夜渐深，乡绅的病势愈发沉重。他昏沉沉地说着胡话，什么都讲——讲酒、讲狗、讲律师；接着他又仿佛在和兄长斯克鲁普说话。正说着，独守在他床边的护士奥利弗太太（Mrs. Oliver），仿佛听见门外有人轻轻地把手搭在门把上，鬼鬼祟祟地想拧动它。"主啊保佑！是谁在那儿？" 她喊道，心都提到了嗓子眼——她想起那个驼背的黑衣人，据说会笑嘻嘻地探头进来招手——"库珀先生！先生！您在吗？" 她喊道。"请您过来，库珀先生，求您了——快！"

老库珀被她从炉边的盹儿中唤醒，踉踉跄跄地从更衣室出来，奥利弗太太一把将他紧紧抓住。

"那个驼背的人刚才一直在拧门，库珀先生，千真万确。" 乡绅正发烧呻吟、含混地嘟囔着，对这一切毫无知觉，她说。"不，不！奥利弗太太，夫人，不可能的，这屋里没有那样一个人：查理少爷在说什么呀？"

"他每过一会儿就喊一声 '斯克鲁普'，也不知道是什么意思，还有——还有——嘘！——听——门把手又响了，" 接着，她发出一声尖叫——"瞧他的脑袋和脖子，在门口那儿！" 她在战栗之中，把老库珀死死地搂在怀里。

===Original===
The candle was flaring, and there was a wavering shadow at the door that looked like the head of a man with a long neck, and a longish sharp nose, peeping in and drawing back.

"Don't be a d﻿—﻿— fool, ma'am!" cried Cooper, very white, and shaking her with all his might. "It's only the candle, I tell you﻿—nothing in life but that. Don't you see?" and he raised the light; "and I'm sure there was no one at the door, and I'll try, if you let me go."

The other nurse was asleep on a sofa, and Mrs. Oliver called her up in a panic, for company, as old Cooper opened the door. There was no one near it, but at the angle of the gallery was a shadow resembling that which he had seen in the room. He raised the candle a little, and it seemed to beckon with a long hand as the head drew back. "Shadow from the candle!" exclaimed Cooper aloud, resolved not to yield to Mrs. Oliver's panic; and, candle in hand, he walked to the corner. There was nothing. He could not forbear peeping down the long gallery from this point, and as he moved the light, he saw precisely the same sort of shadow, a little further down, and as he advanced the same withdrawal, and beckon. "Gammon!" said he; "it is nout but the candle." And on he went, growing half angry and half frightened at the persistency with which this ugly shadow﻿—a literal shadow he was sure it was﻿—presented itself. As he drew near the point where it now appeared, it seemed to collect itself, and nearly dissolve in the central panel of an old carved cabinet which he was now approaching.

In the centre panel of this is a sort of boss carved into a wolf's head. The light fell oddly upon this, and the fugitive shadow seemed to be breaking up, and rearranging itself as oddly. The eyeball gleamed with a point of reflected light, which glittered also upon the grinning mouth, and he saw the long, sharp nose of Scroope Marston, and his fierce eye looking at him, he thought, with a steadfast meaning.

===Chinese===
烛火摇曳着，门口有一道晃动的影子，看着像是一个长脖子、尖鼻头的人头，探进来看一眼又缩了回去。

"别犯傻了，夫人！" 库珀喊道，脸色煞白，拼命地摇晃她。"不过是烛光，我告诉你——除了烛光，什么也没有。你没瞧见吗？" 他把烛台举高了些；"我敢说门口根本没有人，你要是松手，我就去试试。"

另一个护士正在沙发上打盹，奥利弗太太惊慌失措地把她叫醒作伴，这时老库珀打开了门。门口附近空无一人，可是在走廊的转角处，有一道影子，酷似他在屋里看见的那一道。他把烛台略举高了些，那影子随着脑袋的缩回，仿佛伸出一只长长的手在招他。"烛光的影子！" 库珀大声说，决意不向奥利弗太太的惊慌让步；他举着烛台，走到转角处。什么也没有。他忍不住从那里朝长长的走廊尽头窥探了一眼，随着烛光的移动，他看见前方不远处出现了同样的一道影子，他往前走，那影子同样往后缩，又招了招手。"胡扯！" 他说；"不过是烛光罢了。" 他继续往前走，这道丑陋的影子——他确信那不过是一道实实在在的影子——如此执拗地反复出现，让他又恼又怕。等他走到那影子此刻所在之处，它仿佛收拢了自己，几乎消融在他正走近的一只古老雕花橱柜的中央嵌板里。

这橱柜的中央嵌板上，有一个凸出的圆雕，刻成一只狼头的模样。烛光奇异地照在上面，那道飘忽的影子仿佛也在奇异地散开、又重新组合。那狼头的眼珠上有一点反光在闪烁，龇开的嘴上也闪烁着光，他看见了斯克鲁普·马斯顿那又长又尖的鼻子，还有他那只凶狠的眼睛，正——他觉得——带着一种执拗的意味盯着他。

===Original===
Old Cooper stood gazing upon this sight, unable to move, till he saw the face, and the figure that belonged to it, begin gradually to emerge from the wood. At the same time he heard voices approaching rapidly up a side gallery, and Cooper, with a loud "Lord a-mercy on us!" turned and ran back again, pursued by a sound that seemed to shake the old house like a mighty gust of wind.

Into his master's room burst old Cooper, half wild with fear, and clapped the door and turned the key in a twinkling, looking as if he had been pursued by murderers.

"Did you hear it?" whispered Cooper, now standing near the dressing-room door. They all listened, but not a sound from without disturbed the utter stillness of night. "God bless us! I doubt it's my old head that's gone crazy!" exclaimed Cooper.

He would tell them nothing but that he was himself "an old fool," to be frightened by their talk, and that "the rattle of a window, or the dropping o' a pin" was enough to scare him now; and so he helped himself through that night with brandy, and sat up talking by his master's fire.

The Squire recovered slowly from his brain fever, but not perfectly. A very little thing, the doctor said, would suffice to upset him. He was not yet sufficiently strong to remove for change of scene and air, which were necessary for his complete restoration.

===Chinese===
老库珀站在那里目不转睛地盯着这景象，挪不动步子，直到他看见那张脸，以及与之相连的身躯，开始渐渐地从木头里浮现出来。与此同时，他听见有说话声从一条侧廊里急速逼近，库珀大叫一声 "主啊怜悯我们！" 转身就往回跑，身后紧跟着一阵声响，仿佛一阵狂风似的摇撼着这座老宅。

老库珀半吓疯了似的冲进主人的房间，砰地关上门，一眨眼便拧上了钥匙，那副神情，活像被杀人凶犯追着似的。

"你听见了吗？" 库珀这时站在更衣室门边低声说。他们都侧耳倾听，可外面没有任何声响惊扰夜的彻底寂静。"上帝保佑！我看是我这老脑袋瓜发疯了！" 库珀叫道。

他什么也不肯告诉她们，只说自己 "是个老糊涂"，被她们的胡话吓住了，"一扇窗子嘎吱响一下，或者掉下一根针"，如今都足以把他吓一大跳；那一夜，他便靠着白兰地撑了过去，在主人的炉边坐着说了一夜话。

乡绅的脑热病缓缓地见好，却未能痊愈。大夫说，一点极小的事便足以让他反复。他还不够强壮，尚不能易地疗养、换换空气，而那才是他彻底康复所必需的。

===Original===
Cooper slept in the dressing-room, and was now his only nightly attendant. The ways of the invalid were odd: he liked, half sitting up in his bed, to smoke his churchwarden o' nights, and made old Cooper smoke, for company, at the fireside. As the Squire and his humble friend indulged in it, smoking is a taciturn pleasure, and it was not until the Master of Gylingden had finished his third pipe that he essayed conversation, and when he did, the subject was not such as Cooper would have chosen.

"I say, old Cooper, look in my face, and don't be afeared to speak out," said the Squire, looking at him with a steady, cunning smile; "you know all this time, as well as I do, who's in the house. You needn't deny﻿—hey?﻿—Scroope and my father?"

"Don't you be talking like that, Charlie," said old Cooper, rather sternly and frightened, after a long silence; still looking in his face, which did not change.

"What's the good o' shammin', Cooper? Scroope's took the hearin' o' yer right ear﻿—you know he did. He's looking angry. He's nigh took my life wi' this fever. But he's not done wi' me yet, and he looks awful wicked. Ye saw him﻿—ye know ye did."

Cooper was awfully frightened, and the odd smile on the Squire's lips frightened him still more. He dropped his pipe, and stood gazing in silence at his master, and feeling as if he were in a dream.

"If ye think so, ye should not be smiling like that," said Cooper, grimly.

"I'm tired, Cooper, and it's as well to smile as t'other thing; so I'll even smile while I can. You know what they mean to do wi' me. That's all I wanted to say. Now, lad, go on wi' yer pipe﻿—I'm goin' asleep."

So the Squire turned over in his bed, and lay down serenely, with his head on the pillow. Old Cooper looked at him, and glanced at the door, and then half-filled his tumbler with brandy, and drank it off, and felt better, and got to his bed in the dressing-room.

===Chinese===
库珀睡在更衣室里，如今是他唯一的夜间看护。这位病人的脾气有些古怪：他喜欢夜里半靠在床上，抽他那杆长杆烟斗（churchwarden），还要老库珀在炉边陪着抽。正如乡绅和他这位卑微的朋友所沉浸于其中的那样，抽烟是一种沉默的乐趣，直到盖林登的主人抽完第三斗烟，他才试着开口说话，而他一开口，谈的却不是库珀愿意选择的话题。

"我说，老库珀，看着我的脸，别怕，照实说，" 乡绅说，带着一种沉稳而狡黠的微笑看着他；"这一阵子，你跟我一样清楚，这屋里都有谁。你不必否认——嗯？——斯克鲁普和我父亲？"

"你别这么说，查理，" 老库珀沉默良久之后，相当严厉又害怕地说，眼睛仍盯着他的脸，而那张脸纹丝不变。

"装模作样有什么用呢，库珀？斯克鲁普已经取走了你右耳的听力——你知道他取走了。他正怒气冲冲地瞪着。他差点用这场热病要了我的命。可他还没跟我算完呢，他看着凶得很。你见过他——你知道你见过。"

库珀吓得要命，乡绅嘴角那抹古怪的笑，更让他害怕。他的烟斗掉在地上，他默默地站着，盯着主人，觉得自己像在梦里一般。

"你要是这么觉得，就不该这样笑着，" 库珀阴沉地说。

"我累了，库珀，笑一笑总比另一种样子要好些；所以趁我还能笑，就笑一笑吧。你知道他们打算怎么处置我。我要说的就这些。好了，老伙计，接着抽你的烟斗吧——我要睡了。"

于是乡绅在床上翻了个身，安安静静地躺下，头枕在枕头上。老库珀看着他，又瞥了一眼门口，然后往大玻璃杯里倒了半杯白兰地，一饮而尽，觉得好受了些，便回更衣室自己的床上去了。

===Original===
In the dead of night he was suddenly awakened by the Squire, who was standing, in his dressing-gown and slippers, by his bed.

"I've brought you a bit o' a present. I got the rents o' Hazelden yesterday, and ye'll keep that for yourself﻿—it's a fifty﻿—and give t' other to Nelly Carwell, tomorrow; I'll sleep the sounder; and I saw Scroope since; he's not such a bad 'un after all, old fellow! He's got a crape over his face﻿—for I told him I couldn't bear it; and I'd do many a thing for him now. I never could stand shilly-shally. Good night, old Cooper!"

And the Squire laid his trembling hand kindly on the old man's shoulder, and returned to his own room. "I don't half like how he is. Doctor don't come half often enough. I don't like that queer smile o' his, and his hand was as cold as death. I hope in God his brain's not a-turnin'!"

With these reflections, he turned to the pleasanter subject of his present, and at last fell asleep.

In the morning, when he went into the Squire's room, the Squire had left his bed. "Never mind; he'll come back, like a bad shillin'," thought old Cooper, preparing the room as usual. But he did not return. Then began an uneasiness, succeeded by a panic, when it began to be plain that the Squire was not in the house. What had become of him? None of his clothes, but his dressing-gown and slippers, were missing. Had he left the house, in his present sickly state, in that garb? and, if so, could he be in his right senses; and was there a chance of his surviving a cold, damp night, so passed, in the open air?

===Chinese===
深夜里，他突然被乡绅叫醒——乡绅穿着晨衣和拖鞋，正站在他的床边。

"我给你带了件小礼物。昨天我收了哈泽尔登（Hazelden）的租金，这一张五十镑的你自己留着——再那一张明天给内莉·卡韦尔（Nelly Carwell）；我会睡得安稳些；自那以后我又见到了斯克鲁普；他到底也不算太坏，老伙计！他脸上蒙了一块黑纱——因为我跟他说我受不了那张脸；如今我倒愿意为他做许多事了。我向来受不了拖泥带水。晚安，老库珀！"

乡绅把颤抖的手亲切地搭在老人的肩上，回自己的房间去了。"我一点也不喜欢他这副样子。大夫来得也太不勤了。我不喜欢他脸上那种古怪的笑，他的手也冷得像死人的手。但愿上帝保佑，他的脑子别出毛病！"

他一边这样想着，一边把心思转到那件礼物这件较愉快的事上，终于睡着了。

早上，他走进乡绅的房间时，乡绅已经离了床。"不要紧；他会回来的，就像一枚假先令那样总会转回来，" 老库珀心想，照旧收拾着房间。可他没有回来。接着便是一阵不安，继之以惊恐——因为事情渐渐明朗：乡绅不在屋里。他到哪儿去了呢？除了晨衣和拖鞋，他什么衣物也没少。以他眼下这病恹恹的样子，他莫非就穿着这身出了门？若是如此，他神志可还清醒？在户外挨过一个阴冷潮湿的夜晚，他还有活命的指望吗？

===Original===
Tom Edwards was up to the house, and told them, that, walking a mile or so that morning, at four o'clock﻿—there being no moon﻿—along with Farmer Nokes, who was driving his cart to market, in the dark, three men walked, in front of the horse, not twenty yards before them, all the way from near Gylingden Lodge to the burial-ground, the gate of which was opened for them from within, and the three men entered, and the gate was shut. Tom Edwards thought they were gone in to make preparation for a funeral of some member of the Marston family. But the occurrence seemed to Cooper, who knew there was no such thing, horribly ominous.

He now commenced a careful search, and at last bethought him of the lonely upper storey, and King Herod's chamber. He saw nothing changed there, but the closet door was shut, and, dark as was the morning, something, like a large white knot sticking out over the door, caught his eye.

The door resisted his efforts to open it for a time; some great weight forced it down against the floor; at length, however, it did yield a little, and a heavy crash, shaking the whole floor, and sending an echo flying through all the silent corridors, with a sound like receding laughter, half stunned him.

When he pushed open the door, his master was lying dead upon the floor. His cravat was drawn halter-wise tight round his throat, and had done its work well. The body was cold, and had been long dead.

In due course the coroner held his inquest, and the jury pronounced, "that the deceased, Charles Marston, had died by his own hand, in a state of temporary insanity." But old Cooper had his own opinion about the Squire's death, though his lips were sealed, and he never spoke about it. He went and lived for the residue of his days in York, where there are still people who remember him, a taciturn and surly old man, who attended church regularly, and also drank a little, and was known to have saved some money.

===Chinese===
汤姆·爱德华兹（Tom Edwards）上宅子里来，告诉大家，那天早上四点钟——天上没有月亮——他和诺克斯农场主（Farmer Nokes）一道，诺克斯赶着大车去赶集，在黑暗里走着，约莫走了一英里光景，有三个人一直走在马前面，离他们不到二十码，从盖林登门房附近一路走到那片墓地，墓地的门从里头给他们打开了，三个人走了进去，门又关上了。汤姆·爱德华兹以为他们是进去为马斯顿家哪一位成员的葬礼做准备的。可这事在库珀听来——他明知并无其事——却是不祥之至。

他于是开始仔细搜找，末了想起了那冷清的顶楼，以及希律王寝宫。那里一切如旧，只是套间的门关着，尽管天色昏暗，门上方有个东西，像一个大大的白色绳结凸出来，落进了他的眼里。

那门一时推不开；有什么重物从里面把门顶死在了地板上；然而它终于让开了一点缝，一声沉重的撞击，震动了整层地板，一声回响飞过所有寂静的走廊，听起来像渐渐远去的笑声，把他震得半晕过去。

他把门推开时，只见他的主人已经僵死在地板上。他的领巾被勒成绞索的样子，紧紧勒在脖子上，已完成了它的工作。尸体冰凉，已死去多时。

验尸官如期主持了验尸，陪审团裁断："死者查尔斯·马斯顿系在一时精神错乱之下，死于自己之手。" 然而对于乡绅之死，老库珀自有他自己的看法，只是他守口如瓶，从不对外人讲。他后来搬到约克（York）去住了余生，那里至今还有人记得他——一个沉默寡言、脾气乖戾的老人，按时上教堂，也稍微喝点酒，据说还攒下了些积蓄。

## I The Jacobite’s Legacy / 一　詹姆斯党人的遗赠

===Original===
In my youth I heard a great many Irish family traditions, more or less of a supernatural character, some of them very peculiar, and all, to a child at least, highly interesting. One of these I will now relate, though the translation to cold type from oral narrative, with all the aids of animated human voice and countenance, and the appropriate mise-en-scène of the old-fashioned parlour fireside and its listening circle of excited faces, and, outside, the wintry blast and the moan of leafless boughs, with the occasional rattle of the clumsy old window-frame behind shutter and curtain, as the blast swept by, is at best a trying one.

About midway up the romantic glen of Cappercullen, near the point where the counties of Limerick, Clare, and Tipperary converge, upon the then sequestered and forest-bound range of the Slieve-Felim hills, there stood, in the reigns of the two earliest Georges, the picturesque and massive remains of one of the finest of the Anglo-Irish castles of Munster﻿—perhaps of Ireland.

It crowned the precipitous edge of the wooded glen, itself half-buried among the wild forest that covered that long and solitary range. There was no human habitation within a circle of many miles, except the half-dozen hovels and the small thatched chapel composing the little village of Murroa, which lay at the foot of the glen among the straggling skirts of the noble forest.

===Chinese===
少时我曾听过许多爱尔兰家族的旧闻传说，或多或少都带着几分超自然的色彩，其中有些颇为离奇，至少对一个孩子而言，无不引人入胜。这些故事里，我现在要讲一个；虽说口耳相传一旦变成铅字，失去了人声人面的种种生动助力，又失去了那恰到好处的布景——老式客厅的炉火之畔，一圈屏息凝神的面庞围坐倾听，屋外则是凛冬的寒风、枯枝的悲鸣，间或狂风掠过，笨重老旧的窗框在窗板和帷帘之后一阵嘎吱作响——这番光景化为文字，终究是要大打折扣的。

在卡珀卡伦（Cappercullen）那条引人入胜的幽谷里，大约行至半山之处，利默里克（Limerick）、克莱尔（Clare）、蒂珀雷里（Tipperary）三郡交界近旁，那当时还偏僻幽深、林莽蔽天的斯利夫费利姆（Slieve-Felim）群山之中，当最初两位乔治（George）在位之年，曾矗立着一座如画而宏伟的城堡遗址——那是芒斯特（Munster）乃至全爱尔兰最壮丽的盎格鲁-爱尔兰（Anglo-Irish）城堡之一的残迹。

它雄踞林木葱茏的幽谷那悬崖峭壁的边沿，城堡本身也半掩在覆盖这片绵延荒寂山岭的野林之中。方圆数里之内杳无人烟，唯有那座名叫穆罗阿（Murroa）的小村落——六七间茅舍和一座小小的草顶礼拜堂——坐落在幽谷的脚下，散落在那片苍莽森林的边缘。

===Original===
Its remoteness and difficulty of access saved it from demolition. It was worth nobody’s while to pull down and remove the ponderous and clumsy oak, much less the masonry or flagged roofing of the pile. Whatever would pay the cost of removal had been long since carried away. The rest was abandoned to time﻿—the destroyer.

The hereditary owners of this noble building and of a wide territory in the contiguous counties I have named, were English﻿—the De Lacys﻿—long naturalized in Ireland. They had acquired at least this portion of their estate in the reign of Henry VIII, and held it, with some vicissitudes, down to the establishment of the revolution in Ireland, when they suffered attainder, and, like other great families of that period, underwent a final eclipse.

The De Lacy of that day retired to France, and held a brief command in the Irish Brigade, interrupted by sickness. He retired, became a poor hanger-on of the Court of St. Germains, and died early in the eighteenth century﻿—as well as I remember, 1705﻿—leaving an only son, hardly twelve years old, called by the strange but significant name of Ultor.

===Chinese===
正是它的偏远难至，使它免于被拆毁。拆下运走那些笨重粗大的橡料已是得不偿失，更不必说那石砌的墙垣、石板铺就的屋盖了。凡值得费力搬走的，早已被人运去；余下的，便尽归时光——那万物之毁坏者——去处置。

这座华美城堡连同我所言三郡接壤处那片辽阔领地的世袭主人，本是英格兰人——德莱西（De Lacy）一族——早已在爱尔兰扎根入籍。他们至少在亨利八世（Henry VIII）在位时就取得了这片产业，虽几经周折，仍一直保有，直到爱尔兰那场革命确立之时，他们被褫夺公权，与那个时代的其他名门望族一样，最终归于沉沦没落。

那一代的德莱西避居法国，曾在爱尔兰旅（Irish Brigade）中短暂任职，因病中辍。他退了下来，沦为圣日耳曼宫廷（Court of St. Germains）里一名穷酸的食客，于十八世纪初辞世——我记得好像是 1705 年——只留下一个独子，年方十二岁上下，取了一个古怪却意味深长的名字：乌尔托（Ultor）。

===Original===
At this point commences the marvellous ingredient of my tale.

When his father was dying, he had him to his bedside, with no one by except his confessor; and having told him, first, that on reaching the age of twenty-one, he was to lay claim to a certain small estate in the county of Clare, in Ireland, in right of his mother﻿—the title-deeds of which he gave him﻿—and next, having enjoined him not to marry before the age of thirty, on the ground that earlier marriages destroyed the spirit and the power of enterprise, and would incapacitate him from the accomplishment of his destiny﻿—the restoration of his family﻿—he then went on to open to the child a matter which so terrified him that he cried lamentably, trembling all over, clinging to the priest’s gown with one hand and to his father’s cold wrist with the other, and imploring him, with screams of horror, to desist from his communication.

But the priest, impressed, no doubt, himself, with its necessity, compelled him to listen. And then his father showed him a small picture, from which also the child turned with shrieks, until similarly constrained to look. They did not let him go until he had carefully conned the features, and was able to tell them, from memory, the colour of the eyes and hair, and the fashion and hues of the dress. Then his father gave him a black box containing this portrait, which was a full-length miniature, about nine inches long, painted very finely in oils, as smooth as enamel, and folded above it a sheet of paper, written over in a careful and very legible hand.

The deeds and this black box constituted the most important legacy bequeathed to his only child by the ruined Jacobite, and he deposited them in the hands of the priest, in trust, till his boy, Ultor, should have attained to an age to understand their value, and to keep them securely.

===Chinese===
我这故事里离奇的成分，便是从这一点开始的。

他的父亲临终之际，把他唤到床前，当时身侧除听忏悔的神父外并无旁人。父亲先告诉他，满二十一岁时，须凭他母亲的血脉，去认领爱尔兰克莱尔郡一处小小的田产——并把产业的地契交给了他；接着又嘱咐他，三十岁之前不可成亲，理由是过早婚娶会销磨闯荡的心气与建树的胆力，使他无力成就自己的天命——即重振家族——随后便要向他揭开一桩事。那事把孩子吓坏了，他放声大哭，浑身发抖，一只手死死揪住神父的袍子，另一只手攥着他父亲冰凉的手腕，恐怖地连声尖叫，哀求他不要再往下说了。

然而神父想必自己也深知此事的必要，便逼着他听下去。于是父亲又拿出一张小小的画像给他看，孩子一见又尖声惊叫，直躲避不肯看，直到同样被强按着才去看。他们不许他走，直到他把那画上的容貌细细记熟，能够凭记忆说出发与目的颜色、衣裳的式样和色彩，这才作罢。随后父亲交给他一只黑匣子，里头盛着这幅画像——那是一幅全身袖珍像，约莫九英寸来长，是用油画颜料精心绘就的，光润如珐琅；画像上头还折着一张纸，上面密密地写满了一手工整易认的字。

这些地契和这只黑匣子，便是那位倾家荡产的詹姆斯党人（Jacobite）留给独子最重要的遗产。他把它们一并交托在神父手中，托其保管，等到他的孩子乌尔托长到能懂得这些东西的分量、并能妥善保管的年纪，再行交付。

===Original===
When this scene was ended, the dying exile’s mind, I suppose, was relieved, for he spoke cheerily, and said he believed he would recover; and they soothed the crying child, and his father kissed him, and gave him a little silver coin to buy fruit with; and so they sent him off with another boy for a walk, and when he came back his father was dead.

He remained in France under the care of this ecclesiastic until he had attained the age of twenty-one, when he repaired to Ireland, and his title being unaffected by his father’s attainder, he easily made good his claim to the small estate in the county of Clare.

There he settled, making a dismal and solitary tour now and then of the vast territories which had once been his father’s, and nursing those gloomy and impatient thoughts which befitted the enterprises to which he was devoted.

Occasionally he visited Paris, that common centre of English, Irish, and Scottish disaffection; and there, when a little past thirty, he married the daughter of another ruined Irish house. His bride returned with him to the melancholy seclusion of their Munster residence, where she bore him in succession two daughters﻿—Alice, the elder, dark-eyed and dark-haired, grave and sensible﻿—Una, four years younger, with large blue eyes and long and beautiful golden hair.

Their poor mother was, I believe, naturally a lighthearted, sociable, high-spirited little creature; and her gay and childish nature pined in the isolation and gloom of her lot. At all events she died young, and the children were left to the sole care of their melancholy and embittered father. In process of time the girls grew up, tradition says, beautiful. The elder was designed for a convent, the younger her father hoped to mate as nobly as her high blood and splendid beauty seemed to promise, if only the great game on which he had resolved to stake all succeeded.

===Chinese===
这场场面过后，那位垂死的流亡者，我想，心头大石既去，神思为之一松，他竟高高兴兴地说起话来，还说自己觉得会好起来的；他们把哭闹的孩子安抚下来，父亲亲了亲他，给了他一枚小小的银币去买果子吃；于是便打发他跟另一个孩子一道出去散步，等他回来时，父亲已经死了。

他留在法国，由这位教士照管，直到年满二十一岁。那时他前往爱尔兰，由于他的产业继承权并不受父亲被褫夺公权的影响，他轻而易举地便确立了对克莱尔郡那处小小田产的主张。

他便在那里安顿下来，时不时孤身一人、心情抑郁地出游，在那些曾经属于他父亲的辽阔领地间巡行，心中酝酿着阴郁而焦躁的念头——正与他所矢志的那番图谋相称。

偶尔他也去巴黎（Paris）——那英、爱、苏三地离心分子共聚之地；在那里，他过了三十不久，便娶了另一个破落爱尔兰世家的女儿。新娘随他回到了芒斯特那处幽居的宅邸，在那里她先后为他生下两个女儿——姐姐爱丽丝（Alice），眼黑发黑，性情沉稳而明达——妹妹乌娜（Una），小她四岁，有一双湛蓝的大眼睛，一头又长又美的金发。

她们那可怜的母亲，我相信，本是天性轻快、爱热闹、心气很高的一个小可人儿；她那欢快孩子气的心性，在自身命运的孤寂和阴郁之中日渐萎顿。无论如何，她年纪轻轻便香消玉殒，孩子们便由那位阴郁而满怀愤恨的父亲独自抚养。及后，两个女孩渐渐长大，据传闻，都出落得花容月貌。长女被安排将来进修道院，次女呢，父亲则巴望能与她那高贵的血统和绝世的姿容所预示的那样，结一门同样显赫的亲事——只要他所决意孤注一掷的那盘大棋能够得胜。

## Sir Dominick's Bargain A Legend of Dunoran / 多米尼克爵士的交易——一则杜诺兰传奇

===Original===
In the early autumn of the year 1838, business called me to the south of Ireland. The weather was delightful, the scenery and people were new to me, and sending my luggage on by the mail-coach route in charge of a servant, I hired a serviceable nag at a posting-house, and, full of the curiosity of an explorer, I commenced a leisurely journey of five-and-twenty miles on horseback, by sequestered crossroads, to my place of destination. By bog and hill, by plain and ruined castle, and many a winding stream, my picturesque road led me.

I had started late, and having made little more than half my journey, I was thinking of making a short halt at the next convenient place, and letting my horse have a rest and a feed, and making some provision also for the comforts of his rider.

It was about four o’clock when the road, ascending a gradual steep, found a passage through a rocky gorge between the abrupt termination of a range of mountain to my left and a rocky hill, that rose dark and sudden at my right. Below me lay a little thatched village, under a long line of gigantic beech-trees, through the boughs of which the lowly chimneys sent up their thin turf-smoke. To my left, stretched away for miles, ascending the mountain range I have mentioned, a wild park, through whose sward and ferns the rock broke, timeworn and lichen-stained. This park was studded with straggling wood, which thickened to something like a forest, behind and beyond the little village I was approaching, clothing the irregular ascent of the hillsides with beautiful, and in some places discoloured foliage.

As you descend, the road winds slightly, with the grey park-wall, built of loose stone, and mantled here and there with ivy, at its left, and crosses a shallow ford; and as I approached the village, through breaks in the woodlands, I caught glimpses of the long front of an old ruined house, placed among the trees, about halfway up the picturesque mountainside.

===Chinese===
一八三八年早秋时分，因公务之故我前往爱尔兰南部。彼时天气宜人，风物人情于我皆是初见；我让仆人押着行李循驿车路线先行，自己则在驿站雇了一匹结实耐用的矮马，怀着一个探索者满腹的好奇，由僻静的乡间小道，骑马慢悠悠地踏上了前往目的地的二十五英里行程。沿途过沼泽、越山岗，穿平原、见古堡，又经几多蜿蜒溪流，一路景色如画。

我出发得晚，走了不过半程稍多，便已盘算着在前头方便之处稍作歇脚，让马歇一歇、喂一喂草料，也替它这位骑手备些慰藉。

约莫四点钟光景，道路沿一道缓坡攀升，从左侧山脉陡然收束处与右侧突兀而起、黑黝黝的一座石山之间，寻出一条穿过岩隘的通路。在我脚下，一座小小茅舍村落依傍着一长排参天山毛榉掩映而卧，矮矮的烟囱从枝叶间透出，袅袅升起细细的泥炭青烟。我左手方向，一片莽苍的园林沿着前述山脉绵延数里而上，草坪蕨丛之间，嶙峋岩石破土而出，历经风霜、满布苔痕。园中星散着错落的林木，在我临近的那座小村落后方愈发浓密，几近成林，将山坡那不规则起伏的坡面，披上一层秀美的、间或斑驳的树荫。

顺坡而下，道路微微蜿蜒，左侧便是那道用乱石砌成、此一处彼一处披满常春藤的灰色园墙，路又涉过一处浅浅的渡口；待我走近村子，穿过林地的几处缺口，我瞥见一幢破败老宅长长的正面，掩映于林木之间，大约坐落在那如画的山腰的半坡上。

===Original===
The solitude and melancholy of this ruin piqued my curiosity, and when I had reached the rude thatched public-house, with the sign of St. Columbkill, with robes, mitre, and crozier displayed over its lintel, having seen to my horse and made a good meal myself on a rasher and eggs, I began to think again of the wooded park and the ruinous house, and resolved on a ramble of half an hour among its sylvan solitudes.

The name of the place, I found, was Dunoran; and beside the gate a stile admitted to the grounds, through which, with a pensive enjoyment, I began to saunter towards the dilapidated mansion.

A long grass-grown road, with many turns and windings, led up to the old house, under the shadow of the wood.

The road, as it approached the house skirted the edge of a precipitous glen, clothed with hazel, dwarf-oak, and thorn, and the silent house stood with its wide-open hall-door facing this dark ravine, the further edge of which was crowned with towering forest; and great trees stood about the house and its deserted courtyard and stables.

I walked in and looked about me, through passages overgrown with nettles and weeds; from room to room with ceilings rotted, and here and there a great beam dark and worn, with tendrils of ivy trailing over it. The tall walls with rotten plaster were stained and mouldy, and in some rooms the remains of decayed wainscoting crazily swung to and fro. The almost sashless windows were darkened also with ivy, and about the tall chimneys the jackdaws were wheeling, while from the huge trees that overhung the glen in sombre masses at the other side, the rooks kept up a ceaseless cawing.

As I walked through these melancholy passages—peeping only into some of the rooms, for the flooring was quite gone in the middle, and bowed down toward the centre, and the house was very nearly un-roofed, a state of things which made the exploration a little critical—I began to wonder why so grand a house, in the midst of scenery so picturesque, had been permitted to go to decay; I dreamed of the hospitalities of which it had long ago been the rallying place, and I thought what a scene of Redgauntlet revelries it might disclose at midnight.

The great staircase was of oak, which had stood the weather wonderfully, and I sat down upon its steps, musing vaguely on the transitoriness of all things under the sun.

Except for the hoarse and distant clamour of the rooks, hardly audible where I sat, no sound broke the profound stillness of the spot. Such a sense of solitude I have seldom experienced before. The air was stirless, there was not even the rustle of a withered leaf along the passage. It was oppressive. The tall trees that stood close about the building darkened it, and added something of awe to the melancholy of the scene.

===Chinese===
这片废墟的孤寂与萧索，撩动了我的好奇。待我到了那家粗陋的茅顶酒馆——招牌上是圣科伦巴（St. Columbkill），门楣上绘着法袍、主教冠与权杖——安顿好马匹，自己也美美地吃了一顿咸肉煎蛋之后，我不禁又想起那座林木掩映的园子和那幢破败的老宅，便决意到那林间幽处闲逛半个钟头。

一打听，此地名叫杜诺兰（Dunoran）。园门边有一道踏步石阶可入其间，我便怀着一种怅然之乐，信步向那倾颓的宅第踱去。

一条长长的、芳草萋萋的道路，在树荫之下曲折蜿蜒，通向那座老宅。

道路临近宅子时，沿着一道陡峭的幽谷边缘迤逦而过，谷中遍生榛树、矮橡与荆棘；那悄无声息的宅子，敞着宽阔的大厅门，正对着这道幽暗的深谷；谷的对岸顶端，高大的林木如冠盖覆压；而巨树参天，耸立于宅子及其荒废的庭院、马厩四近。

我走进去，四下打量；穿行于荨麻野草丛生的过道，从一间屋子踱到另一间，天花板多已朽烂，间或可见一根根又黑又旧的大梁，上头蜿蜒着常春藤的藤须。高墙上的灰泥早已剥落，斑驳发霉，有几间屋里残存的护墙板在风中摇摇欲坠。那几乎没了窗框的窗户，也叫常春藤遮得严严实实；高高的烟囱周围，寒鸦盘旋不去；而幽谷对岸那一团团阴沉沉压过来的参天大树上，秃鼻鸦聒噪不休。

我穿行于这些阴郁的过道之中——只是探头往几间屋子里张望张望，因为屋子中央的地板早已坍塌，向中腹凹陷下去，宅子的屋顶也差不多没了，此种情形，令这番探访多了几分危险——我不禁纳闷起来：这样一座气派的宅第，地处如此如画的风光之中，怎会任其倾颓败落？我幻想它昔日作为好客聚会之所的繁华，又想象它在午夜时分，或许会现出一场《红冈特利特》式的狂欢场面。

那座大楼梯是橡木打的，历经风雨仍出奇地完好。我在梯级上坐下，思绪茫然地感慨着日光之下万物无常。

除了秃鼻鸦那粗哑而遥远的喧闹——我坐着的地方几乎听不真切——再无声响惊破此地的深沉寂静。这般强烈的孤寂之感，我平生少有所历。空气凝然不动，过道上连一片枯叶沙沙作响的声音也没有。这寂静压得人透不过气。紧贴宅子矗立的高树将它笼罩在阴影里，更给这萧索的景象添了几分敬畏。

===Original===
In this mood I heard, with an unpleasant surprise, close to me, a voice that was drawling, and, I fancied, sneering, repeat the words: “Food for worms, dead and rotten; God over all.”

There was a small window in the wall, here very thick, which had been built up, and in the dark recess of this, deep in the shadow, I now saw a sharp-featured man, sitting with his feet dangling. His keen eyes were fixed on me, and he was smiling cynically, and before I had well recovered my surprise, he repeated the distich:

> “If death was a thing that money could buy,
>
> The rich they would live, and the poor they would die.

“It was a grand house in its day, sir,” he continued, “Dunoran House, and the Sarsfields. Sir Dominick Sarsfield was the last of the old stock. He lost his life not six foot away from where you are sitting.”

As he thus spoke he let himself down, with a little jump, on to the ground.

He was a dark-faced, sharp-featured, little hunchback, and had a walking-stick in his hand, with the end of which he pointed to a rusty stain in the plaster of the wall.

“Do you mind that mark, sir?” he asked.

“Yes,” I said, standing up, and looking at it, with a curious anticipation of something worth hearing.

“That’s about seven or eight feet from the ground, sir, and you’ll not guess what it is.”

“I dare say not,” said I, “unless it is a stain from the weather.”

“’Tis nothing so lucky, sir,” he answered, with the same cynical smile and a wag of his head, still pointing at the mark with his stick. “That’s a splash of brains and blood. It’s there this hundhred years; and it will never leave it while the wall stands.”

“He was murdered, then?”

“Worse than that, sir,” he answered.

“He killed himself, perhaps?”

“Worse than that, itself, this cross between us and harm! I’m oulder than I look, sir; you wouldn’t guess my years.”

He became silent, and looked at me, evidently inviting a guess.

“Well, I should guess you to be about five-and-fifty.”

He laughed, and took a pinch of snuff, and said:

“I’m that, your honour, and something to the back of it. I was seventy last Candlemas. You would not a’ thought that, to look at me.”

“Upon my word I should not; I can hardly believe it even now. Still, you don’t remember Sir Dominick Sarsfield’s death?” I said, glancing up at the ominous stain on the wall.

“No, sir, that was a long while before I was born. But my grandfather was butler here long ago, and many a time I heard tell how Sir Dominick came by his death. There was no masther in the great house ever sinst that happened. But there was two sarvants in care of it, and my aunt was one o’ them; and she kep’ me here wid her till I was nine year old, and she was lavin’ the place to go to Dublin; and from that time it was let to go down. The wind sthript the roof, and the rain rotted the timber, and little by little, in sixty years’ time, it kem to what you see. But I have a likin’ for it still, for the sake of ould times; and I never come this way but I take a look in. I don’t think it’s many more times I’ll be turnin’ to see the ould place, for I’ll be undher the sod myself before long.”

“You’ll outlive younger people,” I said.

And, quitting that trite subject, I ran on:

“I don’t wonder that you like this old place; it is a beautiful spot, such noble trees.”

“I wish ye seen the glin when the nuts is ripe; they’re the sweetest nuts in all Ireland, I think,” he rejoined, with a practical sense of the picturesque. “You’d fill your pockets while you’d be lookin’ about you.”

“These are very fine old woods,” I remarked. “I have not seen any in Ireland I thought so beautiful.”

“Eiah! your honour, the woods about here is nothing to what they wor. Al the mountains along here was wood when my father was a gossoon, and Murroa Wood was the grandest of them all. All oak mostly, and all cut down as bare as the road. Not one left here that’s fit to compare with them. Which way did your honour come hither—from Limerick?”

“No. Killaloe.”

“Well, then, you passed the ground where Murroa Wood was in former times. You kem undher Lisnavourra, the steep knob of a hill about a mile above the village here. ’Twas near that Murroa Wood was, and ’twas there Sir Dominick Sarsfield first met the devil, the Lord between us and harm, and a bad meeting it was for him and his.”

I had become interested in the adventure which had occurred in the very scenery which had so greatly attracted me, and my new acquaintance, the little hunchback, was easily entreated to tell me the story, and spoke thus, so soon as we had each resumed his seat:

===Chinese===
正当此际，我忽然听见近旁——离我极近之处——一个慢悠悠、我听着还带着几分讥诮的声音，把下面这句话又念了一遍："蛆虫之食，朽败之躯；上帝宰治万物。"

这墙上有一扇小窗，墙在此处很厚，窗早被砌死了。就在这幽暗的窗龛深处、浓重的阴影里，我此刻才看见一个面目瘦削的人，坐在那里，两条腿悬空晃荡。他那双犀利的眼睛直盯着我，嘴角挂着一丝冷笑；我尚未从惊讶中回过神来，他又把那副对子念了一遍：

> 若是死亡这种东西能拿钱买，
>
> 富人便会活，穷人便会死。

"这宅子当年可是气派得很哪，先生，"他接着说道，"杜诺兰宅，萨斯菲尔德家（the Sarsfields）的产业。多米尼克·萨斯菲尔德爵士（Sir Dominick Sarsfield）是那一脉老根的最后一个。他送命的地方，离您坐着的那处，不出六英尺。"

他这样说着，便轻轻一纵，跳到了地上。

他是个面色黧黑、面容瘦削的小驼子，手里拄着一根手杖，用杖头指着墙灰上一块铁锈色的斑痕。

"您瞧见那印记了么，先生？"他问。

"瞧见了，"我站起身来，看着那斑痕，心里隐隐生出一种期待，觉得接下来必有值得一听的故事。

"那印记离地大约七八英尺高，先生，您猜不着那是什么。"

"我确是猜不着，"我说，"除非是风雨留下的水渍。"

"哪有那么走运，先生，"他答道，仍是那副冷笑模样，摇了摇头，手中的杖头依旧指着那块印记，"那是一摊脑浆和血溅的痕迹。在那墙上已经留了一百年了；只要这堵墙不倒，它就永远不会消失。"

"那他是被人谋杀的？"

"比那还糟，先生，"他答道。

"莫非是自寻短见？"

"比那还要糟，真是的——上帝保佑我们别沾上这晦气！我比看上去要老些，先生；您可猜不出我的年纪。"

他静了下来，望着我，显然是想让我猜一猜。

"嗯，我猜您大约五十五岁上下。"

他笑了笑，捏了一撮鼻烟，说道：

"不止那些，老爷，还要往上添几岁呢。今年圣烛节我满了七十。您瞧着我，可想不到这一层吧。"

"当真想不到；便是此刻我也难以置信。不过，您总不致还记得多米尼克·萨斯菲尔德爵士是怎么死的吧？"我说着，抬眼望了望墙上那不祥的斑痕。

"是不记得，先生，那是我出生很久以前的事了。不过我祖父从前是这里的管家，多米尼克爵士是怎么送命的，我听人说过的，不下百回。自打那桩事发生之后，这大宅子里再没住过主人。只是留下了两个仆人看守，我姑妈便是其中之一；她把我留在这里带到九岁，才离开此地去都柏林；从那时起，这宅子便任其败落了。风掀了屋顶，雨烂了木料，六十年的光阴，一点点，就成了您眼前这般模样。可我仍然喜欢它，看在往日旧情的份上；每逢打这儿过，我总要进来看一看。我想，再回头来看这老地方的次数也不多了，因为用不了多久，我自己也要躺到青草底下去了。"

"您会熬过比您年轻的人呢，"我说。

撇开这句套话，我接着道：

"您喜欢这处老地方，我也并不奇怪；这地方美得很，树木又这般雄奇。"

"您要是瞧见栗子熟时节的这幽谷就好了；我想，全爱尔兰再没那么甜的栗子了，"他答道，对如画之景别有一种务实的体会，"您东张西望的工夫，口袋便装得满满的了。"

"这些老林子确实极好，"我说，"在爱尔兰我还未曾见过这般秀美的。"

"哎呀！老爷，这一带的林子跟从前比，简直算不得什么。我父亲还是个小子那会儿，这一带的座座山头尽是林木，而穆罗阿林子（Murroa Wood）又是其中最了不起的。多是橡木，却统统砍了个精光，光秃秃的跟大路一般。如今再没一棵能跟它们相提并论的了。老爷您是从哪条路来的——从利默里克（Limerick）那边？"

"不，从基拉洛（Killaloe）来。"

"那您就是打从前穆罗阿林子所在的那片地界过来的了。您从利斯纳武拉（Lisnavourra）底下经过——就是这村子往上约一英里那座陡峭的圆顶小山。穆罗阿林子便在它近旁，正是在那里，多米尼克·萨斯菲尔德爵士头一回遇见了魔鬼——愿主保佑我们免遭祸害——而那一场相会，于他和他的后人，都可谓凶险至极。"

我对这桩恰发生在我如此着迷的景致之中的奇事，业已生出兴趣；我这位新相识的小驼子，也不费什么力气便被劝动，肯把这段故事讲给我听。待我们各自重新落座，他便这样讲了起来：

---

===Original===
It was a fine estate when Sir Dominick came into it; and grand doings there was entirely, feasting and fiddling, free quarters for all the pipers in the counthry round, and a welcome for everyone that liked to come. There was wine, by the hogshead, for the quality; and potteen enough to set a town afire, and beer and cidher enough to float a navy, for the boys and girls, and the likes o’ me. It was kep’ up the best part of a month, till the weather broke, and the rain spoilt the sod for the moneen jigs, and the fair of Allybally Killudeen comin’ on they wor obliged to give over their divarsion, and attind to the pigs.

But Sir Dominick was only beginnin’ when they wor lavin’ off. There was no way of gettin’ rid of his money and estates he did not try—what with drinkin’, dicin’, racin’, cards, and all soarts, it was not many years before the estates wor in debt, and Sir Dominick a distressed man. He showed a bold front to the world as long as he could; and then he sould off his dogs, and most of his horses, and gev out he was going to thraval in France, and the like; and so off with him for awhile; and no one in these parts heard tale or tidings of him for two or three years. Till at last quite unexpected, one night there comes a rapping at the big kitchen window. It was past ten o’clock, and old Connor Hanlon, the butler, my grandfather, was sittin’ by the fire alone, warming his shins over it. There was keen east wind blowing along the mountains that night, and whistling cowld enough, through the tops of the trees, and soundin’ lonesome through the long chimleys.

(And the storyteller glanced up at the nearest stack visible from his seat.)

So he wasn’t quite sure of the knockin’ at the window, and up he gets, and sees his master’s face.

My grandfather was glad to see him safe, for it was a long time since there was any news of him; but he was sorry, too, for it was a changed place and only himself and old Juggy Broadrick in charge of the house, and a man in the stables, and it was a poor thing to see him comin’ back to his own like that.

He shook Con by the hand, and says he:

“I came here to say a word to you. I left my horse with Dick in the stable; I may want him again before morning, or I may never want him.”

And with that he turns into the big kitchen, and draws a stool, and sits down to take an air of the fire.

“Sit down, Connor, opposite me, and listen to what I tell you, and don’t be afeard to say what you think.”

He spoke all the time lookin’ into the fire, with his hands stretched over it, and a tired man he looked.

“An’ why should I be afeard, Masther Dominick?” says my grandfather. “Yourself was a good masther to me, and so was your father, rest his sould, before you, and I’ll say the truth, and dar’ the devil, and more than that, for any Sarsfield of Dunoran, much less yourself, and a good right I’d have.”

“It’s all over with me, Con,” says Sir Dominick.

“Heaven forbid!” says my grandfather.

“’Tis past praying for,” says Sir Dominick. “The last guinea’s gone; the ould place will follow it. It must be sold, and I’m come here, I don’t know why, like a ghost to have a last look round me, and go off in the dark again.”

And with that he tould him to be sure, in case he should hear of his death, to give the oak box, in the closet off his room, to his cousin, Pat Sarsfield, in Dublin, and the sword and pistols his grandfather carried in Aughrim, and two or three thrifling things of the kind.

And says he, “Con, they say if the divil gives you money overnight, you’ll find nothing but a bagful of pebbles, and chips, and nutshells, in the morning. If I thought he played fair, I’m in the humour to make a bargain with him tonight.”

“Lord forbid!” says my grandfather, standing up, with a start and crossing himself.

“They say the country’s full of men, listin’ sogers for the King o’ France. If I light on one o’ them, I’ll not refuse his offer. How contrary things goes! How long is it since me an Captain Waller fought the jewel at New Castle?”

“Six years, Masther Dominick, and ye broke his thigh with the bullet the first shot.”

“I did, Con,” says he, “and I wish, instead, he had shot me through the heart. Have you any whisky?”

My grandfather took it out of the buffet, and the masther pours out some into a bowl, and drank it off.

“I’ll go out and have a look at my horse,” says he, standing up. There was sort of a stare in his eyes, as he pulled his riding-cloak about him, as if there was something bad in his thoughts.

“Sure, I won’t be a minute running out myself to the stable, and looking after the horse for you myself,” says my grandfather.

“I’m not goin’ to the stable,” says Sir Dominick; “I may as well tell you, for I see you found it out already—I’m goin’ across the deer-park; if I come back you’ll see me in an hour’s time. But, anyhow, you’d better not follow me, for if you do I’ll shoot you, and that ’id be a bad ending to our friendship.”

And with that he walks down this passage here, and turns the key in the side door at that end of it, and out wid him on the sod into the moonlight and the cowld wind; and my grandfather seen him walkin’ hard towards the park-wall, and then he comes in and closes the door with a heavy heart.

===Chinese===
多米尼克爵士承继这份家业时，原是丰饶的一片产业；那排场可大极了，又是宴饮，又是奏乐，方圆几个郡的风笛手尽可白吃白住，凡愿来的客人一概欢迎。体面人有成桶的葡萄酒可饮；小伙子、姑娘，还有我这种小人物，则有足以点燃一座市镇的私酿酒（poteen），还有那足以浮起一支舰队的啤酒和苹果酒。这般热闹足足持续了大半个月，直到天公不作美，雨水毁了草皮，叫那暮色中的吉格舞跳不成了；而阿利巴利·基卢丁（Allybally Killudeen）的集市又将近，他们只得收了这份热闹，回去照料那些猪去了。

可是众人散场之时，多米尼克爵士却才刚刚开了个头。但凡能挥霍钱财、败尽家业的法子，他没有不试的——喝酒、掷骰、赛马、打牌，种种门道——不出几年，产业便已负债累累，多米尼克爵士也成了一个焦头烂额之人。他尽可能对着世人撑出一副硬气的面孔；后来到底卖了狗，又卖了大半马匹，放话出去说要往法国及诸如此类的地方游历一番；于是他便走了，离开了一阵子；这一带两三年间竟听不到他半点音讯。直到最后，有一夜，全无预兆地，那大厨房的窗外忽然响起了笃笃的叩击声。那时已过十点，老管家康纳·汉隆（Connor Hanlon）——便是我祖父——独自坐在炉火旁，烤着他的小腿。那一夜，刺骨的东风沿着山岗刮过，从树梢间呼啸而过，寒意彻骨，又在那长长的烟囱里呜咽作响，听来颇为凄清。

（说到此处，讲故事的人抬眼瞟了一下从他座位望得见的最近那座烟囱。）

于是他对那窗上的叩击声一时不敢确定，便起身去看，看见的，正是他主人的脸。

我祖父见他安然无恙，心里是欢喜的——因为许久没听到他的消息了；可同时又难过——因为这地方早已今非昔比，偌大宅子只有他和老朱吉·布罗德里克（Juggy Broadrick）两人看守，再加马厩里一个马夫；他竟这般落魄地回到自己的家，实在令人心酸。

他握了握康的手，说道：

"我来这里，只为跟你说一句话。我把马留在迪克（Dick）那儿，在马厩里；天亮之前我也许还要用它，也许再也不要了。"

说着，他便转身进了大厨房，拖过一张凳子，坐下来烤一烤火。

"坐下，康纳，坐在我对面，听我说什么，也别怕说出你心里的想法。"

他说话时一直盯着炉火，双手伸在火上方，看模样是个疲倦至极的人。

"我有什么好怕的，多米尼克老爷？"我祖父说。"您待我一直是个好主人，您父亲——愿他灵魂安息——在您之前也是一样；我要说真话，就是面对魔鬼我也敢说，为了杜诺兰的任何一位萨斯菲尔德，何况是您，我都敢说，这也是我本分。"

"我完了，康，"多米尼克爵士说。

"上天不容！"我祖父说。

"再也回天无力了，"多米尼克爵士说。"最后一个几尼（guinea）也没了；这老宅子跟着也保不住。非卖不可了。我到这里来，自己也说不清为的什么，像个鬼魂似的，最后再四下看一眼，便又要在黑暗里消失。"

说罢，他嘱咐康纳，万一听到他的死讯，务必把他房间里那间小 closet 里的橡木匣子，交给他在都柏林的表弟帕特·萨斯菲尔德（Pat Sarsfield），还有他祖父在奥格里姆（Aughrim）战役中所佩的刀和手枪，以及两三件这类的小玩意儿。

他又说："康，人都说，若是魔鬼夜里给了你钱，到了早晨，袋子里便只剩些石子、木屑和果壳了。倘若他当真讲信用，我今夜倒有心跟他做一笔交易。"

"上天不容！"我祖父说着，猛地站起，在胸前画了个十字。

"人说乡间遍地都是替法兰西国王招兵买马的人。我若撞上一个，也不会拒绝他的价。世事真会作弄人！我和沃勒上尉（Captain Waller）在新堡（New Castle）决斗，是多久以前的事了？"

"六年了，多米尼克老爷，头一枪您就用子弹打断了他的大腿。"

"是啊，康，"他说，"我倒宁可那一枪是他打穿了我的心。有威士忌么？"

我祖父从餐柜里取出酒，主人倒了一些在碗里，一饮而尽。

"我出去看看我的马，"他说着，站起身来。他把骑马斗篷往身上一裹，眼里有一种直愣愣的神情，仿佛心里盘算着什么不妙的事。

"我这就跑一趟马厩，亲自替您照看马，用不了一盏茶工夫，"我祖父说。

"我不是去马厩，"多米尼克爵士说，"我不妨直说吧——我看你也已经猜着了——我要穿过鹿苑；我若回来，一个钟头之内你便能见着我。但无论如何，你最好不要跟来；你若跟来，我就一枪打死你，那可就把咱俩的交情收得不太体面了。"

说罢，他便从这条过道走下去，在那头的侧门里拧动钥匙，出了门，踏上草地，走进月光与寒风之中；我祖父见他大步流星朝园墙走去，这才回身，心情沉重地关上了门。

===Original===
Sir Dominick stopped to think when he got to the middle of the deer-park, for he had not made up his mind, when he left the house, and the whisky did not clear his head, only it gev him courage.

He did not feel the cowld wind now, nor fear death, nor think much of anything but the shame and fall of the old family.

And he made up his mind, if no better thought came to him between that and there, so soon as he came to Murroa Wood, he’d hang himself from one of the oak branches with his cravat.

It was a bright moonlight night, there was just a bit of a cloud driving across the moon now and then, but, only for that, as light a’most as day.

Down he goes, right for the wood of Murroa. It seemed to him every step he took was as long as three, and it was no time till he was among the big oak-trees with their roots spreading from one to another, and their branches stretching overhead like the timbers of a naked roof, and the moon shining down through them, and casting their shadows thick and twist abroad on the ground as black as my shoe.

He was sobering a bit by this time, and he slacked his pace, and he thought ’twould be better to list in the French king’s army, and thry what that might do for him, for he knew a man might take his own life any time, but it would puzzle him to take it back again when he liked.

Just as he made up his mind not to make away with himself, what should he hear but a step clinkin’ along the dry ground under the trees, and soon he sees a grand gentleman right before him comin’ up to meet him.

He was a handsome young man like himself, and he wore a cocked-hat with gold-lace round it, such as officers wears on their coats, and he had on a dress the same as French officers wore in them times.

He stopped opposite Sir Dominick, and he cum to a standstill also.

The two gentlemen took off their hats to one another, and says the stranger:

“I am recruiting, sir,” says he, “for my sovereign, and you’ll find my money won’t turn into pebbles, chips, and nutshells, by tomorrow.”

At the same time he pulls out a big purse full of gold.

The minute he set eyes on that gentleman, Sir Dominick had his own opinion of him; and at those words he felt the very hair standing up on his head.

“Don’t be afraid,” says he, “the money won’t burn you. If it proves honest gold, and if it prospers with you, I’m willing to make a bargain. This is the last day of February,” says he; “I’ll serve you seven years, and at the end of that time you shall serve me, and I’ll come for you when the seven years is over, when the clock turns the minute between February and March; and the first of March ye’ll come away with me, or never. You’ll not find me a bad master, any more than a bad servant. I love my own; and I command all the pleasures and the glory of the world. The bargain dates from this day, and the lease is out at midnight on the last day I told you; and in the year”—he told him the year, it was easy reckoned, but I forget it—“and if you’d rather wait,” he says, “for eight months and twenty eight days, before you sign the writin’, you may, if you meet me here. But I can’t do a great deal for you in the meantime; and if you don’t sign then, all you get from me, up to that time, will vanish away, and you’ll be just as you are tonight, and ready to hang yourself on the first tree you meet.”

Well, the end of it was, Sir Dominick chose to wait, and he came back to the house with a big bag full of money, as round as your hat a’most.

My grandfather was glad enough, you may be sure, to see the master safe and sound again so soon. Into the kitchen he bangs again, and swings the bag o’ money on the table; and he stands up straight, and heaves up his shoulders like a man that has just got shut of a load; and he looks at the bag, and my grandfather looks at him, and from him to it, and back again. Sir Dominick looked as white as a sheet, and says he:

“I don’t know, Con, what’s in it; it’s the heaviest load I ever carried.”

He seemed shy of openin’ the bag; and he made my grandfather heap up a roaring fire of turf and wood, and then, at last, he opens it, and, sure enough, ’twas stuffed full o’ golden guineas, bright and new, as if they were only that minute out o’ the Mint.

Sir Dominick made my grandfather sit at his elbow while he counted every guinea in the bag.

When he was done countin’, and it wasn’t far from daylight when that time came, Sir Dominick made my grandfather swear not to tell a word about it. And a close secret it was for many a day after.

===Chinese===
多米尼克爵士走到鹿苑中段时，停下脚步想了想——他从屋里出来时其实并未拿定主意；那点威士忌也没能让他脑子清醒，只不过是壮了壮他的胆罢了。

此刻他已感觉不到寒风，也不畏惧死亡，心中盘桓的，唯有这个旧家的颜面与败落这一桩。

他拿定主意：若是一路走到穆罗阿林子再想不出什么更好的法子，他便要在哪根橡树枝上，用自己的领巾了结了自己。

那是一个明亮的月夜，只有一两片云时不时掠过月亮，除却这一点，四下里几乎亮如白昼。

他径直朝穆罗阿林子走下去。他觉得自己每迈一步都长似三步；不消片刻，他便已置身于那些大橡树之间——树根此起彼伏、相互牵连，枝杈在头顶交织，宛如裸露屋顶的椽木，月光透过枝叶倾泻而下，在地上投下浓密扭曲的阴影，黑得跟我的鞋面一般。

走到这时，他酒意已渐渐醒了些，便放慢了脚步；他寻思，倒不如去应募法兰西国王的军，看看那路子能否替他解围——因为他知道，一个人要寻短见，什么时候都行，可一旦死了，想再活回来，那便由不得他了。

他刚刚拿定主意不自寻了断，便听得脚下干枯的地面传来一步一步笃笃的足音；不多时，只见一位气度不凡的绅士迎面朝他走来，与他相会。

那是个与他一样的英俊青年，头戴一缀金丝绦的三角帽，正是军官们挂在军服上的那一款；身上穿的，也是彼时法兰西军官所着的装束。

他在多米尼克爵士对面停住，多米尼克爵士也随之站定了。

两位绅士彼此脱帽致意，那陌生人便开口道：

"先生，我是替我家君主招兵募勇的，"他说，"到了明日，您便会发现我给的钱，并不会化作石子、木屑和果壳。"

说着，他便掏出一只鼓鼓囊囊、装满金币的大钱袋。

多米尼克爵士一照面，便已对这位绅士心存自家的一番揣度；听了这话，他只觉头发一根根在头顶竖了起来。

"不必害怕，"那人说，"这钱烫不着您的。若是这金子果真清白，又于您顺遂，我便愿意与您成交。今天是二月的最后一天，"他说，"我为您效劳七年，七年期满，便由您来侍奉我；待七年之期一满，我便来取您——就在时钟走过二月与三月之间的那一分钟；三月一日，您便随我而去，否则再无机会。您会发觉，我做主子并不刻薄，做仆人也同样得力。我爱我自己的人；世间一切享乐与荣华，尽在我掌握之中。这交易以今日为始，契约在我所说的最后一日的午夜满期；那一年是——"他把那年份告诉了他，年份原是好算的，可惜我忘了——"倘若您宁愿再等上八个月又二十八天，再签那字据，也无不可，届时仍在此地相会便是。只是这期间我能为您做的，相当有限；若到时您不签，那么此前我给您的一切，都将烟消云散，您便会一如今夜这般光景，一心只想随便找棵树吊死自己了。"

结果嘛，多米尼克爵士到底选择了等候；他带着一大袋钱回到了宅子，那袋子鼓得几乎跟您的帽子一般圆。

我祖父见主人这么快便安然无恙地回来，自是喜出望外。他一头闯进厨房，把钱袋往桌上一甩；他挺直了身子，耸了耸肩，活像个刚卸下千斤重担的人；他盯着那袋子看，我祖父盯着他看，目光又从他转到袋子，再从袋子转回他身上。多米尼克爵士面白如纸，说道：

"康，我不知道这里头是什么；这是我平生扛过的最沉的担子。"

他似乎不敢开那只袋子；他叫我祖父生起一炉旺旺的泥炭和木柴火；到了末了，他才把袋子打开——果不其然，里头塞满了金几尼，崭新锃亮，仿佛是刚刚才从造币厂里出来的一般。

多米尼克爵士叫我祖父坐在他身旁，他亲手一枚一枚，把袋里的每一枚几尼都数了个清清楚楚。

待他数完——其时天已将明——多米尼克爵士叫我祖父发誓，对此事半个字也不得向外人提起。此后的许多日子里，这事都是一个严守的秘密。

===Original===
When the eight months and twenty-eight days were pretty near spent and ended, Sir Dominick returned to the house here with a troubled mind, in doubt what was best to be done, and no one alive but my grandfather knew anything about the matter, and he not half what had happened.

As the day drew near, towards the end of October, Sir Dominick grew only more and more troubled in mind.

One time he made up his mind to have no more to say to such things, nor to speak again with the like of them he met with in the wood of Murroa. Then, again, his heart failed him when he thought of his debts, and he not knowing where to turn. Then, only a week before the day, everything began to go wrong with him. One man wrote from London to say that Sir Dominick paid three thousand pounds to the wrong man, and must pay it over again; another demanded a debt he never heard of before; and another, in Dublin, denied the payment of a thundherin’ big bill, and Sir Dominick could nowhere find the receipt, and so on, wid fifty other things as bad.

Well, by the time the night of the 28th of October came round, he was a’most ready to lose his senses with all the demands that was risin’ up again him on all sides, and nothing to meet them but the help of the one dhreadful friend he had to depind on at night in the oak-wood down there below.

So there was nothing for it but to go through with the business that was begun already, and about the same hour as he went last, he takes off the little crucifix he wore round his neck, for he was a Catholic, and his gospel, and his bit o’ the thrue cross that he had in a locket, for since he took the money from the Evil One he was growin’ frightful in himself, and got all he could to guard him from the power of the devil. But tonight, for his life, he daren’t take them with him. So he gives them into my grandfather’s hands without a word, only he looked as white as a sheet o’ paper; and he takes his hat and sword, and telling my grandfather to watch for him, away he goes, to try what would come of it.

It was a fine still night, and the moon—not so bright, though, now as the first time—was shinin’ over heath and rock, and down on the lonesome oak-wood below him.

His heart beat thick as he drew near it. There was not a sound, not even the distant bark of a dog from the village behind him. There was not a lonesomer spot in the country round, and if it wasn’t for his debts and losses that was drivin’ him on half mad, in spite of his fears for his soul and his hopes of paradise, and all his good angel was whisperin’ in his ear, he would a’ turned back, and sent for his clargy, and made his confession and his penance, and changed his ways, and led a good life, for he was frightened enough to have done a great dale.

Softer and slower he stepped as he got, once more, in undher the big branches of the oak-threes; and when he got in a bit, near where he met with the bad spirit before, he stopped and looked round him, and felt himself, every bit, turning as cowld as a dead man, and you may be sure he did not feel much betther when he seen the same man steppin’ from behind the big tree that was touchin’ his elbow a’most.

“You found the money good,” says he, “but it was not enough. No matter, you shall have enough and to spare. I’ll see after your luck, and I’ll give you a hint whenever it can serve you; and any time you want to see me you have only to come down here, and call my face to mind, and wish me present. You shan’t owe a shilling by the end of the year, and you shall never miss the right card, the best throw, and the winning horse. Are you willing?”

The young gentleman’s voice almost stuck in his throat, and his hair was rising on his head, but he did get out a word or two to signify that he consented; and with that the Evil One handed him a needle, and bid him give him three drops of blood from his arm; and he took them in the cup of an acorn, and gave him a pen, and bid him write some words that he repeated, and that Sir Dominick did not understand, on two thin slips of parchment. He took one himself and the other he sunk in Sir Dominick’s arm at the place where he drew the blood, and he closed the flesh over it. And that’s as true as you’re sittin’ there!

Well, Sir Dominick went home. He was a frightened man, and well he might be. But in a little time he began to grow aisier in his mind. Anyhow, he got out of debt very quick, and money came tumbling in to make him richer, and everything he took in hand prospered, and he never made a wager, or played a game, but he won; and for all that, there was not a poor man on the estate that was not happier than Sir Dominick.

===Chinese===
待到那八个月又二十八天快要过尽之时，多米尼克爵士满心烦乱地回到了这宅子里，一时不知何去何从；彼时在世之人中，唯我祖父对此事略知一二，而他所知，也还不及实情的一半。

随着那日子一日一日临近——已到十月末了——多米尼克爵士心里的烦乱只是有增无已。

有一阵子，他下定决心，再不与此类事有所牵连，再不与他在穆罗阿林中所遇的那东西交谈。可转念一想，那些债务便叫他心里发虚，简直不知该何去何从。偏巧在那日子前一周，诸事都不顺遂起来：有人从伦敦写信来，说多米尼克爵士把三千镑付错了人，须得再付一次；又有人追讨一笔他闻所未闻的旧债；都柏林那边又有一人，矢口否认一笔天大的账款已经清偿，而多米尼克爵士怎么也找不到那张收据——如此种种，还有五十桩同样棘手的事。

到了十月二十八日那夜，从四面八方涌来的索债，已逼得他几乎要失了神志；除了那位可怖的朋友——他唯有夜间在底下那片橡木林中可依凭的那位——之外，他再无别法应付。

事已至此，已无可回头，唯有把已经开始的事做到底。约莫上回那个时辰，他摘下颈间所戴的小十字架——他是个天主教徒——又摘下他的福音书，还有他锁在吊坠里的一片真十字架（the true cross）的圣物；因为自从他从那恶者手中接过钱之后，他内心里日益惊惧，便想尽法子护住自己，免遭魔鬼的权势所制。可今夜，他拼了性命，也不敢将这些圣物带在身上。于是他一言不发，只把它们交到我祖父手里，脸色却白得像一张纸；他取了帽子和佩剑，嘱咐我祖父替他守望，便走了出去，要看看此事到底会有什么结果。

那是一个晴朗无风的夜晚，月光——虽已不似头一回那般明亮——洒在石楠与岩石之上，也洒在他脚下那片凄清的橡木林间。

他走近林子时，心头擂鼓般狂跳。四下里阒然无声，连身后村子里远远的一声犬吠也听不见。方圆一带再没有比这更荒凉的去处了；若不是那些债务和亏空逼得他半发疯似的——全然不顾他对自家灵魂的恐惧、对天堂的希冀，以及他那善良的天使在他耳畔的低语——他本会掉头回去，差人去请神父，做一番告解与补赎，改过自新，重新做人；他那时怕得够了，本可以做出许多功德来。

待他再一次走进那些大橡树枝叶之下，他的脚步愈发轻、愈发缓了；往里走了一截，将近他上回遇见那恶灵之处，他便停下脚步，四下环顾，只觉自己浑身上下，凉得如同死人一般；而当他瞧见同一个人从那棵几乎挨着他胳膊的大树背后踱出来时，您可想而知，他心里就更不好受了。

"那些钱，您发觉是好用的吧，"他说，"只是还不够。不打紧，您日后要有足够的，还有富余。我会替您照看着运气，但凡能帮到您处，我便给您一点提点；您什么时候想见我，只管到这里来，在心中唤起我的面目，愿望我到场，便是。到年底，您不会再欠一先令（shilling）；您也绝不会错过那张得胜的牌、那一掷的最妙点数、那一匹跑赢的马。您可愿意？"

那年轻绅士的声音几乎哽在喉间，头发又一根根竖了起来，可他到底挤出只言片语，表示应允；于是那恶者递给他一根针，命他从自己臂上取三滴血；他用一只橡果的杯托接了血，又给他一支笔，命他在两片薄薄的羊皮纸上，写下他所念、而多米尼克爵士并不懂得的一些字句。他自己取了一片，另一片则埋进多米尼克爵士臂上抽血之处，将那皮肉重新合上。这一切，千真万确，正如您坐在此处一般！

于是，多米尼克爵士回了家。他是个被吓破了胆的人，这也不足为怪。可是过不多久，他心里渐渐安生了些。无论如何，他很快便偿清了债务，钱财如潮水般涌来，愈发使他富有；他经手的桩桩件件尽皆顺遂；不论他下注、抑或对弈，从未有不胜之时。然而纵然如此，整个庄园里，再没有一个穷人，不比多米尼克爵士活得更安乐。

===Original===
So he took again to his old ways; for, when the money came back, all came back, and there were hounds and horses, and wine galore, and no end of company, and grand doin’s, and divarsion, up here at the great house. And some said Sir Dominick was thinkin’ of gettin’ married; and more said he wasn’t. But, anyhow, there was somethin’ troublin’ him more than common, and so one night, unknownst to all, away he goes to the lonesome oak-wood. It was something, maybe, my grandfather thought was troublin’ him about a beautiful young lady he was jealous of, and mad in love with her. But that was only guess.

Well, when Sir Dominick got into the wood this time, he grew more in dread than ever; and he was on the point of turnin’ and lavin’ the place, when who should he see, close beside him, but my gentleman, seated on a big stone undher one of the trees. In place of looking the fine young gentleman in goold lace and grand clothes he appeared before, he was now in rags, he looked twice the size he had been, and his face smutted with soot, and he had a murtherin’ big steel hammer, as heavy as a halfhundred, with a handle a yard long, across his knees. It was so dark under the tree, he did not see him quite clear for some time.

He stood up, and he looked awful tall entirely. And what passed between them in that discourse my grandfather never heered. But Sir Dominick was as black as night afterwards, and hadn’t a laugh for anything nor a word a’most for anyone, and he only grew worse and worse, and darker and darker. And now this thing, whatever it was, used to come to him of its own accord, whether he wanted it or no; sometimes in one shape, and sometimes in another, in lonesome places, and sometimes at his side by night when he’d be ridin’ home alone, until at last he lost heart altogether and sent for the priest.

The priest was with him a long time, and when he heered the whole story, he rode off all the way for the bishop, and the bishop came here to the great house next day, and he gev Sir Dominick a good advice. He toult him he must give over dicin’, and swearin’, and drinkin’, and all bad company, and live a vartuous steady life until the seven years bargain was out, and if the divil didn’t come for him the minute afther the stroke of twelve the first morning of the month of March, he was safe out of the bargain. There was not more than eight or ten months to run now before the seven years wor out, and he lived all the time according to the bishop’s advice, as strict as if he was “in retreat.”

Well, you may guess he felt quare enough when the mornin’ of the 28th of February came.

The priest came up by appointment, and Sir Dominick and his raverence wor together in the room you see there, and kep’ up their prayers together till the clock struck twelve, and a good hour after, and not a sign of a disturbance, nor nothing came near them, and the priest slep’ that night in the house in the room next Sir Dominick’s, and all went over as comfortable as could be, and they shook hands and kissed like two comrades after winning a battle.

So, now, Sir Dominick thought he might as well have a pleasant evening, after all his fastin’ and praying; and he sent round to half a dozen of the neighbouring gentlemen to come and dine with him, and his raverence stayed and dined also, and a roarin’ bowl o’ punch they had, and no end o’ wine, and the swearin’ and dice, and cards and guineas changing hands, and songs and stories, that wouldn’t do anyone good to hear, and the priest slipped away, when he seen the turn things was takin’, and it was not far from the stroke of twelve when Sir Dominick, sitting at the head of his table, swears, “this is the best first of March I ever sat down with my friends.”

“It ain’t the first o’ March,” says Mr. Hiffernan of Ballyvoreen. He was a scholard, and always kep’ an almanac.

“What is it, then?” says Sir Dominick, startin’ up, and dhroppin’ the ladle into the bowl, and starin’ at him as if he had two heads.

“’Tis the twenty-ninth of February, leap year,” says he. And just as they were talkin’, the clock strikes twelve; and my grandfather, who was half asleep in a chair by the fire in the hall, openin’ his eyes, sees a short square fellow with a cloak on, and long black hair bushin’ out from under his hat, standin’ just there where you see the bit o’ light shinin’ again’ the wall.

(My hunchbacked friend pointed with his stick to a little patch of red sunset light that relieved the deepening shadow of the passage.)

“Tell your master,” says he, in an awful voice, like the growl of a baist, “that I’m here by appointment, and expect him downstairs this minute.”

Up goes my grandfather, by these very steps you are sittin’ on.

“Tell him I can’t come down yet,” says Sir Dominick, and he turns to the company in the room, and says he with a cold sweat shinin’ on his face, “for God’s sake, gentlemen, will any of you jump from the window and bring the priest here?” One looked at another and no one knew what to make of it, and in the meantime, up comes my grandfather again, and says he, tremblin’, “He says, sir, unless you go down to him, he’ll come up to you.”

“I don’t understand this, gentlemen, I’ll see what it means,” says Sir Dominick, trying to put a face on it, and walkin’ out o’ the room like a man through the press-room, with the hangman waitin’ for him outside. Down the stairs he comes, and two or three of the gentlemen peeping over the banisters, to see. My grandfather was walking six or eight steps behind him, and he seen the stranger take a stride out to meet Sir Dominick, and catch him up in his arms, and whirl his head against the wall, and wi’ that the hall-doore flies open, and out goes the candles, and the turf and wood-ashes flyin’ with the wind out o’ the hall-fire, ran in a drift o’ sparks along the floore by his feet.

Down runs the gintlemen. Bang goes the hall-doore. Some comes runnin’ up, and more runnin’ down, with lights. It was all over with Sir Dominick. They lifted up the corpse, and put its shoulders again’ the wall; but there was not a gasp left in him. He was cowld and stiffenin’ already.

Pat Donovan was comin’ up to the great house late that night and after he passed the little brook, that the carriage track up to the house crosses, and about fifty steps to this side of it, his dog, that was by his side, makes a sudden wheel, and springs over the wall, and sets up a yowlin’ inside you’d hear a mile away; and that minute two men passed him by in silence, goin’ down from the house, one of them short and square, and the other like Sir Dominick in shape, but there was little light under the trees where he was, and they looked only like shadows; and as they passed him by he could not hear the sound of their feet and he drew back to the wall frightened; and when he got up to the great house, he found all in confusion, and the master’s body, with the head smashed to pieces, lying just on *that spot*.

===Chinese===
于是他又重拾起往日那套做派；因为钱一回来，什么都跟着回来了——又有了猎犬和马匹，有了喝不尽的酒，宾客络绎不绝，大宅里又是排场，又是消遣，热闹非凡。有人说多米尼克爵士正想着成亲；也有人说并无此事。但无论如何，有一桩事比往常更使他烦扰；于是有一夜，他瞒着众人，悄然又往那凄清的橡木林去了。据我祖父揣测，许是因一位他倾心爱慕、又满怀嫉妒的美貌少女，有些什么事搅扰着他。但那也只是猜度罢了。

这一回多米尼克爵士一进林子，心中的恐惧更甚从前；他正要转身离开此地，却见身边不远，正是我那位绅士，坐在一棵树下的一块大石头上。这一回，他再不是先前那副身披金丝绦、衣冠华美的翩翩佳公子模样，而是衣衫褴褛，身形比从前大了一倍，脸上抹得满是烟灰，膝上横着一把要命的大钢锤——足有半英担重，锤柄就有一码长。树下昏暗，他竟有好一阵子没看清他。

他站起身来，身量高得骇人。他们两人之间在那番交谈里究竟说了些什么，我祖父终生未曾听说。但事后多米尼克爵士的脸色乌沉如夜，再没有什么能博他一笑，对任何人也几乎无话可讲；他只是一日不如一日，愈发阴沉。而如今，那东西——也不知究竟是何物——竟会不请自来，不论他愿不愿；时而化作这一种形貌，时而化作那一种，在荒僻之处显现，有时夜里他独自骑马回家，它便在他身侧出现。直到末了，他彻底心灰意冷，差人去请了神父。

神父陪了他许久，听完前因后果，便连夜骑马去请主教；主教翌日便亲临大宅，给多米尼克爵士一番良言。他告诫他：必须戒了掷骰、咒骂、酗酒，远离一切损友，过一种端正沉稳的日子，直等那七年之约期满；倘若魔鬼未能在三月一日凌晨钟鸣十二响之后那一分钟之内来取他，他便算是逃出了这场交易。此时距七年之期已不足八到十个月，他这段时日里皆遵主教之诫而行，规规矩矩，犹如在教会里"避静"一般。

好吧，二月二十八日清晨到来之时，您猜他心里是何等滋味。

神父依约前来，多米尼克爵士与他阁下就在您所见的那间屋子里，一同祈禱，直到钟敲十二点，又足足多守了一个钟头，并无半点骚乱之象，也无任何东西近得他们身来。神父那夜便宿在宅中，就住多米尼克爵士隔壁的屋子；一切平平安安地过了去，两人像得胜之后的两名战友，握手拥抱。

于是多米尼克爵士心想：禁食祷告了这许久，今夜总该好好乐一乐了；他便差人去请邻近六七位绅士来赴晚宴，他阁下也留下一同入席。他们喝着一大碗热腾腾的潘趣酒，葡萄酒更是不计其数，又是咒骂，又是掷骰，打牌、几尼易手，还有那些不堪入耳的艳曲与秽语。神父见势头不对，便悄然溜走了。离十二点钟响已不远之时，多米尼克爵士坐在首席，朗声说道："这是我平生所度过的，最快活的一个三月一日。"

"今儿可不是三月一日，"巴利沃林的希弗南先生（Mr. Hiffernan of Ballyvoreen）说道。他是个读书人，案头常年备着一本年鉴。

"那是什么日子？"多米尼克爵士猛地站起，把勺子掉进了酒碗里，瞪着他，仿佛他生了两个脑袋。

"是二月二十九日，闰年，"他说。话音未落，钟敲响了十二点；我祖父那时在门厅炉火旁一张椅子里半睡半醒，一睁眼，便看见一个身披斗篷、矮矮壮壮的汉子，帽檐下披散着长长的黑发，正站在——那里，就是您瞧见的、那块光亮映在墙上的地方。

（我这位驼背朋友用杖头指了指一小片夕阳的红光，那红光正映在过道愈发深沉的阴影之上，颇为醒目。）

"去告诉你家主人，"他用一种骇人的声音——如同野兽的咆哮一般——说道，"我依约到此，要他即刻下楼来见我。"

我祖父便顺着您正坐着的这道楼梯上去。

"告诉他，我还下不了楼，"多米尼克爵士说，随即转向屋里众人，脸上冷汗涔涔，说道："看在上帝的份上，诸位先生，哪位能从窗口跳下去，把神父请到这里来？"众人面面相觑，谁也不明所以；正这时，我祖父又上来了，颤声说道："他说，老爷，您要是不下去，他便上楼来找您。"

"我搞不明白这是怎么回事，诸位先生，我下去看看，"多米尼克爵士说，强作镇定，走出屋子，活像一个穿过死牢、外头刽子手正等着他的人。他走下楼来；有两三位绅士从栏杆上探出头去张望。我祖父走在他身后六到八级开外，只见那陌生人跨上一步迎向多米尼克爵士，一把将他抱起，将他的头狠狠撞向墙壁——霎时间，大厅门洞开，烛火尽数熄灭，炉火里的泥炭与木灰随着风卷了出来，化作一路火星，沿着他脚边飘拂过去。

绅士们纷纷奔下楼来。砰的一声，大厅门关上。有的举着灯往上跑，有的往下跑。多米尼克爵士已经完了。他们抬起那具尸体，让它肩膀靠着墙；可他身上再没有一丝气息。他已然冰冷，正在僵硬。

那天夜里，帕特·多诺万（Pat Donovan）正往大宅走来；他过了那条小溪——通往大宅的车辙要涉过它——再往这边约莫五十步，他身旁那只狗猛地一个回旋，纵身跳过墙去，在墙里头狂吠起来，那一里地之外都能听见；就在那一刻，有两个人默不作声地从他身旁走过，从大宅那边下来；其中一个矮矮壮壮，另一个身形恰似多米尼克爵士；只是他所站之处，树下灯光稀微，那两人看上去不过是两道阴影罢了；他们走过时，他竟听不见他们的脚步声，吓得紧贴住墙根；待他赶到大宅，只见一片混乱，主人的尸首——脑袋已经砸得稀烂——便躺在那个地方。

---

===Original===
The narrator stood up and indicated with the point of his stick the exact site of the body, and, as I looked, the shadow deepened, the red stain of sunlight vanished from the wall, and the sun had gone down behind the distant hill of New Castle, leaving the haunted scene in the deep grey of darkening twilight.

So I and the storyteller parted, not without good wishes on both sides, and a little “tip,” which seemed not unwelcome, from me.

It was dusk and the moon up by the time I reached the village, remounted my nag, and looked my last on the scene of the terrible legend of Dunoran.

===Chinese===
讲述者站起身来，用杖头指了指尸体所卧的确切位置；我循着他的手势望去，阴影更深了，墙上那一片夕阳的红光也消隐不见——太阳已经落到远处的新堡山后去了，将这闹鬼的旧地，留在渐浓暮色的深灰之中。

于是我与这位讲故事的人道别，彼此说了些好话相送；我从兜里掏出一点"小费"给他，看样子倒也并非不受欢迎。

待我回到村里，重新跨上我的矮马，最后回望这杜诺兰那可怕传说之地，天色已暗，月亮升起来了。

## Borrhomeo the Astrologer A Monkish Tale / 占星师博罗梅奥：一则修士的故事

===Original===
At the period of the famous plague of Milan in 1630, a frenzy of superstition seized upon the population high and low. Old prophecies of a diabolical visitation reserved for their city, in that particular year of grace, prepared the way for this wild panic of the imagination. When the plague broke out terror seems to have acted to a degree scarcely paralleled upon the fancy or the credulity of the people. Excitement in very many cases produced absolutely the hallucinations of madness. Persons deposed, in the most solemn and consistent terms, to having themselves witnessed diabolical processions, spoken with an awful impersonation of Satan, and been solicited amidst scenes and personages altogether supernatural, to lend their human agency to the nefarious designs of the fiend, by consenting to disseminate by certain prescribed means, the virus of the pestilence.

Some of the stories related of persons possessed by these awful fancies are in print; and by no means destitute of a certain original and romantic horror. That which I am about to tell, however, has I believe, never been printed. At all events I saw it only in MSS., sewed up in vellum, with a psaltery and half-a-dozen lives of saints, in the library of the old Dominican monastery which stands about two leagues to the northeast of the city. With your permission I am about to give you the best translation I was able to make of this short but odd story, of the truth of which, judging from the company in which I found it, the honest monks entertained no sort of doubt. You are to remember that all sorts of tales of wonder were at that time flying about and believed in Milan, and that many of these were authenticated in such a way as to leave no doubt as to the bona fides of those who believed themselves to have been eyewitnesses of what they told. Monks and country padres of course believed; but so did men who stood highest in the church, and who, unless fame belied them, believed little else.

===Chinese===
1630 年米兰那场大瘟疫肆虐之时，上下人等尽皆为迷信之狂所摄。古老的预言早已扬言，魔祸将在此特定的恩典之年降临他们的城池，由此为先，遂为这想象力中狂乱的恐慌铺平了道路。瘟疫一旦爆发，恐惧之于人心的煽动、之于轻信的撩拨，其烈殆为世所罕匹。许多情形之下，极度亢奋竟真真切切地催生出癫狂的幻觉。有人以最庄严、最首尾相符的言辞宣誓作证，谓己身亲见群魔游行之列，亲与撒旦那可怖的化身对语，又于全然超自然的情景人物之间被多方怂恿，要借其人力以助那凶魔的奸恶图谋——只消应允，便可以某种指定的法子，播散那瘟疫的毒种。

关于被这等可怖妄念所附之人的故事，有些已见诸铅椠，且并非毫无一种别致的、罗曼蒂克的恐怖意味。然而我行将讲述的这一则，我相信从未付梓。无论如何，我只是在手稿中得见——它同一部《诗篇》、半打圣徒传记一道，缝合在一卷羊皮封套之内，藏于城东北约二里格开外那座古老多明我会修道院的藏书室中。如蒙允可，我将把所能作出的最佳译笔，呈奉于这一则短小却离奇的故事；而从它身处的同伴判断，那些诚朴的修士对其所载之事的真实性，毫无半点疑心。诸位当记得，其时米兰城中种种奇谭漫天飞舞、人皆深信，其中许多又被证实得如此确凿，以至于那些自谓亲眼目睹所述之事的人，其诚信已不容置疑。修士和乡间的神父们自然是信的；但教会中位跻极顶的人物也同样深信——据传闻所说，这些人除此之外几乎一无所信。

===Original===
In the year of our Lord, 1630, when Satan, by divine permission, appearing among us in person, afflicted our beautiful city of Milan with a pestilence unheard of in its severity, there lived in the Strada Piana, which has lately been pulled down, an astrologer calling himself Borrhomeo. Some say he came from Perrugia, others from Venice; I know not. He it was who first predicted, in the year of our Lord, 1628, by means of his art, that the pale comet which then appeared would speedily be followed, not by war or by famine, but by pestilence; which accordingly came to pass. Beside his skill in astrology, which was wonderful, he was profoundly versed in alchemy. He was a man great in stature, and strong, though old in years, and with a most reverent beard. But though seemingly austere in his life, it is said that he was given up, in secret, to enormous wickedness.

Having shut himself up in his house for more than a month, with his furnace and crucibles (truly he had made repeated and near approaches to the grand arcanum) he had arrived, as he supposed, at the moment of projection.

===Chinese===
主历 1630 年，撒旦蒙上苍准许，亲临我们中间，以一场惨烈程度前所未闻的瘟疫降罚我美丽的米兰城。彼时在斯特拉达·皮亚纳街上——此街近来已被拆除——住着一位自称博罗梅奥（Borrhomeo）的占星师。有人说他来自佩鲁贾（Perrugia），也有人说他来自威尼斯（Venice）；我不得而知。正是他，于主历 1628 年率先凭其术数预言：当时现身的苍白彗星过后，紧随而至的将不是兵燹，也不是饥荒，而是瘟疫；此事果然后来应验。他的占星术固已神妙绝伦，于炼金术一道亦是造诣极深。其人身形魁伟、筋骨强健，虽已年迈，却蓄一部极令人起敬的须髯。只是，虽说其起居观之似颇清苦严正，据传他暗地里却沉溺于骇人的邪行。

闭门于宅中逾一月之久，守着他的炉火与坩埚（他确实已一次又一次地逼近那"大秘宝"），他自以为，"投点"的时刻已然到来。

===Original===
He collects the powder and tries it on molten lead; it was a failure. He was too wise to be angry; the long pursuit of his art had taught him patience. But while he is pondering in a profound and gloomy reverie, a retort, which he had forgotten in the furnace, explodes.

He sees in the smoke a pale young man, dressed in mourning, with black hair, and viewing him with a sad and reproachful countenance.

Borrhomeo who lived among chimaeras, is not utterly overcome, as another man might be, and confronts him, amazed, indeed, but not terrified.

The stranger shook his head like a holy young confessor, who hears an evil shrift; and says he, rather sternly—"Borrhomeo! Beware of covetousness which is idolatry. On this sordid pursuit which you call a science, have you wasted your days on earth and your peace hereafter."

"Young man," says the alchemist, too much struck by the manner and reproof of the stranger to ask himself how he came there—"Wealth is power to do good as well as evil. To seek it is, therefore, an ambition as honourable as any other."

"We both know why you seek it, and how you would employ it," answers the young man gravely.

===Chinese===
他收拢那粉末，在熔铅上一试，竟告失败。他是聪明人，不至于动怒；多年穷究其术，早已教会他忍耐。正当他沉入一种深沉而阴郁的遐思之时，一只被他遗忘在炉中的曲颈甑猛然炸裂。

硝烟之中，他看见一个面色苍白的青年，身着丧服，一头黑发，正以哀戚而责备的神情望着他。

博罗梅奥久与幻象为伍，并不像旁人那般被彻底压倒，竟迎上前去与他相对，惊固然是惊，却并不恐惧。

那陌生人摇了摇头，其态如一位年轻圣洁的听忏悔神父，听到了一番罪孽的告解；他颇为严厉地开口道——"博罗梅奥！当心贪婪，那便是拜偶像。这桩你所称为'学问'的肮脏营生，已叫你荒废了在世的光阴，也葬送了身后的安宁。"

"年轻人，"炼金术士说——他被这陌生人的气度与训斥太过触动，竟来不及自问他是如何来到此地的——"财富乃是行善亦可行恶的力量。是以求之，乃是与任何抱负一样可敬的雄心。"

"你我二人都心知肚明，你求它的缘由，以及你将如何用它，"那青年神情凝重地答道。

===Original===
The old man's face flushed with anger at this rebuke, and he looked down frowningly to the table whereon lay the book of his spells. But he bethought him this must be a good spirit, and he was abashed. Nevertheless, he roused his courage, and shook his white mane back, and was on the point of answering sternly, when the young man said with a melancholy smile—

"Besides, you will never discover the grand arcanum—the *elixir vitae*, or the philosopher's stone."

His words, which were as soft as snowflakes, fell like an iron mace upon the heart of the seer.

"Perhaps not," said the astrologer frigidly.

"Not perhaps," said the stranger.

"At all events, young man—for as such you appear—and I know what spirits seek who take that shape, the science has its charms for me; and when the pleasures of the young are as harmless as the amusements of the aged I'll hear you question mine."

"You know not what spirit you are of. As for me, I am contrite and humble—well I may," says the stranger faintly with a sigh. "Besides, what you have pursued in vain, and will never by your own researches find, I have discovered."

"What! the—"

"Yes, the tincture that can prolong life to virtual immortality, and the dust that can change that lead into gold; but I care for neither."

===Chinese===
老人闻此斥责，面色因怒而涨红，皱眉俯视桌上那本咒书。可转念一想，这必定是位善灵，他便讪讪地收敛了。然而他重又鼓起勇气，将那头白发如鬃般往后一甩，正欲严厉作答，那青年却带着一丝哀伤的微笑说道——

"况且，你也永远不会参透那大秘宝——那*长生灵药*（elixir vitae），或曰点金石。"

他的话轻柔如雪片，却像一柄铁锤砸在那占星师的心上。

"也许不能，"占星师冷冷地说。

"不是也许，"陌生人道。

"无论如何，年轻人——既然你这般现身——而且我晓得取这副形貌而来的是何种灵体，这门学问自有它的迷人之处；待到年轻人的乐事与老年人的消遣一般无害之时，我再来听你非议我的嗜好不迟。"

"你不知道自己怀的是怎样一种灵。至于我，我是痛悔而谦卑的——我尽可以如此，"陌生人轻声叹息着说。"况且，你所苦苦追寻而不得、凭你自家钻研也永难寻见的东西，我已寻到了。"

"什么！那——"

"是的，那种能将生命延续至几乎不死的灵药，那能把铅化作金的粉末；可这两样，我都不放在心上。"

===Original===
"Why, young man, if this be true," says Borrhomeo in a rapture of wonder, "you stand before me an angel of wisdom, in power and immortality like a god!"

"No," says the stranger, "a long-lived fellow, with a long purse—that's all."

"All?—everything!" cries the old man. "Will you—*will* you—"

"Yes, sir, you shall see," says the young man in black. "Give me that crucible. It is all a matter of proportions. Water, clay, and air are the material of all the vegetable world—the flowers and forests, the wines and the fruits—the seed is both the laboratory and the chemist, and knows how, with the sun's help, to apportion and combine."

While he said this with the abstracted manner of one whose mind is mazed in a double reverie, while his hands work out some familiar problem, he tumbled over the alchemist's papers, and unstopped and stopped his bottles of crystals, precipitates, and elixirs—taking a little from this and a little from that, and throwing all into a small gold cup that stood on the table; but like a juggler, he moved those bottles so deftly, that the quick eyes and retentive soul of the old man vainly sought to catch or keep the order of the process. When he had done there was hardly a thimble-full.

"Is that it?" whispered the old man, twinkling with greedy eyes.

"No," said the stranger, with a sly smile, "there is one very simple ingredient which you have forgotten."

===Chinese===
"哎呀，年轻人，若果然如此，"博罗梅奥惊叹得如痴如狂，"那你站在我面前的，便是一位智慧的天使，权能与不朽皆如神明一般了！"

"不，"陌生人道，"不过是个寿长之人，外加一只鼓鼓的钱袋——如此而已。"

"而已？——那便是一切了！"老人叫道。"你可愿——*你可愿*——"

"愿意，先生，您且看着，"那黑衣青年说。"把那只坩埚递给我。这全不过是个配比的事。水、土、气，乃是一切植物界的原料——花草与林木、美酒与果实——种子既是工坊，又是工匠，懂得如何在日光相助之下分剂调和。"

他这般说着，神情恍忽如一人之心神陷于双重遐思之中，而其双手却在摆弄一桩烂熟的活计；他把炼金术士的纸页翻得乱七八糟，又把那些装着晶体、沉淀物与灵药的瓶子一一启封、封上——这瓶取一点，那瓶取一点，统统抛进桌上一只小小的金杯之中；可他像戏法艺人一般，挪动那些瓶子的手法灵巧之极，老人那双锐利的眼睛与过人的记性，徒然想捉住、记住那道道工序的次序，终归枉然。待他做完，杯中所剩，还不够装满一只顶针。

"就是这个？"老人悄声问，一双贪婪的眼睛灼灼发亮。

"不，"陌生人狡黠地一笑，"还有一样极简单的配料，你却忘了。"

===Original===
He took a large, flat, oval gold box, with some hair set under a crystal in the lid of it, and looking at it for a moment, he seemed to sigh. He tapped it like a snuffbox—there was within it a powder like vermilion, and on the inside of the lid, in the centre, was the small enamel portrait of a beautiful but sinister female face. The features were so very beautiful, and the expression so strangely blended with horror, that it fixed the gaze of the old man for a moment; and—was it illusion?—he thought he saw the face steadily dilating as if it would gradually fill the lid of the box, and even expand to human dimensions.

"Yes," said the stranger, as having taken some of the red powder, he shut the cover down again with a snap, "she was beautiful, and her lineaments are still clear and bright—nothing like darkness to keep them from fading, and so the poor little miniature is again in prison;" and he dropped the box back into his pocket.

Then he took two iron ladles, and heating in the one his powder to a white heat, and bidding the alchemist melt a pellet of lead in the other, and pour it into the ladle which held the powder, there arose a beautiful purple fire in the bottom of it, with an intense fringe of green and yellow; and when it subsided there was a little nut of gold there of the bigness of the leaden pellet.

The fiery eyes of the alchemist almost leaped from their sockets into the iron cup, and he could have clasped his marvellous visitor round the knees and worshipped him.

===Chinese===
他取出一只又大又扁的椭圆形金盒，盒盖的水晶之下压着一绺头发；他朝它端详片刻，似是叹了一口气。他像敲鼻烟壶一般叩了叩盒盖——里面装着一种朱砂般的粉末，盒盖内侧正中，是一幅小小的珐琅画像：一张美艳却阴鸷的女子脸庞。那五官美艳已极，神情又诡异地糅合着可怖之色，竟教老人的目光一时凝住不动；而且——莫非是幻觉？——他觉得那张脸正在稳稳地胀大，仿佛要渐渐充塞整只盒盖，甚至扩张到与真人一般大小。

"是了，"陌生人说着，已取了些许那红色粉末，啪地一声把盒盖重新合上，"她曾是美丽的，她的容颜至今仍清晰鲜亮——唯有黑暗能使之免于褪色，于是这可怜的小画像便又下了狱。"说罢，他把盒子扔回了衣袋。

随后他取了两只铁勺，一只里把他的粉末烧到白热，又命炼金术士在另一只里熔了一粒铅丸，把它倒进盛着粉末的那只勺里；勺底便升起一团美丽的紫色火焰，镶着一圈浓烈的绿黄火边；待火焰熄灭，里面便有了一颗小小的金疙瘩，大小恰与那枚铅丸相当。

炼金术士那双灼灼如火的眼珠，几乎要从眼眶里蹦进那只铁勺去；他简直想一把抱住这位神乎其神的访客的双膝，俯身膜拜。

===Original===
"And now," says the stranger very gently and earnestly, "in return for satisfying your curiosity, I ask only your solemn promise to prosecute this dread science no more. Ha! you'll not give it. Take, then, my warning, and remember the wages of this knowledge is sorrow."

"But won't you tell me how to commute—and—and—you have not produced the elixir," the old man cried.

"'Tis folly—and, as I've told you, worse—a snare," answered the young man, sighing heavily. "I came not to satisfy but to rebuke your dangerous though fruitless frenzy. Besides, I hear my friend still pacing the street. Hark! he taps at the window."

Then came a sharp rattle as of a cane tapping angrily on the window.

The young man bowed, smiling sadly, and somehow got himself away, though without hurry, yet so quickly that the old man could not reach the door till after it had closed and he was gone.

"Oaf that I am!" cried the astrologer, losing patience and stamping on the ground, "how have I let him go? He hesitated—he would have yielded—his scruples, benevolent perhaps, I could have quieted—and yet in the very crisis I was tongue-tied and motionless, and let him go!"

He pushed open the little window, from which he observed the street, and thought he saw the stranger walking round the corner, conversing with a little hunchback in a red cloak, and followed by an ugly dog.

===Chinese===
"那么如今，"陌生人极其温和而恳切地说，"既已满足了你的好奇心，作为回报，我只求你一个庄严的承诺：从此不再穷究这门可怕的学问。哈！你不肯应承。那就收下我的警告吧，记住：这种知识的工价，乃是忧愁。"

"可你难道不愿告诉我如何能消解——而且——而且——你尚未把那灵药造出来呢，"老人叫道。

"那是痴心妄想——而且，如我方才所言，更糟——是个圈套，"青年答道，沉沉地叹了一口气。"我来不为满足，乃是要斥责你这场危险却徒劳的癫狂。况且，我听见我的同伴仍在街上踱步。听！他在叩窗。"

随即响起一阵急促的笃笃声，像是一根手杖怒气冲冲地叩在窗上。

那青年鞠了一躬，凄然微笑，不知怎地便抽身而去，虽不慌不忙，却迅疾之极——老人还没够到门边，门已阖上，人已无踪。

"我这蠢材！"占星师按捺不住，直跺脚，"我竟让他走了！他犹豫了——他本要让步了——他的顾虑，或许是出于善心，我原可劝解的——偏偏在这紧要关头，我舌头打了结，浑身动弹不得，竟任他去了！"

他推开那扇用以窥探街景的小窗，恍惚看见那陌生人正拐过街角，与一个身披红斗篷的小驼子交谈，身后还跟着一只丑陋的狗。

===Original===
At sight of the great white head and beard, and the fierce features of the alchemist, bleared and tanned in the smoke of his furnace, people stopped and looked. So he withdrew, and in haste got him ready for the street, waiting for no refreshment, though he had fasted long; for he had the strength as well as the stature of a giant, and forth he went.

By this time the twilight had passed into night. He had his mantle about him, and his rapier and dagger—for the streets were dangerous, and a feather in his cap, and his white beard hidden behind the fold of his cloak. So he might have passed for a tall soldier of the guard.

The pestilence kept people much within doors, and the streets more solitary than was customary. He had walked through the town two hours and more, before he met with anything to speak of. Then—lo!—on a sudden, near the Fountain of the Lion—it being then moonlight—he discovers, in a solitude, the figure of his visitor, standing with the hunchback and the dog, which he knew by its ungainly bones, and its carrying its huge head so near the ground.

So he shouts along the silent street, "Stay a moment, signor," and he mends his pace.

But they were parting company there, it seemed, and away went the deformed, with his unsightly beast at his heels, and this way came the youth in black.

===Chinese===
人们一见那颗雪白的大头颅与胡须，一见炼金术士那张被炉烟熏黄烤黑、狰狞可怖的面孔，无不驻足而视。他于是退回屋内，匆匆打点停当便要上街，连一点饮食也不肯等，尽管他已久未进食；他既有巨人之躯，亦有巨人之力，便径自出了门。

此时暮色已尽，化为黑夜。他披上斗篷，佩了长剑与匕首——因街途不靖——帽上插一根羽毛，白须则藏于斗篷的褶缝之后。这般装束，他满可以冒充一名高大的禁卫军士。

瘟疫把人多半困在户内，街市比往日更为萧索冷清。他在城中走了两个多钟头，才遇见一桩值得一提的事。随即——瞧哇！——猛然之间，在那雄狮喷泉（Fountain of the Lion）近旁——其时月色正明——他于一片寂寥之中，发现了那位访客的身影，正与那驼子和那只狗立在一处；他之所以认出那狗，是凭它那副粗笨的骨架，又凭它把那颗硕大的脑袋几乎贴着地面拖着。

他便沿着空寂的长街高声喊道："且留步，先生（signor），"一面加快了脚步。

可他们似乎恰在此处分道扬镳，那畸人带着他那丑陋的畜生脚跟脚地去了，那黑衣青年则朝这边走来。

===Original===
So standing full in his way, and doffing his cap, and throwing back his cloak, that his snowy beard and head might appear, and the stranger recognize him when he drew nigh. He cried—

"Borrhomeo implores thee to take pity on his ignorance."

"What! still mad?" said the young man. "This man will waste the small remnant of his years in godless search after gold and immortality; better he should know all, and feel their vanity."

"Better a thousand times!" cried the old man, in ecstacy.

"There is in this city, signor, at this time, in great secrecy, the master who taught me," says the youth, "the master of all alchemists. Many centuries since he found out the *elixir vitae*. From him I've learned the few secrets that I know, and without his leave I dare not impart them. If you desire it, I will bring you before him; but, once in his presence, you cannot recede, and his conditions you must accept."

"All, all, with my whole heart. But some reasonable pleasures—"

"With your pleasures he will not interfere; he cannot change your heart," said the young man, with one of his heavy sighs; "but you know what gold is, and what the elixir is, and power and immortality are not to be had for nothing."

"Lead on, signor, I'm ready," cries the old man, whose face flushed, and his eyes burned with the fires of an evil rapture.

"Take my hand," said the young man, more stern and pale than he had yet appeared. So he did, and his conductor seized it with a cold grip, and they walked swiftly on.

===Chinese===
他便径直拦住他的去路，脱下便帽，往后一甩斗篷，好露出那一头雪白的须发，让陌生人走近时认出他来。他高声叫道——

"博罗梅奥恳求你，可怜可怜他的无知吧。"

"怎么！还疯着？"那青年道。"这人怕是要把残年剩下的那点光阴，都荒废在求金、求长生的不虔之业上了；倒不如让他知道个究竟，好叫他尝尝这两样的虚妄滋味。"

"千真万确，再好不过！"老人如痴如狂地叫道。

"先生，此时此城之中，正有教过我的那位师父，极隐秘地住着，"青年说，"他是一切炼金术士的师父。数百年前，他便已寻得那*长生灵药*（elixir vitae）。我所晓得的几桩秘密，都是从他那里学来的，未经他许可，我不敢擅授于人。你若愿意，我可引你到他跟前；只是，一旦到了他面前，你便再不能退缩，他所开出的条件，你必得应承。"

"一概应承，一概应承，发自肺腑。只是些许合情合理的乐事——"

"你的乐事，他不会过问；他也改不了你的心，"青年说，照例沉重地叹了一声，"可你晓得金子是什么，灵药是什么，权能与不朽，断非可以白白到手的。"

"领路吧，先生，我准备好了，"老人叫道，他满面涨红，双眼燃着一种邪恶的狂喜之火。

"拉住我的手，"青年说，比先前更为严厉、更为苍白。他照办了，引路人以一握冰冷的手攥住他，两人便疾步前行。

===Original===
