Now he led him through several streets, and on their way Borrhomeo passes his notary, and, lingering a moment, asks him whether he has a bond, signed by a certain merchant, with whom he had contracted for a loan. The notary, who was talking to another, says, suddenly, to that other—

"*Per Baccho!* I've just called to mind a matter that must be looked after for Signor Borrhomeo;" and he called him a nickname, which incensed the astrologer, who struck him a lusty box upon the ear.

"There's a humming in my ear tonight," said the notary, going into his house; "I hope it is no sign of the plague."

So on they walked, side by side, till they reached the shop of a vintner of no good repute. It was well known to Borrhomeo—a house of evil resort, where the philosopher sometimes stole, disguised, by night, to be no longer a necromancer, but a man, and, so, from a man to become a beast.

They passed through the shop. The host, with a fat pale face, and a villainous smile, was drawing wine, which a handsome damsel was waiting to take away with her. He kissed her as she paid, and she gave him a cuff on his fat white chops, and laughed.

"What's become of Signor Borrhomeo," said the girl, "that he never comes here now."

"Why, here he is!" cries Borrhomeo, with a saturnine smile, and he slaps his broad palm on her shoulder.

But the girl only shrugged, with a little shiver, and said, "What a chill down my back—they're walking over my grave now."

[The Italian phrase here is very nearly equivalent.]

"Why they neither hear nor see me!" said the astrologer, amazed.

===Chinese===
此时他引着他穿过好几条街，途中博罗梅奥经过他那公证人处，便驻足片刻，问他手里是否还收着某商人签给他的一张借契——他曾与此人谈妥一笔贷款。那公证人正与另一人交谈，忽然对那人说道——

"*以酒神之名！*（Per Baccho！）我刚刚想起一桩事，得替博罗梅奥先生赶紧料理；"他还顺嘴给他起了个浑名，这一下激怒了占星师，便结结实实给了他一记响亮的耳光。

"我今夜耳朵里嗡嗡直响，"那公证人一面进屋一面说，"但愿不是瘟疫的征兆才好。"

于是两人并肩前行，直到来到一家声名狼藉的酒肆门前。此店博罗梅奥再熟悉不过——一所藏污纳垢的去处，这位"哲人"有时趁着夜色，乔装改扮悄悄溜到这里，不再做什么通灵术士，而要做一个凡人，既做了凡人，便进而堕为一头走兽。

他们穿过店堂。店主人一张苍白肥胖的脸，挂着奸恶的笑，正打酒；一个俊俏的姑娘等着把酒端走。她付钱时他趁机亲了她一口，她便在他那白胖的脸颊上回敬了一记耳刮子，笑了起来。

"博罗梅奥先生怎么啦，"那姑娘说，"如今再不上这儿来了。"

"咦，我就在这儿哪！"博罗梅奥叫道，带着阴郁的笑，把一只宽大的巴掌拍在她的肩上。

可那姑娘只是耸了耸肩，打了个寒噤，说道："我背脊上一阵发凉——这会儿怕是有人在踩我的坟地呢。"

［此处的意大利俗语，与英文这层意思几乎完全相当。］

"怎么，他们既听不见我，也看不见我！"占星师诧异地说。

===Original===
They went into the inner room, where guests used to sit and drink. But the plague had stopped all that, and the room was empty.

"He's in there," said the young man; "you'll see him presently."

Borrhomeo was filled with an awful curiosity. He knew the room, he thought, well; and there never had been, he thought, a door where the young man had pointed; but there was now a drapery there like what covers a doorway, and it swelled and swayed slowly in the wind.

"Some centuries?" said the astrologer, looking on the dark drapery. "Geber, perhaps, or Alfarabi—"

"It matters not a pin's point what his name; you'll call him 'my lord,' simply; and—observe—we alchemists are a potent order, and it behoves you to keep your word with us."

"I will be true," said Borrhomeo.

"And use the powers you gain, beneficently," repeated his guide.

"I'm but a sinner. I will strive, with only an exception, in favour of such things as make wealth and life worth having," answered the philosopher.

"See, take this, and do as I bid you," said the youth, giving him a thin round film of human skin.

[How the honest monk who wrote the tale, or even Borrhomeo himself, knew this and many other matters he describes, 'tis for him to say.]

"Breathe on it," said he.

And when he did so he made him stretch it to the size of a sheet of paper, which he did quite easily.

"Now cover your face with it as with a napkin."

So he did.

"'Twill do; give it to me. It is but a picture. See."

And it slowly shrunk until its disc was just the same as that of the lady's miniature in the lid of the box, over which he fixed it.

Borrhomeo beheld his own picture.

===Chinese===
他们进了里间，客人们从前惯常在此围坐饮酒。可瘟疫已把这营生断绝了，屋里空无一人。

"他就在里面，"那青年说，"你马上便能见到他。"

博罗梅奥心中充满了一种可怖的好奇。他自以为对这间屋子再熟不过；他心想，那里向来不曾有过一扇门——青年手指之处；可如今那里却悬着一幅帷幕，状如遮在门洞之前，正缓缓地随风鼓荡、摇摆。

"几百年？"占星师望着那深色的帷幕说。"莫非是贾比尔（Geber），或是阿尔法拉比（Alfarabi）——"

"他姓甚名谁，半个铜钱的价值都不值；你只消唤他'大人'便是；而且——记着——我们炼金术士乃是一个势力强大的门派，你须得对我们守信。"

"我必守约，"博罗梅奥说。

"并以你所获之力，行善事，"引路人又重述了一遍。

"我不过是个罪人。我愿尽力而为——只有一桩例外，凡能使财富与人生值得一享之事，则另当别论，"那"哲人"答道。

"瞧，拿着这个，照我吩咐的去做，"青年说，递给他一片薄薄的、圆形的人皮薄膜。

［那位撰写此篇的诚实修士——甚至博罗梅奥本人——又是如何得知此事、以及他所描述的许多别的事的，那只有他自己才能说得清了。］

"朝它呵口气，"他说。

他依言呵了，青年便教他把那薄膜抻成一张纸那般大小，这事他做来毫不费力。

"如今把它像餐巾一样蒙在脸上。"

他便照办了。

"行了；把它给我。这不过是一幅画像。瞧。"

它便缓缓地缩小，缩到其圆盘恰与那盒盖里仕女袖珍像一般大小，他便把它固定在那像之上。

博罗梅奥看见了自己的画像。

===Original===
"Every adept has his portrait here," said the young man. "So good a likeness is always pleasant; but these have a power beside, and establish a sympathy between their originals and their possessor which secures discipline and silence."

"How does it work?" asked Borrhomeo.

"Have I not been your good angel?" said the young man, sitting before him. He extends his legs—pushing out his feet, and letting his chin sink on his chest—he fixes his eyes upon him with a horrible and sarcastic glare, and one of his feet contracts and divides into a goatish stump.

Borrhomeo would have burst into a yell, but he could not.

"It is a nightinare, is it not?" said the stranger, who seemed delighted to hold him, minute after minute, in that spell. At last the shoe and hose that seemed to have shrunk apart like burning parchment, closed over the goatish shin and hoof; and rising, he shook him by the shoulder. With a gasp, the astrologer started to his feet.

"There, I told you it was a nightmare, or—or what you please. I could not have done it but through the picture. You see how fast we have you. You must for once resemble a Christian, Borrhomeo, and with us deal truly and honestly."

"You've promised me the *elixir vitae*," the old man said, fearful lest the secret should escape him.

"And you shall have it. Go, bring a cup of wine. He'll not see you, nor the wine, nor the cup."

So he brought a cup of Falernian, which he loved the best.

"There's fifty years of life for every drop," said the youth.

"Let me live a thousand years, to begin with," cries Borrhomeo.

"Beware. You'll tire of it—"

"Nay. Give me the twenty drops."

===Chinese===
"每一位入道者，皆在此处留有一幅画像，"那青年说。"如此惟妙惟肖的肖像，自然令人赏心；但这些画像另有一桩神通，能在它的原主与持有人之间结起一种感应，由此确保纪律与缄默。"

"那是怎么作用的？"博罗梅奥问。

"我岂不是一直做你的守护天使么？"那青年在他面前坐下说。他伸出双腿——把脚伸向前去，下巴沉到胸前——一双眼睛以一种可怖而讥诮的目光死死盯住他，他的一只脚随之收缩、裂开，化作一截山羊似的脚桩。

博罗梅奥本要发出一声惨叫，却叫不出来。

"这是场噩梦，是吧？"陌生人说，他似乎颇为得意，能把他一分钟又一分钟地镇在这咒缚里。终于，那鞋袜状如烈火炙过的羊皮纸似的，似已缩开，重又合拢在那山羊的小腿与蹄子之上；他站起身来，摇了摇他的肩膀。占星师猛吸一口气，跳了起来。

"瞧，我早说过这是场噩梦，或者——或者随你怎么叫。若不凭那幅画像，我也办不到。你瞧我们把你攥得多紧。博罗梅奥，这一回你可得像个基督徒的样子，对我们以诚相待、不可欺瞒了。"

"你已应许给我那*长生灵药*（elixir vitae）的，"老人说，惟恐那秘密从他手中溜走。

"你自会得到。去，端一杯酒来。他看不见你，也看不见那酒、那只杯。"

他便去端了一杯法勒纳酒（Falernian）来——这是他最钟爱的酒。

"每一滴，便值五十年的阳寿，"青年说。

"那就先让我活一千年罢，"博罗梅奥叫道。

"当心。你迟早会厌倦——"

"不。给我二十滴。"

===Original===
So he took the cup, and measured the drops; and as they fell, the wine was agitated with a gentle simmer all over, and threw out ring after ring of purple, green, and gold. And Borrhomeo drank it, and sucked in the last drop in ecstacy, and cried out, blaspheming, with joy and sensual delight—

"And I'm to have this secret, too."

"This and all others, when you claim them," said the young man.

"See, 'tis time," he added.

And Borrhomeo saw that the great misshapen dog he had seen in the street, was sniffing by the stranger's feet.

When they went into the inner room there was a large table, and many men at either side; and at the head a gigantic man, with a face like the face of a beast, but the flesh was as of a man. Borrhomeo quaked in his presence.

"I am aware of what hath passed, Borrhomeo," he said. "The condition is this:—You take this vial, and with the fluid it contains and the sponge trace the letter S on every door of every church and religious house within the walls of Milan. The dog will go with you."

It was a fiend in dog's shape, says the monkish writer; and had he failed in his task would have torn him in pieces.

===Chinese===
于是他接过杯，一滴滴量下；那酒液每落下一滴，便起一阵微微的沸腾之状，一圈又一圈泛出紫、绿、金三色的环纹。博罗梅奥一饮而尽，又贪婪地咂尽了最后一滴，如痴如狂地亵渎神明般欢呼起来，满心是肉欲的欢狂——

"而我还将获得这个秘密。"

"这个，以及其余一切，只待你来索取，"那青年说。

"瞧，时候到了，"他又添了一句。

博罗梅奥便看见，他在街上所见的那只硕大畸形的狗，正嗅着在陌生人的脚边。

他们走进里间，里面摆着一张大桌，两旁坐着许多人；上首坐着一个巨人般的男子，一张脸形如兽面，那肉却又是人的血肉。博罗梅奥在他面前瑟瑟发抖。

"所经诸事我已尽知，博罗梅奥，"他说。"条件是这样的：——你拿着这只小瓶，用瓶里所盛的液汁和那块海绵，在米兰城墙之内的每一座教堂、每一所修道院的门上，描出一个字母 S。那只狗会随你同去。"

据那位修士作者所言，那是一只以犬形现身的凶魔；他若在差事上有半点差池，便会被它撕成碎片。

===Original===
So Borrhomeo, that old arch-villain, undertook this office cheerfully, well knowing what its purpose was. For it was a thing notorious, that Satan was himself in a bodily, though phantasmal, shape seen before in Milan, and that he had tempted others to a like fascinorous action; but, happily for their souls, in vain. The Stygian satellites of the fiend had power to smear the door of every unconsecrated house in Milan with that pestilential virus, as, indeed, the citizens with their own eyes, when first the plague broke out, beheld upon their own doors. But they could not defile the church gates, nor the doors of the monasteries; and according to the conditions under which their infernal malice is bound, they could in nowise effect it save by the hand of one who was baptized, which, to the baleful abuse of that holy sacrament, the wretch, Borrhomeo, had been.

He did his accursed and murderous office well and fearlessly. His reward mammon and indefinite long life. The hell-dog by his side compelling him, and the belief in his invisibility making him confident withal. But therein was shown forth to all the world the craft of the fiend, and the just judgment of heaven; for he was plainly seen in the very act by the Sexton of the Church of Saint Mary of the Passion, and by the Pastor of the convent of Saint Justina of Padua, and the same officer of the Olivetans of Saint Victor. So, finding in the morning the only too plain and fatal traces of what he had been doing, with a mob at their heels, who would have had his life but for the guard, they arrested him in his house next morning, and the mob breaking in, smashed all the instruments of his infernal art, and would have burnt the house had they been allowed.

===Chinese===
于是那老魔头博罗梅奥欣然领下这桩差事，原是心知肚明其用途何在。因这事已属众所周知：撒旦此前确曾亲在米兰现出肉身——虽则只是幻形——也曾诱人去做同样妖邪之举；幸而可怜了他们的灵魂，皆未得逞。那凶魔手下的冥河喽啰们，本有权用那疫疠之毒涂抹米兰城中每一所未经祝圣之宅的门扉——事实上，瘟疫初起之时，市民们便曾亲眼看见自家门上有此物事。但他们玷污不了教堂的大门，也玷污不了修道院的门户；而按照他们那地狱的歹念所受的约束，他们无论如何办不到此事，除非借由一个受过洗之人的手——那恶贼博罗梅奥，正曾领受过这圣礼，如今却被他作贱成这等歹毒的用途。

他干这遭天谴的杀人差事，干得卖力而无畏。他的报酬是财神与无尽的阳寿。身边那只地狱犬挟制着他，而他自恃隐身，愈发有恃无恐。然而恰恰在此，向全世界昭然显露的，是那凶魔的诡诈，与上苍公允的裁断；因为就在他下手之际，便被苦难圣母堂（Saint Mary of the Passion）的司事、帕多瓦圣犹斯丁娜修院（convent of Saint Justina of Padua）的牧师，以及圣维克多橄榄山会（Olivetans of Saint Victor）的同一位职事，当场看得清清楚楚。于是，第二天清晨，他们发现了他所为那些再明白不过、再致命不过的痕迹，便领着一群暴民——若非有卫兵弹压，这群人本要当场要了他的命——翌晨在他宅中将他拿下，暴民破门而入，把他那一应通邪之术的家什砸得粉碎，若非有人拦阻，连那宅子也要一把火烧了。

===Original===
He being duly arraigned was, according to law, put to the torture, and forthwith confessed all the particulars I have related. So he was cast into a dungeon to await execution, which secretly he dreaded not, being confident in the efficacy of the elixir he had swallowed.

He was not to be put to death by decapitation. It was justly thought too honourable for so sordid a miscreant. He was sentenced to be hanged, and after hanging a day and a night he was to be laid in an open grave outside the gate on the Roman road, and there impaled, and after three days' exposure to be covered in, and so committed to the keeping of the earth, no more to groan under his living enormities.

The night before his execution, thinking deeply on the virtue of the elixir, and having assured himself, by many notable instances, which he easily brought to remembrance, that they could not deprive him, even by this severity, of his life, he lifted up his eyes and beheld the young man, in mourning suit, whose visit had been his ruin, standing near him in the cell.

This slave of Satan affected a sad countenance at first; and said he, "We are cast down, Borrhomeo, by reason of thy sentence."

"But we've cheated them," answers he, pretending, maybe, more confidence than he had; "they can't kill me."

"That's certain," rejoins the fiend.

"I shall live for a thousand years," says he.

"Ay, you must continue to live for full one thousand years; 'tis a fair term—is it not?"

"A great deal may be done in that time," says the old man, while beads of perspiration covered his puckered forehead, and he thought that, perhaps, he might cheat *him* too, and make his peace with heaven.

===Chinese===
他被正式起诉，依律受刑，当即把我说过的种种细节一一招认。遂被投下地牢，候旨正法，可他心中暗自并不畏惧，因他深信自己既已吞下灵药，定有奇效。

他不会被处以斩首之刑。如此下场对于这般卑污的恶徒，世人公正地以为，未免太过体面。他被判绞刑，悬吊一日一夜之后，移至罗马大道城门外的一座敞坟之中，以木桩贯之，露置三日方才掩土，如此交归大地收管，使他再也无力在阳世为恶作祟。

行刑前夜，他反复玩味那灵药的灵效，又凭许多轻易便能想起的显赫先例，笃定即便施以这般酷烈手段，他们也取不走他的性命。他抬起眼来，只见那位曾给他带来灭顶之灾的黑衣青年，正立于囚室之中、他身旁。

这撒旦的奴仆起初装出一副悲戚之容；他说道："博罗梅奥，因你这场判决，我们可栽了。"

"可我们已经骗过他们了，"他答道，也许装的信心比实有的还足，"他们杀不了我。"

"那是自然，"那凶魔应道。

"我将再活一千年，"他说。

"是呀，你必须再活整整一千年；这期限可观得很——可不是么？"

"这段时间里能做不少事呢，"老人说，一颗颗汗珠却布满他那打褶的额头，他心想，说不定自己也能把*他*骗过去，与上天重修旧好。

===Original===
"They can't hang me," says Borrhomeo.

"Oh! yes, they will certainly hang you; but, then, you'll live through it."

"Ay, the elixir," cried the prisoner.

"Thus stands the case: when an ordinary man is hanged he dies outright; but you can't die."

"No—ha, ha!—I can't die!"

"Therefore, when you are hanged, you feel, think, hear, and soforth during the process."

"St. Anthony! But then 'tis only an hour—one hour of agony—and it ends."

"You are to hang for a whole day and night," continued the fiend; "but that don't signify. Then when they take you down, you continue to feel, hear, think, and, if they leave your eyes open, to see, just as usual."

"Why, yes, certainly, I'm alive," cries Borrhomeo.

"Yes, alive, quite alive, although you appear to be dead," says the demon with a smile.

"Ay; but what's the best moment to make my escape?" says Borrhomeo.

"Escape! why, you *have* escaped. They can't kill you. No one can kill you, until your time is out. Then you know they lay you in an open grave and impale you."

"What! ah, ha!" roared the old sinner, "you are jesting."

"Hush! depend upon it they will go through with it."

The old man shook in every joint.

"Then, after three days and nights, they bury you," said his visitor.

"I'll lose my life, or I'll break from them!" shouts the gigantic astrologer.

"But you can't lose your life, and you can't break from them," says the fiend, softly.

"Why not? Oh! blessed saints! I'm stronger than you think."

"Ay, muscle, bones—you are an old giant!"

"Surely," cries the old man, "and the terror of a dead man rising; ha! don't you see? They fly before me, and so I escape."

"But you can't rise."

"Say—say in heaven's name what you mean," thundered old Borrhomeo.

"Do you remember, signor, that nightmare, as we jocularly called it, at the sign of the 'Red Hat'?"

"Yes."

===Chinese===
"他们吊不死我，"博罗梅奥说。

"哦！吊得死的，他们一定会把你吊起；只不过，你会活着挺过去。"

"是啊，那灵药，"囚徒叫道。

"事情是这样的：寻常人受绞，当即气绝；可你死不了。"

"死不了——哈，哈！——我死不了！"

"所以，受绞之际，你是有感觉、能思想、听得见的，如此等等，整个过程中皆然。"

"圣安东尼（St. Anthony）啊！可那不过是一个钟头——一个钟头的苦痛——便完了。"

"你得整整吊上一日一夜，"那凶魔续道，"可这算不了什么。待他们把你放下来，你照样继续有感觉、听得见、想得着，倘若他们没合上你的眼睛，你还看得见，一如寻常。"

"咦，是啊，那是自然，我是活着的，"博罗梅奥叫道。

"不错，活着，活得好好的，尽管你看上去像死了一般，"那魔物微笑着说。

"也罢；可我何时脱身最好？"博罗梅奥问。

"脱身！咦，你*已经*脱身了。他们杀不了你。谁也杀不了你，除非你的期限已到。到那时，你知道，他们会把你放进一座敞坟，以木桩贯之。"

"什么！啊，哈！"那老罪人咆哮道，"你在说笑。"

"嘘！你只管放心，他们会照办到底的。"

老人每一处关节都在打颤。

"那之后三日三夜，他们才把你埋了，"访客说。

"我宁可送命，也要从他们手里挣脱出去！"那巨人般的占星师吼道。

"可你既送不了命，也挣脱不了，"凶魔柔声道。

"为何不能？哦！可敬的圣徒啊！我比你想象的要强。"

"是啊，筋骨、骨架——你是个老巨人！"

"那是自然，"老人叫道，"再加上死人诈尸那股骇人——哈！你难道看不见？他们一见我便作鸟兽散，我便这样脱身。"

"可你动不了。"

"看在老天分上——你说，你到底什么意思，"老博罗梅奥怒喝道。

"先生，你可记得，在'红帽'（Red Hat）酒肆招牌之下，我们戏称为噩梦的那一桩？"

"记得。"

===Original===
"Well, a man who having swallowed the *elixir vitae*, suffers that sort of shock which in other mortals is a violent death, is afflicted during the remainder of his period of life, whether he be decapitated, or dismembered, or is laid unmutilated in the grave, with that sort of catalepsy, which you experienced for a minute—a catalepsy that does not relax or intermit. For that reason you ought to have carefully avoided this predicament."

"'Tis a lie," roared the old man, and he ground his teeth, "*that's* not living."

"You'll find, upon my honour, that it *is* living," answered the fiend, with a gentle smile, and withdrawing from the cell.

Borrhomeo told all this to a priest, not under seal of confession, but to induce him to plead for his life. But the good man seeing he had already made himself the liegeman and accomplice of Satan, refused. Nor would his intercession have prevailed in any wise.

So Borrhomeo was hanged, impaled, and buried, according to his sentence; and it came to pass that fourteen years afterwards, that grave was opened in making a great drain from the group of houses thereby, and Borrhomeo was found just as he was laid therein, in no wise decayed, but fresh and sound, which, indeed, showed that there did remain in him that sort of life which was supposed to ward off the common consequences of death.

So he was thrown into a great pit, and with many curses, covered in with stones and earth, where his stupendous punishment proceeds.

Get thee hence, Satan.

===Chinese===
"那么，一个吞下*长生灵药*（elixir vitae）的人，若遭受那种在寻常凡人身上足以致暴毙的冲击，在其余生——无论他被斩首、被肢解，还是毫发无损地躺在坟中——都将为一种强直性昏厥所困，正是你方才片刻所经历的那种——一种既不松弛、也不稍歇的强直性昏厥。正因如此，你原该小心翼翼地避开这般境地才是。"

"这是一派胡言，"老人咆哮，咬牙切齿，"*那*算什么活着。"

"凭我的信誉，你自会发现，那*确是*活着，"那凶魔答道，微微一笑，便退出了囚室。

博罗梅奥把这一切告诉了一位神父，并非在告解的封印之下，而是想求他为自己的性命说情。可那善士见他早已自甘沦为撒旦的臣属与同谋，断然拒绝。即便他肯开口求情，也断无济于事。

于是博罗梅奥依判被绞、被贯桩、被掩埋；事有凑巧，十四年之后，因要从那一片屋舍处修一条大排水沟，那座坟被掘开，人们发现博罗梅奥一如当初被安置时那般躺在其中，毫不腐朽，反倒是鲜活完好——这果然印证了：他体内确还残留着那种生命，据说正可以此抵挡死亡寻常的后果。

于是人们把他抛进一口大坑，伴着无数咒骂，用石头和泥土掩埋起来，他那骇人的刑罚，便在那里继续进行。

撒旦啊，退去吧。

## An Account of Some Strange Disturbances in Aungier Street / 昂吉尔街怪异扰攘记

===Original===
It is not worth telling, this story of mine﻿—at least, not worth writing. Told, indeed, as I have sometimes been called upon to tell it, to a circle of intelligent and eager faces, lighted up by a good after-dinner fire on a winter’s evening, with a cold wind rising and wailing outside, and all snug and cosy within, it has gone off﻿—though I say it, who should not﻿—indifferent well. But it is a venture to do as you would have me. Pen, ink, and paper are cold vehicles for the marvellous, and a “reader” decidedly a more critical animal than a “listener.” If, however, you can induce your friends to read it after nightfall, and when the fireside talk has run for a while on thrilling tales of shapeless terror; in short, if you will secure me the *mollia tempora fandi*, I will go to my work, and say my say, with better heart. Well, then, these conditions presupposed, I shall waste no more words, but tell you simply how it all happened.

My cousin (Tom Ludlow) and I studied medicine together. I think he would have succeeded, had he stuck to the profession; but he preferred the Church, poor fellow, and died early, a sacrifice to contagion, contracted in the noble discharge of his duties. For my present purpose, I say enough of his character when I mention that he was of a sedate but frank and cheerful nature; very exact in his observance of truth, and not by any means like myself﻿—of an excitable or nervous temperament.

My Uncle Ludlow﻿—Tom’s father﻿—while we were attending lectures, purchased three or four old houses in Aungier Street, one of which was unoccupied. *He* resided in the country, and Tom proposed that we should take up our abode in the untenanted house, so long as it should continue unlet; a move which would accomplish the double end of settling us nearer alike to our lecture-rooms and to our amusements, and of relieving us from the weekly charge of rent for our lodgings.

Our furniture was very scant﻿—our whole equipage remarkably modest and primitive; and, in short, our arrangements pretty nearly as simple as those of a bivouac. Our new plan was, therefore, executed almost as soon as conceived. The front drawing-room was our sitting-room. I had the bedroom over it, and Tom the back bedroom on the same floor, which nothing could have induced me to occupy.

===Chinese===
我这段故事，实在不值一讲——至少，不值一写。诚然，我有时被人央着讲它，听者是一圈聪颖热切的脸，一张张被冬夜饭后一炉好火映得通红；外头寒风渐起，呜咽作声，屋里却暖融融、安逸适意，这般情境下讲出来——虽是我自己说出来，本不该自夸——倒也颇过得去。可如今你既要我形诸笔墨，便是一场冒险了。笔、墨、纸三者，原是承载奇闻的冷清器具；而一个"读者"，显然比一个"听客"挑剔得多。不过，你若能劝你的朋友在入夜之后再读它，且是炉边闲话已绕着那些无形的恐怖传说盘桓了一阵之后；一言以蔽之，你若肯为我争得那段*mollia tempora fandi*（宜言之时），我便能提起精神，动手做事，把话说明白。那么，既有这些前提，我便不再多费唇舌，单把这事的来龙去脉，原原本本说与你听。

我那位表兄（汤姆·勒德洛，Tom Ludlow）与我一道学医。我想他若坚守此行，本可大有作为；可惜他偏爱了教会，可怜人，早早便去世了——他是在尽职之中染上疫病，作了殉职的牺牲。就我眼下要说的事而言，提一提他的性情便够了：他为人沉稳，却又坦率开朗；立言极重信实，性情与我截然不同——我乃是个易于激动、神经过敏的体质。

我们听课那阵子，我叔叔勒德洛——即汤姆的父亲——在昂吉尔街（Aungier Street）买下三四幢老宅，其中一幢空着无人住。叔叔本人住在乡间，汤姆便提议，我们不妨搬进那幢空宅去住，只要它一日租不出去，我们便一日住着；此举一举两得——既能教我们离课堂和消遣之处都近些，又能省下住旅馆每周须付的房租。

我们的家当少得可怜——全副装备寒酸质朴得很；简而言之，屋里陈设之简陋，几乎与露营无二。因此这新主意一经议定，几乎立刻便付诸实行。前客厅作了我们的起居室；我住其上的那间卧房，汤姆则住同层后卧房——那间屋子，无论何种条件，都不能诱我去住。

===Original===
The house, to begin with, was a very old one. It had been, I believe, newly fronted about fifty years before; but with this exception, it had nothing modern about it. The agent who bought it and looked into the titles for my uncle, told me that it was sold, along with much other forfeited property, at Chichester House, I think, in 1702; and had belonged to Sir Thomas Hacket, who was Lord Mayor of Dublin in James II’s time. How old it was *then*, I can’t say; but, at all events, it had seen years and changes enough to have contracted all that mysterious and saddened air, at once exciting and depressing, which belongs to most old mansions.

There had been very little done in the way of modernising details; and, perhaps, it was better so; for there was something queer and bygone in the very walls and ceilings﻿—in the shape of doors and windows﻿—in the odd diagonal site of the chimneypieces﻿—in the beams and ponderous cornices﻿—not to mention the singular solidity of all the woodwork, from the banisters to the window-frames, which hopelessly defied disguise, and would have emphatically proclaimed their antiquity through any conceivable amount of modern finery and varnish.

An effort had, indeed, been made, to the extent of papering the drawing-rooms; but somehow, the paper looked raw and out of keeping; and the old woman, who kept a little dirt-pie of a shop in the lane, and whose daughter﻿—a girl of two and fifty﻿—was our solitary handmaid, coming in at sunrise, and chastely receding again as soon as she had made all ready for tea in our state apartment;﻿—this woman, I say, remembered it, when old Judge Horrocks (who, having earned the reputation of a particularly “hanging judge,” ended by hanging himself, as the coroner’s jury found, under an impulse of “temporary insanity,” with a child’s skipping-rope, over the massive old bannisters) resided there, entertaining good company, with fine venison and rare old port. In those halcyon days, the drawing-rooms were hung with gilded leather, and, I dare say, cut a good figure, for they were really spacious rooms.

===Chinese===
这宅子，首先一条，是十分古旧的。我相信约莫五十年前才换了新的临街立面；但除此以外，便再无一处称得上时新。替我叔叔买下它、又替他查阅契据的代理人告诉我，这宅子是1702年——我想没记错的话——在奇切斯特府（Chichester House）连同许多被没收的产业一道拍卖出去的；原主是托马斯·哈克特爵士（Sir Thomas Hacket），詹姆斯二世时代曾任都柏林市长。至于*那时*它已有多老，我说不上来；但无论如何，它已阅历了足够的年岁与变故，足以沾染上那一身神秘而忧郁的气息——既令人心神激荡，又令人压抑不振——这是多数古宅通有的气性。

细节上的"现代化"工程做得极少；或许这样反倒好；因为那墙垣、那天花板，那门窗的式样，那壁炉架古怪的斜置方位，那梁木与沉甸甸的飞檐——乃至全部木作的异常坚固，从楼梯扶手到窗框，无一不透着一股古怪而旧日的味道，任凭如何掩饰也无济于事，便是涂上无论多少时髦的漆饰与亮油，它们也要斩钉截铁地宣告自己的古旧。

诚然，也曾有人花过一番心思，给客厅糊了墙纸；可不知怎的，那墙纸看上去生硬扎眼，与屋子格格不入。巷子里开着一家巴掌大的肮脏小铺的老妪——她那个五十二岁的"姑娘"是我们唯一的女佣，每日日出时来，待把"上房"里备茶的一切办妥，便又如处女般悄然退去——我说，这老妪还记得，当年老贺洛克斯法官（Judge Horrocks）住在这里时——这位法官博得了个特别"爱判绞刑"的名声，临了却也把自己吊死了，验尸陪审团裁定乃是出于"一时癫狂"，用的是一根孩童跳绳的绳子，悬在那粗重的旧扶手之上——那时他常在此处款待上宾，席上有上好的鹿肉与罕见的陈年波特酒。在那太平日子里，客厅四壁挂着镶金皮的壁毡，我想必颇为体面，因为那两间屋子着实宽敞。

===Original===
The bedrooms were wainscoted, but the front one was not gloomy; and in it the cosiness of antiquity quite overcame its sombre associations. But the back bedroom, with its two queerly-placed melancholy windows, staring vacantly at the foot of the bed, and with the shadowy recess to be found in most old houses in Dublin, like a large ghostly closet, which, from congeniality of temperament, had amalgamated with the bedchamber, and dissolved the partition. At nighttime, this “alcove”﻿—as our “maid” was wont to call it﻿—had, in my eyes, a specially sinister and suggestive character. Tom’s distant and solitary candle glimmered vainly into its darkness. *There* it was always overlooking him﻿—always itself impenetrable. But this was only part of the effect. The whole room was, I can’t tell how, repulsive to me. There was, I suppose, in its proportions and features, a latent discord﻿—a certain mysterious and indescribable relation, which jarred indistinctly upon some secret sense of the fitting and the safe, and raised indefinable suspicions and apprehensions of the imagination. On the whole, as I began by saying, nothing could have induced me to pass a night alone in it.

I had never pretended to conceal from poor Tom my superstitious weakness; and he, on the other hand, most unaffectedly ridiculed my tremors. The sceptic was, however, destined to receive a lesson, as you shall hear.

We had not been very long in occupation of our respective dormitories, when I began to complain of uneasy nights and disturbed sleep. I was, I suppose, the more impatient under this annoyance, as I was usually a sound sleeper, and by no means prone to nightmares. It was now, however, my destiny, instead of enjoying my customary repose, every night to “sup full of horrors.” After a preliminary course of disagreeable and frightful dreams, my troubles took a definite form, and the same vision, without an appreciable variation in a single detail, visited me at least (on an average) every second night in the week.

===Chinese===
卧房四壁都装着护墙板，前房却并不阴沉；在那里，古旧所带来的那份舒适感，完全盖过了它晦暗的联想。但那间后卧房，两扇位置古怪、神情忧郁的窗，空洞洞地直瞪着床脚；再加上一处都柏林多数老宅里都有的幽暗凹室——仿佛一只硕大的鬼气森森的壁橱，因其气质相投，竟与卧房合而为一，连隔墙都消融了。到了夜间，这处"凹室"——我们的"女佣"惯于这样称呼它——在我眼中便格外带着一种险恶而引人联想的意味。汤姆那一星孤烛，远远地照进去，也只是徒然地在它的黑暗里摇曳。*那里面*永远在俯瞰着他——而它自身却永远深不可测。可这还只是效果的一部分。整间屋子，我说不清怎的，处处令我生厌。我想，在它的比例和形貌之中，潜藏着一种不谐和——某种神秘而难以言喻的关系，隐隐地触动了某个关乎安妥与否的隐秘感官，从而搅起想象中那些说不清道不明的不安与忧惧。总而言之，正如我一开头所说，无论如何都不能诱我独自在那屋里过一夜。

我那迷信的软处，在可怜的汤姆面前从未有意遮掩；而他呢，反过来也最是毫不做作地讥笑我的怯怕。然而，这位怀疑者注定要受一番教训——你且往下听便是。

我们各自住进自己的寝室没多久，我便开始抱怨夜里不安稳、睡不踏实。我平日原是个酣睡的人，也绝少做噩梦，故而对这桩烦恼尤为烦躁。可如今，命运不再让我享受往日的安宁，每夜都要"饱餐恐怖"。先是一连串恼人可怖的梦作个铺垫，随后那些烦扰便渐渐成了定形——同一个幻象，每一细节都不差分毫，每周至少（平均算来）要来造访我两夜。

===Original===
Now, this dream, nightmare, or infernal illusion﻿—which you please﻿—of which I was the miserable sport, was on this wise:﻿—

I saw, or thought I saw, with the most abominable distinctness, although at the time in profound darkness, every article of furniture and accidental arrangement of the chamber in which I lay. This, as you know, is incidental to ordinary nightmare. Well, while in this clairvoyant condition, which seemed but the lighting up of the theatre in which was to be exhibited the monotonous tableau of horror, which made my nights insupportable, my attention invariably became, I know not why, fixed upon the windows opposite the foot of my bed; and, uniformly with the same effect, a sense of dreadful anticipation always took slow but sure possession of me. I became somehow conscious of a sort of horrid but undefined preparation going forward in some unknown quarter, and by some unknown agency, for my torment; and, after an interval, which always seemed to me of the same length, a picture suddenly flew up to the window, where it remained fixed, as if by an electrical attraction, and my discipline of horror then commenced, to last perhaps for hours. The picture thus mysteriously glued to the windowpanes, was the portrait of an old man, in a crimson flowered silk dressing-gown, the folds of which I could now describe, with a countenance embodying a strange mixture of intellect, sensuality, and power, but withal sinister and full of malignant omen. His nose was hooked, like the beak of a vulture; his eyes large, grey, and prominent, and lighted up with a more than mortal cruelty and coldness. These features were surmounted by a crimson velvet cap, the hair that peeped from under which was white with age, while the eyebrows retained their original blackness. Well I remember every line, hue, and shadow of that stony countenance, and well I may! The gaze of this hellish visage was fixed upon me, and mine returned it with the inexplicable fascination of nightmare, for what appeared to me to be hours of agony. At last﻿—

> The cock he crew, away then flew

the fiend who had enslaved me through the awful watches of the night; and, harassed and nervous, I rose to the duties of the day.

===Chinese===
那么，我所深受其苦的这个梦、这夜魇、这邪祟的幻影——随你怎么叫——其情形是这样的：——

我看见，或自以为看见，以一种可憎的清晰，纵然当时四下里漆黑一团，我身卧之处的每一件家具、每一处偶然的陈设，无不了然。这种情形，你也知道，乃是寻常夜魇所伴有的现象。且说，我身处这般"透视力"之中——这仿佛不过是把一座戏台照亮，好在那台上演出那一成不变的恐怖场面，教我的夜苦不堪言——不知为何，我的注意力总是被钉在床脚对面的那两扇窗户上；而每一次都生同样的效果，一种可怖的预感便缓缓地、却无可动摇地攫住了我。我不知怎地觉察到，某处不知名的角落、由某种不知名的力量，正在暗中为一桩可怖却又不甚分明的勾当做准备，专为折磨我；过一段总像是等长的时间，一幅画像便倏地飞到窗前，仿佛被电的吸力吸住一般，钉在那里不动了——于是我那恐怖的酷刑便开了场，往往要持续上好几个钟头。这幅神秘地"贴"在窗玻璃上的画像，是一个老者的肖像，身穿深红底起花的绸质晨衣——那衣褶我至今仍能一一描出——面容上交织着智力、纵欲与权势的奇异混合，却又不祥之至，满是恶兆。他的鼻如钩，似秃鹫之喙；眼大而灰，向外凸出，亮着一种超乎凡人的残忍与冷漠。这副相貌之上戴一顶深红丝绒帽，帽下发丝已因年迈而白，眉毛却仍保留着本来的黑色。那副石像般的面孔，每一线条、每一色泽、每一阴影，我至今记得分明——也理应记得分明！那张地狱般的脸凝视着我，而我的目光也以夜魇那种说不清的魅惑回望着它，仿佛熬过了好几个时辰的苦痛。末了——

> 雄鸡一唱，魔鬼便飞去了

那夜夜奴役我度过可怖守夜的邪祟，便这般去了；我于是带着一身疲惫与心神不宁，起身去应付白日的差事。

===Original===
I had﻿—I can’t say exactly why, but it may have been from the exquisite anguish and profound impressions of unearthly horror, with which this strange phantasmagoria was associated﻿—an insurmountable antipathy to describing the exact nature of my nightly troubles to my friend and comrade. Generally, however, I told him that I was haunted by abominable dreams; and, true to the imputed materialism of medicine, we put our heads together to dispel my horrors, not by exorcism, but by a tonic.

I will do this tonic justice, and frankly admit that the accursed portrait began to intermit its visits under its influence. What of that? Was this singular apparition﻿—as full of character as of terror﻿—therefore the creature of my fancy, or the invention of my poor stomach? Was it, in short, *subjective* (to borrow the technical slang of the day) and not the palpable aggression and intrusion of an external agent? That, good friend, as we will both admit, by no means follows. The evil spirit, who enthralled my senses in the shape of that portrait, may have been just as near me, just as energetic, just as malignant, though I saw him not. What means the whole moral code of revealed religion regarding the due keeping of our own bodies, soberness, temperance, etc.? here is an obvious connection between the material and the invisible; the healthy tone of the system, and its unimpaired energy, may, for aught we can tell, guard us against influences which would otherwise render life itself terrific. The mesmerist and the electro-biologist will fail upon an average with nine patients out of ten﻿—so may the evil spirit. Special conditions of the corporeal system are indispensable to the production of certain spiritual phenomena. The operation succeeds sometimes﻿—sometimes fails﻿—that is all.

===Chinese===
我有一种无法克服的厌恶，不愿把我每夜苦况的确切性质，向我那位朋友兼同伴细细描述——究竟为何，我说不确切，或许是因为这桩怪诞的幻影剧所伴有的那种刺骨的痛苦与深沉得超乎尘世的恐怖印象。大体上我只是告诉他，我被可憎的梦纠缠着；而我们呢，也不愧世人所讥诮的那副医学的唯物做派，两人凑在一处设法驱我的恐怖——不是用驱魔，而是用补剂。

我得当面给这补剂一句公道：我坦白承认，那可诅咒的画像，在它的作用下，确实开始时作时辍了。这又如何？难道这一个性鲜明而又可怖的怪异显形，因此便是我的幻想的产物，或是我这可怜的胃腑所编造出来的么？简而言之，难道它是*主观的*（借用如今那一套行话），而不是某个外在之物公然的侵犯与闯入？好朋友，这一点，你我都得承认，绝不能就此推论出来。那以画像之形惑我感官的恶灵，纵使我看不见他，他或许照样离我那么近、照样精力充沛、照样心怀恶意。启示宗教那一整套关于应当善自保养身体、节制、克己之类的道德规训，究竟所为何事？物质与不可见之物之间，显然有着某种关联；周身的康健气机、无亏的精力，也许——就我们所知——正能护卫我们，抵挡那些否则足以令生命本身化为恐怖的影响。施行催眠术与电生物术的人，十个病人里平均要在九个身上失手——恶灵亦然。某些属灵现象的产生，必须仰赖肉身系统所处的一些特殊条件。手术有时成功，有时失败——如此而已。

===Original===
I found afterwards that my would-be sceptical companion had his troubles too. But of these I knew nothing yet. One night, for a wonder, I was sleeping soundly, when I was roused by a step on the lobby outside my room, followed by the loud clang of what turned out to be a large brass candlestick, flung with all his force by poor Tom Ludlow over the banisters, and rattling with a rebound down the second flight of stairs; and almost concurrently with this, Tom burst open my door, and bounced into my room backwards, in a state of extraordinary agitation.

I had jumped out of bed and clutched him by the arm before I had any distinct idea of my own whereabouts. There we were﻿—in our shirts﻿—standing before the open door﻿—staring through the great old banister opposite, at the lobby window, through which the sickly light of a clouded moon was gleaming.

“What’s the matter, Tom? What’s the matter with you? What the devil’s the matter with you, Tom?” I demanded shaking him with nervous impatience.

He took a long breath before he answered me, and then it was not very coherently.

“It’s nothing, nothing at all﻿—did I speak?﻿—what did I say?﻿—where’s the candle, Richard? It’s dark; I﻿—I had a candle!”

“Yes, dark enough,” I said; “but what’s the matter?﻿—what *is* it?﻿—why don’t you speak, Tom?﻿—have you lost your wits?﻿—what is the matter?”

“The matter?﻿—oh, it is all over. It must have been a dream﻿—nothing at all but a dream﻿—don’t you think so? It could not be anything more than a dream.”

“Of *course*” said I, feeling uncommonly nervous, “it *was* a dream.”

“I thought,” he said, “there was a man in my room, and﻿—and I jumped out of bed; and﻿—and﻿—where’s the candle?”

“In your room, most likely,” I said, “shall I go and bring it?”

“No; stay here﻿—don’t go; it’s no matter﻿—don’t, I tell you; it was all a dream. Bolt the door, Dick; I’ll stay here with you﻿—I feel nervous. So, Dick, like a good fellow, light your candle and open the window﻿—I am in a *shocking state*.”

I did as he asked me, and robing himself like Granuaile in one of my blankets, he seated himself close beside my bed.

===Chinese===
我后来才知道，我那位自命怀疑派的同伴，原来也有他的苦楚。但这些我当时一无所知。一天夜里，难得地，我正睡得酣沉，忽然被房外走廊里的脚步声惊醒，紧接着是一声洪亮的哐啷——原来是可怜的汤姆·勒德洛使尽全力把一只大铜烛台从扶手上方摔了下去，砰砰碰碰一路反弹，滚下第二段楼梯；几乎与此同一瞬间，汤姆撞开了我的房门，倒退着蹦进我的屋里，神情极为激动。

我跳下床，一把抓住他的胳膊——自己一时都没弄清身在何处。我们俩就那么站着——只穿着衬衣——在敞开的门前——透过对面那道粗重的旧扶手，直瞪着走廊尽头那扇窗，窗外一轮被云遮住的月亮，正透出惨淡的光。

"怎么了，汤姆？你怎么了？你到底见了什么鬼，汤姆？"我连声追问，神经质地摇着他。

他长长吸了一口气，才答得上来，答得也不甚连贯。

"没什么，根本没什么——我说话了么？——我说了什么？——蜡烛在哪儿，理查德？好黑呀；我——我本来拿着蜡烛的！"

"是够黑的，"我说，"可到底怎么了？——是*什么*事？——你怎么不说话，汤姆？——你疯了不成？——到底是怎么回事？"

"怎么回事？——啊，全完了。一定是个梦——只不过是个梦——你不觉得么？不可能不是梦的。"

"那*当然*"我说，自己也紧张得非同寻常，"*是*个梦。"

"我原以为，"他说，"屋里进了个人，我——我就跳下床；后来——后来——蜡烛呢？"

"多半在你屋里吧，"我说，"我去给你拿？"

"不；待在这儿——别去；不要紧——我说，别去；那不过是个梦。把门闩上，迪克；我跟你一块儿待着——我心里慌。那么，迪克，好兄弟，替我点上蜡烛，再把窗子打开——我这副*狼狈相*真够呛。"

我依着他办了；他拿我一条毯子像格劳尼娅（Granuaile）似的裹在身上，紧挨着我的床边坐下。

===Original===
Everybody knows how contagious is fear of all sorts, but more especially that particular kind of fear under which poor Tom was at that moment labouring. I would not have heard, nor I believe would he have recapitulated, just at that moment, for half the world, the details of the hideous vision which had so unmanned him.

“Don’t mind telling me anything about your nonsensical dream, Tom,” said I, affecting contempt, really in a panic; “let us talk about something else; but it is quite plain that this dirty old house disagrees with us both, and hang me if I stay here any longer, to be pestered with indigestion and﻿—and﻿—bad nights, so we may as well look out for lodgings﻿—don’t you think so?﻿—at once.”

Tom agreed, and, after an interval, said﻿—

“I have been thinking, Richard, that it is a long time since I saw my father, and I have made up my mind to go down tomorrow and return in a day or two, and you can take rooms for us in the meantime.”

I fancied that this resolution, obviously the result of the vision which had so profoundly scared him, would probably vanish next morning with the damps and shadows of night. But I was mistaken. Off went Tom at peep of day to the country, having agreed that so soon as I had secured suitable lodgings, I was to recall him by letter from his visit to my Uncle Ludlow.

Now, anxious as I was to change my quarters, it so happened, owing to a series of petty procrastinations and accidents, that nearly a week elapsed before my bargain was made and my letter of recall on the wing to Tom; and, in the meantime, a trifling adventure or two had occurred to your humble servant, which, absurd as they now appear, diminished by distance, did certainly at the time serve to whet my appetite for change considerably.

===Chinese===
谁都知道，凡是恐惧，都极易传染，尤其是可怜的汤姆此时所承受的那一种。此刻便拿半个世界来换，我也不愿听——我相信他也不愿重述——那把他吓得如此失魂落魄的骇人幻象的细节。

"你那荒唐的梦，就不必跟我讲了，汤姆，"我说，装出一副鄙夷的样子，其实心里慌得很；"我们谈点别的吧；不过很明白，这所肮脏的破老宅子，对我们俩都不相宜，要是我再赖下去，被消化不良和——和——夜里睡不好所纠缠，那就叫我见鬼去，所以咱们还是赶紧另找住处——你说是不是？——马上就找。"

汤姆应允了，过了一会儿又说——

"我一直在想，理查德，我已经好久没见父亲了，我打定主意明天下乡去，过一两日就回，这段时间你便可以替我们租屋。"

我原以为这个决定——显然是那场把他吓坏了的幻象所致——到第二天早晨，会随着夜里的湿气与阴影一并消散。可我想错了。汤姆天一亮便动身下乡去了，只约定：我一觅得合适的寓所，便写信到勒德洛叔叔家把他召回。

我虽急着搬迁，偏偏因一连串小小的拖延与意外，直到差不多过了一个礼拜，我的租约才算敲定，召回他的信才上了路；而在此期间，敝人又碰上了一两桩小小的奇遇——如今想来固然可笑，相隔既远，也显得无关紧要，但当时确乎大大加重了我急于搬家的心思。

===Original===
A night or two after the departure of my comrade, I was sitting by my bedroom fire, the door locked, and the ingredients of a tumbler of hot whisky-punch upon the crazy spider-table; for, as the best mode of keeping the

> Black spirits and white,

> Blue spirits and grey,

with which I was environed, at bay, I had adopted the practice recommended by the wisdom of my ancestors, and “kept my spirits up by pouring spirits down.” I had thrown aside my volume of Anatomy, and was treating myself by way of a tonic, preparatory to my punch and bed, to half-a-dozen pages of the *Spectator*, when I heard a step on the flight of stairs descending from the attics. It was two o’clock, and the streets were as silent as a churchyard﻿—the sounds were, therefore, perfectly distinct. There was a slow, heavy tread, characterised by the emphasis and deliberation of age, descending by the narrow staircase from above; and, what made the sound more singular, it was plain that the feet which produced it were perfectly bare, measuring the descent with something between a pound and a flop, very ugly to hear.

I knew quite well that my attendant had gone away many hours before, and that nobody but myself had any business in the house. It was quite plain also that the person who was coming downstairs had no intention whatever of concealing his movements; but, on the contrary, appeared disposed to make even more noise, and proceed more deliberately, than was at all necessary. When the step reached the foot of the stairs outside my room, it seemed to stop; and I expected every moment to see my door open spontaneously, and give admission to the original of my detested portrait. I was, however, relieved in a few seconds by hearing the descent renewed, just in the same manner, upon the staircase leading down to the drawing-rooms, and thence, after another pause, down the next flight, and so on to the hall, whence I heard no more.

===Chinese===
同伴走后一两天的一个夜里，我坐在卧室炉边，门已闩上，一张摇摇欲坠的蛛脚小桌上摆着一杯热威士忌潘趣酒的料；因为，要把那围在我四周的——

> 黑的灵，白的灵，

> 蓝的灵，灰的灵，

挡在一定距离之外，最好的法子无过于采纳我先人的智慧——"以酒下肚，提我精神"。我把那卷《解剖学》推到一边，当作补剂的先导，在潘趣与就寝之前，给自己读上六七页《旁观者》（*Spectator*）解闷——就在这时，我听见从顶楼下来的那段楼梯上传来一阵脚步声。此时是两点钟，街上静得如同坟场——因此那声响听得格外分明。那是一种缓慢、沉重的脚步，带着老迈之人特有的那种郑重与从容，从上面那段窄窄的楼梯一级一级走下来；而尤其古怪的是，那双发出声响的脚分明是赤着的，每下一级，都介于"咚"与"啪嗒"之间，听着十分刺耳。

我心里很清楚：伺候我的那个女佣几小时前早已走了，除了我，再无任何人有理由留在这宅子里。也很明白：这位下楼者丝毫没有要掩饰自己动静的意思；相反，倒像是要比实际所需弄出更大的声响、走得更从容些。当那脚步走到我房外的楼梯口时，似乎停住了；我每一刻都等着看我的房门自行开启，把我所深恶的那幅画像的原型放进来。然而，不过几秒钟，我便松了一口气——听得那脚步又照样往下走，沿着通向客厅的那段楼梯下去；再一顿，又下一段，如此一直到了门厅，这才再无声息。

===Original===
Now, by the time the sound had ceased, I was wound up, as they say, to a very unpleasant pitch of excitement. I listened, but there was not a stir. I screwed up my courage to a decisive experiment﻿—opened my door, and in a stentorian voice bawled over the banisters, “Who’s there?” There was no answer but the ringing of my own voice through the empty old house﻿—no renewal of the movement; nothing, in short, to give my unpleasant sensations a definite direction. There is, I think, something most disagreeably disenchanting in the sound of one’s own voice under such circumstances, exerted in solitude, and in vain. It redoubled my sense of isolation, and my misgivings increased on perceiving that the door, which I certainly thought I had left open, was closed behind me; in a vague alarm, lest my retreat should be cut off, I got again into my room as quickly as I could, where I remained in a state of imaginary blockade, and very uncomfortable indeed, till morning.

Next night brought no return of my barefooted fellow-lodger; but the night following, being in my bed, and in the dark﻿—somewhere, I suppose, about the same hour as before, I distinctly heard the old fellow again descending from the garrets.

This time I had had my punch, and the morale of the garrison was consequently excellent. I jumped out of bed, clutched the poker as I passed the expiring fire, and in a moment was upon the lobby. The sound had ceased by this time﻿—the dark and chill were discouraging; and, guess my horror, when I saw, or thought I saw, a black monster, whether in the shape of a man or a bear I could not say, standing, with its back to the wall, on the lobby, facing me, with a pair of great greenish eyes shining dimly out. Now, I must be frank, and confess that the cupboard which displayed our plates and cups stood just there, though at the moment I did not recollect it. At the same time I must honestly say, that making every allowance for an excited imagination, I never could satisfy myself that I was made the dupe of my own fancy in this matter; for this apparition, after one or two shiftings of shape, as if in the act of incipient transformation, began, as it seemed on second thoughts, to advance upon me in its original form. From an instinct of terror rather than of courage, I hurled the poker, with all my force, at its head; and to the music of a horrid crash made my way into my room, and double-locked the door. Then, in a minute more, I heard the horrid bare feet walk down the stairs, till the sound ceased in the hall, as on the former occasion.

===Chinese===
待到那声响完全停息，我已被弄得——俗话所说——神经绷到了极不舒服的紧度。我侧耳细听，一点动静也没有。我鼓起勇气，作一个决断的试验——开了门，扯着洪亮的嗓子朝扶手外头大喊："谁？"回答我的，只有我自己的声音在那空荡荡的旧宅里来回激荡；再没有任何动静；总之，没有任何东西能给我那不快之感一个明确的方向。我想，在这种情形下，独自一人、徒然地高声发问，听见自己的嗓音，其中有一种最能叫人扫兴、最令人心寒的意味。它加倍地让我感到孤孑；而我回头一看，那扇我明明记得是开着的房门竟已在我身后阖上了，这一来我那点疑惧又添了几分；我心头一阵模糊的惊慌，生怕退路被断，便尽快缩回房里，自此便在这自设的"围城"之中——其实极不舒服——一直熬到天亮。

第二夜，那位赤脚的同寓者并未再来；但再下一夜，我已上床，四下漆黑——大约还是先前那个时辰罢——我又分明听见那老家伙从顶楼上下来。

这一回我已喝过潘趣，"守军士气"因此极佳。我跳下床，经过将熄的炉火时顺手抄起拨火棍，一转眼便到了走廊上。这时声响已息——黑暗与寒意叫人泄气；你猜我看见什么——或自以为看见什么——一只黑色的怪物，是人形还是熊形，我说不准，背贴着墙，立在走廊上正对着我，一双泛绿的大眼睛幽幽地发着光。这里我得老实说一句：陈列杯盘的食橱正立在那一处，虽然我那时并没记起来。但同时我也得坦诚地说：纵使把想象力的激动一并算上，我始终不能使自己相信，这件事上我是被自家的幻想所欺；因为这显形，在一两次变相——仿佛初初要变形——之后，又像改了主意，以原来的形态朝我逼来。那是出于恐惧而非出于勇气的一念，我使尽全力把拨火棍朝它的头掷去；伴着一阵骇人的哗啦声，我闯进了自己的屋子，把门反锁了两道。又过一分钟，我听见那可怖的赤脚又一级级走下楼梯，直至——和前次一样——在门厅里消了声息。

===Original===
If the apparition of the night before was an ocular delusion of my fancy sporting with the dark outlines of our cupboard, and if its horrid eyes were nothing but a pair of inverted teacups, I had, at all events, the satisfaction of having launched the poker with admirable effect, and in true “fancy” phrase, “knocked its two daylights into one,” as the commingled fragments of my tea-service testified. I did my best to gather comfort and courage from these evidences; but it would not do. And then what could I say of those horrid bare feet, and the regular tramp, tramp, tramp, which measured the distance of the entire staircase through the solitude of my haunted dwelling, and at an hour when no good influence was stirring? Confound it!﻿—the whole affair was abominable. I was out of spirits, and dreaded the approach of night.

It came, ushered ominously in with a thunderstorm and dull torrents of depressing rain. Earlier than usual the streets grew silent; and by twelve o’clock nothing but the comfortless pattering of the rain was to be heard.

I made myself as snug as I could. I lighted *two* candles instead of one. I forswore bed, and held myself in readiness for a sally, candle in hand; for, *coûte que coûte*, I was resolved to *see* the being, if visible at all, who troubled the nightly stillness of my mansion. I was fidgetty and nervous and tried in vain to interest myself with my books. I walked up and down my room, whistling in turn martial and hilarious music, and listening ever and anon for the dreaded noise. I sat down and stared at the square label on the solemn and reserved-looking black bottle, until “**Flanagan & Co.’s Best Old Malt Whisky**” grew into a sort of subdued accompaniment to all the fantastic and horrible speculations which chased one another through my brain.

===Chinese===
倘若头一夜的显形，不过是我那幻想以食橱的黑色轮廓为戏；倘若那双可怖的眼睛，不过是两只倒扣的茶杯；那么无论如何，我总算有一桩可慰之处：我那一拨火棍掷得漂亮至极，以道地"幻想派"的话来说，便是"把它两眼打成了一只眼"——我那一套破碎的茶具便是明证。我竭力从这些证据里搜求安慰与勇气；却终归无用。再说，我又怎能解释那双可怖的赤脚，那有规律的"咚、咚、咚"——在那闹鬼的孤宅的寂静里，丈量着整段楼梯的距离，又正值那般时分，再无一丝善的力量走动？见鬼去吧！——这整桩事可恶极了。我心绪低落，开始害怕夜的来临。

夜还是来了——先以一场雷雨和一阵阵叫人沮丧的阴沉大雨，不祥地为它开了道。街上比往常更早就静了下来；到十二点钟，除了那恼人的淅沥雨声，再听不见别的。

我把自己尽量安顿舒适。我点了*两*支蜡烛，而不是一支。我决心不上床，整装待发，手持蜡烛，准备出击；因为，*无论如何*，我已铁了心，只要那扰我夜静的东西真能被看见，我定要*亲眼*一见。我坐立不安，神经过敏，想用书引动兴致，却徒然无功。我在屋里踱来踱去，轮番吹着雄壮与欢快的调子，时不时侧耳谛听那叫人胆寒的声响。我又坐下，盯着那庄重而神情矜持的黑色方瓶上那张方标签，直盯到"**弗拉纳根公司极品陈年麦芽威士忌**"几个字，竟成了我脑中那接踵而至的种种荒诞可怖的揣测的一种低声伴奏。

===Original===
Silence, meanwhile, grew more silent, and darkness darker. I listened in vain for the rumble of a vehicle, or the dull clamour of a distant row. There was nothing but the sound of a rising wind, which had succeeded the thunderstorm that had travelled over the Dublin mountains quite out of hearing. In the middle of this great city I began to feel myself alone with nature, and Heaven knows what beside. My courage was ebbing. Punch, however, which makes beasts of so many, made a man of me again﻿—just in time to hear with tolerable nerve and firmness the lumpy, flabby, naked feet deliberately descending the stairs again.

I took a candle, not without a tremour. As I crossed the floor I tried to extemporise a prayer, but stopped short to listen, and never finished it. The steps continued. I confess I hesitated for some seconds at the door before I took heart of grace and opened it. When I peeped out the lobby was perfectly empty﻿—there was no monster standing on the staircase; and as the detested sound ceased, I was reassured enough to venture forward nearly to the banisters. Horror of horrors! within a stair or two beneath the spot where I stood the unearthly tread smote the floor. My eye caught something in motion; it was about the size of Goliah’s foot﻿—it was grey, heavy, and flapped with a dead weight from one step to another. As I am alive, it was the most monstrous grey rat I ever beheld or imagined.

===Chinese===
与此同时，寂静愈发寂静，黑暗愈发黑暗。我徒然地听着，盼能听见一辆车的辚辚，或远处一场骚动的沉闷喧声。什么也没有，只有风声渐起——那是从都柏林群山之外一路滚过去的雷雨之后才起来的风。在这座大城正中，我开始觉得自己是与自然——天晓得还有别的什么——相对孑然。我的勇气正在下落。然而，潘趣酒虽然把许多人喝成了畜生，倒把我重新喝成了汉子——来得正是时候，恰好让我以还算镇定的神经和气魄，听见那臃肿、肥软、赤裸的脚，又从容不迫地一级级走下楼梯。

我取了一支蜡烛，手也不免有些发颤。穿过屋子时，我试着即兴祷告几句，却停下来一听，那祷告始终没有念完。脚步仍在继续。我得承认，在门前我迟疑了几秒，才鼓起勇气把它打开。我探头一望——走廊上空无一人——楼梯口也没有什么怪物站着；那可憎的声响既已止息，我胆子壮了些，竟敢前行，几乎走到扶手边上。可怕呀可怕！就在我所立之处以下一两级楼梯，那非尘世的脚步又踏响了地板。我眼角瞥见一团动的东西；约莫歌利亚（Goliah）的脚那般大小；灰色的，沉甸甸的，以一种死沉的重量从这一级"啪"地翻到那一级。我拿性命打赌，那是我平生所见所想最大的一只灰色老鼠。

===Original===
Shakespeare says﻿—“Some men there are cannot abide a gaping pig, and some that are mad if they behold a cat.” I went well-nigh out of my wits when I beheld this *rat*; for, laugh at me as you may, it fixed upon me, I thought, a perfectly human expression of malice; and, as it shuffled about and looked up into my face almost from between my feet, I saw, I could swear it﻿—I felt it then, and know it now, the infernal gaze and the accursed countenance of my old friend in the portrait, transfused into the visage of the bloated vermin before me.

I bounced into my room again with a feeling of loathing and horror I cannot describe, and locked and bolted my door as if a lion had been at the other side. D﻿—n him or *it*; curse the portrait and its original! I felt in my soul that the rat﻿—yes, the *rat*, the **rat** I had just seen, was that evil being in masquerade, and rambling through the house upon some infernal night lark.

Next morning I was early trudging through the miry streets; and, among other transactions, posted a peremptory note recalling Tom. On my return, however, I found a note from my absent “chum,” announcing his intended return next day. I was doubly rejoiced at this, because I had succeeded in getting rooms; and because the change of scene and return of my comrade were rendered specially pleasant by the last night’s half ridiculous half horrible adventure.

I slept extemporaneously in my new quarters in Digges’ Street that night, and next morning returned for breakfast to the haunted mansion, where I was certain Tom would call immediately on his arrival.

I was quite right﻿—he came; and almost his first question referred to the primary object of our change of residence.

“Thank God,” he said with genuine fervour, on hearing that all was arranged. “On *your* account I am delighted. As to myself, I assure you that no earthly consideration could have induced me ever again to pass a night in this disastrous old house.”

“Confound the house!” I ejaculated, with a genuine mixture of fear and detestation, “we have not had a pleasant hour since we came to live here”; and so I went on, and related incidentally my adventure with the plethoric old rat.

“Well, if that were *all*,” said my cousin, affecting to make light of the matter, “I don’t think I should have minded it very much.”

“Ay, but its eye﻿—its countenance, my dear Tom,” urged I; “if you had seen *that*, you would have felt it might be *anything* but what it seemed.”

“I inclined to think the best conjurer in such a case would be an able-bodied cat,” he said, with a provoking chuckle.

“But let us hear your own adventure,” I said tartly.

At this challenge he looked uneasily round him. I had poked up a very unpleasant recollection.

“You shall hear it, Dick; I’ll tell it to you,” he said. “Begad, sir, I should feel quite queer, though, telling it *here*, though we are too strong a body for ghosts to meddle with just now.”

===Chinese===
莎士比亚说过——"有些人见不得一头张嘴的猪，有些人见了一只猫便要发狂。"我见了这只*老鼠*，几乎也要发狂；因为任你怎么笑我，我却觉得它把一种完全是人所独有的恶毒神情，钉在了我的身上；当它在地上窸窸窣窣地挪动，几乎就在我两脚之间仰起脸来看我——我看得分明，我可以发誓——那时我便感到了，至今也仍明白——那正是我那位画像里的"老朋友"的地狱般的目光与被诅咒的面容，化入了眼前这只鼓胀的害兽的脸上。

我怀着一种无法形容的厌恶与恐怖，又蹦回自己的房间，把门锁了又闩，仿佛对面站着一头狮子。该死的他，或者*它*；诅咒那画像，诅咒那画像的原型！我灵魂里深信——那只鼠——对，那只*鼠*，我刚才看见的那只**鼠**——便是那个恶灵的乔装，趁夜在这宅子里东游西荡，干着地狱式的胡闹。

第二天一早，我便在泥泞的街上奔波办事；其中一桩，便是寄出一封措辞坚决的信，召回汤姆。可等我回来，却看见那位不在家的"室友"留了便条，说他次日便返。我因此加倍欢喜：一则寓所已经觅定；二则换了场景、同伴归来，因着昨夜那场半可笑半可怖的奇遇，尤其显得可喜。

那天夜里我便在新寓所——迪格斯街（Digges' Street）——临时过了一宿，第二天早晨回到那闹鬼的旧宅用早饭，汤姆一到必先来此找我，这是笃定的。

我没料错——他来了；他张口几乎头一句，便问起我们迁居的那桩本意。

"谢天谢地，"他听我说一切妥当，便由衷地热烈说道。"为*你*我高兴。至于我自己，我向你保证，世间没有任何条件能诱我再在这倒霉的破老屋里过一夜。"

"叫这宅子见鬼去！"我脱口而出，恐惧与厌恶交集，"自打搬来此地，我们便没过过一个舒坦时辰"；我便这样说着，顺带把自己与那只血气过盛的老鼠的奇遇讲了一遍。

"嗯，倘若*仅止于此*"，表兄装作轻描淡写地说，"我想我倒也不怎么在乎。"

"哎，可是它的眼——它的神情，我亲爱的汤姆，"我追道；"要是你见了*那个*，你便会觉得，它可能是*任何东西*，唯独不是它表面看来的那样子。"

"我倒以为，这情形下最高明的术士，乃是一只身强力壮的猫，"他说着，发出一声惹人恼的轻笑。

"那么，且听你自己的奇遇罢，"我没好气地说。

被这一激，他不安地四下望望。我显然戳着了他一段极不痛快的旧事。

"你且听罢，迪克；我讲给你听，"他说。"老天在上，先生，可是在*这里*讲，我也要觉得毛骨悚然呢——纵然我们如今人多势众，鬼魂一时也搅扰不了我们。"

===Original===
Though he spoke this like a joke, I think it was serious calculation. Our Hebe was in a corner of the room, packing our cracked delft tea and dinner-services in a basket. She soon suspended operations, and with mouth and eyes wide open became an absorbed listener. Tom’s experiences were told nearly in these words:﻿—

“I saw it three times, Dick﻿—three distinct times; and I am perfectly certain it meant me some infernal harm. I was, I say, in danger﻿—in *extreme* danger; for, if nothing else had happened, my reason would most certainly have failed me, unless I had escaped so soon. Thank God. I *did* escape.

“The first night of this hateful disturbance, I was lying in the attitude of sleep, in that lumbering old bed. I hate to think of it. I was really wide awake, though I had put out my candle, and was lying as quietly as if I had been asleep; and although accidentally restless, my thoughts were running in a cheerful and agreeable channel.

“I think it must have been two o’clock at least when I thought I heard a sound in that﻿—that odious dark recess at the far end of the bedroom. It was as if someone was drawing a piece of cord slowly along the floor, lifting it up, and dropping it softly down again in coils. I sat up once or twice in my bed, but could see nothing, so I concluded it must be mice in the wainscot. I felt no emotion graver than curiosity, and after a few minutes ceased to observe it.

“While lying in this state, strange to say; without at first a suspicion of anything supernatural, on a sudden I saw an old man, rather stout and square, in a sort of roan-red dressing-gown, and with a black cap on his head, moving stiffly and slowly in a diagonal direction, from the recess, across the floor of the bedroom, passing my bed at the foot, and entering the lumber-closet at the left. He had something under his arm; his head hung a little at one side; and, merciful God! when I saw his face.”

Tom stopped for a while, and then said﻿—

“That awful countenance, which living or dying I never can forget, disclosed what he was. Without turning to the right or left, he passed beside me, and entered the closet by the bed’s head.

“While this fearful and indescribable type of death and guilt was passing, I felt that I had no more power to speak or stir than if I had been myself a corpse. For hours after it had disappeared, I was too terrified and weak to move. As soon as daylight came, I took courage, and examined the room, and especially the course which the frightful intruder had seemed to take, but there was not a vestige to indicate anybody’s having passed there; no sign of any disturbing agency visible among the lumber that strewed the floor of the closet.

===Chinese===
他这话虽像句玩笑，我想却是认真算计过的。我们的"赫柏"（Hebe，斟酒的女侍）正蹲在屋角，把那套满是裂纹的粗瓷茶具和餐具往篮里装。她不多时便停了手里的活，嘴眼齐张，听得出了神。汤姆的经历，差不多便是照这些话讲出来的：——

"我见过它三次，迪克——清清楚楚三次；我万分确信，它是要加害于我的——某种地狱式的加害。我那时，我说，处境危险——*极其*危险；因为，便没有别的变故，要不是我逃得早，我的神志必会支撑不住。感谢上帝。我*到底*逃了出来。

"这可憎的骚扰头一夜，我正以睡姿躺在那张笨重的旧床上。我连想都不愿想它。我其实醒得很，虽已熄了蜡烛，却静静地躺着，一如已经睡着；虽说偶有些翻身，心绪却走在一条愉快惬意的道上。

"我想至少总有两点钟了，我忽然听见卧房尽头那处——那处可憎的暗凹里——有一种声响。仿佛有人在地板上慢慢拖一段绳索，提起来，又一圈圈轻轻地放下。我在床上坐起一两回，却什么也看不见，便断定是护墙板里有耗子。我心里除了一丝好奇，别无感触；过几分钟也就不再理会。

"正这般躺着——说来奇怪——初时并无一丝超自然的疑心；忽然之间，我看见一个老者，身子颇壮实方正，穿一件暗红如栗马色的晨衣，头戴一顶黑帽，以一种僵直迟缓的步子，斜斜地从那凹室出来，横过卧房的地板，从我床脚边经过，进了左边那间堆杂物的壁橱。他腋下夹着什么东西；头略略歪向一边；仁慈的上天哪！待我看见他的脸——"

汤姆停了一阵，又说——

"那张可怕的脸，我是到死也忘不了的——无论生死——它把他是什么都揭露了出来。他既不左顾也不右盼，从我身旁经过，从床头那边进了壁橱。

"当这可怖而不可言喻的、象征着死亡与罪孽的东西经过之时，我觉得自己连开口、连动一动的力量都没有，仿佛我自己便是一具尸首。它消失之后的好几个钟头里，我都吓得太甚、太虚弱，动弹不得。一到天亮，我壮起胆子，把屋子细细检查了一遍，尤其查看了那个可怕的闯入者所走过的路径——可是连一丝有人经过的痕迹也没有；壁橱里满地堆着的杂物之间，也找不出任何扰动的迹象。

===Original===
“I now began to recover a little. I was fagged and exhausted, and at last, overpowered by a feverish sleep. I came down late; and finding you out of spirits, on account of your dreams about the portrait, whose *original* I am now certain disclosed himself to me, I did not care to talk about the infernal vision. In fact, I was trying to persuade myself that the whole thing was an illusion, and I did not like to revive in their intensity the hated impressions of the past night﻿—or to risk the constancy of my scepticism, by recounting the tale of my sufferings.

“It required some nerve, I can tell you, to go to my haunted chamber next night, and lie down quietly in the same bed,” continued Tom. “I did so with a degree of trepidation, which, I am not ashamed to say, a very little matter would have sufficed to stimulate to downright panic. This night, however, passed off quietly enough, as also the next; and so too did two or three more. I grew more confident, and began to fancy that I believed in the theories of spectral illusions, with which I had at first vainly tried to impose upon my convictions.

“The apparition had been, indeed, altogether anomalous. It had crossed the room without any recognition of my presence: I had not disturbed *it*, and *it* had no mission to *me*. What, then, was the imaginable use of its crossing the room in a visible shape at all? Of course it might have *been* in the closet instead of *going* there, as easily as it introduced itself into the recess without entering the chamber in a shape discernible by the senses. Besides, how the deuce *had* I seen it? It was a dark night; I had no candle; there was no fire; and yet I saw it as distinctly, in coloring and outline, as ever I beheld human form! A cataleptic dream would explain it all; and I was determined that a dream it should be.

===Chinese===
"我这才稍稍缓过一口气来。我筋疲力尽，憔悴不堪，终于被一阵发烧似的睡眠所压倒。我下楼下得迟；见你因那画像的梦而心境不佳——那画像的*原型*，我现在确信，正是向我显形的同一物——我便不愿把那地狱般的幻象拿出来讲。其实，我也正竭力说服自己，全事不过一场幻觉，我不愿把昨夜那些可憎的印象重新搅得如火如荼——也不愿因重述自己的苦况，而动摇了我那份怀疑论的恒心。

"老实告诉你，第二天夜里再走进那闹鬼的寝室，在那张床上静静地躺下去，是颇需要些胆量的，"汤姆接着说，"我怀着一份战战兢兢去做——说来也不怕难为情——只消一点小事，便足以把这份惊惧推成一场彻底的惊慌。可这一夜却过得相当平静，第二夜也是；其后两三夜亦然。我胆子壮了些，竟开始以为自己相信起那些幽灵幻象的理论来——那些理论，我起初也曾徒然地用来搪塞自己的信念。

"那一次显形，实在反常至极。它横过屋子，对我之在场毫无理会：我没有惊动*它*，*它*与我也没有相干。那么，它究竟何苦要以一个看得见的形状横过屋子呢？它当然大可本来就*待在*壁橱里，而不必*走*到那里去——正如它无需以感官所及之形进入卧房，便能出现在那凹室里。再说，见鬼，我究竟是*怎么*看见它的？那是个黑夜；我没有蜡烛；炉里没有火；可我却看得清清楚楚，颜色轮廓分明，便如我平生所见任何活人一样真切！一场强直性昏睡的梦，便可解释这一切；我便打定主意，它非是一场梦不可。

===Original===
“One of the most remarkable phenomena connected with the practice of mendacity is the vast number of deliberate lies we tell ourselves, whom, of all persons, we can least expect to deceive. In all this, I need hardly tell you, Dick, I was simply lying to myself, and did not believe one word of the wretched humbug. Yet I went on, as men will do, like persevering charlatans and impostors, who tire people into credulity by the mere force of reiteration; so I hoped to win myself over at last to a comfortable scepticism about the ghost.

“He had not appeared a second time﻿—that certainly was a comfort; and what, after all, did I care for him, and his queer old toggery and strange looks? Not a fig! I was nothing the worse for having seen him, and a good story the better. So I tumbled into bed, put out my candle, and, cheered by a loud drunken quarrel in the back lane, went fast asleep.

“From this deep slumber I awoke with a start. I knew I had had a horrible dream; but what it was I could not remember. My heart was thumping furiously; I felt bewildered and feverish; I sat up in the bed and looked about the room. A broad flood of moonlight came in through the curtainless window; everything was as I had last seen it; and though the domestic squabble in the back lane was, unhappily for me, allayed, I yet could hear a pleasant fellow singing, on his way home, the then popular comic ditty called, ‘Murphy Delany.’ Taking advantage of this diversion I lay down again, with my face towards the fireplace, and closing my eyes, did my best to think of nothing else but the song, which was every moment growing fainter in the distance:﻿—

> “ ’Twas Murphy Delany, so funny and frisky,

> Stepped into a shebeen shop to get his skin full;

> He reeled out again pretty well lined with whiskey,

> As fresh as a shamrock, as blind as a bull.

===Chinese===
"行骗这一行当里，有一桩最可注意的现象——便是我们对自己所说出的那无数蓄意的谎话；而在所有人之中，我们偏偏最不可能骗过自己。这全部之中，迪克，我几乎不必告诉你，我不过在对自己撒谎，那套可怜的鬼话，我自己一个字也不信。然而我仍照常人那样，像一个锲而不舍的江湖骗子和冒牌行家，单凭一遍遍重述之力，把人磨到肯信为止；我也如此希望，最终把自己劝服，对那鬼魂抱一份称心的怀疑。

"它没有第二次显形——这固然可慰；再说，我到底何曾在乎它，在乎它那身古怪的旧打扮与那副怪相？一丝一毫也不！我见了它，毫无所损，倒多得了一个好故事。我便一骨碌上床，吹了蜡烛，因后巷里一场喧闹的醉汉口角而壮胆，沉沉睡去。

"我从这酣沉的睡眠里一惊而醒。我晓得自己做了一个可怕的梦；可梦的是什么，却记不起来。心在胸膛里狂跳不止；我不知所措，浑身发烧；我在床上坐起来，把屋里四下打量。一派广阔的月光，从那无帘的窗涌进来；一切如我末次所见；后巷里那场家庭口角——于我颇为不幸——倒已平息，我却还听见一个乐天派的家伙，一边归家一边唱着那时风行的一首滑稽小调，名为《墨菲·德兰尼》（Murphy Delany）。我便借这一段消遣，重新躺下，脸朝着壁炉，闭上眼，竭力只去想那支歌——它正一刻比一刻在远处淡去：——

> "墨菲·德兰尼，滑稽又活泼，

> 踅进一家地下酒铺，灌个满腹；

> 出来时一肚皮威士忌撑得鼓鼓，

> 像三叶草那般精神，像公牛那般眼瞎。

===Original===
“The singer, whose condition I dare say resembled that of his hero, was soon too far off to regale my ears any more; and as his music died away, I myself sank into a doze, neither sound nor refreshing. Somehow the song had got into my head, and I went meandering on through the adventures of my respectable fellow-countryman, who, on emerging from the ‘shebeen shop,’ fell into a river, from which he was fished up to be ‘sat upon’ by a coroner’s jury, who having learned from a ‘horse-doctor’ that he was ‘dead as a doornail, so there was an end,’ returned their verdict accordingly, just as he returned to his senses, when an angry altercation and a pitched battle between the body and the coroner winds up the lay with due spirit and pleasantry.

“Through this ballad I continued with a weary monotony to plod, down to the very last line, and then da capo, and so on, in my uncomfortable half-sleep, for how long, I can’t conjecture. I found myself at last, however, muttering, ‘*dead* as a doornail, so there was an end’; and something like another voice within me, seemed to say, very faintly, but sharply, ‘dead! dead! *dead!* and may the Lord have mercy on your soul!’ and instantaneously I was wide awake, and staring right before me from the pillow.

“Now﻿—will you believe it, Dick?﻿—I saw the same accursed figure standing full front, and gazing at me with its stony and fiendish countenance, not two yards from the bedside.”

Tom stopped here, and wiped the perspiration from his face. I felt very queer. The girl was as pale as Tom; and, assembled as we were in the very scene of these adventures, we were all, I dare say, equally grateful for the clear daylight and the resuming bustle out of doors.

===Chinese===
"那位歌者——我想他的光景与他歌中的主角相去不远——不多时便走得太远，再不能娱我的耳朵了；他的歌声既远，我自己也陷入了一阵不沉、不解乏的瞌睡。不知怎地，那支歌竟钻进了我的脑里，我便随着那位可敬的同乡的奇遇一路漫游：他从那'地下酒铺'出来，跌进一条河里，被人捞了上来，要由验尸陪审团来'过堂'；陪审团从一个'马医'那里听来他已'死得像门钉一般，如此而已'，便照此裁定；偏巧他这时又苏醒过来，于是尸体与验尸官之间爆发了一场怒气冲天的争执与一场恶战，这首俚谣便以应有的神气与谐趣收场。

"我便拖着疲惫而单调的步子，在这首谣曲里一路跋涉，直至末一行；然后再da capo，从头再来；如此这般，在我不舒服的半睡半醒之中，持续了多久，我猜不出。然而末了我发现自己嘴里咕哝着：'死得像门钉一般，如此而已'；我内心深处似乎另有一个声音，极轻却极锐利地说道：'死了！死了！*死了*！愿主怜悯你的灵魂！'——一刹那间我完全清醒过来，从枕上直瞪着前方。

"这一下——迪克，你信不信？——我看见同一副可诅咒的身影，正正地站在我面前，以它那石像般、魔鬼般的面容凝视着我，离床边不出两码远。"

汤姆说到这里便停住，抹了抹脸上的汗。我也觉得浑身不对劲。那姑娘脸色白得和汤姆一样；我们聚集之地，恰恰又是这些奇遇的现场——我想，屋里的人，对那朗朗的白昼和门外重新喧响起来的市声，必定是一样心怀感激的。

===Original===
“For about three seconds only I saw it plainly; then it grew indistinct; but, for a long time, there was something like a column of dark vapour where it had been standing, between me and the wall; and I felt sure that he was still there. After a good while, this appearance went too. I took my clothes downstairs to the hall, and dressed there, with the door half open; then went out into the street, and walked about the town till morning, when I came back, in a miserable state of nervousness and exhaustion. I was such a fool, Dick, as to be ashamed to tell you how I came to be so upset. I thought you would laugh at me; especially as I had always talked philosophy, and treated *your* ghosts with contempt. I concluded you would give me no quarter; and so kept my tale of horror to myself.

“Now, Dick, you will hardly believe me, when I assure you, that for many nights after this last experience, I did not go to my room at all. I used to sit up for a while in the drawing-room after you had gone up to your bed; and then steal down softly to the hall-door, let myself out, and sit in the ‘Robin Hood’ tavern until the last guest went off; and then I got through the night like a sentry, pacing the streets till morning.

“For more than a week I never slept in bed. I sometimes had a snooze on a form in the ‘Robin Hood,’ and sometimes a nap in a chair during the day; but regular sleep I had absolutely none.

“I was quite resolved that we should get into another house; but I could not bring myself to tell you the reason, and I somehow put it off from day to day, although my life was, during every hour of this procrastination, rendered as miserable as that of a felon with the constables on his track. I was growing absolutely ill from this wretched mode of life.

===Chinese===
"我清清楚楚看见它，不过约莫三秒；其后便模糊起来；但很长一段时间，在它方才所立之处——我与墙之间——留有一道仿佛黑色蒸气凝成的柱子；我深信他仍在那儿。过了好一阵，这团形影也散了。我把衣裳拿到楼下门厅，在那里穿戴，门半开着；然后出门上街，在城里走来走去，直走到天亮，才心力交瘁、神经衰弱地回来。我傻到这步田地，迪克，竟不好意思告诉你我是因何这般失态。我以为你会笑我；尤其因为我一向满嘴哲理，又向来鄙视*你的*那些鬼。我断定你必不留情面；便把这一段恐怖的经历闷在心里。

"听着，迪克，你大概不会相信，可我郑重告诉你：自这最后一遭之后，一连许多夜，我根本没回自己的屋里去睡。你上楼就寝之后，我往往在客厅里坐上一阵；然后悄悄溜到大门，放自己出去，在'罗宾汉'（Robin Hood）酒馆坐到末一个客人散去；其后我便像一名哨兵似的，在街上踱来踱去，直踱到天明，以此挨过一夜。

"足足一个多礼拜，我没在床上睡过一回。有时在'罗宾汉'的长凳上打个盹，有时白天在椅子里眯一觉；可正经的睡眠，几乎一点也没有。

"我已铁了心，定要搬出这宅子；可我又说不出口把缘故告诉你，竟一日一日地拖了下来——纵然在这拖延的每一个时辰里，我的日子过得如同被警察追缉的逃犯一般苦。这种可悲的活法，已把我弄得当真要病了。

===Original===
“One afternoon I determined to enjoy an hour’s sleep upon your bed. I hated mine; so that I had never, except in a stealthy visit every day to unmake it, lest Martha should discover the secret of my nightly absence, entered the ill-omened chamber.

“As ill-luck would have it, you had locked your bedroom, and taken away the key. I went into my own to unsettle the bedclothes, as usual, and give the bed the appearance of having been slept in. Now, a variety of circumstances concurred to bring about the dreadful scene through which I was that night to pass. In the first place, I was literally overpowered with fatigue, and longing for sleep; in the next place, the effect of this extreme exhaustion upon my nerves resembled that of a narcotic, and rendered me less susceptible than, perhaps, I should in any other condition have been, of the exciting fears which had become habitual to me. Then again, a little bit of the window was open, a pleasant freshness pervaded the room, and, to crown all, the cheerful sun of day was making the room quite pleasant. What was to prevent my enjoying an hour’s nap *here*? The whole air was resonant with the cheerful hum of life, and the broad matter-of-fact light of day filled every corner of the room.

“I yielded﻿—stifling my qualms﻿—to the almost overpowering temptation; and merely throwing off my coat, and loosening my cravat, I lay down, limiting myself to *half*-an-hour’s doze in the unwonted enjoyment of a feather bed, a coverlet, and a bolster.

“It was horribly insidious; and the demon, no doubt, marked my infatuated preparations. Dolt that I was, I fancied, with mind and body worn out for want of sleep, and an arrear of a full week’s rest to my credit, that such measure as *half*-an-hour’s sleep, in such a situation, was possible. My sleep was deathlike, long, and dreamless.

===Chinese===
"一天下午，我决意在你床上享受一个钟头的睡眠。我自己的床，我早已腻透了；所以那间不祥之屋，除了每日偷偷进去一次把被褥弄乱——免得玛莎（Martha）发现我夜夜不归的秘密——我从未踏入。

"偏巧不巧，你那间卧房锁了门，钥匙也带走了。我便进自己的屋，照例把被褥弄乱，把床弄得像有人睡过的样子。此时种种机缘凑合，酿成了我那一夜所要经历的可怖场面。其一，我简直被疲惫所压倒，渴睡之极；其二，这种极度困乏对我的神经所起的作用，竟如一剂麻醉药，使我对比起平日任何状态之下，更不易受那一向盘踞心头的兴奋的恐惧所侵。再说，窗子也开了一缝，屋里弥漫着一种宜人的清新；尤其要紧的，是那一日的欢快阳光，把屋子照得颇为可人。又有什么能阻止我*在此*享受一个钟头的小睡呢？满空气都和着生命的欢快嗡鸣而震响；那坦坦荡荡、毫无疑问的白日光，填满了屋里的每一个角落。

"我便屈服了——压下心头那一阵翻涌的不安——向这几乎不可抵御的诱惑低头；仅仅脱了上衣，松了领巾，便躺了下来，限定自己在这羽毛褥、被单、长枕的不寻常享受里，只打个*半*小时的盹。

"那是一个恶毒之至的圈套；那魔鬼，无疑正在暗中窥视着我这痴愚的安排。我这一介蠢物，竟以为身心俱因缺睡而疲敝、又有一整周睡眠的亏欠记账在手——*半小时*之睡，于这般境地之中，竟能如我所愿。我的睡眠沉如死，长，而无梦。

===Original===
“Without a start or fearful sensation of any kind, I waked gently, but completely. It was, as you have good reason to remember, long past midnight﻿—I believe, about two o’clock. When sleep has been deep and long enough to satisfy nature thoroughly, one often wakens in this way, suddenly, tranquilly, and completely.

“There was a figure seated in that lumbering, old sofa-chair, near the fireplace. Its back was rather towards me, but I could not be mistaken; it turned slowly round, and, merciful heavens! there was the stony face, with its infernal lineaments of malignity and despair, gloating on me. There was now no doubt as to its consciousness of my presence, and the hellish malice with which it was animated, for it arose, and drew close to the bedside. There was a rope about its neck, and the other end, coiled up, it held stiffly in its hand.

“My good angel nerved me for this horrible crisis. I remained for some seconds transfixed by the gaze of this tremendous phantom. He came close to the bed, and appeared on the point of mounting upon it. The next instant I was upon the floor at the far side, and in a moment more was, I don’t know how, upon the lobby.

“But the spell was not yet broken; the valley of the shadow of death was not yet traversed. The abhorred phantom was before me there; it was standing near the banisters, stooping a little, and with one end of the rope round its own neck, was poising a noose at the other, as if to throw over mine; and while engaged in this baleful pantomime, it wore a smile so sensual, so unspeakably dreadful, that my senses were nearly overpowered. I saw and remember nothing more, until I found myself in your room.

“I had a wonderful escape, Dick﻿—there is no disputing *that*﻿—an escape for which, while I live, I shall bless the mercy of heaven. No one can conceive or imagine what it is for flesh and blood to stand in the presence of such a thing, but one who has had the terrific experience. Dick, Dick, a shadow has passed over me﻿—a chill has crossed my blood and marrow, and I will never be the same again﻿—never, Dick﻿—never!”

===Chinese===
"我并未惊跳，亦无任何可怖之感，只是轻柔地、却又彻底地醒了过来。那时刻——你尽有理由记得——早已过了半夜，我想，约莫两点钟。睡眠若深若长，足以尽慰天性，人便往往这般醒来：突然、宁静、而彻底。

"壁炉旁那张笨重的旧沙发椅上，坐着一个身影。背影多半对着我，但我决不会看错；它慢慢地转过身来——仁慈的上天哪！那正是那张石像般的脸，带着地狱般的恶毒与绝望的神情，贪婪地盯着我。这一回，它之觉察到我在场、其心所怀的地狱式的恶意，已无可置疑——因为它站起身来，挨近了床边。它颈上绕着一根绳，另一端盘成一卷，僵硬地握在手里。

"我的守护善灵，在这可怕关头为我壮了胆。我足有几秒钟，被这可怖幽灵的目光钉住，动弹不得。他走到床前，眼看就要爬上床来。下一个瞬间，我已在床的远侧落地，再一转眼，我已——自己也说不清怎的——到了走廊上。

"可那咒还没破；死荫的幽谷尚未穿尽。我所憎恶的幽灵，又已立在我面前；它站在扶手附近，略略佝偻着身子，一手把绳的一端仍绕在自己颈上，另一端挽成一个套，仿佛要朝我头上抛来；当它做着这恶毒的哑剧之时，唇边挂着一丝笑——那么淫邪，又那么不可言说地可怕，我的感官几乎为之昏乱。其后的所见所记，便一概没有，直到发觉自己已立在你的屋里。

"我这一劫逃得实在离奇，迪克——这一点无可争辩——这一场脱险，我只要活一日，便要祝颂上天的慈悲一日。除非亲身经历过那般可怖之事，无人能想象，肉骨凡胎，立于那样一种东西面前，是何等光景。迪克，迪克，有一道影子掠过了我——有一股寒气穿过我的血与髓，我再也不会是从前的我了——再也不会了，迪克——再也不会！"

===Original===
Our handmaid, a mature girl of two-and-fifty, as I have said, stayed her hand, as Tom’s story proceeded, and by little and little drew near to us, with open mouth, and her brows contracted over her little, beady black eyes, till stealing a glance over her shoulder now and then, she established herself close behind us. During the relation, she had made various earnest comments, in an undertone; but these and her ejaculations, for the sake of brevity and simplicity, I have omitted in my narration.

“It’s often I heard tell of it,” she now said, “but I never believed it rightly till now﻿—though, indeed, why should not I? Does not my mother, down there in the lane, know quare stories, God bless us, beyant telling about it? But you ought not to have slept in the back bedroom. She was loath to let me be going in and out of that room even in the daytime, let alone for any Christian to spend the night in it; for sure she says it was his own bedroom.”

“*Whose* own bedroom?” we asked, in a breath.

“Why, *his*﻿—the ould Judge’s﻿—Judge Horrock’s, to be sure, God rest his sowl;” and she looked fearfully round.

“Amen!” I muttered. “But did he die there?”

“Die there! No, not quite *there*,” she said. “Shure, was not it over the banisters he hung himself, the ould sinner, God be merciful to us all? and was not it in the alcove they found the handles of the skipping-rope cut off, and the knife where he was settling the cord, God bless us, to hang himself with? It was his housekeeper’s daughter owned the rope, my mother often told me, and the child never throve after, and used to be starting up out of her sleep, and screeching in the night time, wid dhrames and frights that cum an her; and they said how it was the speerit of the ould Judge that was tormentin’ her; and she used to be roaring and yelling out to hould back the big ould fellow with the crooked neck; and then she’d screech ‘Oh, the master! the master! he’s stampin’ at me, and beckoning to me! Mother, darling, don’t let me go!’ And so the poor crathure died at last, and the docthers said it was wather on the brain, for it was all they could say.”

===Chinese===
我们的女佣，便是那位五十二岁的"成熟姑娘"，我已说过——汤姆讲故事的当儿，她停了手里的活，一点一点挪近前来，张着嘴，那双珠子般的小黑眼上方眉头紧蹙，时不时从我们肩头偷望过来，末了便立定了，紧贴在我们身后。讲述之中，她屡屡以低声发出种种恳切的议论；这些话连同她的惊呼，为简明起见，我于叙述中一概从略。

"这事我常听人讲起，"她这才说道，"可直到今日我才当真信了——其实，说真的，我怎会不信？我妈就住在下面巷子里，她岂不是知道些古怪故事，上帝保佑我们，简直讲都讲不完？只是你们原不该在那间后卧房里睡觉的。便是我白天进进出出那间屋，她都不大愿意，更莫说让哪个基督徒在里面过夜了；因为她常说，那原是他本人的卧房。"

"*谁的*卧房？"我们异口同声地问。

"嗐，*他*的——那位老法官的——贺洛克斯法官的，没错，愿上帝安他的灵魂；"她说着，怯怯地四下张望。

"阿门！"我低声道。"可他是死在那里的么？"

"死在那里！不，不完全是*死在那里*"，她说。"哎呀，他不是从扶手上头把自己吊死的么，那老罪人，上帝慈悲我们众人？他们岂不是在那凹室里寻见跳绳的把手被割了下来，还有那把刀——他是用那刀整理绳子的，上帝保佑，好把自己吊死？我妈常对我说，那绳原是管家女儿的东西；那孩子自那以后便再没好过，夜里常常从睡中惊起，尖叫不止，因着那些压上她身的梦与惧；人都说，那是老法官的鬼魂在作弄她；她常常又嚎又叫，喊叫着要把那个歪脖子的老家伙挡回去；一会儿又尖叫：'哎，主人！主人！他在跺脚冲我来，又冲我招手！妈呀，好妈，别让我去！'那苦命的人儿末了便这样死了；医生说是水入脑——因为这是他们能说的全部了。"

===Original===
“How long ago was all this?” I asked.

“Oh, then, how would I know?” she answered. “But it must be a wondherful long time ago, for the housekeeper was an ould woman, with a pipe in her mouth, and not a tooth left, and better nor eighty years ould when my mother was first married; and they said she was a rale buxom, fine-dressed woman when the ould Judge come to his end; an’, indeed, my mother’s not far from eighty years ould herself this day; and what made it worse for the unnatural ould villain, God rest his soul, to frighten the little girl out of the world the way he did, was what was mostly thought and believed by everyone. My mother says how the poor little crathure was his own child; for he was by all accounts an ould villain every way, an’ the hangin’est judge that ever was known in Ireland’s ground.”

“From what you said about the danger of sleeping in that bedroom,” said I, “I suppose there were stories about the ghost having appeared there to others.”

“Well, there was things said﻿—quare things, surely,” she answered, as it seemed, with some reluctance. “And why would not there? Sure was it not up in that same room he slept for more than twenty years? and was it not in the *alcove* he got the rope ready that done his own business at last, the way he done many a betther man’s in his lifetime?﻿—and was not the body lying in the same bed after death, and put in the coffin there, too, and carried out to his grave from it in Pether’s churchyard, after the coroner was done? But there was quare stories﻿—my mother has them all﻿—about how one Nicholas Spaight got into trouble on the head of it.”

“And what did they say of this Nicholas Spaight?” I asked.

“Oh, for that matther, it’s soon told,” she answered.

And she certainly did relate a very strange story, which so piqued my curiosity, that I took occasion to visit the ancient lady, her mother, from whom I learned many very curious particulars. Indeed, I am tempted to tell the tale, but my fingers are weary, and I must defer it. But if you wish to hear it another time, I shall do my best.

===Chinese===
"这都是多少年前的事了？"我问。

"哎呀，那我怎会晓得？"她答道。"可一定是好久好以前的事了；因为那管家已是个老妪，嘴里衔着烟斗，一颗牙也没剩，我妈新嫁的那年她已八十出头；听说那老法官死的时候，她还是个体态丰腴、穿戴齐整的妇人呢；再说，我妈本人如今离八十也不远了；那桩更叫这桩丧尽天良的老恶棍——愿上帝安他的灵魂——如此把一个小丫头活活吓出人世的事，据众人所信所想，更是如此。我妈说，那苦命的小东西，原是他自己的亲生女儿；因为据各方所说，他方方面面都是个老恶棍，又是爱尔兰有史以来最嗜判绞刑的法官。"

"听你方才说在那间卧房里睡觉有危险，"我说，"想必也有那鬼在里头向旁人显过形的说法罢。"

"嗯，是有那么些说法——古怪的说法，自然，"她答道，似乎有些不愿。"又怎能没有？他岂不是在那同一间屋里睡了二十多年？那根送了他自己终的绳，岂不是在*那凹室*里备下的，一如他生前送了不知多少比他好的人？他死后，尸首岂不是躺在那张床上，棺材也是在屋里殓的，验尸官验罢，便从那里抬到彼得的墓地安葬？至于那些古怪的说法——我妈都记得——其中有一桩，说的是一个尼古拉斯·斯佩特（Nicholas Spaight）因这事而惹了祸。"

"他们又是怎么说这位尼古拉斯·斯佩特的呢？"我问。

"嗐，这事么，三言两语就说完，"她答道。

她确乎讲了一段十分离奇的故事，把我的好奇心勾得大发；我便趁机去拜访了她母亲那位年高的夫人，从她口中得知许多奇异的细节。其实我也颇想把这故事讲出来，无奈指端已倦，只好按下不表。倘若你异日愿闻，我必尽力一述。

===Original===
When we had heard the strange tale I have *not* told you, we put one or two further questions to her about the alleged spectral visitations, to which the house had, ever since the death of the wicked old Judge, been subjected.

“No one ever had luck in it,” she told us. “There was always cross accidents, sudden deaths, and short times in it. The first that tuck it was a family﻿—I forget their name﻿—but at any rate there was two young ladies and their papa. He was about sixty, and a stout healthy gentleman as you’d wish to see at that age. Well, he slept in that unlucky back bedroom; and, God between us an’ harm! sure enough he was found dead one morning, half out of the bed, with his head as black as a sloe, and swelled like a puddin’, hanging down near the floor. It was a fit, they said. He was as dead as a mackerel, and so *he* could not say what it was; but the ould people was all sure that it was nothing at all but the ould Judge, God bless us! that frightened him out of his senses and his life together.

“Some time after there was a rich old maiden lady took the house. I don’t know which room *she* slept in, but she lived alone; and at any rate, one morning, the servants going down early to their work, found her sitting on the passage-stairs, shivering and talkin’ to herself, quite mad; and never a word more could any of *them* or her friends get from her ever afterwards but, ‘Don’t ask me to go, for I promised to wait for him.’ They never made out from her who it was she meant by *him*, but of course those that knew all about the ould house were at no loss for the meaning of all that happened to her.

“Then afterwards, when the house was let out in lodgings, there was Micky Byrne that took the same room, with his wife and three little children; and sure I heard Mrs. Byrne myself telling how the children used to be lifted up in the bed at night, she could not see by what mains; and how they were starting and screeching every hour, just all as one as the housekeeper’s little girl that died, till at last one night poor Micky had a dhrop in him, the way he used now and again; and what do you think in the middle of the night he thought he heard a noise on the stairs, and being in liquor, nothing less id do him but out he must go himself to see what was wrong. Well, after that, all she ever heard of him was himself sayin’, ‘Oh, God!’ and a tumble that shook the very house; and there, sure enough, he was lying on the lower stairs, under the lobby, with his neck smashed double undher him, where he was flung over the banisters.”

===Chinese===
我们既听了那段我*未曾*讲给你的奇事，便又就这所宅子——自那恶毒的老法官死后——所传承受的种种鬼魂作祟，再向她追问了一两句。

"在这里头，再没人得过福，"她告诉我们，"总有种种横祸、暴卒、短命的事。头一个租下它的，是一户人家——名字我忘了——总而言之，是两位年轻小姐和她们的父亲。父亲约莫六十岁，那样年纪，你再也见不到比他更壮健的绅士了。哎，他睡的便是那间倒霉的后卧房；上帝保佑我们免祸罢！果不其然，一天早晨，人发现他死在床上，半截身子探出床外，头黑如黑刺李，肿得像只布丁，垂在地板边上。人说是一阵急病。他是死得透透的了，所以*他*再不能说那是怎么一回事；可那些老辈人，都一口咬定，那无非是那老法官——上帝保佑我们！——把他的神志和性命一并吓出了窍。

"再过些时，又有一位有钱的老小姐租了这宅子。我不知*她*睡的是哪一间，反正她独居；总之，一天清早，仆人们下去做活，只见她坐在过道的楼梯上，浑身发抖，自言自语，已经完全疯了；其后无论是*那些仆人*还是她的亲友，再也休想从她口里听到别的话，只一句：'别叫我走，因为我答应过等他。'他们始终没能从她口中问出那*他*究竟指谁，但那些深谙这所旧宅底细的人，自然明白这一切所指。

"再后来，这宅子分间出租了。有个叫米基·伯恩（Micky Byrne）的，带着妻子和三个小孩，租的便是同一间屋；我亲耳听伯恩太太讲过，孩子们夜里怎样在床上被人抬起来，她却看不见是何手法；孩子们又是怎样每个钟头便惊起尖叫，全然和那死了的管家小女儿一个模样；直到末了一夜，可怜的米基又带了点酒意——他隔三岔五便是如此；你猜怎么着，半夜里他以为听见楼梯上有声响，借着酒劲，非得自己出去看个究竟。哎，其后她所听见他的，便只有他自己的一声'哦，上帝！'和一声把整所房子都震动的跌落；果不其然，他便躺在扶手下头那段较低的楼梯上，颈骨折成两段，是被从扶手上头抛下来的。"

===Original===
Then the handmaiden added﻿—

“I’ll go down to the lane, and send up Joe Gavvey to pack up the rest of the taythings, and bring all the things across to your new lodgings.”

And so we all sallied out together, each of us breathing more freely, I have no doubt, as we crossed that ill-omened threshold for the last time.

Now, I may add thus much, in compliance with the immemorial usage of the realm of fiction, which sees the hero not only through his adventures, but fairly out of the world. You must have perceived that what the flesh, blood, and bone hero of romance proper is to the regular compounder of fiction, this old house of brick, wood, and mortar is to the humble recorder of this true tale. I, therefore, relate, as in duty bound, the catastrophe which ultimately befell it, which was simply this﻿—that about two years subsequently to my story it was taken by a quack doctor, who called himself Baron Duhlstoerf, and filled the parlour windows with bottles of indescribable horrors preserved in brandy, and the newspapers with the usual grandiloquent and mendacious advertisements. This gentleman among his virtues did not reckon sobriety, and one night, being overcome with much wine, he set fire to his bed curtains, partially burned himself, and totally consumed the house. It was afterwards rebuilt, and for a time an undertaker established himself in the premises.
