The man was still speechless, but he seemed to understand the physician when he forbid his repeating the painful and fruitless attempts which he made to articulate, and he at once resigned himself quietly into his hands.

I left the patient with leeches upon his temples, and bleeding freely, apparently with little of the drowsiness which accompanies apoplexy; indeed, Dr. D﻿—﻿— told me that he had never before witnessed a seizure which seemed to combine the symptoms of so many kinds, and yet which belonged to none of the recognised classes; it certainly was not apoplexy, catalepsy, nor delirium tremens, and yet it seemed, in some degree, to partake of the properties of all. It was strange, but stranger things are coming.

===Chinese===
D—医生立时赶到床畔；一加查验，发现那放血刀口处忽涌出一股汹涌而出的鲜血——无疑正是这一桩，把他从众人皆以为永不再返的人世之外，忽地、近乎超自然地召了回来。那人仍不能言语，但医师既止他再作那些痛苦而无用的发声之试，他似乎颇能领会，便安然将自家交到医师手中。

我离了病人，他两太阳穴上贴着水蛭，血尚畅流，瞧着不似中风昏迷之状；果然，D—医生告我，他从未见过一桩病作，竟将这许多症候集于一身，却又无一与所立之诸类相合；那确非中风、非僵卧、非战栗谵狂，却又似或多或少兼具诸者之性。这已属奇异，更奇之事尚在其后。

===Original===
During two or three days Dr. D﻿—﻿— would not allow his patient to converse in a manner which could excite or exhaust him, with anyone; he suffered him merely as briefly as possible to express his immediate wants. And it was not until the fourth day after my early visit, the particulars of which I have just detailed, that it was thought expedient that I should see him, and then only because it appeared that his extreme importunity and impatience to meet me were likely to retard his recovery more than the mere exhaustion attendant upon a short conversation could possibly do; perhaps, too, my friend entertained some hope that if by holy confession his patient's bosom were eased of the perilous stuff which no doubt oppressed it, his recovery would be more assured and rapid. It was then, as I have said, upon the fourth day after my first professional call, that I found myself once more in the dreary chamber of want and sickness.

===Chinese===
两三日内，D—医生不许他的病人与任何人作那足以激动或耗神之谈，只许他尽可能简短地陈明眼下的需求。直至我前面详述的那次清晨初访之后的第四日，方才议定我应当见他一面，且唯独因为：他求见之心之切、之躁，似更甚于一场短谈所伴之劳顿，恐反有碍于他的康复；再者，吾友或亦存了一线希望：以为若借圣事告解，将病人胸中所积的那沉重的危殆之物倾吐一空，其康复或可更稳、更速。于是，便如我所说，在我那第一次为职分所驱的探访之后第四日，我又一次置身于那间凄凉的匮乏与疾病之室。

===Original===
The man was in bed, and appeared low and restless. On my entering the room he raised himself in the bed, and muttered, twice or thrice:

"Thank God! thank God!"

I signed to those of his family who stood by to leave the room, and took a chair beside the bed. So soon as we were alone, he said, rather doggedly:

"There's no use in telling me of the sinfulness of bad ways﻿—I know it all. I know where they lead to﻿—I seen everything about it with my own eyesight, as plain as I see you." He rolled himself in the bed, as if to hide his face in the clothes; and then suddenly raising himself, he exclaimed with startling vehemence: "Look, sir! there is no use in mincing the matter: I'm blasted with the fires of hell; I have been in hell. What do you think of that? In hell﻿—I'm lost forever﻿—I have not a chance. I am damned already﻿—damned﻿—damned!"

===Chinese===
那人在床上，神气低沉而烦躁。我一进门，他便在床上支起身子，喃喃地说了两三遍：

"感谢上帝！感谢上帝！"

我做手势叫站在床畔的几个家人离房，自己在床边坐下。才得二人独处，他便颇执拗地说道：

"再拿那些邪路如何有罪的话来劝我，已是没用——这一切我都明白。我晓得它们的归宿——它们周遭的一切，我都亲眼见过，看得明明白白，就同我看见您一样明白。"他在床上翻了个身，似要把脸藏进被褥；又忽地支起身子，以一种骇人的激切喊道："您瞧，先生！掩饰也没用了：我已被地狱之火灼焦了；我曾下过地狱。您以为如何？下过地狱——我已永沦——毫无指望。我已经被定了罪——定罪——定罪！"

===Original===
The end of this sentence he actually shouted. His vehemence was perfectly terrific; he threw himself back, and laughed, and sobbed hysterically. I poured some water into a teacup, and gave it to him. After he had swallowed it, I told him if he had anything to communicate, to do so as briefly as he could, and in a manner as little agitating to himself as possible; threatening at the same time, though I had no intention of doing so, to leave him at once, in case he again gave way to such passionate excitement.

"It's only foolishness," he continued, "for me to try to thank you for coming to such a villain as myself at all. It's no use for me to wish good to you, or to bless you; for such as me has no blessings to give."

===Chinese===
这末一句话，他几乎是吼出来的。他那一阵激切可怖之至；他往后一仰，又笑又哭，状如癔发。我倒了一杯水给他。待他咽下，我便对他说，若他有事相告，务求简明，且尽量不使自家过于激动；又吓唬他——虽我并无此意——倘若他再这般情急失控，我便立时离去。

"似我这般恶棍，"他续道，"您竟肯光降，我想要道一声谢，也是痴心。我也不配祝您安好、为您祈福；因为似我这等人，原无福可赐。"

===Original===
I told him that I had but done my duty, and urged him to proceed to the matter which weighed upon his mind. He then spoke nearly as follows:

"I came in drunk on Friday night last, and got to my bed here; I don't remember how. Sometime in the night it seemed to me I wakened, and feeling unasy in myself, I got up out of the bed. I wanted the fresh air; but I would not make a noise to open the window, for fear I'd waken the crathurs. It was very dark and throublesome to find the door; but at last I did get it, and I groped my way out, and went down as asy as I could. I felt quite sober, and I counted the steps one after another, as I was going down, that I might not stumble at the bottom.

"When I came to the first landing-place﻿—God be about us always!﻿—the floor of it sunk under me, and I went down﻿—down﻿—down, till the senses almost left me. I do not know how long I was falling, but it seemed to me a great while. When I came rightly to myself at last, I was sitting near the top of a great table; and I could not see the end of it, if it had any, it was so far off. And there was men beyond reckoning, sitting down all along by it, at each side, as far as I could see at all. I did not know at first was it in the open air; but there was a close smothering feel in it that was not natural. And there was a kind of light that my eyesight never saw before, red and unsteady; and I did not see for a long time where it was coming from, until I looked straight up, and then I seen that it came from great balls of blood-coloured fire that were rolling high over head with a sort of rushing, trembling sound, and I perceived that they shone on the ribs of a great roof of rock that was arched overhead instead of the sky. When I seen this, scarce knowing what I did, I got up, and I said, 'I have no right to be here; I must go.' And the man that was sitting at my left hand only smiled, and said, 'Sit down again; you can *never* leave this place.' And his voice was weaker than any child's voice I ever heerd; and when he was done speaking he smiled again.

===Chinese===
我告他，我不过尽了本分罢了，便劝他把压在心头之事说出来。他遂大约这般讲道：

"上礼拜五夜里我醉醺醺地回来，上了这张床；怎么上的，我记不得了。夜半我仿佛一觉醒来，觉着心头不安，便从床上起来。我渴念新鲜空气；可我不肯弄出声响去开窗，怕把那几个苦命的惊醒。屋里漆黑，连摸那扇门都艰难之至；到底摸到了，我便摸黑出去，尽可能放轻脚步下楼。我神志倒清爽得很，下楼时一级一级数着，好不至于在最底下一级绊倒。

"到了头一个歇脚平台——上帝永远护佑我们！——那楼板在我脚下一软，我便坠下去——坠下去——坠下去，直坠到几乎失了知觉。我不知坠落了多久，只觉是很长一段时候。待我终于神志全清，我正坐在一张大桌子的近顶处；那张桌子倘若真有个尽头，我也是望不见的——太远了。桌子两旁坐着数不清的人，沿着两边一直排到我目力所及之处。我起初不知自己是在露天之下，还是屋宇之中；可那一种闷窒窒息之感，不似寻常。那里又有一种我目力所未曾见过的光——红的，摇曳不定；好一阵子我看不见它从何处来，直待我抬头直望，方才看见那光是从几团血色火球里发出的，火球在高空滚动，发出一种急掠而颤动的声响；我又察觉，那光照在一座巨大穹隆的岩肋之上——是岩石的穹顶，遮在我头顶，代替了天空。我见了这光景，也几乎不省自家在做什么，便立起身，说道：'我无权在此；我得走。'坐在我左手的那人只是笑了笑，说道：'再坐下罢；你*永远*不能离开此地。'他的声音比我听过的任何孩童的都还要轻弱；说罢，又笑了一笑。

===Original===
"Then I spoke out very loud and bold, and I said, 'In the name of God, let me out of this bad place.' And there was a great man that I did not see before, sitting at the end of the table that I was near; and he was taller than twelve men, and his face was very proud and terrible to look at. And he stood up and stretched out his hand before him; and when he stood up, all that was there, great and small, bowed down with a sighing sound, and a dread came on my heart, and he looked at me, and I could not speak. I felt I was his own, to do what he liked with, for I knew at once who he was; and he said, 'If you promise to return, you may depart for a season;' and the voice he spoke with was terrible and mournful, and the echoes of it went rolling and swelling down the endless cave, and mixing with the trembling of the fire overhead; so that when he sat down there was a sound after him, all through the place, like the roaring of a furnace, and I said, with all the strength I had, 'I promise to come back﻿—in God's name let me go!'

"And with that I lost the sight and the hearing of all that was there, and when my senses came to me again, I was sitting in the bed with the blood all over me, and you and the rest praying around the room."

===Chinese===
"于是我放胆高声说道：'奉上帝之名，让我出这恶地。'便有一个我先前未见的高大之人，坐在我所靠近的那一头；他比十二个汉子叠起来还高，面孔极傲慢、可怖，叫人不忍逼视。他站起来，把一只手向前一伸；他一站起来，在场众人无论大小，皆叹一声、俯伏下去；我心上一阵惧怕袭来；他看着我，我便再不能言语。我觉出我已属他，任他处置——因为我立时知道他是谁；他说道：'你若许诺再来，可暂时离去'；他说话的声音又可怖、又悲凉，那回声在那无尽的洞穴中翻滚、汹涌，与头顶之火的颤动相和；待他坐下，那满洞之中尚有一阵余响，如熔炉之吼；我便竭尽气力答道：'我许诺必再回来——奉上帝之名，放我去罢！'

"我便失了对那一切的视听，待神志回转，我已坐在床上，周身是血，您和众人围着屋子祷告。"

===Original===
Here he paused and wiped away the chill drops of horror which hung upon his forehead.

I remained silent for some moments. The vision which he had just described struck my imagination not a little, for this was long before Vathek and the "Hall of Eblis" had delighted the world; and the description which he gave had, as I received it, all the attractions of novelty beside the impressiveness which always belongs to the narration of an *eyewitness*, whether in the body or in the spirit, of the scenes which he describes. There was something, too, in the stern horror with which the man related these things, and in the incongruity of his description, with the vulgarly received notions of the great place of punishment, and of its presiding spirit, which struck my mind with awe, almost with fear. At length he said, with an expression of horrible, imploring earnestness, which I shall never forget﻿—"Well, sir, is there any hope; is there any chance at all? or, is my soul pledged and promised away forever? is it gone out of my power? must I go back to the place?"

In answering him, I had no easy task to perform; for however clear might be my internal conviction of the groundlessness of his fears, and however strong my scepticism respecting the reality of what he had described, I nevertheless felt that his impression to the contrary, and his humility and terror resulting from it, might be made available as no mean engines in the work of his conversion from prodigacy, and of his restoration to decent habits, and to religious feeling.

===Chinese===
说到此处他住了口，抹去额上挂着的几点寒惧之汗。

我默然片刻。他所描述的那一梦颇动我的想象；盖其时《瓦提克》（Vathek）与"埃布利斯之厅"（Hall of Eblis）尚未倾动天下；他所言之状，在我听来，既有新异之趣，又兼一种凡属目击者——无论肉身之目击，抑或魂魄之目击——叙述其所历之景时所特有的那种撼人之力。再者，那人讲述这些事时所带的那种冷峻的战栗，加之他所言与我们素所承袭的、关于那大刑之地与其主宰的凡俗之见之不相吻合，皆令我心生敬畏，近乎恐惧。终是他带着一副我毕生难忘的、可怖而哀求之至的恳切，说道——"那么，先生，可有指望？可有半点指望？抑或，我的灵魂已许了出去、永不再返？已非我力所能挽？我必得回到那地方去？"

答他这话，于我并非易事；盖无论我心内如何深信他所惧者毫无根据，无论我对所述之事的真伪如何深抱怀疑，我却仍觉：他那相反的执念，以及由此而生出的谦卑与恐惧，未尝不可化为有力的机括——用在他从浪荡归正、复返良俗与虔信这一桩工程之上。

===Original===
I therefore told him that he was to regard his dream rather in the light of a warning than in that of a prophecy; that our salvation depended not upon the word or deed of a moment, but upon the habits of a life; that, in fine, if he at once discarded his idle companions and evil habits, and firmly adhered to a sober, industrious, and religious course of life, the powers of darkness might claim his soul in vain, for that there were higher and firmer pledges than human tongue could utter, which promised salvation to him who should repent and lead a new life.

===Chinese===
于是我告他：他当把这梦视作警戒，而非谶语；我们的得救，不系于一时的言与行，而系于一生的习与行；总之，他若当即弃绝那班损友与恶习，坚定地守住一条清醒、勤勉、敬虔的人生之路，那黑暗之权势要索取他的灵魂，亦是徒然——因为有比人口所能发的更高、更坚的凭据，许下救恩给那悔改而行新生之人。

===Original===
I left him much comforted, and with a promise to return upon the next day. I did so, and found him much more cheerful and without any remains of the dogged sullenness which I suppose had arisen from his despair. His promises of amendment were given in that tone of deliberate earnestness, which belongs to deep and solemn determination; and it was with no small delight that I observed, after repeated visits, that his good resolutions, so far from failing, did but gather strength by time; and when I saw that man shake off the idle and debauched companions, whose society had for years formed alike his amusement and his ruin, and revive his long discarded habits of industry and sobriety, I said within myself, there is something more in all this than the operation of an idle dream.

One day, sometime after his perfect restoration to health, I was surprised on ascending the stairs, for the purpose of visiting this man, to find him busily employed in nailing down some planks upon the landing-place, through which, at the commencement of his mysterious vision, it seemed to him that he had sunk. I perceived at once that he was strengthening the floor with a view to securing himself against such a catastrophe, and could scarcely forbear a smile as I bid "God bless his work."

He perceived my thoughts, I suppose, for he immediately said:

===Chinese===
我留他得着不少安慰，许诺次日再来。我果然去了，见他心境爽朗得多，全无先前那副执拗沉郁之态——我想那沉郁原是从绝望里生出来的。他改过之诺，是以一种从容恳切的口吻道出的——那种口吻唯属于深沉而庄重的决心。我屡屡往访之后，欣喜地看见他的善念非但不衰，反与时俱增；及至我看见那人摆脱了那班游手好闲、纵酒荒唐的旧伴——他们的交游多年来既是他消遣，又是他祸殃——又拾起久已弃置的勤勉与清醒的旧习，我便心下自语：这一切之中，必有胜过一个闲梦之力者。

一日，在他完全康复之后不久，我登楼去探他，却见他正忙着在那歇脚平台上钉几块木板——他起初坠入玄梦之时，似即是从那处楼板陷落下去的。我一看便知，他是在加固那楼板，以防再有同类之变；我几乎忍俊不禁，含笑祝他"上帝佑其工事"。

我想他看出了我的心绪，便立时说道：

===Original===
"I can never pass over that floor without trembling. I'd leave this house if I could, but I can't find another lodging in the town so cheap, and I'll not take a better till I've paid off all my debts, please God; but I could not be asy in my mind till I made it as safe as I could. You'll hardly believe me, your honour, that while I'm working, maybe a mile away, my heart is in a flutter the whole way back, with the bare thoughts of the two little steps I have to walk upon this bit of a floor. So it's no wonder, sir, I'd thry to make it sound and firm with any idle timber I have."

I applauded his resolution to pay off his debts, and the steadiness with which he perused his plans of conscientious economy, and passed on.

===Chinese===
"我每回走过那楼板，没有一回不打颤。若能搬离这屋子，我早搬了；可镇上再也寻不着比这更便宜的住处，我也无意寻更好的——待我把欠下的债一笔笔还清了，那才叫好，上帝愿意；可我心里总不踏实，非得把它弄得越稳越牢不可。您只怕不肯信，老爷，我在外头做活，也许离这儿一英里之遥，可一想到回来还要在那两步小楼板上踏过，心便扑通扑通直跳，一路跳到家里。所以，先生，我自然要拣些零碎木板，把它弄得又结实又稳当。"

我赞他偿债的决心，以及他恪守那出于良心之节俭计划的坚毅，便过去了。

===Original===
Many months elapsed, and still there appeared no alteration in his resolutions of amendment. He was a good workman, and with his better habits he recovered his former extensive and profitable employment. Everything seemed to promise comfort and respectability. I have little more to add, and that shall be told quickly. I had one evening met Pat Connell, as he returned from his work, and as usual, after a mutual, and on his side respectful salutation, I spoke a few words of encouragement and approval. I left him industrious, active, healthy﻿—when next I saw him, not three days after, he was a corpse.

The circumstances which marked the event of his death were somewhat strange﻿—I might say fearful. The unfortunate man had accidentally met an early friend just returned, after a long absence, and in a moment of excitement, forgetting everything in the warmth of his joy, he yielded to his urgent invitation to accompany him into a public-house, which lay close by the spot where the encounter had taken place. Connell, however, previously to entering the room, had announced his determination to take nothing more than the strictest temperance would warrant.

But oh! who can describe the inveterate tenacity with which a drunkard's habits cling to him through life? He may repent﻿—he may reform﻿—he may look with actual abhorrence upon his past profligacy; but amid all this reformation and compunction, who can tell the moment in which the base and ruinous propensity may not recur, triumphing over resolution, remorse, shame, everything, and prostrating its victim once more in all that is destructive and revolting in that fatal vice?

===Chinese===
数月过去，他改过之志仍不见有丝毫动摇。他是个好工匠，随着旧习的复返，昔日那广泛而获利的营生亦随之而复。一切似都预示着安乐与体面。我所余要补的已不多，且可匆匆道尽。某日傍晚，我遇见帕特·康奈尔从工地上回来；彼此寒暄——他照例恭而敬之——之后，我如常说了几句勉励嘉许之语。我离开他时，他勤勉、活泼、康健——待我下次见他，不出三日，他已是一具尸首。

标识他身亡一事的几桩情形，颇有些奇异——我几乎可以说可怖。这不幸的人，偶然遇见一位阔别多年、方才归来的旧友；一时情动，忘乎所以，竟应了他殷殷之邀，陪他走进近旁一家酒肆——就在相遇之地紧隔壁。然而康奈尔未入座之前，已先声言：他此次所饮，绝不超过最严格之节制所许的限度。

可嗟！谁人能描摹一个醉汉之习，一生之中是如何根深蒂固、纠缠不去？他或可悔悟——或可自新——或可怀着真切的憎恶回望昔日的荒唐；可在这一切自新与悔痛之间，谁又能料定那一刻——那下贱而毁灭性的癖好猝然复萌，凌驾于决心、悔痛、羞耻以及一切之上，将其牺牲品再一次按倒在那致命恶习之中一切毁人、一切令人作呕之物的脚下？

===Original===
The wretched man left the place in a state of utter intoxication. He was brought home nearly insensible, and placed in his bed, where he lay in the deep calm lethargy of drunkenness. The younger part of the family retired to rest much after their usual hour; but the poor wife remained up sitting by the fire, too much grieved and shocked at the occurrence of what she had so little expected, to settle to rest; fatigue, however, at length overcame her, and she sank gradually into an uneasy slumber. She could not tell how long she had remained in this state, when she awakened, and immediately on opening her eyes, she perceived by the faint red light of the smouldering turf embers, two persons, one of whom she recognised as her husband, noiselessly gliding out of the room.

"Pat, darling, where are you going?" said she. There was no answer﻿—the door closed after them; but in a moment she was startled and terrified by a loud and heavy crash, as if some ponderous body had been hurled down the stair. Much alarmed, she started up, and going to the head of the staircase, she called repeatedly upon her husband, but in vain. She returned to the room, and with the assistance of her daughter, whom I had occasion to mention before, she succeeded in finding and lighting a candle, with which she hurried again to the head of the staircase.

At the bottom lay what seemed to be a bundle of clothes, heaped together, motionless, lifeless﻿—it was her husband. In going down the stair, for what purpose can never now be known, he had fallen helplessly and violently to the bottom, and coming head foremost, the spine at the neck had been dislocated by the shock, and instant death must have ensued. The body lay upon that landing-place to which his dream had referred. It is scarcely worth endeavouring to clear up a single point in a narrative where all is mystery; yet I could not help suspecting that the second figure which had been seen in the room by Connell's wife on the night of his death, might have been no other than his own shadow. I suggested this solution of the difficulty; but she told me that the unknown person had been considerably in advance of the other, and on reaching the door, had turned back as if to communicate something to his companion. It was then a mystery.

===Chinese===
那苦命人离了酒肆之时，已是酩酊大醉之至。人几乎是抬他回家，半昏半醒地放上床；他躺在那儿，沉入醉酒之人那种深沉恬静的昏睡之中。家中年幼的几个，比平日迟了许多方才就寝；那可怜的妻子却独自守在火边——她万不料会有此一变，悲恸震惊之下，无法安息；然疲乏到底胜了她，她渐沉入一段不安的睡眠。她说不清自己睡了多久，便醒了；一睁眼，借着那行将熄灭的泥炭余烬所发的微弱红光，看见两个人——其中一个她认出是她的丈夫——悄无声息地溜出屋去。

"帕特，亲爱的，你去哪儿？"她问道。无人作答——门在他们身后关上了；可不多时她便被一声又沉又闷的巨响吓得魂飞天外——仿佛有什么沉重之物被从楼梯上一路掷下。她大惊之下跃起身，奔到楼梯口，一遍遍唤她丈夫的名字——却无人应。她回到屋里，在那女儿——即我前文曾提过的那一位——的帮衬下，寻见并点起一支蜡烛，又慌忙奔回楼梯口。

最底下一层，堆着一团衣裳似的东西，纹丝不动、毫无生息——那正是她的丈夫。他下楼究竟所为何事，再无人能知晓；他失足跌落，又狠又重，一路栽到底；头先着地，颈上的脊椎一震之间便已脱臼，立时毙命。尸身正卧在那个他在梦中所指的歇脚平台之上。这叙事之中，处处皆是谜团，再去廓清一二点，已属无谓；然我不禁疑心：康奈尔之妻在丈夫亡故之夜于室内所见的第二个人影，或不过是他自家的影子。我把这一解法道出；她却告我，那未明之人较另一人着实在前数步；及至到了门口，又回过头来，似要与其同伴说些什么。此事遂成一谜。

===Original===
Was the dream verified?﻿—whither had the disembodied spirit sped?﻿—who can say? We know not. But I left the house of death that day in a state of horror which I could not describe. It seemed to me that I was scarce awake. I heard and saw everything as if under the spell of a nightmare. The coincidence was terrible.

===Chinese===
那梦可曾应验？——那脱窍的魂魄飞向何方？——谁能说？我们不知。可那一日我离那死人之宅时，心头所压的恐怖，非笔墨所能状。我只觉自家恍若未醒。所见所闻一切，皆如被梦魇的咒所制。那巧合，可怖之至。

## Jim Sulivan's Adventures in the Great Snow Being a Ninth Extract from the Legacy of the Late Francis Purcell, P.P. of Drumcoolagh. / 吉姆·苏利文的大雪奇遇——已故德鲁姆库拉（Drumcoolagh）教区神父（P.P.）弗朗西斯·珀塞尔（Francis Purcell）遗稿之第九则摘录

===Original===
Jim Sulivan was a dacent, honest boy as you'd find in the seven parishes, an' he was a beautiful singer, an' an illegant dancer intirely, an' a mighty plisant boy in himself; but he had the divil's bad luck, for he married for love, an 'av coorse he niver had an asy minute afther.
Nell Gorman was the girl he fancied, an' a beautiful slip of a girl she was, jist twinty to the minute when he married her. She was as round an' as complate in all her shapes as a firkin, you'd think, an' her two cheeks was as fat an' as red, it id open your heart to look at them.
But beauty is not the thing all through, an' as beautiful as she was she had the divil's tongue, an' the divil's timper, an' the divil's behaviour all out; an' it was impossible for him to be in the house with her for while you'd count tin without havin' an argymint, an' as sure as she riz an argymnt with him she'd hit him a wipe iv a skillet or whatever lay next to her hand.
Well, this wasn't at all plasin' to Jim Sulivan you may be sure, an' there was scarce a week that his head wasn't plasthered up, or his back bint double, or his nose swelled as big as a pittaty, with the vilence iv her timper, an' his heart was scalded everlastin'ly with her tongue; so he had no pace or quietness in body or soul at all at all, with the way she was goin' an.

===Chinese===
吉姆·苏利文（Jim Sulivan）是方圆七个堂区里头数得上的本分老实汉子，他嗓子好，唱起歌来动人，跳起舞来更是利落漂亮，脾性也随和可亲；偏偏他倒霉透顶——他是为着爱情成的亲，自然，打那以后就没过过一天安生日子。
他相中的姑娘叫内尔·戈尔曼（Nell Gorman），是个水灵灵的俏丫头，成亲那年刚满二十，生得周周正正、该胖的地方胖、该瘦的地方瘦，像只小木桶似的；两颊又红又圆，叫人看着就打心眼里欢喜。
可模样俊俏并不能当饭吃，她生得虽美，嘴皮子却毒得要命，脾气也坏得出奇，举止更是撒泼惯了的；吉姆和她同在一个屋檐下，你数不到十她便要挑起一场口角，而只要她起了口角，跟着便是顺手抄起平底锅——或是手边够得着的什么东西——朝他砸过来。
这一来，吉姆·苏利文心里自然老大不痛快，这是可想而知的；几乎每个礼拜，他不是头上缠着绷带，就是腰背疼得直不起来，再不然鼻子肿得像个土豆——全是拜她那暴脾气所赐；她那张嘴更把他的心都磨出了老茧；于是他浑身上下、里里外外，再没有半点太平清静，全是叫她闹的。

===Original===
Well, your honour, one cowld snowin' evenin' he kim in afther his day's work regulatin' the men in the farm, an' he sat down very quite by the fire, for he had a scrimmidge with her in the mornin', an' all he wanted was an air iv the fire in pace; so divil a word he said but dhrew a stool an' sat down close to the fire. Well, as soon as the woman saw him,
"Move aff," says she, "an' don't be inthrudin' an the fire," says she.
Well, he kept never mindin', an' didn't let an' to hear a word she was sayin', so she kem over an' she had a spoon in her hand, an' she took jist the smallest taste in life iv the boilin' wather out iv the pot, an' she dhropped it down an his shins, an' with that he let a roar you'd think the roof id fly aff iv the house.
"Hould your tongue, you barbarrian," says she; "you'll waken the child," says she.
"An' if I done right," says he, for the spoonful of boilin' wather riz him entirely, "I'd take yourself," says he, "an' I'd stuff you into the pot an the fire, an' boil you," says he, "into castor oil," says he.
"That's purty behavour," says she; "it's fine usage you're givin' me, isn't it?" says she, gettin' wickeder every minute; "but before I'm boiled," says she, "thry how you like *that*," says she; an', sure enough, before he had time to put up his guard, she hot him a rale terrible clink iv the iron spoon acrass the jaw.
"Hould me, some iv ye, or I'll murdher her," says he.
"Will you?" says she, an' with that she hot him another tin times as good as the first.
"By jabers," says he, slappin' himself behind, "that's the last salute you'll ever give me," says he; "so take my last blessin'," says he, "you ungovernable baste!" says he—an' with that he pulled an his hat an' walked out iv the door.

===Chinese===
话说，老爷，有个下雪的傍晚，他在农庄里指派完长工们一天的活儿回到家里，悄悄地在火炉边坐下——清早他跟她拌过几句嘴，这会儿只想图个清静，烤烤火；于是他一言不发，拖过一张小凳，紧挨着炉火坐下。哪知那女人一瞧见他——
"滚开，"她说道，"别在这儿碍手碍脚地挤着火，"她说。
他权当没听见，装作她一个字也没说；她便走过来，手里拿着一把勺子，从锅里舀了那么一丁点儿滚开的水，滴在他小腿上——这一下他嗷的一声嚎起来，您准以为那房顶都要给掀飞了。
"闭嘴，你这个野蛮人，"她说道；"会把孩子吵醒的，"她说。
"我要是做得对，"他说道——那一勺滚水把他整个人都激起来了——"我就该把你，"他说，"塞进锅里架在火上，把你煮成蓖麻油，"他说。
"好哇，这话说得真好听，"她说道；"你可真会疼我，是不是？"她说着，火气一秒大过一秒；"不过在我被煮之前，"她说，"你先尝尝这个，"她说；果不其然，他还来不及招架，她一铁勺就结结实实敲在他下巴上，打得那叫一个狠。
"谁来拉我一把，不然我要把她宰了，"他说道。
"你敢？"她说道，跟着又是十倍于头一下的狠劲，又敲了他一下。
"我的老天爷，"他一巴掌拍在自己后屁股上，说道，"这是你给我的最后一个吻了，"他说；"那就收下我这最后的祝福吧，"他说，"你这管不住的畜生！"他说——说着，他一把扣上帽子，径直走出了门。

===Original===
Well, she never minded a word he said, for he used to say the same thing all as one every time she dhrew blood; an' she had no expectation at all but he'd be back by the time supper id be ready; but faix the story didn't go quite so simple this time, for while he was walkin', lonesome enough, down the borheen, with his heart almost broke with the pain, for his shins an' his jaw was mighty troublesome, av course, with the thratement he got, who did he see but Mick Hanlon, his uncle's sarvint by, ridin' down, quite an asy, an the ould black horse, with a halter as long as himself.
"Is that Mr. Soolivan?" says the by, says he, as soon as he saw him a good bit aff.
"To be sure it is, ye spalpeen, you," says Jim, roarin' out; "what do you want wid me this time a-day?" says he.
"Don't you know me?" says the gossoon, "it's Mick Hanlon that's in it," says he.
"Oh, blur an agers, thin, it's welcome you are, Micky asthore," says Jim; "how is all wid the man an' the woman beyant?" says he.
"Oh!" says Micky, "bad enough," says he; "the ould man's jist aff, an' if you don't hurry like shot," says he, "he'll be in glory before you get there," says he.
"It's jokin' ye are," says Jim, sorrowful enough, for he was mighty partial to his uncle intirely.
"Oh, not in the smallest taste," says Micky; "the breath was jist out iv him," says he, "when I left the farm. 'An',' says he, 'take the ould black horse,' says he, 'for he's shure-footed for the road,' says he, 'an' bring Jim Soolivan here,' says he, 'for I think I'd die asy af I could see him onst,' says he."
"Well," says Jim, "will I have time," says he, "to go back to the house, for it would be a consolation," says he, "to tell the bad news to the woman?" says he.
"It's too late you are already," says Micky, "so come up behind me, for God's sake," says he, "an' don't waste time;" an' with that he brought the horse up beside the ditch, an' Jim Soolivan mounted up behind Micky, an' they rode off; an' tin good miles it was iv a road, an' at the other side iv Keeper intirely; an' it was snowin' so fast that the ould baste could hardly go an at all at all, an' the two bys an his back was jist like a snowball all as one, an' almost fruz an' smothered at the same time, your honour; an' they wor both mighty sorrowful intirely, an' their toes almost dhroppin' aff wid the could.
And when Jim got to the farm his uncle was gettin' an illegantly, an' he was sittin' up sthrong an' warm in the bed, an' improvin' every minute, an' no signs av dyin' an him at all at all; so he had all his throuble for nothin'.
But this wasn't all, for the snow kem so thick that it was impassible to get along the roads at all at all; an' faix, instead iv gettin' betther, next mornin' it was only tin times worse; so Jim had jist to take it asy, an' stay wid his uncle antil such times as the snow id melt.

===Chinese===
那么，他那些话她一个字也没往心里去，因为每逢她打得他见血，他都是这一套说辞；她也只当他不消到吃晚饭的时辰便会回来；可这一回的事儿，偏没有那么顺当。原来他正孤零零地顺着那条小巷子往前走，心疼得几乎要碎了——小腿和下巴疼得厉害，受了那样一番"款待"，自是难免——谁知迎面竟遇见了米克·汉伦（Mick Hanlon），他伯父家那个雇工的小厮，正骑着那匹老黑马，稳稳当当、不慌不忙地过来，手里还牵着一条比他人还长的笼头绳。
"是苏利文少爷吗？"那小厮隔着老远便喊道，他一瞧见他影儿。
"可不就是我吗，你这小浑蛋，"吉姆扯着嗓子吼道；"这大白天的我有什么事儿？"他说。
"您不认得我啦？"那小厮说，"我是米克·汉伦呀，"他说。
"哎呀，活见鬼，那可太好了，亲爱的米克，"吉姆说道；"家里那两位老人家可好？"他问。
"唉！"米克说道，"好不哪儿去，"他说；"老人家刚咽气，您要是不像放枪一样飞奔回去，"他说，"只怕还没等到，他老人家已经升天啦，"他说。
"你莫不是在说笑吧，"吉姆说道，心头颇为沉痛，因为他一向最是亲近这位伯父。
"哎呀，一星半点儿也不是说笑，"米克说道；"我离开农庄那工夫，"他说，"他刚没了气儿。'还有，'他说，'牵那匹老黑马去，'他说，'它脚程稳，赶路靠得住，'他说，'把吉姆·苏利文带来，'他说，'我想着我能见他一面，死也瞑目了，'他说。"
"那么，"吉姆说道，"我还有工夫，"他说，"回家一趟不？也好把这坏消息，"他说，"跟那女人说一声？"他问。
"您已经迟啦，"米克说道，"看在上帝份上，快上来坐我后头吧，"他说，"别耽搁了；"说着他把马牵到沟渠边上，吉姆·苏利文便翻身坐到米克身后，两人策马而去；那是整整十英里的好路，而且全在基珀山（Keeper）的那一头；雪下得那个急呀，那匹老牲口几乎寸步难行，马背上两个汉子浑身上下裹满了雪，活脱脱像一只滚成的大雪球，又冻又闷，几乎喘不过气来，老爷；他俩心里头都沉重得很，脚趾头都快给冻掉了。
可等吉姆赶到农庄，他伯父竟正精神抖擞地见好，在床上坐得又稳又暖，一刻比一刻见起色，一点儿要死的迹象都没有；于是他这一趟算是白忙活了。
可这还不算完，雪下得太大，路上根本没法通行；而且，老天爷，非但没见好转，第二天早晨反倒比先前更糟了十倍；于是吉姆只好既来之则安之，留在伯父家里，等着雪化。

===Original===
Well, your honour, the evenin' Jim Soolivan wint away, whin the dark was closin' in, Nell Gorman, his wife, beginned to get mighty anasy in herself whin she didn't see him comin' back at all; an' she was gettin' more an' more frightful in herself every minute till the dark kem an', an' divil a taste iv her husband was coming at all at all.
"Oh!" says she, "there's no use in purtendin', I know he's kilt himself; he has committed infantycide an himself," says she, "like a dissipated bliggard as he always was," says she, "God rest his soul. Oh, thin, isn't it me an' not you, Jim Soolivan, that's the unforthunate woman," says she, "for ain't I cryin' here, an' isn't he in heaven, the bliggard," says she. "Oh, voh, voh, it's not at home comfortable with your wife an' family that you are, Jim Soolivan," says she, "but in the other world, you aumathaun, in glory wid the saints I hope," says she. "It's I that's the unforthunate famale," says she, "an' not yourself, Jim Soolivan," says she.
An' this way she kep' an till mornin', cryin' and lamintin; an' wid the first light she called up all the sarvint bys, an' she tould them to go out an' to sarch every inch iv ground to find the corpse, "for I'm sure," says she, "it's not to go hide himself he would," says she.

===Chinese===
话说，老爷，吉姆·苏利文走掉的那个傍晚，天色将黑未黑的时候，他妻子内尔·戈尔曼见他迟迟不归，心里便开始七上八下地不安生起来；她越想越发毛，天色越黑，心里越发毛，可她那个丈夫，连个影儿都没有。
"哎呀！"她说道，"装也没用了，我知道他是寻了短见啦；他把自己给结果啦，"她说道，"就像他一向那样的，一个没出息的泼皮，"她说，"愿上帝宽恕他的灵魂。唉，可不是我，而不是你，吉姆·苏利文，才是那个苦命的女人哪，"她说道，"我不在这儿哭吗？他倒好，上了天堂啦，那个泼皮，"她说。"唉，呜呜呜，你哪儿是舒舒服服地在家里守着老婆孩子呀，吉姆·苏利文，"她说道，"你是到了那另一个世界去了呀，你这个没良心的，但愿你正和圣人们一起享着荣光哪，"她说。"苦命的是我呀，"她说道，"不是我那个苦命的丈夫，吉姆·苏利文，"她说。
她就这么一把鼻涕一把眼泪地哭嚎到天亮；天刚一亮，她便把家里所有的雇工都叫了起来，吩咐他们出去，把每一寸地皮都翻个遍，把尸首找出来——"因为我知道，"她说道，"他绝不是自己躲起来的那种人，"她说。

===Original===
Well, they went as well as they could, rummagin' through the snow, antil, at last, what should they come to, sure enough, but the corpse of a poor thravelling man, that fell over the quarry the night before by rason of the snow and some liquor he had, maybe; but, at any rate, he was as dead as a herrin', an' his face was knocked all to pieces jist like an over-boiled pitaty, glory be to God; an' divil a taste iv a nose or a chin, or a hill or a hollow from one end av his face to the other but was all as flat as a pancake. An' he was about Jim Soolivan's size, an' dhressed out exactly the same, wid a ridin' coat an' new corderhoys; so they carried him home, an' they were all as sure as daylight it was Jim Soolivan himself, an' they were wondhering he'd do sich a dirty turn as to go kill himself for spite.
Well, your honour, they waked him as well as they could, with what neighbours they could git togither, but by rason iv the snow, there wasn't enough gothered to make much divarsion; however it was a plisint wake enough, an' the churchyard an' the priest bein' convanient, as soon as the youngsthers had their bit iv fun and divarsion out iv the corpse, they burried it without a great dale iv throuble; an' about three days afther the berrin, ould Jim Mallowney, from th'other side iv the little hill, her own cousin by the mother's side—he had a snug bit iv a farm an' a house close by, by the same token—kem walkin' in to see how she was in her health, an' he dhrew a chair, an' he sot down an' beginned to convarse her about one thing an' another, antil he got her quite an' asy into middlin' good humour, an' as soon as he seen it was time:
"I'm wondherin'," says he, "Nell Gorman, sich a handsome, likely girl, id be thinkin' iv nothin' but lamintin' an' the likes," says he, "an' lingerin' away her days without any consolation, or gettin' a husband," says he.
"Oh," says she, "isn't it only three days since I burried the poor man," says she, "an' isn't it rather soon to be talkin iv marryin' agin?" says she.
"Divil a taste," says he, "three days is jist the time to a minute for cryin' afther a husband, an' there's no occasion in life to be keepin' it up," says he; "an' besides all that," says he, "Shrovetide is almost over, an' if you don't be sturrin' yourself an' lookin' about you, you'll be late," says he, "for this year at any rate, an' that's twelve months lost; an' who's to look afther the farm all that time," says he, "an' to keep the men to their work?" says he.
"It's thrue for you, Jim Mallowney," says she, "but I'm afeard the neighbours will be all talkin' about it," says she.
"Divil's cure to the word," says he.
"An' who would you advise?" says she.
"Young Andy Curtis is the boy," says he.
"He's a likely boy in himself," says she.
"An' as handy a gossoon as is out," says he.
"Well, thin, Jim Mallowney," says she, "here's my hand, an' you may be talkin' to Andy Curtis, an' if he's willin' I'm agreeble—is that enough?" says she.

===Chinese===
于是他们能怎么找就怎么找，在雪堆里翻来翻去，最后，果不其然，竟然真找着一具尸首——是个可怜的过路客，大约是头天夜里因为大雪，又加上灌了些黄汤，从采石场边上摔下去的；不管怎么说，他是死得透透的了，脸摔得稀烂，活像一只煮过头的土豆，赞美上帝；从他这张脸的这一头到那一头，鼻子也扁、下巴也扁，坑洼全无，一马平川，全像摊薄饼似的。再者他的身量跟吉姆·苏利文相仿，穿戴也一模一样——一件骑马外套，一条崭新的灯芯绒裤子；于是他们便把他抬了回去，一个个都信誓旦旦地以为这就是吉姆·苏利文本人，都纳闷他怎么会做出这种卑鄙事，竟为了赌气去寻了短见。
话说，老爷，他们尽量凑合着给他守了灵，左邻右舍能请到的都请了，可因为大雪的缘故，到场的人不多，也闹不出多少热闹来；不过这场守灵倒也算过得去，加上坟地近、神父也方便，小伙子们从尸首身上找完他们那点乐子和热闹之后，没费多大周折便把他给葬了；下葬之后约莫三天，小山那边的老吉姆·马洛尼（Jim Mallowney）——她娘家那头的表兄——他有一小块安逸的田产，还有一处宅子就在近旁，顺便提一句——走进来看望她身子可好，他拖过一把椅子坐下，便东拉西扯地跟她聊起这聊起那，直到把她哄得心情颇为舒畅，一见火候到了：
"我倒是纳闷，"他说道，"内尔·戈尔曼，你这么个标致体面的姑娘，"他说，"怎会成天除了哭丧就不想别的，"他说，"白白蹉跎着日子，既不找个依靠，也不肯再嫁个人，"他说。
"哎呀，"她说道，"我那可怜的人才下葬三天哪，"她说，"这么快就谈再嫁，是不是太早了些？"她问。
"早个屁，"他说道，"哭丈夫，三天刚刚好，一分不多一分不少，再哭下去就完全没必要了，"他说；"再说，"他说，"狂欢节（Shrovetide）眼看就要过完了，你要是不赶紧活动活动、四处张罗张罗，"他说，"今年至少是赶不上了，"他说，"那可就白白耽误了十二个月；这十二个月里，谁来照看农庄，"他说，"谁来管着那些长工干活？"他问。
"你说得也是，吉姆·马洛尼，"她说道，"就怕邻里们都要说闲话，"她说。
"他们爱说什么，让他们说去，"他说道。
"那你瞧着谁合适？"她问。
"小安迪·柯蒂斯（Andy Curtis）那小伙子就挺好，"他说道。
"小伙子人倒是不错，"她说道。
"手脚又勤快，十里八乡也挑不出第二个，"他说。
"那么好吧，吉姆·马洛尼，"她说道，"一言为定，"她说着伸出手去，"你可以去跟安迪·柯蒂斯提一提，他要是愿意，我没意见——这样够了吧？"她问。

===Original===
So with that he made off with himself straight to Andy Curtis; an' before three days more was past, the weddin' kem an', an' Nell Gorman an' Andy Curtis was married as complate as possible; an' if the wake was plisint the weddin' was tin times as agreeble, an' all the neighbours that could make their way to it was there, an' there was three fiddlers an' lots iv pipers, an' ould Connor Shamus6 the piper himself was in it—by the same token it was the last weddin' he ever played music at, for the next mornin', whin he was goin' home, bein' mighty hearty an' plisint in himself, he was smothered in the snow, undher the ould castle; an' by my sowl he was a sore loss to the bys an' girls twenty miles round, for he was the illigantest piper, barrin' the liquor alone, that ever worked a bellas.
Well, a week passed over smart enough, an' Nell an' her new husband was mighty well continted with one another, for it was too soon for her to begin to regulate him the way she used with poor Jim Soolivan, so they wor comfortable enough; but this was too good to last, for the thaw kem an', an' you may be sure Jim Soolivan didn't lose a minute's time as soon as the heavy dhrift iv snow was melted enough between him and home to let him pass, for he didn't hear a word iv news from home sinst he lift it, by rason that no one, good nor bad, could thraval at all, with the way the snow was dhrifted.

===Chinese===
于是他立马动身，径直去找安迪·柯蒂斯；没过三天，婚事便办起来了，内尔·戈尔曼和安迪·柯蒂斯风风光光地成了亲；守灵若是热闹，这场婚礼便热闹十倍，能赶来的邻里悉数到场，席间有三个提琴手、好几个风笛手，连老风笛手康纳·谢默斯（Connor Shamus）也亲自来了——顺便说一句，这是他生平最后一次在婚礼上吹奏，因为第二天早晨他回家的时候，兴致正高、心情正好，竟在古堡底下被大雪活活闷死了；老天在上，方圆二十里的小伙子和大姑娘们没有不为他心疼的，因为论吹风笛，他可算头一把好手——除了贪杯这一桩毛病之外——再没有谁像他那样会鼓捣风箱的了。
一星期过得飞快，内尔和她新丈夫你恩我爱，十分融洽，因为日子尚浅，她还来不及像整治可怜的吉姆·苏利文那样整治他，所以日子还算太平；可这种好日子长不了，因为雪开始化了，雪一化，您可以想见，吉姆·苏利文是一刻也不会耽误的，只要挡在他和家之间的那道厚厚的雪堆化得能让人通行，他便立刻动身——因为自打他离家，家里没传过来半点音信，这全怪雪堆得太厚，不论好人歹人，谁都别想挪动半步。

===Original===
So one night, when Nell Gorman an' her new husband, Andy Curtis, was snug an' warm in bed, an' fast asleep, an' everything quite, who should come to the door, sure enough, but Jim Soolivan himself, an' he beginned flakin' the door wid a big blackthorn stick he had, an' roarin' out like the divil to open the door, for he had a dhrop taken.
"What the divil's the matther?" says Andy Curtis, wakenin' out iv his sleep.
"Who's batin' the door?" says Nell; "what's all the noise for?" says she.
"Who's in it?" says Andy.
"It's me," says Jim.
"Who are you?" says Andy; "what's your name?"
"Jim Soolivan," says he.
"By jabers, you lie," says Andy.
"Wait till I get at you," says Jim, hittin' the door a lick iv the wattle you'd hear half a mile off.
"It's him, sure enough," says Nell; "I know his speech; it's his wandherin' sowl that can't get rest, the crass o' Christ betune us an' harm."
"Let me in," says Jim, "or I'll dhrive the door in a top iv yis."
"Jim Soolivan—Jim Soolivan," says Nell, sittin' up in the bed, an' gropin' for a quart bottle iv holy wather she used to hang by the back iv the bed, "don't come in, darlin'—there's holy wather here," says she; "but tell me from where you are is there anything that's throublin' your poor sinful sowl?" says she. "An' tell me how many masses 'ill make you asy, an' by this crass, I'll buy you as many as you want," says she.
"I don't know what the divil you mane," says Jim.
"Go back," says she, "go back to glory, for God's sake," says she.
"Divil's cure to the bit iv me 'ill go back to glory, or anywhere else," says he, "this blessed night; so open the door at onst' an' let me in," says he.
"The Lord forbid," says she.
"By jabers, you'd betther," says he, "or it 'ill be the worse for you," says he; an' wid that he fell to wallopin' the door till he was fairly tired, an' Andy an' his wife crassin' themselves an' sayin' their prayers for the bare life all the time.
"Jim Soolivan," says she, as soon as he was done, "go back, for God's sake, an' don't be freakenin' me an' your poor fatherless childhren," says she.
"Why, you bosthoon, you," says Jim, "won't you let your husband in," says he, "to his own house?" says he.
"You *wor* my husband, sure enough," says she, "but it's well you know, Jim Soolivan, you're not my husband *now*," says she.
"You're as dhrunk as can be consaved," says Jim.
"Go back, in God's name, pacibly to your grave," says Nell.
"By my soul, it's to my grave you'll sind me, sure enough," says he, "you hardhearted bain', for I'm jist aff wid the cowld," says he.
"Jim Sulivan," says she, "it's in your dacent coffin you should be, you unforthunate sperit," says she; "what is it's annoyin' your sowl, in the wide world, at all?" says she; "hadn't you everything complate?" says she, "the oil, an' the wake, an' the berrin'?" says she.
"Och, by the hoky," says Jim, "it's too long I'm makin' a fool iv mysilf, gostherin' wid you outside iv my own door," says he, "for it's plain to be seen," says he, "you don't know what your're sayin', an' no one *else* knows what you mane, you unforthunate fool," says he; "so, onst for all, open the door quietly," says he, "or, by my sowkins, I'll not lave a splinther together," says he.

===Chinese===
于是在一天夜里，内尔·戈尔曼和她新丈夫安迪·柯蒂斯正暖暖和和、舒舒服服地躺在床上，睡得正熟，四下里静悄悄的——果不其然，除了吉姆·苏利文本人，还有谁会找上门来？他抄起一根粗黑刺木棍子，劈头盖脸地敲那门，又像魔鬼附身似的扯着嗓子吼"开门"，因为他灌了几口黄汤。
"出什么鬼事了？"安迪·柯蒂斯从睡梦中惊醒，说道。
"谁在砸门？"内尔说道；"嚷嚷什么呢？"她问。
"外头是谁？"安迪问。
"是我，"吉姆说道。
"你是谁？"安迪问，"你叫什么名字？"
"吉姆·苏利文，"他说道。
"见鬼，你胡扯，"安迪说道。
"等我进去收拾你，"吉姆说道，抡起棍子狠狠敲了门一下，那响声半里地外都听得见。
"是他，没错，"内尔说道；"我听得出他的腔调；是他那游荡不安的灵魂，基督的十字架保佑我们别遭祸事。"
"让我进去，"吉姆说道，"不然我把这门连框砸到你们头顶上。"
"吉姆·苏利文——吉姆·苏利文，"内尔从床上坐起来，伸手去摸床背后她常挂的那一小瓶圣水，说道，"别进来，亲爱的——我这儿有圣水，"她说；"可你站在那儿告诉我，是不是有什么事在折磨你那可怜有罪的灵魂？"她问。"告诉我做几台弥撒能让你安息，我对着这十字架发誓，你要多少台我给你买多少台，"她说。
"我哪知道你见鬼的在说什么，"吉姆说道。
"回去吧，"她说道，"看在上帝份上，回你的天堂去吧，"她说。
"我见鬼的哪儿也不去，既不回天堂，也不去别的什么地方，"他说道，"今儿个这大好夜里；所以马上把门打开，让我进去，"他说。
"主啊，万万不可，"她说道。
"老天在上，你最好识相点，"他说道，"不然有你好看的，"他说；说着他便抡起棍子乒乒乓乓地砸门，直砸到筋疲力尽，安迪和他老婆一整工夫都在画十字、拼了命地念祷告。
"吉姆·苏利文，"等他砸完了，她才说道，"看在上帝份上回去吧，"她说，"别再吓唬我和你那些没爹的可怜孩子们了，"她说。
"嗐，你这蠢货，"吉姆说道，"你不让你丈夫进，"他说，"回他自己的家？"他问。
"你*曾经*是我丈夫，这没错，"她说道，"可你心里也明白，吉姆·苏利文，你*现在*已经不是我的丈夫了，"她说。
"你醉得简直不成样子，"吉姆说道。
"奉上帝的名，你安安生生地回你的坟里去吧，"内尔说道。
"老天在上，是你准会把我送进坟里去，没错，"他说道，"你这个狠心肠的婆娘，我这会儿冻得快不行了，"他说。
"吉姆·苏利文，"她说道，"你本该好好躺在你那体面的棺材里，你这倒霉的游魂，"她说；"到底是在这世上什么事在作弄你的灵魂？"她问；"你什么没备齐？"她问，"圣油也涂了，灵也守了，丧也出了？"她问。
"哎呀，活见鬼，"吉姆说道，"我在自家门口跟你扯这么久的淡，白白像个傻子，"他说，"因为明眼人一看便知，"他说，"你根本不知道自己在说什么，也没*别人*知道你想说什么，你这倒霉的蠢货，"他说；"所以，我最后说一次，乖乖把门打开，"他说，"不然，我对着灵魂起誓，我非把这屋子拆得连一根木片都不剩，"他说。

===Original===
Well, whin Nell an' Andy seen he was getting vexed, they beginned to bawl out their prayers, with the fright, as if the life was lavin' them; an' the more he bate the door, the louder they prayed, until at last Jim was fairly tired out.
"Bad luck to you," says he; "for a rale divil av a woman," says he. I "can't get any advantage av you, any way; but wait till I get hould iv you, that's all," says he. An' he turned aff from the door, an' wint round to the cowhouse, an' settled himself as well as he could, in the sthraw; an' he was tired enough wid the thravellin' he had in the daytime, an' a good dale bothered with what liquor he had taken; so he was purty sure of sleepin' wherever he thrun himself.
But, by my sowl, it wasn't the same way with the man an' the woman in the house—for divil a wink iv sleep, good or bad, could they get at all, wid the fright iv the sperit, as they supposed; an' with the first light they sint a little gossoon, as fast as he could wag, straight off, like a shot, to the priest, an' to desire him, for the love o' God, to come to them an the minute, an' to bring, if it was plasin' to his raverence, all the little things he had for sayin' mass, an' savin' sowls, an' banishin' sperits, an' freakenin' the divil, an' the likes iv that. An' it wasn't long till his raverence kem down, sure enough, on the ould grey mare, wid the little mass-boy behind him, an' the prayer-books an' Bibles, an' all the other mystarious articles that was wantin', along wid him; an' as soon as he kem in, "God save all here," says he.
"God save ye, kindly, your raverence," says they.
"An' what's gone wrong wid ye?" says he; "ye must be very bad," says he, "entirely, to disturb my devotions," says he, "this way, jist at breakfast-time," says he.
"By my sowkins," says Nell, "it's bad enough we are, your raverence," says she, "for it's poor Jim's sperit," says she; "God rest his sowl, wherever it is," says she, "that was wandherin' up an' down, opossite the door all night," says she, "in the way it was no use at all, thryin' to get a wink iv sleep," says she.
"It's to lay it, you want me, I suppose," says the priest.
"If your raverence 'id do that same, it 'id be plasin' to us," says Andy.
"It'll be rather expinsive," says the priest.
"We'll not differ about the price, your raverence," says Andy.
"Did the sperit stop long?" says the priest.
"Most part iv the night," says Nell, "the Lord be merciful to us all!" says she.
"That'll make it more costly than I thought," says he. "An' did it make much noise?" says he.
"By my soul, it's it that did," says Andy; "leatherin' the door wid sticks and stones," says he, "antil I fairly thought every minute," says he, "the ould boords id smash, an' the sperit id be in an top iv us—God bless us," says he.
"Phiew!" says the priest; "it'll cost a power iv money."
"Well, your raverence," says Andy, "take whatever you like," says he; "only make sure it won't annoy us any more," says he.
"Oh! by my sowkins," says the priest, "it'll be the quarest ghost in the siven parishes," says he, "if it has the courage to come back," says he, "afther what I'll do this mornin', plase God," says he; "so we'll say twelve pounds; an' God knows it's chape enough," says he, "considherin' all the sarcumstances," says he.

===Chinese===
那么，内尔和安迪见他动了真火，吓得赶紧扯开嗓子念起祷告来，那架势，活像命都要没了；他越是砸门，他们越是念得起劲，直到最后吉姆实在累得不行了。
"让你倒大霉吧，"他说道；"你这婆娘，真是少有的恶鬼，"他说。"我怎么也占不到你半点上风；不过，等我抓到你再说，"他说。于是他离开门口，绕到牛棚那边去，在稻草堆里尽可能安顿下来；他白天赶了一天的路，实在乏得慌，又因为灌了几口酒，脑袋晕乎乎的；所以这一躺下去，哪儿还管睡得着睡不着，保准睡得跟死猪一样。
可是，老天在上，屋里那汉子与那婆娘可就没这么好过了——因为被那"鬼魂"一吓，他俩是大眼瞪小眼，一宿没合一下眼；天一亮，他们便打发一个小厮，撒腿就跑，像离弦的箭一样，直奔神父那里去，求他看在上帝份上，立马赶到他们家来，并且——若是神父他老人家赏脸——把做弥撒、救灵魂、驱邪祟、镇魔鬼那些零七八碎的小物件都一并带来。没过多久，神父他老人家果然骑着那匹老灰母马赶到了，辅祭的小童坐在他身后，连同祷告书、《圣经》以及一切所需的神秘法器，都带了来；他一进门便道："愿上帝保佑这一家子。"
"多谢您老人家好意，神父，"他们答道。
"你们这是怎么了？"他问道；"你们一定是糟糕透顶了，"他说，"才会这样，"他说，"来搅扰我做晨祷，"他说，"偏偏又赶在吃早饭的时辰，"他说。
"老天在上，"内尔说道，"我们确实糟糕得很，神父，"她说，"因为那是可怜的吉姆的鬼魂呀，"她说；"愿上帝宽恕他的灵魂，无论他如今身在何处，"她说，"他整整一夜在门前晃来晃去，"她说，"闹得我们一丁点儿觉都睡不成，"她说。
"你们是想让我来超度它，我猜，"神父说道。
"您老人家肯赏这个脸，我们就感激不尽了，"安迪说道。
"这可不便宜呢，"神父说道。
"价钱的事好商量，神父，"安迪说道。
"那鬼魂待得久吗？"神父问。
"大半夜呢，"内尔说道，"主啊，发发慈悲吧！"她说。
"那就比我预想的还要贵了，"他说道。"它吵得厉害吗？"他问。
"老天在上，可不是厉害嘛，"安迪说道；"又是棍子又是石头地砸门，"他说，"我每时每刻都在想，"他说，"那几块旧木板就要裂开了，那鬼魂就要扑到我们头上了——上帝保佑，"他说。
"嘶——"神父倒吸一口凉气；"这要花一大笔钱哪。"
"那么，神父，"安迪说道，"您要多少给多少，"他说；"只要保证它不再来作祟就行，"他说。
"哦！老天在上，"神父说道，"那它就是方圆七个堂区里最稀奇的鬼了，"他说，"要是它在我今儿个——上帝保佑——要做完这桩法事之后，"他说，"还敢有胆子回来的话，"他说；"那么我们就说十二镑吧；老天知道，这已经是便宜得不能再便宜了，"他说，"把种种情形都算进去，"他说。

===Original===
Well, there wasn't a second word to the bargain; so they paid him the money down, an' he sot the table doun like an althar, before the door, an' he settled it out wid all the things he had wid him; an' he lit a bit iv a holy candle, an' he scathered his holy wather right an' left; an' he took up a big book, an' he wint an readin' for half an hour, good; an' whin he kem to the end, he tuck hould iv his little bell, and he beginned to ring it for the bare life; an', by my soul, he rung it so well, that he wakened Jim Sulivan in the cowhouse, where he was sleepin', an' up he jumped, widout a minute's delay, an' med right for the house, where all the family, an' the priest, an' the little mass-boy was assimbled, layin' the ghost; an' as soon as his raverence seen him comin' in at the door, wid the fair fright, he flung the bell at his head, an' hot him sich a lick iv it in the forehead, that he sthretched him on the floor; but fain; he didn't wait to ax any questions, but he cut round the table as if the divil was afther him, an' out at the door, an' didn't stop even as much as to mount an his mare, but leathered away down the borheen as fast as his legs could carry him, though the mud was up to his knees, savin' your presence.

===Chinese===
那么，这桩买卖再没人多嘴；他们当下付了钱，他便在门前把桌子摆成祭坛的样子，把他带来的那些物件一一铺排停当；他点起一截圣烛，又把圣水东洒西洒地撒了一遍；他捧起一本厚厚的大书，足足念了半个多钟头；念到末尾，他抓起那只小铃铛，便拼命地摇起来；老天在上，他摇得那叫一个卖力，竟把睡在牛棚里的吉姆·苏利文给吵醒了，他一骨碌爬起来，一刻也不耽误，径直奔向正屋——那儿一家老小、神父、还有那辅祭小童正聚在一处，做那驱鬼的法事；神父他老人家一见他从门口走进来，吓得魂飞魄散，把手里的铃铛朝他脑袋就扔过去，正正地砸在他额头上，一下就把他撂倒在地；可他哪儿还顾得上问什么缘由，绕过桌子就跑，那架势，活像魔鬼正撵在他屁股后头，一头冲出门去，连上马都顾不上，撒开两条腿便顺着那条小巷子飞奔而去，顾不得泥浆没到了膝盖——恕我直言。

===Original===
Well, by the time Jim kem to himself, the family persaved the mistake, an' Andy wint home, lavin' Nell to make the explanation. An' as soon as Jim heerd it all, he said he was quite contint to lave her to Andy, entirely; but the priest would not hear iv it; an' he jist med him marry his wife over again, an' a merry weddin' it was, an' a fine collection for his raverence. An' Andy was there along wid the rest, an' the priest put a small pinnance upon him, for bein' in too great a hurry to marry a widdy.
An' bad luck to the word he'd allow anyone to say an the business, ever after, at all, at all; so, av coorse, no one offinded his raverence, by spakin' iv the twelve pounds he got for layin' the sperit.
An' the neighbours wor all mighty well plased, to be sure, for gettin' all the divarsion of a wake, an' two weddin's for nothin'.

===Chinese===
那么，等吉姆清醒过来，一家人这才发觉闹了乌龙，安迪便回了家，留下内尔来把事情的原委说清楚。吉姆听完这一切，便说他十分乐意把她整个儿让给安迪；可神父死活不依；他硬是叫吉姆把妻子重新娶了一回——那可是一场热热闹闹的婚礼，神父他老人家的钱袋也鼓鼓囊囊地收了一笔。安迪也在场，与众宾客同乐；神父还罚他做了一点小小的补赎，因为他急着娶寡妇，未免太心急了些。
而从此之后，神父绝不容许任何人对这桩事嚼半个字的舌根，一点口风都不许漏；所以自然也没人敢去触他老人家的霉头，提那为了驱鬼收下的十二镑钱。
至于邻里们呢，一个个都乐开了花——这是自然的——白白瞧了一场守灵的热闹，外加两场婚礼，一个子儿不花。

## The Fatal Bride Being a Second Contribution from the Reminiscences of a Bachelor. / 致命新娘——摘自一位单身汉回忆录的第二篇来稿

===Original===
I am now an old man, and, what is perhaps less excusable, an old bachelor too; and yet, sir, I am not a bachelor of malice prepense—I am no professed railer against wedlock. I would not, for my grandmother’s enamel *bonbonniere*, which catches my eye this moment, nor for my honoured uncle’s silver-mounted and inlaid steel barrels—both of them family relics dear in their own several ways—that your fair readers should set me down as guilty of premeditated and deliberate celibacy. No such thing. I have more than once narrowly escaped—I should say *missed*—the fate-matrimonial, and that by pure accident—by no cowardice or perfidy of mine. No; my tendencies were all conjugal—my blessedness, however, has been single; and so far am I from thanking my stars, or taking merit to myself for this state of things, that, sooth to say, even the seventy-and-five winters and summers that have bleached and baked me in succession, still find me, now and then, sighing over the tender recollections and bitter disappointments, which are now for me, the sad and only relics of the romance of early days.

===Chinese===
我如今已是个上了年纪的人，而且——或许更难叫人原谅——还是个老单身汉；然而，先生，我并非蓄意要做单身汉——我也不是那种专门诋毁婚姻的人。我此刻瞧见祖母那只珐琅糖果盒（*bonbonniere*）就在眼前，又想到叔父那对镶银嵌钢的枪管——两件都是家传旧物，各有各的可爱——便是拿这两样来换，我也不愿让诸位高雅的读者把我当作一个蓄谋已久、存心独身的罪人。绝无此事。我不止一回险些——应当说，是与姻缘擦肩而过——而那全是出于偶然，并非我的怯懦或薄情所致。不；我的天性原是向着成家立室的——只是我的福分偏偏落了单；我也绝不因今日这般光景而去感谢星辰，或自诩有什么功劳——说句老实话，便是这七十五个寒暑接连将我晒白又烤枯，如今偶尔仍叫我叹息的，仍是那些缱绻的回忆与辛酸的失意，它们于我，已是早年那段浪漫仅存的、凄凉的余烬。

===Original===
But though I have had my passages of love, as well as those of the sterner passions, in my day; and though I sometimes take a whim to rummage among old trinkets, lockets, and likenesses, each of them to me a little history in itself, yet I would not have you suppose me a superannuated sentimentalist either. No, sir. I have my tender, and, jesting aside, my melancholy retrospections; but I have also my pleasant, and, even at this time of day, my exciting recollections, too. I would be almost ashamed to tell you how often it comes to pass, that, my solitary pint of old port finished, I find myself sunk in my comfortable, ancient, leathern chair, gazing between my knees into the clear red embers, between which and me are rising and floating, like mystic shapes from an enchanted cauldron, the forms and faces long lost to life, which have mingled in the mazes of early adventure; and some of whom have left upon my time-chilled heart, traces that eternity itself, mayhap, will fail to obliterate.

===Chinese===
然而，虽说我也曾有过几段恋爱的经历，以及那些更为酷烈的情事；虽说我也时常心血来潮，翻翻那些旧首饰、小匣子和画像——每一件于我都是一部小小的掌故——您可别因此就把我当成一个老来多情的感伤主义者。不，先生。我有我的柔情，也有——说正经的——我的悒郁回首；但我也有我的快慰，甚至到了这般年纪，仍有令我激荡的回忆。我几乎不好意思向您招认，这样的事发生得有多频繁：独饮的那一品脱陈年波特酒喝完，我便陷进那张舒适的旧皮椅里，目光从两膝之间投向那一炉通红的余烬；在余烬与我之间，如同一口魔锅里升起的幻影一般，冉冉浮动着的，是那些早已作古的身影和面容——他们曾在我早年种种奇遇的迷宫里出没；其中有几位，在我这颗被岁月冻冷了的心上，留下的印记只怕连永恒也难以抹去。

===Original===
Thus it is, that in long winter’s evenings, as I sit alone and musing, memory calls up, with chastened colouring and softened outline, the chequered past before me. Passive, as though the pageant were the creation of some Prospero, and I his wondering visitor, I sit by and see, while memory and association crowd my vision with their filmy troops, fragments of old adventure, and glimpses of thrilling scenes, with all their actors duly accoutred, and looking just as they did—how many years ago! The lighthearted and the moody—the loved and the worthless—the prosperous and the ruined—the changed, and the dead and gone—all, in defiance of time and death, take their old places, and wear their old looks and liveries, as they drift by me in sad and wayward procession. Leaving these recollections to themselves, to rise, and shift, and unroll before my listless gaze, as chance, or some unknown law of suggestion wills it, it often happens that strange occurrences, and striking and mournful histories, which had passed from my ordinary remembrances, are thrown up again, like long-buried treasures from the restless sea, and startle me almost with the vividness of novelty.

===Chinese===
于是，在漫长的冬夜，我独坐凝思，记忆便以收敛了色泽、柔化了轮廓的笔法，将那跌宕的往事召到我眼前。我无所作为，仿佛这场盛景是某位普洛斯彼罗（Prospero）的造物，而我不过是个惊叹的看客，在一旁坐着观看；记忆与联想以他们缥缈的队伍挤满我的视野，旧日奇遇的断片、惊心场景的剪影，一一带着应有的装束浮现，模样一如当年——那是多少年前的事了！轻快的与沉郁的——所爱的与薄情的——得意的与败落的——变了的、死了的、去了的——一齐无视时间与死亡，各归其位，各复其旧貌、各穿其旧服，在我面前飘然而过，排成一列凄凉而又变幻无常的行列。我任这些回忆自生自长、自移自展，在我慵懒的目光之前铺陈，听凭偶然、或某种未知的联想之法来安排；于是常常有这样的事：那些早已从我寻常记忆中淡去的怪事、那些动人而悲惨的旧闻，竟又一一浮现，如同久埋海底的宝物被不宁的海浪冲上岸来，以其崭新般的鲜明，叫我几乎为之悚然一惊。

===Original===
It may be, that feeling, in most of these stories, that interest which attaches to an acquaintance with the individuals who have taken a part in them, I am unduly predisposed to exaggerate the degree of favour with which an ordinary reader may be presumed to regard them. Incidents well worth recording, as having happened to my lord or lady this, that, or t’other, may yet prove dull enough in the abstract, and unsupported by the borrowed importance of the aforesaid distinguished titles. But whatever interest I might have thrown over these pages, by particularizing individuals, and publishing real names, I feel bound—in some cases by humanity, in others by honour, but in *all* effectually—to forego. A *chronique scandaleuse* is not quite the thing for your respectable pages, nor, independently of other and higher considerations, are the tease and worry to which such authorship would expose your humble servant, quite the thing for an easy old bachelor, who has not handled a pistol in anger for full five-and-thirty years, who wishes well to all mankind, and hates trouble, almost as much as law or bloodshed.

===Chinese===
或许，由于这些故事里，我大多因与当事人相识而生出一份关切，我便难免有所偏颇，夸大了一位寻常读者可能对它们青睐的程度。那些因发生在某位大人、某位夫人身上而值得一录的事，一旦抽去了来龙去脉，又没了前述显赫头衔借来的分量，读来或许会乏味得很。然而，本可以借点出真人、刊出真名而为本卷增添的色彩，我却觉得有义务——有些出于人情，有些出于道义，但无论哪一种都一概有效——尽数放弃。一份"*丑闻录*"（*chronique scandaleuse*）登在您那体面的篇幅上未免不妥；再者，撇开其他更高尚的考量不谈，此种笔墨招来的麻烦与纠缠，对一个三十五年来未曾真正动过手枪、愿与世人皆相安无事、并且讨厌打官司几乎如同讨厌流血的老单身汉而言，也着实不合适。

===Original===
The tales I send you, therefore, shall not record the *names* of those whose acts, follies, or sufferings, they recite. In all other respects they shall be faithful narratives of fact—in this alone fictitious. They may prove wondrous dull, as old men’s stories sometimes do. Of their merits, I am, for every reason, the worst possible judge. Decide, then, yourself—put them into your Magazine or into your fire, just as your critical acumen shall determine. As for me, I prize my snug obscurity too justly to aspire to literary honours, or to participate in literary resentments. Blot, burn, or print, just as you please; I have nothing of the *genus irritabile*, except, perhaps, some symptoms of the *cacoëthes scribendi* about me. I perceive, indeed, with complacency, that you have admitted my former contribution to a place in your November number; this has determined me to despatch another, which, with like encouragement, may be followed by a third, and so on; I, all the while, with your good leave, maintaining my incognito, and despatching my scribblings through that mysterious agency, the penny-post. Should you cease to hear from me, without sufficient apparent cause for the suspension of my correspondence; should, I say, this series—for such, with your permission, I mean to make it—be abruptly and finally cut short, why then you may conclude that the “brief candle,” in whose flickering light I ply this my self-imposed task, has at last gone out, and left your old and unknown correspondent to the darkness and repose to which time is hurrying us all.

===Chinese===
因此，我寄给您的这些故事，绝不记载其中人物所作所为、所愚所苦的*真名实姓*。其余一应细节，皆忠实于事实——唯有在这一处上才是虚构。它们也许会乏味得可怕，正如老人的絮叨有时那样。论其优劣，我因种种缘故，是最不配下判断的人。那么，您自家定夺吧——是刊在您的杂志上，还是丢进火里，全凭您的眼光裁度。至于我，我太珍惜自己这份安逸的隐姓埋名，去觊觎什么文坛的荣名，或者卷入文人的恩怨。涂抹、焚烧、付梓，悉听尊便；我身上没有那种"*易怒之族*"（*genus irritabile*）的脾气，或许唯有几分"*写作之癖*"（*cacoëthes scribendi*）的症状罢了。我确实颇为欣慰地注意到，您已将我前次来稿收入了贵刊十一月号；这便促使我再寄上一篇，若蒙同等的鼓励，或许还有第三篇，如此接续下去；而我，经您恩准，自始至终隐姓埋名，仅凭便邮政——这神秘的媒介——投递我这些笔墨。倘若您不再收到我的来鸿，而又找不出充分的明显缘由来解释这通信的中断；倘若，我说，这一系列——蒙您允准，我正有意把它做成一个系列——竟戛然而止、再无下文，那您便可以断定：借了那摇曳不定的"短烛"之光、勉力从事这件自找差事的老翁，那支烛终归熄了，您这位年迈而不见真容的通信人，便已被留给那正将我辈一同催赶向前的黑暗与安息。

===Original===
With these few preliminary remarks, now offered once for all, I shall end the tedious task of introduction, and plunge at once into the business of my story, merely reiterating, by way of supplemental caution, that names and titles, and a few details of locality, which I fancied might indicate individuals, and lead to detection, have been suppressed and altered; but that in the substance, and, indeed, with those exceptions, in all the minor details of these narratives, I shall observe a strict adherence to the facts, as they were either related to me, or came within my own personal knowledge.

===Chinese===
几句开场白，就此一次说尽；我也要结束这段冗长的引介，径直扑入故事的正题。只是再赘一句，以为补充的告诫：凡是我认为可能牵出真人、招致识破的人名、头衔，以及若干地名细节，都已删去或改易；但除此之外，无论事关大旨还是细枝末节，我必严格依从事实——这些事，要么是别人讲给我听的，要么是我亲历亲知的。

===Original===
The story which I am about to relate, carries me back somewhere about half a century; at which time, it is needless to say, Dublin was, in point of society, a very different city from what it now is. It had then a resident aristocracy, and one whose equipages and housekeeping were maintained upon a scale which put plebeian competition wholly out of the question. I do not mean to offer any ungracious reflections upon the existing state of Dublin society. We have now, alas! more tuft-hunters than tufts to boast of; magnificent pretensions, based, like the Brahmin’s world, nobody can exactly say upon what, strive and strain to fill the void, which a legitimate aristocracy have left; and men, whose grandfathers—but what matters it? the thing is after all but natural. What was a metropolis, is a capital no longer; and it is but lost time sighing after the things that once were, or snarling at those that are.

===Chinese===
我即将讲述的这个故事，把我带回到大约半个世纪以前；那时，都柏林在社交界这一层上，毋庸说是与今日截然不同的一座城。彼时城中尚有定居的贵族，其车马仪仗、门庭排场之阔绰，绝非平民所能攀比。我并不想对都柏林眼下的社交风气作什么刻薄的议论。唉！如今我们这儿，攀附缨冠之徒倒比缨冠之辈还多；种种堂皇的做派，如同婆罗门的那方天地一般，谁也说不出究竟建立在什么之上，却竭力挣扎着去填补一个名正言顺的贵族阶级所留下的空缺；还有那么一些人，其祖父辈——可是，这又有什么要紧？事情到底不出常理。昔日一座都会，如今已不再是首都；既已如此，再去追怀旧物、或对现状龇牙咧嘴，不过是白费光阴罢了。

===Original===
At the time of which I speak, there resided in Dublin a certain worthy baronet, whom I shall call Sir Arthur Chadleigh. He was then considerably past sixty, and was a venerable monument of what was called hard living, in all its departments. He had been, until gout disabled him, a knowing gentleman on the turf; he was a deep player and a deep drinker, and covered, with an exterior of boisterous jollity, a very cold and selfish heart. He was thoroughly a man of the world, and what was then an essential ingredient in that amiable character, whenever occasion prompted, a very determined duellist. Whatever good nature he was possessed of, was expended upon society at large. In his dealings with his own family, he was arbitrary and severe; and if he did possess any natural affections, he had managed to get them all admirably under control, and never was known, under any circumstances, to suffer from their overindulgence. This old gentleman had been blessed, in his prime, with an helpmate; but Lady Chadleigh, having been, in her own way, about as domestic a person as Sir Arthur, one fine morning, at three o’clock precisely, when her spouse was entering upon his fourth bottle of claret in the parlour, absconded with young Lord Kildalkin. The happy pair were overtaken at Havre by the baronet, who, at ten paces, duly measured, shot off Kildalkin’s thumb—a feat which satisfied his honour, as some of the sterner brethren of the hair-trigger averred, at much too reasonable a rate. The worthy baronet, however, on his return, explained satisfactorily to a select circle of friends. “For,” said he, “had I shot him through the head, I should not have known what the ——— to do with Lady C.” As it was, he left his wife in the hands of his rival, as a moderate equivalent for the joint.

===Chinese===
在我所讲的那个年代，都柏林住着一位值得称道的准男爵，姑且唤他亚瑟·查德利爵士（Sir Arthur Chadleigh）。他彼时已年逾六旬，是所谓"豪饮重肉之生活"——各方面皆是——的一座行走的旧标本。在痛风将他撂倒之前，他原是赛马场上一位精明的行家；他赌得深、喝得凶，用一副喧嚷豪爽的外表，遮着一颗极冷漠自私的心。他是个彻头彻尾的世路老手，而要做成这种"讨喜"的人物，彼时有一条必不可少的质素——一旦时机相催，他便是一个说一不二的决斗家。他身上无论还残存多少和气，尽数都抛洒给了外头的应酬。待自家人，他专横而严苛；他纵有几分天伦之情，也已将它们调理得服服帖帖，从不曾在任何情形下，因纵情而吃过苦头。这位老先生壮年时，曾有幸得一位贤内助；然而查德利夫人（Lady Chadleigh），按她自家的路数，原与查德利爵士一样不着家：某个晴朗的清晨，整三点钟光景——彼时她丈夫正在客厅里开他那第四瓶红葡萄酒——她竟与年轻的基尔达尔金勋爵（Lord Kildalkin）私奔了。这一对璧人在勒阿弗尔被准男爵追上，他以规矩量好的十步之距，打掉了基尔达尔金的一根拇指——此举既已雪了他的名节，照几位更见硬气的"扳机兄弟"所说，代价未免太便宜了些。然而这位可敬的准男爵归乡之后，对一干至交好友作了令人满意的解释。"因为，"他说，"我若一枪打穿了他的脑袋，可就不知道——该拿查夫人怎么办了。"既已如此，他便将妻子留在情敌手中，权作一笔中等的补偿，抵了那一桩婚姻的纠葛。

===Original===
Lady Chadleigh had not been cruel enough to leave her lord without some objects on which to exercise those domestic virtues, for which he was so justly celebrated. She had been just five years married, when she took her departure, as I have stated; and she left behind her, for the consolation of her spouse, along with an extensive assortment of macaws, avadavats, lapdogs, and other sundries, three children—two sons and a girl. The macaws, etc., were easily disposed of, but there was no getting rid of the children; so Sir Arthur called in a grim old spinster sister, who, for fourteen years, dating from that day, presided at the baronet’s tea-table, and ruled his little flock. At the end of this period she died, and much about the same time died also the unfortunate Lady Chadleigh, forsaken and heartbroken, in some obscure town in France.

===Chinese===
查德利夫人到底没有残忍到丢下丈夫，不给他留下些许施展那套家室美德的用武之地——这套美德，他向来是出了名的。她婚后恰满五年便如前述一走了之；她留给丈夫作慰藉的，除了一大堆鹦鹉、文鸟、哈巴狗以及其他零碎，还有三个孩子——两男一女。鹦鹉之类倒好打发，孩子却是甩不脱的；于是亚瑟爵士把他那位面色严峻的老处女妹妹请了来，从那天起整整十四年，由她主持准男爵的茶桌、统管他那一小群儿女。这一程到了头，她也死了；大约也就在前后不久，那位不幸的查德利夫人也在法国某座无名小城里，孤苦伶仃、心碎而亡。

===Original===
Lady Chadleigh’s name had been proscribed—in Sir Arthur’s presence none dared to mention it; and, with the exception of little Mary, the daughter who, since infancy, had never seen her, no human being appeared to feel the smallest concern about the event. Little Mary Chadleigh, however, felt it deeply; with the yearnings of unavailing affection, she had always clung to the idea, that some time or other her mother would come back, and be fond of her. The reasons of the separation were, of course, wholly unknown to her, and her childish eagerness to learn something of her mother, had been systematically repulsed with a mysterious discouragement, in which she had come gradually to acquiesce. But though she had long learned to look upon her mother’s absence as in some way a necessary and unavoidable privation, and even as a natural thing, and a matter of course, which scarcely required to be accounted for, yet her mind had been constantly busied with the one thought, that at last she would return, and love her as she wished to be loved. And now came these strange tidings, never looked for in her childish dreams, and these black dresses, to tell her that all the little plans and hopes that had silently fluttered her innocent heart so many a time for so many years, must end forever; that the being for whose return she had been watching and wishing ever since she could remember, was never to come again. This was a sore shock to the poor girl, and she wept, in the solitude of her chamber, over this, to her, most bitter calamity, with a vehemence of grief and a sense of desolation, which, to one unacquainted with the cherished reveries, the castle-building of the heart, which had been her secret happiness from earliest childhood, would have been unaccountable.

===Chinese===
查德利夫人的名字在府中已被禁提——在亚瑟爵士跟前，无人敢提它一句；除了小玛丽——那个自襁褓以来便未曾见过母亲的小女儿——之外，似乎再没有第二个人，对这件事表现出丝毫关切。然而小玛丽·查德利却痛彻心扉；怀着那份无以寄托的眷恋，她一直死死抱着一个念头：母亲终有一日会回来，会疼爱她。分离的缘由，她自然一无所知；她孩童式地急于打听母亲的一点消息，却屡遭神秘而断然的回绝，久而久之，她也就默默顺从了。然而，虽然她早已学着把母亲的缺席看作某种必要而无可奈何的亏欠，甚至看成自然而然、理所当然、根本不必深究的事，她的心思却始终绕着同一个念头打转：母亲终会回来，会如她所愿那般爱她。如今这噩耗传来——这是她孩提时的梦里都不曾料到的——还有那一身黑衣，告诉她：多年来无数次悄然撩动她那颗纯真心的小小盘算和希望，都要就此了结，再无回旋；那个她自打记事起便日夜盼望、翘首以待其归来的人，再也不会回来了。这对那可怜的姑娘是一次沉重的打击；她在闺房的静寂中，为这场于她而言最惨痛的灾祸痛哭失声，那份悲恸之烈、那份被遗弃之感之深，对一个并不知晓她自幼秘藏的那些珍重幻想、那些心头的空中楼阁——正是她自小以来的隐秘快乐——的人而言，恐怕是难以理解的。

===Original===
Years passed on—new objects and associations began to fill her reveries; her secret sorrow wore away, and this early grief became but a sad, and scarcely unpleasing remembrance. I was a very young man when first I saw Miss Chadleigh, and I have seldom been so much struck by any combination of beauty, grace, and expression, as when she entered the room at one of Lady ———’s balls. She was at this time about nineteen, beautifully formed, and with the bearing of natural nobility; her complexion was clear, and rather pale; her eyes dark and lustrous; and her features, as I thought, exquisitely beautiful. The prevailing expression of her face was melancholy, with perhaps some slight character of haughtiness; but when she smiled, there was such a rippling of dimples, such an arch merriment in her lovely eyes, and such a revelation of little, even, pearly teeth, as made her perfectly enchanting. “Well,” thought I, as I watched with absolute fascination the movements of this lovely being, “if beauty the most enchanting be any longer the potent influence it once was, there is no scheme of ambition to whose realization such loveliness as yours may not aspire.” How little did I dream of what was coming!

===Chinese===
光阴荏苒——新的目标和新的交游渐渐填满了她的遐思；她那份隐秘的哀伤磨蚀了去，这一桩早年的伤心事，也只剩下一段凄凉、却又未尝不略带悦意的回忆。我初见查德利小姐那年，还是个十分年轻的小伙子；在某位夫人（Lady ———）的舞会上，她走进大厅的那一瞬，我为其容貌、仪态与神情合而为一的美所打动之深，一生中罕有。她那时约莫十九岁，身段姣好，举止间有一种与生俱来的高贵；肤色明净，略见苍白；一双眸子黝黑而流光；五官，在我看来，精致绝伦。她面上的主调是悒郁，或许还带着些许矜持的傲气；然而一旦她微笑，那酒窝便如春水般漾开，那双美目里便漾出俏皮的欢意，那一口细密齐整、珍珠般的小牙便一并显露，直叫人神魂颠倒。"好哇，"我一面出神地注视着这位可人儿的一举一动，一面暗想，"倘若倾国之姿仍如往昔那般是种通天的魔力，那么天底下便没有什么雄心所图，是您这般姿色所不能攀得的了。"我哪里想得到，接下来竟会是那样一番光景！

===Original===
I was so much attracted—my interest and attention so irresistibly engaged, by this beautiful girl, that I observed her, with scarcely any intermission, during the entire evening. It would be ridiculous to say that I was actually in love; I was not absurd or romantic enough (which you will) to get up a sentimental and hopeless passion at a moment’s notice, and that, too, without having exchanged one word with the object of my aspirations. No such thing. The feeling with which I gazed on Miss Chadleigh, was one of the profoundest admiration, I admit, yet untinctured with any, the least, admixture of actual tenderness. I observed her with the deep and silent pleasure with which beauty of the highest order may be contemplated, without the smallest danger to the heart; and, indeed, of the philosophical nature of my admiration, I had full assurance in the fact, that I remarked, with hardly one flutter of jealousy, the attentions, evidently not ill-received, which were devotedly paid her by a singularly handsome young officer, in a perfectly irresistible cavalry uniform. This gentleman was the afterwards too-celebrated Captain Jennings.

===Chinese===
这位美丽的姑娘牢牢地吸引了我的目光——我的兴致与注意都被她不可抗拒地牵了去，整晚我几乎目不转睛地打量着她。若说我当时当真已堕入情网，未免荒唐；我还不至于荒谬或浪漫到（您固然会如此）一眨眼便炮制出一桩感伤而无望的痴情来，何况这痴情的对象，我与她连一句话都未曾交换过。绝非如此。我凝视查德利小姐时所怀的心情，我承认，是一种最深刻的倾慕，却并未掺入哪怕一丁点真正的柔情。我以一种深沉而默然的愉悦观察着她——这种愉悦，乃是凝赏绝色时所能有的，对心毫无危险；而我这份倾慕之纯粹出于哲思一途，更有一桩事实足以为证：我眼睁睁看着一位英俊非凡的青年军官——身着一套简直无人能挡的骑兵制服——殷勤备至地伺候在她身边，而她显然也并不反感，我看着这一切，竟几乎未曾有一丝妒意的颤动。这位先生，便是日后那位声名太过的詹宁斯上尉（Captain Jennings）。

===Original===
That evening remains impressed upon my memory with the vividness—what do I say?—with fifty times the vividness of yesterday. I think I see old Sir Arthur now, as he sat at the whist-table, with his crutch beside him—for gout had claimed him as its own—his fiery face and heavy brows, overcast with the profound calculations of his favourite game, and his massive frame, shaking all over with the stentorian chuckle with which he greeted the conclusion of each successful rubber, while he slyly pocketed the guineas, and rallied and quizzed his discomfited opponents, with ferocious good-humour. I looked at this old man with some curiosity. I had never seen him before, and in his past life were not a few passages of vicissitude, daring, and adventure, such as might well warrant that qualified degree of interest which, as a young man, I not unnaturally felt in him. As I observed this hero of a hundred stories in the gossip of the day—his massive, but now crippled form—his bloated face, in which few could have traced a vestige of the handsome traits which rumour assigned to his early youth, and upon which, in the intervals of his tempestuous good-humour, I thought I could clearly discover the stamp of those sterner and imperious attributes with which general report had invested him;—as I looked on this fierce, crafty, intemperate, but at the same time, strangely enough, by no means unpopular man of the world, it was impossible to avoid the trite but natural contrast which, in a thousand such cases, is forced upon the mind, as often as, turning from him, my eye rested upon his beautiful child. How could a creature so exquisitely lovely, so accomplished in every natural grace—and, if expression might be trusted, at once so refined, so noble, and so sensitive—have ever sprung from a root so gnarled, bitter, and unsightly! Yet his child she doubtless was; for the world, with all its jealous and censorious curiosity, had never once questioned the parentage of Sir Arthur’s children, and in this the world was right. For poor Lady Chadleigh had begun her married life a good and faithful wife, and under circumstances less unhappy, might have been pure and honoured to the last. But the insults of callous profligacy had alienated and exasperated a heart at once proud and impetuous. She had been a spoiled child, and became a ruined woman. Habitually ungoverned, she was incapable of forbearance. With little principle and less prudence, she suffered a restless sense of wrong to hurry her into extravagances of conduct—intended, but without effect, to pique Sir Arthur, and wound at least his pride into jealousy; and in this mad enterprise the unhappy woman had at last effectually compromised herself, and was forced to the terrible necessity of flight. Her fall was not that of an impure, but of a vengeful spirit. It was the act of a bitter and passionate suicide, who would squander fifty lives to bring home one pang of remorse, or any other feeling, to the heart of callous indifference. Poor thing! the world understood her character, and despised her; for want of a due contempt for Sir Arthur’s apathy, and a proper acquiescence in his profligate courses, she had given herself to ruin.

===Chinese===
那一晚的情景，铭刻在我记忆中的鲜明程度——我说什么来着？——是昨日的五十倍。我此刻仿佛还看得见老亚瑟爵士：他坐在惠斯特牌桌前，手边搁着拐杖——因痛风早已将他收归己有——那张火红的脸、那两道浓眉，笼罩着他所钟爱的那局牌的深谋算计；他庞大的身躯，每赢一局便发出洪钟般的怪笑，笑得整个人直颤；他一面狡黠地把几尼（guinea）扫进腰包，一面以一种凶狠的好脾气打趣、讥嘲他那几个败阵的对手。我带着几分好奇打量这位老人。我从未见过他，而他一生的过往里，不乏几段跌宕、大胆、惊险的事迹，足以让我这个年轻人对他生出这等——也算不上不自然的——有节制的兴致。这位彼时街谈巷议中上百桩轶闻的主角——他魁伟而如今残废的身躯——他那浮肿的脸，几乎无人能从中辨出一丝当年传闻中他青年时俊秀的影子，而在他那阵暴风骤雨般的好脾气的间隙里，我以为自己能清清楚楚地看出，众人相传的他那些冷硬专横的气性的烙印；——我看着这样一个凶狠、狡黠、纵欲无度、却怪得很、并不见得招人厌的世路老手，便不能不生出那一种陈腐却又不由自主的对比来——这种对比，在千百桩类似的情形里都强行涌上心头——每回我从他身上移开目光，落到他那个美丽的孩子身上时，便油然而生。一个如此精雕细琢、天然风姿无不周备——并且，若神情可凭，则既娴雅、又高贵、又敏感的人儿——怎会从一截如此虬曲、苦涩、丑陋的根上生出来！然而她无疑确是他的孩子；因为世人尽管好妒好议、处处窥探，却从未对亚瑟爵士几个孩子的出身起过疑心，在这一点上，世人是对的。可怜的查德利夫人，新婚之初原是个贤良忠贞的妻子，若境遇不那么悲惨，她本可以清白而受人敬重地走到最后。可是冷漠荒淫的折辱，激恼了一颗又傲又烈的心，把它推得更远。她原是个被惯坏了的孩子，结果成了一个身败名裂的女人。她一向任性惯了，学不会隐忍。她既无多少原则，更少几分审慎，任由一种按捺不住的委屈之感驱使她做出种种越轨之举——本想借此激一激亚瑟爵士，至少刺痛他的自尊，引他妒火中烧，却毫无成效；就在这一桩疯狂的谋划里，那不幸的女人到底把自己彻底搭了进去，被迫走上那条可怕的、非走不可的逃亡之路。她的失足，并非出自一颗不洁的心，而是出自一颗报复的心。那是一个满怀怨毒、激情难抑的自毁者之举——她宁肯掷出五十条性命，只为把一缕悔恨、或任何一种情感，送进那颗冷漠无情的心里。可怜的人！世人看懂了她的脾性，便瞧不起她；只因她未能恰如其分地鄙夷亚瑟爵士的麻木，又未能得体地顺从他的荒唐，她便亲手把自己交给了毁灭。

===Original===
“Who is that officer,” I asked a friend, whom accident brought close to me in the crowded room—“that good-looking fellow, who has been so marked in his devotions to Miss Chadleigh all the evening?”

“Oh! that—don’t you know?” he replied. “Why that is Captain Jennings—Jennings the aide-de-camp—a devilish handsome fellow; the women are quite mad about him, and he knows it.”

“Miss Chadleigh appears intimate with him,” I observed.

“Yes, so she is; he was a friend of young Chadleigh’s, who died, or was taken in some battle in India,” he answered.

“So, one of her brothers is dead, then?” I interrupted.

“Yes; I believe the native army made him a prisoner, and treated him in the usual way,” replied he. “I heard the particulars; they were deuced horrid; but I don’t quite recollect them now.”

“And, Miss Chadleigh—has not she a second brother?” I inquired.

“A second brother! Yes,” he answered. “A pleasant fellow; but a perfect devil for wildness. She was fond of the other brother, and in a sad way, I believe, when the news came; but that is a year and a-half since. There, now, you can see young Chadleigh—the young man going to take Miss Chadleigh away.”

He nodded to indicate the party, and I followed the direction of his eye.

===Chinese===
"那位军官是谁？"我向一位被人群挤到我身边的朋友打听，"那个好看的家伙，整晚都对查德利小姐殷勤得那么显眼？"

"哦！那位——你不认识？"他答道，"嘿，那就是詹宁斯上尉——副官詹宁斯——一个俊得过分的家伙；女人们为他疯了似的，他自己也心知肚明。"

"查德利小姐似乎和他很熟。"我道。

"是的，确实如此；他是小查德利的朋友，小查德利在印度阵亡了，或者是在哪场战役里被俘了。"他答。

"那她有一个哥哥是死了？"我插嘴。

"是的；我听说印度土著军队俘虏了他，照老法子处置了他，"他答，"详情我也听人说过；骇人得很；不过如今我记不太清了。"

"那么，查德利小姐——她不是还有一个哥哥吗？"我问。

"还有一个哥哥！有的，"他答，"一个挺有趣的家伙；可是野得跟个十足的魔鬼似的。她喜欢那个阵亡的哥哥，噩耗传来时，想必难过得很；不过那都是一年半以前的事了。瞧，现在你能看见小查德利了——就是去带查德利小姐走的那个年轻人。"

他点点头，把那几位指给我看，我便顺着他的目光望去。

===Original===
Young Chadleigh was a decidedly well-looking man, with a frank and rather distinguished air, and dressed with an almost foppish attention to the prevailing fashion. I had just time to observe that he and Jennings chatted familiarly for a minute or two, and appeared to be on the friendliest terms of intimacy.

“Well,” thought I, “after all, he may be but a friend.”

Whether it be impossible to contemplate such beauty as Miss Chadleigh’s with perfect stoicism, and that, without knowing it, I was really a little jealous, I can’t say; but I certainly had watched the young captain’s attentions with a slight but disagreeable sense of restlessness, and experienced, I know not how, a certain relief in the reflection I had just made. It had, however, hardly visited my mind, when it was again disturbed.

===Chinese===
小查德利是个长得着实不错的人，神情坦率、还带着几分不俗的气度，衣着上对时兴样式几乎是煞费苦心，到了近乎花花公子的地步。我只来得及瞧上一眼，便见他跟詹宁斯熟络地攀谈了一两分钟，看样子交情极为亲密。

"也罢，"我心想，"他毕竟不过是个朋友罢了。"

像查德利小姐这般姿色，是否真有人能以十足的斯多葛式的冷静去凝视，而我虽不自知、其实已生出了几分醋意，这我说不准；但那晚我望着那位年轻上尉的殷勤，心中确有一种隐隐的、却又颇不舒服的不宁，而我刚才那一转念，不知怎地，竟让我松了一口气。然而这念头方才落下，心思便又被搅起。

===Original===
Miss Chadleigh, leaning on her brother’s arm, was passing so close as almost to touch me, whom she had unconsciously inspired with so much admiration, when Jennings, following, presented her with her fan, accidentally forgotten. As she took it with a gracious smile, she blushed. Yes, I could not be mistaken, for a more beautiful blush I never beheld in my existence; and, to make the matter worse, I thought I perceived that, as he placed the light weapon of coquetry in her hand, his own rested upon hers for a second longer than was strictly necessary, and in doing so conveyed the slightest possible *pressure* to her little ivory fingers. I felt, I know not how, disposed to be affronted and incensed, and actually stared, with no very inviting expression, full upon Captain Jennings, as he made his retreat, with a lurking smile of vanity and triumph on his lip. My ill-bred stare was unobserved, and I could, on reflection, scarcely help laughing at the absurdity of the emotion which had inspired it. But, after all, why should I?—the nature of the beast pervades us all. The presence of beauty is a woeful stimulus to unprovoked combativeness, and I do believe there is a lurking idea universally in the mind of man, that beauty should be, somehow, the prize of the fiercest and strongest—the

> “Viribus editior ut in grege taurus.”

I know it was ever the case with me—I never saw, at least in my young days, a pretty girl, without feeling a disposition to fight with somebody—and this, although, under ordinary circumstances, as peaceable a fellow as any among her majesty’s liege subjects.

===Chinese===
查德利小姐挽着她哥哥的手臂经过时，离我近得几乎要擦到我——这位不知不觉间令我生出那般倾慕的小姐——这时，跟在后头的詹宁斯上前，把她一时忘下的扇子递还给她。她含笑接过，嫣然一笑间，竟红了脸。是的，我决没有看错，我这辈子还不曾见过比这更美的红晕；而更糟的是，我恍惚觉得，他把那柄卖弄风情的轻巧兵器放进她手里时，他自己的手在她手上多停了那么一秒——比规矩所严加要求的还多了一秒——就在这一刻，又向她那几根象牙般的小指头，传达了一丝几不可察的*一握*。我不知怎地，竟生出一种受冒犯、被激怒的心情，竟当真以一种绝称不上友善的神情，直直盯住了向后退去的詹宁斯上尉——他嘴角正挂着一抹藏不住的、虚荣而得意的笑。我那失礼的凝视他并未察觉，事后一想，连我自己也忍不住要为这情绪的荒唐发笑。可说到底，我又何必呢？——兽性原是我们人人共通的。美色当前，便是一桩无缘无故的战斗欲的劣性刺激；我也深信，人心之中普遍潜伏着这样一个念头，以为美色，在某种意义上，便该是那最凶、最强者的战利品——正如——

> "Viribus editior ut in grege taurus."（如牛群中之最强壮之牡牛。）

我知道我一向如此——至少在年轻时，我每见一个漂亮姑娘，便要生出一种想跟人打一架的兴致——虽说在寻常境况下，我是女王陛下子民之中最和气不过的一个人。

===Original===
In pursuing this narrative, I am forced occasionally to rely upon the report of others; in some of its oddest scenes, however, as the reader will perceive, I was present, and myself a secondary actor. What I did not myself witness, I shall, as I have said, supply from the testimony of others, and thus present your readers with a connected recital of this eccentric piece of Irish biography.

If fortune had condemned Captain Jennings to the torments of love, she was, at all events, resolved to grant him every reasonable mitigation in his distressed condition. For upwards of a month, during that summer, he had the happiness of being a guest at Lord ———’s, where Miss Chadleigh and her brother were also visitors; whether he had succeeded, or not, in making any impression upon the young lady’s heart, was not then known; but as his attentions were, if possible, more marked and devoted than ever, the affair began to be talked of, and, soon after this visit terminated, was mentioned by a friend to Sir Arthur himself.

===Chinese===
在追述这段故事时，我不得不偶尔借助他人的转述；然而其中几处最为离奇的场景——读者自会看出——我恰好在场，并且自己还是个次要的角色。我所未能亲见的部分，如前所述，将从他人的证言中加以补缀，从而为您的读者奉上一篇前后贯通的记叙，记述这段古怪的爱尔兰轶事。

倘若命运已将詹宁斯上尉判入了相思的苦刑，那么，至少它已决意在这困窘之境中，给他一切合理的宽减。那年夏天，他有幸在某勋爵（Lord ———）府上做客达一月有余；查德利小姐和她哥哥也是同府的客人——他是否已在那位小姐的心上留下丝毫印记，彼时尚不可知；然而他的殷勤，竟比从前更显眼、更专注了几分，此事渐渐为人议论，这一场造访才了，便有好事者把它当作一桩新闻，告诉了亚瑟爵士本人。

===Original===
The baronet forthwith instituted inquiries respecting Captain Jennings’ ways and means—the result was unsatisfactory—and, one day, as the gay young gentleman sat chatting, at an early visit, with Chadleigh and his fair sister, the old baronet hobbled into the room, and set himself down as one of the party—a procedure quite contrary to his ordinary habits. There was nothing ominous in his countenance and bearing, however; on the contrary, he seemed more than usually frank and good-humoured, shook Jennings more heartily by the hand, and laughed more boisterously at all his jokes and stories than ever he had done before. Chadleigh had already gone, and Sir Arthur having dispatched Mary to superintend some customary arrangements affecting his own comforts, the door was closed upon him and Captain Jennings.

===Chinese===
准男爵随即着手打听詹宁斯上尉的家底——结果并不令人满意——一日，这位风流少年趁早来走访，正与小查德利和他那位美貌的妹妹闲谈，老准男爵竟一瘸一拐地踱了进来，挨着他们坐下，成了这一伙里的一员——此举与他平素的做派全然相悖。然而他神色举止间并无半点不祥之兆；恰恰相反，他似乎比往常更坦率、更和悦，握詹宁斯的手握得分外热切，对他所有的笑话和掌故，笑得比以往任何时候都更放肆。小查德利这时已经走了，亚瑟爵士又把玛丽支使开去，让她去督办几桩关系他老人家舒适的例行安排，门一关，便只剩下他和詹宁斯上尉两人。

===Original===
“Jennings,” said the baronet.

“Well, sir.”

“You’re a devilish good fellow—Jennings, a devilish pleasant fellow,” said the baronet, “and I’ve no doubt will get on in the world—with *prudence*, that is, with *prudence*.”

Jennings bowed his acknowledgments, and looked a little surprised.

“And, as it strikes me, Jennings, my boy,” continued the baronet, in the same jolly tone—“about the most *im*prudent thing you could possibly do, at the outset, would be to *marry*; and marriage being out of the question in point of prudence—totally and entirely out of the question—I should not, you understand me, like to have Miss Chadleigh, my daughter, talked of in connection with such an absurdity.”

“Really, Sir Arthur,” interrupted Jennings, changing colour slightly, and affecting a cool hauteur, which he was far from feeling—“I don’t precisely know to what particular circumstances you are pleased to allude.”

“Come, come, my dear fellow,” said Sir Arthur, in the same tone of rough good humour, which, in all his dealings, alike with friend or foe, whether with the dice-box or the pistol, he had ever maintained—“we are, both of us, men of the world—eh? I an old, and you a young one; but both of us unquestionably men of the world, and perfectly wide awake. You know just as well as *I*, and *I* as well as *you*, what is usually termed, ‘paying attentions to a young lady’—let us have no shamming at either side—we both of us know this; and I don’t approve of Miss Chadleigh’s receiving any such distinction from *you*, my dear Jennings; and now I hope I have made myself perfectly intelligible.”

Jennings bowed stiffly, and the baronet continued—
