He said this in his most engaging and conciliatory manner; but, as I bowed in acknowledgment of the preference, I felt my original dislike of him rather increased than abated.

“I offer no defence whatever for my conduct; God knows I blame myself as severely as anybody else can possibly do,” he continued, with a contrite shake of the head; “I ran blindly into extreme temptation, and have compromised, not only myself, but a young lady, whom I would gladly die to extricate from the unfortunate position into which I have unguardedly led her.”

Equivocal as had been his agitation that morning, it was, at all events, genuine; but now he had recalled all the artificial graces of his manner. I saw in the polished ease of his remorse, and in the studied melancholy of his compassion, something indescribably repulsive and abominable.

“Without further tasking your patience,” he resumed, at the same time taking a paper from his desk, “I have to entreat your consent to become the depository of this paper. It is a piece of evidence which may throw an important light upon this affair; the copy of a document, which I keep in my possession, and which you will, perhaps, oblige me by retaining in yours; the nature of it you will see at a glance, and I have endorsed upon it the name and address of the party whose testimony it is, so that, if need be, there can be no difficulty in applying it properly. All I ask of you is, to guard it equally from destruction, and from the eyes of all others, but yourself; and that, whenever I write to you to that effect, you will kindly hand it to my law-agent in town, whom I will name to you, whenever it becomes necessary to employ one. Will you kindly undertake this commission?”

I could hardly decline an office, as it seemed, so easily performed. I so little liked the applicant himself, however, that a slight, and not very gracious hesitation, preceded my acceptance of its duties. He thanked me, however, profusely; and I had risen for the purpose of taking my departure, when a vehicle of some kind stopped at the hall-door, and a thundering double-knock announced the arrival of a visitor.

“Tell them I’m dressing,” said Jennings to the servant, who appeared at the room-door; and, in the next moment, the summons at the hall-door was answered.

“Captain Jennings is dressing for the evening,” I heard the servant say, in reply to the inquiry of the footman who had knocked.

This intimation, however, had not the desired effect, for the steps of the carriage were let down with a sharp clang, and, almost at the same moment, I heard a different voice, that, I presumed, of the visitor in person, demand—

“Is your master at home?”

The same answer was repeated, and the applicant for admission replied in a sharp decisive tone—

“Ha! dressing for the evening, very good; then he *is* at home?”

“But, sir, I beg pardon; he positively cannot see anybody at present,” urged the man.

“He shall certainly see me,” retorted the visitor, in the same tone. “I know the way—don’t mind.”

From the moment the clatter of the carriage-steps smote my ear, my mind unaccountably misgave me, and a foreboding of impending collision and mischief, filled me with an almost painful suspense. My instinctive apprehensions did not deceive me. The drawing-room door was pushed abruptly open, and young Chadleigh entered the room.

===Chinese===
我方才所闻，已叫我确信：无论结局为何，那一日之灾已为时不远；怀着与事变之迫近成正比的焦虑——此事我无法不致以最深的关切——我叩响了厅门，随即被引上楼，便与詹宁斯上尉相对而坐了。

只见他披着晨衣、趿着拖鞋。他面色苍白、神色焦灼，但此时已完全恢复了冷静与从容。

"给您添这许多麻烦，我实在于心难安，深知此举唐突已极。"寒暄既毕、我落座之后，他接着说，"只是，除罗伯逊医生外——我和他的交情，也同与您一样浅——这一桩最不幸的事里，我再无可托付的君子了——"（说到这里，他略略耸了耸肩，带着一种悻悻与不满的神气，这神气竟比方才一切所言，更深地令我确信：他那自私的冷漠，正是他性格的底色——这正与我向来所信不谋而合）——"此事的详情，您与罗伯逊医生两位尽知，那么，我仅有的一桩隐衷，宁可托付给您、而不托付于他——这一选择，或也算不得怎么不近人情——还望您海涵。"

这番话，他是以最动人、最委婉的姿态说出来的；然而，当我还礼以谢他的青睐时，我反倒觉得，我对他的那份原初的反感，不减反增了。

"对于我的行径，我不作任何辩解；天知道，我责备我自己，已不亚于旁人所能加之于我的责备。"他接着说，带着一副痛悔的神气摇了摇头，"我一时盲目，投身于极度的诱惑之中，结果连累了一位小姐——我宁愿以死相赎，把她从我这莽撞将她引入的不幸境地中救拔出来。"

那天早晨他那番激动，尽管可疑，到底还算真诚；可如今他已把一切做作的仪态都重拾了回来。在他那圆熟的悔恨里，在他那精心雕琢的悲悯里，我瞧见了一种难以言喻的、令人憎厌的、可鄙的东西。

"不再多费您的耐心了，"他又道，一面从书桌里取出一份文件，"我不得不恳请您，做这份文件的保管者。这是一份证据，或可为此事投下重要的光亮；是我手边一份文书的抄本，还望您不吝替我收存；其性质您一望便知，我已在上面注明了作证一方的姓名住址，一旦需用，必能妥为调取。我所求于您的只是：一不失毁，二则除您之外，勿令旁人过目；再有，若我日后有信相索，请您将其转交我在城里的律师代理——其姓名我届时相告，待须用他之时。劳您承下这桩差事，可否？"

这样一桩差事，办来似是轻而易举，我几乎无从推却。然而我如此不喜欢这位相托之人，以致在应承之前，难免有几分不甚热络的迟疑。他仍是千恩万谢；我已起身欲辞，忽然一辆车在厅门外停了下来，一阵如雷的双叩，宣告了一位访客的驾到。

"就说我在更衣。"詹宁斯对出现在门口的仆人道；下一刻，厅门外的叩门声便得了回音。

"詹宁斯上尉正更衣，准备出门赴晚宴。"我听见那仆人这样回答叩门的随从。

然而这番示意并未奏效，只因车阶被放下时，发出一声清脆的金属响；几乎同时，我听见了另一个声音——想必是来客本人——喝道——

"你家老爷在家么？"

同样的回答又重复了一遍，求见之人以尖锐而果决的口吻回道——

"哈！更衣赴晚宴，很好；那么他*在*家喽？"

"可是，先生，恕罪；他实在不能此刻见客。"那仆人苦劝。

"他必得见我。"那来客以同样的口吻驳道，"路我认得——不必费心。"

自车阶那声金属响传入我耳中之刻起，我心头便无端地打起鼓来，一种大祸将至、冲突将临的预感，叫我几乎坐立不安。我那本能的忧虑并未骗我。客厅的门被一把推开，小查德利闯了进来。

===Original===
The moment I saw him, I perceived that in his face which warned me of the truth of my vague anticipations. Pale, stern, and collected, he walked slowly a few steps into the room, bowed with an ominous and icy formality to Captain Jennings, and, in a tone so cold and deadly, as I think I never heard before, or since, said—

“Captain Jennings, I presume you apprehend the subject of my visit?”

It was scarcely necessary to put the question. He had advanced to receive Chadleigh with his usual air of frank and easy gaiety, their eyes met, and in the encounter he read the truth—the smile passed away in an instant from his countenance, and was succeeded by a look, to the full as stern and ominous as that which confronted him. The young men felt that a deadly quarrel lay between them, and I think I never saw a more portentous greeting.

“You have not announced it, sir,” said Jennings, with cold and measured politeness; “but I have no hesitation in saying, that I *do* suspect the cause of your visit.”

“Good, sir!” replied Chadleigh, in the same constrained voice; “I came on behalf of Miss Mary Chadleigh’s father, and in my own right, as her brother, to demand of you, in the first place, where that young lady at present is.”

“Without meaning to dispute *your* right to put that question,” replied Jennings, “I mean to stand upon *mine*, to decline answering it.”

“You refuse to answer?” said his visitor, while his countenance darkened.

“I do—most distinctly refuse,” repeated he.

“Pray, think better of it, sir,” retorted Chadleigh, with a ghastly mimicry of courtesy.

“Mr. Chadleigh,” replied Jennings, haughtily, “I recommend you strongly to act as a man of the world in this business. The mischief, whatever it be, is now past cure. If you will only allow events to take their course, scandal may be avoided, and a great deal of unnecessary trouble, exposure, and violence spared. If you will persist in pushing this matter to extremity, do so; upon your head be the consequences.”

“Sir,” said Chadleigh, “you greatly mistake me, if you fancy that your mean and perfidious conduct, in spiriting away the daughter of a gentleman, who frankly told you that he peremptorily declined the connection which your conduct seemed to offer—if you fancy that your base and mercenary conduct in inveigling her, a young lady entitled to a fortune, and with most suitable prospects before her, into a marriage with you, a mere adventurer—”

“Mr. Chadleigh, before you proceed further, let me ask you, *have* you actually made up your mind to push this affair to a public quarrel?” insisted Jennings.

“Yes, sir,” retorted Chadleigh, proudly and bitterly. “Mary Chadleigh has selected for herself—embraced her own degradation—married a man whom her father expressly forbid his house, because he suspected him of entertaining the schemes he has but too securely realized. She is now, and henceforward, to Sir Arthur and to me, a stranger; we renounce and disown her; and by ———, she shall not stand between you and the punishment you deserve.” He paused; and added emphatically—“I presume you will be at home by eleven o’clock tonight?”

“Certainly, sir,” answered Jennings, calmly.

His visitor bowed sternly, and began to withdraw.

===Chinese===
我一看他的脸，便瞧出了那神色——它印证了我方才那点模糊的预感。他面色苍白、神情冷峻而镇定，缓步向房中踱了几步，以一种阴沉、冰冷地郑重的姿态，朝詹宁斯上尉一躬身；又以一种我自问前所未闻、此后也未再闻的、冷得可怕的口吻道——

"詹宁斯上尉，我想，您当明白我此来所为何事吧？"

这话原也无须问。他已依着惯常那种坦率而洒脱的快活神气，迎上前去接待查德利；两人的目光相遇，就在这一交锋里，他读出了实情——那笑容瞬间从他脸上褪去，换上了一副神色，与他所对的那副神色同样严峻、同样不祥。两位年轻人都感到，他们之间横着一桩你死我活的过节；我想我从未见过比这更为凶险的"寒暄"。

"您尚未明言，先生，"詹宁斯以冷峻而有分寸的客气说，"但我并不讳言，我*确*已猜到此番造访的因由。"

"好，先生！"查德利以同样压抑的嗓音答道，"我以玛丽·查德利小姐之父的名义，并以我作为她兄长的本分，来向你——首先要向你来讨一句话——那位小姐此刻在哪里。"

"我并非要质疑*您*提出此问的权利，"詹宁斯答，"但我也要坚持*我*的权利——不予作答。"

"你拒绝作答？"来客说着，脸色阴沉下来。

"正是——我最明白不过地拒绝。"他重复道。

"先生，还请三思。"查德利以一副煞有介事的、令人毛骨悚然的客套回敬道。

"查德利先生，"詹宁斯傲然答道，"我恳切奉劝您，在此事中以一个世路中人的姿态行事。既铸成之祸，无论是什么，如今都无从挽救。您若肯听任事态自然发展，风言风语或可避免，许多不必要的麻烦、张扬与冲突，亦可一并省去。您若执意将此事推到极处，那便随您——后果自负。"

"先生，"查德利道，"你若是以为，你那卑鄙而背信的行径——你把一位君子之女拐走，而那位君子当初明白告诉你，他断然拒绝你那行径所暗含的姻缘——你若是以为，你那贪婪无耻的行径，竟能诱骗她——一位原有一笔财产、又有最相宜之前程的小姐——与你这么个冒险家成婚——"

"查德利先生，您再说下去之前，容我问一句，您*当真*打定主意，要把这事闹成一场公开的争执么？"詹宁斯追问道。

"正是，先生。"查德利傲然而苦涩地驳道。"玛丽·查德利已自择其路——拥抱了她的自我作贱——嫁了一个她父亲明令逐出门墙的人，因为他疑心此人心怀叵测，而那些叵测之心，如今已被他得逞得太彻底了。她从今往后，无论对亚瑟爵士还是对我，都已是路人；我们与她断绝、不认；我对天起誓，她绝不能横在你与你应得的惩罚之间。"他顿了顿；又加重了语气补一句——"今晚十一点，我想，您在寓所吧？"

"当然，先生。"詹宁斯平静地答。

来客冷冷一躬，便要退去。

===Original===
“I wish, if you please, to add one word,” said Jennings.

“Certainly,” said Chadleigh, returning.

Jennings looked down for a moment, in agitated and guilty abstraction—bit his lips, and grew deadly pale, as though inwardly agonized with a mortal struggle.

“I have to request *your* attention, too, Mr. ———,” he said, addressing me, and arresting my departure. “It is, unfortunately, due to myself that you should hear what I am about to say.”

“Be so good as to say, without further delay, what you desire me to hear,” said Chadleigh.

“Yes, sir; you have forced me to it,” said Jennings, drawing himself up, and looking with a steady, and singularly evil scowl, full in his visitor’s face. “You talked of marriage?”

“Yes, sir,” replied Chadleigh.

“Well, sir, as you *will* have it a quarrel between us, it is, unfortunately, due to myself to say, that there is no such thing as marriage in the case.”

Jennings spoke these words with a resolute and measured distinctness, which left no room for misapprehension.

“No!—no marriage!” said Chadleigh, after a hideous pause of some seconds, and speaking almost in a whisper, like one half-stunned, while he returned the guilty gaze of his transformed friend with a stare of actual horror.

For my own part, I confess I was scarcely one degree less astounded than Chadleigh, at this utterly unlooked-for declaration.

“Not married—not married! Why, great God, can it—is it credible! You monstrous, measureless villain—”

The flimsy varnish of affected courtesy was gone, and the hell-born passions it had masked broke forth in an instant, in undisguised and titanic revelation. With one hoarse execration, shrieked rather than spoken, Chadleigh advanced toward Jennings.

“Take care, Chadleigh—take care; I would not harm you,” said Jennings, sternly.

“Hold, for God’s sake,” I cried, interposing between the two young men. “Mr. Chadleigh, I implore of you—remember, consider; what can come of this?”

“Let me go, sir,” cried Chadleigh, hoarsely.

“Mr. Jennings,” I cried, still clinging to Chadleigh, for in his furious paroxysm of excitement, I could not tell what dreadful results might possibly attend a physical encounter, “for God’s sake, avoid this; you’ll have bloodshed else. Mr. Chadleigh, reflect; stay for one moment.”

“Let me go, sir; let me go, or by ———, I’ll strike you down,” cried Chadleigh, straining and struggling to reach the object of his fury.

“Get into your room, Mr. Jennings, unless you wish for murder. Go, for Heaven’s sake,” I repeated. “I can’t prevent it longer. I tell you go—go, in God’s name. *Will* you go, or not?”

Jennings’ momentary agitation had entirely disappeared with the immediate menace of such an encounter as that which threatened him. His physical courage no one had ever doubted; and the moment *it* was tasked, his intrepid calmness instantly returned. He hesitated for a second; then, with one glance of mingled remorse and disdain at Chadleigh, he turned, and strode sullenly into his chamber, flinging the door close after him. The key was, fortunately, in the outside; and, without giving Chadleigh time to get before me, I sprang to the door, locked it, and, placing the key in my pocket, stood facing the baffled assailant.

“Sir,” he said bitterly, “by ———, you shall answer for this.”

“When and how you please, Mr. Chadleigh,” I replied, sadly. “I have done my duty, and no more, in preventing a murderous fray; and I thank God I have succeeded.”

He stood undecided for a few seconds. At last he said—

“Perhaps you were right, sir; and *I* ought to ask *your* pardon. You *were* right, sir, and I was wrong. Pardon me.”

I gave him the assurance he required, and he added abruptly—

“This is no place for me. Good night, sir.”

===Chinese===
"我愿再附一言，不知可否？"詹宁斯道。

"请讲。"查德利回身道。

詹宁斯低头沉吟了片刻，神色激动而愧疚，心如乱麻——他咬着唇，脸白得发青，似在内心经历一场殊死的挣扎。

"———先生，我也有劳*您*留意。"他对我说，止住我的离去。"很不幸，您理应听听我接下来要说的话，这对得起我自己。"

"劳驾，请不要再耽搁，把您要我听的话说出来吧。"查德利道。

"是的，先生；是您逼我至此的。"詹宁斯挺直身子，以一种沉稳而、怪异地凶狠的怒容，直直盯住来客的脸。"您方才提到了婚姻？"

"是的，先生。"查德利答。

"好，先生，既是您*执意*要我们之间有一场龃龉，那么，很不幸，为对得起我自己，我不得不说——此事之中，并无婚姻一说。"

詹宁斯以一种坚定、从容而清晰的可分明的口吻，说出这几句话，绝无令人误解的余地。

"没有！——没有婚姻！"查德利停了几秒，那几秒骇人地漫长，才像被雷击一般、近乎耳语地说了出来，而以真正惊骇的目光，回视着那位已变了脸的朋友那心虚的凝视。

至于我，我承认，我对这全然始料未及的宣告所感到的震骇，较之查德利只少不多。

"未成婚——未成婚！老天啊，怎会——怎能令人置信！你这罪大恶极、天理难容的恶棍——"

那层薄薄的、做作的客气之漆，转瞬剥落；它所掩盖的那几样地狱所生的情欲，顷刻之间赤裸裸地、如泰坦般倾泻而出。查德利一声嘶哑的咒骂——与其说是说出，不如说是嚎出——便朝詹宁斯扑了上去。

"当心，查德利——当心；我不想伤你。"詹宁斯冷峻地说。

"看在老天的份上，住手！"我嚷道，挡在两个年轻人之间。"查德利先生，我求您——想想，三思；这能有什么好处？"

"放开我，先生。"查德利嘶声道。

"詹宁斯先生，"我仍紧紧揪住查德利，喊道——他既已激愤若狂，一旦动起手来，会酿出何等惨祸，我实难预料——"看在老天的份上，避一避吧；否则要见血的。查德利先生，您想想；稍停一刻。"

"放开我，先生；放开我，否则我对天发誓，我要把你打翻在地。"查德利嚷着，挣扎着要够到他怒火所向的人。

"詹宁斯先生，您回自己房里去，除非您想闹出人命。去呀，看在老天的份上，"我又道，"我拦不了多久了。我让您去——去呀，以上天的名义。您*到底*去不去？"

詹宁斯方才那阵短暂的激动，随着那威胁逼近的搏斗的当头一险，已经消失得无影无踪。他的血气之勇，从未有人怀疑；而这一勇气一经考验，他那临危不乱的镇定立时回归。他迟疑了一秒；随即以一种悔恨与轻蔑交加的目光，朝查德利一瞥，转身阴沉地大步走进自己的卧室，把门"砰"地带上。所幸钥匙插在外头；我不给查德利抢先的机会，一个箭步扑到门前，把门锁上，将钥匙揣进口袋，转身面对那个功亏一篑的袭扰者。

"先生，"他恨恨地说，"我对天发誓，您要为此付出代价。"

"随时奉陪，悉听尊便，查德利先生。"我黯然答道，"我阻止了一场流血的厮杀，不过是尽了本分，再无其他；我感谢上天，我做到了。"

他踌躇了几秒。末了他说——

"先生，也许您是对的；该说*对不起*的是*我*。您*确实*是对的，先生，是我错了。恕罪。"

我给了他所要的保证，他又突兀地补一句——

"此地非我所留。晚安，先生。"

===Original===
So saying, he left the room; and I, from the window, saw him reenter the carriage, and drive away, ere I returned to turn the key in Jennings’ room. I did so, and called him; there was no answer. I pushed the door open a little, and looked in. He had thrown himself into a chair, and was sitting close by a table, his forehead laid upon his arm, and his face concealed—he was sobbing. He started up abruptly, on becoming aware of my presence, and with a violent effort commanded himself.

“Mr. ———,” said he, “pray don’t leave me, for a few minutes. Mr. ———, you don’t know what I am suffering, and what I have suffered. I am about the most miserable and unfortunate mortal you have ever seen or heard of—indeed I am. Sir, you can’t understand—I can’t explain to you the horrors of my position.”

“The poor young lady,” I said, coldly, “is certainly impressed with the belief that she is legally married. Dr. Robertson distinctly told me so—nay, he himself believed it.”

“Yes, yes, yes,” he interrupted, vehemently; “but I can prove it is not so. The paper I have placed in your hand will show you that there has been no such thing. She thinks it—she believes, no doubt, poor creature; but she’s wrong—quite wrong.”

I was greatly shocked at the sinister eagerness with which Jennings laboured to impress this fact, which, of all others, I thought he ought naturally to be most anxious to conceal for the present, upon my conviction; and I could not forbear saying—

“At all events, you will not fail to make all the reparation now in your power, and—”

“What reparation?” he asked, vehemently.

“There is but one,” I answered, “which you can now offer; and that is, *marriage*.”

“You are right, indeed,” he answered, sullenly, after a long pause; “it is the only—the *only* reparation for such a wrong.”

He sank into a moody and compunctious silence. At last he said, abruptly—

“They talk of generosity, and impulse, and all that, but take my word for it, *prudence* is worth them all. My own utter want of reflection has done it. I have been drawn into a situation in which I am powerless, at least for good; but do me justice, sir; you *must* do me justice, for, by ———, I designed no wrong; I am not a cold-blooded wretch. I was led away by passion—misguided and betrayed into a position, as I told you, where I am no longer a free agent, and then my conduct is criticised, as if I could do just as I pleased. Is this justice or honesty? I’m railed at like a cold, scheming villain, and damned for not making reparation—I, that never laid a deliberate plot in my life, or hesitated to make atonement where I could. By heavens, sir, I tell you truth. Is this fair dealing—is it candour—is it common toleration?”

I reminded Jennings that I had no right to judge in the matter; and also intimated that I had already stayed too long, and so rose to take my departure.

“Well, well, well,” he said, with a dreary sort of shrug; “patience, and shuffle the cards—who knows what may turn up—who knows? Though, egad, take it which way you will, it is about as cursed, black a looking business, as ever man was in for. It is hard—hard, by ———. It looks as if they were all in a savage conspiracy to ruin me; and what good, in the devil’s name, can come of it—a pack of fools!”

===Chinese===
说着，他便出了房；我从窗口看着他重又上了车，疾驰而去，方才回去，开了詹宁斯房门上的锁。我开了锁，唤他；却无回应。我把门推开一线，朝里张望。他瘫在一张椅子上，紧挨着一张桌子坐着，前额枕在臂上，脸埋着不见——他在抽泣。他一发觉我在，便猛地一惊坐直，拼命地强自镇定下来。

"———先生，"他道，"请别离我而去，哪怕几分钟。———先生，你不知道我正在受、而且已经受了怎样的罪。我大约是你平生所见所闻的，最不幸、最苦命的人——当真是的。先生，你不会明白——我也无法向你说明我所处境地的种种可怖。"

"那位可怜的小姐，"我冷冷地说，"显然坚信她自己是合法完婚的。罗伯逊医生明明白白地告诉过我——不但如此，他自己也这么相信。"

"是的，是的，是的，"他激烈地打断，"可我能证明并非如此。我交到你手上的那份文件，便足以叫你看出，绝无此事。她是这么以为的——她自然深信不疑，可怜的人；可她错了——大错特错。"

詹宁斯竟以这等阴险的急切，要把这一件——在我看来他此刻最该隐瞒的事——烙进我的信念里，叫我大为震惊；我忍不住说道——

"无论如何，您不会不愿尽您目前所能，作出一切补救，而且——"

"什么补救？"他激动地问。

"唯有一桩，"我答，"是您如今能作的；那便是——*成婚*。"

"您说得对，确实如此。"他停了好一阵，才阴郁地答道，"那是唯一——对这等亏负*唯一*的补救。"

他陷入了悒郁而悔恨的沉默。末了他突兀地说——

"世人说什么慷慨、冲动、诸如此类，可请信我一句话，*审慎*比这一切都值钱。我之铸成大错，全因自己全然不加思量。我已陷入一个我无力自拔——至少无力自拔向善——的境地；然而，先生，请公正待我；您*必须*公正待我，因为我对天发誓，我从未设计过害人；我绝非冷血的恶棍。我是被激情牵着走了——如我所说，被人误导、被人诱入了一个我再不能自主的境地，而众人却对我的行径指手画脚，仿佛我能为所欲为似的。这是公道么？这是诚实么？我被当作一个冷血阴谋的恶棍来唾骂，被咒骂着为何不作补救——我，这辈子从未设过一个深思熟虑的局，但凡能补救之处，从不曾犹豫不前。皇天在上，先生，我句句是实。这算得公平交易么——算得坦诚么——算得最起码的宽宥么？"

我提醒詹宁斯，我并无资格评判此事；又示意我已耽搁太久，便起身告辞。

"也罢，也罢，也罢。"他说，疲乏地耸了耸肩，"且忍耐，且洗牌发牌——谁知会翻出什么来——谁知呢？虽说，哎呀，无论你怎么看，这都是一个人所能卷入的、最该死、最阴暗的一桩烂事了。太难了——太难了，我对天发誓。倒像他们全都串通一气，要合伙毁了我似的；可是，凭魔鬼之名，这又能有什么好处——一群蠢货！"

===Original===
I now took my leave. A feeling of curiosity, and, still more strongly, one of intense interest in the unfortunate young lady, with whose fate he was so disastrously connected, had tempted me, minute after minute, to prolong my visit. It was already nearly dark, and the streetlamps were burning. I had reached the corner of Grafton-street, buried in profound abstraction, when I was suddenly accosted by a familiar voice. It was that of my friend Fitzgerald, a wild fellow, and a pleasant one to boot, and an accomplished adept in all the then important mysteries of the small-sword and pistol, and learned in all the lore of points of honour.

“Can you tell me,” said he, after our greeting, and taking me at the same time by the arm, and drawing me with him, “whether Dick Chadleigh has got into a scrape?”

“What kind of a scrape do you mean?” I asked, evasively.

“Why, he called on me when I was out, not half-an-hour ago,” he replied, “and left a hurried note, telling me I must go to him without a moment’s delay, on my return, about a little business. Now, there is but one kind of business I understand”—here he raised his arm once or twice significantly, as if balancing a pistol—“and I strongly suspect it must be upon *that* he has called me to counsel; all my friends make use of me, you know, on such occasions. Have you heard anything of Chadleigh’s being likely to want my services in *that* way—eh?”

I told him I knew that high words had passed between him and Captain Jennings.

“Jennings—ho, ho!” said he, with a serious air—“a cool hand, I fancy. Egad, from the little I’ve seen of him, I’m inclined to think, if *he* is the man, it will be a matter of flints and powder—egad, it does look like business.”

I was not at all sorry to comply with Fitzgerald’s suggestion, to the effect that I should await his return in Brown’s coffeehouse, and end the evening there in his company. My anxiety to learn the issue of the business was such, that I would gladly have done much more to satisfy it. Accordingly, I dropt into that public resort of idleness, while Fitzgerald, having called a coach, rumbled away to his interview with Chadleigh.

===Chinese===
我便告辞而去。一份好奇，以及——更强烈地——对那位与他命运惨烈相连的不幸小姐的关切，使我一分一分地把这趟拜访拖延了下来。其时天色将黑，街灯已燃。我已走到格拉夫顿街（Grafton-street）的拐角，正深陷沉思，忽被一个熟悉的声音叫住。那是我朋友菲茨杰拉德（Fitzgerald）——一个性情放浪、却讨人喜欢的家伙，又是当时备受看重的剑术与手枪两门的精通者，于名誉之一切学问无所不通。

"你能告诉我么，"寒暄既毕，他一面挽起我的手臂、把我带着同走，一面道，"迪克·查德利可是惹上麻烦了？"

"你指哪种麻烦？"我闪烁其词地问。

"嘿，半小时前他来找我，我不在家，"他答，"留下一张匆匆写的便条，说我一回来就得上他那儿去，一刻也耽误不得，说是有点儿小事。可是，我懂的营生，只有那么一种——"他说着，意味深长地把胳膊举了一两下，像是在掂一把手枪——"我疑心他要我参谋的，必是*那*一桩；我的朋友们每逢这种场合，都用得上我，你是知道的。你可曾听说，查德利可能要借重我*那*方面的效力么——嗯？"

我告诉他，我确知他与詹宁斯上尉之间曾有过一番激烈的言语。

"詹宁斯——嗬，嗬！"他神色凝重地说——"我瞧是个沉得住气的家伙。哎呀，就我所见的那一点儿而言，我倒以为，若*他*便是其人，那这回定是火石火药之交了——哎呀，这事瞧起来当真像要动真格的了。"

菲茨杰拉德提议我在布朗咖啡馆（Brown's coffeehouse）等他回来，与他一同在那里消磨这一晚，我欣然从命。我急于知此事之结局，其情之切，纵要我做更多的事，也在所不辞。于是，我便踅进那间闲人聚集之所，而菲茨杰拉德叫了一辆马车，辚辚而去，赴他与查德利之约。

===Original===
“I had sat there for considerably more than an hour, and was beginning to give up all hope of his return, when he entered.

“Well,” said he, when we had established ourselves at a table apart from the rest, “I have had a couple of odd—devilish odd conversations—since I saw you. I don’t know, indeed, whether I am at liberty to tell you the subject of the quarrel.”

I interrupted him by assuring him that I already knew it; and having satisfied him upon this point, he proceeded to detail the particulars, which I shall condense for the benefit of the reader.

He had, it seemed, found Chadleigh still much excited, and quite determined upon a hostile meeting; indeed, so resolute upon the point, that he would not so much as hear of anything to the contrary. His directions were peremptory, and amounted simply to this—that arrangements for a meeting were to be completed without a moment’s delay. All details, of course, were left to the direction of his friend; with respect to the quarrel itself, however, he was not invested with any right of diplomacy. Finding Chadleigh thus implacably resolved, Fitzgerald undertook the affair, which for other parties he had so often filled with singular efficiency, and was duly invested with the important functions of a “second” in the affair. Leaving Chadleigh, however, and being still of opinion that, if possible, the matter ought, for every reason, to be quietly adjusted, he resolved, upon his own responsibility, to make one final effort to prevent a catastrophe which, even if unattended by any more tragical consequences, must, at all events, have the effect of irreparably disgracing Miss Chadleigh. His belief was, that there remained one chance, and one only, of saving the unfortunate young lady, and that was, a private marriage with the author of her shame, accomplished without the delay of a single hour, if possible, so that the public might hear of the elopement and the marriage at one and the same time. Filled with this project, Fitzgerald hurried up the stairs of Jennings’ lodgings. The servant announced him as he entered the drawing-room. Jennings had altered his purpose, and determined, after what had passed, to remain at home. He was still in his dressing-gown, and, when his visitor entered, was sitting before his open desk, the candles burning beside him, and what seemed like a miniature in his hands. He was looking intently upon it, with no very loving aspect, when Fitzgerald entered; but he hastily thrust it, face downward, among the open letters, which lay in multitudinous confusion in the profundity of the old-fashioned desk, and shutting all up quickly, he locked it fast, and rose to receive him. Fitzgerald observed, also, that some torn papers were burning on the fire, and Jennings glanced quickly towards them, to see that they were actually destroyed.

“I have the honour, Captain Jennings, to wait upon you with a communication from Mr. Chadleigh,” said Fitzgerald.

“Pray, sir, take a chair,” said Jennings, coldly, and with a formal bow.

Fitzgerald complied, and resumed—

“I need scarcely, I apprehend, detail the reasons which have induced this step. You have already had an interview with my principal, Mr. Chadleigh.”

“There is certainly no occasion, sir, to say more. I do perfectly understand the nature of your visit, which I have, indeed, been expecting; and have only to say, as Mr. Chadleigh has pushed matters to extremity, I apprehend your instructions are very brief, and that our present business may be quickly arranged; if you will favour me with your card, my friend shall wait upon you at whatever hour you name.

“To say the truth, Mr. Jennings,” replied Fitzgerald, “you are right in supposing that my instructions have been very brief—in a word, they were those of absolute and unconditional hostility; this, however, is a case of such very peculiar delicacy—a case in which forbearance is so eminently important—so imperatively called for by all the circumstances, that I have resolved to take a responsibility upon myself, and endeavour to arrange this matter amicably, if, indeed, it be possible.”

Jennings continued to regard him with earnest attention, but did not speak.

“In short, as far as my influence goes, I would guarantee such an adjustment, upon one condition, which you can have no possible objection in submitting to—that you repair the dishonour you have done Miss Chadleigh, by *marrying* her, before her present unhappy position becomes public.”

Jennings grew deadly pale, and his features seemed to contract with the intensity of acute suffering, as he gazed for a few seconds upon the speaker, and then, abruptly rising, with a gesture like wringing his hands, he turned towards the fire, and remained standing for a time with his face averted.

“Well, sir,” exclaimed Fitzgerald, after a pause of considerable surprise—for he had expected a prompt and grateful acceptance of his proffered interposition—“what do you say—what am I to understand?”

Jennings heaved a dreary sigh, and said, gloomily and desperately enough—

“What you propose is absolutely out of the question—impracticable.”

“Then, sir, take the consequences,” said Fitzgerald, with irrepressible indignation; “you have, at least, quieted my scruples in acting against you—there is but one way of settling the matter now.”

“Just so, sir,” said Jennings, who had recovered his haughty coldness; “and, as I must leave details to the discretion of my friend, I have only to ask you at what hour precisely it will be convenient to you to see him?”

Fitzgerald named ten o’clock that night, and placed his card in Jennings’ hand.

“Very good, sir,” replied the latter, having glanced at it; “I presume that both parties are equally anxious to have this affair concluded with all possible despatch; my friend shall attend at the appointed hour.”

With these words they parted.

===Chinese===
我在那里坐了一个多钟头，正要不再指望他回来，他便走了进来。

"嗳，"我们在一张远离众人的桌前坐定后，他说，"自见你之后，我接连谈了两桩怪——怪得离奇的——话。说真的，我都不知道我能否把那场龃龉的因由告诉你。"

我打断他，向他保证我早已知晓；他见我确实知情，便从头细细说来，我则将其要旨为读者 condensed如下：

他找到查德利时，查德利仍旧激动得很，且已下定决心要来一场兵戎相见；而且在这件事上执拗得连半句异议都听不进去。他的吩咐斩钉截铁，归结起来不外一句——会面的诸般安排须立刻办妥，一刻不得延误。至于一切细节，当然悉由其友裁度；但就龃龉本身而言，他却未授其友任何斡旋之权。菲茨杰拉德见查德利如此决绝，便接下了这件差事——这种角色他从前替旁人担过不止一回，每每干练异常——于是顺理成章地负起了这一桩事件里"副手"的重任。然而，离开查德利之后，他仍以为此事若能设法悄悄了结，无论于公于私都更为妥当，便自作主张，要作最后一次努力，阻止一场灾难——这场灾难即便不致更悲惨的后果，至少也必将使查德利小姐名誉扫地、无可挽回。他相信，救那位不幸的小姐，唯有一线生机，且仅此一线——即与她身败名裂的祸首秘密成婚，若有可能，一个钟头也不耽搁，好叫世人同时听闻私奔与成婚两事。怀着这一盘算，菲茨杰拉德三步并作两步奔上詹宁斯寓所的楼梯。仆人通报他进客厅时，詹宁斯已改了主意——既已出了那档子事，他决定索性留在家中。他仍穿着晨衣，客人进来时，他正坐在敞开的书桌前，旁边点着蜡烛，手里似拿着一幅袖珍画像。菲茨杰拉德进门时，他正凝神看着那画像，神色颇不温柔；但他匆匆把画像反扣在那一堆凌乱不堪、堆在老式书桌深处的打开的信件里，迅速合上一切，牢牢锁好，起身相迎。菲茨杰拉德还瞧见，炉子里正烧着几张撕碎的纸，詹宁斯急忙朝它们瞥了一眼，要确认它们当真已烧毁。

"詹宁斯上尉，我有幸奉查德利先生之命，前来传话。"菲茨杰拉德道。

"先生请坐。"詹宁斯冷冷地说，客气地一躬身。

菲茨杰拉德依言落座，又道——

"我想，我无须赘述促成此番举动的缘由。您已与我方当事人查德利先生见过一面了。"

"先生，确实无须再多说。您此番造访的性质，我了然于胸——事实上我也一直在等；我只想说一句，查德利先生既已将事情推到极处，我想您的指令也极为简短，我们眼前这桩事可望速战速决；您若肯惠赐您的名片，我的朋友会在您所指定的任何时辰前去拜访。"

"说句实话，詹宁斯先生，"菲茨杰拉德答，"您所料不错，我的指令确是极为简短——一句话，那便是绝对而无条件的敌对；然而，此案情状极为特殊、极为微妙——此案之中，克制尤为重要——一切情形都迫切地呼唤着它——是以我决意自负其责，设法将此事善了，果能如此的话。"

詹宁斯仍以殷切的注意看着他，却不开口。

"简而言之，在我的影响所及的范围之内，我愿担保此事可得如此料理，唯有一个条件——您想必不可反对——那便是：趁这位小姐眼下的不幸处境尚未为世人所知之前，您以*成婚*来弥补您对查德利小姐所造成的玷辱。"

詹宁斯的脸色顿时惨白，五官似因剧痛而紧缩，他凝视着说话之人几秒，便突兀地站起身来，做出一个仿佛要绞扭双手的姿势，转身面向炉火，背对着众人，立了好一会儿。

"那么，先生，"菲茨杰拉德大出意料，停了好一阵才开口——他原以为对方会立刻、并心怀感激地接受他这番斡旋——"您怎么说——我该作何理解？"

詹宁斯叹了一口气，凄凉而绝望地答道——

"您所提议之事，根本无从谈起——行不通。"

"那么，先生，自负其果吧。"菲茨杰拉德抑不住愤怒地说，"您至少已使我对此番与您为敌，再无半点不安——此事如今唯有一途可了。"

"正是如此，先生。"詹宁斯恢复了那副高傲的冷淡，"既要把细节交由我友裁度，我只想请问，您何时与他相见为宜？"

菲茨杰拉德约定当晚十点，并把名片交到詹宁斯手中。

"很好，先生。"后者瞥了一眼名片，答道，"我想双方都一样地急于把此事了结，越快越好；我的朋友必于约定之时到场。"

言讫而别。

===Original===
“I don’t know how it is,” said Fitzgerald, after he had concluded his narrative, “but this thing has put me quite out of spirits—it is a bad affair, a d——d bad business; and, mark my words, so sure as you sit there, one or other of them will lose his life by it; they are both of them game—game to the backbone—game every inch, sir; and Chadleigh is in a murderous, black temper, too. Somehow, this is the first business of the sort, I ever had a hand in, that made me mopish; d——n me, but it smells all over of death and winding-sheets.”

As the mortal crisis of this strange tragedy approached, my interest in its denouement became more and more intense. At my entreaty, Fitzgerald undertook to let me know, so soon as they were completed, the detailed arrangements for the approaching duel. As he had sundry preparations to make, he was obliged to leave me, and I walked home, in dejected solitude, to my lodgings.

I was no sooner alone in my apartment, than I recollected the paper which had been entrusted to my care by Jennings. He had not only omitted to prohibit its perusal in my case, but had actually told me, in so many words, that I was at liberty to read it. There was, therefore, no impediment to the honourable gratification of my curiosity; and, secure from interruption, I proceeded to examine the document.

It purported to be a statement of certain occurrences, in connection with a clandestine visit made by the deponent, one “Benjamin Cruise, clerk, resident next door to the Cow and Cleaver, in Smithfield, in the city of Dublin;” at the solicitation of Mrs. Martha Keating, at the house of Sir Arthur Chadleigh, in St. Stephen’s-green. The narrative was to the effect, that the reverend gentleman in question was applied to, on or about a certain day, nearly a year preceding the date of the document in question, to attend at the back entrance of the said mansion; where, according to arrangement, he waited until about one o’clock, when he was admitted, and conveyed with great precaution up a backstair, and into a chamber, where was a young lady, as it seemed, in much agitation; and whom, as he was then and there informed by the old woman, his conductress, he believes to have been Miss Mary Chadleigh; by which name, he was afterwards directed to marry her to a certain young gentleman, whom he now knows to be Captain Jennings, and who, shortly after his, Cruise’s arrival, joined the party in the said chamber, with like caution; that he, Cruise, had then, at the desire of the party, proceeded to unite Miss Chadleigh and Captain Jennings, according to the ritual of the Church of England; and that a noise in another part of the house having alarmed them, the ceremony was interrupted in the introductory part, and before the giving of the ring; and he and Captain Jennings, were together hurried out from the house the same way; and, that he never before, or since then, saw Miss Mary Chadleigh, and knew not of her having been married by any other clergyman. This statement, which was given with great aggravation of detail, was duly dated, and signed in full, by the reverend gentleman, in those days, a not very creditably-notorious personage.

===Chinese===
"我也不知怎么的，"菲茨杰拉德讲完了这段事后说，"这事叫我意气消沉得很——这是一桩坏事，一桩该死的坏事；请记住我的话，正如你坐在此处一般确凿，他们两人之中，必有一个要为此送命；他们俩都是有种的——骨子里都是有种的——每一寸都是有种的，先生；而查德利这会儿正在一种杀气腾腾、阴鸷狠毒的心境之中。也不知怎的，我经手过的这等事里，这是头一桩叫我郁郁寡欢的；该死的，这事里有一股子死与寿衣的气味，扑鼻而来。"

随着这桩离奇悲剧的生死关头临近，我对结局的关切也愈发炽烈。在我的恳请之下，菲茨杰拉德答应一俟即将到来的决斗诸事安排停当，便立刻告知我。他尚有几样准备要做，不得不与我暂别；我则郁郁独归寓所。

我一独自回到房中，便想起詹宁斯托我保管的那份文书。他不仅未曾禁止我过目，还曾明明白白地说过，我尽可一读。那么，我这点好奇心之满足，乃是君子所为，并无窒碍；我便避开一切打扰，着手研读那份文书。

文书自称，是关于某几桩事项的陈述，牵涉到具陈人某次的秘密造访——此人名叫"本杰明·克鲁斯，书记官，住都柏林城史密斯菲尔德区（Smithfield）'母牛与屠斧'酒馆隔壁"；系应圣斯蒂芬草地亚瑟·查德利爵士府上玛莎·基廷夫人（Mrs. Martha Keating）之请而行。文书大意称：所述这位可敬的教士，于本文日期之前约一年的某日，应邀前往上述宅第的后门候命；依约等候至约莫一时许，方被引入，并极其谨慎地经由一道后楼梯，被带到一间内室，室内有一位小姐，神色颇为激动；据彼时彼地引他前来的老妇人相告，他相信她便是玛丽·查德利小姐；他随后受命以此名，将她与一位青年绅士行礼成婚——此绅士他如今方知是詹宁斯上尉；在克鲁斯到达后不久，此人亦以同样谨慎的方式加入室内众人；克鲁斯旋即应众人之请，依英国国教仪式，为查德利小姐与詹宁斯上尉主持婚礼；然因宅中他处传来一阵声响，众人受了惊，婚礼乃于开场部分、尚未交换戒指之前便被打断；他与詹宁斯上尉一同循原路被匆匆送出宅外；他自那以后，无论此前此后，再未见过玛丽·查德利小姐，亦不知她曾由任何其他教士为她主持婚礼。这份陈述，细节详尽得令人发指，日期俱全，由那位可敬的教士亲笔署名——此人当年是个颇有些不大光彩的、声名狼藉之人。

===Original===
The perusal of this document impressed me still more unfavourably respecting Jennings. There was something sinister and equivocal about the whole thing. The infamous character of the degraded man who signed it; the industrious detail with which it had been prepared; and, above all, the unaccountable precaution which had suggested the adoption of such a measure, filled me with painful misgivings, to the effect that some gross and horrible delusion had been practised upon poor Miss Chadleigh; and I could not forbear deeply regretting, that I had suffered myself, under conditions of secrecy, to be made the depository of so suspicious a document.

I was pursuing this unsatisfactory train of reflections, when a note was placed in my hand; it was couched in the following terms:—

> “Dear ———,
> “At seven o’clock tomorrow morning, on the Fifteen Acres.
> “Yours in haste,
> “Fitzgerald.”

I spent a restless night, and was up long before dawn. Having completed my toilet, I walked some way into town, in the grey twilight of coming morning; and when I had, as I calculated, consumed the greater part of the necessary interval, I got into a hackney-coach, and drove directly to the place of rendezvous. Availing myself of a screen of bushes, I stopped the carriage, and got out, unobserved from the scene of action. As soon as I obtained a view of the ground, I observed there a coach, and a little group of three persons, who were standing, listlessly, close beside it; two or three gentlemen on horseback—mere spectators, of course, like myself—were also on the ground. I walked as near as I decently could to the group I have mentioned, and saw that Chadleigh and Fitzgerald were two of the number. The latter looked at his watch, and mounted the coach-box, to command a more extended view; shading his eyes with his hand, he looked along the skirting of wood which bounds the place, in the direction of the city, and at last his eye seemed to settle upon a distant object. I followed the direction of his gaze, and saw the top of a carriage moving in the distance.

“Here,” I thought, “comes Jennings; which of them is to leave the field unhurt, and which—” I shrank from the inquiry, merely mental as it was, with something like a shudder.

“Poor Mary Chadleigh! whichever way it ends, its issue must be, to her, a tragedy.”

Fitzgerald had descended from his post of observation, and recognizing me, he walked up, and shook me by the hand. He looked pale and stern.

“They are coming,” said he, glancing towards the vehicle which was now rapidly approaching.

“Rather late—are they?” I asked—more from want of something to say than any other cause.

“No, no; a quarter past seven was fixed on, subsequently to my note, last night; we should scarcely have had light earlier,” he said.

“The weapons are pistols?” I asked.

“Yes,” he answered; “and we may as well begin to make our preparations. Come with me; you’ll not be in the way; I won’t stand on ceremony when the time comes for you to withdraw and leave Major Gurney and myself to our deliberations.”

So saying, he drew me with him to the side of the carriage.

“Take out the case,” he said to the man who stood by the carriage-door; “not that—those are the instruments; leave it where Dr. ——— placed it—the *flat* case—that’s right; just keep it in your hand; and when I beckon to you, bring it over to me quickly; there, don’t shake it.”

===Chinese===
这份文书读毕，我对詹宁斯的观感更为不堪。整件事里，有一种阴险而暧昧的东西。署名那位被褫夺圣职之人的恶名昭彰；文书准备得这般煞费苦心、事无巨细；尤其是——不知出于何故竟有人想出此等防备之策——这一切都令我满心忐忑，只觉可怜的查德利小姐，被人施了一桩极其可恶、极其骇人的骗局；而我，竟在缄默之诺下，做了这般可疑文书的保管者，我禁不住深自懊悔。

我正沿着这条不快的思路冥想，忽有一封信递到我手中；信上写的是：——

> "亲爱的———：
> 明晨七时，十五英亩地（the Fifteen Acres）见。
> 匆匆。
> 菲茨杰拉德。"

我彻夜辗转，天未亮便起了床。盥洗穿戴既毕，在将明未明的晨光里，我徒步向城里走了一程；待我盘算着已耗去所需时间的大半，便雇了一辆出租马车，直奔约会之地。借着一片灌木丛的遮挡，我叫车停下，下车时并未被场上的人瞧见。我一得窥场地的全貌，便看见那里停着一辆马车，旁边有三人一小群，懒洋洋地立着；两三位骑马的绅士——自然是和我一般的旁观者——也在场。我尽量得体地走近我方才所说的那一小群人，看见其中两人正是查德利和菲茨杰拉德。后者看了看表，登上了车夫座，以便望得更远些；他以手遮眼，沿着场地边上那一线树林、朝都柏林方向眺望，末了他的目光似落在远处一个物件上。我顺他所望的方向看去，瞧见一辆马车的顶篷，正在远处移动。

"来了，"我心想，"詹宁斯来了；他们俩，哪一个能完好无损地离开这块地，哪一个——"我不敢再想下去，纵然只是心底一念，也叫我几欲打一个寒噤。

"可怜的玛丽·查德利！无论结局如何，此事之收场，于她，注定是一出悲剧。"

菲茨杰拉德已从他的瞭望之位下来，认出我，便走上前与我握手。他面色苍白、神情凝重。

"他们来了。"他说，朝那辆此刻正疾驰而来的车望了一眼。

"他们——略迟了些吧？"我问——倒不是为别的，不过是没话找话罢了。

"不，不；昨晚在我那便笺之后，又改定为七点一刻；再早我们怕是还没有光呢。"他说。

"用家伙是手枪么？"我问。

"是的，"他答，"我们也不妨着手预备了。随我来；您不会碍事；到了该您退场、由我和古尔尼少校（Major Gurney）议事之时，我不会跟您见外的。"

说着，他把我拉到马车旁边。

"把那匣子拿出来。"他对站在车门边的仆人道，"不是那个——那些是器具；把它放在———医生放的地方——那只*扁*匣子——对了；就这样，拿在手里；我招手时，你赶紧给我送来；好，别晃。"

===Original===
We now walked up to Chadleigh, who stood moodily and doggedly, with his surtout buttoned up to the chin; and exchanging, now and then, a brief word or two with his companion—a slim, pale-faced, young surgeon, who was, evidently, but one degree less frightened than if he had been himself a principal. Fitzgerald dropped my arm as he approached, and leaving me at a little distance, observed, consulting his watch—

“Eight minutes before their time.”

Chadleigh nodded.

“They have brought advice, too,” suggested the little surgeon, timidly; “there is a second carriage.”

“There’s no need to waste time,” said Chadleigh; “we had better walk on a little to meet them.”

The steps of the first carriage had, by this time, been let down; and Jennings, followed by a stiff, elderly gentleman, with a red, important face, and a military air, descended upon the turf. After, as it seemed, a few directions to the servants, they began to walk towards us, briskly, followed by an attendant, carrying a pistol-case; and with the carriage, which carried their medical friend, a little in the rear.

My heart swelled within me as those two little groups approached one another, in grim silence, over the smooth sward. Gracious God! what an awful account for eternity was to be closed ere they parted!

On they came, briskly and steadily, through the keen and misty morning air—nearer and nearer—until the interposing space became so limited that each party, as it were, by mutual consent, slackening their pace, came slowly to a halt, at some dozen steps apart, and interchanged, in silence, a stern and formal salutation. Fitzgerald stepped forward, and was met about halfway by the grim elderly gentleman whom I have described. After another salutation, as formal, they withdrew a little, and conducted a brief conference, in short, decisive whispers. Meanwhile, those who, either accidentally, or by design, had been spectators of the proceedings, began to gather about the spot on which the combatants were placed.

I had thought, once or twice, that Jennings perceived my presence, and now I was assured of it.

“Mr. ———,” he said, in a low, hurried tone, “I have a request to make.”

“Pray, state it, sir,” I replied, approaching.

“It is just this—should I happen to fall, remain here for a few moments, as I may feel it necessary to make a communication to you of the last importance, not to myself, but to others.”

I undertook to comply with this request, and withdrew.

There was not the slightest perceptible tremor, not the least indication of excitement, in his manner, voice, or aspect, excepting that he was, perhaps, a little paler than usual, and his eyes were unusually dilated. With the restlessness of suspense, I walked to the spot where Chadleigh was standing, and, almost at the same moment, Fitzgerald returned.

“What is the distance?” asked Chadleigh.

“Ten paces,” rejoined Fitzgerald.

“Too much,” said he, gruffly.

“It is the usual thing; you don’t want to have us look bloodthirsty,” retorted Fitzgerald.

“And for that reason, I’d like to have it settled one way or other at the first shot.”

“It will be settled time enough,” said the second, and, unlocking the pistol-case, he proceeded to load the weapons; a silence, hardly broken by a whisper, followed, during which the click of ramrods, and the cramming home of wadded bullets were ominously audible.

“Are you ready, Mr. Fitzgerald?” inquired Jennings’ second; “if so, we had better place our men at once.”

A piece of money was thrown up for choice of ground; Jennings won.

“Luck’s so far with us, sir; I hope it may not turn,” remarked the veteran, with a ghastly jocularity.

Chadleigh disencumbered himself of his surtout, and the combatants took their ground respectively.

“Gentlemen,” said the major, addressing the spectators, “have the goodness to draw back a little; some of you may be hurt, else.”

The suggestion was complied with, and a breathless silence followed.

“Are you ready, gentlemen,” inquired the major.

Each answered in the affirmative.

===Chinese===
我们随即走到查德利跟前，他闷闷地、倔头倔脑地站着，紧身外套的扣子一直扣到下巴；偶尔与他身边那位同伴——一位瘦削、面色苍白的年轻外科医生，瞧那惊惶之色，比他自己当当事人也好不了多少——交换一两句简短的话。菲茨杰拉德走到跟前时松开了我的手臂，把我留在稍远处，看了看表，道——

"他们还差八分钟。"

查德利点了点头。

"他们也带了医士，"那小个子外科医生怯怯地说，"还有第二辆车呢。"

"用不着耽搁工夫，"查德利道，"我们不妨往前迎一迎。"

第一辆车的车阶此时已被放下；詹宁斯下了车，踩在草地上，身后跟着一位板着脸、上了年纪的绅士，面色红润、神气活现，一副戎马气度。他似向仆从吩咐了几句，便带着一位拎着手枪匣的随从，朝我们这边快步走来；载着他们那位医士朋友的马车，稍稍落在后头。

那两小群人，在死一般的寂静里，踏着平整的草皮，彼此走近——我的心在胸膛里发胀。仁慈的上天啊！他们分手之前，竟要了结一笔何等可怖的、要向永恒交代的账啊！

他们来了，又轻快又稳当地，穿过清冷雾蒙的晨气——越来越近——直到中间的间隔所剩无几，两边的人便仿佛心照不宣，一同放慢步子，缓缓地停了下来，相隔约莫十来步远，默默交换了一个冷峻而客套的致意。菲茨杰拉德上前几步，在半道与我方才所描写的那位板着脸的上了年纪的绅士相遇。又彼此如仪地一礼之后，他们退开一点，以短促、果决的低语，进行了简短的磋商。与此同时，那些或偶然、或有意目睹此情此景的人，开始在两位当事人所立之处附近聚拢起来。

我一两回以为詹宁斯察觉到了我在场，此刻我则确信了这一点。

"———先生，"他以低而急促的口吻道，"我有一事相求。"

"请讲，先生。"我答着，走近一些。

"就是这一桩——我若万一倒下，请在此地稍留片刻，因为或有一桩至要之言，我须向您交代——此事不关我自己，却关系旁人。"

我答应照办，便退开了。

他的神态、嗓音、面色，都察觉不出一丝一毫的颤抖或激动，只是脸色或许比平日略白，瞳孔也异乎寻常地张得很大。我在悬虑的焦躁中，走到查德利所立之处，几乎同时，菲茨杰拉德也回来了。

"距离多少？"查德利问。

"十步。"菲茨杰拉德答。

"太多了。"他粗声道。

"这是惯例；您总不希望我们显得嗜血吧。"菲茨杰拉德驳道。

"正因如此，我才愿一枪便了结此事，无论结局如何。"

"了结之时自会了结。"副手说罢，开了手枪匣，开始装填家伙；一阵沉默随之而来，几乎连耳语也无；其间通条轻叩、裹布弹丸被填入膛的声响，不祥地可闻。

"菲茨杰拉德先生，您可预备好了？"詹宁斯的副手问，"如已齐备，我们便把人各就位。"

一枚钱币被抛起，以择场地；詹宁斯赢了。

"运气暂时在我们这边，先生；但愿它莫要中途转向。"老兵带着一种惨然的诙谐道。

查德利脱下紧身外套，双方当事人各就各位。

"先生们，"少校对旁观者道，"劳驾后退一点儿；否则难免有人被误伤。"

众人依言后退，随之而来的是屏息般的静默。

"先生们，预备好了么？"少校问。

两边都答：好了。

===Original===
After a brief pause the word “fire” was given, each raised his weapon, but Chadleigh only fired. Jennings must have had a narrow escape, for he shook his head, put his hand to his ear, as if a hornet had stung him, then, quickly raising the pistol, he fired into the air, threw the weapon up, and caught it by the muzzle as it descended.

“D——e, sir, that won’t do,” exclaimed Chadleigh, in a tone of bitter exasperation, “you may throw away your shot, if you will, but I’m cursed if you get out of the business on these terms; it is the act of a poltroon and a scoundrel to sneak out of a quarrel that way; I’ll baulk your scheme, for you—”

“Don’t say a word,” said Jennings, sternly, interrupting Fitzgerald, who was about to interfere, “I call you all to witness I have stood his fire, and without returning it—that’s all; let him take the consequences of his vindictive obstinacy. I’ll not stand to be shot at like a target; I’ve a right to defend myself, and by ——— I’ll do it.”

“Certainly; ’tis very just and sensible; the very point I was going to put,” said the major, with a brisk approval, that strongly contrasted with the savage intensity of Jennings’ tone.

It was plain that the angry and mortal passions of combat were, in Jennings, at last thoroughly aroused. I heard him say to Major Gurney, once or twice, impatiently, “make haste,” and saw him dart one or two lowering glances at Chadleigh. The preliminaries for a second exchange of shots were completed in a few moments—the signal was given—and both fired so exactly together, that, from the report, one would have believed the explosion a single one. Jennings’ shot was well directed, though accident defeated its aim; it struck the trigger guard of Chadleigh’s pistol, which was nearly forced from his hand by the shock, and glancing off, the ball buried itself in the sod. Jennings, on the other hand, stood immovable, while one might slowly count three, then staggered a little, dropped his pistol, and fell suddenly to the ground. Chadleigh walked forward a few hesitating steps, checked himself, and, in an agitated voice, said to the surgeon who had accompanied him—

“You may be wanted here—by ——— he’s hurt! Fitzgerald, come away—come, I say.”

Meanwhile, amid a babel of conflicting and exciting suggestions, the surgeon, ordering the crowd to stand back, had the wounded man raised a little on the carriage cushions, and was proceeding to examine the injury, but Jennings said, faintly—

“Don’t—don’t—it’s all of no use.”

He invited me, with a glance and a slight gesture, to approach.

“One word,” he said, speaking with great difficulty. I stooped down, to bring my ear as near him as I could. “It’s all a lie—all that—the paper—see the man, and tell him I said so—poor Mary—I made him do it, but I could not help it—there’s no use in maintaining the cheat any longer—I’m dying. Keep him away,” he continued, faintly turning his gaze for a moment on the surgeon, who was approaching, and then on me, “he can do nothing for me—only listen to me—my last word—that paper is—is a lie—we were married—I can—I can scarcely speak—don’t—don’t-—are you going—hold me—oh God!”

===Chinese===
短暂一停之后，"放"字令下，双方皆举枪，但开枪的只有查德利一人。詹宁斯定是九死一生，只见他摇了摇头，把手举到耳边，仿佛被一只大黄蜂螫了一下；随即他迅疾举起手枪，朝天放了一枪，把枪向上一抛，枪落下时又一把接住了枪口。

"该——的，先生，这可不行，"查德利以极其愤激的口吻嚷道，"你大可浪费你那一枪，随你的便，可你休想就此脱身；这等溜出一场争执的做派，乃是懦夫和无赖之所为；你的算盘，我非要打破不可——"

"一个字也别说。"詹宁斯冷峻地说，打断了正要上前干预的菲茨杰拉德，"我请诸位作证，我已承受了他的枪火，却未还击——仅此而已；让他自食他那睚眦必报的固执之果吧。我可不愿像靶子似的站着挨打；我有自卫之权，我对天发誓，必行之。"

"当然；这话再公道、再在理不过；这正是我方要说的。"少校以一种轻快的赞许道，与詹宁斯那凶狠的语气恰成强烈对比。

显然，詹宁斯那战斗的、要人性命的怒火，终于被彻底点燃了。我听见他一两回不耐烦地对古尔尼少校说"快点"，又见他朝查德利投去一两道阴沉的目光。第二轮对射的诸般预备，片刻间便已停当——令下——两边一齐开枪，时机分毫不差，以致单听枪声，简直会以为是同一响。詹宁斯那一枪瞄得极准，虽则意外毁了它的准头；它击中了查德利手枪的扳机护圈，那枪几乎被这一震从他手中脱手；子弹一偏，便扎进了草皮里。詹宁斯这边呢，一动不动地立着，慢数到三的工夫，身子晃了一晃，手枪落地，便突然栽倒在地。查德利犹犹豫豫地向前走了几步，又收住脚，神色激动地对随行的外科医生道——

"您怕是用得上了——我对天发誓，他受伤了！菲茨杰拉德，我们走——来呀，我说。"

与此同时，众人七嘴八舌、议论纷纭，外科医生一面喝令众人后退，一面叫人把伤者稍稍扶起，靠在马车的座垫上，着手检验伤处，詹宁斯却虚弱地说——

"别——别——这一切都无济于事了。"

他以一道目光和一个微微的手势，示意我上前。

"一句话。"他说，说话极其吃力。我弯下腰，把耳朵凑得离他尽可能的近。"全是假的——那纸上所说一切——找到那个人，告诉他我亲口说的——可怜的玛丽——是我逼他做的，可我也是身不由己——这骗局再撑下去也无益了——我要死了。叫他离我远些，"他虚弱地接下去，把目光转向正走近的外科医生，停了停，又转向我，"他为我已无能为力——你只管听我说——我的临终之言——那纸文书——是——是一派谎言——我们成过婚——我——我几乎说不出话——别——别——你是要走么——扶着我——哦，老天！"

===Original===
I can never forget the look that Jennings fixed on me—the fearful, imploring gaze of his dilated eyes, filled with the wild, deep, awful meaning of death—the strangling effort to speak—the ghastly pallor—and then, the dropping of the jaw—the mouth, through which the breath of life was never more to stir, helplessly agape—the eyes, with the deep earnestness of their awful meaning, fixed forever—and the stern movelessness of the darkened brow. Was this the gay, vain, reckless Jennings? Was this mute but fearful monitor of death, propped-up before us, indeed the frivolous, lighthearted, sensual man of the world, among whose dreams and calculations the warning shadow of death had never glided?

“By ——— he is dead,” said one of the bystanders, breaking the breathless silence that had followed.

The surgeon kneeled down beside him, placed his hand over the dead man’s heart, raised his arm, and held his pulse for a moment—then replaced the hand by his side in silence. I remember seeing the grass that he had plucked, dropping from the stiffening fingers.

“Lift the body into the carriage, and drive to Kildare-street,” said the physician, addressing the servants.

---

===Chinese===
詹宁斯望着我、定在我身上的那一道目光，我永生不能忘——那双瞪大的眼睛里，流露着可怖而哀恳的神色，充溢着死亡之狂乱、深沉而骇人的意涵——那挣扎着、几乎要噎住地要说出话来的努力——那死人般的惨白——随后，下颌松垂——那张嘴，生命的气息再也无从在其中掠动，无力地张着——那双眼睛，带着它们可怖意涵的深沉而凝重，永远地凝住了——那阴沉了的眉宇，那铁一般的凝然不动。这难道就是那个轻佻、浮华、孟浪的詹宁斯么？这位被支在我们面前的、无言却可怖的死亡之诫，难道当真就是那个浮薄、轻快、沉溺声色的世路中人？死亡的警示之影，可曾在他的迷梦和算计之间掠过半丝么？

"我对天发誓，他死了。"沉默既久，一位旁观者打破了那屏息的寂静。

外科医生在他身旁跪下，把手按在死者的胸口，举起他的胳膊，按了一刻脉——然后把那只手默默地放回他身侧。我记得看见他从那僵硬的手指间，拈起的几根青草，纷纷落下。

"把遗体抬上车，开到基尔代尔街去。"医师对仆从们说。

---

===Original===
Poor Mary Chadleigh was long held in ignorance of this, to her, overwhelming catastrophe. At length, however, it could be no longer concealed; and the revelation was followed by a brain-fever, which first threatened her life, and then her reason. She recovered, however, with a mind unimpaired, although with a shattered constitution. With her younger brother and her child, the youthful widow found an asylum for years in England, until the death of Sir Arthur put her in possession of the fortune which his will could not control.

One circumstance connected with the history of Jennings’ fate, however, never reached her ear. I had taken care to procure, though not without considerable difficulty at starting, the fullest evidence of the marriage—and afterwards learned, from the younger brother, whose return had, perhaps, precipitated the catastrophe, a circumstance which accounted for what had, for a time, appeared to me the gratuitous villany of Jennings, in himself denying, and suborning others to deny, a marriage, whose existence was necessary to protect Miss Chadleigh from the agonizing degradation, the appalling ruin, with which she had been so imminently, though unconsciously, threatened. Jennings, it seemed, had actually married a woman of very equivocal rank, and more than equivocal character, in India. There were circumstances, however, which made the validity of this marriage doubtful, and the woman herself had left him, and formed a vicious connection there; so that he had regarded the marriage as dissolved by mutual consent, and never reckoned upon the remote contingency of her turning up, by any accident. By a fatal coincidence, however, it happened, that, of the few individuals who knew of this connection, his intimate and confidential friend, Captain Chadleigh, had been one. His supposed death had, however, quieted those alarms, which would have precluded the moral possibility of Jennings’ hazarding the audacious step which ended so fatally for himself, and the unexpected and impending return of Chadleigh was the first event which recalled the reckless and unprincipled man to a sense of his actual position. How often is crime unavailing for its meditated purpose, and effective only for the ruin of him who plans it. While Jennings was stoutly denying his marriage with Mary Chadleigh, to avoid the fancied danger of a prosecution, the poor young lady’s brother was bringing with him tidings of the death (long previous to his marriage with Miss Chadleigh) of the profligate woman, whose claim upon his hand had driven him to the selfish and desperate expedient of denying his union with the too-confiding creature whom his ardent and impetuous pursuit had won to lifelong sorrow. Yet I have lived to see the offspring of this inauspicious marriage, Arthur Chadleigh, a member of parliament, and the sole inheritor of the great Chadleigh estates in Ireland.

===Chinese===
可怜的玛丽·查德利，长久以来都被瞒在鼓里，不知这一桩于她而言、足以压垮一切的惨祸。然而，事情终究瞒不下去；一旦揭明，紧随而来的便是一场脑热病，先是要了她的命，又险些夺去她的神志。不过她终于熬了过来，心智无损，只是身子已大伤元气。这位年轻的寡妇，带着她的幼弟和孩子，在英国觅得一处避难之所，一住多年，直到亚瑟爵士去世，使她得以继承那笔他的遗嘱也无从左右的财产。

然而，与詹宁斯命运相关的一桩情由，她始终不曾听人提起。我曾费心——虽说初时颇为不易——搜罗了这场婚姻最充分的证据；其后又从那位幼弟——他的归来或许正是促成这场惨祸的导火索——口中，得知了一桩情由，正好解释了一件事：詹宁斯曾亲口否认、又收买他人否认一桩婚事，而此事之存在，原可庇护查德利小姐免受那种痛切的玷辱、免于那种骇人的倾覆——而这一切当时正迫在眉睫地、虽则全然不自觉地威胁着她——这一度在我看来，无异于无端的作恶。原来，詹宁斯早年在印度，确曾与一位身份极为可疑、品行尤甚可疑的女子成过婚。只是有几桩情形，使这桩婚事的有效性颇为可疑；那女子自己也离他而去，在印度另结了一段苟且之情；是以他便把这段婚姻视作双方默许地解除，再不曾把那女子有朝一日偶然出现的渺远可能放在心上。然而命运弄人——知情者寥寥无几之中，竟有他的至交、心腹之友查德利上尉其人。这位友人之"死讯"，原已平息了詹宁斯的种种忧惧——若无此"死讯"，他绝无可能在道义上冒那胆大包天的一步，并最终酿成自己的横祸；而查德利出人意料、迫在眉睫的归来，乃是头一桩事，把这位孟浪而无原则之人，唤回到对自身实际处境的清醒之中。世间多少罪恶，于其图谋的目的毫无裨益，却只促成图谋者自身的败亡。当詹宁斯为了规避他所设想的被追诉之险，而矢口否认自己与玛丽·查德利的婚事之时，那位可怜小姐的兄长，正带在身边一个消息——那荒淫女子久已身故（远在詹宁斯与查德利小姐成婚之前），正是这女子昔日对他这一只手的索求，逼得他铤而走险，自私而绝望地否认自己与那位过于轻信的姑娘的结合——正是他当年一番热烈而急切的追逐，赢得了她，也赢来了她终生的哀愁。然而，我竟活到了看见这段不祥姻缘的血脉——亚瑟·查德利——成为国会议员，并独继承了查德利家在爱尔兰的广大地产。

## The Fortunes of Sir Robert Ardagh, Being a Second Extract from the Papers of the Late Father Purcell. / 罗伯特·阿达格爵士的命运——已故珀塞尔神父遗稿之第二篇摘录

> "大地亦有泡沫，一如流水——
>
> 此物即属其中。"

===Original===
In the south of Ireland, and on the borders of the county of Limerick, there lies a district of two or three miles in length, which is rendered interesting by the fact that it is one of the very few spots throughout this country, in which some vestiges of aboriginal forest still remain. It has little or none of the lordly character of the American forest, for the axe has felled its oldest and its grandest trees; but in the close wood which survives, live all the wild and pleasing peculiarities of nature: its complete irregularity, its vistas, in whose perspective the quiet cattle are peacefully browsing; its refreshing glades, where the grey rocks arise from amid the nodding fern; the silvery shafts of the old birch trees; the knotted trunks of the hoary oak, the grotesque but graceful branches which never shed their honours under the tyrant pruning-hook; the soft green sward; the chequered light and shade; the wild luxuriant weeds; the lichen and the moss—all, all are beautiful alike in the green freshness of spring, or in the sadness and sere of autumn. Their beauty is of that kind which makes the heart full with joy—appealing to the affections with a power which belongs to nature only. This wood runs up, from below the base, to the ridge of a long line of irregular hills, having perhaps, in primitive times, formed but the skirting of some mighty forest which occupied the level below.

But now, alas! whither have we drifted? whither has the tide of civilisation borne us? It has passed over a land unprepared for it—it has left nakedness behind it; we have lost our forests, but our marauders remain; we have destroyed all that is picturesque, while we have retained everything that is revolting in barbarism. Through the midst of this woodland there runs a deep gully or glen, where the stillness of the scene is broken in upon by the brawling of a mountain-stream, which, however, in the winter season, swells into a rapid and formidable torrent.

===Chinese===
爱尔兰南部、利默里克郡（Limerick）的边界上，有一处长约二三英里的地带，其所以引人注目，乃因它是我国境内所剩无几、犹存几分原始林踪迹的所在之一。它几乎没有美洲森林那般雄浑气派，因为最古老、最壮伟的树木早已倒在了斧斤之下；然而在那片劫后余生的密林之中，大自然一切野趣与可爱之处都还活着：全然无章的布局，那一条条透视深处的远景，恬静的牛群正在其间安然吃草；那沁人心脾的林间空地，灰色岩石从摇曳的蕨丛中探出头来；老桦树银白的树干；苍老橡树虬结的躯干，那些古怪却优美、从不在暴君般的修枝钩下屈尊落叶的枝桠；柔软如茵的草地；斑驳明灭的光影；野性疯长的杂草；地衣与青苔——这一切，一切，无论在春天的新绿里，还是在秋日的萧瑟中，都同样美丽。这种美，属于那种令人心头充盈喜悦的美——它以一种唯大自然才有的力量，叩动着人的情思。这片林子从山脚一路攀上一列参差绵延的山脊，或许在远古时代，它不过是占据下方平地的那片莽莽大森林的一道边裙罢了。

然而如今，唉！我们漂泊到了何方？文明的潮水又把我们卷向了何处？它漫过了一片尚未为之备好的土地——身后只留下满目疮痍；我们丢了森林，劫掠者却还在；我们毁掉了一切如画之物，却把野蛮中一切令人作呕的东西都原封不动地保留了下来。穿过这片林地中部，有一道深陷的沟壑或山涧，山涧溪流潺潺作响，打破了此处的宁静；只是到了冬季，这溪水便涨成一条湍急而凶猛的洪流。

===Original===
There is one point at which the glen becomes extremely deep and narrow; the sides descend to the depth of some hundred feet, and are so steep as to be nearly perpendicular. The wild trees which have taken root in the crannies and chasms of the rock have so intersected and entangled, that one can with difficulty catch a glimpse of the stream, which wheels, flashes, and foams below, as if exulting in the surrounding silence and solitude.

This spot was not unwisely chosen, as a point of no ordinary strength, for the erection of a massive square tower or keep, one side of which rises as if in continuation of the precipitous cliff on which it is based. Originally, the only mode of ingress was by a narrow portal in the very wall which overtopped the precipice, opening upon a ledge of rock which afforded a precarious pathway, cautiously intersected, however, by a deep trench cut with great labour in the living rock; so that, in its original state, and before the introduction of artillery into the art of war, this tower might have been pronounced, and that not presumptuously, almost impregnable.

The progress of improvement and the increasing security of the times had, however, tempted its successive proprietors, if not to adorn, at least to enlarge their premises, and at about the middle of the last century, when the castle was last inhabited, the original square tower formed but a small part of the edifice.

===Chinese===
在某一处，山涧变得格外深窄；两岸陡降至数百尺之深，几乎是直上直下。扎根于岩缝与裂隙间的野树盘根错节、相互绞缠，人很难瞥见底下那道在回旋、闪烁、翻腾的溪水，它仿佛在四围的死寂与荒僻之中怡然自得。

这处地方被选作一处非同寻常的险要之地来营造一座厚重方正的塔楼或曰堡垒，倒也不算失策；塔楼的一侧拔地而起，仿佛是它脚下的悬崖陡壁的延续。最初，唯一的入口就是悬在峭壁之上的那面墙里的一道窄门，门外是一条狭长的岩架，作为一条岌岌可危的通道；这条通道又被人小心翼翼地用一道深沟切断，那沟是费了好大气力在活岩上凿出来的；因此，在最初的状态下，在火炮尚未引入战争艺术之前，说这座塔楼几乎固若金汤，倒也算不得狂妄。

然而时世日趋承平、改良日益推进，历代主人纵使无意装点，至少也动了扩建旧业的念头；约莫上世纪中叶、城堡最后一次有人居住时，那座最初的方塔，已不过是整座建筑的一小部分了。

===Original===
The castle, and a wide tract of the surrounding country, had from time immemorial belonged to a family which, for distinctness, we shall call by the name of Ardagh; and owing to the associations which, in Ireland, almost always attach to scenes which have long witnessed alike the exercise of stern feudal authority, and of that savage hospitality which distinguished the good old times, this building has become the subject and the scene of many wild and extraordinary traditions. One of them I have been enabled, by a personal acquaintance with an eyewitness of the events, to trace to its origin; and yet it is hard to say whether the events which I am about to record appear more strange or improbable as seen through the distorting medium of tradition, or in the appalling dimness of uncertainty which surrounds the reality.

Tradition says that, sometime in the last century, Sir Robert Ardagh, a young man, and the last heir of that family, went abroad and served in foreign armies; and that, having acquired considerable honour and emolument, he settled at Castle Ardagh, the building we have just now attempted to describe. He was what the country people call a "dark" man; that is, he was considered morose, reserved, and ill-tempered; and, as it was supposed from the utter solitude of his life, was upon no terms of cordiality with the other members of his family.

The only occasion upon which he broke through the solitary monotony of his life was during the continuance of the racing season, and immediately subsequent to it; at which time he was to be seen among the busiest upon the course, betting deeply and unhesitatingly, and invariably with success. Sir Robert was, however, too well known as a man of honour, and of too high a family, to be suspected of any unfair dealing. He was, moreover, a soldier, and a man of an intrepid as well as of a haughty character; and no one cared to hazard a surmise, the consequences of which would be felt most probably by its originator only.

===Chinese===
这座城堡，连同周围一大片乡野，自古以来便属于一个家族——为行文清楚起见，我们且称其为阿达格（Ardagh）家族；由于这处所在历经岁月，早已既见证了严酷的封建威权之行使，又见证了昔日好时光里那种粗豪的好客之道——而在爱尔兰，这两种记忆几乎总会附着于此类场景之上——这座建筑也因此成了许多离奇诡谲之传说的题材与舞台。其中一桩传说，我有幸因与一位事件目击者相熟，得以追溯其源头；然而实在难说，我即将记述的这些事件，是透过传统这道扭曲的媒介去看时显得更加离奇、更加不可思议呢，还是当真相被那层令人颤栗的、朦胧莫测的迷雾笼罩时，显得更加离奇、更加不可思议。

传说云：上世纪某时，罗伯特·阿达格爵士（Sir Robert Ardagh），此族中一位青年，也是末代继承人，远赴异国，投身外邦军旅；既已博得相当的声名与财利，便定居于阿达格城堡（Castle Ardagh），即我们方才竭力描摹的那座建筑。他是乡民口中所谓的一个"阴沉"（dark）之人；所谓"阴沉"，便是说他被视作性情乖戾、缄默寡言、脾气很坏；而且——据他那与世隔绝的生活推断——他与家中其他成员素无亲近之情。

他打破自己孤寂单调之生活的唯一场合，便是在赛马季持续期间及其后紧随的一段时日；每到那时，人们便能在赛场上瞧见他，是最忙忙碌碌的人之一，下注之深、之果决，从不稍逊，而每每稳操胜券。然而，罗伯特爵士素以重信守诺著称，又出身于太高贵的门第，断不至于被人疑心有何舞弊勾当。况且他是个军人，生性既刚毅又倨傲；谁也不敢贸然胡乱猜测，因为这种猜测的后果，多半只会落到此发话者自己的头上。

===Original===
Gossip, however, was not silent; it was remarked that Sir Robert never appeared at the race-ground, which was the only place of public resort which he frequented, except in company with a certain strange-looking person, who was never seen elsewhere, or under other circumstances. It was remarked, too, that this man, whose relation to Sir Robert was never distinctly ascertained, was the only person to whom he seemed to speak unnecessarily; it was observed that while with the country gentry he exchanged no further communication than what was unavoidable in arranging his sporting transactions, with this person he would converse earnestly and frequently. Tradition asserts that, to enhance the curiosity which this unaccountable and exclusive preference excited, the stranger possessed some striking and unpleasant peculiarities of person and of garb—she does not say, however, what these were—but they, in conjunction with Sir Robert's secluded habits and extraordinary run of luck—a success which was supposed to result from the suggestions and immediate advice of the unknown—were sufficient to warrant report in pronouncing that there was something *queer* in the wind, and in surmising that Sir Robert was playing a fearful and a hazardous game, and that, in short, his strange companion was little better than the devil himself.

Years, however, rolled quietly away, and nothing novel occurred in the arrangements of Castle Ardagh, excepting that Sir Robert parted with his odd companion, but as nobody could tell whence he came, so nobody could say whither he had gone. Sir Robert's habits, however, underwent no consequent change; he continued regularly to frequent the race meetings, without mixing at all in the convivialities of the gentry, and immediately afterwards to relapse into the secluded monotony of his ordinary life.

===Chinese===
然而流言并不缄默；人们注意到，罗伯特爵士出现在赛马场——这是他唯一肯涉足的公共场所——从不曾不带一位形容怪异之人同行；而此人，旁处从未得见，别的场合也从未得见。人们又注意到，这个与罗伯特爵士之关系始终无人能确指的男人，竟是他唯一会与之多费口舌的人；人们观察到，他与乡间绅士们除了为赛马之事作必要交接之外，再无多余来往，可与此人却能恳切而频繁地长谈。传说又谓，为着给这份莫名其妙的、独占性的偏爱所激起的好奇心火上浇油，那陌生人本人在容貌与衣着上还有些触目而令人不快的古怪之处——至于究竟是哪些古怪，传说却并未明言——但这些古怪之处，连同罗伯特爵士离群索居的习性，以及他那令人称奇的连连好运——据信这好运正是出自那陌生人的暗示与当面指点——已足以让风声断言：这事里头必有蹊跷，并揣测罗伯特爵士正在玩一局可怖而险恶的把戏，简而言之，他那位怪同伴，与魔鬼本人相差无几。

然而岁月悄然流逝，阿达格城堡的种种营生再无新事，只是罗伯特爵士遣走了他那位怪同伴；可正如当初没人说得出他从何处来，如今也没人说得出他往何处去了。然而罗伯特爵士的习性并未因此有何改变；他照旧准时出席赛马会，毫不掺和绅士们的杯酒酬酢，会一散便立即重新堕回他平日里那种离群索居、了无生趣的单调生活中去。

===Original===
It was said that he had accumulated vast sums of money—and, as his bets were always successful, and always large, such must have been the case. He did not suffer the acquisition of wealth, however, to influence his hospitality or his housekeeping—he neither purchased land, nor extended his establishment; and his mode of enjoying his money must have been altogether that of the miser—consisting merely in the pleasure of touching and telling his gold, and in the consciousness of wealth.

Sir Robert's temper, so far from improving, became more than ever gloomy and morose. He sometimes carried the indulgence of his evil dispositions to such a height that it bordered upon insanity. During these paroxysms he would neither eat, drink, nor sleep. On such occasions he insisted on perfect privacy, even from the intrusion of his most trusted servants; his voice was frequently heard, sometimes in earnest supplication, sometime as if in loud and angry altercation with some unknown visitant; sometimes he would, for hours together, walk to and fro throughout the long oak wainscoted apartment, which he generally occupied, with wild gesticulations and agitated pace, in the manner of one who has been roused to a state of unnatural excitement by some sudden and appalling intimation.

These paroxysms of apparent lunacy were so frightful, that during their continuance even his oldest and most-faithful domestics dared not approach him; consequently, his hours of agony were never intruded upon, and the mysterious causes of his sufferings appeared likely to remain hidden forever.

===Chinese===
据传他积攒下了大宗钱财——既然他的赌注每每命中，且数目一贯可观，情形想必备如此。然而他并不让这财富的聚敛左右自己待客的殷勤或家中的用度——他既不购置田产，也不扩充门庭；他享受钱财的方式，必然完全是守财奴式的——只在于触摸、点数黄金所带来的那份愉悦，以及那份拥有财富的自觉罢了。

罗伯特爵士的脾气非但未见好转，反而比从前更加阴沉暴戾。他有时把那邪僻性子的发作纵容到几近癫狂的地步。发作起来，他不吃、不喝、不睡。每逢这种时候，他严令任何人不许近前，即便他最亲信的仆人也不得擅入；只听得他的声音时时传出，有时是在恳切地哀求，有时又仿佛在与某个来路不明的访客高声怒争；有时他会一连数小时在那间橡木镶壁的长屋里来回踱步——他平日便多居于此屋——步履踉跄，手势狂乱，宛如一个被某种突至而可怖的消息激起了反常亢奋之人。

这等近乎癫狂的发作，可怖到了这般田地：发作之时，连他最老、最忠心的仆人都胆敢不近身；因此，他独自煎熬的时辰从未被人擅扰，他所受折磨的隐秘缘由，看来也注定要永远隐没于黑暗之中。

===Original===
On one occasion a fit of this kind continued for an unusual time, the ordinary term of their duration—about two days—had been long past, and the old servant who generally waited upon Sir Robert after these visitations, having in vain listened for the well-known tinkle of his master's hand-bell, began to feel extremely anxious; he feared that his master might have died from sheer exhaustion, or perhaps put an end to his own existence during his miserable depression. These fears at length became so strong, that having in vain urged some of his brother servants to accompany him, he determined to go up alone, and himself see whether any accident had befallen Sir Robert.

He traversed the several passages which conducted from the new to the more ancient parts of the mansion, and having arrived in the old hall of the castle, the utter silence of the hour, for it was very late in the night, the idea of the nature of the enterprise in which he was engaging himself, a sensation of remoteness from anything like human companionship, but, more than all, the vivid but undefined anticipation of something horrible, came upon him with such oppressive weight that he hesitated as to whether he should proceed. Real uneasiness, however, respecting the fate of his master, for whom he felt that kind of attachment which the force of habitual intercourse not unfrequently engenders respecting objects not in themselves amiable, and also a latent unwillingness to expose his weakness to the ridicule of his fellow-servants, combined to overcome his reluctance; and he had just placed his foot upon the first step of the staircase which conducted to his master's chamber, when his attention was arrested by a low but distinct knocking at the hall-door. Not, perhaps, very sorry at finding thus an excuse even for deferring his intended expedition, he placed the candle upon a stone block which lay in the hall, and approached the door, uncertain whether his ears had not deceived him. This doubt was justified by the circumstance that the hall entrance had been for nearly fifty years disused as a mode of ingress to the castle. The situation of this gate also, which we have endeavoured to describe, opening upon a narrow ledge of rock which overhangs a perilous cliff, rendered it at all times, but particularly at night, a dangerous entrance. This shelving platform of rock, which formed the only avenue to the door, was divided, as I have already stated, by a broad chasm, the planks across which had long disappeared by decay or otherwise, so that it seemed at least highly improbable that any man could have found his way across the passage in safety to the door, more particularly on a night like that, of singular darkness. The old man, therefore, listened attentively, to ascertain whether the first application should be followed by another. He had not long to wait; the same low but singularly distinct knocking was repeated; so low that it seemed as if the applicant had employed no harder or heavier instrument than his hand, and yet, despite the immense thickness of the door, with such strength that the sound was distinctly audible.

===Chinese===
有一回，这种发作延续了异乎寻常的时辰——寻常发作的期限，约莫两天，早已远远过了——那位素来在这些发作之后侍候罗伯特爵士的老仆，左等右等也听不到主人手铃那熟稔的叮当声，便开始惴惴不安起来；他怕主人莫不是已在一气之下虚脱而亡，又或者在苦痛的颓丧之中寻了短见。这恐惧终至强烈难抑，他先是白费口舌地劝几位同仆陪他同去，未果，便决意独自上楼，亲眼看一看主人是否出了什么岔子。

他穿过好几道连接宅子新部与古部的回廊，到了城堡的古大厅里；此刻夜已极深，四下里万籁俱寂，加之念及自己所行之事的性质，加之一种与人间陪伴相去甚远、孑然一身之感，更兼某种虽鲜明却说不清道不明的、对可怖之事的预感——一齐以令人窒息的分量压将上来，他不禁踟蹰，要不要继续往前。然而对主人安危的真切挂念——他对主人怀有那种由朝夕相处之力所生、纵使对象本身并不可爱也照旧滋生的情分——再加一股不愿在同仆面前露怯、招人耻笑的潜在心思——合力压过了他的不情愿；他刚把脚踏上通往主人卧房的那道楼梯的第一级，注意力便被大厅门口一阵低而分明的叩门声引了去。他多半倒也不太遗憾，竟由此寻得了一个借口，哪怕是推迟一下所拟的这趟探查也好；他把蜡烛搁在大厅里一方石墩上，走到门边，心里犹疑着自己的耳朵是不是听岔了。这犹疑倒也情有可原，因为大厅这道入口，作为进入城堡的一条通道，已有将近五十年弃置不用了。再加上这门的位置——我们已竭力描摹过了——门外是一条悬于凶险峭壁之上的狭长岩架，使得它无论何时、尤其在夜里，都是一道凶险的入口。这条倾斜的岩石平台，是通往此门的唯一通道，如前所述，中间被一道宽阔的裂谷断开，横跨其上的木板早已因朽烂或其他缘故消失殆尽；由此看来，任何人竟能安然无恙地摸过这条通道、走到门前，至少是极不可能的事——更何况像那样一个夜色特别浓黑的晚上。于是老人凝神细听，要弄清这头一次叩门之后，是否还有第二次。他没等多久；同样低沉却分外分明的叩门声再次响起；那声响低得，仿佛叩门者所用之物，并无比他自己的手掌更硬更重的东西，然而——尽管门厚得惊人——那声响却强得足以被听得清清楚楚。

===Original===
The knock was repeated a third time, without any increase of loudness; and the old man, obeying an impulse for which to his dying hour he could never account, proceeded to remove, one by one, the three great oaken bars which secured the door. Time and damp had effectually corroded the iron chambers of the lock, so that it afforded little resistance. With some effort, as he believed, assisted from without, the old servant succeeded in opening the door; and a low, square-built figure, apparently that of a man wrapped in a large black cloak, entered the hall. The servant could not see much of this visitant with any distinctness; his dress appeared foreign, the skirt of his ample cloak was thrown over one shoulder; he wore a large felt hat, with a very heavy leaf, from under which escaped what appeared to be a mass of long sooty-black hair; his feet were cased in heavy riding-boots. Such were the few particulars which the servant had time and light to observe. The stranger desired him to let his master know instantly that a friend had come, by appointment, to settle some business with him. The servant hesitated, but a slight motion on the part of his visitor, as if to possess himself of the candle, determined him; so, taking it in his hand, he ascended the castle stairs, leaving his guest in the hall.

On reaching the apartment which opened upon the oak-chamber he was surprised to observe the door of that room partly open, and the room itself lit up. He paused, but there was no sound; he looked in, and saw Sir Robert, his head and the upper part of his body reclining on a table, upon which burned a lamp; his arms were stretched forward on either side, and perfectly motionless; it appeared that, having been sitting at the table, he had thus sunk forward, either dead or in a swoon. There was no sound of breathing; all was silent, except the sharp ticking of a watch, which lay beside the lamp. The servant coughed twice or thrice, but with no effect; his fears now almost amounted to certainty, and he was approaching the table on which his master partly lay, to satisfy himself of his death, when Sir Robert slowly raised his head, and throwing himself back in his chair, fixed his eyes in a ghastly and uncertain gaze upon his attendant. At length he said, slowly and painfully, as if he dreaded the answer:

"In God's name, what are you?"

"Sir," said the servant, "a strange gentleman wants to see you below."

===Chinese===
叩门声第三次响起，仍未加重分毫；老人听凭一股冲动——这股冲动他至死也无法说清缘由——动手一一卸下那三道护门的大橡木横闩。岁月与潮气早已将锁的铁芯锈蚀殆尽，它几乎不作抵抗。老人颇费了些力气——他只觉得有股力量从门外帮衬着他——总算把门拉开了；一个矮胖敦实、显然是个裹在宽大黑斗篷里的男人的身影，进了大厅。仆人借着光，没能把这位访客瞧得太清；他的衣装像是异邦式样，宽大斗篷的下摆甩在一侧肩头；他戴一顶阔边厚重的毡帽，帽檐下溢出一大绺烟黑的长发；脚上蹬着沉重的马靴。这些便是仆人有工夫、有光亮能看清的寥寥几许细节。陌生人命他立刻通报主人，说有一位朋友，依约前来，要与主人了结一桩事务。仆人踌躇了一下，可访客只朝蜡烛略一动势，似要伸手来夺，仆人便拿定了主意；于是他抄起蜡烛，登上城堡的楼梯，把客人留在大厅里。

到了那间与橡木厅相连的屋子跟前，他惊讶地发现那屋门半掩着，里头还亮着灯。他驻足一听，没有声响；他探头一瞧，只见罗伯特爵士头颅与上半身伏在桌上，桌上点着一盏灯；他双臂向两侧摊开，纹丝不动；看起来，像是他原本坐在桌前，就这么向前一栽，要么死了，要么昏厥过去。听不到一丝呼吸声；四下死寂，只有桌上灯旁一只怀表在发出尖利的嘀嗒。仆人咳了两三声，毫无反应；此刻他的恐惧几已成定局，正要凑近那张主人半伏其上的桌子，确认他的死讯——这时罗伯特爵士缓缓抬起头来，身子往椅背一靠，一双眼睛以一种惨白而游移的目光，定定地盯着他的侍者。良久，他才缓慢而吃力地开口，仿佛生怕听到那个回答：

"以上帝之名，你是什么？"

"老爷，"仆人说，"底下有位陌生先生要见您。"

===Original===
At this intimation Sir Robert, starting on his feet and tossing his arms wildly upwards, uttered a shriek of such appalling and despairing terror that it was almost too fearful for human endurance; and long after the sound had ceased it seemed to the terrified imagination of the old servant to roll through the deserted passages in bursts of unnatural laughter. After a few moments Sir Robert said:

"Can't you send him away? Why does he come so soon? O God! O God! let him leave me for an hour; a little time. I can't see him now; try to get him away. You see I can't go down now; I have not strength. O God! O God! let him come back in an hour; it is not long to wait. He cannot lose anything by it; nothing, nothing, nothing. Tell him that; say anything to him."

The servant went down. In his own words, he did not feel the stairs under him till he got to the hall. The figure stood exactly as he had left it. He delivered his master's message as coherently as he could. The stranger replied in a careless tone:

"If Sir Robert will not come down to me, I must go up to him."

The man returned, and to his surprise he found his master much more composed in manner. He listened to the message, and though the cold perspiration rose in drops upon his forehead faster than he could wipe it away, his manner had lost the dreadful agitation which had marked it before. He rose feebly, and casting a last look of agony behind him, passed from the room to the lobby, where he signed to his attendant not to follow him. The man moved as far as the head of the staircase, from whence he had a tolerably distinct view of the hall, which was imperfectly lighted by the candle he had left there.

===Chinese===
听了这话，罗伯特爵士猛地跳将起来，双臂狂乱地向上一甩，发出一声尖叫——那可怖而绝望的惊惧之声，直叫人肉身难捱；待那声音早已止歇，在那老仆惶怖的想象里，它却仍一程一程地滚过空荡荡的回廊，化作一阵阵反常的大笑。过了片刻，罗伯特爵士说道：

"你就不能打发他走吗？他怎么来得这么快？哦，上帝！哦，上帝！让他放我一小时的假吧；就一小会儿。我现在见不得他；想想法子把他支开。你也瞧见了，我现在下不了楼；我没那个气力。哦，上帝！哦，上帝！让他一个钟头之后再回来吧；等的工夫不算长。他什么也不会因此错过；什么也不会，什么也不会，什么也不会。你就这么告诉他；随便你怎么说都成。"

仆人下了楼。用他自己的话说，他直到进了大厅，才觉出脚下有楼梯。那个身影分毫未动，正与他离去时一般无二。他竭力把主人的话转述得有条理些。陌生人漫不经心地答道：

"罗伯特爵士要是不肯下楼见我，那我只好上楼去见他。"

仆人回了上去，出乎他意料的是，他发觉主人神态已镇定了许多。主人听了这话，虽然额上冷汗涔涔，涔涔得比他措拭的工夫还快，举止间却已没了先前那可怖的激乱。他勉强撑起身子，朝身后投去最后一道苦痛的目光，从屋里走到门厅，在那里打了个手势，叫侍者不必跟来。侍者只挪到楼梯口为止，从那里能把大厅瞧得相当清楚——大厅里只靠他方才留下的那支蜡烛，照得昏昏黄黄。

===Original===
He saw his master reel, rather than walk down the stairs, clinging all the way to the banisters. He walked on, as if about to sink every moment from weakness. The figure advanced as if to meet him, and in passing struck down the light. The servant could see no more; but there was a sound of struggling, renewed at intervals with silent but fearful energy. It was evident, however, that the parties were approaching the door, for he heard the solid oak sound twice or thrice, as the feet of the combatants, in shuffling hither and thither over the floor, struck upon it. After a slight pause he heard the door thrown open with such violence that the leaf seemed to strike the sidewall of the hall, for it was so dark without that this could only be surmised by the sound. The struggle was renewed with an agony and intenseness of energy that betrayed itself in deep-drawn gasps. One desperate effort, which terminated in the breaking of some part of the door, producing a sound as if the doorpost was wrenched from its position, was followed by another wrestle, evidently upon the narrow ledge which ran outside the door, overtopping the precipice. This proved to be the final struggle, for it was followed by a crashing sound as if some heavy body had fallen over, and was rushing down the precipice, through the light boughs that crossed near the top. All then became still as the grave, except when the moan of the night wind sighed up the wooded glen.

The old servant had not nerve to return through the hall, and to him the darkness seemed all but endless; but morning at length came, and with it the disclosure of the events of the night. Near the door, upon the ground, lay Sir Robert's sword-belt, which had given way in the scuffle. A huge splinter from the massive doorpost had been wrenched off by an almost superhuman effort—one which nothing but the grip of a despairing man could have severed—and on the rock outside were left the marks of the slipping and sliding of feet.

At the foot of the precipice, not immediately under the castle, but dragged some way up the glen, were found the remains of Sir Robert, with hardly a vestige of a limb or feature left distinguishable. The right hand, however, was uninjured, and in its fingers were clutched, with the fixedness of death, a long lock of coarse sooty hair—the only direct circumstantial evidence of the presence of a second person. So says tradition.

===Chinese===
他瞧见主人与其说是走下楼梯，不如说是摇晃着蹭下楼去，一路紧紧攀着栏杆。他往前挪，仿佛每时每刻都要因虚脱而瘫倒。那身影迎上前去，仿佛是去接他，错身之际，一掌打灭了那支蜡烛。仆人再也看不见什么了；却传来一阵挣扎之声，每隔一阵便又以一种无声却可怖的劲头重新发作。然而很显然，双方正朝门口移去，因为他听得那实心橡木地板响了两三下，那是搏斗者的脚在地板上拖来拽去、撞到门上所发。略一停顿之后，他听见门被猛地撞开，那扇门扇仿佛直直拍到了大厅的侧墙——因为外头一片漆黑，这只能凭声音揣度。搏斗再度发作，那股子苦痛而竭力的劲头，从一声声深吸的粗气里泄露无遗。又是一次拼死的较劲，以门上某处断裂告终，发出一声仿佛门框从原位被生生抽离的声响；紧接着又是一番扭打，显然已挪到了门外那条悬于峭壁之上的狭长岩架上。这便是最后的搏斗了，因为紧随其后，便是一阵咔嚓的巨响，仿佛有什么沉重之物翻将下去，正顺着峭壁坠下，一路穿过崖顶附近那些细细的枝桠。其后一切便如坟墓般死寂，唯有夜风的长叹，沿着林木葱茏的山涧一声声呜咽而上。

老仆再没那个胆量穿过大厅折回了，在他看来，那黑暗仿佛无穷无尽；然而清晨终于来临，随之而来的是昨夜之事的真相大白。门边的地上，落着罗伯特爵士的佩剑绶带，那是扭打中被扯断的。那厚重的门框上，有一大块木条被一股近乎超人的蛮力生生扳断——除了绝望之人的死死一攥，再无别物能将其扯断——门外的岩石上，则留着一串脚下滑蹭拖拽的痕迹。

在峭壁脚下——并非正对城堡之下，而是被拖到了山涧上游一段路的地方——人们找到了罗伯特爵士的遗骸，四肢与面目几乎无一处理辨。然而他的右手完好无损，五指之间以死之紧握，攥着一绺长长的、粗硬的烟黑头发——这是有人曾在场的唯一直接物证。传说如此云云。

===Original===
This story, as I have mentioned, was current among the dealers in such lore; but the original facts are so dissimilar in all but the name of the principal person mentioned and his mode of life, and the fact that his death was accompanied with circumstances of extraordinary mystery, that the two narratives are totally irreconcilable (even allowing the utmost for the exaggerating influence of tradition), except by supposing report to have combined and blended together the fabulous histories of several distinct bearers of the family name. However this may be, I shall lay before the reader a distinct recital of the events from which the foregoing tradition arose. With respect to these there can be no mistake; they are authenticated as fully as anything can be by human testimony; and I state them principally upon the evidence of a lady who herself bore a prominent part in the strange events which she related, and which I now record as being among the few well-attested tales of the marvellous which it has been my fate to hear. I shall, as far as I am able, arrange in one combined narrative the evidence of several distinct persons who were eyewitnesses of what they related, and with the truth of whose testimony I am solemnly and deeply impressed.

Sir Robert Ardagh, as we choose to call him, was the heir and representative of the family whose name he bore; but owing to the prodigality of his father, the estates descended to him in a very impaired condition. Urged by the restless spirit of youth, or more probably by a feeling of pride which could not submit to witness, in the paternal mansion, what he considered a humiliating alteration in the style and hospitality which up to that time had distinguished his family, Sir Robert left Ireland and went abroad. How he occupied himself, or what countries he visited during his absence, was never known, nor did he afterwards make any allusion or encourage any inquiries touching his foreign sojourn. He left Ireland in the year 1742, being then just of age, and was not heard of until the year 1760—about eighteen years afterwards—at which time he returned. His personal appearance was, as might have been expected, very greatly altered, more altered, indeed, than the time of his absence might have warranted one in supposing likely. But to counterbalance the unfavourable change which time had wrought in his form and features, he had acquired all the advantages of polish of manner and refinement of taste which foreign travel is supposed to bestow. But what was truly surprising was that it soon became evident that Sir Robert was very wealthy—wealthy to an extraordinary and unaccountable degree; and this fact was made manifest, not only by his expensive style of living, but by his proceeding to disembarrass his property, and to purchase extensive estates in addition.
