Moreover, there could be nothing deceptive in these appearances, for he paid ready money for everything, from the most important purchase to the most trifling.

===Chinese===
我已说过，这个故事在那一类奇闻的贩夫走卒之间口耳相传；然而原初的事实，除了主要人物之名与其生活方式、以及其死亡伴有非同寻常的神秘情节之外，与上述传说几乎处处相左，以至于两套叙述根本无法调和（即便最大限度地体谅传说的夸饰之力），除非我们假定：风传是把这一姓氏之下几个不同人物各自的传奇，糅合混编在了一处。无论究竟如何，我都要把催生上述传说的那些事件，原原本本地摆在读者面前。这些事件不容置疑；它们已为人力所能给予的任何证词所充分证实；我之所以记述，主要依据的是一位女士的证言——她本人便在她所述、亦即我如今所记的这些离奇事件中担当过要角；我之所以记下这些，也因为它们是我命中难得听闻的、为数不多、证据确凿的奇谈之一。我将尽我所能，把几位不同的目击者各自所述的证词汇为一篇连贯的叙述，他们的证词之真实，令我深为肃然动容。

罗伯特·阿达格爵士——我们姑且如此称他——乃是其姓氏所在家族的继承人与代表；然因乃父挥霍无度，家产传到他手时，已是大损元气。罗伯特爵士之远走异国，或为青年那不安分的心气所驱，或更可能为一种自尊心所驱——他自尊太甚，不忍在祖宅之中亲睹他视为家门素来风度与好客之道的一种屈辱性的式微——总之他离开了爱尔兰，远赴他乡。他在外何以为业、游历过哪些国度，始终无人知晓；日后再不曾听他就此有过只言片语的提及，也不曾鼓励过任何人就其海外羁旅之事探问。他于 1742 年离开爱尔兰，其时方才及冠，直到 1760 年——约莫十八年之后——才再度有他的消息传来，其时他已归乡。他的容颜在意料之中大变，变得比他那离家时日所能令人想见的还要厉害。然而为时间在其形貌上所施的不利改动相抵的，是他已尽得了海外游历所应有的那份举止之圆熟与趣味之雅致。可真正叫人惊异的，是很快便看得明白：罗伯特爵士极为豪富——豪富到了一个非同寻常、无由解释的地步；这事不仅显于他阔绰的起居排场，更由他着手清理旧业之负债、又另购大片地产之举坐实。再者，这些表象不会有半点虚假，因为他凡事皆现钱交易——从最要紧的大宗购置到最微末的小笔花销，概不例外。

===Original===
Sir Robert was a remarkably agreeable man, and possessing the combined advantages of birth and property, he was, as a matter of course, gladly received into the highest society which the metropolis then commanded. It was thus that he became acquainted with the two beautiful Miss F——ds, then among the brightest ornaments of the highest circle of Dublin fashion. Their family was in more than one direction allied to nobility; and Lady D——, their elder sister by many years, and sometime married to a once well-known nobleman, was now their protectress. These considerations, beside the fact that the young ladies were what is usually termed heiresses, though not to a very great amount, secured to them a high position in the best society which Ireland then produced. The two young ladies differed strongly, alike in appearance and in character. The elder of the two, Emily, was generally considered the handsomer—for her beauty was of that impressive kind which never failed to strike even at the first glance, possessing as it did all the advantages of a fine person and a commanding carriage. The beauty of her features strikingly assorted in character with that of her figure and deportment. Her hair was raven-black and richly luxuriant, beautifully contrasting with the perfect whiteness of her forehead—her finely pencilled brows were black as the ringlets that clustered near them—and her blue eyes, full, lustrous, and animated, possessed all the power and brilliancy of brown ones, with more than their softness and variety of expression. She was not, however, merely the tragedy queen. When she smiled, and that was not seldom, the dimpling of cheek and chin, the laughing display of the small and beautiful teeth—but, more than all, the roguish archness of her deep, bright eye, showed that nature had not neglected in her the lighter and the softer characteristics of woman.

Her younger sister Mary was, as I believe not unfrequently occurs in the case of sisters, quite in the opposite style of beauty. She was light-haired, had more colour, had nearly equal grace, with much more liveliness of manner. Her eyes were of that dark grey which poets so much admire—full of expression and vivacity. She was altogether a very beautiful and animated girl—though as unlike her sister as the presence of those two qualities would permit her to be. Their dissimilarity did not stop here—it was deeper than mere appearance—the character of their minds differed almost as strikingly as did their complexion. The fair-haired beauty had a large proportion of that softness and pliability of temper which physiognomists assign as the characteristics of such complexions. She was much more the creature of impulse than of feeling, and consequently more the victim of extrinsic circumstances than was her sister. Emily, on the contrary, possessed considerable firmness and decision. She was less excitable, but when excited her feelings were more intense and enduring. She wanted much of the gaiety, but with it the volatility of her younger sister. Her opinions were adopted, and her friendships formed more reflectively, and her affections seemed to move, as it were, more slowly, but more determinedly. This firmness of character did not amount to anything masculine, and did not at all impair the feminine grace of her manners.

罗伯特爵士是个极讨人喜欢的人，兼有出身与财产两般好处，理所当然地被京城上流社会——其时京城所能攀到的最高一层——欣然接纳。他便由此结识了两位美丽的 F——d 小姐，其时她们是都柏林时尚最高圈子里最耀眼的两位装饰。她们的家世在不止一个方向上与贵族联姻；她们的姐姐 D—— 夫人比她们年长许多，曾嫁给一位昔日颇负盛名的贵族，如今是她们的保护人。有这些缘由，再加上两位小姐乃通常所谓"嗣女"——虽则所嗣不算太丰——便为她们在爱尔兰彼时所能产出的最好社交圈中，稳稳保住了一个高位。这两位小姐无论容貌还是性情都迥然不同。姐姐埃米莉（Emily）一般被认为更美——因为她的美属于那种动人心魄的美，便是一眼之间也不会不令人心动，盖因她兼具一副好身段与一种雍容自持的气度。她的五官之美，与她的身段与气度之美，惊人地相得益彰。她的秀发乌黑丰茂，与那莹白的额头相映成趣——她描得细细的蛾眉，黑如簇在眉畔的鬈发——而她那一双蓝色的眼眸，饱满、明亮、灵动，既有褐色眼眸的力度与光彩，又胜过褐色眼眸的柔和与神情之多端。然而她并非仅是个悲剧女王。她笑起来——而她笑的次数并不少——脸颊与下巴的酒窝、那一口细小美齿的展露——更兼那双深邃明亮的眼中那一抹俏皮的狡黠——都显示大自然并未在她身上疏忽了女子那份更轻盈、更柔软的特质。

妹妹玛丽（Mary）——我相信这在姐妹之间也不算罕见——其美完全是另一种路数。她头发颜色浅，血色更足，风度与她姐姐几乎不相上下，举止却活泼得多。她的眼眸是那种诗人们极力称赏的深灰——神情与灵动兼备。她整个儿是个极美、极活泼的姑娘——尽管在那两种品质所容许的范围内，她与她姐姐判若两人。两人的不同不止于此——比容貌更深——她们的性情之别，几乎与肤色之别一样判然。那位金发的美人，性情中含了大量的温柔与柔顺——相术家们正以此种肤色为其特征。她与其说是感情的造物，不如说是冲动的造物，因而比姐姐更易成为外在境遇的牺牲品。埃米莉则恰恰相反，颇有几分坚毅与决断。她不易激动，可一旦激动起来，感情便更浓烈、更持久。她少了妹妹的几分轻快，却也少了妹妹的几分浮薄。她的主见之形成、她的友谊之缔结，都更为深思，而她的情意，仿佛行得更缓，却也更断然。这种性情的坚毅，并未达到阳刚之地，也丝毫未损她举止间那份女子气之娴雅。

===Original===
Sir Robert Ardagh was for a long time apparently equally attentive to the two sisters, and many were the conjectures and the surmises as to which would be the lady of his choice. At length, however, these doubts were determined; he proposed for and was accepted by the dark beauty, Emily F——d.

The bridals were celebrated in a manner becoming the wealth and connections of the parties; and Sir Robert and Lady Ardagh left Dublin to pass the honeymoon at the family mansion, Castle Ardagh, which had lately been fitted up in a style bordering upon magnificent. Whether in compliance with the wishes of his lady, or owing to some whim of his own, his habits were henceforward strikingly altered; and from having moved among the gayest if not the most profligate of the votaries of fashion, he suddenly settled down into a quiet, domestic, country gentleman, and seldom, if ever, visited the capital, and then his sojourns were as brief as the nature of his business would permit.

Lady Ardagh, however, did not suffer from this change further than in being secluded from general society; for Sir Robert's wealth, and the hospitality which he had established in the family mansion, commanded that of such of his lady's friends and relatives as had leisure or inclination to visit the castle; and as their style of living was very handsome, and its internal resources of amusement considerable, few invitations from Sir Robert or his lady were neglected.

===Chinese===
很长一段时间里，罗伯特·阿达格爵士对两姐妹似乎一视同仁，于是闲言中猜测纷纭，揣度哪一位将成为他的意中人。然而这些疑团终归有了分晓；他向那位黑发美人埃米莉·F——d 求婚，并得了允准。

婚礼办得与双方家资及人脉相称；罗伯特爵士与阿达格夫人随后离开都柏林，到祖宅阿达格城堡去度蜜月——这座城堡近日方才修饰一新，其排场近乎奢华。无论是依从夫人的意愿，还是出于他自己的一时兴起，他的习性从此判若两人；昔日他混迹于时尚信徒之中——纵然不是最放浪的一群，也是最热闹的一群——如今他竟骤然安顿下来，成了一个沉静的、居家型的乡间绅士，难得进一趟城，即便进城，也是事务性质所容许的最短勾留。

然而阿达格夫人并未因这一变故受苦，所苦的不过是退出了寻常应酬；因为罗伯特爵士的财力，以及他在祖宅所立下的那份好客之风，足以把夫人那班有闲、有兴的亲戚朋友一并招来城堡小住；再加上府中起居奢华、府内消遣颇多，爵士夫妇所发的请帖，几乎无人肯轻慢。

===Original===
Many years passed quietly away, during which Sir Robert's and Lady Ardagh's hopes of issue were several times disappointed. In the lapse of all this time there occurred but one event worth recording. Sir Robert had brought with him from abroad a valet, who sometimes professed himself to be French, at others Italian, and at others again German. He spoke all these languages with equal fluency, and seemed to take a kind of pleasure in puzzling the sagacity and balk the curiosity of such of the visitors at the castle as at any time happened to enter into conversation with him, or who, struck by his singularities, became inquisitive respecting his country and origin. Sir Robert called him by the French name, **Jacque**, and among the lower orders he was familiarly known by the title of "Jack, the devil," an appellation which originated in a supposed malignity of disposition and a real reluctance to mix in the society of those who were believed to be his equals. This morose reserve, coupled with the mystery which enveloped all about him, rendered him an object of suspicion and inquiry to his fellow-servants, amongst whom it was whispered that this man in secret governed the actions of Sir Robert with a despotic dictation, and that, as if to indemnify himself for his public and apparent servitude and self-denial, he in private exacted a degree of respectful homage from his so-called master, totally inconsistent with the relation generally supposed to exist between them.

This man's personal appearance was, to say the least of it, extremely odd; he was low in stature; and this defect was enhanced by a distortion of the spine, so considerable as almost to amount to a hunch; his features, too, had all that sharpness and sickliness of hue which generally accompany deformity; he wore his hair, which was black as soot, in heavy neglected ringlets about his shoulders, and always without powder—a peculiarity in those days. There was something unpleasant, too, in the circumstance that he never raised his eyes to meet those of another; this fact was often cited as a proof of his being something not quite right, and said to result not from the timidity which is supposed in most cases to induce this habit, but from a consciousness that his eye possessed a power which, if exhibited, would betray a supernatural origin. Once, and once only, had he violated this sinister observance: it was on the occasion of Sir Robert's hopes having been most bitterly disappointed; his lady, after a severe and dangerous confinement, gave birth to a dead child. Immediately after the intelligence had been made known, a servant, having upon some business passed outside the gate of the castle-yard, was met by Jacque, who, contrary to his wont, accosted him, observing, "So, after all the pother, the son and heir is stillborn." This remark was accompanied by a chuckling laugh, the only approach to merriment which he was ever known to exhibit. The servant, who was really disappointed, having hoped for holiday times, feasting and debauchery with impunity during the rejoicings which would have accompanied a christening, turned tartly upon the little valet, telling him that he should let Sir Robert know how he had received the tidings which should have filled any faithful servant with sorrow; and having once broken the ice, he was proceeding with increasing fluency, when his harangue was cut short and his temerity punished, by the little man raising his head and treating him to a scowl so fearful, half-demoniac, half-insane, that it haunted his imagination in nightmares and nervous tremors for months after.

===Chinese===
许多年头悄然流逝，其间罗伯特爵士与阿达格夫人一再盼嗣，一再落空。在这漫长的光阴里，只发生过一桩事值得一提。罗伯特爵士从海外带回了一名贴身侍仆，这人有时自称是法国人，有时自称意大利人，有时又自称德意志人。这几种语言他说来无一不通、同样流利，似乎还颇以难倒那些在城堡里与他搭话的客人——或因他种种古怪而生异、探问其国族来历的客人——之明察、挫其好奇心为乐。罗伯特爵士以法语名称"**雅克**（Jacque）"唤他，而在下等人之中，他便以"魔鬼杰克（Jack, the devil）"这一诨号广为人知——此诨号一则源于人们所揣度的他性情之阴毒，二则源于他实在不肯与那些被认为是其同辈之辈为伍。这种阴郁的缄默，加之他周身所笼罩的那层神秘，使他成了同仆们疑忌探问的对象；同仆之间私下风传，此人暗中以专制之令辖制着罗伯特爵士的一举一动，仿佛是为着在台面上的奴颜婢膝与自我克制求一补偿，他在私下里竟反过来向他那位所谓主人索取一种恭敬之礼，与人们通常设想的主仆之分全然相悖。

此人的形容，说得再轻些，也是古怪之极；他身量矮小；这一短处又因脊骨之畸变而更显——那畸变之剧，几乎已成了驼背；他的五官也带了一股畸形之体所常有的那种尖削与病色；他的头发烟黑，梳成厚厚的、疏于打理的鬈发披在肩头，且从不扑粉——这在当时可谓一桩异数。还有一桩事令人不快：他从不抬眼与人相视；这一节常被引为他"不大对头"之明证，据说此习之成，并非出于多数情形下诱发此习的那种怯懦，而是由于他自知那一双眼中藏着一股力量，一旦显露，便会泄露其超自然之来历。他平生只有一回破了这道阴森的规矩：那是在罗伯特爵士所盼最苦地落了空之际——夫人经过一场凶险万分的难产，产下一名死婴。消息传开不多时，一名仆人因事走过城堡庭院门外，迎面撞见雅克，此人一反常态，竟开口搭话道："怎着，闹了这半天的动静，原来这位少爷兼继承人，是个死胎。"这话还伴着一阵嘿嘿的笑——这是旁人见他露过的、最接近欢愉之色的一种神情。那仆人当真有些失望——他原盼着一番节日般的日子、借着洗礼之庆大吃大喝、放浪形骸而无忌——便悻悻地冲那小厮发作道，他定要把爵士之子如何听这本来该叫任何忠仆悲恸的消息的情形禀告爵士；话头一旦打开，他便越说越溜，正滔滔不绝之际，却被那小矮个儿一抬头、一道狠瞪堵了回去——那一瞪之可怖，半似魔鬼、半似癫狂，竟使他此后数月之间，在噩梦与神经质的战栗中再三为想象所萦回。

===Original===
To this man Lady Ardagh had, at first sight, conceived an antipathy amounting to horror, a mixture of loathing and dread so very powerful that she had made it a particular and urgent request to Sir Robert, that he would dismiss him, offering herself, from that property which Sir Robert had by the marriage settlements left at her own disposal, to provide handsomely for him, provided only she might be relieved from the continual anxiety and discomfort which the fear of encountering him induced.

Sir Robert, however, would not hear of it; the request seemed at first to agitate and distress him; but when still urged in defiance of his peremptory refusal, he burst into a violent fit of fury; he spoke darkly of great sacrifices which he had made, and threatened that if the request were at any time renewed he would leave both her and the country forever. This was, however, a solitary instance of violence; his general conduct towards Lady Ardagh, though at no time uxorious, was certainly kind and respectful, and he was more than repaid in the fervent attachment which she bore him in return.

===Chinese===
这人，阿达格夫人自第一眼起，便生出一种近于惊惧的憎恶——厌恶与畏惧交织，其势之烈，竟使她郑重而急切地向罗伯特爵士请求，求他将此人遣走；她并以爵士在婚约中留给她自行处置的那笔财产，主动提出要厚给此人之资，只要能免去她日日那番怕与他撞见的焦虑不安。

然而罗伯特爵士连听也不肯听；这一请求初时似乎令他心绪不宁、苦痛不堪；可当夫人不顾他的断然拒绝仍苦苦相劝时，他勃然大怒；他闪烁其词地说到自己曾作过何等重大的牺牲，并威胁道，此事若再有提起，他定会离她、离这个国家而去，永不回头。不过，这是他仅有的一次暴烈之举；他对阿达格夫人的一贯态度，虽则算不上多么怜爱，却无疑是和蔼而敬重的；而她对他所怀的那份炽烈的依恋，也已是过之而无不及的回报。

===Original===
Some short time after this strange interview between Sir Robert and Lady Ardagh; one night after the family had retired to bed, and when everything had been quiet for some time, the bell of Sir Robert's dressing-room rang suddenly and violently; the ringing was repeated again and again at still shorter intervals, and with increasing violence, as if the person who pulled the bell was agitated by the presence of some terrifying and imminent danger. A servant named Donovan was the first to answer it; he threw on his clothes, and hurried to the room.

Sir Robert had selected for his private room an apartment remote from the bedchambers of the castle, most of which lay in the more modern parts of the mansion, and secured at its entrance by a double door. As the servant opened the first of these, Sir Robert's bell again sounded with a longer and louder peal; the inner door resisted his efforts to open it; but after a few violent struggles, not having been perfectly secured, or owing to the inadequacy of the bolt itself, it gave way, and the servant rushed into the apartment, advancing several paces before he could recover himself. As he entered, he heard Sir Robert's voice exclaiming loudly—"Wait without, do not come in yet;" but the prohibition came too late. Near a low truckle-bed, upon which Sir Robert sometimes slept, for he was a whimsical man, in a large armchair, sat, or rather lounged, the form of the valet Jacque, his arms folded, and his heels stretched forward on the floor, so as fully to exhibit his misshapen legs, his head thrown back, and his eyes fixed upon his master with a look of indescribable defiance and derision, while, as if to add to the strange insolence of his attitude and expression, he had placed upon his head the black cloth cap which it was his habit to wear.

Sir Robert was standing before him, at the distance of several yards, in a posture expressive of despair, terror, and what might be called an agony of humility. He waved his hand twice or thrice, as if to dismiss the servant, who, however, remained fixed on the spot where he had first stood; and then, as if forgetting everything but the agony within him, he pressed his clenched hands on his cold damp brow, and dashed away the heavy drops that gathered chill and thickly there.

===Chinese===
罗伯特爵士与阿达格夫人这番古怪的晤谈之后不久；某夜，全府上下都已就寝，四下里早已静了一阵，罗伯特爵士更衣室的铃却骤然猛烈地响了起来；铃声一阵接一阵，间隔越来越短，力道越来越猛，仿佛那拉铃之人正为某种可怖而迫在眉睫的危险所惊扰。一名唤作多诺万（Donovan）的仆人第一个赶去应铃；他胡乱披上衣裳，三步并作两步赶往那间屋子。

罗伯特爵士挑作私室的，是远离城堡诸卧房的一间屋子——那些卧房多半在宅子的新部——其门口还设了两重门。仆人刚把第一重门拉开，爵士的铃声又是一长一促、比先前更响；里头那重门却推它不开；可几番猛撞之后，许是门未上紧、又许是门闩本身不够结实，它终于让开了，仆人一个收势不住，冲进屋去好几步方才站定。他一进门，便听得罗伯特爵士在高声呼喝——"在外头候着，先别进来；"可这一禁为时已晚。一张矮矮的滚轮床边——爵士有时就在此床上歇息，因他是个性情乖僻之人——一张大扶手椅里，坐着、不如说是瘫坐着贴身侍仆雅克的身影；他双臂抱胸，两脚脚跟朝前伸在地板上，将他那一双畸形的腿尽行展露；他头往后仰，两眼定定地盯着自家主人，那一副神情之骄横、之讥诮，难以言表；而仿佛为着给他这一身姿态与神情那股子古怪的傲慢再加一层劲儿，他竟把那顶他素日所戴的黑布便帽，戴在了自己头上。

罗伯特爵士立在他面前，相距数码之遥，那一副姿态，写满了绝望、惊惧，以及一种不妨称之为"谦卑之苦痛"的东西。他挥了两三下手，仿佛是要打发那仆人走，可那仆人却钉在了他最初立足之处，动也没动；随即，爵士仿佛忘却了一切，唯独忘不了心头的苦痛，他把攥紧的双手按上自己冷冰冰、湿漉漉的额角，把那一头密密聚拢、凉透透的汗珠一抹而散。

===Original===
Jacque broke the silence.

"Donovan," said he, "shake up that drone and drunkard, Carlton; tell him that his master directs that the travelling carriage shall be at the door within half-an-hour."

The servant paused, as if in doubt as to what he should do; but his scruples were resolved by Sir Robert's saying hurriedly, "Go—go, do whatever he directs; his commands are mine; tell Carlton the same."

The servant hurried to obey, and in about half-an-hour the carriage was at the door, and Jacque, having directed the coachman to drive to B——n, a small town at about the distance of twelve miles—the nearest point, however, at which post-horses could be obtained—stepped into the vehicle, which accordingly quitted the castle immediately.

Although it was a fine moonlight night, the carriage made its way but very slowly, and after the lapse of two hours the travellers had arrived at a point about eight miles from the castle, at which the road strikes through a desolate and heathy flat, sloping up distantly at either side into bleak undulatory hills, in whose monotonous sweep the imagination beholds the heaving of some dark sluggish sea, arrested in its first commotion by some preternatural power. It is a gloomy and divested spot; there is neither tree nor habitation near it; its monotony is unbroken, except by here and there the grey front of a rock peering above the heath, and the effect is rendered yet more dreary and spectral by the exaggerated and misty shadows which the moon casts along the sloping sides of the hills.

===Chinese===
雅克打破了沉默。

"多诺万，"他说，"把那懒骨头、醉鬼卡尔顿（Carlton）给我叫起来；告诉他，主人吩咐，旅行马车半个钟头之内得停到门口。"

仆人迟疑了一下，似乎不知如何是好；可罗伯特爵士匆匆一句便解了他的为难："去——去，他叫你干什么你就干什么；他的命令便是我的命令；这话也同样转告卡尔顿。"

仆人匆匆而去照办，约莫半个钟头之后，马车已停在门口，雅克吩咐车夫驶往 B——n——一座约莫十二英里外的小镇——然而那也是能换到驿马的最近一处——随即钻进车厢，马车当即驶离了城堡。

虽是个月色清朗之夜，马车走得却极慢，两个钟头过后，一行人到了离城堡约八英里的一处地方，此间道路穿过一片荒凉、长满石楠的平地，平地两侧遥遥斜升为苍凉的、波状起伏的丘陵，那一片单调的绵延之中，叫人恍惚看见某片晦暗沉滞的大海，刚一开始翻腾便被某种超自然之力所遏住。这是一处阴郁、剥落之所；近旁既无树木、也无人居；其单调唯一被打破之处，便是这里那里探出石楠之上的一带灰色岩面；而那月光沿丘陵斜坡所投下的、夸大了的、朦胧的影子，又使这一带的景况更显凄清、更显鬼气森森。

===Original===
When they had gained about the centre of this tract, Carlton, the coachman, was surprised to see a figure standing at some distance in advance, immediately beside the road, and still more so when, on coming up, he observed that it was no other than Jacque whom he believed to be at that moment quietly seated in the carriage; the coachman drew up, and nodding to him, the little valet exclaimed:

"Carlton, I have got the start of you; the roads are heavy, so I shall even take care of myself the rest of the way. Do you make your way back as best you can, and I shall follow my own nose."

So saying, he chucked a purse into the lap of the coachman, and turning off at a right angle with the road, he began to move rapidly away in the direction of the dark ridge that lowered in the distance.

The servant watched him until he was lost in the shadowy haze of night; and neither he nor any of the inmates of the castle saw Jacque again. His disappearance, as might have been expected, did not cause any regret among the servants and dependants at the castle; and Lady Ardagh did not attempt to conceal her delight; but with Sir Robert matters were different, for two or three days subsequent to this event he confined himself to his room, and when he did return to his ordinary occupations, it was with a gloomy indifference, which showed that he did so more from habit than from any interest he felt in them. He appeared from that moment unaccountably and strikingly changed, and thenceforward walked through life as a thing from which he could derive neither profit nor pleasure. His temper, however, so far from growing wayward or morose, became, though gloomy, very—almost unnaturally—placid and cold; but his spirits totally failed, and he grew silent and abstracted.

These sombre habits of mind, as might have been anticipated, very materially affected the gay housekeeping of the castle; and the dark and melancholy spirit of its master seemed to have communicated itself to the very domestics, almost to the very walls of the mansion.

===Chinese===
待他们行至约莫这片平地的中央，车夫卡尔顿惊讶地瞧见前方不远处、紧贴着路边站着一个人影；更叫他惊异的是，行近一看，此人不是别个，正是雅克——他还道此公此刻正安安稳稳坐在车厢里呢；车夫勒住马，朝他一点头，那小个子侍仆便喊道：

"卡尔顿，我抢在你前头啦；路难走得很，剩下的路我索性自己照应自己罢。你呢，想方设法往回赶罢，我可要顺着自家鼻子的方向走啦。"

说罢，他把一只钱袋朝车夫膝头一抛，与大道成一个直角地一拐，便朝着远处那道黑沉沉压下来的山脊，快步离去了。

仆人目送着他，直到他消失在夜色的朦胧雾霭之中；自此而后，他、连同堡中上下任何一人，再没见过雅克。他的失踪，一如所料，并未在堡中仆役与依附之人间引起一丝惋惜；阿达格夫人也毫不掩饰她的欣喜；可罗伯特爵士这边却另当别论——此事之后两三日，他闭门不出；待他重理旧业时，已是带着一股阴郁的漠然，可见他之所以如此，乃是出于积习，而非对此间之事还有丝毫兴致。自那一刻起，他变了个叫人说不上所以然、却十分显眼的人，从此走过人生，一如走在一桩既无利可图、也无情趣的事物之中。然而他的脾气，非但没有变得乖戾、暴戾，反倒——虽则阴郁——变得非常、几乎是反常地平和、冷漠起来；可他的精神气却全然垮了，变得沉默寡言、神不守舍。

这种阴郁的心性，一如所料，大大地影响了城堡里往日热闹的起居；而主人那股子阴沉、悒郁之气，似乎也传染给了府里的仆役，几乎传染给了宅子的墙壁本身。

===Original===
Several years rolled on in this way, and the sounds of mirth and wassail had long been strangers to the castle, when Sir Robert requested his lady, to her great astonishment, to invite some twenty or thirty of their friends to spend the Christmas, which was fast approaching, at the castle. Lady Ardagh gladly complied, and her sister Mary, who still continued unmarried, and Lady D—— were of course included in the invitations. Lady Ardagh had requested her sisters to set forward as early as possible, in order that she might enjoy a little of their society before the arrival of the other guests; and in compliance with this request they left Dublin almost immediately upon receiving the invitation, a little more than a week before the arrival of the festival which was to be the period at which the whole party were to muster.

For expedition's sake it was arranged that they should post, while Lady D——'s groom was to follow with her horses, she taking with herself her own maid and one male servant. They left the city when the day was considerably spent, and consequently made but three stages in the first day; upon the second, at about eight in the evening, they had reached the town of K——k, distant about fifteen miles from Castle Ardagh. Here, owing to Miss F——d's great fatigue, she having been for a considerable time in a very delicate state of health, it was determined to put up for the night. They, accordingly, took possession of the best sitting-room which the inn commanded, and Lady D—— remained in it to direct and urge the preparations for some refreshment, which the fatigues of the day had rendered necessary, while her younger sister retired to her bedchamber to rest there for a little time, as the parlour commanded no such luxury as a sofa.

===Chinese===
如此又过了好几年，欢声与酣饮之声早已成了城堡的稀客，这时罗伯特爵士竟——大大出乎夫人之意料——请夫人发帖，邀约二三十位好友前来城堡共度即将到来的圣诞。阿达格夫人欣然照办，她的妹妹玛丽——其时仍未出阁——以及 D—— 夫人，自也在被邀之列。阿达格夫人请两位姐妹尽可能早些启程，好在大批客人到之前，先行与她们聚上几日；两位姐妹应其所请，得帖之后几乎立即就离开了都柏林，其时距那合府宾客齐至的节庆，不过一周有余。

为求迅捷，她们议定乘驿车前往，而 D—— 夫人的马夫则随后赶着她的马匹跟来，夫人身边只带自家一名贴身侍女、一名男仆。她们离城时，白日已过了大半，因而头一日仅行了三个驿站；第二日傍晚八时上下，她们到了 K——k 镇，距阿达格城堡约莫十五英里之遥。在此，因 F——d 小姐疲乏已极——她身子一向十分娇弱，已有一段时日——众人议定就此投宿一宵。于是她们占了客栈里最好的一间起居室，D—— 夫人留在里头亲自指挥、催促预备些茶点——一日劳顿已使此为必需——而她的小妹则退入自己的卧房略作歇息，因那起居室并无沙发此等奢物可得享用。

===Original===
Miss F——d was, as I have already stated, at this time in very delicate health; and upon this occasion the exhaustion of fatigue, and the dreary badness of the weather, combined to depress her spirits. Lady D—— had not been left long to herself, when the door communicating with the passage was abruptly opened, and her sister Mary entered in a state of great agitation; she sat down pale and trembling upon one of the chairs, and it was not until a copious flood of tears had relieved her, that she became sufficiently calm to relate the cause of her excitement and distress. It was simply this. Almost immediately upon lying down upon the bed she sank into a feverish and unrefreshing slumber; images of all grotesque shapes and startling colours flitted before her sleeping fancy with all the rapidity and variety of the changes in a kaleidoscope. At length, as she described it, a mist seemed to interpose itself between her sight and the ever-shifting scenery which sported before her imagination, and out of this cloudy shadow gradually emerged a figure whose back seemed turned towards the sleeper; it was that of a lady, who, in perfect silence, was expressing as far as pantomimic gesture could, by wringing her hands, and throwing her head from side to side, in the manner of one who is exhausted by the over indulgence, by the very sickness and impatience of grief; the extremity of misery. For a long time she sought in vain to catch a glimpse of the face of the apparition, who thus seemed to stir and live before her. But at length the figure seemed to move with an air of authority, as if about to give directions to some inferior, and in doing so, it turned its head so as to display, with a ghastly distinctness, the features of Lady Ardagh, pale as death, with her dark hair all dishevelled, and her eyes dim and sunken with weeping. The revulsion of feeling which Miss F——d experienced at this disclosure—for up to that point she had contemplated the appearance rather with a sense of curiosity and of interest, than of anything deeper—was so horrible, that the shock awoke her perfectly. She sat up in the bed, and looked fearfully around the room, which was imperfectly lighted by a single candle burning dimly, as if she almost expected to see the reality of her dreadful vision lurking in some corner of the chamber. Her fears were, however, verified, though not in the way she expected; yet in a manner sufficiently horrible—for she had hardly time to breathe and to collect her thoughts, when she heard, or thought she heard, the voice of her sister, Lady Ardagh, sometimes sobbing violently, and sometimes almost shrieking as if in terror, and calling upon her and Lady D——, with the most imploring earnestness of despair, for God's sake to lose no time in coming to her. All this was so horribly distinct, that it seemed as if the mourner was standing within a few yards of the spot where Miss F——d lay. She sprang from the bed, and leaving the candle in the room behind her, she made her way in the dark through the passage, the voice still following her, until as she arrived at the door of the sitting-room it seemed to die away in low sobbing.

===Chinese===
F——d 小姐，如我已述，此际身子正十分娇弱；此番又是劳顿之疲乏，又是天气之阴凄恶劣，两般相合，越发压低了她的心绪。D—— 夫人独处未久，通往过道的那扇门便被猛地推开，她妹妹玛丽神色大乱地走了进来；她脸色煞白、浑身颤抖，跌坐在一张椅子上，直待一汪眼泪如泉涌般倾泻而出、稍稍解了心头之压，她才平静下来，足以道出自己惊惧苦痛的缘由。缘由说来也简单。她几乎是一沾床便沉入了一阵燥热而不得舒爽的昏睡；种种形状古怪、色彩惊心之幻象，以一种万花筒变幻般的迅疾与繁多，在她睡梦的想象之前纷至沓来。终于，照她所描述的那样，似有一层薄雾插进了她的视线与那在她想象之前嬉戏变幻的情景之间，从这云雾般的影里，渐渐浮出了一个身影，那身影的背似乎朝着睡眠者；那是位女士的身影，她一言不发，却尽哑剧手势之所能，把——绞着双手、把头左右甩动，那样子，正像一个被过度的放纵所榨干、被悲伤本身那种反胃与不耐所榨干的人；苦难之极。她久久地、徒劳地想瞥见那显形之人的脸，那在她眼前仿佛活生生动着的脸。可终于，那身影似以一种权威之态动了起来，仿佛正要向某个下人发号施令，便在这一动之间，它把头转了过来，以惨白分明的清晰，露出了阿达格夫人的面容——苍白如死，一头黑发纷披凌乱，一双眼睛因哭泣而昏暗、而深陷。F——d 小姐此刻所感受的那一番心情之逆转——因在那一刻之前，她注视这显形，与其说是出于一种比好奇与关切更深之物，不如说便是好奇与关切——可怖到了这般地步，这一惊竟把她完完全全惊醒了。她从床上坐起，惶然四顾这间屋子——屋子里只靠一支燃得暗淡的蜡烛照得昏黄——她几乎像是盼着、又怕着，要瞧见自己那可怖幻象的真身，正潜伏在屋中某一隅。然而她的恐惧竟应验了，虽说并非以她所想的那种方式应验；可应验之法也足够可怖——因她几乎还没工夫喘一口气、收一收神，便听见、又像是自以为听见，她姐姐阿达格夫人的声音，时而剧烈抽泣，时而近乎惊叫，声声唤着她与 D—— 夫人，以一种绝望之中最最恳切的哀求，求她们看在上帝份上，一刻也别耽搁，速速到她身边来。这一切清清楚楚得可怕，仿佛那哀哭之人便站在离 F——d 小姐所卧之地不过几码之处。她从床上一跃而起，把蜡烛留在屋里，摸黑穿过过道，那声音仍一路相随，待她到了起居室门口，那声音方似在低低的抽泣之中，渐渐隐没。

===Original===
As soon as Miss F——d was tolerably recovered, she declared her determination to proceed directly, and without further loss of time, to Castle Ardagh. It was not without much difficulty that Lady D—— at length prevailed upon her to consent to remain where they then were, until morning should arrive, when it was to be expected that the young lady would be much refreshed by at least remaining quiet for the night, even though sleep were out of the question. Lady D—— was convinced, from the nervous and feverish symptoms which her sister exhibited, that she had already done too much, and was more than ever satisfied of the necessity of prosecuting the journey no further upon that day. After some time she persuaded her sister to return to her room, where she remained with her until she had gone to bed, and appeared comparatively composed. Lady D—— then returned to the parlour, and not finding herself sleepy, she remained sitting by the fire. Her solitude was a second time broken in upon, by the entrance of her sister, who now appeared, if possible, more agitated than before. She said that Lady D—— had not long left the room, when she was roused by a repetition of the same wailing and lamentations, accompanied by the wildest and most agonized supplications that no time should be lost in coming to Castle Ardagh, and all in her sister's voice, and uttered at the same proximity as before. This time the voice had followed her to the very door of the sitting-room, and until she closed it, seemed to pour forth its cries and sobs at the very threshold.

Miss F——d now most positively declared that nothing should prevent her proceeding instantly to the castle, adding that if Lady D—— would not accompany her, she would go on by herself. Superstitious feelings are at all times more or less contagious, and the last century afforded a soil much more congenial to their growth than the present. Lady D—— was so far affected by her sister's terrors, that she became, at least, uneasy; and seeing that her sister was immovably determined upon setting forward immediately, she consented to accompany her forthwith. After a slight delay, fresh horses were procured, and the two ladies and their attendants renewed their journey, with strong injunctions to the driver to quicken their rate of travelling as much as possible, and promises of reward in case of his doing so.

待 F——d 小姐稍稍复原，她便声言决意即刻、毫不耽搁地赶往阿达格城堡。D—— 夫人费了好大的劲，才总算劝得她答应暂留此地、待到天明，那时小姐纵使睡不着，至少静养一夜，也该养回几分精神。D—— 夫人从妹妹所显露的那一番神经质、发热的症状里断定，她已操劳太过，越发认定今日断不可再向前赶路。她又劝了妹妹一阵，劝她回房去，自己也陪在她房里，直到她上了床、看上去已较为安定。D—— 夫人这才回到起居室，自觉并无睡意，便在炉边坐着。她的清静第二度被人打破——她妹妹又走了进来，这一回，倘若可能，比先前更加神乱。她说，D—— 夫人前脚刚走，她便又被同一番号泣与哀哭所惊起，伴着那最最狂乱、最最苦痛的恳求，求她们一刻也别耽搁、速到阿达格城堡来——一切仍是姐姐的声音，仍是与先前一般无二的近。这一回，那声音竟一路追到起居室门口，直到她把门关上，仿佛还把那一腔号哭与抽泣，都倾在了门槛之上。

===Original===
Roads were then in much worse condition throughout the south, even than they now are; and the fifteen miles which modern posting would have passed in little more than an hour and a half, were not completed even with every possible exertion in twice the time. Miss F——d had been nervously restless during the journey. Her head had been constantly out of the carriage window; and as they approached the entrance to the castle demesne, which lay about a mile from the building, her anxiety began to communicate itself to her sister. The postillion had just dismounted, and was endeavouring to open the gate—at that time a necessary trouble; for in the middle of the last century porter's lodges were not common in the south of Ireland, and locks and keys almost unknown. He had just succeeded in rolling back the heavy oaken gate so as to admit the vehicle, when a mounted servant rode rapidly down the avenue, and drawing up at the carriage, asked of the postillion who the party were; and on hearing, he rode round to the carriage window and handed in a note, which Lady D—— received. By the assistance of one of the coach-lamps they succeeded in deciphering it. It was scrawled in great agitation, and ran thus:

> "**My Dear Sister—My Dear Sisters both**—In God's name lose no time, I am frightened and miserable; I cannot explain all till you come. I am too much terrified to write coherently; but understand me—hasten—do not waste a minute. I am afraid you will come too late.
> "E. A."

The servant could tell nothing more than that the castle was in great confusion, and that Lady Ardagh had been crying bitterly all the night. Sir Robert was perfectly well. Altogether at a loss as to the cause of Lady Ardagh's great distress, they urged their way up the steep and broken avenue which wound through the crowding trees, whose wild and grotesque branches, now left stripped and naked by the blasts of winter, stretched drearily across the road. As the carriage drew up in the area before the door, the anxiety of the ladies almost amounted to agony; and scarcely waiting for the assistance of their attendant, they sprang to the ground, and in an instant stood at the castle door. From within were distinctly audible the sounds of lamentation and weeping, and the suppressed hum of voices as if of those endeavouring to soothe the mourner. The door was speedily opened, and when the ladies entered, the first object which met their view was their sister, Lady Ardagh, sitting on a form in the hall, weeping and wringing her hands in deep agony. Beside her stood two old, withered crones, who were each endeavouring in their own way to administer consolation, without even knowing or caring what the subject of her grief might be.

那仆人也说不出更多的，只说堡中已乱作一团，阿达格夫人整夜哭得厉害。罗伯特爵士则安然无恙。她们对阿达格夫人何以如此苦痛，全然摸不着头脑，便催着车登上那道陡峭、坎坷的林荫道——道在簇簇树丛之间蜿蜒而上，那些狂怪嶙峋的枝桠，如今已被冬日的寒风剥得精光、赤裸，惨淡地横斜在路的上空。马车在门前空地上停住之际，两位夫人的焦虑已近苦痛；她们几乎等不及随从搀扶，便纵身跳下车来，转眼便立于城堡门口。从里头清清楚楚传来哀号与啼泣之声，还夹着一阵压低了的嗡嗡人语，仿佛有人在劝慰那哀哭之人。门很快开了，两位夫人进门所见头一物，便是她们姐妹阿达格夫人，正坐在大厅里一张长凳上，哀哀痛哭、绞着双手，苦痛至深。她身旁站着两个干瘪老妪，各以各的法子，竭力劝慰，至于夫人所苦何事，她们既不知、也并不在意。

===Original===
Immediately on Lady Ardagh's seeing her sisters, she started up, fell on their necks, and kissed them again and again without speaking, and then taking them each by a hand, still weeping bitterly, she led them into a small room adjoining the hall, in which burned a light, and, having closed the door, she sat down between them. After thanking them for the haste they had made, she proceeded to tell them, in words incoherent from agitation, that Sir Robert had in private, and in the most solemn manner, told her that he should die upon that night, and that he had occupied himself during the evening in giving minute directions respecting the arrangements of his funeral. Lady D—— here suggested the possibility of his labouring under the hallucinations of a fever; but to this Lady Ardagh quickly replied:

"Oh! no, no! Would to God I could think it. Oh! no, no! Wait till you have seen him. There is a frightful calmness about all he says and does; and his directions are all so clear, and his mind so perfectly collected, it is impossible, quite impossible." And she wept yet more bitterly.

At that moment Sir Robert's voice was heard in issuing some directions, as he came downstairs; and Lady Ardagh exclaimed, hurriedly:

"Go now and see him yourself. He is in the hall."

Lady D—— accordingly went out into the hall, where Sir Robert met her; and, saluting her with kind politeness, he said, after a pause:

"You are come upon a melancholy mission—the house is in great confusion, and some of its inmates in considerable grief." He took her hand, and looking fixedly in her face, continued: "I shall not live to see tomorrow's sun shine."

"You are ill, sir, I have no doubt," replied she; "but I am very certain we shall see you much better tomorrow, and still better the day following."

"I am *not* ill, sister," replied he. "Feel my temples, they are cool; lay your finger to my pulse, its throb is slow and temperate. I never was more perfectly in health, and yet do I know that ere three hours be past, I shall be no more."

"Sir, sir," said she, a good deal startled, but wishing to conceal the impression which the calm solemnity of his manner had, in her own despite, made upon her, "Sir, you should not jest; you should not even speak lightly upon such subjects. You trifle with what is sacred—you are sporting with the best affections of your wife—"

"Stay, my good lady," said he; "if when this clock shall strike the hour of three, I shall be anything but a helpless clod, then upbraid me. Pray return now to your sister. Lady Ardagh is, indeed, much to be pitied; but what is past cannot now be helped. I have now a few papers to arrange, and some to destroy. I shall see you and Lady Ardagh before my death; try to compose her—her sufferings distress me much; but what is past cannot now be mended."

Thus saying, he went upstairs, and Lady D—— returned to the room where her sisters were sitting.

阿达格夫人一见两位姐妹，便霍然起身，扑到她们颈间，一言不发地亲了又亲，随后一手牵着一个，仍哀哀痛哭不止，把她们领进了大厅旁一间点着灯的小屋，关上门，在她们中间坐下。她先谢过她们一路赶路的火速，这才——因心绪激荡而语无伦次地——告诉她们：罗伯特爵士已私下里、以最最郑重的方式，对她说他必死于今夜，又说，他这一晚都忙着就自己葬礼的种种安排，一一作了细致的吩咐。D—— 夫人这时插话，说爵士莫不是发了热病、生了谵妄；对此阿达格夫人急急答道：

"哦！不，不！我要是能这么想就好啦，上帝啊。哦！不，不！等您见了他就知道了。他一举一动、一言一语，都有一种可怖的镇定；他的吩咐条理分明，神志清醒至极，不可能，绝不可能的。"她说着，越发痛哭起来。

就在这一刻，只听得罗伯特爵士一边下楼、一边在吩咐什么事的声音；阿达格夫人急忙喊道：

"您这就去见他罢。他在大厅里。"

D—— 夫人便走进大厅，罗伯特爵士迎了上来；他殷勤有礼地向她致意，顿了一顿，说道：

"您此来是为一桩哀伤之事——府中眼下乱作一团，府里也有人悲恸得不轻。"他握住她的手，目不转睛地盯着她的脸，继续道，"我活不到明日太阳出来之时了。"

"先生，您一定是病了，"她答道，"可我十分确信，明日我们便会见您好得多，后日更好。"

"我**没有**病，姐姐，"他答道，"摸摸我的额角，是凉的；把您的手指搭在我的脉上，跳得又慢又稳。我身子从来没有比此刻更康健过，可我也明知，不出三个钟头，我便不在人世了。"

"先生，先生，"她说道，颇受了些惊吓，却又不愿叫人瞧出爵士那种平静郑重之态在她违心之下所留下的印象，"先生，您不该拿这话开玩笑；这种事连轻飘飘地提一句也不该。您是在亵渎神圣之物——您是在作践您妻子那一片最最深情——"

"且住，好夫人，"他说，"等这座钟敲响三点之时，我若不是一具无用的泥土，那时您再来责备我。现在，请回到您妹妹身边去罢。阿达格夫人固然深可怜悯，可过去之事，如今已无可挽回。我眼下还要整理几份文件，还要销毁几份。我死之前还会见您和阿达格夫人一面的；想法子让她定一定神——她那番苦楚令我很是不安；可过去之事，如今已无可补救了。"

说罢，他便上楼去了，D—— 夫人也回到了两位姐妹所坐的那间屋子。

===Original===
"Well," exclaimed Lady Ardagh, as she reentered, "is it not so?—do you still doubt?—do you think there is any hope?"

Lady D—— was silent.

"Oh! none, none, none," continued she; "I see, I see you are convinced." And she wrung her hands in bitter agony.

"My dear sister," said Lady D——, "there is, no doubt, something strange in all that has appeared in this matter; but still I cannot but hope that there may be something deceptive in all the apparent calmness of Sir Robert. I still must believe that some latent fever has affected his mind, or that, owing to the state of nervous depression into which he has been sinking, some trivial occurrence has been converted, in his disordered imagination, into an augury foreboding his immediate dissolution."

In such suggestions, unsatisfactory even to those who originated them, and doubly so to her whom they were intended to comfort, more than two hours passed; and Lady D—— was beginning to hope that the fated term might elapse without the occurrence of any tragical event, when Sir Robert entered the room. On coming in, he placed his finger with a warning gesture upon his lips, as if to enjoin silence; and then having successively pressed the hands of his two sisters-in-law, he stooped sadly over the fainting form of his lady, and twice pressed her cold, pale forehead, with his lips, and then passed silently out of the room.

Lady D——, starting up, followed to the door, and saw him take a candle in the hall, and walk deliberately up the stairs. Stimulated by a feeling of horrible curiosity, she continued to follow him at a distance. She saw him enter his own private room, and heard him close and lock the door after him. Continuing to follow him as far as she could, she placed herself at the door of the chamber, as noiselessly as possible, where after a little time she was joined by her two sisters, Lady Ardagh and Miss F——d. In breathless silence they listened to what should pass within. They distinctly heard Sir Robert pacing up and down the room for some time; and then, after a pause, a sound as if someone had thrown himself heavily upon the bed. At this moment Lady D——, forgetting that the door had been secured within, turned the handle for the purpose of entering; when someone from the inside, close to the door, said, "Hush! hush!" The same lady, now much alarmed, knocked violently at the door; there was no answer. She knocked again more violently, with no further success. Lady Ardagh, now uttering a piercing shriek, sank in a swoon upon the floor. Three or four servants, alarmed by the noise, now hurried upstairs, and Lady Ardagh was carried apparently lifeless to her own chamber. They then, after having knocked long and loudly in vain, applied themselves to forcing an entrance into Sir Robert's room. After resisting some violent efforts, the door at length gave way, and all entered the room nearly together. There was a single candle burning upon a table at the far end of the apartment; and stretched upon the bed lay Sir Robert Ardagh. He was a corpse—the eyes were open—no convulsion had passed over the features, or distorted the limbs—it seemed as if the soul had sped from the body without a struggle to remain there. On touching the body it was found to be cold as clay—all lingering of the vital heat had left it. They closed the ghastly eyes of the corpse, and leaving it to the care of those who seem to consider it a privilege of their age and sex to gloat over the revolting spectacle of death in all its stages, they returned to Lady Ardagh, now a widow. The party assembled at the castle, but the atmosphere was tainted with death. Grief there was not much, but awe and panic were expressed in every face. The guests talked in whispers, and the servants walked on tiptoe, as if afraid of the very noise of their own footsteps.

The funeral was conducted almost with splendour. The body, having been conveyed, in compliance with Sir Robert's last directions, to Dublin, was there laid within the ancient walls of St. Audoen's Church—where I have read the epitaph, telling the age and titles of the departed dust. Neither painted escutcheon, nor marble slab, have served to rescue from oblivion the story of the dead, whose very name will ere long moulder from their tracery,

> "Et sunt sua fata sepulchris."1

The events which I have recorded are not imaginary. They are *facts*; and there lives one whose authority none would venture to question, who could vindicate the accuracy of every statement which I have set down, and that, too, with all the circumstantiality of an eyewitness.2

D—— 夫人默然不语。

"哦！没有了，没有了，没有了，"她继续道，"我看得出来，我看得出来，您信了。"她便在苦痛之中，绞着双手。

"我亲爱的妹妹，"D—— 夫人说，"此事种种表见，诚然有些古怪；可我仍旧不能不存一线希望——罗伯特爵士这一身的平静，许是有什么叫人看不真的地方。我仍须相信，是某种潜伏的热病扰乱了他的心神；又或者，因他近来日沉一日地陷入一种神志颓丧之境，某一桩微末小事，便在他错乱的想象之中，化作了一道预言他将立时殒命的凶兆。"

如此这般的劝解——便是对劝解之人自己也难令人满意，对那本欲宽慰之人更添一倍之不足——便如此过了两个多钟头；D—— 夫人正开始盼望那个命定的时辰或可不致有何惨事发生，便在此时，罗伯特爵士进了屋。他一进来，便把一根手指竖在唇上，作警示之态，仿佛在命众人噤声；随即他依次握了握两位姨妹的手，又悲戚戚地俯身在他那将昏厥过去的夫人身上，用嘴唇在她那冰凉苍白的额头上印了两下，便默默走出了屋子。

D—— 夫人霍地起身，追到门口，瞧见他在大厅里取了一支蜡烛，从容不迫地上了楼。她受一股可怖的好奇心所驱，仍远远地跟着他。她瞧见他进了自家的私室，又听得他随手把门关上、落了锁。她尽可能无声无息地跟到所能跟到的最远之处，便在那屋子的门口站定，不多时，她两位姐妹——阿达格夫人和 F——d 小姐——也来了，与她同立。她们屏息静气，听着里头会有何动静。她们清清楚楚听见罗伯特爵士在屋里来回踱了好一阵；随后，停了片刻，便传来一声响，仿佛有人重重地把自己摔到了床上。就在这一刻，D—— 夫人忘了门已从里头锁上，转动把手，想要进去——这时紧贴着门、从里头传来一声，"嘘！嘘！"这一位夫人此刻大惊之下，猛力敲门；无人答应。她再敲，越发猛烈，依旧毫无所获。阿达格夫人此时发出一声尖锐的惊叫，昏厥过去，倒在地上。三四名仆人闻声惊起，匆匆上楼，阿达格夫人被抬回自己屋里，已是一动不动、状若死尸。众人随后在长久而大声的敲门皆归徒劳之后，便合力动手强撞罗伯特爵士的房门。几番猛撞之后，门终于让开了，众人几乎一齐涌入。屋子最里头的桌上，燃着一支孤烛；床上直挺挺躺着罗伯特·阿达格爵士。他已是一具尸体——双眼圆睁——五官未曾受过任何抽搐之扰，四肢也不曾有任何扭曲——仿佛灵魂已从躯壳里逸去，不曾费过一丝挣扎以求留下。一触之下，尸体冷如黏土——一切生命余温，俱已离他而去。他们把那双惨不忍视的死眼合上，把遗体留给那一类似乎把"细看死亡各阶段的可怖景象"视作其年纪与性别之特权的人去照管，便回到如今已成寡妇的阿达格夫人身边。堡中聚起了一众人等，可空气里弥漫着死亡的气息。悲恸并不甚多，敬畏与惊恐却写在每张脸上。客人们低声细语，仆人们踮着脚走路，仿佛生怕自己脚步的一丝声响。

葬礼办得几乎称得上隆重。遗体遵照罗伯特爵士的临终吩咐，运到了都柏林，安葬在圣奥多恩教堂（St. Audoen's Church）的古墙之内——我曾在那里读过那方墓志铭，铭文记着这抔尘土的年纪与头衔。然而无论是彩绘的纹章，还是大理石的墓碑，都未能将死者之事从遗忘之中救出，他连那个名字，不久也将从那雕凿的字痕间一同剥落，

> "坟墓亦各有其命。"1

我所记下的这些事件，并非凭空虚构。它们是**事实**；而今尚有一位在世之人，其权威无人敢于质询，足可为我所记下的每一句话之无误作辩，且能以一个目击者所能有的那种种细枝末节为之佐证。2

## Strange Event in the Life of Schalken the Painter Being a Seventh Extract from the Legacy of the Late Francis Purcell, P.P. of Drumcoolagh. / 画家沙尔肯生平中的一桩怪事——已故德鲁姆库拉（Drumcoolagh）教区神父（P.P.）弗朗西斯·珀塞尔（Francis Purcell）遗稿之第七则摘录

===Original===
You will no doubt be surprised, my dear friend, at the subject of the following narrative. What had I to do with Schalken, or Schalken with me? He had returned to his native land, and was probably dead and buried, before I was born; I never visited Holland nor spoke with a native of that country. So much I believe you already know. I must, then, give you my authority, and state to you frankly the ground upon which rests the credibility of the strange story which I am, about to lay before you.

I was acquainted, in my early days, with a Captain Vandael, whose father had served King William in the Low Countries, and also in my own unhappy land during the Irish campaigns. I know not how it happened that I liked this man’s society, spite of his politics and religion: but so it was; and it was by means of the free intercourse to which our intimacy gave rise that I became possessed of the curious tale which you are about to hear.

I had often been struck, while visiting Vandael, by a remarkable picture, in which, though no connoisseur myself, I could not fail to discern some very strong peculiarities, particularly in the distribution of light and shade, as also a certain oddity in the design itself, which interested my curiosity. It represented the interior of what might be a chamber in some antique religious building﻿—the foreground was occupied by a female figure, arrayed in a species of white robe, part of which is arranged so as to form a veil. The dress, however, is not strictly that of any religious order. In its hand the figure bears a lamp, by whose light alone the form and face are illuminated; the features are marked by an arch smile, such as pretty women wear when engaged in successfully practising some roguish trick; in the background, and, excepting where the dim red light of an expiring fire serves to define the form, totally in the shade, stands the figure of a man equipped in the old fashion, with doublet and so forth, in an attitude of alarm, his hand being placed upon the hilt of his sword, which he appears to be in the act of drawing.

===Chinese===
我的挚友，下面这则故事的主题，想必会让你大感意外。我与沙尔肯（Schalken）又有何干，沙尔肯又与我何干？早在我降生之前，他便已返回故土，多半早已作古入土；我从未踏足荷兰（Holland），也不曾与那个国度的人有过只言片语。这些，我想你早已知晓。那么，我须得向你交代我所依据的来源，坦白地陈明这桩即将呈列于你面前的怪事，其所凭据究竟何在。

早年我曾结识一位范达尔上尉（Captain Vandael），其父曾在低地国家（Low Countries）追随威廉国王（King William）麾下效命，也曾随军来到我那不幸的故土，参与征讨爱尔兰（Irish）的战事。我说不清何以竟喜好与这人来往——尽管他的政见与信仰都与我相左：然而事实便是如此；也正因我们这份交情往来无拘，我才得以听闻你即将听到的那桩奇闻。

每次造访范达尔，我总不免为一幅引人注目的画作所打动；我虽算不得什么鉴赏里手，却也看得出画中有几处十分鲜明的奇特之处，尤其在明暗分布之上，且那构图本身亦带着某种古怪，引动了我的好奇心。画中所绘，是某座古老宗教建筑内一间屋子的内景——前景之上立着一名女子，身披一袭白袍，袍幅的一角被拢成面纱之状。然而这装束，严格说来，并不属于哪一修会。那女子手中擎着一盏油灯，周身与面容唯有这灯火得以照亮；她眉目间挂着一抹促狭的笑意，正如俊俏女子得手了某种顽皮把戏时所流露的那种神情；而在画面深处，除了一炉将熄之火透出暗红微光、勾出人影轮廓之外，全然隐没于阴影之中，立着一名男子，装束是旧时的款式，身着紧身短上衣等等，神情惊惶，一只手已按在剑柄之上，看那模样，正要拔剑出鞘。

===Original===
“There are some pictures,” said I to my friend, “which impress one, I know not how, with a conviction that they represent not the mere ideal shapes and combinations which have floated through the imagination of the artist, but scenes, faces, and situations which have actually existed. When I look upon that picture, something assures me that I behold the representation of a reality.”

Vandael smiled, and, fixing his eyes upon the painting musingly, he said:

“Your fancy has not deceived you, my good friend, for that picture is the record, and I believe a faithful one, of a remarkable and mysterious occurrence. It was painted by Schalken, and contains, in the face of the female figure, which occupies the most prominent place in the design, an accurate portrait of Rose Velderkaust, the niece of Gerard Douw, the first and, I believe, the only love of Godfrey Schalken. My father knew the painter well, and from Schalken himself he learned the story of the mysterious drama, one scene of which the picture has embodied. This painting, which is accounted a fine specimen of Schalken’s style, was bequeathed to my father by the artist’s will, and, as you have observed, is a very striking and interesting production.”

I had only to request Vandael to tell the story of the painting in order to be gratified; and thus it is that I am enabled to submit to you a faithful recital of what I heard myself, leaving you to reject or to allow the evidence upon which the truth of the tradition depends, with this one assurance, that Schalken was an honest, blunt Dutchman, and, I believe, wholly incapable of committing a flight of imagination; and further, that Vandael, from whom I heard the story, appeared firmly convinced of its truth.

===Chinese===
“有些画作，”我对朋友说，“会以一种我说不清的方式，让人心中生出一种确信：它们所绘的，并非仅是画家脑中飘忽掠过的那些虚想之形与幻设之局，而是当真存在过的场景、面容与境遇。我每每凝视这幅画，心中便有某种声音告诉我：我所见的，乃是一桩真实之事的写照。”

范达尔微微一笑，凝目沉思地望着那画，说道：

“你的直觉未曾欺瞒你，我的好朋友，因为那幅画所录的——我相信所录不差——确是一桩离奇而神秘的事。此画出自沙尔肯的手笔，画中那位在构图之上占据最显要位置的女子面容，便是罗丝·费尔德考斯特（Rose Velderkaust）的精确写像——她是杰拉德·道（Gerard Douw）的甥女，也是戈弗雷·沙尔肯（Godfrey Schalken）最初的、我相信也是一生惟一的心上人。家父与那位画家交情颇厚，正是从沙尔肯亲口，家父得知了这桩神秘戏剧的始末，而这幅画所凝固的，不过是其中的一幕。这幅画被公认为沙尔肯风格的精妙典范，乃画家临终以遗嘱相赠，留给了家父；正如你所察觉的，这确是一幅极为动人、极堪玩味的作品。”

我只需请范达尔讲讲这幅画背后的故事，便能如愿以偿；正因如此，我方能将我所亲耳听闻的一切，忠实地转述与你，至于那桩传说的真伪所据的证据，是采信还是摈弃，尽由你自行裁夺。我仅可保一点：沙尔肯为人质朴直率，是个地道的荷兰人，我想他断不至于凭空捏造一通异想天开的情节；再者，将此事讲给我听的范达尔，对此事之确凿，亦是深信不疑。

===Original===
There are few forms upon which the mantle of mystery and romance could seem to hang more ungracefully than upon that of the uncouth and clownish Schalken﻿—the Dutch boor﻿—the rude and dogged, but most cunning worker in oils, whose pieces delight the initiated of the present day almost as much as his manners disgusted the refined of his own; and yet this man, so rude, so dogged, so slovenly, I had almost said so savage, in mien and manner, during his after successes, had been selected by the capricious goddess, in his early life, to figure as the hero of a romance by no means devoid of interest or of mystery.

Who can tell how meet he may have been in his young days to play the part of the lover or of the hero﻿—who can say that in early life he had been the same harsh, unlicked, and rugged boor that, in his maturer age, he proved﻿—or how far the neglected rudeness which afterwards marked his air, and garb, and manners, may not have been the growth of that reckless apathy not unfrequently produced by bitter misfortunes and disappointments in early life?

These questions can never now be answered.

We must content ourselves, then, with a plain statement of facts, or what have been received and transmitted as such, leaving matters of speculation to those who like them.

===Chinese===
神秘与传奇的氅衣，披在再没有比沙尔肯——那个粗鄙、村气的荷兰乡人——身上更显格格不入的了：他生性粗鲁、执拗，却在油彩一道上精巧绝伦，他的画作令今日行家赏玩不已的程度，几乎与他当日令同代风雅之人嫌恶厌憎的程度相当；然而这个人，这般的粗鲁、执拗、邋遢——我几乎想说这般的粗野——在他日后功成名就之时，举止仪态皆是如此，却偏偏在早年，被那位反复无常的女神相中，教他在一出丝毫不乏趣味、不乏神秘的传奇之中，扮演了一回主角。

谁能断言，他年少之时，未必不曾有资格充当一回情人、做一回主角呢——谁又能说，早年生涯中的他，就必与那日后成熟之年所证实的他，是同一个粗厉、未加驯化、不解风情的乡野之夫呢——又或者，后来那般笼罩其周身气度、装束、言谈举止的、为人所忽视的粗粝，究竟在多大程度上，未尝不是一种漠然冷漠的滋长之物，而这种漠然，又恰是早年的沉痛挫折与失意所常常催生出来的？

这些问题，如今已无从解答。

那么，我们唯有满足于一桩朴实的陈述——陈述那些被作为事实接收、又被作为事实传下来的情节——至于种种揣测，便留给那些喜好揣测之人吧。

===Original===
When Schalken studied under the immortal Gerard Douw, he was a young man; and in spite of the phlegmatic constitution and unexcitable manner which he shared, we believe, with his countrymen, he was not incapable of deep and vivid impressions, for it is an established fact that the young painter looked with considerable interest upon the beautiful niece of his wealthy master.

Rose Velderkaust was very young, having, at the period of which we speak, not yet attained her seventeenth year, and, if tradition speaks truth, possessed all the soft dimpling charms of the fair, light-haired Flemish maidens. Schalken had not studied long in the school of Gerard Douw, when he felt this interest deepening into something of a keener and intenser feeling than was quite consistent with the tranquillity of his honest Dutch heart; and at the same time he perceived, or thought he perceived, flattering symptoms of a reciprocity of liking, and this was quite sufficient to determine whatever indecision he might have heretofore experienced, and to lead him to devote exclusively to her every hope and feeling of his heart. In short, he was as much in love as a Dutchman could be. He was not long in making his passion known to the pretty maiden herself, and his declaration was followed by a corresponding confession upon her part.

Schalken, however, was a poor man, and he possessed no counterbalancing advantages of birth or position to induce the old man to consent to a union which must involve his niece and ward in the strugglings and difficulties of a young and nearly friendless artist. He was, therefore, to wait until time had furnished him with opportunity, and accident with success; and then, if his labours were found sufficiently lucrative, it was to be hoped that his proposals might at least be listened to by her jealous guardian. Months passed away, and, cheered by the smiles of the little Rose, Schalken’s labours were redoubled, and with such effect and improvement as reasonably to promise the realisation of his hopes, and no contemptible eminence in his art, before many years should have elapsed.

===Chinese===
当沙尔肯在那位不朽的杰拉德·道门下习艺之时，他还年轻；尽管他生性淡漠、举止不易激动——这性情，我们相信，乃是与他的同胞们所共有的——但他却并非不能体味深沉而鲜明的感动，因为有一桩既定的事实摆在那里：这位年轻的画家，对他那位阔绰师父的美丽甥女，已怀着相当深切的关注。

罗丝·费尔德考斯特年纪尚轻，在我们所述的这段时光，她尚未满十七岁；倘若传说不假，她集齐了金发佛兰德斯（Flemish）少女那种柔润含笑、双靥生春的万般娇媚。沙尔肯在杰拉德·道的门下习艺未久，便觉这份关注正逐渐深化，化作某种比他那颗老实的荷兰心所能安享的、更为炽烈、更为迫切的情思；与此同时，他察觉——或者说自以为察觉——了几分两情相悦的可喜端倪，而这，已足令他打消此前或曾有过的种种犹豫，将他心头所有的期盼与情思，悉数倾注于她一人之身。简而言之，他已堕入情网，其深其切，已到一个荷兰人所能有的地步。他不久便向那俏丽的少女倾诉了衷肠，而他的告白，也随即得到了她相应的回应。

然而沙尔肯是个穷汉，他亦无门第或身份上的种种相抵之利，足以打动那位老人，使他首肯一桩必将使其甥女兼被监护人陷入一个年轻而几近无依无靠的画师之挣扎与困顿的姻缘。于是，他唯有等待——等岁月赐他机遇，等机缘成全其事；待到那时，倘若他的劳作收益颇丰，那么他所提的亲事，至少有望为那位戒备森严的监护人俯听。数月流转，在小罗丝笑靥的鼓舞之下，沙尔肯加倍地勤勉，画艺精进之速之佳，大可指望在不出数年之内，一遂其愿，并于画道之上跻身一席不可小觑的地位。

===Original===
The even course of this cheering prosperity was, however, destined to experience a sudden and formidable interruption, and that, too, in a manner so strange and mysterious as to baffle all investigation, and throw upon the events themselves a shadow of almost supernatural horror.

Schalken had one evening remained in the master’s studio considerably longer than his more volatile companions, who had gladly availed themselves of the excuse which the dusk of evening afforded, to withdraw from their several tasks, in order to finish a day of labour in the jollity and conviviality of the tavern.

But Schalken worked for improvement, or rather for love. Besides, he was now engaged merely in sketching a design, an operation which, unlike that of colouring, might be continued as long as there was light sufficient to distinguish between canvas and charcoal. He had not then, nor, indeed, until long after, discovered the peculiar powers of his pencil, and he was engaged in composing a group of extremely roguish-looking and grotesque imps and demons, who were inflicting various ingenious torments upon a perspiring and potbellied St. Anthony, who reclined in the midst of them, apparently in the last stage of drunkenness.

===Chinese===
然而，这一帆风顺、令人宽慰的顺境，注定要遭一场突如其来的、可怕的打断；且那打断的方式，又是如此离奇、如此神秘，竟至一切查究皆无从着手，更给事件本身投上了一重近乎超自然的恐怖阴翳。

某日傍晚，沙尔肯在师父的画室里逗留得较那些性情轻快的同伴们长久得多——他的同伴们早已趁着暮色四合所给的借口，欣然搁下各自的活计，溜到酒馆里寻欢作乐、把盏言欢去了。

然而沙尔肯作画，是为求精进，或者更直白地说，是为着爱情。再者，他此刻所从事的，不过是勾勒一幅草稿，这种勾画与着色不同，只要还有足以辨认画布与炭笔的光线，便可一直做下去。那时他还未——其实直到许久之后也未曾——发现自己画笔所独具的种种奇能，他此刻正埋首构图，画的是一群模样极促狭、极怪诞的小鬼与恶魔，正在一位汗流浃背、大腹便便的圣安东尼（St. Anthony）身上施用种种别出心裁的酷刑，那位圣徒则瘫坐在众鬼之中，看模样已醉到了最后一程。

===Original===
The young artist, however, though incapable of executing, or even of appreciating, anything of true sublimity, had nevertheless discernment enough to prevent his being by any means satisfied with his work; and many were the patient erasures and corrections which the limbs and features of saint and devil underwent, yet all without producing in their new arrangement anything of improvement or increased effect.

The large, old-fashioned room was silent, and, with the exception of himself, quite deserted by its usual inmates. An hour had passed﻿—nearly two﻿—without any improved result. Daylight had already declined, and twilight was fast giving way to the darkness of night. The patience of the young man was exhausted, and he stood before his unfinished production, absorbed in no very pleasing ruminations, one hand buried in the folds of his long dark hair, and the other holding the piece of charcoal which had so ill executed its office, and which he now rubbed, without much regard to the sable streaks which it produced, with irritable pressure upon his ample Flemish inexpressibles.

“Pshaw!” said the young man aloud, “would that picture, devils, saint, and all, were where they should be﻿—in hell!”

===Chinese===
这位年轻的画家，虽无能执笔、甚至连鉴赏任何真正崇高的东西都谈不上，却也还有几分眼力，足以教他无论如何都对自己的作品心生不满；于是圣徒与魔鬼的四肢五官，耐着性子擦了又擦、改了又改，纵经这许多删改，重新排布之后，却仍不见丝毫的长进，也不见半点的增色。

那间宽敞的、旧式格局的屋子一片寂静，除了他自己之外，平日栖身其中的众人都已散尽。一个钟头过去了——将近两个了——仍无丝毫起色。天光早已暗淡，暮色正迅速地让位于黑夜。年轻人的耐性已然耗尽，他立于那幅未竟之作前，沉浸在一桩并不怎么惬意的冥想之中，一只手埋进他那深色长发的发缕之间，另一只手握着那截失职的炭笔，此刻正毫无顾忌地在一条条黑色的涂痕之中，烦躁地用力抹擦着他那条宽大的佛兰德斯式的肥大裤子。

“呸！”年轻人高声说道，“巴不得那幅画——魔鬼、圣徒，连带所有——都到它们该去的地方——地狱里去！”

===Original===
A short, sudden laugh, uttered startlingly close to his ear, instantly responded to the ejaculation.

The artist turned sharply round, and now for the first time became aware that his labours had been overlooked by a stranger.

Within about a yard and a half, and rather behind him, there stood what was, or appeared to be, the figure of an elderly man: he wore a short cloak, and broad-brimmed hat with a conical crown, and in his hand, which was protected with a heavy, gauntlet-shaped glove, he carried a long ebony walking-stick, surmounted with what appeared, as it glittered dimly in the twilight, to be a massive head of gold, and upon his breast, through the folds of the cloak, there shone what appeared to be the links of a rich chain of the same metal.

The room was so obscure that nothing further of the appearance of the figure could be ascertained, and the face was altogether overshadowed by the heavy flap of the beaver which overhung it, so that not a feature could be discerned. A quantity of dark hair escaped from beneath this sombre hat, a circumstance which, connected with the firm, upright carriage of the intruder, proved that his years could not yet exceed threescore or thereabouts.

There was an air of gravity and importance about the garb of this person, and something indescribably odd, I might say awful, in the perfect, stone-like movelessness of the figure, that effectually checked the testy comment which had at once risen to the lips of the irritated artist. He therefore, as soon as he had sufficiently recovered the surprise, asked the stranger, civilly, to be seated, and desired to know if he had any message to leave for his master.

===Chinese===
一声短促而突兀的笑，就在他耳畔惊雷般地近处响起，立刻答了这一句咒诅。

画家猛地转过身，这才头一回发觉，自己的劳作竟一直被一个陌生人注视着。

在距他约莫一码半、略略偏后的地方，立着一个——或者说一个看起来像是——老者的身影：他披着一件短斗篷，头戴一顶阔檐、尖顶的帽子，一只手——戴着重重的、连指手套模样的护手——拄着一根长长的乌木手杖，杖头之上，就那暮色中隐隐闪烁的微光看来，似是一颗硕大的黄金杖首；而在他胸前，透过斗篷的褶皱，隐约可见一条同质地的、贵重链子的链环。

屋内幽暗至极，那身影的外观此外再无可辨；他的面庞更被那顶海狸皮帽沉甸甸地下垂的帽檐整个儿笼在阴影之下，连一个五官都看不清。一绺绺深色的头发从这顶阴沉的帽子底下逸出，此情此景，再连同那闯入者挺直、稳健的举止看来，可见其年岁应尚未过六十，或六十上下。

此人的装束之上带着一种庄重与气派，而那身影那种绝然的、如石像一般的纹丝不动之中，又透出一种说不清的——我几乎可以说——可怖的意味，竟将那已到那恼怒画家唇边的几句冲撞之言，生生堵了回去。于是，待他稍稍从惊异之中回过神来，便客气地请那陌生人落座，并问他是否有口信要留给他师父。

===Original===
“Tell Gerard Douw,” said the unknown, without altering his attitude in the smallest degree, “that Mynher Vanderhauseny of Rotterdam, desires to speak with him tomorrow evening at this hour, and, if he please, in this room, upon matters of weight﻿—that is all. Good night.”

The stranger, having finished this message, turned abruptly, and, with a quick but silent step, quitted the room, before Schalken had time to say a word in reply.

The young man felt a curiosity to see in what direction the burgher of Rotterdam would turn on quitting the studio, and for that purpose he went directly to the window which commanded the door.

A lobby of considerable extent intervened between the inner door of the painter’s room and the street entrance, so that Schalken occupied the post of observation before the old man could possibly have reached the street.

He watched in vain, however. There was no other mode of exit.

Had the old man vanished, or was he lurking about the recesses of the lobby for some bad purpose? This last suggestion filled the mind of Schalken with a vague horror, which was so unaccountably intense as to make him alike afraid to remain in the room alone and reluctant to pass through the lobby.

However, with an effort which appeared very disproportioned to the occasion, he summoned resolution to leave the room, and, having double-locked the door and thrust the key in his pocket, without looking to the right or left, he traversed the passage which had so recently, perhaps still, contained the person of his mysterious visitant, scarcely venturing to breathe till he had arrived in the open street.

===Chinese===
“告诉杰拉德·道，”那陌生人说道，身姿分毫未移，“鹿特丹（Rotterdam）的米恩赫尔（Mynher）范德豪森（Vanderhausen），希望明日傍晚这个时辰与他相见，若他愿意，就在此屋之中，所谈之事关系重大——就这些。晚安。”

陌生人传罢这话，便蓦地转过身，迈着快捷却无声的步子，径自出了屋子，沙尔肯竟来不及回他半个字。

年轻人心中好奇，想看看这位鹿特丹的市民出了画室之后往哪个方向走，于是径直走到那扇可以俯瞰大门的窗前。

画家屋子的内门与通街的大门之间，隔着一段颇长的门廊，所以沙尔肯抢先一步占据了观察的哨位，那老人按理是无论如何也走不到街上去的。

然而他白等了。此外再无别的出口。

那老人究竟是凭空消失了，还是为了什么不轨的目的，正潜伏在门廊的幽暗角落里？这后一种念头一旦浮上沙尔肯心头，便叫满心充斥起一种说不清道不明的恐怖，那恐怖之莫名地剧烈，竟使他既不敢独留屋中，又不愿穿过那门廊。

然而，他鼓起了一股与此事的轻重似乎颇为不相当的决心，唤起勇气离开了屋子，将门上了两道反锁，钥匙揣进衣袋，目不斜视地穿过那段方才——或许此刻仍——容留着那位神秘访客身影的过道，直到他抵达开阔的街面上，方才敢放心喘一口气。

===Original===
“Mynher Vanderhausen,” said Gerard Douw within himself, as the appointed hour approached, “Mynher Vanderhausen of Rotterdam! I never heard of the man till yesterday. What can he want of me? A portrait, perhaps, to be painted; or a younger son or a poor relation to be apprenticed; or a collection to be valued; or﻿—pshaw! there’s no one in Rotterdam to leave me a legacy. Well, whatever the business may be, we shall soon know it all.”

It was now the close of day, and every easel, except that of Schalken, was deserted. Gerard Douw was pacing the apartment with the restless step of impatient expectation, every now and then humming a passage from a piece of music which he was himself composing; for, though no great proficient, he admired the art; sometimes pausing to glance over the work of one of his absent pupils, but more frequently placing himself at the window, from whence he might observe the passengers who threaded the obscure by-street in which his studio was placed.

“Said you not, Godfrey,” exclaimed Douw, after a long and fruitless gaze from his post of observation, and turning to Schalken﻿—“said you not the hour of appointment was at about seven by the clock of the Stadhouse?”

“It had just told seven when I first saw him, sir,” answered the student.

“The hour is close at hand, then,” said the master, consulting a horologe as large and as round as a full-grown orange. “Mynher Vanderhausen, from Rotterdam﻿—is it not so?”

“Such was the name.”

“And an elderly man, richly clad?” continued Douw.

“As well as I might see,” replied his pupil; “he could not be young, nor yet very old neither, and his dress was rich and grave, as might become a citizen of wealth and consideration.”

===Chinese===
“米恩赫尔·范德豪森，”杰拉德·道自语道，约定的时辰渐近，“鹿特丹的米恩赫尔·范德豪森！我昨日之前竟从未听过此人。他找我何事？许是来求画一幅肖像；或要把哪个庶出的儿子、穷亲戚送来拜师学艺；或是请人估一估什么收藏；又或者——呸！鹿特丹哪有什么人会遗我一份财产呢。罢了罢了，无论何事，咱们不久自会知晓。”

此刻已是日暮时分，除了沙尔肯那一张之外，每一座画架都已空无一人。杰拉德·道正以那不耐的期待所激起的不安步履，在屋里来回踱着，时不时哼上两句他自己正谱写的一段乐曲——他虽算不得什么高手，却雅好此道；有时也停下来，扫一眼某个不在的弟子的功课，但更多的时候，是站到窗前，从那里窥望那些穿行于他画室所在的这条偏僻小街之上的行人。

“戈弗雷，你不是说，”道在那观察哨前长久而无果地凝望了一番之后，转过身来对沙尔肯说——“你不是说，约定的时辰按市政厅（Stadhouse）的钟，是七点上下吗？”

“我初见他时，钟刚敲过七点，师父。”那学生答道。

“那么时辰将至了，”那师父说着，掏出一只怀表，那怀表足有一个长成的橙子那般大、那般圆。“米恩赫尔·范德豪森，鹿特丹来的——是这个名字吧？”

“正是此名。”

“一位衣饰华贵的老人？”道又追问。

“就我所能看清的而言，”弟子答道，“他既不算年轻，却也未太老，衣着华贵而庄重，正合一位有身家、有地位的市民身份。”

===Original===
At this moment the sonorous boom of the Stadhouse clock told, stroke after stroke, the hour of seven; the eyes of both master and student were directed to the door; and it was not until the last peal of the old bell had ceased to vibrate, that Douw exclaimed:

“So, so; we shall have his worship presently﻿—that is, if he means to keep his hour; if not, thou mayst wait for him, Godfrey, if you court the acquaintance of a capricious burgomaster. As for me, I think our old Leiden contains a sufficiency of such commodities, without an importation from Rotterdam.”

Schalken laughed, as in duty bound; and after a pause of some minutes, Douw suddenly exclaimed:

“What if it should all prove a jest, a piece of mummery got up by Vankarp, or some such worthy! I wish you had run all risks, and cudgelled the old burgomaster, stadholder, or whatever else he may be, soundly. I would wager a dozen of Rhenish, his worship would have pleaded old acquaintance before the third application.”

“Here he comes, sir,” said Schalken, in a low admonitory tone; and instantly, upon turning towards the door, Gerard Douw observed the same figure which had, on the day before, so unexpectedly greeted the vision of his pupil Schalken.

There was something in the air and mien of the figure which at once satisfied the painter that there was no mummery in the case, and that he really stood in the presence of a man of worship; and so, without hesitation, he doffed his cap, and courteously saluting the stranger, requested him to be seated.

The visitor waved his hand slightly, as, if in acknowledgment of the courtesy, but remained standing.

===Chinese===
正在此时，市政厅那洪亮深沉的钟声一声一声地敲响了七点；师父与弟子两人的目光齐齐投向门口；直到那座老钟最后一声余响止歇，道才叫出声来：

“好了，好了；阁下马上就到——这是说，倘若他守时的话；倘若不然，戈弗雷，你尽可去等他，若你竟愿结交一位喜怒无常的市长。至于我，我以为咱们这古老的莱顿（Leiden）城里，此等人物已够多的了，何须再从鹿特丹进口一位。”

沙尔肯依礼赔笑；过了几分钟，道忽然又叫起来：

“倘若这全是某个恶作剧呢？是范卡普（Vankarp）那一伙人搞的什么装神弄鬼的把戏呢！我巴不得你当初不顾一切，把那位老市长、旧总长或者随他到底是什么人物，结结实实揍上一顿。我敢赌一打莱茵葡萄酒（Rhenish），不出第三棍，阁下就要拿旧交情来求饶了。”

“他来了，师父。”沙尔肯压低声音提醒道；话音刚落，杰拉德·道一转身，便瞧见了那幅昨日在他弟子沙尔肯眼底突如其来地现过一回的身影。

那身影的气度举止之中带着某种东西，顿时叫这位画家心中了然：此事绝非装神弄鬼，他确确实实立在一位有身份的人物面前；于是他毫不犹豫地脱下便帽，客气地向那陌生人致意，并请他落座。

访客微微挥了挥手，仿佛是答谢这一礼数，却仍站着不动。

===Original===
“I have the honour to see Mynher Vanderhausen, of Rotterdam?” said Gerard Douw.

“The same,” was the laconic reply of his visitant.

“I understand your worship desires to speak with me,” continued Douw, “and I am here by appointment to wait your commands.”

“Is that a man of trust?” said Vanderhausen, turning towards Schalken, who stood at a little distance behind his master.

“Certainly,” replied Gerard.

“Then let him take this box and get the nearest jeweller or goldsmith to value its contents, and let him return hither with a certificate of the valuation.”

At the same time he placed a small case, about nine inches square, in the hands of Gerard Douw, who was as much amazed at its weight as at the strange abruptness with which it was handed to him.

In accordance with the wishes of the stranger, he delivered it into the hands of Schalken, and repeating *his* directions, despatched him upon the mission.

===Chinese===
“我有幸见到鹿特丹的米恩赫尔·范德豪森吗？”杰拉德·道问道。

“正是。”来客简短地答道。

“我听说阁下有意与我商谈，”道接着说，“我依约在此恭候吩咐。”

“这人靠得住吗？”范德豪森说着，转向站在师父身后不远处沙尔肯那边。

“靠得住。”杰拉德答。

“那么叫他拿着这只匣子，去找最近的珠宝匠或者金匠，估一估里头的东西值多少，再叫他带一张估价的字据回来。”

说着，他将一只约莫九英寸见方的小匣子放到杰拉德·道手里，道既惊于这匣子的分量之沉，又惊于它被递过来的这等古怪而突兀。

依照那陌生人的吩咐，他把匣子交到沙尔肯手里，又把那些吩咐重复了一遍，便打发他去了。

===Original===
Schalken disposed his precious charge securely beneath the folds of his cloak, and rapidly traversing two or three narrow streets, he stopped at a corner house, the lower part of which was then occupied by the shop of a Jewish goldsmith.

Schalken entered the shop, and calling the little Hebrew into the obscurity of its back recesses, he proceeded to lay before him Vanderhausen’s packet.

On being examined by the light of a lamp, it appeared entirely cased with lead, the outer surface of which was much scraped and soiled, and nearly white with age. This was with difficulty partially removed, and disclosed beneath a box of some dark and singularly hard wood; this, too, was forced, and after the removal of two or three folds of linen, its contents proved to be a mass of golden ingots, close packed, and, as the Jew declared, of the most perfect quality.

Every ingot underwent the scrutiny of the little Jew, who seemed to feel an epicurean delight in touching and testing these morsels of the glorious metal; and each one of them was replaced in the box with the exclamation:

“Mein Gott, how very perfect! not one grain of alloy﻿—beautiful, beautiful!”

The task was at length finished, and the Jew certified under his hand the value of the ingots submitted to his examination to amount to many thousand rix-dollars.

With the desired document in his bosom, and the rich box of gold carefully pressed under his arm, and concealed by his cloak, he retraced his way, and entering the studio, found his master and the stranger in close conference.

===Chinese===
沙尔肯将他这贵重的托付妥帖地藏在斗篷的褶皱之下，快步穿过两三条窄巷，在一所拐角处的屋子前停下，那屋子下方的铺面，彼时正是一个犹太金匠的店铺。

沙尔肯进了铺子，把那个矮小的希伯来人叫到铺子后头幽暗的深处，便将范德豪森的包裹摆到了他面前。

借灯光一验，那包裹外头整个儿裹着一层铅皮，铅皮表面已被刮得斑驳、污损不堪，年深日久已近灰白。这层铅皮好不容易才揭去一部分，底下露出一只某种深色、质地异常坚硬的木头匣子；这木匣也被撬开，揭去两三层麻布之后，里面的物件竟是一整堆金锭，紧紧挨挨地码在一起，据那犹太人宣称，成色精纯无比。

每一锭金子都经那矮小犹太人一一过目审视，他似乎在抚摸、检验这些灿灿金属的碎块之时，体味到一种老饕般的愉悦；每验完一锭，便放回匣中，口中叫道：

“我的天主啊，成色多完美！没有一星半点的杂质——美极了，美极了！”

这一番检验终于做完了，那犹太人便亲手开具了一张字据，证明他所验过的金锭，价值达数千里克斯银元（rix-dollars）之多。

沙尔肯怀中揣着那张所要的字据，腋下紧紧夹着那匣沉甸甸的金子，用斗篷遮掩妥当，原路折回，进了画室，只见师父正与那陌生人密谈。

===Original===
Schalken had no sooner left the room, in order to execute the commission he had taken in charge, than Vanderhausen addressed Gerard Douw in the following terms:

“I may not tarry with you tonight more than a few minutes, and so I shall briefly tell you the matter upon which I come. You visited the town of Rotterdam some four months ago, and then I saw in the church of St. Lawrence your niece, Rose Velderkaust. I desire to marry her, and if I satisfy you as to the fact that I am very wealthy﻿—more wealthy than any husband you could dream of for her﻿—I expect that you will forward my views to the utmost of your authority. If you approve my proposal, you must close with it at once, for I cannot command time enough to wait for calculations and delays.”

Gerard Douw was, perhaps, as much astonished as anyone could be by the very unexpected nature of Mynher Vanderhausen’s communication; but he did not give vent to any unseemly expression of surprise, for besides the motives supplied by prudence and politeness, the painter experienced a kind of chill and oppressive sensation, something like that which is supposed to affect a man who is placed unconsciously in immediate contact with something to which he has a natural antipathy﻿—an undefined horror and dread while standing in the presence of the eccentric stranger, which made him very unwilling to say anything which might reasonably prove offensive.

===Chinese===
沙尔肯刚刚离开屋子去办所托之事，范德豪森便对杰拉德·道说了下面这番话：

“今夜我不能在此久留，多则几分钟而已，所以我便开门见山，把来意简短地告诉你。约莫四个月之前，你曾造访鹿特丹城，那时我是在圣劳伦斯（St. Lawrence）教堂里见到你甥女罗丝·费尔德考斯特的。我意欲娶她为妻，倘若我能向你证明我极为富有——比她所能梦想的任何夫婿都更富有——那么我指望你能尽你作为监护人之权柄，成全我的心愿。你若赞成我这一提议，便须当场应承下来，因为我没有那么多的工夫，去等你盘算拖延。”

杰拉德·道听米恩赫尔·范德豪森这一番话，其所出之突兀，也许不下于任何人所能感到的惊愕；但他并未失态，流露任何不得体的惊讶之色，因为除了审慎与礼数所给的种种理由之外，这位画家心头还泛起一种阴冷压抑之感，颇似一个人在不知不觉之中，与一种他天性上深恶痛绝的东西紧挨在一起时所感到的那种——一种说不清的恐怖与畏惧，就在这位古怪的陌生人面前立着之时，这感觉一直萦绕心头，使他极不愿说出任何可能合理地触怒对方的话来。

===Original===
“I have no doubt,” said Gerard, after two or three prefatory hems, “that the connection which you propose would prove alike advantageous and honourable to my niece; but you must be aware that she has a will of her own, and may not acquiesce in what *we* may design for her advantage.”

“Do not seek to deceive me, Sir Painter,” said Vanderhausen; “you are her guardian﻿—she is your ward. She is mine if *you* like to make her so.”

The man of Rotterdam moved forward a little as he spoke, and Gerard Douw, he scarce knew why, inwardly prayed for the speedy return of Schalken.

“I desire,” said the mysterious gentleman, “to place in your hands at once an evidence of my wealth, and a security for my liberal dealing with your niece. The lad will return in a minute or two with a sum in value five times the fortune which she has a right to expect from a husband. This shall lie in your hands, together with her dowry, and you may apply the united sum as suits her interest best; it shall be all exclusively hers while she lives. Is that liberal?”

Douw assented, and inwardly thought that fortune had been extraordinarily kind to his niece. The stranger, he thought, must be both wealthy and generous, and such an offer was not to be despised, though made by a humourist, and one of no very prepossessing presence.

===Chinese===
“我毫不怀疑，”杰拉德咳了两三声开场之后说道，“您所提的这桩姻缘，对我的甥女而言，必是既体面又实惠的；但您想必也明白，她自有她的主意，未必肯顺着‘我们’替她谋划的好处行事。”

“休要骗我，画家先生，”范德豪森说，“你是她的监护人——她是你的被监护人。只要‘你’愿意把她许我，她便是我的。”

那鹿特丹人说话间往前挪了一步，杰拉德·道也不知怎的，心里暗暗祈盼沙尔肯早些回来。

“我意欲，”那神秘的绅士说，“当即在你手中放下一笔信物，一则证我之富，二则保我对令甥女之慷慨不虚。那小伙子一两分钟便带着一笔款项回来了，其值是她从一个夫婿那里理当期望所得财产的五倍。这笔款项，连同她的嫁妆，一并放在你手里，你可将两项合并，怎么合乎她的利益便怎么用；这笔钱在她有生之年，尽数归她一人所有。这算不算慷慨？”

道点头称是，心里暗想命运对他这甥女可谓格外垂青。他想，这陌生人必是一位既富且慨之人，这般一门亲事，纵然出自一个怪脾气、仪表也并不怎么讨喜之人之口，也断不可轻慢。

===Original===
Rose had no very high pretensions, for she was almost without dowry; indeed, altogether so, excepting so far as the deficiency had been supplied by the generosity of her uncle. Neither had she any right to raise any scruples against the match on the score of birth, for her own origin was by no means elevated; and as to other objections, Gerard resolved, and, indeed, by the usages of the time was warranted in resolving, not to listen to them for a moment.

“Sir,” said he, addressing the stranger, “your offer is most liberal, and whatever hesitation I may feel in closing with it immediately, arises solely from my not having the honour of knowing anything of your family or station. Upon these points you can, of course, satisfy me without difficulty?”

“As to my respectability,” said the stranger, drily, “you must take that for granted at present; pester me with no inquiries; you can discover nothing more about me than I choose to make known. You shall have sufficient security for my respectability﻿—my word, if you are honourable: if you are sordid, my gold.”

“A testy old gentleman,” thought Douw; “he must have his own way. But, all things considered, I am justified in giving my niece to him. Were she my own daughter, I would do the like by her. I will not pledge myself unnecessarily, however.”

“You will not pledge yourself unnecessarily,” said Vanderhausen, strangely uttering the very words which had just floated through the mind of his companion; “but you will do so if it *is* necessary, I presume; and I will show you that I consider it indispensable. If the gold I mean to leave in your hands satisfy you, and if you desire that my proposal shall not be at once withdrawn, you must, before I leave this room, write your name to this engagement.”

Having thus spoken, he placed a paper in the hands of Gerard, the contents of which expressed an engagement entered into by Gerard Douw, to give to Wilken Vanderhausen, of Rotterdam, in marriage, Rose Velderkaust, and so forth, within one week of the date hereof.

===Chinese===
罗丝原本也攀不上什么高门大户，因为她几乎身无嫁资；说起来简直是全无——除了她叔父慷慨解囊，才略略补上了这一桩缺憾。她也没有资格以门第为由，对这门亲事提出异议，因为她自己的出身也说不上多么高贵；至于别种反对的理由，杰拉德已下定决心不予理会——而以当时的风俗而论，他这般决心也是有根据的。

“先生，”他对那陌生人说，“您所开出的条件实在慷慨，我之所以未敢即时应承，所犹豫的，无非是我还无缘得知半点关于您家世出身、地位身份的消息。这些方面，您当然可以毫不费力地令我释怀？”

“至于我的体面与地位，”那陌生人冷冷地说，“此刻你只能姑且信之；休要以任何探问来烦我；除了我自愿告知之外，你再查不出半点关于我的消息。关于我的体面，你将得到充分的担保——你若是个讲信义的人，便以我的话为凭；你若是个见钱眼开的人，便以我的金子为凭。”

“一位脾气古怪的老先生，”道心想，“非得由着他不可。不过，权衡下来，我把甥女许他，也是理直气壮的。她若是我亲生的女儿，我也要同样办理。然而，能不轻许之时，我且不轻许。”

“能不轻许之时，你且不轻许，”范德豪森竟把方才浮过他同伴心头的几个字一字不差地说了出来，“但倘若‘确属’必要，我想你便会应承了；我且告诉你，我视此为不可或缺。倘若我打算留于你手的那笔金子，能叫你满意；倘若你不愿我这提议当即撤回，那么，在我离开此屋之前，你必须在这张文书之上签下你的名字。”

说罢，他将一张纸放到杰拉德手里，纸上所书，乃是一纸契约：杰拉德·道允诺自即日起，一周之内，将罗丝·费尔德考斯特许配与鹿特丹的威尔肯·范德豪森（Wilken Vanderhausen）为妻，云云。

===Original===
While the painter was employed in reading this covenant, Schalken, as we have stated, entered the studio, and having delivered the box and the valuation of the Jew into the hands of the stranger, he was about to retire, when Vanderhausen called to him to wait; and, presenting the case and the certificate to Gerard Douw, he waited in silence until he had satisfied himself by an inspection of both as to the value of the pledge left in his hands. At length he said:

“Are you content?”

The painter said he would fain have another day to consider.

“Not an hour,” said the suitor, coolly.

“Well, then,” said Douw, “I am content; it is a bargain.”

“Then sign at once,” said Vanderhausen; “I am weary.”

At the same time he produced a small case of writing materials, and Gerard signed the important document.

“Let this youth witness the covenant,” said the old man; and Godfrey Schalken unconsciously signed the instrument which bestowed upon another that hand which he had so long regarded as the object and reward of all his labours.

The compact being thus completed, the strange visitor folded up the paper, and stowed it safely in an inner pocket.

“I will visit you tomorrow night, at nine of the clock, at your house, Gerard Douw, and will see the subject of our contract. Farewell.” And so saying, Wilken Vanderhausen moved stiffly, but rapidly out of the room.

===Chinese===
画家正读着这契约，沙尔肯——如我们方才所说——进了画室，把匣子与那犹太人的估价字据一并交到陌生人手里，正要退下，范德豪森却叫住他等候；他把匣子和字据呈到杰拉德·道面前，便默然站在一旁，等他验过两样东西、确认留在手中的担保之价值。终于，他问道：

“你满意了吗？”

那画家说，他但愿能再宽限一日斟酌。

“一个时辰也不行。”那求婚者冷冷地说。

“那么，好吧，”道说，“我满意了；一言为定。”

“那么即刻签字，”范德豪森说，“我已倦了。”

说着，他取出一只小小的文具匣，杰拉德便在那张重要的文书上签了字。

“叫这青年为这契约做个见证。”老人说；于是戈弗雷·沙尔肯浑然不觉地，在那一纸文书上签了字——而这一纸文书，便将那只他久久视作毕生劳作之目标与酬报的手，拱手让与了旁人。

契约既已如此订下，那位古怪的访客便将那张纸折好，妥帖地收进了贴身的衣袋。

“明晚九点，我到你的宅子里拜访你，杰拉德·道，来看一看咱们契约之中的那个人。再会。”说完，威尔肯·范德豪森便迈着僵硬却快捷的步子，出了屋子。

===Original===
Schalken, eager to resolve his doubts, had placed himself by the window in order to watch the street entrance; but the experiment served only to support his suspicions, for the old man did not issue from the door. This was very strange, very odd, very fearful. He and his master returned together, and talked but little on the way, for each had his own subjects of reflection, of anxiety, and of hope.

Schalken, however, did not know the ruin which threatened his cherished schemes.

Gerard Douw knew nothing of the attachment which had sprung up between his pupil and his niece; and even if he had, it is doubtful whether he would have regarded its existence as any serious obstruction to the wishes of Mynher Vanderhausen.

Marriages were then and there matters of traffic and calculation; and it would have appeared as absurd in the eyes of the guardian to make a mutual attachment an essential element in a contract of marriage, as it would have been to draw up his bonds and receipts in the language of chivalrous romance.

The painter, however, did not communicate to his niece the important step which he had taken in her behalf, and his resolution arose not from any anticipation of opposition on her part, but solely from a ludicrous consciousness that if his ward were, as she very naturally might do, to ask him to describe the appearance of the bridegroom whom he destined for her, he would be forced to confess that he had not seen his face, and, if called upon, would find it impossible to identify him.

===Chinese===
沙尔肯急于一解心头之疑，便站到窗前，以监视那通街的大门；然而这一番试验，不过坐实了他的疑心而已——那老人并未从那门里走出来。这真是太奇怪了，太古怪了，太可怕了。师徒二人结伴而归，一路上相对无言，只因两人各怀各的心事——一份思索，一份焦灼，一份希冀。

然而，沙尔肯并不知道，一场毁坏正悄然逼近他那苦心经营的种种盘算。

杰拉德·道对自己弟子与甥女之间悄然滋生的那段情愫一无所知；即便他知情，这情愫能否构成对米恩赫尔·范德豪森之意愿的什么严重阻碍，也还是大可存疑的事。

那时的婚姻，在彼处之地，本是盘算与交易之物；在一位监护人眼中，把两情相悦当作一桩婚约之中不可或缺的要件，正如同叫他拿骑士传奇里的腔调来起草他的债券字据一般荒唐。

然而这位画家并未将他已经替甥女定下的这桩重要一步告知于她，他之所以如此决心，并非出于预感到她会反对，而仅仅是出于一种滑稽的意识：倘若他的被监护人——她这般做乃是极为自然之事——当真要他描绘一下那位他为她所选的新郎是何模样，他便不得不承认，自己连他的脸都未曾见过，纵然叫他去认，他也认他不出。

===Original===
Upon the next day, Gerard Douw having dined, called his niece to him, and having scanned her person with an air of satisfaction, he took her hand, and looking upon her pretty, innocent face with a smile of kindness, he said:

“Rose, my girl, that face of yours will make your fortune.” Rose blushed and smiled. “Such faces and such tempers seldom go together, and, when they do, the compound is a love-potion which few heads or hearts can resist. Trust me, thou wilt soon be a bride, girl. But this is trifling, and I am pressed for time, so make ready the large room by eight o’clock tonight, and give directions for supper at nine. I expect a friend tonight; and observe me, child, do thou trick thyself out handsomely. I would not have him think us poor or sluttish.”

With these words he left the chamber, and took his way to the room to which we have already had occasion to introduce our readers﻿—that in which his pupils worked.
