这份文书，加上两人亲自登门的干脆利落，再加上那位方济各会修士的有案可查的身份，已经足以令希思科特心悦诚服——除了尽行公开之外，再没什么能比这更令他信服的了。而他这番信服并未走眼。

德怀尔临走之前，向希思科特反复叮嘱，这事必须严守秘密，绝不可走漏到奥玛拉上校耳中——若传到上校耳朵里，于各方都是身败名裂的下场。他又拒绝让希思科特见女儿一面，连她在何处都不肯告知，非等情形到了能让希思科特去探望而无碍的地步再说。

希思科特是个性情粗厉、闷闷不乐的人；虽说他的脾气再难驾驭不过，可这件事里却有那么多叫他欢喜、几乎叫他眼花缭乱之处，于是他便接受了德怀尔所开列的条件，除了一摇头、一句粗声粗气的"但愿这一切都是好事"之外，再无半点不悦之色。

将近两个月过去了，小奥玛拉却仍未启程赴英。他的来信寥寥无几，间隔又长；总之，他的种种行径终于促使奥玛拉上校提前返回爱尔兰，同时又敦请———勋爵及其子N———上尉、还有埃米莉小姐履行一桩前约——他们已答应到他府上小住数周。

一封信送到了小奥玛拉手里，告知他这一安排，并要他前往都柏林侍候；他随即便赶去了。

===Original===
He arrived, with Dwyer, in time to welcome his father and his distinguished guests. He resolved to break off his embarrassing connection with Lady Emily, without, however, stating the real motive, which he felt would exasperate the resentment which his father and Lord ——— would no doubt feel at his conduct.

He strongly felt how dishonourably he would act if, in obedience to Dwyer's advice, he seemed tacitly to acquiesce in an engagement which it was impossible for him to fulfil. He knew that Lady Emily was not capable of anything like strong attachment; and that even if she were, he had no reason whatever to suppose that she cared at all for him.

He had not at any time desired the alliance; nor had he any reason to suppose the young lady in any degree less indifferent. He regarded it now, and not without some appearance of justice, as nothing more than a kind of understood stipulation, entered into by their parents, and to be considered rather as a matter of business and calculation than as involving anything of mutual inclination on the part of the parties most nearly interested in the matter.

He anxiously, therefore, watched for an opportunity of making known his feelings to Lord ———, as he could not with propriety do so to Lady Emily; but what at a distance appeared to be a matter of easy accomplishment, now, upon a nearer approach, and when the immediate impulse which had prompted the act had subsided, appeared so full of difficulty and almost inextricable embarrassments, that he involuntarily shrunk from the task day after day.

Though it was a source of indescribable anxiety to him, he did not venture to write to Ellen, for he could not disguise from himself the danger which the secrecy of his connection with her must incur by his communicating with her, even through a public office, where their letters might be permitted to lie longer than the gossiping inquisitiveness of a country town would warrant him in supposing safe.

===Chinese===
他与德怀尔一同抵达，正好赶上迎接他父亲及其贵宾。他决意要割断与埃米莉小姐之间那桩令他为难的瓜葛，只是不愿说出真正的缘由——他觉得，那缘由只会火上浇油，激怒他父亲和———勋爵——对于他的行事，他俩无疑会恼怒。

他痛切地感到，自己若依德怀尔之劝，便等于默然默认一桩自己根本无法履行的婚约，这是何等不光彩的勾当。他知道埃米莉小姐并非那种能生出强烈依恋之人；即便她是，他也毫无理由设想她对自己有半分在意。

这门亲事他从来便不愿攀；他也无任何理由设想这位小姐有半分不冷淡。如今他把这事——倒也不无几分道理地——视为不过是双方父母订立的一种心照不允的契约，与其说它牵涉到两个最切身相关之人的相互情意，倒不如说它更像一桩生意、一笔算计。

于是他焦急地等候一个机会，好向———勋爵吐露心曲——他不能得体地直接向埃米莉小姐吐露；可这件事在远处看时似乎轻而易举，一旦挨近身来，再加上当初促使他下决心的那股直接的冲动已经平息，便显得处处为难、处处是几乎解不开的纠葛，以至于他一天又一天地、身不由己地避着这桩差事。

虽说他为此焦虑得难以言表，却也不敢给埃伦写信。他无法对自己隐瞒，他与她那层秘密关系一旦因通信而暴露，便要招致何等危险——哪怕经由公共邮局也不行，乡下小镇那些多嘴多舌的好奇心，断不会让他们的信件安稳地在那儿耽搁多久。

===Original===
It was about a fortnight after young O'Mara had arrived in Dublin, where all things, and places, and amusements; and persons seemed thoroughly stale, flat, and unprofitable, when one day, tempted by the unusual fineness of the weather, Lady Emily proposed a walk in the College Park, a favourite promenade at that time. She therefore with young O'Mara, accompanied by Dwyer (who, by the by, when he pleased, could act the gentleman sufficiently well), proceeded to the place proposed, where they continued to walk for some time.

"Why, Richard," said Lady Emily, after a tedious and unbroken pause of some minutes, "you are becoming worse and worse every day. You are growing absolutely intolerable; perfectly stupid! not one good thing have I heard since I left the house."

O'Mara smiled, and was seeking for a suitable reply, when his design was interrupted, and his attention suddenly and painfully arrested, by the appearance of two figures, who were slowly passing the broad walk on which he and his party moved; the one was that of Captain N———, the other was the form of—Martin Heathcote!

O'Mara felt confounded, almost stunned; the anticipation of some impending mischief—of an immediate and violent collision with a young man whom he had ever regarded as his friend, were apprehensions which such a juxtaposition could not fail to produce.

"Is Heathcote mad?" thought he. "What devil can have brought him here?"

Dwyer having exchanged a significant glance with O'Mara, said slightly to Lady Emily:

"Will your ladyship excuse me for a moment? I have a word to say to Captain N———, and will, with your permission, immediately rejoin you."

He bowed, and walking rapidly on, was in a few moments beside the object of his and his patron's uneasiness.

Whatever Heathcote's object might be, he certainly had not yet declared the secret, whose safety O'Mara had so naturally desired, for Captain N——— appeared in good spirits; and on coming up to his sister and her companion, he joined them for a moment, telling O'Mara, laughingly, that an old quiz had come from the country for the express purpose of telling tales, as it was to be supposed, of him (young O'Mara), in whose neighbourhood he lived.

During this speech it required all the effort which it was possible to exert to prevent O'Mara's betraying the extreme agitation to which his situation gave rise. Captain N———, however, suspected nothing, and passed on without further delay.

Dinner was an early meal in those days, and Lady Emily was obliged to leave the Park in less than half an hour after the unpleasant meeting which we have just mentioned.

小奥玛拉到都柏林约莫两周之后——在那里，一切事物、一切场所、一切娱乐，连一切人等，于他似乎都透着一股索然无味、淡而无味、了无意趣的味儿——有一天，难得天气好得出奇，埃米莉小姐便动了游兴，提议到大学公园（the College Park）去散散步——那地方是当时颇受人青睐的一处散步胜地。于是她便与小奥玛拉一道，由德怀尔作陪（顺便说一句，德怀尔若是高兴起来，也能把一位绅士扮得有模有样），一同前往说定的那处地方，在那儿溜达了好一会儿。

"哎呀，理查德，"在一段令人难熬的、一连好几分钟都没人打破的沉默之后，埃米莉小姐说道，"你这是一天比一天不像样了。你简直变得叫人受不了；呆头呆脑的！我自从出了家门，就没听你说过一句像样的话。"

奥玛拉笑了笑，正要寻一句得体的回话，他这打算便被打断了；他的注意力突然被一阵刺痛般地摄住——只见两个身影正缓缓穿过他和同伴们所踱的那条宽阔的步道：一个是N———上尉，另一个的身影却是——马丁·希思科特！

奥玛拉只觉如遭雷击，几乎呆住了；一场即将临头的祸事——一场与一个他向来视作朋友的年轻人立刻就要发生的激烈冲突——凡此种种忧虑，这样的一场照面自难免叫他一齐生出。

"希思科特是疯了吗？"他心想，"是哪个魔鬼把他弄到这儿来的？"

德怀尔与奥玛拉交换了一个意味深长的眼色，便对埃米莉小姐随口说道：

"小姐可否容我失陪片刻？我有一句话要跟N———上尉说，您若允准，我即刻便回来陪您。"

他一躬身，便快步走开，不多时已到了叫他和他主子都放心不下的那个人身旁。

不论希思科特所来何为，那桩奥玛拉自然要为之担忧安危的秘密，他显然尚未吐露半个字，因为N———上尉神情甚是舒畅；他走到妹妹及其同伴跟前，与他们应酬了片刻，笑着告诉奥玛拉，说是乡间来了一个怪老头，专程赶来告状的——想必是告他（小奥玛拉）的状，因为这老头就住在他左近。

在N———上尉说这番话的当儿，奥玛拉为使自己不致流露出那处境所带来的极端激动，可谓竭尽了人之所能。然而N———上尉毫无所疑，径自走过去了，并未再作停留。

那个年月，正餐是一顿吃得很早的饭；埃米莉小姐不得不在我们方才所说的那场不快的照面之后不到半小时，便离开了公园。

===Original===
Young O'Mara and, at a sign from him, Dwyer having escorted the lady to the door of Colonel O'Mara's house, pretended an engagement, and departed together.

Richard O'Mara instantly questioned his comrade upon the subject of his anxiety; but Dwyer had nothing to communicate of a satisfactory nature. He had only time, while the captain had been engaged with Lady Emily and her companion, to say to Heathcote:

"Be secret, as you value your existence: everything will be right, if you be but secret."

To this Heathcote had replied: "Never fear me; I understand what I am about."

This was said in such an ambiguous manner that it was impossible to conjecture whether he intended or not to act upon Dwyer's exhortation. The conclusion which appeared most natural, was by no means an agreeable one.

It was much to be feared that Heathcote having heard some vague report of O'Mara's engagement with Lady Emily, perhaps exaggerated, by the repetition, into a speedily approaching marriage, had become alarmed for his daughter's interest, and had taken this decisive step in order to prevent, by a disclosure of the circumstances of his clandestine union with Ellen, the possibility of his completing a guilty alliance with Captain N———'s sister. If he entertained the suspicions which they attributed to him, he had certainly taken the most effectual means to prevent their being realised. Whatever his object might be, his presence in Dublin, in company with Captain N———, boded nothing good to O'Mara.

They entered ———'s tavern, in Dame Street, together; and there, over a hasty and by no means a comfortable meal, they talked over their plans and conjectures. Evening closed in, and found them still closeted together, with nothing to interrupt, and a large tankard of claret to sustain their desultory conversation.

Nothing had been determined upon, except that Dwyer and O'Mara should proceed under cover of the darkness to search the town for Heathcote, and by minute inquiries at the most frequented houses of entertainment, to ascertain his place of residence, in order to procuring a full and explanatory interview with him. They had each filled their last glass, and were sipping it slowly, seated with their feet stretched towards a bright cheerful fire; the small table which sustained the flagon of which we have spoken, together with two pair of wax candles, placed between them, so as to afford a convenient resting-place for the long glasses out of which they drank.

"One good result, at all events, will be effected by Heathcote's visit," said O'Mara. "Before twenty-four hours I shall do that which I should have done long ago. I shall, without reserve, state everything. I can no longer endure this suspense—this dishonourable secrecy—this apparent dissimulation. Every moment I have passed since my departure from the country has been one of embarrassment, of pain, of humiliation. Tomorrow I will brave the storm, whether successfully or not is doubtful; but I had rather walk the high roads a beggar, than submit a day longer to be made the degraded sport of every accident—the miserable dependent upon a successful system of deception. Though *passive* deception, it is still unmanly, unworthy, unjustifiable deception. I cannot bear to think of it. I despise myself, but I will cease to be the despicable thing I have become. Tomorrow sees me free, and this harassing subject forever at rest."

===Chinese===
小奥玛拉，以及在他示意下一同相随的德怀尔，把这位小姐送到了奥玛拉上校府邸门口，便托辞有事，一道走了。

理查德·奥玛拉当即就他忧心之事盘问同伴；可德怀尔并无半点叫人宽慰的消息可报。他只来得及——趁上尉与埃米莉小姐及其同伴应酬之时——向希思科特说了这么一句：

"千万保密，性命攸关——只要你保密，一切自会无事。"

对此，希思科特答道："不用怕我；我自有分数。"

这话答得模棱两可，无从揣测他到底是打算依德怀尔的劝诫去做，还是不打算。看来最合情理的推断，却绝不是令人愉快的那种。

极可忧虑的是：希思科特风闻了奥玛拉与埃米莉小姐议婚的某种模糊风声——经一传再传，或许已被夸大成婚期在即——便为女儿的利益担惊受怕起来，于是索性走出了这决定性的一步，借披露他与埃伦那桩秘密婚事的内情，断绝他与N———上尉之妹结成一桩罪孽姻缘的可能。他若当真怀有他们所归于他的那般猜疑，那便是用了最有效的法子去阻止这些猜疑成为现实。无论他意欲何为，他与N———上尉结伴现身都柏林，于奥玛拉而言都不是什么好兆头。

他们一同进了达姆街（Dame Street）上的———酒馆；在那里，匆匆用了顿绝谈不上舒心的小餐，一边合计着他们的种种计策和推测。夜色降临，他们仍关在屋里密谈，无人搅扰，一罐子大杯的红酒，则支撑着他们东拉西扯的闲话。

除了一件事，他们什么也没议定：德怀尔与奥玛拉将趁着夜色，在城里各处搜寻希思科特，通过在最热闹的几家酒肆里细细打听，查出他的落脚之处，以便与他作一次彻底而明白的当面谈话。两人各斟了最后一杯，正坐着慢慢地呷，双腿朝着明亮旺畅的炉火伸着；那张撑着方才所说的酒罐的小桌，连同两对蜡烛，就放在他们二人之间，恰好给他们手里那两只长杯提供了一个方便搁置的所在。

"无论如何，希思科特这一趟，至少要促成一桩好结果，"奥玛拉说。"不出二十四个钟头，我便要做一件早该做的事。我要毫无保留地把一切都摊开。这种悬念——这种不光彩的隐瞒——这种表面上的虚与委蛇，我再受不了啦。自离乡以来，我所过的每一刻，都是尴尬、是痛苦、是羞辱。明日我便去闯这场风暴；成与不成，未可知；可我宁可去做个在大路上讨饭的叫花子，也不愿再多忍一天，做那被一桩桩意外随意作践的可怜虫——做那全靠一套得逞的欺骗勾当来维系的可怜附庸。这欺骗纵是*消极*的，到底还是个怯懦、不光彩、无可辩解的欺骗。我连想都不能去想它。我看不起我自己，可我再也不做我现在这副可鄙模样了。明日我便是自由之身，这桩恼人的事也就永远了结。"

===Original===
He was interrupted here by the sound of footsteps heavily but rapidly ascending the tavern staircase. The room door opened, and Captain N———, accompanied by a fashionably-attired young man, entered the room.

Young O'Mara had risen from his seat on the entrance of their unexpected visitants; and the moment Captain N——— recognised his person, an evident and ominous change passed over his countenance. He turned hastily to withdraw, but, as it seemed, almost instantly changed his mind, for he turned again abruptly.

"This chamber is engaged, sir," said the waiter.

"Leave the room, sir," was his only reply.

"The room is engaged, sir," repeated the waiter, probably believing that his first suggestion had been unheard.

"Leave the room, or go to hell!" shouted Captain N———; at the same time seizing the astounded waiter by the shoulder, he hurled him headlong into the passage, and flung the door to with a crash that shook the walls. "Sir," continued he, addressing himself to O'Mara, "I did not hope to have met you until tomorrow. Fortune has been kind to me—draw, and defend yourself."

At the same time he drew his sword, and placed himself in an attitude of attack.

"I will not draw upon *you*," said O'Mara. "I have, indeed, wronged you. I have given you just cause for resentment; but against your life I will never lift my hand."

"You are a coward, sir," replied Captain N———, with almost frightful vehemence, "as every trickster and swindler *is*. You are a contemptible dastard—a despicable, damned villain! Draw your sword, sir, and defend your life, or every post and pillar in this town shall tell your infamy."

"Perhaps," said his friend, with a sneer, "the gentleman can do better without his honour than without his wife."

"Yes," shouted the captain, "his wife—a trull—a common—"

"Silence, sir!" cried O'Mara, all the fierceness of his nature roused by this last insult—"your object is gained; your blood be upon your own head." At the same time he sprang across a bench which stood in his way, and pushing aside the table which supported the lights, in an instant their swords crossed, and they were engaged in close and deadly strife.

他正说着，却被一阵脚步声打断——那脚步沉重却急促地登上酒馆的楼梯。房门一开，N———上尉在一个衣着入时的年轻人陪伴下，走了进来。

两位不速之客进门之时，小奥玛拉已从座上站起；N———上尉一认出他，脸上便掠过一阵明显的、不祥的变化。他急急转身欲走，可看那模样，几乎在转眼之间又改了主意，猛地又转了回来。

"先生，这间房已经被人包下了，"侍者说道。

"出去，先生，"是他唯一的回答。

"先生，这间房已经被人包下了，"侍者重复道，大概是以为他方才那一句没被听见。

"出去，不然就下地狱去！"N———上尉吼道；同时一把抓住那惊得目瞪口呆的侍者的肩膀，把他头朝外扔进了过道，砰的一声把门带上，震得四壁嗡然。"先生，"他转向奥玛拉接着说道，"我本来不指望明日之前能碰见您。命运待我真不薄——拔剑吧，自卫。"

同时他便抽出剑来，摆出进攻的架势。

"我不会与*你*拔剑相斗，"奥玛拉说道，"我确实做了对不起你的事。我给了你怨恨我的正当缘由；可要我取你的性命，我绝不动手。"

"你是个懦夫，先生，"N———上尉答道，那股激烈劲儿几乎骇人，"正如每一个骗子和无赖*都是*的那样。你是个可鄙的胆小鬼——一个下流、该死的恶棍！拔剑，先生，自卫你的性命，否则这城里每一根柱子、每一块招牌，都要宣扬你的丑行。"

"也许吧，"他的朋友冷笑一声说道，"这位先生丢了名誉比丢了老婆，日子还能过得好些。"

"不错，"上尉吼道，"他的老婆——一个贱货——一个人尽可——"

"住口，先生！"奥玛拉叫道，他天性中全部的凶猛都被这最后一重侮辱激了起来——"你的目的达到了；你的血要算在你自己头上。"同时他纵身跃过挡道的一条长凳，把搁着烛火的那张桌子一推，转眼之间，两人的剑已交上了锋，他们便投入了一场近身的、你死我活的厮杀。

===Original===
Captain N——— was far the stronger of the two; but, on the other hand, O'Mara possessed far more skill in the use of the fatal weapon which they employed. But the narrowness of the room rendered this advantage hardly available.

Almost instantly O'Mara received a slight wound upon the forehead, which, though little more than a scratch, bled so fast as to obstruct his sight considerably.

Those who have used the foil can tell how slight a derangement of eye or of hand is sufficient to determine a contest of this kind; and this knowledge will prevent their being surprised when I say, that, spite of O'Mara's superior skill and practice, his adversary's sword passed twice through and through his body, and he fell heavily and helplessly upon the floor of the chamber.

Without saying a word, the successful combatant quitted the room along with his companion, leaving Dwyer to shift as best he might for his fallen comrade.

With the assistance of some of the wondering menials of the place, Dwyer succeeded in conveying the wounded man into an adjoining room, where he was laid upon a bed, in a state bordering upon insensibility—the blood flowing, I might say *welling*, from the wounds so fast as to show that unless the bleeding were speedily and effectually stopped, he could not live for half an hour.

Medical aid was, of course, instantly procured, and Colonel O'Mara, though at the time seriously indisposed, was urgently requested to attend without loss of time. He did so; but human succour and support were all too late. The wound had been truly dealt—the tide of life had ebbed; and his father had not arrived five minutes when young O'Mara was a corpse. His body rests in the vaults of Christ Church, in Dublin, without a stone to mark the spot.

===Chinese===
N———上尉在两人之中力气大得多；但另一面，奥玛拉在操使这件夺命兵器上，本事却远胜对方。可惜房间太窄，这一长处几乎无从施展。

几乎在转眼之间，奥玛拉额头便受了一处轻伤，这道伤虽不过是擦破一点皮，血流得却极急，几乎把他的视线都遮住了。

用过花剑的人都知道，眼睛或手上多么微小的一点错乱，便足以决定这一类比斗的胜负；这一点读者既知，便不会因我下面这话而惊奇：尽管奥玛拉本事更高、阅历更深，对手的剑却两度将他身体贯穿，他沉重地、毫无办法地，倒在了屋子的地板上。

得胜的那一位一言不发，便与同伴一同离开了房间，只把德怀尔留下，任他竭尽全力去照应倒地的同伴。

靠着这地方几个看得目瞪口呆的底下人帮衬，德怀尔总算把伤者抬到了隔壁一间屋里，安置在一张床上——此时他已近乎不省人事；血从伤口涌出，我可以说是*喷涌*——流得那样急，分明可见：若不能立刻、有效地止住血，他连半个钟头也活不了。

医生自然立刻请到，奥玛拉上校虽那时正抱重病，也被人十万火急地请来，一刻不敢耽搁。他来了；可一切人世的救助都已太晚。那一剑刺得又准又狠——生命的潮水已经退尽；他父亲到了还不到五分钟，小奥玛拉便成了一具尸骸。他的遗体安息在都柏林基督教堂（Christ Church）的地下墓穴之中，连一块标明所在之处的石碑都没有。

===Original===
The counsels of the wicked are always dark, and their motives often beyond fathoming; and strange, unaccountable, incredible as it may seem, I do believe, and that upon evidence so clear as to amount almost to demonstration, that Heathcote's visit to Dublin—his betrayal of the secret—and the final and terrible catastrophe which laid O'Mara in the grave, were brought about by no other agent than Dwyer himself.

I have myself seen the letter which induced that visit. The handwriting is exactly what I have seen in other alleged specimens of Dwyer's penmanship. It is written with an affectation of honest alarm at O'Mara's conduct, and expresses a conviction that if some of Lady Emily's family be not informed of O'Mara's real situation, nothing could prevent his concluding with her an advantageous alliance, then upon the tapis, and altogether throwing off his allegiance to Ellen—a step which, as the writer candidly asserted, would finally conduce as inevitably to his own disgrace as it immediately would to her ruin and misery.

The production was formally signed with Dwyer's name, and the postscript contained a strict injunction of secrecy, asserting that if it were ascertained that such an epistle had been despatched from such a quarter, it would be attended with the total ruin of the writer.

It is true that Dwyer, many years after, when this letter came to light, alleged it to be a forgery, an assertion whose truth, even to his dying hour, and long after he had apparently ceased to feel the lash of public scorn, he continued obstinately to maintain. Indeed this matter is full of mystery, for, revenge alone excepted, which I believe, in such minds as Dwyer's, seldom overcomes the sense of interest, the only intelligible motive which could have prompted him to such an act was the hope that since he had, through young O'Mara's interest, procured from the colonel a lease of a small farm upon the terms which he had originally stipulated, he might prosecute his plan touching the property of Martin Heathcote, rendering his daughter's hand free by the removal of young O'Mara. This appears to me too complicated a plan of villany to have entered the mind even of such a man as Dwyer. I must, therefore, suppose his motives to have originated out of circumstances connected with this story which may not have come to my ear, and perhaps never will.

===Chinese===
恶人所谋，从来幽暗，其用意每每深不可测；尽管这事看似离奇、不可解、甚至难以置信，我却深信——而且是凭着几乎可作定论的确凿证据——希思科特此番都柏林之行、他对那桩秘密的告发，以及最终把奥玛拉送入坟墓的那场骇人惨祸，主使者不是别人，正是德怀尔自己。

那封促使此行的信，我亲眼见过。笔迹正与我所见过的、据说是德怀尔手笔的其它样本一般无二。信里装出一番出于公心的惊惶，为奥玛拉的行径而大感不安；信中并称，若不把奥玛拉的真实处境告知埃米莉小姐家中某位至亲，便无人能阻止他与她缔结一桩有利可图的姻缘——此议当时正悬而未决——并彻底摆脱对埃伦的义务；信里又坦白断言，此一步骤最终必使他自取其辱，正如眼下立即使她身败名裂、陷于苦海一般无可挽回。

这封东西末尾端端正正署着德怀尔的名字，附笔里又严嘱保密，声称一旦被人查知此信出自他这一处，写信人便要遭到彻底的毁灭。

诚然，多年之后这封信东窗事发之时，德怀尔坚称此信乃是伪作；这一套说辞的真实性，他至死都顽固地加以坚持——哪怕后来他分明已对世人唾骂的鞭笞毫无感觉了，也未曾改口。此事确乎处处迷雾重重，因为，除开报仇这一条——而我相信，在德怀尔这一类心性的人那里，报仇之念极少能压过利益的盘算——唯一可解的动机，便只能是这般一种指望：既然他已借小奥玛拉之力，从上校手里按最初谈妥的条件弄到了一小块田产的租契，那么他大可继续推进他关于马丁·希思科特那份产业的计划，只消除掉小奥玛拉，便可使他女儿的一只手重获自由。在我看来，这便是称为恶棍，也未免太过周密的一套恶谋了，连德怀尔这种人也不见得想得出来。因此我只能设想，他的动机实出自与这个故事相关、却不曾传到我耳中、或许永远也不会传到我耳中的某些情由。

===Original===
Colonel O'Mara felt the death of his son more deeply than I should have thought possible; but that son had been the last being who had continued to interest his cold heart. Perhaps the pride which he felt in his child had in it more of selfishness than of any generous feeling. But, be this as it may, the melancholy circumstances connected with Ellen Heathcote had reached him, and his conduct towards her proved, more strongly than anything else could have done, that he felt keenly and justly, and, to a certain degree, with a softened heart, the fatal event of which she had been, in some manner, alike the cause and the victim.

He evinced not towards her, as might have been expected, any unreasonable resentment. On the contrary, he exhibited great consideration, even tenderness, for her situation; and having ascertained where his son had placed her, he issued strict orders that she should not be disturbed, and that the fatal tidings, which had not yet reached her, should be withheld until they might be communicated in such a way as to soften as much as possible the inevitable shock.

These last directions were acted upon too scrupulously and too long; and, indeed, I am satisfied that had the event been communicated at once, however terrible and overwhelming the shock might have been, much of the bitterest anguish, of sickening doubts, of harassing suspense, would have been spared her, and the first tempestuous burst of sorrow having passed over, her chastened spirit might have recovered its tone, and her life have been spared. But the mistaken kindness which concealed from her the dreadful truth, instead of relieving her mind of a burden which it could not support, laid upon it a weight of horrible fears and doubts as to the affection of O'Mara, compared with which even the certainty of his death would have been tolerable.

===Chinese===
奥玛拉上校丧子之痛之深，远出乎我所能想象；然则这个儿子，原是他那颗冷淡的心所仍肯眷注的最后一个对象。他对这个孩子所感到的那份骄傲里头，自私的成分或许多于任何一种慷慨之情。但无论此说是否成立，那桩与埃伦·希思科特相关的凄惨情由到底传到了他耳中；而他对她所表现出的态度，比任何旁的什么都能更有力地证明：他对那场致命的变故感得深切、感得公正，且在某种程度上，是怀着一颗已经软下来的心去感的——而那场变故，她既是某种意义上的祸首，又是它的牺牲。

他并未像人们所预期的那样，对她流露半分不近情理的怨恨。恰恰相反，他对她的处境表现出了极大的体恤，甚至可说是温存；既已查明儿子把她安置在何处，他便下了一道严令：不得搅扰她；而那尚未传到她耳中的噩耗，必须暂缓告知，直到能以一种尽可能减轻那无可避免之打击的方式说与她知。

这最后一道吩咐被执行得未免过于谨慎、又过于长久了；我深信，倘若这件事当初便径直告知于她，那么无论那打击何等骇人、何等势不可挡，她都能免去许多最苦的痛楚、许多令人作呕的疑虑、许多令人焦灼的悬念；待到第一阵如暴风骤雨般的悲恸过去之后，她那颗历经磨折的心灵未尝不能恢复常态，她这条命也未尝不能保住。然而这一份搞错了的善意，对她隐瞒了那可怖的真相，非但未能卸下她那副承受不住的心头重担，反倒在她心头压上了一重对奥玛拉情意的可怖猜疑和疑惧，与之相比，就连他已死这一确凿无疑的事实，也会变得可以忍受。

===Original===
One evening I had just seated myself beside a cheerful turf fire, with that true relish which a long cold ride through a bleak and shelterless country affords, stretching my chilled limbs to meet the genial influence, and imbibing the warmth at every pore, when my comfortable meditations were interrupted by a long and sonorous ringing at the doorbell evidently effected by no timid hand.

A messenger had arrived to request my attendance at the Lodge—such was the name which distinguished a small and somewhat antiquated building, occupying a peculiarly secluded position among the bleak and heathy hills which varied the surface of that not altogether uninteresting district, and which had, I believe, been employed by the keen and hardy ancestors of the O'Mara family as a convenient temporary residence during the sporting season.

Thither my attendance was required, in order to administer to a deeply distressed lady such comforts as an afflicted mind can gather from the sublime hopes and consolations of Christianity.

I had long suspected that the occupant of this sequestered, I might say desolate, dwelling-house was the poor girl whose brief story we are following; and feeling a keen interest in her fate—as who that had ever seen her *did not*?—I started from my comfortable seat with more eager alacrity than, I will confess it, I might have evinced had my duty called me in another direction.

In a few minutes I was trotting rapidly onward, preceded by my guide, who urged his horse with the remorseless rapidity of one who seeks by the speed of his progress to escape observation. Over roads and through bogs we splashed and clattered, until at length traversing the brow of a wild and rocky hill, whose aspect seemed so barren and forbidding that it might have been a lasting barrier alike to mortal sight and step, the lonely building became visible, lying in a kind of swampy flat, with a broad reedy pond or lake stretching away to its side, and backed by a farther range of monotonous sweeping hills, marked with irregular lines of grey rock, which, in the distance, bore a rude and colossal resemblance to the walls of a fortification.

Riding with undiminished speed along a kind of wild horse-track, we turned the corner of a high and somewhat ruinous wall of loose stones, and making a sudden wheel we found ourselves in a small quadrangle, surmounted on two sides by dilapidated stables and kennels, on another by a broken stone wall, and upon the fourth by the front of the lodge itself.

The whole character of the place was that of dreary desertion and decay, which would of itself have predisposed the mind for melancholy impressions. My guide dismounted, and with respectful attention held my horse's bridle while I got down; and knocking at the door with the handle of his whip, it was speedily opened by a neatly-dressed female domestic, and I was admitted to the interior of the house, and conducted into a small room, where a fire in some degree dispelled the cheerless air, which would otherwise have prevailed to a painful degree throughout the place.

===Chinese===
有一天傍晚，我刚在一炉旺畅的泥炭火边坐下——那是经过一番长途跋涉、骑马穿过一片荒凉不避风的山野之后，所感到的那一种真切的惬意——正把冻僵了的四肢伸向那和煦的暖意，每一个毛孔都在汲取着热气，我这舒坦的沉思却被一阵长而响亮的门铃声打断，那铃声显然并非出于一只怯生生的手。

来了一位信使，请我前往"小屋"（the Lodge）——这是那一座小巧却颇有些年头、坐落在那片荒丘野岭之中格外偏僻一隅的房子的别号。那片地方表面起伏不平，倒也并非毫无可观之处；那小屋，我相信，本是奥玛拉家族那些精悍、耐苦的祖辈们在狩猎时节当作一处便当的临时落脚之地用的。

我之所以被请到那里去，是为了给一位悲苦已极的夫人，送去一颗受创之心所能从基督教的崇高指望与慰藉之中汲取的那份安慰。

那座偏僻——我甚至可说荒凉——的住宅里住的是何人，我早已疑心便是我们正追踪其简短生平的那位可怜姑娘；我既对她的命运关怀备至——但凡见过她的人，*哪个不*关怀备至呢？——便从那舒服的座椅上一跃而起，那份急切之情，我坦白说，若是我当尽之责把我唤向别一处，我未必便能表现得如此。

不消几分钟，我便策马疾行起来，前面由向导领路；那向导催马催得毫不留情，那速度像是想借着疾行来躲开旁人的目光。一路之上，过道路、穿泥塘，我们溅着水、踏着响，终于翻过了一座嶙峋荒山的山脊——那山的模样如此荒芜、如此拒人于千里之外，简直可作一道挡住凡人目光与脚步的永久屏障——这时那座孤零零的屋宇便显现出来：它卧在一片沼泽似的平地上，一侧延展开一片宽阔的、长满芦苇的池塘或曰小湖；背后则是一带连绵单调的远山，山体上留着一道道参差不齐的灰岩条纹，远远望去，粗粗大大地酷似一道道城墙。

我们沿着一条荒野的马道，速度丝毫不减地策马前行，拐过一道高而颇有些倾颓的乱石墙角，猛地一转，便进了一个小小的四方的院子：院子两边是破败的马厩和犬舍，另一边是一堵塌了的石墙，第四边便是那小屋的正面。

这地方的整个气韵，是一种阴郁的废弃与衰败；单是这一点，便足以使人的心绪预先染上忧思。我的向导下了马，恭恭敬敬地替我拉着马缰，让我下马；他用马鞭的柄敲了敲门，不多时门便由一个穿戴整洁的女仆开了，我被让进宅子的里头，被引到一间小屋子里——那里头生着一炉火，多少驱散了一些这屋里否则便会弥漫到令人难受的阴冷气。

===Original===
I had been waiting but for a very few minutes when another female servant, somewhat older than the first, entered the room. She made some apology on the part of the person whom I had come to visit, for the slight delay which had already occurred, and requested me further to wait for a few minutes longer, intimating that the lady's grief was so violent, that without great effort she could not bring herself to speak calmly at all. As if to beguile the time, the good dame went on in a highly communicative strain to tell me, amongst much that could not interest me, a little of what I had desired to hear. I discovered that the grief of her whom I had come to visit was excited by the sudden death of a little boy, her only child, who was then lying dead in his mother's chamber.

"And the mother's name?" said I, inquiringly.

The woman looked at me for a moment, smiled, and shook her head with the air of mingled mystery and importance which seems to say, "I am unfathomable." I did not care to press the question, though I suspected that much of her apparent reluctance was affected, knowing that my doubts respecting the identity of the person whom I had come to visit must soon be set at rest, and after a little pause the worthy Abigail went on as fluently as ever. She told me that her young mistress had been, for the time she had been with her—that was, for about a year and a half—in declining health and spirits, and that she had loved her little child to a degree beyond expression—so devotedly that she could not, in all probability, survive it long.

While she was running on in this way the bell rang, and signing me to follow, she opened the room door, but stopped in the hall, and taking me a little aside, and speaking in a whisper, she told me, as I valued the life of the poor lady, not to say one word of the death of young O'Mara. I nodded acquiescence, and ascending a narrow and ill-constructed staircase, she stopped at a chamber door and knocked.

"Come in," said a gentle voice from within, and, preceded by my conductress, I entered a moderately-sized, but rather gloomy chamber.

There was but one living form within it—it was the light and graceful figure of a young woman. She had risen as I entered the room; but owing to the obscurity of the apartment, and to the circumstance that her face, as she looked towards the door, was turned away from the light, which found its way in dimly through the narrow windows, I could not instantly recognise the features.

"You do not remember me, sir?" said the same low, mournful voice. "I am—I *was*—Ellen Heathcote."

"I do remember you, my poor child," said I, taking her hand; "I do remember you very well. Speak to me frankly—speak to me as a friend. Whatever I can do or say for you, is yours already; only speak."

"You were always very kind, sir, to those—to those that *wanted* kindness."

===Chinese===
我只等了不多几分钟，另一个女仆——比头一个略长几岁——便进了屋。她替我所要探望的那人，为方才那点小小的耽搁道了歉，又请我再多等几分钟，并暗示我：那位夫人的悲恸来得极猛，若非竭力克制，根本不能平静地开口说话。仿佛是为了打发这段等候的工夫，这位好心的大娘话匣子一打开便滔滔不绝，说的多是些与我无关的话，其中却也夹着一星半点我正想听闻的内容。我这才知道，我所要探望的那人的悲恸，乃是由一个小男孩的猝然夭折所致——那是她唯一的孩子，此刻正停尸在他母亲的卧室里。

"那么，这位母亲叫什么名字？"我问道。

那妇人瞧了我一眼，笑了笑，摇了摇头，那一副神情又神秘又自得，仿佛在说："我这水深着呢。"我不愿再追问下去，尽管我疑心她这份半推半就多半是装出来的——我知道，关于我所要探望之人到底是谁，我的种种疑虑很快便会有个分晓。这位热心的阿比盖尔（Abigail）【注：旧时对女仆的泛称】略一停顿，便又口若悬河地说了下去。她告诉我，她这位少奶奶自从到她这儿——前后约莫一年半——身体和精神便一日不如一日；又说她爱她那个小娃娃，爱到了言语所不能形容的地步——爱得那样痴，多半连娃娃自己也活不久了。

她正这么絮絮不止，门铃响了，她朝我招手让我跟上，开了房门，却在过道里停下，把我拉到一旁，压低了声音告诉我，我若还顾念那可怜夫人的一条命，便千万不可对小奥玛拉的死吐露半个字。我点了点头，表示依她；她便登上又窄又造得不像样的楼梯，在一扇卧房的门前停下，敲了敲门。

"进来吧，"屋里一个柔和的声音说道；我在引路之人身后，走进了一间不大不小、却相当阴沉的卧房。

屋里只有一个活着的身影——那是一个轻盈、优雅的年轻女子的身段。我进屋时她已站起身来；但因屋内昏暗，又因她朝门望过来时脸背着光——光只是昏昏地透过狭窄的窗户照进来——我一时竟认不出她的容貌。

"您不记得我了吧，先生？"还是那低沉、哀婉的声音。"我是——我*曾经是*——埃伦·希思科特。"

"我记着你呢，我可怜的孩子，"我说着，握住了她的手，"我清清楚楚地记着你。坦坦白白地跟我说——把我当一个朋友。凡我所能为你做、所能为你说的，如今都已是你的了；你只管开口便是。"

"您向来待人厚道，先生——对那些——对那些*渴求*一点善意的人。"

===Original===
The tears were almost overflowing, but she checked them; and as if an accession of fortitude had followed the momentary weakness, she continued, in a subdued but firm tone, to tell me briefly the circumstances of her marriage with O'Mara. When she had concluded the recital, she paused for a moment; and I asked again:

"Can I aid you in any way—by advice or otherwise?"

"I wish, sir, to tell you all I have been thinking about," she continued. "I am sure, sir, that Master Richard loved me once—I am sure he did not think to deceive me; but there were bad, hardhearted people about him, and his family were all rich and high, and I am sure he wishes *now* he had never, never seen me. Well, sir, it is not in my heart to blame him. What was *I* that I should look at him?—an ignorant, poor, country girl—and he so high and great, and so beautiful. The blame was all mine—it was all my fault; I could not think or hope he would care for me more than a little time. Well, sir, I thought over and over again that since his love was gone from me forever, I should not stand in his way, and hinder whatever great thing his family wished for him. So I thought often and often to write him a letter to get the marriage broken, and to send me home; but for one reason, I would have done it long ago: there was a little child, his and mine—the dearest, the loveliest." She could not go on for a minute or two. "The little child that is lying there, on that bed; but it is dead and gone, and there is no reason *now* why I should delay any more about it."

She put her hand into her breast, and took out a letter, which she opened. She put it into my hands. It ran thus:

===Chinese===
那一眶眼泪几乎要夺眶而出，可她强自忍住；仿佛那一阵子的软弱过后，反倒添了一股刚强；她便以低抑却坚定的口吻，把她与奥玛拉成婚的前后情由，简略地告诉了我。她说完这段叙述，停了一停；我又问了一遍：

"我能帮你什么忙吗——出个主意，或别的什么？"

"先生，我想把我这些日子所想的，都对您说了吧，"她接着说道，"我相信，先生，理查德少爷曾经是爱过我的——我相信他并未存心骗我；可他身边尽是些歹毒、心硬的人，他的家人又个个有钱、有地位；我如今想必，他巴不得自己从没、从没见过我才好。也好，先生，我心里并不怨他。*我*是个什么东西，竟配高攀他？——不过是个无知的、穷苦的乡下姑娘——而他是那样高、那样大，又是那样俊。错全在我——是我一个人的不是；我也本不该指望、不该奢望他能长久地把我放在心上。也好，先生，我一再再地想过，既然他的爱已经一去不返、永远不再属于我，我便不该挡在他路上，不该拦阻他家里替他筹谋的什么大好前程。所以我一次又一次地想给他写一封信，请他把这门亲事作废，把我打发回家；可为了一个缘由，我直到今日才肯下手：曾经有过一个小娃娃，他的，也是我的——最亲爱的，最可爱的。"她有一两分钟说不下去。"那个小娃娃，就躺在那边，那张床上；可如今他已不在了，再没有道理，*为何*我还要在这件事上拖延下去。"

她把手伸进怀里，取出一封信，把它拆开。她把它放到我手里。信上写道：

===Original===
> "Dear Master Richard,
> "My little child is dead, and your happiness is all I care about now. Your marriage with me is displeasing to your family, and I would be a burden to you, and in your way in the fine places, and among the great friends where you must be. You ought, therefore, to break the marriage, and I will sign whatever *you* wish, or your family. I will never try to blame you, Master Richard—do not think it—for I never deserved your love, and must not complain now that I have lost it; but I will always pray for you, and be thinking of you while I live."

While I read this letter, I was satisfied that so far from adding to the poor girl's grief, a full disclosure of what had happened would, on the contrary, mitigate her sorrow, and deprive it of its sharpest sting.

"Ellen," said I solemnly, "Richard O'Mara was never unfaithful to you; he is now where human reproach can reach him no more."

As I said this, the hectic flush upon her cheek gave place to a paleness so deadly, that I almost thought she would drop lifeless upon the spot.

"Is he—is he dead, then?" said she, wildly.

I took her hand in mine, and told her the sad story as best I could. She listened with a calmness which appeared almost unnatural, until I had finished the mournful narration. She then arose, and going to the bedside, she drew the curtain and gazed silently and fixedly on the quiet face of the child: but the feelings which swelled at her heart could not be suppressed; the tears gushed forth, and sobbing as if her heart would break, she leant over the bed and took the dead child in her arms.

She wept and kissed it, and kissed it and wept again, in grief so passionate, so heartrending, as to draw bitter tears from my eyes. I said what little I could to calm her—to have sought to do more would have been a mockery; and observing that the darkness had closed in, I took my leave and departed, being favoured with the services of my former guide.

===Chinese===
> "亲爱的理查德少爷：
> "我的小娃娃死了，您的幸福是我如今唯一挂在心上的事。您与我的这门亲事，您家里不乐意；我又会成了您的累赘，挡您在那些体面场合、在那些您不得不周旋的显贵朋友之间的道儿。所以，您该把这门亲事作废，无论*您*、还是您家里，要我怎么签字，我便怎么签。我决不怨您，理查德少爷——千万别这么想——因为我从来不配您爱，如今失了这份爱，也无从抱怨；可我会一辈子为您祈祷，一辈子念着您，直到我咽气为止。"

我读着这封信，便确信：把真相和盘托出，非但不会加重这可怜姑娘的悲恸，反倒会减轻她的愁苦，拔去这愁苦中最尖锐的那根毒刺。

"埃伦，"我郑重地说道，"理查德·奥玛拉从未对你负心；他如今所在之处，世人的责难再也及不到他了。"

我说这话时，她颊上那病态的潮红便褪成了一种死一般的苍白，我几乎以为她当场便要倒下断气。

"那么他——他可是死了？"她神志狂乱地说道。

我握住她的手，尽我所能把那桩悲惨的事讲给她听。她以一种近乎不近人情的镇定听着，直到我把这段哀婉的叙述讲完。然后她站起身，走到床边，拉开床帷，默默而定定地凝视着孩子那张安静的小脸：可她心头涌起的那股情感却压不住；泪如泉涌，她抽抽搭搭地哭得肝肠寸断，俯身在床上，把那已死的孩子抱进了怀里。

她哭着亲他，亲了又哭，哭了又亲；那份悲伤如此激烈，如此叫人断肠，连我都禁不住落下苦泪。我尽力说几句所能想到的、稍稍能宽慰她的话——再要硬去劝慰，便是嘲弄了；我见夜色已深，便告辞出来，由我那位先前的向导领着，回去了。

===Original===
I expected to have been soon called upon again to visit the poor girl; but the Lodge lay beyond the boundary of my parish, and I felt a reluctance to trespass upon the precincts of my brother minister, and a certain degree of hesitation in intruding upon one whose situation was so very peculiar, and who would, I had no doubt, feel no scruple in requesting my attendance if she desired it.

A month, however, passed away, and I did not hear anything of Ellen. I called at the Lodge, and to my inquiries they answered that she was very much worse in health, and that since the death of the child she had been sinking fast, and so weak that she had been chiefly confined to her bed. I sent frequently to inquire, and often called myself, and all that I heard convinced me that she was rapidly sinking into the grave.

Late one night I was summoned from my rest, by a visit from the person who had upon the former occasion acted as my guide; he had come to summon me to the deathbed of her whom I had then attended. With all celerity I made my preparations, and, not without considerable difficulty and some danger, we made a rapid night-ride to the Lodge, a distance of five miles at least. We arrived safely, and in a very short time—but too late.

I stood by the bed upon which lay the once beautiful form of Ellen Heathcote. The brief but sorrowful trial was past—the desolate mourner was gone to that land where the pangs of grief, the tumults of passion, regrets and cold neglect, are felt no more. I leant over the lifeless face, and scanned the beautiful features which, living, had wrought such magic on all that looked upon them. They were, indeed, much wasted; but it was impossible for the fingers of death or of decay altogether to obliterate the traces of that exquisite beauty which had so distinguished her. As I gazed on this most sad and striking spectacle, remembrances thronged fast upon my mind, and tear after tear fell upon the cold form that slept tranquilly and forever.

A few days afterwards I was told that a funeral had left the Lodge at the dead of night, and had been conducted with the most scrupulous secrecy. It was, of course, to me no mystery.

Heathcote lived to a very advanced age, being of that hard mould which is not easily impressionable. The selfish and the hardhearted survive where nobler, more generous, and, above all, more sympathising natures would have sunk forever.

Dwyer certainly succeeded in extorting, I cannot say how, considerable and advantageous leases from Colonel O'Mara; but after his death he disposed of his interest in these, and having for a time launched into a sea of profligate extravagance, he became bankrupt, and for a long time I totally lost sight of him.

The rebellion of '98, and the events which immediately followed, called him forth from his lurking-places, in the character of an informer; and I myself have seen the hoary-headed, paralytic perjurer, with a scowl of derision and defiance, brave the hootings and the execrations of the indignant multitude.

===Chinese===
我本以为很快便会被再次请去探望这可怜的姑娘；可那"小屋"已在我堂区的边界之外，我有些不愿踏进同工前辈的辖地，又有些迟疑，是否要去叨扰一位处境如此特殊之人——她若当真要我前来，我毫不怀疑，她自会毫无顾忌地开口相请。

然而一个月过去了，我竟未听到关于埃伦的半点消息。我亲到小屋探问，他们答我说她身子已大不如前，自孩子死后便一日日衰弱下去，已虚弱到几乎终日卧床不起的地步。我屡屡差人探问，也屡屡亲自登门；我所听到的种种，都叫我确信，她正在飞速地滑入坟墓。

有一天深夜，我被人从睡梦中唤起——来人正是上次替我引路的那一位；他是来请我去赴那一位我曾探视过之人的临终之床的。我连忙打点停当，虽不无相当的艰难与几分险阻，我们仍连夜快马赶赴小屋，前后至少五英里路。我们平安抵达，所费的时辰也不多——可一切都太晚了。

我站在床边，床上躺着的，便是埃伦·希思科特那曾经美丽的身躯。这一场短暂而悲苦的试炼已经过去——那孤苦无依的哀痛者已经去了那样一片国土：在那里，悲伤的刺痛、激情的翻涌、悔恨与冷酷的疏弃，再也感觉不到了。我俯身在那张了无生气的脸上，端详着那一副生时曾对一切看她之人施过那般魔力的、美丽的五官。它们确已大大消损；可死亡与朽坏的手指，却终究抹不尽那曾使她如此出众的、精微动人的美的痕迹。我凝视着这一幅至悲而至触目的景象，种种往事纷纷涌上心头，一滴一滴的眼泪，落在那已永远静静地沉睡了的、冰冷的躯体上。

几天之后，我听说有一支送葬的队伍在半夜里从小屋出发，全程极尽隐秘地举行。这事于我，自然算不得什么秘密。

希思科特则活到了很大的岁数，他那副硬心肠原是那种不易受触动之辈。自私而心硬之人往往能在更为高尚、更为宽厚，尤其是更富同情之心的人早已沉沦之际，苟活下去。

德怀尔倒是确实设法——我也说不上是怎么设法——从奥玛拉上校手里榨取了几份颇有油水的、有利的租契；可上校一死，他便把这些权益转手卖了出去，一度纵身跳入奢靡放荡的汪洋之中，终至破产，有很长一段时间，我全然不知他的下落。

一七九八年的起义，及其后紧接而来的种种事变，把他从藏身之处赶了出来，以一个告密者的身份露了面；我亲眼见过这个头发花白、半身不遂的作伪证者，一脸讥嘲与挑衅的怒容，公然迎着愤怒人群的哄骂与咒诅。

# Being a Tenth Extract from the Legacy of the Late Francis Purcell, P.P. of Drumcoolagh / 已故德鲁姆库拉教区神父弗朗西斯·珀塞尔遗稿之第十则摘录

### Introduction / 引言

===Original===
In the following narrative, I have endeavoured to give as nearly as possible the ipsissima verba of the valued friend from whom I received it, conscious that any aberration from *her* mode of telling the tale of her own life would at once impair its accuracy and its effect.

Would that, with her words, I could also bring before you her animated gesture, her expressive countenance, the solemn and thrilling air and accent with which she related the dark passages in her strange story; and, above all, that I could communicate the impressive consciousness that the narrator had seen with her own eyes, and personally acted in the scenes which she described; these accompaniments, taken with the additional circumstance that she who told the tale was one far too deeply and sadly impressed with religious principle to misrepresent or fabricate what she repeated as fact, gave to the tale a depth of interest which the events recorded could hardly, themselves, have produced.

I became acquainted with the lady from whose lips I heard this narrative nearly twenty years since, and the story struck my fancy so much that I committed it to paper while it was still fresh in my mind; and should its perusal afford you entertainment for a listless half hour, my labour shall not have been bestowed in vain.

I find that I have taken the story down as she told it, in the first person, and perhaps this is as it should be.

She began as follows:

===Chinese===
在下面这篇记述里，我已竭力把那位我珍重的友人——我正是从*她*口中听得此篇——的原话（ipsissima verba），尽可能如实地呈现出来；因为我深知，但凡偏离了她讲述自己一生时所用的那种口吻，便会立刻既损其准确，又减其感染力。

但愿我在转述她的言辞之时，也能将她那生动的手势、她那富有表情的容颜、她讲述自己离奇往事中那些阴森篇章时所带的那庄重而动人心魄的神情声调，一并呈现在诸君面前；更但愿我能传达出那种令人肃然的切身之感——讲述者是亲眼所见、亲身参与了她所描绘的那些场景的。这些伴随讲述而来的种种，再加上另一层情由——这位讲述者，是一位宗教信念浸润至深、至为凝重之人，断不至于将她当作事实复述之事加以歪曲或编造——遂使这故事生出一重深沉的意味，而这层意味，单凭所记之事本身，恐怕是难以引发的。

约莫二十年前，我结识了这位女士——此篇记述便是从她口中听来的。这故事深得我心，我趁其在脑海中尚且鲜明之时，便录之于纸；倘若展卷一读，能为诸君消遣一个百无聊赖的半点钟，我这番工夫便不算白费。

我发现，我是照着她所讲的样子、用第一人称把这故事记下来的，而这或许也正是它应有的样子。

她这样开头道：

## The Last Heir of Castle Connor / 康纳城堡的最后嗣子
### Being a Third Extract from the Legacy of the Late Francis Purcell, P.P. of Drumcoolagh. / 已故德鲁姆库拉教区神父弗朗西斯·珀塞尔遗稿之第三则摘录

===Original===
There is something in the decay of ancient grandeur to interest even the most unconcerned spectator﻿—the evidences of greatness, of power, and of pride that survive the wreck of time, proving, in mournful contrast with present desolation and decay, what *was* in other days, appeal, with a resistless power, to the sympathies of our nature. And when, as we gaze on the scion of some ruined family, the first impulse of nature that bids us regard his fate with interest and respect is justified by the recollection of great exertions and self-devotion and sacrifices in the cause of a lost country and of a despised religion﻿—sacrifices and efforts made with all the motives of faithfulness and of honour, and terminating in ruin﻿—in such a case respect becomes veneration, and the interest we feel amounts almost to a passion.

It is this feeling which has thrown the magic veil of romance over every roofless castle and ruined turret throughout our country; it is this feeling that, so long as a tower remains above the level of the soil, so long as one scion of a prostrate and impoverished family survives, will never suffer Ireland to yield to the stranger more than the “mouth honour” which fear compels.3 I who have conversed *viva voce et propria persona* with those whose recollections could run back so far as the times previous to the confiscations which followed the Revolution of 1688﻿—whose memory could repeople halls long roofless and desolate, and point out the places where greatness once had been, may feel all this more strongly, and with a more vivid interest, than can those whose sympathies are awakened by the feebler influence of what may be called the *picturesque* effects of ruin and decay.

There do, indeed, still exist some fragments of the ancient Catholic families of Ireland; but, alas! what *very* fragments! They linger like the remnants of her aboriginal forests, reft indeed of their strength and greatness, but proud even in decay. Every winter thins their ranks, and strews the ground with the wreck of their loftiest branches; they are at best but tolerated in the land which gave them birth﻿—objects of curiosity, perhaps of pity, to one class, but of veneration to another.

===Chinese===
古老荣光的衰败之中，总有某种东西，纵使最漠然的旁观者也不能不动容——那些见证过伟大、权势与骄傲的痕迹，历经岁月的摧折而犹存，以其与今日的荒凉败落所形成的可悲对照，昭示着旧日的模样，以一种不可抗拒之力，叩击着我们天性中的同情。而当我们凝望某个没落家族的孤苗，那种令我们怀着关切与敬意去注视其命运的本能冲动，若又因一段记忆而获得印证——记忆中他们曾为一个沦亡的故国、一种受轻蔑的信仰而竭尽全力、舍生忘死、作出种种牺牲，那些牺牲与努力皆出于忠诚与道义，最终却以倾覆告终——在这种情形下，敬意便升华为崇敬，我们所感到的关切，几近于一种痴情。

正是这种感情，为我国每一座没了屋顶的城堡、每一处坍塌的角楼，都披上了一袭浪漫的魔幻轻纱；也正是这种感情，只要还有一座塔楼高出地面，只要还有一个倾颓困窘的家族尚有子嗣存世，便决不容爱尔兰向异族屈服——所献出的，不过是恐惧所迫的那一点"口头上的敬意"。我曾亲口、亲面地与一些人交谈过，他们的记忆可以一直追溯到 1688 年革命之后那场没收风潮之前的岁月——他们的记忆能重新住满早已没了屋顶、一片荒凉的厅堂，能一一指点昔日显赫曾经所在之处；唯其如此，我对这一切的感受，或许比旁人更为强烈，也更为鲜活——旁人的同情，不过是被所谓废墟与衰败的"如画"效果这等微弱的影响所唤起罢了。

爱尔兰古老的天主教家族，今日确实还残留着几支；然而，唉！残存的是何等的"几支"啊！他们正如这片土地原生森林的残株一般苟延——气力与伟岸虽已被褫夺殆尽，却纵在衰朽之中仍保有几分傲骨。每一个寒冬都削薄他们的行列，将他们最高枝的残骸铺满一地；他们充其量不过是在生养自己的这片土地上勉为见容——于一类人是猎奇的对象，或许是怜悯的对象，于另一类人却是崇敬的所在。

===Original===
The O’Connors, of Castle Connor, were an ancient Irish family. The name recurs frequently in our history, and is generally to be found in a prominent place whenever periods of tumult or of peril called forth the courage and the enterprise of this country. After the accession of William III, the storm of confiscation which swept over the land made woeful havoc in their broad domains. Some fragments of property, however, did remain to them, and with it the building which had for ages formed the family residence.

About the year 17﻿—, my uncle, a Catholic priest, became acquainted with the inmates of Castle Connor, and after a time introduced me, then a lad of about fifteen, full of spirits, and little dreaming that a profession so grave as his should ever become mine.

The family at that time consisted of but two members, a widow lady and her only son, a young man aged about eighteen. In our early days the progress from acquaintance to intimacy, and from intimacy to friendship is proverbially rapid; and young O’Connor and I became, in less than a month, close and confidential companions﻿—an intercourse which ripened gradually into an attachment ardent, deep, and devoted﻿—such as I believe young hearts only are capable of forming.

===Chinese===
康纳城堡的奥康纳家族（the O'Connors），是爱尔兰一支古老的世家。这个姓氏在我们的史册中屡见不斑，每逢动荡或危难之秋，唤起这片土地的勇气与进取之处时，它往往赫然在列。威廉三世（William III）即位之后，那场横扫全国的没收风暴，在他们辽阔的领地上造成了可悲的破坏。然而他们毕竟还保留下了一些零星的产业，连同那座数百年来作为家族宅邸的古老建筑。

大约在 17——年，我的叔父——一位天主教神父——与康纳城堡里的人家结识，过了一段时日，便引荐了我：那时我还是个十五岁上下的少年，意气风发，做梦也想不到他那般庄重的职业，有朝一日竟会成为我毕生的职业。

那一家当时只有两口人：一位孀居的夫人和她的独子，一个约莫十八岁的青年。少年人之间，由相识到相熟、由相熟到相交，其迅疾历来为人称道；小奥康纳（O'Connor）与我不出一个月，便成了无话不谈的密友——这段交往日渐深厚，终于化为一种热烈、深沉、矢志不渝的情谊——我想，唯有少年人的心，才结得出这样的情谊吧。

===Original===
He had been left early fatherless, and the representative and heir of his family. His mother’s affection for him was intense in proportion as there existed no other object to divide it﻿—indeed﻿—such love as that she bore him I have never seen elsewhere. Her love was better bestowed than that of mothers generally is, for young O’Connor, not without some of the faults, had certainly many of the most engaging qualities of youth. He had all the frankness and gaiety which attract, and the generosity of heart which confirms friendship; indeed, I never saw a person so universally popular; his very faults seemed to recommend him; he was wild, extravagant, thoughtless, and fearlessly adventurous﻿—defects of character which, among the peasantry of Ireland, are honoured as virtues. The combination of these qualities, and the position which O’Connor occupied as representative of an ancient Irish Catholic family﻿—a peculiarly interesting one to me, one of the old faith﻿—endeared him to me so much that I have never felt the pangs of parting more keenly than when it became necessary, for the finishing of his education, that he should go abroad.

===Chinese===
他自幼失怙，便是这一家族的继承人与代表。母亲对他的疼爱，因再无别的对象来分走这份情而格外炽烈——实在说来——她对他的那份爱，我在别处从未见过。她的爱，比寻常母亲的爱所投更为得其所哉，因为小奥康纳虽也不无少年人的一些毛病，却确乎具备青春最讨人欢喜的诸多品性。他有着那种令人一见倾心的坦率与活泼，也有着足以坐实友谊的那副慷慨心肠；我从未见过哪个人能如此广得人心；连他的种种短处，仿佛都成了讨人喜欢的由头——他狂放、挥霍、少心机、又胆大妄为——这些性情上的毛病，在爱尔兰乡民之间，倒被当作美德来看待。这些品性凑在一起，加之奥康纳作为一支古老的爱尔兰天主教世家之代表所处的地位——对我这个旧教徒而言，这是一个格外令人系念的身份——使他对我而言可亲可宝之至；后来为了完成学业他不得不远赴海外，我与他分别时所感到的那阵锥心之痛，此生再没有更甚的。

===Original===
Three years had passed away before I saw him again. During the interval, however, I had frequently heard from him, so that absence had not abated the warmth of our attachment. Who could tell of the rejoicings that marked the evening of his return? The horses were removed from the chaise at the distance of a mile from the castle, while it and its contents were borne rapidly onward almost by the pressure of the multitude, like a log upon a torrent. Bonfires blared far and near﻿—bagpipes roared and fiddles squeaked; and, amid the thundering shouts of thousands, the carriage drew up before the castle.

In an instant young O’Connor was upon the ground, crying, “Thank you, boys﻿—thank you, boys;” while a thousand hands were stretched out from all sides to grasp even a finger of his. Still, amid shouts of “God bless your honour﻿—long may you reign!” and “Make room there, boys! clear the road for the masther!” he reached the threshold of the castle, where stood his mother weeping for joy.

Oh! who could describe that embrace, or the enthusiasm with which it was witnessed? “God bless him to you, my lady﻿—glory to ye both!” and “Oh, but he is a fine young gentleman, God bless him!” resounded on all sides, while hats flew up in volleys that darkened the moon; and when at length, amid the broad delighted grins of the thronging domestics, whose sense of decorum precluded any more boisterous evidence of joy, they reached the parlour, then giving way to the fullness of her joy the widowed mother kissed and blessed him and wept in turn. Well might any parent be proud to claim as son the handsome stripling who now represented the Castle Connor family; but to her his beauty had a peculiar charm, for it bore a striking resemblance to that of her husband, the last O’Connor.

===Chinese===
三年过去了，我才又见着他。这期间我屡屡收到他的来信，是以别离并未消减我们情谊的温度。他归来的那个傍晚，那番欢腾的景象，谁能描摹得尽呢？马车离城堡还有一英里，套车的马便被卸了下来，连车带人几乎是被人群的挤拥裹挟着疾驰向前，活像洪流之上漂浮的一段木头。远近四方，篝火熊熊——风笛轰鸣，提琴尖啸；在千人雷动般的欢呼里，马车停在了城堡前。

转眼之间，小奥康纳便已跳到地上，喊着："多谢各位，伙计们——多谢各位，伙计们；"四面八方伸过来上千只手，只为能摸到他一根手指头。他在阵阵呼喊里向前——"上帝保佑老爷——愿您长长久久地当家做主！"还有"让开些，伙计们！给少爷清出条路来！"——他就这样走到了城堡的门槛前，他母亲正站在那里，喜极而泣。

啊！那一个拥抱，还有众人目睹此情此景时所迸发的热忱，谁能写得出来呢？"上帝保佑他平安归来，夫人——恭喜您二位！"还有"哎呀，他可真是个俊俏的少爷啊，上帝保佑他！"四下里响成一片；帽子一排接一排地抛上半空，把月亮都遮暗了；待到他们终于在那一群簇拥而来的仆人宽宽的喜笑颜中——仆人们碍于体统，不敢再有更放肆的欢喜表示——走进客厅，那位孀居的母亲这才任由满腔的欢喜尽情倾泻，又吻他、又祝福他、又落泪，三者轮替不息。任何一个做父母的，若能认眼前这个英俊少年为子，都该引以为傲——他如今便是康纳城堡这一家族的代表；然而于她而言，他的俊美别有一番动人之处，因为他那张脸，与她丈夫——已故的末代奥康纳——极其相像。

===Original===
I know not whether partiality blinded me, or that I did no more than justice to my friend in believing that I had never seen so handsome a young man. I am inclined to think the latter. He was rather tall, very slightly and elegantly made; his face was oval, and his features decidedly Spanish in cast and complexion, but with far more vivacity of expression than generally belongs to the beauty of that nation. The extreme delicacy of his features and the varied animation of his countenance made him appear even younger than his years﻿—an illusion which the total absence of everything studied in his manners seemed to confirm. Time had wrought no small change in me, alike in mind and spirits; but in the case of O’Connor it seemed to have lost its power to alter. His gaiety was undamped, his generosity unchilled; and though the space which had intervened between our parting and reunion was but brief, yet at the period of life at which we were, even a shorter interval than that of three years has frequently served to form or *de*form a character.

===Chinese===
究竟是我偏心蔽了明见，还是我对我这位朋友并未溢美——我当真从未见过如此俊美的青年——我至今分辨不清。我倒是倾向于后者。他身量略高，体态轻盈而优雅；一张脸是椭圆形的，五官与肤色明显带着西班牙人的轮廓，然而神情之活泼，又远胜那个民族通常所有的美。他五官的精致和脸上变幻无穷的生气，使他看上去比实际年纪还要年轻——而他举手投足之间毫无半点矫揉造作，似乎又坐实了这一错觉。岁月在我身上所造成的变化不小，无论心境还是性情都为之改观；然而在奥康纳身上，岁月仿佛失去了改变他的力量。他的活泼未减，他的慷慨未冷；虽然我们分别与重逢之间相隔的时日本属短暂，但在我们当时所处的年岁，即便比三年更短的间隙，也往往足以塑造或者毁掉一个人的性情。

===Original===
Weeks had passed away since the return of O’Connor, and scarce a day had elapsed without my seeing him, when the neighbourhood was thrown into an unusual state of excitement by the announcement of a race-ball to be celebrated at the assembly-room of the town of T﻿—﻿—, distant scarcely two miles from Castle Connor.

Young O’Connor, as I had expected, determined at once to attend it; and having directed in vain all the powers of his rhetoric to persuade his mother to accompany him, he turned the whole battery of his logic upon me, who, at that time, felt a reluctance stronger than that of mere apathy to mixing in any of these scenes of noisy pleasure for which for many reasons I felt myself unfitted. He was so urgent and persevering, however, that I could not refuse; and I found myself reluctantly obliged to make up my mind to attend him upon the important night to the spacious but ill-finished building, which the fashion and beauty of the county were pleased to term an assembly-room.

===Chinese===
奥康纳归来后又过了几个礼拜，这期间几乎没有哪一天我不与他相见；忽然，四邻之间陷入了一阵异乎寻常的骚动——据说在 T——镇（那镇子离康纳城堡不足两英里）的集会厅里，将举办一场赛马舞会。

不出我所料，小奥康纳当即决定赴会；他先是费尽唇舌，想劝他母亲同去，劝之无果，便把整套辩才的炮火都对准了我——而我彼时对卷入任何这类喧闹作乐的场合，都怀着一种比单纯的冷淡更为强烈的抗拒，因为种种缘故，我觉得自己于此颇不相宜。无奈他百般相劝、死缠不休，我无法推却；只得勉强打定主意，在那个要紧的夜晚陪他同赴那座宽敞却粗糙的所在——郡中的时髦人物与佳丽们乐于称之为"集会厅"的那座建筑。

===Original===
When we entered the apartment, we found a select few, surrounded by a crowd of spectators, busily performing a minuet, with all the congees and flourishes which belonged to that courtly dance; and my companion, infected by the contagion of example, was soon, as I had anticipated, waving his chapeau bras, and gracefully bowing before one of the prettiest girls in the room. I had neither skill nor spirits to qualify me to follow his example; and as the fullness of the room rendered it easy to do so without its appearing singular, I determined to be merely a spectator of the scene which surrounded me, without taking an active part in its amusements.

The room was indeed very much crowded, so that its various groups, formed as design or accident had thrown the parties together, afforded no small fund of entertainment to the contemplative observer. There were the dancers, all gaiety and good-humour; a little further off were the tables at which sat the cardplayers, some plying their vocation with deep and silent anxiety﻿—for in those days gaming often ran very high in such places﻿—and others disputing with all the vociferous pertinacity of undisguised ill-temper. There, again, were the sallow, blue-nosed, grey-eyed dealers in whispered scandal; and, in short, there is scarcely a group or combination to be met with in the court of kings which might not have found a humble parallel in the assembly-room of T﻿—﻿—.

===Chinese===
我们走进大厅时，只见寥寥几位人物，在一群围观者簇拥之下，正卖力地跳着一支小步舞，带着那种宫廷舞所应有的一应屈膝礼与花哨动作；我这位同伴，受了众人作乐的感染，果然不出我所料，不多时便扬起他那顶两角帽，在一屋子最标致的姑娘之一面前风度翩翩地躬身施礼。我既无技艺、也无兴致去学他的样；恰好大厅里人头攒动，置身事外并不显眼，我便索性打定主意，只作一个冷眼旁观的人，看着眼前这一幕，并不亲身参与其中的种种消遣。

大厅里当真是拥挤不堪，各色人等或因刻意结伴、或因偶然凑合，分作一团一簇，给那好沉思的旁观者提供了不少可供玩味的材料。那里有跳舞的人，一个个欢天喜地、和颜悦色；稍远一点是牌桌，牌客们围坐其旁，有的屏息凝神、一声不响地埋头于他们的营生——在那个年月，这种地方的赌博往往下注极重——有的则在争得面红耳赤，毫不掩饰其暴躁的脾气。再那边，是几个面色蜡黄、鼻子发青、灰眼珠的货色，凑在一起低声搬弄着耳语般的丑闻；简而言之，王公朝廷里所能见到的几乎任何一种人物或组合，在这 T——镇的集会厅里，都不难找到一个寒微的对影。

===Original===
I was allowed to indulge in undisturbed contemplation, for I suppose I was not known to more than five or six in the room. I thus had leisure not only to observe the different classes into which the company had divided itself, but to amuse myself by speculating as to the rank and character of many of the individual actors in the drama.

Among many who have long since passed from my memory, one person for some time engaged my attention, and that person, for many reasons, I shall not soon forget. He was a tall, square-shouldered man, who stood in a careless attitude, leaning with his back to the wall; he seemed to have secluded himself from the busy multitudes which moved noisily and gaily around him, and nobody seemed to observe or to converse with him. He was fashionably dressed, but perhaps rather extravagantly; his face was full and heavy, expressive of sullenness and stupidity, and marked with the lines of strong vulgarity; his age might be somewhere between forty and fifty. Such as I have endeavoured to describe him, he remained motionless, his arms doggedly folded across his broad chest, and turning his sullen eyes from corner to corner of the room, as if eager to detect some object on which to vent his ill-humour.

===Chinese===
众人容我静静地出神，无人搅扰——我估摸满屋子认识我的人也不过五六个。于是我不独有余暇观察场中宾客自然分成的各个群落，还可借着揣度这出戏里不少个中人物的身份与性情，聊以自娱。

在许多早已从我记忆中淡去的人影里，有一个曾有一阵子引住了我的目光；而这个人，出于种种缘故，我久久不能忘怀。他是个高个子、宽肩膀的男人，懒懒地靠着墙站着，一副漫不经心的姿态；他仿佛刻意把自己从身边那些喧闹快活、往来穿梭的人群里隔绝出来，也没人留意他、或与他搭话。他衣着时髦，也许还过于奢华了些；他那张脸肉厚而沉重，一副阴沉、愚钝的神情，刻着粗鄙之徒特有的那些深刻纹路；年纪大约在四十到五十之间。他便如我所努力描绘的这般，一动不动地立着，两条胳膊执拗地交叠在宽阔的胸前，一双阴鸷的眼睛从大厅的这一角扫到那一角，仿佛急于找出一个可以发泄他满腔戾气的对象。

===Original===
It is strange, and yet it is true, that one sometimes finds even in the most commonplace countenance an undefinable something, which fascinates the attention, and forces it to recur again and again, while it is impossible to tell whether the peculiarity which thus attracts us lies in feature or in expression, or in both combined, and why it is that our observation should be engrossed by an object which, when analysed, seems to possess no claim to interest or even to notice. This unaccountable feeling I have often experienced, and I believe I am not singular, but never in so remarkable a degree as upon this occasion. My friend O’Connor, having disposed of his fair partner, was crossing the room for the purpose of joining me, in doing which I was surprised to see him exchange a familiar, almost a cordial, greeting with the object of my curiosity. I say I was surprised, for independent of his very questionable appearance, it struck me as strange that though so constantly associated with O’Connor, and, as I thought, personally acquainted with all his intimates, I had never before even seen this individual. I did not fail immediately to ask him who this gentleman was. I thought he seemed slightly embarrassed, but after a moment’s pause he laughingly said that his friend over the way was too mysterious a personage to have his name announced in so giddy a scene as the present; but that on the morrow he would furnish me with all the information which I could desire. There was, I thought, in his affected jocularity a real awkwardness which appeared to me unaccountable, and consequently increased my curiosity; its gratification, however, I was obliged to defer. At length, wearied with witnessing amusements in which I could not sympathise, I left the room, and did not see O’Connor until late in the next day.

===Chinese===
说来也怪，却又确有其事：一个人有时竟会在最平庸不过的一张脸上，发现某种难以言说的东西，它攫住你的注意，逼着你一遍又一遍地回过头去，而你又说不出这种吸引我们的特质究竟在五官、在神情，还是二者兼而有之，也说不清为什么我们的目光竟会被一个一经分析便毫无可取、甚至不值一顾的对象所独占。这种无可名状的感觉我时常有所体会，我相信有此感的并非我一人；然而从来没有哪一次，像这次这般强烈。我的朋友奥康纳与他那位漂亮舞伴周旋已毕，正穿过大厅朝我走来——令我诧异的是，他在走过那个引我注目的人身边时，竟与他交换了一个熟稔的、近乎热络的招呼。我之所以诧异，是因为撇开那人极可质疑的外表不谈，我觉得奇怪：我既与奥康纳朝夕相伴，又自以为结识他所有的密友，这个人我却连见也不曾见过。我立刻不失时机地问他，这位绅士是谁。我看他似乎微微有些窘，然而沉吟片刻，便笑着答道：他那位对面的朋友，是个太神秘的人物，不宜在眼下这般轻浮的场合通报姓名；明日他定会把我想知道的一切和盘托出。我总觉得，他那故作的诙谐之下，藏着一层实实在在的局促——这局促在我看来全无来由，反倒更勾起了我的好奇；然而这份好奇的满足，却不得不暂且搁下。到后来，我对眼前这场自己全然不能共鸣的作乐看得厌了，便离了大厅，直到第二天日头偏西，才又见着奥康纳。

===Original===
I had ridden down towards the castle for the purpose of visiting the O’Connors, and had nearly reached the avenue leading to the mansion, when I met my friend. He was also mounted; and having answered my inquiries respecting his mother, he easily persuaded me to accompany him in his ramble. We had chatted as usual for some time, when, after a pause, O’Connor said:

“By the way, Purcell, you expressed some curiosity respecting the tall, handsome fellow to whom I spoke last night.”

“I certainly did question you about a *tall* gentleman, but was not aware of his claims to beauty,” replied I.

“Well, that is as it may be,” said he; “the ladies think him handsome, and their opinion upon that score is more valuable than yours or mine. Do you know,” he continued, “I sometimes feel half sorry that I ever made the fellow’s acquaintance: he is quite a marked man here, and they tell stories of him that are anything but reputable, though I am sure without foundation. I think I know enough about him to warrant me in saying so.”

“May I ask his name?” inquired I.

“Oh! did not I tell you his name?” rejoined he. “You should have heard that first; he and his name are equally well known. You will recognise the individual at once when I tell you that his name is﻿—Fitzgerald.”

“Fitzgerald!” I repeated. “Fitzgerald!﻿—can it be Fitzgerald the duellist?”

===Chinese===
我骑马朝城堡那边去，为的是拜访奥康纳一家，快到通往宅邸的那条林荫道时，正好遇见了我这位朋友。他也骑着马；他答过我对他母亲安好的问候，便轻而易举地说动我陪他一同闲逛。我们照旧谈了一阵，忽然，奥康纳顿了一顿，说道：

"对了，珀塞尔，昨晚你对我与之搭话的那个高个子、还算英俊的家伙，颇有些好奇。"

"我确曾问过你一位'高个子'绅士的事，却不知他竟称得上英俊，"我答道。

"也好，这也见仁见智，"他说；"姑娘家倒觉得他生得俊，论这一点，她们的见解可比你我值钱得多。你可知道，"他接着说，"我有时竟颇悔当初结识了这家伙：他在这一带可算是个挂了号的人物，人们讲的那些关于他的事，没有一桩是体面的——虽然我确信都属无稽之谈。关于他，我想我知道得够多了，足以下此断语。"

"敢问他尊姓大名？"我问。

"噢！我没把他的名字告诉你吗？"他应道，"这本该先说的；他这个人，和他的名字一样，尽人皆知。我一说出他的名字，你立刻便能认出此人——他姓菲茨杰拉德（Fitzgerald）。"

"菲茨杰拉德！"我重复了一遍，"菲茨杰拉德！——莫不是那个决斗家菲茨杰拉德？"

===Original===
“Upon my word you have hit it,” replied he, laughing; “but you have accompanied the discovery with a look of horror more tragic than appropriate. He is not the monster you take him for﻿—he has a good deal of old Irish pride; his temper is hasty, and he has been unfortunately thrown in the way of men who have not made allowance for these things. I am convinced that in every case in which Fitzgerald has fought, if the truth could be discovered, he would be found to have acted throughout upon the defensive. No man is mad enough to risk his own life, except when the doing so is an alternative to submitting tamely to what he considers an insult. I am certain that no man ever engaged in a duel under the consciousness that he had acted an intentionally aggressive part.”

“When did you make his acquaintance?” said I.

“About two years ago,” he replied. “I met him in France, and you know when one is abroad it is an ungracious task to reject the advances of one’s countryman, otherwise I think I should have avoided his society﻿—less upon my own account than because I am sure the acquaintance would be a source of continual though groundless uneasiness to my mother. I know, therefore, that you will not unnecessarily mention its existence to her.”

I gave him the desired assurance, and added:

“May I ask you. O’Connor, if, indeed, it be a fair question, whether this Fitzgerald at any time attempted to engage you in anything like gaming?”

===Chinese===
"果真一语中的，"他笑着答道，"不过你这一发现，还配了一副过于悲壮、不合时宜的神情。他并非你所想的那等怪物——他身上颇有几分爱尔兰旧家的傲气；脾气急些，又不幸总与一些不肯体谅这些的人周旋在一起。我深信，菲茨杰拉德所卷入的每一桩决斗，倘若真相可查，他都必定是自始至终出于守势。一个人除非面临两难——要么冒死一搏，要么默默咽下他所认为的侮辱——否则没有人会疯到去拿自己的性命做赌注。我敢断言，决没有哪个人，是在明知自己有意挑衅的前提下，还去与人决斗的。"

"你何时与他结识的？"我问。

"约莫两年前，"他答，"我是在法国与他相识的。你也知道，一个人身在异国，要回绝一位同胞的示好，未免不近人情；若非如此，我想我本会回避他的往来——倒不全是为我自己着想，而更多地是因为，我深知这段交情会成为我母亲持续不断、却又全无来由的不安之源。所以我知道，你不会在她面前多嘴提及此事的。"

我依他所请作了保证，又问：

"我可不可以问你，奥康纳——倘若这问得不算冒犯的话——那位菲茨杰拉德，可曾有过什么企图，拉你卷入诸如赌博一类的事？"

===Original===
This question was suggested by my having frequently heard Fitzgerald mentioned as a noted gambler, and sometimes even as a blackleg. O’Connor seemed, I thought, slightly embarrassed. He answered:

“No, no﻿—I cannot say that he ever attempted anything of the kind. I certainly have played with him, but never lost to any serious amount; nor can I recollect that he ever solicited me﻿—indeed he knows that I have a strong objection to deep play. *You* must be aware that my finances could not bear much pruning down. I never lost more to him at a sitting than about five pounds, which you know is nothing. No, you wrong him if you imagine that he attached himself to me merely for the sake of such contemptible winnings as those which a broken-down Irish gentleman could afford him. Come, Purcell, you are too hard upon him﻿—you judge only by report; you must see him, and decide for yourself.﻿—Suppose we call upon him now; he is at the inn, in the High Street, not a mile off.”

I declined the proposal drily.

“Your caution is too easily alarmed,” said he. “I do not wish you to make this man your bosom friend: I merely desire that you should see and speak to him, and if you form any acquaintance with him, it must be of that slight nature which can be dropped or continued at pleasure.”

===Chinese===
我之所以有此一问，是因为我屡屡听人提起菲茨杰拉德，说他是出名的赌棍，有时甚至被称作赌局骗子。我看奥康纳似乎微微有些窘。他答道：

"没有，没有——我不能说他有过任何这类的企图。我确曾与他同赌过，却从未输到值得一说的数目；我也想不起他何时主动邀过我——他其实是知道我对重注豪赌深恶痛绝的。你总该明白，我那点家底，经不起多少削剃。我每回与他同坐一局，最多不过输上五镑上下，你知道这算不了什么。不，你若以为他之所以与我交结，只为图谋一个穷途末路的爱尔兰绅士所能奉上的那点寒酸进项，那你便是冤枉了他。得了，珀塞尔，你对他未免太苛刻了——你不过是凭传闻下判断；你总该见见他，再自己定夺。——不如我们现在就去拜望他；他就在高街那家客栈里，不足一英里远。"

我冷冷地回绝了这一提议。

"你这未免过于草木皆兵了，"他说，"我并非要你与此人结为至交：我不过想让你见见他、与他说几句话；纵使你与他结下什么交情，那也不过是浅尝辄止的那一种，想断便断，想续便续。"

===Original===
From the time that O’Connor had announced the fact that his friend was no other than the notorious Fitzgerald, a foreboding of something calamitous had come upon me, and it now occurred to me that if any unpleasantness were to be feared as likely to result to O’Connor from their connection, I might find my attempts to extricate him much facilitated by my being acquainted, however slightly, with Fitzgerald. I know not whether the idea was reasonable﻿—it was certainly natural; and I told O’Connor that upon second thoughts I would ride down with him to the town, and wait upon Mr. Fitzgerald.

We found him at home; and chatted with him for a considerable time. To my surprise his manners were perfectly those of a gentleman, and his conversation, if not peculiarly engaging, was certainly amusing. The politeness of his demeanour, and the easy fluency with which he told his stories and his anecdotes, many of them curious, and all more or less entertaining, accounted to my mind at once for the facility with which he had improved his acquaintance with O’Connor; and when he pressed upon us an invitation to sup with him that night, I had almost joined O’Connor in accepting it. I determined, however, against doing so, for I had no wish to be on terms of familiarity with Mr. Fitzgerald; and I knew that one evening spent together as he proposed would go further towards establishing an intimacy between us than fifty morning visits could do. When I arose to depart, it was with feelings almost favourable to Fitzgerald; indeed I was more than half ashamed to acknowledge to my companion how complete a revolution in my opinion respecting his friend half an hour’s conversation with him had wrought. His appearance certainly *was* against him; but then, under the influence of his manner, one lost sight of much of its ungainliness, and of nearly all its vulgarity; and, on the whole, I felt convinced that report had done him grievous wrong, inasmuch as anybody, by an observance of the common courtesies of society, might easily avoid coming into personal collision with a gentleman so studiously polite as Fitzgerald. At parting, O’Connor requested me to call upon him the next day, as he intended to make trial of the merits of a pair of greyhounds, which he had thoughts of purchasing; adding, that if he could escape in anything like tolerable time from Fitzgerald’s supper-party, he would take the field soon after ten on the next morning. At the appointed hour, or perhaps a little later, I dismounted at Castle Connor; and, on entering the hall, I observed a gentleman issuing from O’Connor’s private room. I recognised him, as he approached, as a Mr. McDonough, and, being but slightly acquainted with him, was about to pass him with a bow, when he stopped me. There was something in his manner which struck me as odd; he seemed a good deal flurried if not agitated, and said, in a hurried tone:

“This is a very foolish business, Mr. Purcell. You have some influence with my friend O’Connor; I hope you can induce him to adopt some more moderate line of conduct than that he has decided upon. If you will allow me, I will return for a moment with you, and talk over the matter again with O’Connor.”

===Chinese===
自奥康纳道破他的朋友不是别人，正是那个声名狼藉的菲茨杰拉德之时起，一种大祸将临的预感便压上了我的心头；此刻我又暗想，若说这段交情会给奥康纳招来什么不堪的麻烦，那么我与菲茨杰拉德纵使只是泛泛之交，也或许能使我搭救朋友的努力更为顺手。这念头是否合乎情理，我不得而知——它确乎是人之常情；于是我告诉奥康纳，再三思之下，我愿与他一同骑马进城，去拜望菲茨杰拉德先生。

我们见他正在客栈里，便与他闲谈了颇有一阵。出乎我意料，他的举止完全是绅士派头，谈吐虽不见得怎样迷人，却着实有趣。他举止之有礼，讲故事、说掌故之时那份从容流利——那些掌故有不少颇为新奇，无一不多少带些趣味——在我心中顿时说明了他何以能那样轻易地与奥康纳熟络起来；当他殷勤留我们当晚与他共进夜宵时，我几乎已随奥康纳一同应允。然而我终于打定主意不去——我并不愿与菲茨杰拉德先生有什么熟稔的往来；我深知，按他所提议的那样同过一晚，其足以在我等之间催生亲近，胜过五十回晨间拜访。待我起身告辞时，对菲茨杰拉德的心情已近乎有好感；说实在的，我颇为不好意思向我这位同伴承认，与他那位朋友区区半个钟头的交谈，已使我观感为之大变。他的外表确实与他不利；然而在他的风度笼罩之下，人便会忽略其大半的笨拙，几乎全部的粗鄙；总而言之，我深信传闻委实冤屈了他，因为任何人，只要稍稍恪守社交的寻常礼数，便不难避免与一位如此处处讲礼的绅士发生正面冲突。临别之际，奥康纳请我次日去访他，因为他要试一对灵缇犬的脚力，有意买下；他又说，若能从菲茨杰拉德那场夜宴里抽身不太晚的话，次日上午十点过后他便要带着猎犬下田。到了约定时辰，也许略晚一些，我在康纳城堡前下了马；一进大厅，便见一位绅士从奥康纳的私室里走出来。他走近时，我认出那是麦克多诺先生（Mr. McDonough），我与他不过泛泛之交，正欲颔首而过，他却叫住了我。他神色之中有几分异样，颇为惹眼；他似乎颇有些慌乱，若非激动的话，匆匆说道：

"这可真是一桩极荒唐的事，珀塞尔先生。你对我朋友奥康纳还有几分影响力；但愿你能劝他改采一条比我朋友所选更为持重的路。若蒙允许，我与你一道回去片刻，与奥康纳再把这事好生商量一番。"

===Original===
As McDonough uttered these words, I felt that sudden sinking of the heart which accompanies the immediate anticipation of something dreaded and dreadful. I was instantly convinced that O’Connor had quarrelled with Fitzgerald, and I knew that if such were the case, nothing short of a miracle could extricate him from the consequences. I signed to McDonough to lead the way, and we entered the little study together. O’Connor was standing with his back to the fire; on the table lay the breakfast-things in the disorder in which a hurried meal had left them; and on another smaller table, placed near the hearth, lay pen, ink, and paper. As soon as O’Connor saw me, he came forward and shook me cordially by the hand.

“My dear Purcell,” said he, “you are the very man I wanted. I have got into an ugly scrape, and I trust to my friends to get me out of it.”

“You have not had a dispute with that man﻿—that Fitzgerald, I hope,” said I, giving utterance to the conjecture whose truth I most dreaded.

“Faith, I cannot say exactly what passed between us,” said he, “inasmuch as I was at the time nearly half seas over; but of this much I am certain, that we exchanged angry words last night. I lost my temper most confoundedly; but, as well as I can recollect, he appeared perfectly cool and collected. What he said was, therefore, deliberately said, and on that account must be resented.”

“My dear O’Connor, are you mad?” I exclaimed. “Why will you seek to drive to a deadly issue a few hasty words, uttered under the influence of wine, and forgotten almost as soon as uttered? A quarrel with Fitzgerald it is twenty chances to one would terminate fatally to you.”

===Chinese===
麦克多诺说出这番话时，我心中猛地一沉——那种骤然下沉之感，正是人对所畏惧、所恐惧之事行将到来时的预感。我立刻断定，奥康纳已与菲茨杰拉德起了冲突；而我深知，倘若如此，除非有奇迹，再无他法能把他从其后果里救拔出来。我示意麦克多诺先行，我们一同走进了那间小小的书房。奥康纳正背对着炉火站着；桌上摆着早餐用具，因匆匆用过而凌乱不堪；炉边另一张小些的桌上，则摆着笔、墨、纸。奥康纳一见我，便上前来，热络地与我握手。

"我亲爱的珀塞尔，"他说，"你正是我此刻最想见的人。我惹上了一桩极麻烦的事，全靠朋友们帮我脱身了。"

"你莫不是与那个人——那个菲茨杰拉德——起了争执吧，但愿不是，"我说，道出了那个我最惧其为真的揣测。

"哎，说真的，我俩之间究竟说了些什么，我也说不大准，"他说，"因为那会儿我已差不多半醉了；但有一点我是确定的：昨夜我们交换了几句恶言。我的火气发得实在厉害；不过凭我所能记得的，他倒是自始至终十分冷静沉着。可见他所说的话，都是经深思熟虑才说的，单凭这一点，就不能不跟他计较。"

"我亲爱的奥康纳，你疯了不成？"我失声叫道，"几句酒后的冲口之言，说过便几近忘却，你何苦非要把这事逼到生死相搏的地步不可？与菲茨杰拉德结怨，二十条命里怕也未必能保得住一条。"

===Original===
“It is exactly because Fitzgerald *is* such an accomplished shot,” said he, “that I become liable to the most injurious and intolerable suspicions if I submit to anything from him which could be construed into an affront; and for that reason Fitzgerald is the very last man to whom I would concede an inch in a case of honour.”

“I do not require you to make any, the slightest sacrifice of what you term your honour,” I replied; “but if you have actually written a challenge to Fitzgerald, as I suspect you have done, I conjure you to reconsider the matter before you despatch it. From all that I have heard you say, Fitzgerald has more to complain of in the altercation which has taken place than you. You owe it to your only surviving parent not to thrust yourself thus wantonly upon﻿—I will say it, the most appalling danger. Nobody, my dear O’Connor, can have a doubt of your courage; and if at any time, which God forbid, you shall be called upon thus to risk your life, you should have it in your power to enter the field under the consciousness that you have acted throughout temperately and like a man, and not, as I fear you now would do, having rashly and most causelessly endangered your own life and that of your friend.”

“I believe, Purcell, your are right,” said he. “I believe I *have* viewed the matter in too decided a light; my note, I think, scarcely allows him an honourable alternative, and that is certainly going a step too far﻿—further than I intended. Mr. McDonough, I’ll thank you to hand me the note.”

He broke the seal, and, casting his eye hastily over it, he continued:

“It is, indeed, a monument of folly. I am very glad, Purcell, you happened to come in, otherwise it would have reached its destination by this time.”

He threw it into the fire; and, after a moment’s pause, resumed:

“You must not mistake me, however. I am perfectly satisfied as to the propriety, nay, the necessity, of communicating with Fitzgerald. The difficulty is in what tone I should address him. I cannot say that the man directly affronted me﻿—I cannot recollect any one expression which I could lay hold upon as offensive﻿—but his language was ambiguous, and admitted frequently of the most insulting construction, and his manner throughout was insupportably domineering. I know it impressed me with the idea that he presumed upon his reputation as a ‘dead shot,’ and that would be utterly unendurable.”

===Chinese===
"正因为菲茨杰拉德是这样一位神枪手，"他说，"所以倘若我对他有任何可以被视为冒犯的举动却默默忍受，那各种最恶毒、最难堪的猜疑便会加到我头上；正因如此，在有关荣誉的事上，我最后一个肯让步的，便是菲茨杰拉德。"

"我并非要你对你所谓的荣誉作出丝毫的牺牲，"我答道，"可是你若果真如我所疑，已向菲茨杰拉德写下了战书，那么我恳求你，在送出之前务必三思。据我所听你说的那些话来看，在那场口角里，该抱怨的，与其说是你，不如说是菲茨杰拉德。你上有孀母在堂，唯一的至亲，你便不该这样无谓地把自己推到——我便直说了吧——最骇人的险境里去。我亲爱的奥康纳，谁也不会怀疑你的勇气；万一有朝一日——但愿上帝不容——你当真不得不如此以身犯险，你也该能坦然走上决斗场，自知自始至终行事持重、不失君子之风，而不是像我所担心你现在这样——鲁莽而又毫无来由地，把自己的性命与朋友的性命，一同置于险地。"

"我相信，珀塞尔，你说得对，"他说，"我想我确是把这事看得过于决绝了；我的便笺，怕是没有给他留下什么体面的退路，这一步确实走得太远——超出了我的本意。麦克多诺先生，劳烦你把那便笺递给我。"

他拆开封口，匆匆扫了一眼，又道：

"这实在是一座愚行的纪念碑。珀塞尔，我很庆幸你恰好走了进来，不然的话，这封信此刻怕已送到他手里了。"

他把信扔进了火里；顿了一顿，又道：

"但你不可误会我。至于与菲茨杰拉德通消息的得当——甚至必要——我毫无异言。难只难在我该用什么口吻去写信给他。我不能说他直接冒犯了我——我记不起有哪一句话我可以抓作把柄、指为侮辱——但他的言辞含糊，往往可以作最侮辱人的解读；他自始至终的态度，更是盛气凌人，叫人难以忍受。我知道，他给我的印象是：他仗着自己'指哪打哪'的名头而有恃无恐，这便是万难容忍的了。"

===Original===
“I would now recommend, as I have already done,” said McDonough, “that if you write to Fitzgerald, it should be in such a strain as to leave him at perfect liberty, without a compromise of honour, in a friendly way, to satisfy your doubts as to his conduct.”

I seconded the proposal warmly, and O’Connor, in a few minutes, finished a note, which he desired us to read. It was to this effect:

> “O’Connor, of Castle Connor, feeling that some expressions employed by Mr. Fitzgerald upon last night, admitted of a construction offensive to him, and injurious to his character, requests to know whether Mr. Fitzgerald intended to convey such a meaning.
> “Castle Connor, Thursday morning.”

This note was consigned to the care of Mr. McDonough, who forthwith departed to execute his mission. The sound of his horse’s hoofs, as he rode rapidly away, struck heavily at my heart; but I found some satisfaction in the reflection that McDonough appeared as averse from extreme measures as I was myself, for I well knew, with respect to the final result of the affair, that as much depended upon the tone adopted by the *second*, as upon the nature of the written communication.

===Chinese===
"那我便再进一言，与我先前所说的一样，"麦克多诺道，"你若写信给菲茨杰拉德，措辞便该留他在不损荣誉的前提下，完全可以友善地消除你对他的举动所生的疑虑。"

我热切地附议此议。不多时，奥康纳便写就一笺，请我们过目。大意如下：

> "昨夜菲茨杰拉德先生所用的若干言辞，康纳城堡之奥康纳深感其或可被解读为有损其人格及名誉的冒犯，故特此函询：菲茨杰拉德先生当时是否确有此意，尚祈见告。
> 康纳城堡，星期四晨。"

这封信交托给了麦克多诺先生，他随即动身前去办事。他策马疾驰而去，马蹄声声，重击在我的心上；但转念一想，麦克多诺看来与我自己一样不喜走极端，我便略觉宽慰——因为我深知，此事的最终结局，副手所取的口吻与书函本身的措辞，关系同等重大。

===Original===
I have seldom passed a more anxious hour than that which intervened between the departure and the return of that gentleman. Every instant I imagined I heard the tramp of a horse approaching, and every time that a door opened I fancied it was to give entrance to the eagerly expected courier. At length I did hear the hollow and rapid tread of a horse’s hoof upon the avenue. It approached﻿—it stopped﻿—a hurried step traversed the hall﻿—the room door opened, and McDonough entered.

“You have made great haste,” said O’Connor; “did you find him at home?”

“I did,” replied McDonough, “and made the greater haste as Fitzgerald did not let me know the contents of his reply.”

At the same time he handed a note to O’Connor, who instantly broke the seal. The words were as follow:

> “Mr. Fitzgerald regrets that anything which has fallen from him should have appeared to Mr. O’Connor to be intended to convey a reflection upon his honour (none such having been meant), and begs leave to disavow any wish to quarrel unnecessarily with Mr. O’Connor.
> “T﻿—﻿— Inn, Thursday morning.”

===Chinese===
那位先生离去与归来之间的那一个钟头，是我平生所度过的最为焦灼的一个钟头，少有例外。我每一刻都仿佛听见一匹马正向这边走近的蹄声；每一扇门开，我都以为是放那位翘首以盼的信使进来。终于，我真的听见了林荫道上一阵空洞而急促的马蹄声。它近了——停了——一阵匆忙的脚步穿过大厅——房门开了，麦克多诺走了进来。

"你可真够快的，"奥康纳说，"在家里撞见他了吗？"

"撞见了，"麦克多诺答道，"也正因菲茨杰拉德没有让我知晓他回函的内容，我才更加快了脚步。"

说着，他把一封信递给奥康纳，奥康纳即刻拆了封。信中写道：

> "菲茨杰拉德先生深以为憾：他所发表的任何言辞，竟在奥康纳先生看来似有影射其荣誉之嫌（此绝非本意）；并恳请声明，他绝无与奥康纳先生无端起衅之意。
> T——客栈，星期四晨。"

===Original===
I cannot describe how much I felt relieved on reading the above communication. I took O’Connor’s hand and pressed it warmly, but my emotions were deeper and stronger than I cared to show, for I was convinced that he had escaped a most imminent danger. Nobody whose notions upon the subject are derived from the duelling of modern times, in which matters are conducted without any very sanguinary determination upon either side, and with equal want of skill and coolness by both parties, can form a just estimate of the danger incurred by one who ventured to encounter a duellist of the old school. Perfect coolness in the field, and a steadiness and accuracy (which to the unpractised appeared almost miraculous) in the use of the pistol, formed the characteristics of this class; and in addition to this there generally existed a kind of professional pride, which prompted the duellist, in default of any more malignant feeling, from motives of mere vanity, to seek the life of his antagonist. Fitzgerald’s career had been a remarkably successful one, and I knew that out of thirteen duels which he had fought in Ireland, in nine cases he had *killed* his man. In those days one never heard of the parties leaving the field, as not unfrequently now occurs, without blood having been spilt; and the odds were, of course, in all cases tremendously against a young and unpractised man, when matched with an experienced antagonist. My impression respecting the magnitude of the danger which my friend had incurred was therefore by no means unwarranted.

===Chinese===
读了上面这封信，我心中的轻松实非言语所能形容。我握住奥康纳的手，紧紧地握；但我内心的情感，比我所愿表露的更深、更烈——因为我确信，他已躲过了一场迫在眉睫的大祸。今人的决斗观念得自近世，决斗双方皆无十分凶残的决心，又同样地既无技艺又无冷静，凭这种观念，谁也估量不出一个胆敢与旧学派的决斗家对阵之人，所冒的是何等大险。场上的绝对冷静，使枪时那份在生手看来近乎神技的稳健与精准，构成了这一流人物的标志；除此而外，他们通常还有一种近乎职业自尊的心理，驱使着决斗家在没有更恶毒念头的情形下，单凭虚荣之心，便要取对手的性命。菲茨杰拉德的生涯可谓战果赫赫，我知道他在爱尔兰所经历的十三场决斗里，有九场取了对手的性命。在那个年月，双方不曾流血便离场的事——这种情形如今倒并不少见——是闻所未闻的；一个年轻而毫无经验的生手，与一位久经沙场的对手相敌之时，胜算之微，自不待言。所以我对于我这位朋友所冒的危险之大，所作的判断，绝非过甚其词。

===Original===
I now questioned O’Connor more accurately respecting the circumstances of his quarrel with Fitzgerald. It arose from some dispute respecting the application of a rule of piquet, at which game they had been playing, each interpreting it favourably to himself, and O’Connor, having lost considerably, was in no mood to conduct an argument with temper﻿—an altercation ensued, and that of rather a pungent nature, and the result was that he left Fitzgerald’s room rather abruptly, determined to demand an explanation in the most peremptory tone. For this purpose he had sent for McDonough, and had commissioned him to deliver the note, which my arrival had fortunately intercepted.

As it was now past noon, O’Connor made me promise to remain with him to dinner; and we sat down a party of three, all in high spirits at the termination of our anxieties. It is necessary to mention, for the purpose of accounting for what follows, that Mrs. O’Connor, or, as she was more euphoniously styled, the lady of Castle Connor, was precluded by ill-health from taking her place at the dinner-table, and, indeed, seldom left her room before four o’clock.4 We were sitting after dinner sipping our claret, and talking, and laughing, and enjoying ourselves exceedingly, when a servant, stepping into the room, informed his master that a gentleman wanted to speak with him.
