“Yes, sir—the cedar chamber.”

“I know it—the very thing. No—no punch for me. By and by, perhaps.”

===Chinese===
"我全说'是'——从达代尔沼泽来的，黑得像沥青，烂得像坟坑，爬上你们叫做路的那道曲里拐弯的墙壁，在月光下白得像粉笔，穿过邓纳峡谷，黑得像煤矿井，再下坡到这里，到了'乔治与龙'——你们有旺旺的炉火、聪明的脑袋、上好的潘趣酒——这就来了——还有一具尸首搁在马车房里。尸首所在之处，鹰也必聚在那里。来吧，掌柜的，把花蜜舀出来。喝吧，先生们——喝吧，都喝。在吧台上再调一盆。瞧瞧这酒气，芬芳得何等神圣！诸位怕是喜欢的吧：它浑身上下散发着香料的味道，跟一具木乃伊似的。喝吧，朋友们。舀吧，掌柜的。喝吧，都来。斟上了。"

客人伸手在口袋里摸了摸，摸出三几尼来，塞进了特恩布尔那只肥厚的手掌里。

"这些酒钱喝光了再算。我是这店里的老主顾了。我来来去去，常打这儿过。特恩布尔，我跟你熟得很呢，只是你认不得我罢了。"

"您认得我，我却不认得您，先生，这可失敬了，"特恩布尔先生说道，一双眼睛直盯着那张阴沉险恶的面孔——他可以发誓，这张脸，或者任何与它相似的脸，他这辈子从未见过。不过那几尼的分量和成色倒叫人喜欢，他把它们丢进了口袋。"希望您在此住得舒坦。"

"你给我收拾了卧室没有？"

"收拾了，先生——雪松间。"

"我知道那间——正合适。不——潘趣酒我不喝。待会儿再说吧。"

===Original===
The talk went on, but the stranger had grown silent. He had seated himself on an oak bench by the fire, towards which he extended his feet and hands with seeming enjoyment; his cocked hat being, however, a little over his face.

Gradually the company began to thin. Sir Geoffrey Mardykes was the first to go; then some of the humbler townsfolk. The last bowl of punch was on its last legs. The stranger walked into the passage and said to the drawer:

“Fetch me a lantern. I must see my nag. Light it—hey! That will do. No—you need not come.”

The gaunt traveller took it from the man’s hand and strode along the passage to the door of the stable-yard, which he opened and passed out.

===Chinese===
谈话还在继续，但陌生人已经沉默下来。他在炉边一条橡木长凳上坐了，把手脚都伸向炉火，一副很受用的样子；只是那顶三角帽压得有点低，遮住了脸。

人渐渐散了。杰弗里·马迪克斯爵士头一个走的；接着是一些身份较低的镇民。最后一盆潘趣酒也快见底了。陌生人踱到过道里，对跑堂的说：

"给我拿一盏灯笼来。我得去看看我的马。点上——嗳！行了。不用——你不用跟来。"

那瘦长的旅人从他手里接过灯笼，大步穿过过道，推开马厩院的门，走了出去。

===Original===
Tom Scales, standing on the pavement, was looking through the stable window at the horses when the stranger plucked his shirtsleeve. With an inward shock the hostler found himself alone in presence of the very person he had been thinking of.

“I say—they tell me you have something to look at in there”—he pointed with his thumb at the old coach-house door. “Let us have a peep.”

Tom Scales happened to be at that moment in a state of mind highly favourable to anyone in search of a submissive instrument. He was in great perplexity, and even perturbation. He suffered the stranger to lead him to the coach-house gate.

“You must come in and hold the lantern,” said he. “I’ll pay you handsomely.”

The old hostler applied his key and removed the padlock.

“What are you afraid of? Step in and throw the light on his face,” said the stranger grimly. “Throw open the lantern: stand *there*. Stoop over him a little—he won’t bite you. Steady, or you may pass the night with him!”

===Chinese===
汤姆·斯凯尔斯正站在石板地上，隔着马厩的窗户朝里看马，忽然觉得衬衫袖子被人一扯。马夫心中一凛——他发现自己不知怎的，竟已和方才满脑子想的那个人面对面地单独站在了一处。

"我说——他们告诉我，那里头有样东西值得一看，"他用大拇指朝马车房的大门一指。"让我也瞧瞧。"

汤姆·斯凯尔斯此刻的心境，正有利于任何想找一个俯首帖耳的工具的人。他正惶惑不安，甚至惊慌失措。他任由那陌生人牵着自己，走到了马车房门前。

"你得进来替我擎着灯笼，"那人说。"我重重赏你。"

老马夫掏出钥匙，卸下了挂锁。

"你怕什么？进去，把光照在他脸上，"陌生人阴沉沉地说。"把灯笼打开：站*那儿*。俯下身去看看他——他不会咬你的。稳着点，不然你可就要陪他过夜了！"

---

===Original===
In the meantime the company at the George had dispersed; and, shortly after, Anthony Turnbull—who, like a good landlord, was always last in bed, and first up, in his house—was taking, alone, his last look round the kitchen before making his final visit to the stable-yard, when Tom Scales tottered into the kitchen, looking like death, his hair standing upright; and he sat down on an oak chair, all in a tremble, wiped his forehead with his hand, and, instead of speaking, heaved a great sigh or two.

It was not till after he had swallowed a dram of brandy that he found his voice, and said:

“We’ve the deaul himsel’ in t’ house! By Jen! ye’d best send fo t’ sir” (the clergyman). “Happen he’ll tak him in hand wi’ holy writ, and send him elsewhidder deftly. Lord atween us and harm! I’m a sinfu’ man. I tell ye, Mr. Turnbull, I dar’n’t stop in t’ George tonight under the same roof wi’ him.”

“Ye mean the ra-beyoned, black-feyaced lad, wi’ the brocken neb? Why, that’s a gentleman wi’ a pocket ful o’ guineas, man, and a horse worth fifty pounds!”

“That horse is no better nor his rider. The nags that were in the stable wi’ him, they all tuk the creepins, and sweated like rain down a thack. I tuk them all out o’ that, away from him, into the hack-stable, and I thocht I cud never get them past him. But that’s not all. When I was keekin inta t’ winda at the nags, he comes behint me and claps his claw on ma shouther, and he gars me gang wi’ him, and open the aad coach-house door, and haad the cannle for him, till he pearked into the deed man’t feyace; and, as God’s my judge, I sid the corpse open its eyes and wark its mouth, like a man smoorin’ and strivin’ to talk. I cudna move or say a word, though I felt my hair rising on my heed; but at lang-last I gev a yelloch, and say I, ‘La! what is that?’ And he himsel’ looked round on me, like the devil he is; and, wi’ a skirl o’ a laugh, he strikes the lantern out o’ my hand. When I cum to myself we were outside the coach-house door. The moon was shinin’ in, ad I cud see the corpse stretched on the table whar we left it; and he kicked the door to wi’ a purr o’ his foot. ‘Lock it,’ says he; and so I did. And here’s the key for ye—tak it yoursel’, sir. He offer’d me money: he said he’d mak me a rich man if I’d sell him the corpse, and help him awa’ wi’ it.”

===Chinese===
与此同时，"乔治与龙"里的客人已尽数散了；过了不多时，安东尼·特恩布尔——他做掌柜做得尽心，每晚总是最后一个就寝，每早总是头一个起身——独自在厨房里四下巡视了一番，正打算最后去马厩院看一眼，这时汤姆·斯凯尔斯跌跌撞撞地闯进了厨房，面无人色，头发根根倒竖；他一屁股坐在一张橡木椅上，浑身哆嗦，用手抹了抹额头，张了张嘴却说不出话来，只长长地叹了两三口粗气。

直灌下一口白兰地之后，他才找回了嗓子，说道：

"魔鬼他本人进了咱店里了！老天！你赶紧去请老爷子来（指牧师）。兴许他能拿经文治住他，把他打发到别处去。主啊，保佑我们免受灾祸！我是个罪人。特恩布尔先生，我告诉你，今夜我可不敢跟他待在一个屋檐底下。"

"你说那个黑脸的、塌鼻子的家伙？嗳，那可是位君子，口袋里装满了几尼，还有一匹值五十镑的马呢！"

"那匹马也好不到哪儿去，跟他那骑手一路货色。跟它同厩的那几匹马，全都起了鸡皮疙瘩，汗出得跟雨水顺着稻草往下淌似的。我把它们全牵了出来，躲开它，弄到散客马厩那边去了，我本以为这辈子都牵不过它跟前呢。可这还不算完。我正隔着窗子瞅那几匹马呢，他从背后走过来，把爪子搭在我肩膀上，逼着我跟他走，去开马车房的门，替他擎着蜡烛，让他细瞧那死人的脸；我拿上帝起誓，我亲眼看见那尸首睁开了眼睛，嘴巴一张一合的，像个人憋着气、拼命想说话似的。我动弹不得，也说不出一个字，只觉得头发一根根地在头顶上竖起来；可到末了我尖叫了一声，说：'老天！那是什么？'他自己回过头来看着我，那模样就像他本身就是魔鬼；接着他发出一声尖笑，一巴掌把我手里的灯笼打飞了。等我回过神来，我们已经站在马车房门外头了。月光照进来，我看得见那尸首直挺挺地躺在搁板上，跟咱们先前放的一样；他用脚后跟一磕，把门踢上了。'锁上，'他说；我就锁上了。钥匙在这儿——您自己拿去吧，先生。他拿钱给我来着：他说只要我把那尸首卖给他，帮他弄走，就让我发财。"

===Original===
“Hout, man! What cud he want o’ t’ corpse? He’s not doctor, to do a’ that lids. He was takin’ a rise out o’ ye, lad,” said Turnbull.

“Na, na—he wants the corpse. There’s summat you a’ me can’t tell he wants to do wi’ ’t; and he’d liefer get it wi’ sin and thievin’, and the damage of my soul. He’s one of them freytens a boo or a dobbies off Dardale Moss, that’s always astir wi’ the like after nightfall; unless—Lord save us!—he be the deaul himsel’.”

“Whar is he noo?” asked the landlord, who was growing uncomfortable.

“He spang’d up the back stair to his room. I wonder you didn’t hear him trampin’ like a wild horse; and he clapt his door that the house shook again—but Lord knows whar he is noo. Let us gang awa’s up to the Vicar’s, and gan *him* come down, and talk wi’ him.”

“Hoity toity, man—you’re too easy scared,” said the landlord, pale enough by this time. “’Twould be a fine thing, truly, to send abroad that the house was haunted by the deaul himsel’! Why, ’twould be the ruin o’ the George. You’re sure ye locked the door on the corpse?”

“Aye, sir—sartain.”

“Come wi’ me, Tom—we’ll gi’ a last look round the yard.”

===Chinese===
"得了吧，老兄！他要那尸首做什么？他又不是大夫，犯不着干那种勾当。他是在耍你呢，小子，"特恩布尔说。

"不，不——他要那尸首。这里头有桩咱们谁也说不清的事，他要用那尸首做什么；他宁可以罪孽和偷盗来弄到手，哪怕赔上我的灵魂。他是达代尔沼泽来的那种装神弄鬼的东西，天一黑就出来兴风作浪；除非——主啊救我们！——他就是魔鬼本人。"

"这会儿他在哪儿呢？"掌柜问道，渐渐也觉得不自在了。

"他从后楼梯蹦上了他的房间。你竟然没听见他咚咚咚地像匹野马似的踩？他把门一摔，整座屋子都晃了三晃——可这会儿他在哪儿，只有天晓得了。咱们一块儿上牧师家去，请*他*下来，跟他谈一谈。"

"得了得了，老兄——你也太不经吓了，"掌柜说道，这会儿脸色也白了。"把消息传出去，说这店里闹鬼、闹的是魔鬼本人——那可真是太好了！这岂不是要了'乔治与龙'的命？你确实把那门锁好了？"

"锁好了，先生——错不了。"

"跟我来，汤姆——咱们再到院子里走一圈，最后看一眼。"

===Original===
So, side by side, with many a jealous look right and left, and over their shoulders, they went in silence. On entering the old-fashioned quadrangle, surrounded by stables and other offices—built in the antique cagework fashion—they stopped for a while under the shadow of the inn gable, and looked round the yard, and listened. All was silent—nothing stirring.

The stable lantern was lighted; and with it in his hand Tony Turnbull, holding Tom Scales by the shoulder, advanced. He hauled Tom after him for a step or two; then stood still and shoved him before him for a step or two more; and thus cautiously—as a pair of skirmishers under fire—they approached the coach-house door.

“There, ye see—all safe,” whispered Tom, pointing to the lock, which hung—distinct in the moonlight—in its place. “Cum back, I say!”

“Cum on, say I!” retorted the landlord valorously. “It would never do to allow any tricks to be played with the chap in there”—he pointed to the coach-house door.

“The coroner here in the morning, and never a corpse to sit on!” He unlocked the padlock with these words, having handed the lantern to Tom. “Here, keck in, Tom,” he continued; “ye hev the lantern—and see if all’s as ye left it.”

“Not me—na, not for the George and a’ that’s in it!” said Tom, with a shudder, sternly, as he took a step backward.

“What the—what are ye afraid on? Gi’ me the lantern—it is all one: *I* will.”

And cautiously, little by little, he opened the door; and, holding the lantern over his head in the narrow slit, he peeped in—frowning and pale—with one eye, as if he expected something to fly in his face. He closed the door without speaking, and locked it again.

“As safe as a thief in a mill,” he whispered with a nod to his companion. And at that moment a harsh laugh overhead broke the silence startlingly, and set all the poultry in the yard gabbling.

===Chinese===
于是两人并肩而行，左右张望、时不时回头瞄一眼，一声不吭地走着。一走进那座老式的四合院——四周围着马厩和各色杂房，是古旧的木架结构——他们在客栈山墙的阴影下站住了，四下张望了一回，侧耳听了听。万籁俱寂——什么动静也没有。

马厩灯笼点上了；安东尼·特恩布尔一手提着灯笼，一手按着汤姆·斯凯尔斯的肩膀，往前走去。他拽着汤姆跟自己走了两步；又站住，把他往前面推了两步；就这样小心翼翼地——像两个在枪林弹雨下匍匐的散兵——靠近了马车房的大门。

"瞧，你看——万事大吉，"汤姆悄声说，指着月光下清清楚楚地挂在原处的锁。"我说，回去吧！"

"我说，往前走！"掌柜壮着胆子顶了一句。"里头那位可不能叫人捣了鬼，"他朝马车房门一指。

"明儿一早验尸官来了，连个尸首都没有，怎么验！"他嘴里说着这话，把灯笼递给汤姆，打开了挂锁。"来，瞧一眼，汤姆，"他接着说，"灯笼在你手里——看看是不是跟你走时一样。"

"我才不瞧——不，就算把'乔治与龙'连同里头所有的一切给我，我也不瞧！"汤姆打了个寒噤，生硬地说着，往后退了一步。

"搞什么——你怕什么？把灯笼给我——反正都一样：*我来*。"

他小心翼翼地、一点一点地把门推开了；把灯笼举过头顶，从那道窄窄的门缝里，皱着眉头、面色惨白地眯着一只眼往里窥探——仿佛怕有什么东西劈面飞来。他一言不发地把门又关上了，重新锁好。

"万无一失，跟贼进了磨坊一样妥当，"他朝同伴一点头，悄声说道。就在这一瞬间，头顶上一声刺耳的大笑，骤然划破了寂静，惊得满院的鸡鸭咕咕嘎嘎地叫成一片。

===Original===
“Thar he be!” said Tom, clutching the landlord’s arm—“in the winda—see!”

The window of the cedar-room, up two pair of stairs, was open; and in the shadow a darker outline was visible of a man, with his elbows on the window-stone, looking down upon them.

“Look at his eyes—like two live coals!” gasped Tom.

The landlord could not see all this so sharply, being confused, and not so long-sighted as Tom.

“Time, sir,” called Tony Turnbull, turning cold as he thought he saw a pair of eyes shining down redly at him—“time for honest folk to be in their beds, and asleep!”

“As sound as your sexton!” said the jeering voice from above.

“Come out of this,” whispered the landlord fiercely to his hostler, plucking him hard by the sleeve.

They got into the house, and shut the door.

“I wish we were shot of him,” said the landlord, with something like a groan, as he leaned against the wall of the passage. “I’ll sit up, anyhow—and, Tom, you’ll sit wi’ me. Cum into the gun-room. No one shall steal the dead man out of my yard while I can draw a trigger.”

===Chinese===
"他在那儿！"汤姆一把抓住掌柜的胳膊——"窗户那儿——瞧！"

雪松间——在两层楼梯之上的那间——的窗户开着；暗影里可以看见一个更深的轮廓：一个男人，两肘撑在窗台上，居高临下地俯视着他们。

"你瞧他那双眼睛——像两块烧红的炭！"汤姆喘着气说。

掌柜眼神不如汤姆好使，脑子也正发懵，没看得那么分明。

"该歇了，先生，"安东尼·特恩布尔喊道，只觉得有一双眼睛红通通地从上面盯着自己，顿时凉了半截——"老实人该上床睡了！"

"睡得跟你们的司事一样沉！"上面传来那嘲弄的声音。

"走，离开这儿，"掌柜恶狠狠地凑在马夫耳边说，使劲拽了他一把袖子。

两人进了屋，关上了门。

"巴不得他早点滚蛋才好，"掌柜往过道的墙上一靠，像呻吟似的说了一句。"无论如何我今夜不睡了——汤姆，你陪我一块儿。到枪房里来。只要我还能扣扳机，谁也别想把我院子里的死人偷走。"

===Original===
The gun-room in the George is about twelve feet square. It projects into the stable-yard and commands a full view of the old coach-house; and, through a narrow side window, a flanking view of the back door of the inn, through which the yard is reached.

Tony Turnbull took down the blunderbuss—which was the great ordnance of the house—and loaded it with a stiff charge of pistol bullets.

He put on a greatcoat which hung there, and was his covering when he went out at night, to shoot wild ducks. Tom made himself comfortable likewise. They then sat down at the window, which was open, looking into the yard, the opposite side of which was white in the brilliant moonlight.

The landlord laid the blunderbuss across his knees, and stared into the yard. His comrade stared also. The door of the gun-room was locked; so they felt tolerably secure.

An hour passed; nothing had occurred. Another. The clock struck one. The shadows had shifted a little; but still the moon shone full on the old coach-house, and the stable where the guest’s horse stood.

===Chinese===
"乔治与龙"的枪房约莫十二英尺见方。它凸出在马厩院中，正对着旧马车房，一览无余；另有一扇窄窄的侧窗，可以侧望到客栈的后门——从后门出去便是那个院子。

安东尼·特恩布尔取下那杆大口径短火铳（blunderbuss）——这是店里的"重炮"——满满地装了一铳膛的手枪弹。

他披上一件挂在那里的厚大衣——那是他夜里出去打野鸭时穿的。汤姆也把自己安顿舒坦了。两人在窗前坐下，窗户开着，对着院子；院子对面那堵墙在皎洁的月光下白得晃眼。

掌柜把火铳横搁在膝上，目不转睛地盯着院子。他的同伴也盯着。枪房的门锁上了；两人觉得还算稳当。

一个钟头过去了；什么事也没发生。又是一个钟头。钟敲了一点。影子挪移了一些；但月光依然满满地照在旧马车房上，照在客人那匹马所在的马厩上。

===Original===
Turnbull thought he heard a step on the backstair. Tom was watching the backdoor through the side window, with eyes glazing with the intensity of his stare. Anthony Turnbull, holding his breath, listened at the room door. It was a false alarm.

When he came back to the window looking into the yard:

“Hish! Look thar!” said he in a vehement whisper.

From the shadow at the left they saw the figure of the gaunt horseman, in short cloak and jackboots, emerge. He pushed open the stable door, and led out his powerful black horse. He walked it across the front of the building till he reached the old coach-house door; and there, with its bridle on its neck, he left it standing, while he stalked to the yard gate; and, dealing it a kick with his heel, it sprang back with the rebound, shaking from top to bottom, and stood open. The stranger returned to the side of his horse; and the door which secured the corpse of the dead sexton seemed to swing slowly open of itself as he entered, and returned with the corpse in his arms, and swung it across the shoulders of the horse, and instantly sprang into the saddle.

“Fire!” shouted Tom, and bang went the blunderbuss with a stunning crack. A thousand sparrows’ wings winnowed through the air from the thick ivy. The watchdog yelled a furious bark. There was a strange ring and whistle in the air. The blunderbuss had burst to shivers right down to the very breech. The recoil rolled the innkeeper upon his back on the floor, and Tom Scales was flung against the side of the recess of the window, which had saved him from a tumble as violent. In this position they heard the searing laugh of the departing horseman, and saw him ride out of the gate with his ghastly burden.

===Chinese===
特恩布尔觉得自己听见了后楼梯上有脚步声。汤姆正透过侧窗盯着后门，瞪得两眼发直。安东尼·特恩布尔屏住呼吸，贴着房门听了听。虚惊一场。

他回到对着院子的窗前时：

"嘘！瞧那儿！"他急切地低声说。

从左边的暗影里，他们看见那瘦长骑手的身影出现了——穿着短斗篷、长筒马靴。他推开马厩门，牵出他那匹神骏的黑马。他牵着马走过房屋正面，一直走到旧马车房门前；到了那里，他把缰绳搭在马脖子上，任它站着，自己大步走到院门口；用脚后跟朝门上一踢，门便借着弹力往后一弹，从上到下晃了一晃，弹开了。陌生人回到马旁；而那扇锁着死去的司事之尸的门，似乎随着他走进去，便自行缓缓地荡开了；他从里面出来时，臂弯里已抱着那具尸首，他将它甩上了马背，随即翻身上马。

"开火！"汤姆大喊一声，火铳砰地一声巨响，震耳欲聋。成千只麻雀的翅膀从浓密的常春藤丛中扑棱棱地飞上天。看门狗发出一声狂吠。空气中有一阵奇异的尖啸和呼哨声。那火铳从枪膛一直炸到了枪尾，碎成了齑粉。后坐力把掌柜掀了个仰面朝天，摔在地板上；汤姆·斯凯尔斯也被抛到了窗框的侧壁上——幸亏有那凹壁挡着，才没摔得同样惨。就在这狼狈的当口，他们听见了那远去的骑手刺耳的笑声，只见他驮着那具阴森的负担，骑马出了院门。

---

===Original===
Perhaps some of my readers, like myself, have heard this story told by Roger Turnbull, now host of the George and Dragon, the grandson of the very Tony who then swayed the spigot and keys of that inn, in the identical kitchen of which the fiend treated so many of the neighbours to punch.

===Chinese===
也许有些读者和我一样，曾听罗杰·特恩布尔（Roger Turnbull）亲口讲过这桩故事——他如今是"乔治与龙"的掌柜，正是当年那位把持着客栈酒桶钥匙的安东尼的孙子；而那间厨房，也正是当年那恶魔请了那么多街坊喝潘趣酒的同一间厨房。

---

===Original===
What infernal object was subserved by the possession of the dead villain’s body, I have not learned. But a very curious story, in which a vampire resuscitation of Crooke the sexton figures, may throw a light upon this part of the tale.

The result of Turnbull’s shot at the disappearing fiend certainly justifies old Andrew Moreton’s dictum, which is thus expressed in his curious “History of Apparitions”: “I warn rash brands who, pretending not to fear the devil, are for using the ordinary violences with him, which affect one man from another—or with an apparition, in which they may be sure to receive some mischief. I knew one fired a gun at an apparition and the gun burst in a hundred pieces in his hand; another struck at an apparition with a sword, and broke his sword in pieces and wounded his hand grievously; and ’tis next to madness for anyone to go that way to work with any spirit, be it angel or be it devil.”

===Chinese===
那恶灵攫取那个死去的恶棍的尸首，究竟为着怎样一桩不可告人的目的，我至今未能查明。不过，另有一篇十分离奇的故事，其中涉及了司事克鲁克被吸血鬼复活（vampire）复生的情节——或许可以为这段故事的后半投下一线光亮。

特恩布尔朝那远去的恶魔开了一铳，其后果恰好印证了老安德鲁·莫顿（Andrew Moreton）的一句箴言——他在那部奇特的《幽灵史》（History of Apparitions）中如此写道："我在此警告那些冒失的亡命之徒——他们自称不怕魔鬼，偏要像对付常人一般对魔鬼动粗，或对付一个幽灵——他们大可确信，此举必遭祸殃。我曾认识一人，朝一个幽灵开了一枪，枪在他手中炸成了碎片；又有一人拔剑砍向一个幽灵，剑断成了数截，他的手也伤得不轻。无论对任何灵体——天使也罢、魔鬼也罢——以这种蛮力相向，与疯狂何异。"

### Prologue / 前言

===Original===
Out of about two hundred and thirty cases, more or less nearly akin to that I have entitled “Green Tea,” I select the following, which I call “The Familiar.”
To this MS., Doctor Hesselius has, after his wont, attached some sheets of letter-paper, on which are written, in his hand nearly as compact as print, his own remarks upon the case. He says—

===Chinese===
在我名之为"绿茶（Green Tea）"的那一桩医案之外，尚有约二百三十桩或多或少与之相近的案子，我兹从中拣选出以下这一桩，称之为"熟人（The Familiar）"。
关于这份手稿，赫塞利乌斯医生（Doctor Hesselius）一仍旧贯，附上了几张信笺，上面以他那几与排印无异的密行手迹，写下了他本人对此案的按语。他写道——

===Original===
“In point of conscience, no more unexceptionable narrator, than the venerable Irish Clergyman who has given me this paper, on Mr. Barton’s case, could have been chosen. The statement is, however, medically imperfect. The report of an intelligent physician, who had marked its progress, and attended the patient, from its earlier stages to its close, would have supplied what is wanting to enable me to pronounce with confidence. I should have been acquainted with Mr. Barton’s probable hereditary predispositions; I should have known, possibly, by very early indications, something of a remoter origin of the disease than can now be ascertained.

===Chinese===
"凭良心而论，再没有比那位令人敬重的爱尔兰神职人员更为无可挑剔的叙述者了——正是他把这份关于巴顿先生（Mr. Barton）之案的文稿交予我手。然而，从医学的角度看，这份陈述并不完备。倘若有一位精明的医生，从该病初起直至终局一路留心其病程、诊治其病人，并写下报告，那便恰好可以补我之所缺，使我得以满怀把握地作出判断。我本应知悉巴顿先生可能具有的遗传性体质倾向；我本应——或许能从极为早期的征兆之中——了解到此疾某种比现今所能查考的更为久远的源头。

===Original===
“In a rough way, we may reduce all similar cases to three distinct classes. They are founded on the primary distinction between the subjective and the objective. Of those whose senses are alleged to be subject to supernatural impressions—some are simply visionaries, and propagate the illusions of which they complain, from diseased brain or nerves. Others are, unquestionably, infested by, as we term them, spiritual agencies, exterior to themselves. Others, again, owe their sufferings to a mixed condition. The interior sense, it is true, is opened; but it has been and continues open by the action of disease. This form of disease may, in one sense, be compared to the loss of the scarf-skin, and a consequent exposure of surfaces for whose excessive sensitiveness, nature has provided a muffling. The loss of this covering is attended by an habitual impassability, by influences against which we were intended to be guarded. But in the case of the brain, and the nerves immediately connected with its functions and its sensuous impressions, the cerebral circulation undergoes periodically that vibratory disturbance, which, I believe, I have satisfactorily examined and demonstrated, in my MS. essay, ‘A. 17.’ This vibratory disturbance differs, as I there prove, essentially from the congestive disturbance, the phenomena of which are examined in ‘A. 19.’ It is, when excessive, invariably accompanied by *illusions*.

===Chinese===
"粗略而言，我们可将一切同类病例归为截然不同的三类。其划分所本，在于主观与客观这一根本的区分。在那些据说感官遭受超自然印象侵扰的人当中——有一部分不过是妄想着，他们所抱怨的种种幻象，皆起于有病的大脑或神经。另一些人，则无可置疑地受到了我们所谓的灵异力量的侵扰，而这些力量是外在于他们自身的。还有一些人，其所受的苦楚则源自一种混合的病况。其内在感官（the interior sense）固然是开启了的；然而它之开启，一向是、并且始终是由于疾病的作用。这一形式的疾病，在某种意义上，不妨比作表皮的脱落，由此致使本应被掩覆的组织暴露于外——这些组织敏感异常，造化本已为之备下一重裹覆。这一层裹覆一旦失去，便伴随着一种习常的易受侵扰性，所侵者，正是我们本该被防护以免其害的那些影响。至于大脑、以及与大脑机能及其感官印象直接相连的那些神经，脑部的血液循环则会周期性地发生一种震颤性的扰动——我相信，我已在自己那篇题为《A. 17.》的手稿论文中，对其作了颇为圆满的考察与论证。这一震颤性扰动，一如我在该处所证，与充血性扰动有着本质的区别，后者的种种现象则在《A. 19.》中加以探讨。这种扰动一旦过度，便必然伴有种种*幻象（illusions）*。

===Original===
“Had I seen Mr. Barton, and examined him upon the points, in his case, which need elucidation, I should have without difficulty referred those phenomena to their proper disease. My diagnosis is now, necessarily, conjectural.”
Thus writes Doctor Hesselius; and adds a great deal which is of interest only to a scientific physician.

===Chinese===
"倘若我曾亲见巴顿先生，并就他这桩案子中几处有待阐明的疑点上对他加以详询，我便能毫无困难地将那些现象归之于其应有的病名之下。是故，我此刻的诊断，不得不出于推断了。"
赫塞利乌斯医生便如此写道；此外他还加了许多内容，然而唯有对于通晓科学的医者方才具有兴味。

===Original===
The narrative of the Rev. Thomas Herbert, which furnishes all that is known of the case, will be found in the chapters that follow.

===Chinese===
关于此案，今人所知的一切，皆出自托马斯·赫伯特牧师（the Rev. Thomas Herbert）的记述，下文诸章所载，即是。

## The Ghost and the Bonesetter / 鬼魂与接骨师

===Original===
In looking over the papers of my late valued and respected friend, Francis Purcell, who for nearly fifty years discharged the arduous duties of a parish priest in the south of Ireland, I met with the following document. It is one of many such; for he was a curious and industrious collector of old local traditions—a commodity in which the quarter where he resided mightily abounded. The collection and arrangement of such legends was, as long as I can remember him, his hobby; but I had never learned that his love of the marvellous and whimsical had carried him so far as to prompt him to commit the results of his inquiries to writing, until, in the character of residuary legatee, his will put me in possession of all his manuscript papers. To such as may think the composing of such productions as these inconsistent with the character and habits of a country priest, it is necessary to observe, that there did exist a race of priests—those of the old school, a race now nearly extinct—whose education abroad tended to produce in them tastes more literary than have yet been evinced by the alumni of Maynooth.

It is perhaps necessary to add that the superstition illustrated by the following story, namely, that the corpse last buried is obliged, during his juniority of interment, to supply his brother tenants of the churchyard in which he lies, with fresh water to allay the burning thirst of purgatory, is prevalent throughout the south of Ireland.

The writer can vouch for a case in which a respectable and wealthy farmer, on the borders of Tipperary, in tenderness to the corns of his departed helpmate, enclosed in her coffin two pair of brogues, a light and a heavy, the one for dry, the other for sloppy weather; seeking thus to mitigate the fatigues of her inevitable perambulations in procuring water and administering it to the thirsty souls of purgatory. Fierce and desperate conflicts have ensued in the case of two funeral parties approaching the same churchyard together, each endeavouring to secure to his own dead priority of sepulture, and a consequent immunity from the tax levied upon the pedestrian powers of the last-comer. An instance not long since occurred, in which one of two such parties, through fear of losing to their deceased friend this inestimable advantage, made their way to the churchyard by a shortcut, and, in violation of one of their strongest prejudices, actually threw the coffin over the wall, lest time should be lost in making their entrance through the gate. Innumerable instances of the same kind might be quoted, all tending to show how strongly among the peasantry of the south this superstition is entertained. However, I shall not detain the reader further by any prefatory remarks, but shall proceed to lay before him the following:

===Chinese===
检视我那位已故的、素所敬重的好友弗朗西斯·珀塞尔神父（Francis Purcell）的遗稿时——他在爱尔兰南部担任教区神父，辛勤履职将近五十年——我发现了下面这份文献。此类文稿他遗下甚多；他生前酷爱搜集、整理乡野旧闻，是个勤勉的搜罗者，而他所居之处，这类材料可谓俯拾皆是。据我所知，搜集编次这类传说，乃是他毕生的癖好；只是我一直不知他这份对奇闻异事的痴迷，竟已到了动笔录之的程度——直到我以剩余遗产承受人的身份，凭他的遗嘱接管了他全部的手稿，方才知晓。或许有人以为，乡间神父竟作此类文字，与其身份习性不符；在此须得说明一句：昔日确有过那样一代神职人员——即所谓旧学派，如今已几近绝迹——他们负笈海外所受的教养，使其性情较之梅努斯（Maynooth）出身的后学，更添几分文人气。

或许还有必要补充一句：下文故事所印证的那种迷信——即墓地里最后一个下葬的尸骸，在其"葬期尚浅"之时，须为同卧那片坟茔的"同穴邻人"打来清水，以解炼狱中那灼烧的干渴——此种说法在爱尔兰南部一带颇为盛行。

笔者可以担保一桩真事：蒂珀雷里（Tipperary）边界上一位殷实富农，体恤亡妻脚上的鸡眼，竟在她的棺木里放了两双鞋——一双轻便、一双厚实，一作晴天之用、一作泥泞之用——只为减轻她日后往返取水、浇灌炼狱中干渴亡魂那番无可逃避的辛劳。又曾有两支送葬队伍同趋一处坟地，为使自家亡人抢先入土、从而免却"后来者"须跋涉取水的差役，竟至大打出手、拼个你死我活。不久之前还有过这样一桩事：两队送葬人之中的一队，唯恐亡友失去这天大的便宜，竟抄近道赶赴坟地，更不顾他们最深重的忌讳，索性把棺材从墙头扔了进去——只怕从大门进去那点工夫，便要误了大事。同类的事例不胜枚举，皆可证明这一迷信在南部乡民之中根深蒂固到了何等地步。闲话休提，我不再用这番开场白耽搁读者，这就把下面这篇文字呈上：

### Extract from the MS. Papers of the late Rev. Francis Purcell, of Drumcoolagh. / 摘自已故德鲁姆库拉教区弗朗西斯·珀塞尔神父手稿

===Original===
I tell the following particulars, as nearly as I can recollect them, in the words of the narrator. It may be necessary to observe that he was what is termed a well-spoken man, having for a considerable time instructed the ingenious youth of his native parish in such of the liberal arts and sciences as he found it convenient to profess—a circumstance which may account for the occurrence of several big words in the course of this narrative, more distinguished for euphonious effect than for correctness of application. I proceed then, without further preface, to lay before you the wonderful adventures of Terry Neil.

===Chinese===
下面这些情节，我尽可能依照讲述者的原话，凭记忆复述出来。或许有必要说明一句：此公是所谓"会说话"的人，在本堂区那些聪颖的少年中间，曾教导过一段时日的"文艺与科学"——凡是他觉得便于传授的，都曾开课讲授；正因如此，这段叙述之中屡屡冒出几个冠冕堂皇的大词，其音韵之悦耳，远胜其用度之精当。闲言少叙，我便将特里·尼尔（Terry Neil）的种种奇遇，呈列于诸君之前。

---

===Original===
"Why, thin, 'tis a quare story, an' as thrue as you're sittin' there; and I'd make bould to say there isn't a boy in the seven parishes could tell it better nor crickther than myself, for 'twas my father himself it happened to, an' many's the time I heerd it out iv his own mouth; an' I can say, an' I'm proud av that same, my father's word was as incredible as any squire's oath in the counthry; and so signs an' if a poor man got into any unlucky throuble, he was the boy id go into the court an' prove; but that doesn't signify—he was as honest and as sober a man, barrin' he was a little bit too partial to the glass, as you'd find in a day's walk; and there wasn't the likes of him in the counthry round for nate labourin' an' *baan* diggin'; and he was mighty handy entirely for carpenther's work, and mendin' ould spudethrees, an' the likes i' that. An' so he tuk up with bone-settin', as was most nathural, for none of them could come up to him in mendin' the leg iv a stool or a table; an' sure, there never was a bonesetter got so much custom—man an' child, young an' ould—there never was such breakin' and mendin' of bones known in the memory of man. Well, Terry Neil—for that was my father's name—began to feel his heart growin' light, and his purse heavy; an' he took a bit iv a farm in Squire Phelim's ground, just undher the ould castle, an' a pleasant little spot it was; an' day an' mornin' poor crathurs not able to put a foot to the ground, with broken arms and broken legs, id be comin' ramblin' in from all quarters to have their bones spliced up. Well, yer honour, all this was as well as well could be; but it was customary when Sir Phelim id go anywhere out iv the country, for some iv the tinants to sit up to watch in the ould castle, just for a kind of compliment to the ould family—an' a mighty unplisant compliment it was for the tinants, for there wasn't a man of them but knew there was something quare about the ould castle. The neighbours had it, that the squire's ould grandfather, as good a gintleman—God be with him—as I heer'd, as ever stood in shoe-leather, used to keep walkin' about in the middle iv the night, ever sinst he bursted a blood vessel pullin' out a cork out iv a bottle, as you or I might be doin', and will too, plase God—but that doesn't signify. So, as I was sayin', the ould squire used to come down out of the frame, where his picthur was hung up, and to break the bottles and glasses—God be marciful to us all—an' dthrink all he could come at—an' small blame to him for that same; and then if any of the family id be comin' in, he id be up again in his place, looking as quite an' as innocent as if he didn't know anything about it—the mischievous ould chap.

===Chinese===
嘿，这可是桩怪事，千真万确，就跟您坐在那儿一样实在；我敢夸口说，方圆七个堂区里头，再没哪个汉子能讲得比我更地道——这事儿就出在我亲爹身上，我打小不知听他亲口讲过多少回；我也敢说——这一点我颇为得意——我爹说话的分量，跟乡里哪位乡绅宣了誓一般无二；所以嘛，每逢穷苦人遭了什么倒霉运，他便是那种肯上堂作证的汉子；这且不提——他这个人，又本分又规矩，只是有那么一点点贪杯，您打着灯笼也难找第二个；至于庄稼活儿、精耕细作，乡邻四近没一个比得上他；木匠活儿也是一把好手，修修旧纺车什么的，无所不通。就这样，他自然而然地干起了接骨这一行——您想啊，修板凳腿、拼桌子脚，这一带谁也比不过他；也从来没有哪个接骨师接过这么多的营生——男女老少，人山人海——打从有人记事起，就没见过这般接骨断骨、又断又接的热闹景况。哎，特里·尼尔——这便是我爹的名字——心里头渐渐畅快起来，钱袋也沉了起来；他在费利姆乡绅（Squire Phelim）的地界上，紧挨着那座古堡底下，置了一小块田产，那地方着实宜人；日里夜里，苦命的伤号——脚不沾地的、断胳膊折腿的——从四面八方蹒跚而至，求他给接上。哎，老爷，这一切本来好得很；只是有这么一条老规矩：费利姆乡绅每逢出门离乡，总有几户佃户得轮着去那古堡里守夜，权当是给这旧人家一点礼数——可对佃户们而言，这份礼数实在讨人喜欢不起来，因为他们里头没一个不知道，那古堡是有几分古怪的。邻舍间都传：乡绅的那位老祖父——但愿上帝保佑他——据我所闻，是位一等的好绅士，站着也是个人样——自打有一回拔酒瓶塞子，把一根血管崩断了之后（这事儿您我兴许也会干，上帝愿意的话咱也得干——可这且不说），每逢夜半三更，便要从坟里出来到处溜达。据说，这位老乡绅会从挂着他的画像的画框里走下来，把瓶瓶罐罐砸个稀烂——上帝慈悲啊——凡是他够得着的酒，通通灌下肚去——这倒也怨不得他；可要是家中有人进来，他便又倏地回到原位，神色安详、一脸无辜，活像他对此事一无所知——这老捣蛋鬼。

===Original===
"Well, your honour, as I was sayin', one time the family up at the castle was stayin' in Dublin for a week or two; and so, as usual, some of the tinants had to sit up in the castle, and the third night it kem to my father's turn. 'Oh, tare an' ouns!' says he unto himself, 'an' must I sit up all night, and that ould vagabone of a sperit, glory be to God,' says he, 'serenadin' through the house, an' doin' all sorts iv mischief?' However, there was no gettin' aff, and so he put a bould face on it, an' he went up at nightfall with a bottle of pottieen, and another of holy wather.

"It was rainin' smart enough, an' the evenin' was darksome and gloomy, when my father got in; and what with the rain he got, and the holy wather he sprinkled on himself, it wasn't long till he had to swally a cup iv the pottieen, to keep the cowld out iv his heart. It was the ould steward, Lawrence Connor, that opened the door—an' he an' my father wor always very great. So when he seen who it was, an' my father tould him how it was his turn to watch in the castle, he offered to sit up along with him; and you may be sure my father wasn't sorry for that same. So says Larry:

===Chinese===
哎，老爷，我刚才说到哪儿了——有一回，堡里那户人家上都柏林住了一两个礼拜；于是照老规矩，佃户们又得轮着去古堡守夜，第三夜便轮到了我爹。"哎呀，老天爷呀！"他自个儿嘀咕，"难道要我整整守它一夜，还要忍受那个老流氓鬼——赞美上帝——在屋里头晃来晃去，变着法儿地捣乱？"话虽如此，却躲是躲不掉的，他只好硬着头皮，天擦黑时便揣上一瓶私酿酒（poteen），又带了一瓶圣水，上堡里去了。

我爹赶到时，雨下得正急，天色又暗又阴沉；一路上淋的雨，再加上他往自己身上洒的那点圣水，没多大工夫，他便不得不灌下一杯私酿，好把那股寒气从心头驱出去。给他开门的是老管家劳伦斯·康纳（Lawrence Connor）——他与我爹向来交情深厚。劳伦斯看清来人是谁，又听我爹说今夜轮到他守堡，便主动提出陪他一同熬夜；您可想而知，我爹自然是求之不得。于是拉里（Larry）说道：

===Original===
"'We'll have a bit iv fire in the parlour,' says he.

"'An' why not in the hall?' says my father, for he knew that the squire's picthur was hung in the parlour.

"'No fire can be lit in the hall,' says Lawrence, 'for there's an ould jackdaw's nest in the chimney.'

"'Oh thin,' says my father, 'let us stop in the kitchen, for it's very unproper for the likes iv me to be sittin' in the parlour,' says he.

"'Oh, Terry, that can't be,' says Lawrence; 'if we keep up the ould custom at all, we may as well keep it up properly,' says he.

"'Divil sweep the ould custom!' says my father—to himself, do ye mind, for he didn't like to let Lawrence see that he was more afeard himself.

"'Oh, very well,' says he. 'I'm agreeable, Lawrence,' says he; and so down they both wint to the kitchen, until the fire id be lit in the parlour—an' that same wasn't long doin'.

"Well, your honour, they soon wint up again, an' sat down mighty comfortable by the parlour fire, and they beginned to talk, an' to smoke, an' to dhrink a small taste iv the pottieen; and, moreover, they had a good rousin' fire o' bogwood and turf, to warm their shins over.

===Chinese===
"咱们在客厅里生一摊火吧，"他说。

"干嘛不在大厅里？"我爹说，因为他知道乡绅的画像就挂在客厅里。

"大厅里生不得火，"劳伦斯说，"烟囱里有个老寒鸦窝。"

"那就在厨房里待着吧，"我爹说，"像我这种人，坐在客厅里头，太不像话了，"他说。

"哎呀，特里，那可不行，"劳伦斯说，"既然要守这老规矩，索性就规规矩矩地守，"他说。

"叫魔鬼收了这老规矩去！"我爹说——这话是搁在心里嘀咕的，您明白，因为他不愿让劳伦斯瞧出，其实他自己怕得更厉害。

"哦，那好，"他说，"我没意见，劳伦斯，"他说；于是两人一同下到厨房，等着客厅那摊火生好——这倒也没费多大工夫。

哎，老爷，两人不多时又上楼，舒舒服服地在客厅炉火旁坐下，便你一言我一语地聊起天来，又抽起烟，还呷了一小口私酿；再说，他们面前烧着一炉旺旺的沼泽木和泥炭，正好把小腿烤得暖烘烘的。

===Original===
"Well, sir, as I was sayin' they kep' convarsin' and smokin' together most agreeable, until Lawrence beginn'd to get sleepy, as was but nathural for him, for he was an ould sarvint man, and was used to a great dale iv sleep.

"'Sure it's impossible,' says my father, 'it's gettin' sleepy you are?'

"'Oh, divil a taste,' says Larry; 'I'm only shuttin' my eyes,' says he, 'to keep out the parfume o' the tibacky smoke, that's makin' them wather,' says he. 'So don't you mind other people's business,' says he, stiff enough, for he had a mighty high stomach av his own (rest his sowl), 'and go on,' says he, 'with your story, for I'm listenin',' says he, shuttin' down his eyes.

"Well, when my father seen spakin' was no use, he went on with his story. By the same token, it was the story of Jim Soolivan and his ould goat he was tellin'—an' a plisant story it is—an' there was so much divarsion in it, that it was enough to waken a dormouse, let alone to pervint a Christian goin' asleep. But, faix, the way my father tould it, I believe there never was the likes heerd sinst nor before, for he bawled out every word av it, as if the life was fairly lavin' him, thrying to keep ould Larry awake; but, faix, it was no use, for the hoorsness came an him, an' before he kem to the end of his story Larry O'Connor beginned to snore like a bagpipes.

===Chinese===
哎，老爷，我刚才说啦，他们俩谈得十分投契，烟也抽得痛快，直谈到劳伦斯开始犯困——这也是人之常情，他到底是个上了年纪的老仆，素来觉多。

"嘿，"我爹说，"不会吧，你竟犯起困来了？"

"嗨，困个屁，"拉里说，"我不过是把眼睛闭上，"他说，"好挡住那烟草的味儿——熏得我直淌眼泪，"他说。"所以你少管人家的闲事，"他说，口气颇为生硬，因为他这人性子傲得很（愿他的灵魂安息），"你只管，"他说，"接着讲你的故事，我听着呢，"他说着，把眼睛合上了。

哎，我爹见再说也不顶用，便接着往下讲。顺带提一句，他讲的是吉姆·苏利文（Jim Soolivan）和他那只老山羊的故事——那可是个顶逗趣的故事——里头的笑料之多，便是只睡鼠听了也要笑醒，更不用说叫一个活人别打瞌睡了。可是，老天爷，我爹那个讲法，我想前无古人、后无来者——他每个字都扯着嗓子吼出来，好像这条命眼见就要搭进去了，一心只想把老拉里吵醒；可是，唉，全然无用，那瞌睡虫一来，故事还没讲到结尾，拉里·奥康纳（Larry O'Connor）已经鼾声大作，活像一具风袋。

===Original===
"'Oh, blur an' agres,' says my father, 'isn't this a hard case,' says he, 'that ould villain, lettin' on to be my friend, and to go asleep this way, an' us both in the very room with a sperit,' says he. 'The crass o' Christ about us!' says he; and with that he was goin' to shake Lawrence to waken him, but he just remimbered if he roused him, that he'd surely go off to his bed, an' lave him complately alone, an' that id be by far worse.

"'Oh thin,' says my father, 'I'll not disturb the poor boy. It id be neither friendly nor good-nathured,' says he, 'to tormint him while he is asleep,' says he; 'only I wish I was the same way, myself,' says he.

"An' with that he beginned to walk up an' down, an' sayin' his prayers, until he worked himself into a sweat, savin' your presence. But it was all no good; so he dthrunk about a pint of sperits, to compose his mind.

"'Oh,' says he, 'I wish to the Lord I was as asy in my mind as Larry there. Maybe,' says he, 'if I thried I could go asleep;' an' with that he pulled a big armchair close beside Lawrence, an' settled himself in it as well as he could.

===Chinese===
"哎呀，该死的瘟病！"我爹说，"这也太不讲理了，"他说，"那老东西，装得跟我多亲近似的，竟这样睡死过去，咱俩可是在一间屋里守着个鬼魂啊，"他说。"基督的十字架保佑我们！"他说；说着便要去摇醒劳伦斯，可转念一想：要是把他弄醒了，他准得回自家床上去，把自己撇在这屋里，孤零零一个人——那可就更糟了。

"也罢，"我爹说，"我不搅这可怜人。趁人家睡着了去折腾他，"他说，"既不厚道，也不够朋友，"他说；"只盼我自己也能像他那样才好，"他说。

说着，他便在屋里来回踱起步子，嘴里念念有词地祷告，直念得自己出了一身透汗——恕我直言。可这全不顶事；于是他灌下约莫一品脱烈酒，好叫心神定一定。

"唉，"他说，"我要是能像拉里那样心宽就好啦。说不定，"他说，"我使劲儿试试，也能睡着；"说着，他把一张宽大的扶手椅拖到劳伦斯跟前，尽可能舒舒服服地坐了进去。

===Original===
"But there was one quare thing I forgot to tell you. He couldn't help, in spite av himself, lookin' now an' thin at the picthur, an' he immediately obsarved that the eyes av it was follyin' him about, an' starin' at him, an' winkin' at him, wheriver he wint. 'Oh,' says he, when he seen that, 'it's a poor chance I have,' says he; 'an' bad luck was with me the day I kem into this unforthunate place,' says he. 'But anyway there's no use in bein' freckened now,' says he; 'for if I am to die, I may as well parspire undaunted,' says he.

"Well, your honour, he thried to keep himself quite an' asy, an' he thought two or three times he might have wint asleep, but for the way the storm was groanin' and creakin' through the great heavy branches outside, an' whistlin' through the ould chimleys iv the castle. Well, afther one great roarin' blast iv the wind, you'd think the walls iv the castle was just goin' to fall, quite an' clane, with the shakin' iv it. All av a suddint the storm stopped, as silent an' as quite as if it was a July evenin'. Well, your honour, it wasn't stopped blowin' for three minnites, before he thought he hard a sort iv a noise over the chimley-piece; an' with that my father just opened his eyes the smallest taste in life, an' sure enough he seen the ould squire gettin' out iv the picthur, for all the world as if he was throwin' aff his ridin' coat, until he stepped out clane an' complate, out av the chimley-piece, an' thrun himself down an the floor. Well, the slieveen ould chap—an' my father thought it was the dirtiest turn iv all—before he beginned to do anything out iv the way, he stopped for a while to listen wor they both asleep; an' as soon as he thought all was quite, he put out his hand and tuk hould iv the whisky bottle, an dhrank at laste a pint iv it. Well, your honour, when he tuk his turn out iv it, he settled it back mighty cute entirely, in the very same spot it was in before. An' he beginned to walk up an' down the room, lookin' as sober an' as solid as if he never done the likes at all. An' whinever he went apast my father, he thought he felt a great scent of brimstone, an' it was that that freckened him entirely; for he knew it was brimstone that was burned in hell, savin' your presence. At any rate, he often heerd it from Father Murphy, an' he had a right to know what belonged to it—he's dead since, God rest him. Well, your honour, my father was asy enough until the sperit kem past him; so close, God be marciful to us all, that the smell iv the sulphur tuk the breath clane out iv him; an' with that he tuk such a fit iv coughin', that it al-a-most shuk him out iv the chair he was sittin' in.

===Chinese===
可还有一桩怪事我忘了告诉您。他不由自主地，时不时就要去瞟那画像一眼；他立刻就发觉，画上那双眼睛正跟着他滴溜溜地转，盯着他瞧，冲他眨眼，不管他走到哪里都一样。"唉，"他见此情景，说道，"我这下是没活路了，"他说；"我踏进这倒霉地方的那一日，霉运就跟着我来了，"他说。"不过事到如今，怕也无用了，"他说；"反正要死，我索性大胆地出透这身汗，"他说。

哎，老爷，他竭力让自己安安静静、心平气和，有两三回他觉得自己本可以睡过去的，要不是外面那场风暴——狂风在粗大沉重的树枝间呜呜咽咽、吱吱呀呀地穿行，又在那古堡的老烟囱里呼啸。哎，刮过一阵惊天动地的狂风之后，您准会以为那古堡的墙都要给摇得轰然倒塌、四分五裂。可忽然之间，那风暴竟戛然而止，四周静悄悄的，悄无声息，活像是个七月的黄昏。哎，老爷，风停下还不到三分钟，他便听见壁炉架上方传来一阵窸窸窣窣的响动；我爹便把眼睛眯开那么一丁点儿——果不其然，只见那老乡绅正从画里往外迈，那模样，活像是脱下骑马外套一般，直到他整个人清清爽爽、完完整整地从壁炉架上跨了出来，一纵身跳到了地上。哎，这老滑头——我爹说，这是最损的一招——他在动手干出什么出格事之前，竟先站住脚听了一会儿，听听他俩是不是都睡着了；待他认定一切寂然无声，便伸出手去，抓起威士忌酒瓶，少说也灌下一品脱去。哎，老爷，他喝完那一口，又狡猾地把酒瓶放回原处，分毫不差，就跟没动过一样。接着他便在屋里来回踱起步子，神色凝重、稳稳当当，活像他根本没干过这等事。每逢他从我爹跟前经过，我爹就闻到一股浓烈的硫磺气味——正是这气味把他吓得魂飞魄散；因为他知道——恕我直言——地狱里烧的便是硫磺。这是他时常听墨菲神父（Father Murphy）说的，神父对此道自是颇有研究——他已去世多年，愿他安息。哎，老爷，我爹本来倒还安之若素，直到那鬼魂从他身旁经过——靠得那么近——上帝慈悲啊——那硫磺味儿简直把他的气儿都憋没了；他登时一阵剧烈的咳嗽，咳得几乎要从椅子里翻出来。

===Original===
"'Ho, ho!' says the squire, stoppin' short about two steps aff, and turnin' round facin' my father, 'is it you that's in it?—an' how's all with you, Terry Neil?'

"'At your honour's sarvice,' says my father (as well as the fright id let him, for he was more dead than alive), 'an' it's proud I am to see your honour tonight,' says he.

"'Terence,' says the squire, 'you're a respectable man' (an' it was thrue for him), 'an industhrious, sober man, an' an example of inebriety to the whole parish,' says he.

"'Thank your honour,' says my father, gettin' courage, 'you were always a civil spoken gintleman, God rest your honour.'

"'Rest my honour?' says the sperit (fairly gettin' red in the face with the madness), 'Rest my honour?' says he. 'Why, you ignorant spalpeen,' says he, 'you mane, niggarly ignoramush,' says he, 'where did you lave your manners?' says he. 'If I am dead, it's no fault iv mine,' says he; 'an' it's not to be thrun in my teeth at every hand's turn, by the likes iv you,' says he, stampin' his foot an the flure, that you'd think the boords id smash undther him.

"'Oh,' says my father, 'I'm only a foolish, ignorant poor man,' says he.

===Chinese===
"嗬，嗬！"乡绅说道，在两步开外收住脚，转过身来正对着我爹，"原来是你在这儿？——特里·尼尔，你近来可好啊？"

"听凭老爷差遣，"我爹说（吓得只能挤出这么一句，他早已半死不活了），"今夜得见老爷，小的三生有幸，"他说。

"特伦斯（Terence），"乡绅说，"你是个体面人，"（这话倒也不假）"又勤快、又本分，全堂区节制饮酒的楷模，"他说。

"多谢老爷夸奖，"我爹说着，胆子壮了几分，"老爷您素来是个和颜悦色的君子，愿上帝保佑老爷。"

"保佑我？"那鬼魂说（气得脸都涨红了），"保佑我？"他又道。"嘿，你这无知的浑小子，"他说，"你这小气巴拉、不识好歹的蠢材，"他说，"你的规矩都学到狗肚子里去了？"他说。"我纵然是死了，那也不是我的过错，"他说；"岂能由着你这种货色，动不动就拿这话来寒碜我，"他说着，一脚踏在地板上，那架势，您准以为那木板都要叫他踩个粉碎。

"哎哟，"我爹说，"我不过是个愚昧无知的穷汉子，"他说。

===Original===
"'You're nothing else,' says the squire: 'but anyway,' says he, 'it's not to be listenin' to your gosther, nor convarsin' with the likes iv you, that I came up—down I mane,' says he—(an' as little as the mistake was, my father tuk notice iv it). 'Listen to me now, Terence Neil,' says he: 'I was always a good masther to Pathrick Neil, your grandfather,' says he.

"''Tis thrue for your honour,' says my father.

"'And, moreover, I think I was always a sober, riglar gintleman,' says the squire.

"'That's your name, sure enough,' says my father (though it was a big lie for him, but he could not help it).

"'Well,' says the sperit, 'although I was as sober as most men—at laste as most gintlemin,' says he; 'an' though I was at different pariods a most extempory Christian, and most charitable and inhuman to the poor,' says he; 'for all that I'm not as asy where I am now,' says he, 'as I had a right to expect,' says he.

===Chinese===
"除此之外你也算不得别的什么，"乡绅说："不过，"他说，"我来此可不是来——听你瞎扯，也不是来跟你这种人闲话的——我是上来说的——我是说下来的，"他说——（这个口误虽小，我爹却记在了心上）。"你且听好，特伦斯·尼尔，"他说："我待你祖父帕特里克·尼尔（Patrick Neil），向来是个好东家，"他说。

"老爷说的千真万确，"我爹说。

"再者，"乡绅说，"我想我向来是个本分、正经的君子，"他说。

"您当之无愧，"我爹说（这话于他可是句天大的谎话，却也无可奈何）。

"好吧，"那鬼魂说，"虽说我和大多数人一样本分——至少和大多数君子一样，"他说；"虽说我有段时日可谓是个顶顶了不起的基督徒，对穷苦人又乐善好施、又慈悲为怀，"他说；"尽管如此，我现在待的这个去处，可没我本该指望的那般舒坦，"他说。

===Original===
"'An' more's the pity,' says my father. 'Maybe your honour id wish to have a word with Father Murphy?'

"'Hould your tongue, you misherable bliggard,' says the squire; 'it's not iv my sowl I'm thinkin'—an' I wondther you'd have the impitence to talk to a gintleman consarnin' his sowl; and when I want that fixed,' says he, slappin' his thigh, 'I'll go to them that knows what belongs to the likes,' says he. 'It's not my sowl,' says he, sittin' down opossite my father; 'it's not my sowl that's annoyin' me most—I'm unasy on my right leg,' says he, 'that I bruk at Glenvarloch cover the day I killed black Barney.'

"My father found out afther, it was a favourite horse that fell undher him, afther leapin' the big fence that runs along by the glin.

"'I hope,' says my father, 'your honour's not unasy about the killin' iv him?'

"'Hould your tongue, ye fool,' said the squire, 'an' I'll tell you why I'm unasy on my leg,' says he. 'In the place, where I spend most iv my time,' says he, 'except the little leisure I have for lookin' about me here,' says he, 'I have to walk a great dale more than I was ever used to,' says he, 'and by far more than is good for me either,' says he; 'for I must tell you,' says he, 'the people where I am is ancommonly fond iv cowld wather, for there is nothin' betther to be had; an', moreover, the weather is hotter than is altogether plisant,' says he; 'and I'm appinted,' says he, 'to assist in carryin' the wather, an' gets a mighty poor share iv it myself,' says he, 'an' a mighty throublesome, wearin' job it is, I can tell you,' says he; 'for they're all iv them surprisinly dthry, an' dthrinks it as fast as my legs can carry it,' says he; 'but what kills me intirely,' says he, 'is the wakeness in my leg,' says he, 'an' I want you to give it a pull or two to bring it to shape,' says he, 'and that's the long an' the short iv it,' says he.

===Chinese===
"那真是可惜，"我爹说。"莫非老爷想找墨菲神父说句话？"

"闭上你的嘴，你这可怜的无赖，"乡绅说；"我想的又不是我的灵魂——你这放肆的东西，竟敢跟一位君子谈他的灵魂；待我当真要料理那桩事的时候，"他说着，一拍大腿，"自会去找懂行的人，"他说。"不是我的灵魂，"他说着，在我爹对面坐下；"叫我烦心的，不是我的灵魂——是右腿不舒坦，"他说，"那条腿是我在格伦瓦洛奇（Glenvarloch）猎场打断的，就是我打死黑巴尼（black Barney）那天。"

我爹后来才知道，那是匹心爱的坐骑，跳过谷地边上那道大篱笆时，把他从马背上掀了下来。

"但愿，"我爹说，"老爷不是为了打死它那档子事不安吧？"

"闭上你的嘴，你这蠢货，"乡绅说，"我告诉你我这条腿为何不舒坦，"他说。"在我消磨大部分光阴的那个去处，"他说，"——除了偶尔回来这儿走走、四下瞧瞧那点工夫不算，"他说，"我得走的路，可比我从前行惯的多得多了，"他说，"多得多，远不是好事，"他说；"因为我不妨告诉你，"他说，"我待的那地方，那些人稀罕凉水，爱得不得了，因为再没更好的东西可弄；再者，那地方天气酷热，热得着实不痛快，"他说；"于是派了我一个差事，"他说，"专门帮着运水，可我自己能到嘴的，却少得可怜，"他说，"这活儿又累人、又熬人，我可以告诉您，"他说；"因为他们每一个都渴得要命，我这两条腿跑得多快，他们就喝得多快，"他说；"可最要命的，"他说，"还是我这条腿不中用，"他说，"所以我要你拽它两下，把它拽顺了，"他说，"事情就是这样，一句不多，一句不少，"他说。

===Original===
"'Oh, plase your honour,' says my father (for he didn't like to handle the sperit at all), 'I wouldn't have the impidence to do the likes to your honour,' says he; 'it's only to poor crathurs like myself I'd do it to,' says he.

"'None iv your blarney,' says the squire. 'Here's my leg,' says he, cockin' it up to him—'pull it for the bare life,' says he; an' 'if you don't, by the immortial powers I'll not lave a bone in your carcish I'll not powdher,' says he.

"When my father heerd that, he seen there was no use in purtendin', so he tuk hould iv the leg, an' he kep' pullin' an' pullin', till the sweat, God bless us, beginned to pour down his face.

===Chinese===
"哎哟，老爷恕罪，"我爹说（他压根儿不愿去碰那鬼魂），"我可不敢对老爷您这般放肆，"他说；"我那是只给苦命人接的，跟我一样的穷汉子，"他说。

"少来这一套花言巧语，"乡绅说。"腿在这儿，"他说着，把腿往他跟前一翘——"拼了命地拽，"他说；"你要是不拽，我对着不朽的神明起誓，你身上每一根骨头，我都要敲得粉碎，"他说。

我爹听见这话，便知再装也无用，于是一把抓住那条腿，拽了又拽，直拽得——老天保佑——汗珠子顺着脸往下直淌。

===Original===
"'Pull, you divil!' says the squire.

"'At your sarvice, your honour,' says my father.

"'Pull harder,' says the squire.

"My father pulled like the divil.

"'I'll take a little sup,' says the squire, rachin' over his hand to the bottle, 'to keep up my courage,' says he, lettin' an to be very wake in himself intirely. But, as cute as he was, he was out here, for he tuk the wrong one. 'Here's to your good health, Terence,' says he; 'an' now pull like the very divil.' An' with that he lifted the bottle of holy wather, but it was hardly to his mouth, whin he let a screech out, you'd think the room id fairly split with it, an' made one chuck that sent the leg clane aff his body in my father's hands. Down wint the squire over the table, an' bang wint my father halfway across the room on his back, upon the flure. Whin he kem to himself the cheerful mornin' sun was shinin' through the windy shutthers, an' he was lying flat an his back, with the leg iv one of the great ould chairs pulled clane out iv the socket an' tight in his hand, pintin' up to the ceilin', an' ould Larry fast asleep, an' snorin' as loud as ever. My father wint that mornin' to Father Murphy, an' from that to the day of his death, he never neglected confission nor mass, an' what he tould was betther believed that he spake av it but seldom. An', as for the squire, that is the sperit, whether it was that he did not like his liquor, or by rason iv the loss iv his leg, he was never known to walk agin."

===Chinese===
"使劲拽，你这恶魔！"乡绅说。

"遵命，老爷，"我爹说。

"再使劲些，"乡绅说。

我爹拼了老命地拽。

"我来抿一小口，"乡绅说着，把手伸向酒瓶，"好壮壮胆，"他说，装出一副身子骨虚弱不堪的模样。可他再精明，这一回却失了手——抓错了瓶子。"祝你康健，特伦斯，"他说；"这一下你给我拼了老命地拽。"说着，他端起那瓶圣水，可酒瓶还没凑到嘴边，他便发出一声尖叫——您准以为那屋子都要给叫得裂开了——猛地一抽，竟把那条腿整个儿从他身上抽脱，留在我爹手里。那乡绅一头栽倒在桌上，我爹呢，向后一仰，砰地摔出去半个屋子，仰面朝天躺在地板上。待他神志清醒过来，明媚的晨光正从窗板缝隙里透进来，他直挺挺仰躺在地上，手里紧紧攥着一条腿——原来是从一张又大又旧的扶手椅上整个儿拔出来的椅腿，笔直地指向天花板——老拉里还在呼呼大睡，鼾声如旧。我爹那天一早就去找墨菲神父，从那日起直到寿终正寝，他再没有缺过一次告解，也没有漏过一台弥撒；他既难得开口，他说的话便越发为人所信。至于那位乡绅——也就是那个鬼魂——也不知是他不喜欢那"酒"呢，还是因为丢了那条腿的缘故，从此再没见他出来走动过。"

### Part I / 第一部

===Original===
About the year 1822 I resided in a comfortable and roomy old house, the exact locality of which I need not particularise, further than to say that it was not very far from Old Brompton, in the immediate neighbourhood, or rather continuity (as even my Connemara readers perfectly well know), of the renowned city of London.

Though this house was roomy and comfortable, as I have said, it was not, by any means, a handsome one. It was composed of dark red brick, with small windows, and thick white sashes; a porch, too﻿—none of your flimsy trellis-work, but a solid projection of the same vermillion masonry﻿—surmounted by a leaded balcony, with heavy, half-rotten balustrades, darkened the hall-door with a perennial gloom. The mansion itself stood in a walled enclosure, which had, perhaps, from the date of the erection itself, been devoted to shrubs and flowers. Some of the former had grown there almost to the dignity of trees; and two dark little yews stood at each side of the porch, like swart and inauspicious dwarfs, guarding the entrance of an enchanted castle. Not that my domicile in any respect deserved the comparison: it had no reputation as a haunted house; if it ever had any ghosts, nobody remembered them. Its history was not known to me: it may have witnessed plots, cabals, and forgeries, bloody suicides and cruel murders. It was certainly old enough to have become acquainted with iniquity; a small stone slab, under the balustrade, and over the arch of the porch I mentioned, had the date 1672, and a half-effaced coat of arms, which I might have deciphered any day, had I taken the trouble to get a ladder, but always put it off. All I can say for the house is, that it was well stricken in years, with a certain air of sombre comfort about it; contained a vast number of rooms and closets; and, what was of far greater importance, was got by me a dead bargain.

===Chinese===
大约一八二二年，我住在一幢宽敞舒适的旧宅子里。宅子的确切所在，我无须细说，只消提一句便够了——它离老布朗普顿（Old Brompton）不远，就在那座名城伦敦（London）的紧隔壁，或者说，本就是伦敦连绵不绝的一部分（这一点便是我康内马拉（Connemara）的读者也是再清楚不过的）。

这宅子虽说如我所言宽敞舒适，却算不得体面。它是暗红色的砖墙所砌，窗子小，窗框漆成厚厚的白色；门前一道门廊——不是那种单薄的格子棚，而是同样暗红砖石砌成的结实突出的建筑——上方是一道铅皮阳台，栏杆又粗又半朽，使大门常年笼罩在一层阴翳之中。宅子本身坐落在一片有围墙的院子里；这院子，怕是从宅子落成之日起，便辟作栽花植灌之用了。其中一些灌木几乎已长成了树木的模样；门廊两侧各立着一株深色的小紫杉，活像两个黝黑、不祥的侏儒，替一座魔堡把守着门口。倒并非我这住处当真配得上这般比譬：它素来没有凶宅的名声；纵然曾经闹过鬼，也没人记得了。它的来历我并不清楚：它或许目睹过阴谋、结党、伪造文书，目睹过血腥的自尽与残忍的凶杀。它的年纪确实已老到足以与种种罪孽相识；就在我方才所说的门廊拱顶之上、栏杆之下，嵌着一块小石板，上头刻着一六七二的年份，还有一面磨去了一半的纹章——只要我肯费事架一把梯子，哪一天都能辨认出来，却总是拖了又拖。关于这宅子，我能说的只是：它已届暮年，自有一股阴郁而安适的气息；里头的房间和储物小屋多得不可胜数；而更要紧的是，我是以极便宜的价钱把它弄到手的。

===Original===
Its individuality attracted me. I grew fond of it for itself, and for its associations, until other associations of a hateful kind first disturbed, and then destroyed, their charm. I forgave its dull red brick, and pinched white windows, for the sake of the beloved and cheerful faces within: its ugliness was softened by its age; and its sombre evergreens, and moss-grown stone flowerpots, were relieved by the brilliant hues of a thousand gay and graceful flowers that peeped among them, or nodded over the grass.

Within that old house lay my life’s treasure! I had a darling little girl of nine, and another little darling﻿—a boy﻿—just four years of age; and dearer, unspeakably, than either﻿—a wife﻿—the prettiest, gayest, best little wife in all London. When I tell you that our income was scarcely £380 a year, you will perceive that our establishment cannot have been a magnificent one; yet, I do assure you, we were more comfortable than a great many lords, and happier, I dare say, than the whole peerage put together.

This happiness was not, however, what it ought to have been. The reader will understand at once, and save me a world of moralising circumlocution, when he learns, bluntly and nakedly, that, among all my comforts and blessings, I was an infidel.

===Chinese===
正是它这份独特的脾性吸引了我。我因它本身、因它与我的种种牵系，渐渐生出眷恋——直到后来另一种可憎的牵缠先将这份情趣搅扰，又把它彻底毁了。我原谅它那暗沉的红砖和逼仄的白窗，全是为了屋里那些我钟爱的、欢快的容颜：岁月的痕迹冲淡了它的丑陋；它那些阴郁的常青灌木、生了青苔的石花盆，也因千万朵明艳婀娜、妍丽多姿的花儿——有的从灌丛中探出头来，有的在草地上方摇曳——而添了几分生气。

我这一生的珍宝，就安放在那座旧宅之中！我有一个心爱的小女儿，年方九岁；还有一个心爱的小宝贝——是个男孩——刚满四岁；而比这两个都更令我钟爱、爱到无以言表的——是我的妻子——全伦敦最美丽、最活泼、最贤良的小妻子。我告诉您，我们一年的进项不过区区三百八十镑，您便明白我们的排场断不会多么阔绰；然而，我可以向您保证，我们比许多贵族都过得舒坦，我甚至敢说，比整个上议院全体贵族加在一起都要快活。

然而，这份幸福却并不如它本该的那样。读者诸君一看便知，也省去我一番迂回的道德说教——只要坦白而直白地说出来就够了：在种种安逸与福分之中，我是个不信神的人。

===Original===
I had not been without religious training; on the contrary, more than average pains had been bestowed upon my religious instruction from my earliest childhood. My father, a good, plain, country clergyman, had worked hard to make me as good as himself; and had succeeded, at least, in training me in godly habits. He died, however, when I was but twelve years of age; and fate had long before deprived me of the gentle care of a mother. A boarding-school, followed by a college life, where nobody having any very direct interest in realising in my behalf the ancient blessing, that in fullness of time I should “die a good old man,” I was left very much to my own devices, which, in truth, were none of the best.

Among these were the study of Voltaire, Tom Paine, Hume, Shelley, and the whole school of infidels, poetical as well as prose. This pursuit, and the all but blasphemous vehemence with which I gave myself up to it, was, perhaps, partly reactionary. A somewhat injudicious austerity and precision had indissolubly associated in my childish days the ideas of restraint and gloom with religion. I bore it a grudge; and so, when I became thus early my own master, I set about paying off, after my own fashion, the old score I owed it. I was besides, like every other young infidel whom it has been my fate to meet, a conceited coxcomb. A smattering of literature, without any real knowledge, and a great assortment of all the cut-and-dry flippancies of the school I had embraced, constituted my intellectual stock in trade. I was, like most of my school of philosophy, very proud of being an unbeliever; and fancied myself, in the complacency of my wretched ignorance, at an immeasurable elevation above the churchgoing, Bible-reading herd, whom I treated with a good-humoured superciliousness which I thought vastly indulgent.

===Chinese===
我并非没有受过宗教的薰陶；恰恰相反，自幼年起，我所受的宗教教育便比常人更为用心。我的父亲是一位朴实善良的乡村牧师，他竭力想把我造就得同他一样善良；至少在培养我敬虔的习惯这一点上，他是成功的。然而，在我才十二岁那年，他便去世了；而命运更早之前便夺去了我母亲的温柔照料。先是一段寄宿学校的生活，继之以大学岁月——在那儿，没有谁对实现那句古老的祝福——"待时日圆满，我必善终高龄"——对我有什么直接的利害关系——我便任由自己胡作非为，而这些"主张"，老实说，没有几样是好的。

其中之一，便是研读伏尔泰（Voltaire）、汤姆·潘恩（Tom Paine）、休谟（Hume）、雪莱（Shelley），以及那一整个不信派的阵营——无论作诗的、为文的，统统包括在内。这份嗜好，以及我沉溺其中时那种近乎亵渎的狂热，或许有一部分是出于反激。幼时一种不甚得宜的严苛与刻板，竟将"拘束"与"阴郁"这两个观念与宗教牢牢绑在了一起，难分难解。我对它心存怨恨；于是，这么早便能自主之后，我便以自己的方式，开始清算这笔积年的旧账。再说，我与我所结识的每一个年轻的不信派一样，是个自负的花花公子。一星半点的文学皮毛，谈不上真知灼见，加上我所归附的那一派成套现成的轻薄辞令，便构成了我全部的智力家当。我同我那派"哲学家"里的大多数人一样，以做一个不信者而颇为自得；在我那可悲的无知的自满之中，我幻想自己高踞于那些上教堂、读《圣经》的芸芸众生之上，相去不可以道里计；我待他们以和颜悦色的傲慢，还自以为宽宏大量得很呢。

===Original===
My wife was an excellent little creature and truly pious. She had married me in the full confidence that my levity was merely put on, and would at once give way before the influence she hoped to exert upon my mind. Poor little thing! she deceived herself. I allowed her, indeed, to do entirely as she pleased; but for myself, I carried my infidelity to the length of an absolute superstition. I made an ostentation of it. I would rather have been in a “hell” than in a church on Sunday; and though I did not prevent my wife’s instilling her own principles into the minds of our children, I, in turn, took especial care to deliver mine upon all occasions in their hearing, by which means I trusted to sow the seeds of that unprejudiced scepticism in which I prided myself, at least as early as my good little partner dropped those of her own gentle “superstition” into their infant minds. Had I had my own absurd and impious will in this matter, my children should have had absolutely no religious education whatsoever, and been left wholly unshackled to choose for themselves among all existing systems, infidelity included, precisely as chance, fancy, or interest might hereafter determine.

It is not to be supposed that such a state of things did not afford her great uneasiness. Nevertheless, we were so very fond of one another, and in our humble way enjoyed so many blessings, that we were as entirely happy as any pair can be without the holy influence of religious sympathy.

===Chinese===
我的妻子是个极好的小可人儿，真心地敬虔。她嫁给我时，满心以为我的轻浮不过是装出来的，在她期望能施加于我心智的影响之下，便会立刻烟消云散。可怜的小东西！她是自欺欺人。我固然任由她完全自行其是；至于我自己，我把不信神奉到了一种近乎迷信的地步。我以之为炫耀的资本。礼拜日我宁肯进"地狱"也不进教堂；我虽不阻拦妻子把她自己的信条灌输给孩子们，反过来，我却格外留心，一有机会便要在他们听得见的地方发表我自己的主张——我指望借此把我引以为豪的那种不偏不倚的怀疑论的种子，至少与我那位贤良的伴侣把她那温柔的"迷信"的种子播进孩子们幼小的心田一样早地播下去。倘若在这件事上能由着我那荒谬而亵渎的心意，我的孩子们就根本不该受任何宗教教育，完全不受拘束地在世间一切现有的体系——包括不信派在内——之间自行选择，恰如日后机缘、喜好或利害所决定的那样。

这样的局面，自然不会不令她大为不安。然而，我们彼此又是这般恩爱，又在我们简朴的日子里享着这许多福分，所以若说没有宗教同情那份神圣的感化，我们便算得上一对顶顶美满的夫妻了。

===Original===
But the even flow of prosperity which had for so long gladdened my little household was not destined to last forever. It was ordained that I should experience the bitter truth of more than one of the wise man’s proverbs, and first, especially, of that which declares that “he that hateth suretyship is sure.” I found myself involved (as how many have been before) by a “d﻿—﻿—﻿d good-natured friend,” for more than two hundred pounds. This agreeable intelligence was conveyed to me in an attorney’s letter, which, to obviate unpleasant measures, considerately advised my paying the entire amount within just one week of the date of his pleasant epistle. Had I been called upon within that time to produce the Pitt diamond, or to make title to the Buckingham estates, the demand would have been just as easily complied with.

I have no wish to bore my reader further with this little worry﻿—a very serious one to me, however﻿—and it will be enough to mention, that the kindness of a friend extricated me from the clutches of the law by a timely advance, which, however, I was bound to replace within two years. To enable me to fulfill this engagement, my wife and I, after repeated consultations, resolved upon the course which resulted in the odd and unpleasant consequences which form the subject of this narrative.

We resolved to advertise for a lodger, with or without board, etc.; and by resolutely submitting, for a single year, to the economy we had prescribed for ourselves, as well as to the annoyance of a stranger’s intrusion, we calculated that at the end of that term we should have liquidated our debt.

===Chinese===
然而，长久以来让我这小家充满欢喜的那一帆风顺的顺境，注定不能永驻。命定我要亲身体验智者不止一句箴言的苦涩真理，而首先、尤其是这一句："厌弃作保的，得以安稳。"我发觉自己（正如从前许多人那样）被一位"该死的好心朋友"牵连进去，背了二百多镑的债务。这桩"可喜的消息"，是由一位律师的来信通知我的；为了避免不愉快的措施，那封信体贴入微地劝我在他这封"愉快的信函"发出之后短短一星期之内，便将全数付清。纵然在此时限之内要我拿出皮特钻石（Pitt diamond），或证明我对白金汉（Buckingham）家产享有继承权，这要求也同样容易应承。

我不愿用这桩小小的烦恼——于我却是十分严重的一桩——再为难读者，只消说一句便够：一位朋友的善意及时垫款，将我从法律的魔爪中解救出来；然而这笔款子，我却有义务在两年之内归还。为了让我能履行这一承诺，我和妻子几经商议，终于定下了一条计策——其结果，便是那桩古怪而不愉快的后果，构成了本篇叙事的题材。

我们决意登报招租一位房客，不论是否包伙食，等等；只要我们硬着头皮，忍上区区一年，既受自己定下的俭省之苦，又忍一个外人闯入的烦恼，我们盘算着到了年终，便能还清这笔债。

===Original===
Accordingly, without losing time, we composed an advertisement in the most tempting phraseology we could devise, consistently with that economic laconism which the cost per line in the columns of the *Times* newspaper imposes upon the rhetoric of the advertising public.

Somehow we were unlucky; for although we repeated our public notification three times in the course of a fortnight, we had but two applications. The one was from a clergyman in ill health﻿—a man of great ability and zealous piety, whom we both knew by reputation, and who has since been called to his rest. My good little wife was very anxious that we should close with his offer, which was very considerably under what we had fixed upon; and I have no doubt that she was influenced by the hope that his talents and zeal might exert a happy influence upon my stubborn and unbelieving heart. For my part, his religious character displeased me. I did not wish my children’s heads to be filled with mythic dogmas﻿—for so I judged the doctrines of our holy faith﻿—and instinctively wished him away. I therefore declined his offer; and I have often since thought not quite so graciously as I ought to have done. The other offer﻿—if so it can be called﻿—was so very inadequate that we could not entertain it.

===Chinese===
于是，我们毫不耽搁，拟出一则广告，措辞力求诱人，却又不得不迁就《泰晤士报》（*Times*）栏目里按行计费所带来的那种节俭简短——这种简短，强加在登广告的公众的辞藻之上。

不知怎的，我们运气不佳；虽然在一 fortnight——两周之内，我们将这则公示登了三次，应征者却只有两个。一位是个体弱多病的牧师——此人学问渊博、敬虔热忱，我们两人都久闻其名，他如今已被主召去安息了。我那贤良的小妻子巴不得我们答应他的提议，虽然他出的价钱比我们定的要低得多；我毫不怀疑，她是寄望于他的才学与热忱，能在我这顽固不信的心上施加一点良好的影响。至于我呢，他那宗教的脾气却令我不快。我不愿我孩子们的脑袋里塞满神话式的教条——我那时便是这样判断我们神圣信仰的诸般教义的——本能地不愿他来。于是我回绝了他；事后回想，我常觉得当时回绝得未免太不客气了些。另一个提议——若是称得上"提议"的话——价钱实在太低，我们根本无法考虑。

===Original===
I was now beginning to grow seriously uneasy﻿—our little project, so far from bringing in the gains on which we had calculated, had put me considerably out of pocket; for, independently of the cost of the advertisement I have mentioned, there were sundry little expenses involved in preparing for the meet reception of our expected inmate, which, under ordinary circumstances, we should not have dreamed of. Matters were in this posture, when an occurrence took place which immediately revived my flagging hopes.

As we had no superfluity of servants, our children were early obliged to acquire habits of independence; and my little girl, then just nine years of age, was frequently consigned with no other care than that of her own good sense, to the companionship of a little band of playmates, pretty similarly circumstanced, with whom it was her wont to play. Having one fine summer afternoon gone out as usual with these little companions, she did not return quite so soon as we had expected her; when she did so, she was out of breath, and excited.

===Chinese===
我如今当真开始着急起来——我们这点小盘算，不仅没有带来所指望的进项，反倒叫我贴了不少钱；因为除了方才所说的广告费之外，为了体面地接待我们期待的房客，还免不了有些零碎的开销，这些东西在寻常时日里，我们做梦也不会想到。事情正处在这般田地，忽然发生了一件事，顿时叫我那渐渐低落的心气又振作了起来。

我们家仆人不多，孩子们早早便不得不养成自立的习惯；我的小女儿，那年刚满九岁，常常只凭她自己的机灵，便被交托给一小群玩伴——那些孩子的境况与她相去无几——和她们一块儿玩耍。一个晴朗的夏日午后，她照旧和这些小伙伴一道出门，却没有像我们预期的那样早早回来；待到回来时，气喘吁吁，一脸兴奋。


===Original===
"Oh, papa," she said, "I have seen such a nice old, kind gentleman, and he told me to tell you that he has a particular friend who wants a lodging in a quiet place, and that he thinks your house would suit him exactly, and ever so much more; and, look here, he gave me this."

She opened her hand, and showed me a sovereign.

"Well, this does look promisingly," I said, my wife and I having first exchanged a smiling glance.

"And what kind of gentleman was he, dear?" inquired she. "Was he well dressed﻿—whom was he like?"

"He was not like anyone that I know," she answered; "but he had very nice new clothes on, and he was one of the fattest men I ever saw; and I am sure he is sick, for he looks very pale, and he had a crutch beside him."

"Dear me, how strange!" exclaimed my wife; though, in truth there was nothing very wonderful in the matter. "Go on, child," I said; "let us hear it all out."

"Well, papa, he had such an immense yellow waistcoat!﻿—I never did see such a waistcoat," she resumed; "and he was sitting or leaning, I can't say which, against the bank of the green lane; I suppose to rest himself, for he seems very weak, poor gentleman!"

"And how did you happen to speak to him?" asked my wife.

"When we were passing by, none of us saw him at all but I suppose he heard them talking to me, and saying my name; for he said, 'Fanny﻿—little Fanny﻿—so, that's your name﻿—come here child, I have a question to ask you.'"

"And so you went to him?" I said.

"Yes," she continued, "he beckoned to me, and I did go over to him, but not very near, for I was greatly afraid of him at first."

"Afraid! dear, and why afraid?" asked I.

"I was afraid, because he looked very old, very frightful, and as if he would hurt me."

"What was there so old and frightful about him?" I asked.

She paused and reflected a little, and then said﻿—

"His face was very large and pale, and it was looking upwards: it seemed very angry, I thought, but maybe it was angry from pain; and sometimes one side of it used to twitch and tremble for a minute, and then to grow quite still again; and all the time he was speaking to me, he never looked at me once, but always kept his face and eyes turned upwards; but his voice was very soft, and he called me little Fanny, and gave me this pound to buy toys with; so I was not so frightened in a little time, and then he sent a long message to you, papa, and told me if I forgot it he would beat me; but I knew he was only joking, so that did not frighten me either."

"And what was the message, my girl?" I asked, patting her pretty head with my hand.

"Now, let me remember it all," she said, reflectively; "for he told it to me twice. He asked me if there was a good bedroom at the top of the house, standing by itself﻿—and you know there is, so I told him so; it was exactly the kind of room that he described. And then he said that his friend would pay two hundred pounds a year for that bedroom, his board and attendance; and he told me to ask you, and have your answer when he should next meet me."

"Two hundred pounds!" ejaculated my poor little wife; "why that is nearly twice as much as we expected."

"But did he say that his friend was sick, or very old; or that he had any servant to be supported also?" I asked.

"Oh! no; he told me that he was quite able to take care of himself, and that he had, I think he called it, an asthma, but nothing else the matter; and that he would give no trouble at all, and that any friend who came to see him, he would see, not in the house, but only in the garden."

"In the garden!" I echoed, laughing in spite of myself.

"Yes, indeed he said so; and he told me to say that he would pay one hundred pounds when he came here, and the next hundred in six months, and so on," continued she.

"Oh, ho! half-yearly in advance﻿—better and better," said I.

"And he bid me say, too, if you should ask about his character, that he is just as good as the master of the house himself," she added; "and when he said that, he laughed a little."

===Chinese===
"哦，爸爸，"她说，"我遇见了一位又好又和气的老先生！他让我告诉您，他有一位特别的朋友，想在一处清静的地方租间房住，他觉得您这宅子再合适不过了，还有好多好多话呢；您瞧，他给了我这个。"

她摊开手心，给我看一枚索维林（sovereign）。

"嗯，这事儿看着倒有几分指望。"我说着，与妻子先交换了一个会心的微笑。

"他是个什么样的人呢，亲爱的？"妻子问道，"他穿得体面吗——长得像谁？"

"他不像我认识的任何人，"她答道，"不过他穿着很讲究的新衣裳，是我所见过的最胖的男人之一；我敢说他准是生了病，因为他脸色很苍白，身边还放着一根拐杖。"

"哎呀，好奇怪！"我妻子嚷道——虽说这事其实并无甚稀奇。"接着讲，孩子，"我说，"让我们把话听完。"

"是这样的，爸爸，他穿了一件好大好大的黄马甲！——我从来没见过那样的马甲，"她接着说，"他坐在、或者靠在——我说不清是坐着还是靠着——那条绿径的土坡上；我猜是在歇脚吧，因为他看起来虚弱得很，可怜的先生！"

"那你是怎么同他搭上话的呢？"妻子问。

"我们一行人经过的时候，谁都没瞧见他，可我猜他是听见她们跟我说话、叫我的名字了；因为他说：'范妮——小范妮——哦，原来你叫这个名儿——过来，孩子，我有句话要问你。'"

"于是你就走到他跟前去了？"我说。

"是的，"她接着说，"他朝我招手，我确实走了过去，却没敢靠得太近，因为起先我怕他怕得厉害。"

"怕！亲爱的，怕什么呢？"我问。

"我怕，是因为他看起来很老、很吓人，好像要伤害我似的。"

"他哪里老、哪里吓人了？"我问。

她顿了顿，想了一想，然后说——

"他的脸又大又白，脸是朝上仰着的：我看那神气像是很愤怒，不过也许是疼得发怒；有时候，他半边脸会抽搐、颤抖上一阵，然后又完全静下来；他跟我说话的工夫，一次也没看过我，脸和眼睛老是一直朝上翻着；可他的声音却很温和，他叫我小范妮，又给我这一镑钱买玩具；所以过了一会儿我就不那么怕了；接着他托我给你捎一段好长的话，爸爸，还说要是我忘了，他就打我；可我知道他不过是开玩笑，所以这一点也没叫我害怕。"

"那话是怎么说的，我的好姑娘？"我问，伸手拍拍她那漂亮的小脑袋。

"让我好好把它全想起来，"她若有所思地说，"因为他跟我讲了两遍呢。他问我，房子顶上有没有一间好卧室，是单独一间——您知道的，确实有，我便告诉了他；那正是他所形容的那种房间。然后他说，他的朋友愿意为那间卧室、连同伙食和照应，一年付二百镑；他叫我回来问问您，等他下次见我时，把您的回话带给他。"

"二百镑！"我那可怜的小妻子失声惊呼，"哎呀，这可比我们预期的几乎多出一倍呢。"

"可他有没有说，他那位朋友是不是有病，或者上了年纪；又或者还要带个仆人一块儿来，也得供他吃住？"我问。

"哦！没有；他对我说，他那位朋友完全能照料自己，他好像说是有——我想他是这么叫的——气喘病，可旁的没什么毛病；还说一点也不费事；又说凡是有朋友来看他，他都不在屋里见，只在花园里见。"

"在花园里！"我不禁失笑，重复了一句。

"是的，他确实这么说的；他还叫我对您说，他来的时候先付一百镑，半年后再付下一个一百镑，往后以此类推，"她接着说。

"哦嗬！每半年预付一次——越来越好了。"我说。

"他还叫我说，倘若您问起他的为人，他跟这宅子的主人一样靠得住呢，"她又补充道，"他说这话的时候，还笑了笑。"


===Original===
"Why, if he gives us a hundred pounds in advance," I answered, turning to my wife, "we are safe enough; for he will not find half that value in plate and jewels in the entire household, if he is disposed to rob us. So I see no reason against closing with the offer, should it be seriously meant﻿—do you, dear?"

"Quite the contrary, love," said she. "I think it most desirable﻿—indeed, most *providential*."

"Providential! my dear little bigot!" I repeated, with a smile. "Well, be it so. I call it *lucky* merely; but, perhaps, you are happier in your faith, than I in my philosophy. Yes, you are *grateful* for the chance that I only rejoice at. You receive it as a proof of a divine and tender love﻿—I as an accident. Delusions are often more elevating than truth."

And so saying, I kissed away the saddened cloud that for a moment overcast her face.

"Papa, he bid me be sure to have an answer for him when we meet again," resumed the child. "What shall I say to him when he asks me?"

"Say that we agree to his proposal, my dear﻿—or stay," I said, addressing my wife, "may it not be prudent to reduce what the child says to writing, and accept the offer so? This will prevent misunderstanding, as she may possibly have made some mistake."

===Chinese===
"嘿，他要是预付咱们一百镑，"我转过身对妻子说，"我们就稳妥得很了；他纵然存心打劫，把这全家上下的金银器皿和珠宝加在一块儿，也凑不到这数的一半呢。所以我看不出有什么理由不答应这桩买卖——倘若他是当真的——你说呢，亲爱的？"

"岂止是没有理由不答应，亲爱的，"她说，"我看这事再称心不过了——简直是上天的眷顾。"

"上天的眷顾！我亲爱的小教徒！"我微笑着重复道，"好吧，便算是吧。我不过叫它走运罢了；不过，你守着你的信仰，或许比我守着我的哲学要快活些。是啊，你把这机缘当作恩赐而心存感激，我不过是逢着喜事而高兴。你把它当作神那温柔慈爱的明证——我则当作一桩偶然。迷误往往比真理更能令人升华。"

说着，我以亲吻驱散了一瞬间掠过她脸上的那层愁云。

"爸爸，他叫我一定得有个回话，等下次见面时给他，"孩子又开口道，"他问我的时候，我该怎么说呢？"

"就说我们答应他的提议，亲爱的——或者，等等，"我转向妻子说道，"把孩子的话落笔写成字据，照此应承下来，岂不更稳妥？这样免得生出误会，她说不定已记岔了什么。"


===Original===
My wife agreed, and I wrote a brief note, stating that I was willing to receive an inmate upon the terms recounted by little Fanny, and which I distinctly specified, so that no mistake could possibly arise owing to the vagueness of what lawyers term a parole agreement. This important memorandum I placed in the hands of my little girl, who was to deliver it whenever the old gentleman in the yellow waistcoat should chance to meet her. And all these arrangements completed, I awaited the issue of the affair with as much patience as I could affect. Meanwhile, my wife and I talked it over incessantly; and she, good little soul, almost wore herself to death in settling and unsettling the furniture and decorations of our expected inmate’s apartments. Days passed away﻿—days of hopes deferred, tedious and anxious. We were beginning to despond again, when one morning our little girl ran into the breakfast-parlour, more excited even than she had been before, and fresh from a new interview with the gentleman in the yellow waistcoat. She had encountered him suddenly, pretty nearly where she had met him before, and the result was, that he had read the little note I have mentioned, and desired the child to inform me that his friend, *Mr. Smith*, would take possession of the apartments I proposed setting, on the terms agreed between us, that very evening.

"This evening!" exclaimed my wife and I simultaneously﻿—*I* full of the idea of making a first instalment on the day following; *she*, of the hundred-and-one preparations which still remained to be completed.

"And so Smith is his name! Well, that does not tell us much," said I; "but where did you meet your friend on this occasion, and how long is it since?"

"Near the corner of the wallflower lane (so we indicated one which abounded in these fragrant plants); he was leaning with his back against the old tree you cut my name on, and his crutch was under his arm."

"But how long ago?" I urged.

"Only this moment; I ran home as fast as I could," she replied.

"Why, you little blockhead, you should have told me that at first," I cried, snatching up my hat, and darting away in pursuit of the yellow waistcoat, whose acquaintance I not unnaturally coveted, inasmuch as a man who, for the first time, admits a stranger into his house, on the footing of permanent residence, desires generally to know a little more about him than that his name is Smith.

The place indicated was only, as we say, a step away; and as yellow waistcoat was fat, and used a crutch, I calculated on easily overtaking him. I was, however, disappointed; crutch, waistcoat, and all had disappeared. I climbed to the top of the wall, and from this commanding point of view made a sweeping observation﻿—but in vain. I returned home, cursing my ill-luck, the child’s dullness, and the fat old fellow’s activity.

===Chinese===
妻子应允了，我便写了一张简短的便条，说明我愿按小范妮所述的条件接待一位房客——这些条件我一一条陈分明，以免因律师所谓的"口头约定"含糊不清而横生误会。这张要紧的字据，我交到了小女儿手上，嘱咐她但逢那位穿黄马甲的老先生碰见她，便当面交付与他。这一切安排妥当之后，我便尽可能装出一副耐心的模样，静候此事的结局。与此同时，我和妻子不住地谈论这件事；她呀，这个好心肠的小人儿，为了张罗我们这位未来房客房里的家具摆设，搬来搬去、摆来弄去，几乎把自己折腾得半死。日子一天天过去——尽是些希望落空、既沉闷又焦灼的日子。我们正又开始灰心的时候，一天早上，我们的小女儿冲进早餐间，比上次还要兴奋，刚跟那位黄马甲先生见过了第二面。她是几乎就在原先遇见他的地方，猝不及防地又撞见了他，结果是：他已读过我所写的那张便条，并嘱咐孩子告诉我，他的朋友史密斯先生（Mr. Smith），将于当天傍晚，按我们谈定的条件，搬进我所腾出的那几间屋子。

"今天傍晚！"我和妻子不约而同地失声叫起来——我满脑子想的是第二天便能拿到头一笔款子；她呢，想到的则是尚待完成的那一百零一样预备功夫。

"哦，原来他叫史密斯！嘿，这名字也没告诉咱们多少，"我说，"可这回你在哪儿遇见你那位朋友的，多久以前的事？"

"就在桂竹香小径的拐角附近（我们平日里把那条长满了这种香花的小径这么叫）；他背靠着您刻我名字的那棵老树站着，腋下夹着他的拐杖。"

"可这有多久了？"我追问。

"就这一会儿；我拼命跑回来的。"她答道。

"哎呀，你这小笨蛋，该先说这个才对啊！"我嚷道，一把抓起帽子，飞也似的追那件黄马甲去了——我巴不得结识他，原也是人之常情：一个人头一回把一个生人接进自己家里、当作长住客，自然想知道些那人的底细，总不能光知道他姓史密斯便罢了。

所说的那个地方，照我们的说法，不过几步路；黄马甲既胖，又拄着拐杖，我盘算着轻易便能追上。然而我失望了——拐杖也好，马甲也好，连人带物，统统不见了。我爬上墙头，从这一处居高临下的地势四下张望——却是枉然。我满腹牢骚地回了家，咒自己的晦气，咒孩子的迟钝，也咒那胖老头儿腿脚竟这般利索。


===Original===
I need hardly say that Mr. Smith, in all his aspects, moral, social, physical, and monetary, formed a fruitful and interesting topic of speculation during dinner. How many phantom Smiths, short and long, stout and lean, ill-tempered and well-tempered﻿—rich, respectable, or highly dangerous merchants, spies, forgers, nabobs, swindlers, danced before us, in the endless mazes of fanciful conjecture, during that anxious tête-à-tête, which was probably to be interrupted by the arrival of the gentleman himself.

My wife and I puzzled over the problem as people would over the possible denouement of a French novel; and at last, by mutual consent, we came to the conclusion that Smith could, and would turn out to be no other than the good-natured valetudinarian in the yellow waistcoat himself, a humorist, as was evident enough, and a millionaire, as we unhesitatingly pronounced, who had no immediate relatives, and as I hoped, and my wife "was certain," taken a decided fancy to our little Fanny; I patted the child’s head with something akin to pride, as I thought of the magnificent, though remote possibilities, in store for her.

Meanwhile, hour after hour stole away. It was a beautiful autumn evening, and the amber lustre of the declining sun fell softly upon the yews and flowers, and gave an air, half melancholy, half cheerful, to the dark-red brick piers surmounted with their cracked and grass-grown stone urns, and furnished with the light foliage of untended creeping plants. Down the short broad walk leading to this sombre entrance, my eye constantly wandered; but no impatient rattle on the latch, no battering at the gate, indicated the presence of a visitor, and the lazy bell hung dumbly among the honeysuckles.

"When will he come? Yellow waistcoat promised *this evening*! It has been evening a good hour and a half, and yet he is not here. When will he come? It will soon be dark﻿—the evening will have passed﻿—will he come at all?"

Such were the uneasy speculations which began to trouble us. Redder and duskier grew the light of the setting sun, till it saddened into the mists of night. Twilight came, and then darkness, and still no arrival, no summons at the gate. I would not admit even to my wife the excess of my own impatience. I could, however, stand it no longer; so I took my hat and walked to the gate, where I stood by the side of the public road, watching every vehicle and person that approached, in a fever of expectation. Even these, however, began to fail me, and the road grew comparatively quiet and deserted. Having kept guard like a sentinel for more than half an hour, I returned in no very good humour, with the punctuality of an expected inmate﻿—ordered the servant to draw the curtains and secure the hall-door; and so my wife and I sat down to our disconsolate cup of tea. It must have been about ten o’clock, and we were both sitting silently﻿—she working, I looking moodily into a paper﻿—and neither of us any longer entertaining a hope that anything but disappointment would come of the matter, when a sudden tapping, very loud and sustained, upon the window pane, startled us both in an instant from our reveries.

===Chinese===
不消说，晚饭席上，史密斯先生其人——无论从道德、社交、形貌、财力哪一面看——都成了一个聊不尽、想不完的话题。在那一场惴惴不安、又或许随时会被这位先生本人登门打断的夫妻对谈中，有多少个影影绰绰的史密斯——高矮不一，胖瘦不等，脾气或好或坏——富商、体面客，或险恶的买卖人、奸细、伪造文书者、巨富、骗子——在我们眼前翩翩起舞，走进了无尽无休、异想天开的迷宫里去。

我和妻子埋头猜这道谜，犹如世人猜一部法国小说可能的结局那般；末了，我们不谋而合地得出结论：史密斯非他，必是那位好脾气的、穿黄马甲的半病老头儿本人无疑——此人显然是个怪人，而我们则一口咬定是个百万富翁，膝下并无至亲；如我所盼、如妻子所"断言"的那样，他已经对我们的小范妮生了十分的喜爱；我抚摸着孩子的头，心里头竟有几分与有荣焉之感，一面琢磨着那虽则遥远、却辉煌万分的种种可能，正等候着她呢。

其时，一个钟头又一个钟头悄无声息地溜走了。那是个美丽的秋夕，将落的太阳投下一层琥珀色的柔光，洒在紫杉和花丛之上，给那暗红色的砖砌门柱——柱顶安着开裂生草的石瓮，攀着无人料理的藤蔓疏落的绿叶——添上半忧半喜的情致。通往这道阴沉入口的那条又短又宽的小径，我的目光不住地往那儿溜；然而门闩上没有急不可耐的哐当声，大门上也没有敲击声，显示有客来临；那口懒洋洋的铃铛，在忍冬藤间默然无语。

"他什么时候来呢？黄马甲明明说的是今天傍晚！傍晚已过去了一个半钟头，他还是没到。他什么时候来呢？天就要黑了——傍晚就要过去了——他到底还来不来了？"

这般惴惴不安的揣测，开始搅扰起我们来。落日的光焰越变越红、越变越暗，终于沉入夜的薄雾里去了。暮色降临，继之以黑暗，却仍不见人来，也不见门口有何动静。我甚至不愿向妻子承认我自己的焦躁已到了何等地步。然而，我到底再也捱不住了；于是戴上帽子，走到大门口，站在大路旁，满怀期望地盯着每一辆驶来、每一个走近的车马行人。然而，连这些也渐渐稀少了，路上变得相对清静、空寂起来。我像哨兵似的守了半个多钟头，满心不痛快地回了家——料想那位该来的房客倒是比我还守时——吩咐仆人拉上窗帘，关好大门；于是我和妻子相对坐下，闷闷地喝起茶来。大约是十点钟光景，我们俩默默坐着——她做针线，我闷闷地盯着一张报纸——彼此都不再指望这事会有什么好结局，除了失望而外，就在这时，窗玻璃上忽然传来一阵叩击声，又急又响，持续不断，霎时间把我们俩都从遐想中惊醒了。


===Original===
I am not sure whether I mentioned before that the sitting-room we occupied was upon the ground-floor, and the sward came close under the window. I drew the curtains, and opened the shutters with a revived hope; and looking out, saw a very tall thin figure, a good deal wrapped up, standing about a yard before me, and motioning with head and hand impatiently towards the hall-door. Though the night was clear, there was no moon, and therefore I could see no more than the black outline, like that of an *ombre chinoise* figure, signing to me with mop and moe. In a moment I was at the hall-door, candle in hand; the stranger stepped in﻿—his long fingers clutched in the handle of a valise, and a bag which trailed upon the ground behind him.

The light fell full upon him. He wore a long, ill-made, black surtout, buttoned across, and which wrinkled and bagged about his lank figure; his hat was none of the best, and rather broad in the brim; a sort of white woollen muffler enveloped the lower part of his face; a pair of prominent green goggles, fenced round with leather, completely concealed his eyes; and nothing of the genuine man, but a little bit of yellow forehead, and a small transverse segment of equally yellow cheek and nose, encountered the curious gaze of your humble servant.

"You are﻿—I suppose﻿—" I began; for I really was a little doubtful about my man.

"Mr. Smith﻿—the same; be good enough to show me to my bedchamber," interrupted the stranger, brusquely, and in a tone which, spite of the muffler that enveloped his mouth, was sharp and grating enough.

"Ha!﻿—Mr. Smith﻿—so I supposed. I hope you may find everything as comfortable as we desire to make it﻿—"

I was about making a speech, but was cut short by a slight bow, and a decisive gesture of the hand in the direction of the staircase. It was plain that the stranger hated ceremony.

Together, accordingly, we mounted the staircase; he still pulling his luggage after him, and striding lightly up without articulating a word; and on reaching his bedroom, he immediately removed his hat, showing a sinister, black scratch-wig underneath, and then began unrolling the mighty woolen wrapping of his mouth and chin.

"Come," thought I, "we *shall* see something of your face after all."

This something, however, proved to be very little; for under his muffler was a loose cravat, which stood up in front of his chin and upon his mouth, he wore a respirator﻿—an instrument which I had never seen before, and of the use of which I was wholly ignorant.

There was something so excessively odd in the effect of this piece of unknown mechanism upon his mouth, surmounted by the huge goggles which encased his eyes, that I believe I should have laughed outright, were it not for a certain unpleasant and peculiar impressiveness in the *tout ensemble* of the narrow-chested, long-limbed, and cadaverous figure in black.
