As it was, we stood looking at one another in silence for several seconds.

"Thank you, sir," at last he said, abruptly. "I shan’t want anything whatever tonight; if you can only spare me this candle."

I assented; and, becoming more communicative, he added﻿—

"I am, though an invalid, an independent sort of fellow enough. I am a bit of a philosopher; I am my own servant, and, I hope, my own master, too. I rely upon myself in matters of the body and of the mind. I place valets and priests in the same category﻿—fellows who live by our laziness, intellectual or corporeal. I am a Voltaire, without his luxuries﻿—a Robinson Crusoe, without his Bible﻿—an anchorite, without a superstition﻿—in short, my indulgence is asceticism, and my faith infidelity. Therefore, I shan’t disturb your servants much with my bell, nor yourselves with my psalmody. You have got a rational lodger, who knows how to attend upon himself."

===Chinese===
我一时记不清先前可曾提过：我们坐的那间起居室是在底楼，窗下便是草坪。我拉开窗帘，怀着一线重生的希望推开窗板；往外一瞧，只见一个又高又瘦的身影，裹得严严实实，离我约莫一码远站着，正不耐烦地以头和手朝大门那边比划。夜色虽清，却没有月亮，因此我也只能看见一个黑黝黝的轮廓，活像中国皮影（ombre chinoise）里的人形，冲我连连点头招手。一转眼我便提着蜡烛到了大门口；那位生客一步跨了进来——他瘦长的手指攥着一只旅行提箱的把手，身后还拖着一只在地上蹭的口袋。

灯光直直地照在他身上。他穿一件又长又做得蹩脚的黑色礼服大衣，从前胸一路扣过来，在他那瘦骨嶙峋的身上皱成一团、坠成一个个袋；帽子也谈不上好，帽檐还挺宽；下半张脸裹着一条白毛线围脖似的东西；一副鼓鼓的绿色风镜，镶着一圈皮边，把眼睛遮得严严实实；至于真正的人脸，露出来的不过是一小片蜡黄的额头，外加一小条横着的、同样蜡黄的脸颊和鼻子——这便是落进鄙人好奇眼帘的全部了。

"您是——我想是——"我开口道；因为我当真有点拿不准我这人。

"史密斯——正是本人；劳驾领我到我的卧室去。"这位生客粗声粗气地打断我，那嗓音虽隔着裹嘴的围脖，依旧又尖又刺耳。

"哈！——史密斯先生——我正是这么猜的。但愿您会觉得一切都如我们愿意做的那样妥帖——"

我正要说上一番客套话，却被他微微一鞠躬、又朝楼梯那边果断地一挥手，打断了。很显然，这位生客讨厌客套。

于是我们便一道上了楼；他依旧拖着行李，步履轻捷地拾级而上，一言不发；到了他的卧室，他立刻摘下帽子，露出底下一顶阴森森的黑色粗毛假发，接着便动手解开裹在嘴和下巴上那一大团毛线围裹。

"好啊，"我心想，"这一回总该能瞧见你几分真容了。"

然而这"几分"结果却是少之又少；因为围脖底下是一条松松的领巾，竖在下巴和嘴的前面，他嘴上还戴着一个口鼻罩——一种我从未见过的器械——，更不知它的用处。

这件叫人摸不着头脑的玩意儿安在他嘴上，上头又压着那副罩住双眼的大风镜，那效果古怪到了极点，我想要不是他那一身黑衣、窄胸、长肢、死灰般的人影，整体的气派里有一种说不出的、叫人很不舒服却又别具慑人力量的东西，我准会当场失笑。但事实上，我们俩默默相对，对看了好几秒钟。

"谢谢您，先生，"末了他突兀地说，"今夜我什么都不需要；您只消把这根蜡烛留给我就成。"

我应承了；他便话多起来，又添了几句——

"我虽说是个病夫，倒是个顶独立的人。我算得上半个哲学家；我自己的仆人是我自己，我希望我自己的主人也是我自己。无论身子的事、还是心的事，我一概仰仗自己。我把贴身男仆和神父归为一类——都是靠我们的懒惰——无论是智识上的还是肉体上的懒惰——而活命的家伙。我是个没有伏尔泰那些奢华的伏尔泰——是个没有《圣经》的鲁滨逊（Robinson Crusoe）——是个没有迷信的苦行僧——一句话，我的放纵便是苦行，我的信仰便是不信。所以，我打铃不会怎么搅扰您的仆人，唱圣诗也不会搅扰您二位。您得到的是一位讲理性的房客，懂得如何伺候自己。"


===Original===
During this singular address he was drawing off his ill-fitting black gloves, and when he had done so, a banknote, which had been slipped underneath for safety, remained in his hand.

"Punctuality, sir, is one of my poor pleasures," he said; "will you allow me to enjoy it now? Tomorrow you may acknowledge this; I should not rest were you to decline it."

He extended his bony and discoloured fingers, and placed the note in my hand. Oh, Fortune and Plutus! It was a £100 banknote.

"Pray, not one word, my dear sir," he continued, unbending still further; "it is simply done pursuant to agreement. We shall know one another better, I hope, in a little time; you will find me always equally punctual. At present pray give yourself no further trouble; I require nothing more. Good night."

I returned the valediction, closed his door, and groped my way down the stairs. It was not until I had nearly reached the hall, that I recollected that I had omitted to ask our new inmate at what hour he would desire to be called in the morning, and so I groped my way back again. As I reached the lobby on which his chamber opened, I perceived a long line of light issuing from the partially-opened door, within which stood Mr. Smith, the same odd figure I had just left; while along the boards was creeping towards him across the lobby, a great, big-headed, buff-coloured cat. I had never seen this ugly animal before; and it had reached the threshold of his door, arching its back, and rubbing itself on the post, before either appeared conscious of my approach, when, with an angry growl, it sprang into the stranger’s room.

"What do you want?" he demanded, sharply, standing in the doorway.

I explained my errand.

"I shall call myself," was his sole reply; and he shut the door with a crash that indicated no very pleasurable emotions.

I cared very little about my lodger’s temper. The stealthy rustle of his banknote in my waistcoat pocket was music enough to sweeten the harshest tones of his voice, and to keep alive a cheerful good humour in my heart; and although there was, indisputably, something queer about him, I was, on the whole, very well pleased with my bargain.

===Chinese===
他发表这番奇特的演说时，正把那双不合手的黑手套一只只褪下来；褪完之后，底下夹着的一张为稳妥起见塞在里头的钞票，便留在了他手里。

"准时，先生，是我这可怜人的一点小小乐趣，"他说，"您肯让我此刻便享受一番吗？明日您再正式收下这张收据不迟；您若是推却，我反倒不得安生了。"

他伸出那骨节嶙峋、颜色发暗的手指，把那张钞票放到我手里。哦，命运女神和财神爷啊！那是一张一百镑的钞票。

"求您，一个字也别说了，亲爱的先生，"他接着说，态度越发随和起来，"这不过是按约定办事罢了。但愿不久之后，咱们彼此便能熟稔些；您会发现我一向都是这般守时的。眼下，请不必再费神了；我别无所求。晚安。"

我回了声晚安，替他带上门，摸黑下了楼。直到我几乎走到门厅，才想起我忘了问我们这位新房客，早上要几点叫醒他，于是又摸黑折返回去。我刚走到他房间门口的那段过道，便瞧见一道长长的灯光从半开的门缝里泻出来——门里站着史密斯先生，正是我方才离开的那个古怪身影；而沿着地板，正有一只大脑袋、黄褐色的肥大猫咪，蹑手蹑脚地穿过过道朝他爬去。这只丑陋的畜生我从未见过；它已走到了他门槛前，弓起脊背，在门柱上蹭来蹭去，这一人一猫方才像是察觉我走近了——紧接着，它喉咙里发出一声怒吼，便蹿进了那位生客的房里。

"你要做什么？"他厉声喝问，站在门口。

我便把来意说了一遍。

"我自己会叫自己，"这是他唯一的回话；说罢砰地一声摔上了门——那动静听不出半点高兴的意思。

我这位房客的脾气如何，我是毫不在乎的。他那张钞票在我背心口袋里悄悄窸窣作响，于我便已是够美的乐章，足以把他的嗓音里最刺耳的调子都调成甜的，足以叫我心头一团和气；虽说此公身上，无可争辩地，确实有几分古怪，可总的说来，我对这桩买卖还是相当满意的。


===Original===
The next day our new inmate did not ring his bell until noon. As soon as he had had some breakfast, of which he very sparingly partook, he told the servant that, for the future, he desired that a certain quantity of milk and bread might be left outside his door; and this being done, he would dispense with regular meals. He desired, too, that, on my return, I should be acquainted that he wished to see me in his own room at about nine o’clock; and, meanwhile, he directed that he should be left undisturbed. I found my little wife full of astonishment at Mr. Smith’s strange frugality and seclusion, and very curious to learn the object of the interview he had desired with me. At nine o’clock I repaired to his room.

I found him in precisely the costume in which I had left him﻿—the same green goggles﻿—the same muffling of the mouth, except that being now no more than a broadly-folded black silk handkerchief, very loose, and covering even the lower part of the nose, it was obviously intended for the sole purpose of concealment. It was plain I was not to see more of his features than he had chosen to disclose at our first interview. The effect was as if the lower part of his face had some hideous wound or sore. He closed the door with his own hand on my entrance, nodded slightly, and took his seat. I expected him to begin, but he was so long silent that I was at last constrained to address him.

I said, for want of something more to the purpose, that I hoped he had not been tormented by the strange cat the night before.

"What cat?" he asked, abruptly; "what the plague do you mean?"

"Why, I certainly did see a cat go into your room last night," I resumed.

"Hey, and what if you did﻿—though I fancy you dreamed it﻿—I’m not afraid of a cat; are you?" he interrupted, tartly.

At this moment there came a low growling mew from the closet which opened from the room in which we sat.

"Talk of the devil," said I, pointing towards the closet. My companion, without any exact change of expression, looked, I thought, somehow still more sinister and lowering; and I felt for a moment a sort of superstitious misgiving, which made the rest of the sentence die away on my lips.

Perhaps Mr. Smith perceived this, for he said, in a tone calculated to reassure me﻿—

"Well, sir, I think I am bound to tell you that I like my apartments very well; they suit me, and I shall probably be your tenant for much longer than at first you anticipated."

I expressed my gratification.

===Chinese===
第二天，我们这位新房客直到正午才打铃。他极少量地用了些早餐，便吩咐仆人说，往后请每日在门外放一定分量的牛奶和面包；如此安排之后，他便不再需要正点了。他又交代，等我回来时通知他一声，他想在九点钟左右在他自己房里见我；在这之前，他吩咐道，不许任何人打扰。我发现我那小妻子对史密斯先生这古怪的俭省与避居大为惊奇，也极想知道他约我相见究竟所为何事。九点钟，我便去了他的房里。

我见他穿戴与昨夜我离开时一模一样——还是那副绿风镜——嘴上还是那样的裹束，只是这一回不过是一条叠得宽宽的黑丝巾，松松地搭着，连鼻梁下半截也遮住了，分明是专为遮掩而设。很显然，除了初次见面时他已肯露给我的那一点，我休想再多看他的面目半分。那效果，活像他下半张脸上有某处可怖的创伤或溃疡。他亲手替我带上门，微微一点头，便坐下了。我本以为他会先开口，他却沉默良久，末了我到底按捺不住，只得先与他搭话。

我一时寻不着更切题的话，便说我但愿昨夜那只怪猫没有搅扰了他。

"什么猫？"他没好气地问，"你见鬼地说什么？"

"嘿，我昨夜分明瞧见一只猫钻进了您的房里。"我接道。

"嗬，就算你瞧见了——我瞧你是做梦呢——我总不至于怕一只猫吧；你怕不成？"他没好气地打断我。

正说着，从我们所坐这间屋子通出去的那间小壁橱里头，传来一声低低的、咕噜咕噜的猫叫。

"说曹操，曹操到。"我说着，朝那壁橱一指。我的同伴脸上倒没什么确切的变动，我却觉得他那一副神情益发显得阴沉可怖了；我一时间竟生出一种近乎迷信的不安，剩下的话便在嘴边噎了下去，说不出来了。

许是史密斯先生察觉了这一点，他便用一种有意安抚我的口气说道——

"那么，先生，我想我不妨告诉您，我挺喜欢这几间屋子；很合我的意，我做起您这里的房客，怕要比您起初所想的久得多。"

我表示这于我甚是欣慰。


===Original===
He then began to talk, something in the strain in which he had spoken of his own peculiarities of habit and thinking upon the previous evening. He disposed of all classes and denominations of superstition with an easy sarcastic slang, which for me was so captivating, that I soon lost all reserve, and found myself listening and suggesting by turns﻿—acquiescent and pleased﻿—sometimes hazarding dissent; but whenever I did, foiled and floored by a few pointed satirical sentences, whose sophistry, for such I must now believe it, confounded me with a rapidity which, were it not for the admiration with which he had insensibly inspired me, would have piqued and irritated my vanity not a little.

While this was going on, from time to time the mewing and growling of a cat within the closet became more and more audible. At last these sounds became so loud, accompanied by scratching at the door, that I paused in the midst of a sentence, and observed﻿—

"There certainly is a cat shut up in the closet?"

"Is there?" he ejaculated, in a surprised tone; "nay, I do not hear it."

He rose abruptly and approached the door; his back was towards me, but I observed he raised the goggles which usually covered his eyes, and looked steadfastly at the closet door. The angry sounds all died away into a low, protracted growl, which again subsided into silence. He continued in the same attitude for some moments, and then returned.

"I do not hear it," he said, as he resumed his place, and taking a book from his capacious pocket, asked me if I had seen it before? I never had, and this surprised me, for I had flattered myself that I knew, at least by name, every work published in England during the last fifty years in favour of that philosophy in which we both delighted. The book, moreover, was an odd one, as both its title and table of contents demonstrated.

While we were discoursing upon these subjects, I became more and more distinctly conscious of a new class of sounds proceeding from the same closet. I plainly heard a measured and heavy tread, accompanied by the tapping of some hard and heavy substance like the end of a staff, pass up and down the floor﻿—first, as it seemed, stealthily, and then more and more unconcealedly. I began to feel very uncomfortable and suspicious. As the noise proceeded, and became more and more unequivocal, Mr. Smith abruptly rose, opened the closet door, just enough to admit his own lath-like person, and steal within the threshold for some seconds. What he did I could not see﻿—I felt conscious he had an associate concealed there; and though my eyes remained fixed on the book, I could not avoid listening for some audible words, or signal of caution. I heard, however, nothing of the kind. Mr. Smith turned back﻿—walked a step or two towards me, and said﻿—

"I fancied I heard a sound from that closet, but there is nothing﻿—nothing﻿—nothing whatever; bring the candle, let us both look."

===Chinese===
接着他便谈开了，口气与昨夜谈及他自己的癖性和想法时大同小异。他以一种轻巧的、讥讽的俚语，把形形色色、各门各派的迷信通通打发掉——这一套于我有着莫大的吸引力，我不一会儿便全无保留，自己也时而倾听、时而献疑——既赞同又快活——偶尔还斗胆异议几句；然而每逢我异议，便被他三两句尖刻的讥诮驳得体无完肤——那些诡辩——如今我不得不这么认为了——以一种令人头晕目眩的速度把我搅得糊涂透顶；若不是我已不知不觉对他生出了钦慕之心，这份功夫本该大大地刺伤、激怒我的虚荣心才是。

正谈着，壁橱里头猫儿喵喵咕噜的叫声越来越清晰可闻，此起彼伏。到后来，那声响竟大到伴着抓门声了，我便一句话说到半截，停了下来，说道——

"壁橱里头，关着一只猫，错不了吧？"

"是吗？"他诧异地脱口道，"嗳，我可没听见。"

他霍地站起身，朝那门走去；他背对着我，我却瞧见他抬起了平日罩着双眼的风镜，目不转睛地盯着壁橱的门。那一阵怒叫渐渐低落下去，化作一声低沉而拖长的咆哮，复又归于寂静。他维持着那姿势片刻，才回过身来。

"我没听见啊，"他说着回到原座，又从他那宽大的口袋里掏出一本书，问我可曾见过？我从未见过，这倒叫我吃了一惊，因为我一向自诩，近五十年来英国出版的、拥护我和他所同好的那门哲学的著作，我至少也熟知其名。再者，这本书本身也古怪，无论书名还是目录都可作证。

我们正谈着这些，我越来越分明地觉察到，同一间壁橱里又传出一种新的声响。我清清楚楚地听见一种有节律的、沉重的脚步声，伴着某种又硬又重的东西——像是手杖的末端——叩击地板的笃笃声，在屋里来回踱步——起初听来鬼鬼祟祟，后来越来越不加掩饰。我开始觉得十分不自在，满腹狐疑。那声响不住传来，越来越明确无疑，史密斯先生霍然起身，打开壁橱的门，只开到刚够他那一根麻秆似的身形挤进去的宽度，悄没声地迈过门槛，在里头待了几秒。他做了什么，我看不真切——我心里明白，他在那壁橱里藏着个同伙；我两眼虽盯着那本书，却忍不住竖起耳朵，想听一两句出口的话，或是某个示警的暗号。然而我什么也没听着。史密斯先生回过身来——朝我这边走了两步，说道——

"我恍惚听见那壁橱里有动静，其实什么也没有——什么也没有——绝对什么也没有；拿上蜡烛，咱们俩一道瞧瞧。"


===Original===
I obeyed with some little trepidation, for I fully anticipated that I should detect the intruder, of whose presence my own ears had given me, for nearly half an hour, the most unequivocal proofs. We entered the closet together; it contained but a few chairs and a small spider table. At the far end of the room there was a sort of grey woollen cloth upon the floor, and a bundle of something underneath it. I looked jealously at it, and half thought I could trace the outline of a human figure; but, if so, it was perfectly motionless.

"Some of my poor wardrobe," he muttered, as he pointed his lean finger in the direction. "It did not sound like a cat, did it﻿—hey﻿—did it?" he muttered; and without attending to my answer, he went about the apartment, clapping his hands, and crying, "Hish﻿—hish﻿—hish!"

The game, however, whatever it was, did not start. As I entered I had seen, however, a large crutch reposing against the wall in the corner opposite to the door. This was the only article in the room, except that I have mentioned, with which I was not familiar. With the exception of our two selves, there was not a living creature to be seen there; no shadow but ours upon the bare walls; no feet but our own upon the comfortless floor.

I had never before felt so strange and unpleasant a sensation.

"There is nothing unusual in the room but that crutch," I said.

"What crutch, you dolt? I see no crutch," he ejaculated, in a tone of sudden but suppressed fury.

"Why, *that* crutch," I answered (for somehow I neither felt nor resented his rudeness), turning and pointing to the spot where I had seen it. It was gone!﻿—it was neither there nor anywhere else. It must have been an illusion﻿—rather an odd one, to be sure. And yet I could at this moment, with a safe conscience, *swear* that I never saw an object more distinctly than I had seen it but a second before.

My companion was muttering fast to himself as we withdrew; his presence rather scared than reassured me; and I felt something almost amounting to horror, as, holding the candle above his cadaverous and sable figure, he stood at his threshold, while I descended the stairs, and said, in a sort of whisper﻿—

"Why, but that I am, like yourself, a philosopher, I should say that your house is﻿—is﻿—a﻿—ha! ha! ha!﻿—*haunted*!"

===Chinese===
我怀着几分惴惴不安依了他，因为我满心以为，定能把那个闯入者逮个正着——我这两只耳朵，足有半个钟头之久，已把他存在的最确凿的证据呈给了我。我们一同走进壁橱里头；里头不过几把椅子和一张小小的蛛脚桌。屋子的那一头，地板上有一块灰扑扑的毛呢布，底下鼓着一包东西。我狐疑地盯着它，恍惚觉得能辨出一个人影的轮廓；纵然果真如此，那影子也是纹丝不动的。

"是我的一点可怜的衣裳。"他含含糊糊地说着，瘦骨嶙峋的指头朝那一指。"那声响可不像是猫，是吧——嗳——是不是？"他嘟囔道；也不等我回答，便在屋里走来走去，一面拍着手，一面"嘘——嘘——嘘"地赶着。

然而，那东西——管它是什么——却并没有惊起来。不过我一进门，便瞧见门对面的墙角里，斜倚着一根大拐杖。这是屋里唯一一件我不认得的东西，除我方才所提的之外。除了我们两人而外，这里头连一个活物也瞧不见；光秃秃的墙上，除了我们俩的影子之外再无别影；那叫人浑身不自在的地板上，也只踏着我们两人的脚。

我从未有过这般古怪、这般叫人不舒服的感觉。

"这屋里除了那根拐杖，没有什么不寻常的东西。"我说。

"什么拐杖，你这呆子？我可没瞧见什么拐杖。"他脱口而出，语气突如其来，却被压抑着的狂怒憋得发紧。

"嘿，就那根拐杖，"我答道（不知怎的，我既不觉得、也不计较他的粗鲁），转过身去，朝我方才瞧见它的地方一指。它竟不见了！——既不在那儿，也不在任何地方。这一定是个幻觉——说实在的，倒是桩怪得出奇的幻觉。然而此时此刻，我大可以凭良心起誓：我生平从未把哪样东西看得比一秒钟之前我所看见的那根拐杖更真切过。

我们退出来时，我的同伴嘴里飞快地自言自语着；有他在场，与其说是叫我安心，不如说是叫我害怕；待我下楼时，只见他举着蜡烛，立在他那死灰般、一身玄黑的身影之上，站在门槛边，以一种近乎耳语的声音对我说——我心中几乎生出一种近乎恐惧的感觉——

"嗳，要不是我也和你一样，是个哲学家，我简直要说，你这宅子是——是——是个——哈！哈！哈！——闹鬼的！"


===Original===
"You look very pale, my love," said my wife, as I entered the drawing-room, where she had been long awaiting my return. "Nothing unpleasant has happened?"

"Nothing, nothing, I assure you. Pale!﻿—*do* I look pale?" I answered. "We are excellent friends, I assure you. So far from having had the smallest disagreement, there is every prospect of our agreeing but too well, as you will say; for I find that he holds all my opinions upon speculative subjects. We have had a great deal of conversation this evening, I assure you; and I never met, I think, so scholarlike and able a man."

"I am sorry for it, dearest," she said, sadly. "The greater his talents, if such be his opinions, the more dangerous a companion is he."

We turned, however, to more cheerful topics, and it was late before we retired to rest. I believe it was pride﻿—perhaps only vanity﻿—but, at all events, some obstructive and stubborn instinct of my nature, which I could not overcome﻿—that prevented my telling my wife the odd occurrences which had disturbed my visit to our guest. I was unable or ashamed to confess that so slight a matter had disturbed me; and, above all, that any accident could possibly have clouded, even for a moment, the frosty clearness of my pure and lofty scepticism with the shadows of superstition.

Almost every day seemed to develop some new eccentricity of our strange guest. His dietary consisted, without any variety or relief, of the monotonous bread and milk with which he started; his bed had not been made for nearly a week; nobody had been admitted into his room since my visit, just described; and he never ventured downstairs, or out of doors, until after nightfall, when he used sometimes to glide swiftly round our little enclosed shrubbery, and at others stand quite motionless, composed, as if in an attitude of deep attention. After employing about an hour in this way, he would return, and steal upstairs to his room, when he would shut himself up, and not be seen again until the next night﻿—or, it might be, the night after that﻿—when, perhaps, he would repeat his odd excursion.

Strange as his habits were, their eccentricity was all upon the side least troublesome to us. He required literally no attendance; and as to his occasional night ramble, even *it* caused not the slightest disturbance of our routine hour for securing the house and locking up the hall-door for the night, inasmuch as he had invariably retired before that hour arrived.

===Chinese===
"你脸色好白啊，亲爱的。"我走进客厅时，妻子说道——她在那儿已等候我许久。"没出什么不愉快的事吧？"

"没有，没有，我向你保证。脸色白！——我很白吗？"我答道，"我们处得顶好呢，我向你保证。非但没起半点口角，照这情形，咱们还要投契得过分呢——你准会这么说的；因为我发觉，凡属思辨之事，他的见解与我的全然一致。今晚我们谈了许多，我可以向你保证；这么博学多能的人，我想我从没遇见过。"

"这倒叫我为难了，最亲爱的，"她黯然道，"他若是这般见解，那才学越高，做起同伴来便越凶险。"

然而我们转到了更愉快的话题上，夜深了才去歇息。我想，这是自尊心——或许不过是虚荣心——但无论如何，是我天性中一种执拗而顽固的、无法克服的本能——使我不能把拜访我们这位客人时所遇的种种怪事告诉妻子。我无法、也羞于承认，这么一桩小事竟搅扰了我；更羞于承认，世间竟有什么变故，哪怕只是一时半刻，能用迷信的暗影，罩住我那纯正而高妙的怀疑论所结的霜一般清明的光泽。

我们这位怪客，几乎每日都要生出些新的怪癖来。他的吃食，自打头一日定了牛奶面包之后，便再无变化、再无半点调剂；他的床近一个礼拜不曾铺过；自打我那次拜访之后，再无人进过他的房；天黑之前，他绝不下楼、也绝不出门——天黑之后，他有时会飞快地绕着我们那片有围墙的小灌木丛兜上一圈，有时又一动不动地站着，神情凝重，仿佛在凝神细听什么。如此消磨上一个钟头左右，他便回来，蹑手蹑脚地上楼回房，把自己关在里头，直到第二天夜里——或者，隔上一天——才再现身，或许再重复他这趟古怪的出游。

他的习惯虽怪，怪却怪在最不打扰我们的一面。他简直是一点伺候也不需要；至于他偶尔的夜游，就连那一点儿，也丝毫搅不着我们每晚按时闩门、关大门的习惯，因为不等那个钟点到了，他总是早已回房去了。


===Original===
All this stimulated curiosity, and, in no small degree, that of my wife, who, notwithstanding her vigilance and her anxiety to see our strange inmate, had been hitherto foiled by a series of cross accidents. We were sitting together somewhere about ten o’clock at night, when there came a tap at the room-door. We had just been discussing the unaccountable Smith; and I felt a sheepish consciousness that he might be himself at the door, and have possibly even overheard our speculation﻿—some of them anything but complimentary, respecting himself.

"Come in," cried, I, with an effort; and the tall form of our lodger glided into the room. My wife was positively frightened, and stood looking at him, as he advanced, with a stare of manifest apprehension, and even recoiled mechanically, and caught my hand.

Sensitiveness, however, was not his fault: he made a kind of stiff nod as I mumbled an introduction; and seating himself unasked, began at once to chat in that odd, offhand, and sneering style, in which he excelled, and which had, as he wielded it, a sort of fascination of which I can pretend to convey no idea.

My wife’s alarm subsided, and although she still manifestly felt some sort of misgiving about our visitor, she yet listened to his conversation, and, spite of herself, soon began to enjoy it. He stayed for nearly half an hour. But although he glanced at a great variety of topics, he did not approach the subject of religion. As soon as he was gone, my wife delivered judgment upon him in form. She admitted he was agreeable; but then he was such an unnatural, awful-looking object: there was, besides, something indescribably frightful, she thought, in his manner﻿—the very tone of his voice was strange and hateful; and, on the whole, she felt unutterably relieved at his departure.

A few days after, on my return, I found my poor little wife agitated and dispirited. Mr. Smith had paid her a visit, and brought with him a book, which he stated he had been reading, and which contained some references to the Bible which he begged of her to explain in that profounder and less obvious sense in which they had been cited. This she had endeavoured to do; and affecting to be much gratified by her satisfactory exposition, he had requested her to reconcile some discrepancies which he said had often troubled him when reading the Scriptures. Some of them were quite new to my good little wife; they startled and even horrified her. He pursued this theme, still pretending only to seek for information to quiet his own doubts, while in reality he was sowing in her mind the seeds of the first perturbations that had ever troubled the sources of her peace. He had been with her, she thought, no more than a quarter of an hour; but he had contrived to leave her abundant topics on which to ruminate for days. I found her shocked and horrified at the doubts which this potent Magus had summoned from the pit﻿—doubts which she knew not how to combat, and from the torment of which she could not escape.

"He has made me very miserable with his deceitful questions. I never thought of them before; and, merciful Heaven! I cannot answer them! What am I to do? My serenity is gone; I shall never be happy again."

===Chinese===
这一切越发撩拨起人的好奇心来，尤其是我妻子的好奇心——她虽百般留意、急欲一睹我们这位怪房客的真容，却屡屡被一连串阴差阳错的事绊住，至今不得如愿。一日夜晚十点光景，我们正坐在一起，忽然有人叩起居室的门。我们方才正在议论这位莫测高深的史密斯；我心里不禁有些发窘，只怕来人正是他本人，甚至说不定已偷听了我们的揣测——其中几句谈到他，可不大是什么好话呢。

"进来。"我硬着头皮喊了一声；只见我们这位房客那瘦长的身形一闪身进了屋。我妻子当真吓了一跳，他往前走时，她直勾勾地盯着他，满脸的惶恐，甚至下意识地往后一缩，一把抓住了我的手。

不过神经过敏却算不得他的毛病：我含含糊糊地把两人引见了一下，他便僵硬地点了点头；也不等人让，便自顾自地坐下，一开口便滔滔不绝地聊起来——正是他最擅长的那种古怪、随便、又带讥诮的腔调，这腔调经他运用起来，自有一种说不出的魅力，这魅力我是无法描摹于万一的。

我妻子的惊惶渐渐平息，虽说她显然仍对我们的来客存着几分疑虑，却还是听得入了神，而且不知不觉间竟也乐在其中了。他坐了差不多半个钟头。然而他虽然话题海阔天空，却始终不曾触及宗教二字。他一走，我妻子便郑重其事地下了判语。她承认此人谈吐可喜；可是他那副模样又那样不自然、那样怕人：再者，他的举止里有一种她说不出来的可怖之处——便是那嗓音，也叫人觉得又怪又可憎；总而言之，他这一走，她如释重负，松了好大一口气。

几天之后，有一回我回到家中，只见我那可怜的小妻子一脸惶乱、神情沮丧。原来史密斯先生拜访过她，还带了一本书来，说是他正在读的，里头有好几处引到《圣经》，他恳求她按那些引文所指的、更深一层而不那么显明的含义，替他讲解一番。她便尽力照办了；他又装出对她这番圆满的讲解大为满意的样子，转而请她替他调和几处矛盾——他说自己读《圣经》时，这些矛盾常常搅扰他。其中几处，对我那善良的小妻子而言是闻所未闻的；叫她又惊又怕。他顺着这个话头说下去，嘴上仍只说是为了求解、好平息自己的疑虑，实则是在她心里播下了头一粒骚动的种子，这骚动从此搅扰了她素来平静的心源。她想，他待了不过一刻钟的工夫；却已变着法儿给她留下了一大堆够她想上好几天的话头。我只见她又惊又怕，被那位了不起的术士从地窟里唤出来的种种疑团所折磨——这些疑团她既不知如何抵挡，其苦又无从逃脱。

"他那些虚情假意的问话，把我折磨得好苦。这些事我从前想也没想过；仁慈的上天啊！我又答不上来！我该怎么办？我心里的安宁没了；我再也快活不起来了。"


===Original===
In truth, she was so very miserable, and, as it seemed to me, so disproportionately excited, that, inconsistent in me as the task would have been, I would gladly have explained away her difficulties, and restored to her mind its wonted confidence and serenity, had I possessed sufficient knowledge for the purpose. I really pitied her, and heartily wished Mr. Smith, for the nonce, at the devil.

I observed after this that my wife’s spirits appeared permanently affected. There was a constantly-recurring anxiety, and I thought something was lying still more heavily at her heart than the uncertainties inspired by our lodger.

One evening, as we two were sitting together, after a long silence, she suddenly laid her hand upon my arm, and said﻿—

"Oh, Richard, my darling! would to God you could pray for me!"

There was something so agitated, and even terrified, in her manner, that I was absolutely startled. I urged her to disclose whatever preyed upon her mind.

"You can’t sympathise with me﻿—you can’t help me﻿—you can scarcely compassionate me in my misery! Oh, dearest Richard! Some evil influence has been gaining upon my heart, dulling and destroying my convictions, killing all my holy affections, and﻿—and absolutely transforming me. I look inward upon myself with amazement, with terror﻿—with﻿—oh, God!﻿—with actual despair!"

Saying this, she threw herself on her knees, and wept an agonised flood of tears, with her head reposing in my lap.

Poor little thing, my heart bled for her! But what could I do or say?

All I could suggest was what I really thought, that she was unwell﻿—hysterical﻿—and needed to take better care of her precious self; that her change of feeling was fancied, not real; and that a few days would restore her to her old health and former spirits and serenity.

"And sometimes," she resumed, after I had ended a consolatory discussion, which it was but too manifest had fallen unprofitably upon her ear, "such dreadful, impious thoughts come into my mind, whether I choose it or not; they come, and stay, and return, strive as I may; and I can’t pray against them. They are forced upon me with the strength of an independent will; and oh!﻿—horrible﻿—frightful﻿—they blaspheme the character of God himself. They upbraid the Almighty upon his throne, and I can’t pray against them; there is something in me now that resists prayer."

There was such a real and fearful anguish in the agitation of my gentle companion, that it shook my very soul within me, even while I was affecting to make light of her confessions. I had never before witnessed a struggle at all like this, and I was awestruck at the spectacle.

At length she became comparatively calm. I did gradually succeed, though very imperfectly, in reassuring her. She strove hard against her depression, and recovered a little of her wonted cheerfulness.

After a while, however, the cloud returned. She grew sad and earnest, though no longer excited; and entreated, or rather implored, of me to grant her one special favour, and this was, to avoid the society of our lodger.

===Chinese===
说实在的，她是那样的痛苦，在我看又是那样的过度激动，以至于这桩差事纵然由我来做未免自相矛盾，可只要我有足够的学问，我便巴不得替她把这些疑难一一化解，好让她那颗心恢复往日的自信与安宁。我当真可怜她，打心眼里巴不得史密斯先生这会儿就给魔鬼抓了去才好。

这以后我便留意到，我妻子的精神像是受了永久的创伤。她老是反反复复地焦虑，我还觉得，压在她心头的，另有一桩比我们这位房客所挑起的那些疑惧更沉重的事。

一天傍晚，我们俩坐在一起，沉默了许久之后，她忽然把一只手搭在我臂上，说——

"哦，理查德（Richard），我的心肝！要是你能替我祷告，该多好啊！"

她的神气是那样激动，甚至带着惊恐，我当真吓了一跳。我苦苦劝她把压在心头的事都说出来。

"你不会与我同心——你帮不了我——我这般苦命，你怕是连怜悯也怜悯不来！哦，最亲爱的理查德！有一股邪气的势力，正一点点爬上我的心头，把我的信念磨钝、磨灭，把我一切圣洁的情感尽数扼杀，而且——而且当真把我变了一个人。我往自己心里瞧，又是惊奇，又是害怕——简直是——哦，上帝啊！——简直是绝望！"

说着，她扑通一声跪倒在地，把头枕在我膝上，痛哭失声，泪下如雨。

可怜的小东西，我的心都为她滴血了！可我能说什么、又能做什么呢？

我所能想到的，也不过就是我心里头真正的想法：她是身子不爽——是癔症发作——该好好将息自己这金贵的身子了；她这种心绪的改变不过是幻觉，并非实情；过不了几天，她便能恢复往日的康健、从前的兴致与安宁。

"还有的时候，"我那番劝慰的话显然是对牛弹琴，她听罢又接着说，"我心里会涌进一些极其可怕、亵渎的念头，不管我愿不愿意；它们来了，赖着不走，又转回来，我再怎么抵挡也无用；我连祷告都抵挡不住。它们凭着一股独立的意志之力，硬塞进我心里；哦！——可怕——可怖——它们亵渎上帝自己的品性。它们当着宝座上的全能者百般责难，我连祷告都抵挡不住；我里头如今有了什么，竟抗拒起祷告来了。"

我这位温柔的伴侣，她那激动之中有一种如此真切、如此可怖的苦痛，连我自己的灵魂都被震动了——哪怕我嘴上还在装作把她的吐露当作小事一桩。我从未见过这样的挣扎，这场面叫我敬畏不已。

末了她总算相对平静了下来。我渐渐地、虽则极不圆满地，安抚下了她。她极力与那消沉相抗，稍稍恢复了一点往日的欢快。

然而过了一阵，那团阴云又回来了。她变得沉郁而恳切，虽不再激动；她求我——不如说是哀求我——答应她一桩特别的请求，这便是：躲着我们那位房客，别与他来往。


===Original===
"I never," she said, "could understand till now the instinctive dread with which poor Margaret, in *Faust*, shrinks from the hateful presence of Mephistopheles. I now feel it in myself. The dislike and suspicion I first felt for that man﻿—Smith, or whatever else he may call himself﻿—has grown into literal detestation and terror. I hate him﻿—I am afraid of him﻿—I never knew what anguish of mind was until he entered our doors; and would to God﻿—would to God he were gone."

I reasoned with her﻿—kissed her﻿—laughed at her; but could not dissipate, in the least degree, the intense and preternatural horror with which she had grown to regard the poor philosophic invalid, who was probably, at that moment, poring over some metaphysical book in his solitary bedchamber.

The circumstance I am about to mention will give you some notion of the extreme to which these excited feelings had worked upon her nerves. I was that night suddenly awakened by a piercing scream﻿—I started upright in the bed, and saw my wife standing at the bedside, white as ashes with terror. It was some seconds, so startled was I, before I could find words to ask her the cause of her affright. She caught my wrist in her icy grasp, and climbed, trembling violently, into bed. Notwithstanding my repeated entreaties, she continued for a long time stupified and dumb. At length, however, she told me, that having lain awake for a long time, she felt, on a sudden, that she could pray, and lighting the candle, she had stolen from beside me, and kneeled down for the purpose. She had, however, scarcely assumed the attitude of prayer, when somebody, she said, clutched her arm violently near the wrist, and she heard, at the same instant, some blasphemous menace, the import of which escaped her the moment it was spoken, muttered close in her ear. This terrifying interruption was the cause of the scream which had awakened me; and the condition in which she continued during the remainder of the night confirmed me more than ever in the conviction, that she was suffering under some morbid action of the nervous system.

After this event, which *I* had no hesitation in attributing to fancy, she became literally afraid to pray, and her misery and despondency increased proportionately.

===Chinese===
"从前我总也不明白，"她说，"《浮士德》（*Faust*）里可怜的玛格丽特（Margaret），何以那样本能地畏惧、躲避梅菲斯托费勒斯（Mephistopheles）那可憎的身影。如今我自身觉着了。我起先对那人——史密斯也罢，随他唤什么名儿也罢——所怀的厌恶和疑心，已长成了切切实实的憎恨与恐惧。我恨他——我怕他——自打他踏进我们家门，我才头一遭知道什么叫心里的苦楚；但愿上帝——但愿上帝叫他走了才好。"

我同她说理——吻她——笑她；却丝毫也不能驱散她心头已生出的一种强烈而超乎常情的恐怖——她正是怀着这恐怖，看待楼上那位可怜的、养病的哲学家，而此时此刻，那人多半正在他那孤寂的卧室里埋头读着某本形而上学的书呢。

我下面要讲的那桩事，可以让您略略明白，她这些激荡的情绪，已把她的神经折腾到了何等极端的地步。那天夜里，我突然被一声尖叫惊醒——我从床上猛地坐起，只见妻子站在床边，吓得面如死灰。我惊得有好几秒钟说不出话来，问她到底出了什么事。她伸出冰凉的手死死攥住我的手腕，哆哆嗦嗦地爬回床上。不管我怎么反复追问，她许久都僵着不出一声。末了她才告诉我，她躺下之后好久睡不着，后来忽然觉得自己能祷告了，便点了蜡烛，悄悄从我身边溜下床，跪下来祷告。谁知她刚摆出祷告的姿势，便有人——她说——在她腕子附近狠狠一把攥住了她的胳膊，与此同时，她耳边还听见一句亵渎的威吓，那话刚出口便从她记忆里溜掉了，不知所云。这桩可怕的打断，便是惊醒我的那声尖叫的缘由；她下半夜的模样，越发叫我深信不疑：她这是神经系统出了某种病态的毛病。

这事过后——我毫不迟疑地把它归之于幻觉——她当真怕起祷告来了，她的痛苦和消沉也与之成正比地加重了。


===Original===
It was shortly after this that an unusual pressure of business called me into town one evening after office hours. I had left my dear little wife tolerably well, and little Fanny was to be her companion until I returned. She and her little companion occupied the same room in which we sat on the memorable evening which witnessed the arrival of our eccentric guest. Though usually a lively child, it most provokingly happened upon this night that Fanny was heavy and drowsy to excess. Her mamma would have sent her to bed, but that she now literally feared to be left alone; although, however, she could not so far overcome her horror of solitude as to do this, she yet would not persist in combating the poor child’s sleepiness.

Accordingly, little Fanny was soon locked in a sound sleep, while her mamma quietly pursued her work beside her. They had been perhaps some ten minutes thus circumstanced, when my wife heard the window softly raised from without﻿—a bony hand parted the curtains, and Mr. Smith leaned into the room.

She was so utterly overpowered at sight of this apparition, that even had it, as she expected, climbed into the room, she told me she could not have uttered a sound, or stirred from the spot where she sat transfixed and petrified.

"Ha, ha!" he said gently, "I hope you’ll excuse this, I must admit, very odd intrusion; but I knew I should find you here, and could not resist the opportunity of raising the window just for a moment, to look in upon a little family picture, and say a word to yourself. I understand that you are troubled, because for some cause you cannot say your prayers﻿—because what you call your ‘faith’ is, so to speak, dead and gone, and also because what *you* consider bad thoughts are constantly recurring to your mind. Now, all that is very silly. If it is really impossible for you to believe and to pray, what are you to infer from that? It is perfectly plain your Christian system can’t be a true one﻿—faith and *prayer* it everywhere represents as the conditions of grace, acceptance, and salvation; and yet your Creator will not *permit* you either to believe or pray. The Christian system is, forsooth, a *free* gift, and yet he who formed *you* and *it*, makes it absolutely impossible for you to accept it. *Is* it, I ask you, from your own experience﻿—is it a free gift? And if your own experience, in which you can’t be mistaken, gives its pretensions the lie, why, in the name of common sense, will you persist in believing it? I say it is downright blasphemy to think it has emanated from the Good Spirit﻿—assuming that there is one. It tells you that you must be tormented hereafter in a way only to be made intelligible by the image of eternal fires﻿—pretty strong, we must all allow﻿—unless you comply with certain conditions, which it pretends are so easy that it is a positive pleasure to embrace and perform them; and yet, for the life of you, you can’t﻿—physically *can’t**—do either. Is this truth and mercy?﻿—or is it swindling and cruelty? Is it the part of the Redeemer, or that of the tyrant, deceiver, and tormentor?"

Up to that moment, my wife had sat breathless and motionless, listening, in the catalepsy of nightmare, to a sort of echo of the vile and impious reasoning which had haunted her for so long. At the last words of the sentence his voice became harsh and thrilling; and his whole manner bespoke a sort of crouching and terrific hatred, the like of which she could not have conceived.

Whatever may have been the cause, she was on a sudden disenchanted. She started to her feet; and, freezing with horror though she was, in a shrill cry of agony commanded him, in the name of God, to depart from her. His whole frame seemed to darken; he drew back silently; the curtains dropped into their places, the window was let down again as stealthily as it had just been raised; and my wife found herself alone in the chamber with our little child, who had been startled from her sleep by her mother’s cry of anguish, and with the fearful words, "tempter," "destroyer," "devil," still ringing in her ears, was weeping bitterly, and holding her terrified mother’s hand.

===Chinese===
就在此事之后不久，有一晚我因公事格外繁忙，下了班还得进城去一趟。出门时，我那亲爱的小妻子精神尚可，我便让小范妮陪着她，等我回来。她们母女俩所占的，正是我们那位古怪房客登门那个难忘的夜晚所坐的那间屋子。范妮平日是个活泼的孩子，偏生这一晚困倦异常，睡意浓得叫人恼。她妈妈本想打发她去睡，可她如今当真怕一个人独处；然而她又不能完全战胜自己对孤寂的恐惧，便也不忍硬撑着与这可怜孩子的瞌睡作对。

于是，小范妮不多时便沉沉睡去，她妈妈则在一旁静静地做针线。这般光景约莫过了十分钟，我妻子忽然听见窗子被人从外头轻轻推开了——一只骨瘦如柴的手拨开窗帘，史密斯先生探身进来。

她一见这副景象，登时魂飞魄散，浑身瘫软；她对我说，纵然那身影如她所料当真爬进屋来，她也喊不出一声、动不了一步，只僵坐在那儿，如泥塑木雕一般。

"哈，哈！"他语调柔和地说，"这一番冒昧打搅，我得承认，是怪了些，还望您见谅；可我算准了能在这儿撞见您，忍不住要趁这机会把窗子推开一会儿，瞧瞧这家庭小景，再同您说句话。我听说您心里烦扰，因为不知什么缘故，您祷告不成了——因为您所谓的'信心'，可以说，已经死了、没了；又因为那些您当作恶念的心绪，老是在您心里翻来覆去。哎，这一切都蠢得很。您若是当真信不了、也祷告不了，由此该得出什么结论呢？明摆着的——您那套基督教的体系不可能是真的——它处处把信心和祷告说成是蒙恩、悦纳、得救的条件；可您的造物主偏偏不'容许'您信、也不容许您祷告。基督教这套东西，据说是一份白送的礼物，然而造了您、又造了它的那一位，却叫您压根儿没法接受它。我问您——凭您自己的亲身体验——这算是一份白送的礼物吗？倘若您自己的体验——这体验您决不会弄错——戳穿了它的虚张声势，那么凭常识之名，您又何必死抱着它信呢？我索性说吧：倘若这套东西当真是善灵所赐——假设真有个善灵的话——那么以为它出自善灵，简直就是亵渎。它告诉您，您日后必受一番折磨，那折磨唯有借用永火之象方能形容——咱们都得承认，这话够狠的——除非您依从某些条件；据它说，这些条件容易得很，遵行起来简直是一桩乐事；然而您拼了命也办不到——生理上就是办不到——一样也办不到。这是真理与慈悲吗？——还是欺诈与残忍？这是救赎者所当为，还是暴君、骗子、折磨者所当为？"

直到那一刻，我妻子一直屏息端坐，一动不动，如堕梦魇的僵直之中，听着那一套她久已萦绕心头的、卑污而亵渎的论调的回声。说到末了几句，他的嗓音变得又尖利又激越；他整个人神情大变，透出一种蛰伏而可怖的恨意——其可怖是她万万设想不出的。

也不知究竟是什么缘故，她忽然间如梦初醒。她霍地站起身来；虽则吓得浑身冰冷，却在一声痛苦的尖叫中，奉上帝之名，命他离开她。他整个人影似乎暗了一暗；他悄没声地缩了回去；窗帘落回原处，窗子又像方才推开时那样悄悄地放了下来；我妻子这才发觉自己独自和我们的孩子待在屋里——那孩子已被母亲痛苦的呼喊从睡梦中惊醒，"诱惑者"、"毁灭者"、"魔鬼"这几个可怕的字眼还萦绕在她耳畔，她哭得伤心，紧紧握着她那吓坏了的母亲的手。


===Original===
There is nothing, I believe, more infectious than that species of nervousness which shows itself in superstitious fears. I began﻿—although I could not bring myself to admit anything the least like it﻿—to partake insensibly, but strongly of the peculiar feelings with which my wife, and indeed my whole household, already regarded the lodger upstairs. The fact was, beside, that the state of my poor wife’s mind began to make me seriously uneasy; and, although I was fully sensible of the pecuniary and other advantages attendant upon his stay, they were yet far from outweighing the constant gloom and frequent misery in which the protracted sojourn was involving my once cheerful house. I resolved, therefore, at whatever monetary sacrifice, to put an end to these commotions; and, after several debates with my wife, in which the subject was, as usual, turned in all its possible and impossible bearings, we agreed that, deducting a fair proportion for his five weeks’ sojourn, I should return the remainder of his £100, and request immediate possession of his apartments. Like a man suddenly relieved of an insufferable load, and breathing freely once more, I instantly prepared to carry into effect the result of our deliberations.

In pursuance of this resolution, I waited upon Mr. Smith. This time my call was made in the morning, somewhere about nine o’clock. He received me at his door, standing as usual in the stealthy opening which barely admitted his lank person. There he stood, fully equipped with goggles and respirator, and swathed, rather than dressed, in his puckered black garments.

As he did not seem disposed to invite me into his apartment, although I had announced my visit as one of business, I was obliged to open my errand where I stood; and after a great deal of fumbling and muttering, I contrived to place before him distinctly the resolution to which I had come.

"But I can’t think of taking back any portion of the sum I have paid you," said he, with a cool, dry emphasis.

"Your reluctance to do so, Mr. Smith, is most handsome, and I assure you, appreciated," I replied. "It is very generous; but, at the same time, it is quite impossible for me to accept what I have no right to take, and I must beg of you not to mention that part of the subject again."

"And why should *I* take it?" demanded Mr. Smith.

"Because you have paid this hundred pounds for six months, and you are leaving me with nearly five months of the term still unexpired," I replied. "I expect to receive fair play myself, and always give it."

"But who on earth said that I was going away so soon?" pursued Mr. Smith, in the same dry, sarcastic key. "*I* have not said so﻿—because I really don’t intend it; I mean to stay here to the last day of the six months for which I have paid you. I have no notion of vacating my hired lodgings, simply because you say, *go*. I shan’t quarrel with you﻿—I never quarrel with anybody. I’m as much your friend as ever; but, without the least wish to disoblige, I can’t do this, positively I cannot. Is there anything else?"

===Chinese===
我相信，再没有比那种以迷信的恐惧表现出来的神经质更具传染性的了。我也开始——虽则我还不肯向自己承认有半分这样的意思——不知不觉却又强烈地沾染上了我妻子、其实也是我全家上下，对楼上那位房客所怀的那种独特的心绪。再者，我那可怜的妻子的心境，也开始叫我当真忧心起来；虽说我也完全明白他住在这里，于钱财和其他方面自有种种好处，然而这些好处，远远抵不过这场拖延不绝的寄居，给我那曾经欢乐的家所招致的、长久的阴霾与频频的苦痛。于是我横下心来，不惜在钱财上吃亏，也要了结这一场纷扰；与妻子反复商议了几回——这桩事照例被我们从方方面面、能想得到与想不到的角度掂量了个遍——我们议定：扣除他那五周寄居应摊的公道份额之后，我把他那一百镑的余数退还给他，并请他立即腾出房间。我如同一个忽然卸下万斤重担、重又能畅快呼吸的人，立时着手把我们议定的办法付诸实施。

为照这主意行事，我便去拜访史密斯先生。这一回我是早上登门的，大约九点钟光景。他在自己门口接见我，照例站在那道刚够容他那瘦长身形挤过的、鬼鬼祟祟的半开的门缝里。只见他全副武装，风镜口鼻罩一件不缺，身上与其说是穿着、不如说是裹着一身皱巴巴的黑衣裳。

他既无意请我进屋——虽说我已声明此番拜访是为谈公事——我也只好站在原地开口了；我支支吾吾、嘟嘟囔囔了好一阵，总算把我已拿定的主意，明白无误地摆在了他面前。

"不过，我已经付给你的那笔钱，要我收回其中任何一部分，我是想也不愿想的。"他说道，语气又冷淡又干涩，字字着力。

"史密斯先生，您这般推却，真是大方之至，我向您保证，我心领了。"我答道，"您真是慷慨；可与此同时，我决无权利收下这笔钱，自然也不能接受，所以这件事，求您再也不要提了。"

"那又凭什么要我收回呢？"史密斯先生质问道。

"因为您这一百镑是为期六个月的房租，如今您走时，这六个月还剩将近五个月未满。"我答道，"我待人指望公平待人，也一向公平待人。"

"可到底是谁说我这么快就要走的？"史密斯先生以同样干涩、讥诮的口吻追问道，"我可没说过这话——因为我实在没这个打算；我打算在这儿住满我付了钱的六个月的最后一天。我没那个意思，单凭你一句'走'，便空出我租下的房间来。我不跟你吵架——我从不跟人吵架。我还是像从前一样待你以朋友之谊；可是，虽然毫无拂逆之意，这事我却办不到，断断办不到。还有别的事吗？"


===Original===
I had not anticipated in the least the difficulty which thus encountered and upset our plans. I had so set my heart upon effecting the immediate retirement of our inauspicious inmate, that the disappointment literally stunned me for a moment. I, however, returned to the charge: I urged, and prayed, and almost besought him to give up his apartments, and to leave us. I offered to repay every farthing of the sum he had paid me﻿—reserving nothing on account of the time he had already been with us. I suggested all the disadvantages of the house. I shifted my ground, and told him that my wife wanted the rooms; I pressed his gallantry﻿—his good nature﻿—his economy; in short, I assailed him upon every point﻿—but in vain, he did not even take the trouble of repeating what he had said before﻿—he neither relented, nor showed the least irritation, but simply said﻿—

"I can’t do this; here I am, and here I stay until the half-year has expired. You wanted a lodger, and you have got one﻿—the quietest, least troublesome, least expensive person you could have; and though your house, servants, and furniture are none of the best, I don’t care for that. I pursue my own poor business and enjoyments here entirely to my satisfaction."

Having thus spoken, he gave me a sort of nod, and closed the door.

So, instead of getting rid of him the next day, as we had hoped, we had nearly five months more of his company in expectancy; I hated, and my wife dreaded the prospect. She was literally miserable and panic-struck at her disappointment﻿—and grew so nervous and wretched that I made up my mind to look out for lodgings for her and the children (subversive of all our schemes of retrenchment as such a step would be), and surrendering the house absolutely to Mr. Smith and the servants during the remainder of his term.

Circumstances, however, occurred to prevent our putting this plan in execution. My wife, meanwhile, was, if possible, more depressed and nervous every day. The servants seemed to sympathise in the dread and gloom which involved ourselves; the very children grew timid and spiritless, without knowing why﻿—and the entire house was pervaded with an atmosphere of uncertainty and fear. A poorhouse or a dungeon would have been cheerful, compared with a dwelling haunted unceasingly with unearthly suspicions and alarms. I would have made any sacrifice short of ruin, to emancipate our household from the odious mental and moral thraldom which was invisibly established over us﻿—overcasting us with strange anxieties and an undefined terror.

===Chinese===
我万万没有料到，竟会撞上这般棘手的难处，把我们定下的计划全然打翻。我一门心思想叫我们这位不祥的房客立时三刻搬走，这一下落空，直把我惊得当场发懵。然而我重又发起进攻：我好说歹说，几乎是哀求他腾出房间、离我们而去。我提出把他付给我的钱一文不少地全数退还——对他已在我们这里住过的日子，一文也不扣留。我把这宅子的种种不是一一摆出来。我又改口，说我妻子要用那几间屋子；我抬出他的侠义心肠——他的好脾气——他的节俭——总之，我从四面八方围攻他——却全是白费唇舌，他甚至连重复一遍方才那番话的力气都不屑花——既不心软，也不动半点气，只平平淡淡地说了一句——

"这事我办不到；我既在这儿，便在这儿待下去，直待这半年期满。你要的是一位房客，你也得到了一位——再安静不过、再不麻烦不过、再省事不过的人，你再也找不出第二个来了；虽说你的宅子、仆人、家具没一样算得上好的，我可不在乎这些。我在此地办我自己的那点琐事、享我自己的那点乐趣，全都称了我的心。"

说完这番话，他朝我点了点头，便把门关上了。

于是，我们非但不能像原先指望的那样第二天便摆脱他，反倒还要再熬上将近五个月有他作伴的日子；我恨这前景，我妻子则怕这前景。落了空之后，她简直痛苦万状、惊慌失措——神经越发衰弱，神情越发凄苦，我便横下心来，打算替她和孩子们另寻一处住所（这一着虽与我们一切节省的计策背道而驰），把这座宅子，在他租期剩下的日子里，全然拱手让给史密斯先生和仆人们。

然而事不凑巧，有些变故发生，叫我们没能把这计划付诸实行。这其间，我妻子若是可能的话，是一天比一天更消沉、更神经质了。仆人们似乎也与我们同感那笼罩着我们全家的恐惧与阴霾；便连孩子们也不知怎的，都变得胆小怯懦、没精打采起来——整座宅子，弥漫着一种疑惧交加的气氛。一所济贫院、一座地牢，与一座无时无刻不被超乎人间的疑神疑鬼与惊惶不安所搅扰的住宅相比，怕都要算得上明朗欢快了。只要不至倾家荡产，无论什么代价我都肯付，好把我们这一家子，从那已不知不觉笼罩在我们头上的、可憎的精神与心灵的枷锁之中解救出来——那枷锁以种种古怪的忧惧和一种说不清道不明的恐怖，把我们罩得严严实实。


===Original===
About this time my wife had a dream which troubled her much, although she could not explain its supposed significance satisfactorily by any of the ordinary rules of interpretation in such matters. The vision was as follows.

She dreamed that we were busily employed in carrying out our scheme of removal, and that I came into the parlour where she was making some arrangements, and, with rather an agitated manner, told her that the carriage had come for the children. She thought she went out to the hall, in consequence, holding little Fanny by one hand, and the boy﻿—or, as we still called him, "baby,"﻿—by the other, and feeling, as she did so, an unaccountable gloom, almost amounting to terror, steal over her. The children, too, seemed, she thought, frightened, and disposed to cry.

So close to the hall-door as to exclude the light, stood some kind of vehicle, of which she could see nothing but that its door was wide open, and the interior involved in total darkness. The children, she thought, shrunk back in great trepidation, and she addressed herself to induce them, by persuasion, to enter, telling them that they were only "going to their new home." So, in a while, little Fanny approached it; but, at the same instant, some person came swiftly up from behind, and, raising the little boy in his hands, said fiercely, "No, the baby first"; and placed him in the carriage. This person was our lodger, Mr. Smith, and was gone as soon as seen. My wife, even in her dream, could not act or speak; but as the child was lifted into the carriage-door, a man, whose face was full of beautiful tenderness and compassion, leaned forward from the carriage and received the little child, which, stretching his arms to the stranger, looked back with a strange smile upon his mother.

"He is safe with me, and I will deliver him to you when you come."

These words the man spoke, looking upon her, as he received him, and immediately the carriage-door shut, and the noise of its closing wakened my wife from her nightmare.

This dream troubled her very much, and even haunted my mind unpleasantly too. We agreed, however, not to speak of it to anybody, not to divulge any of our misgivings respecting the stranger. We were anxious that neither the children nor the servants should catch the contagion of those fears which had seized upon my poor little wife, and, if truth were spoken, upon myself in some degree also. But this precaution was, I believe, needless, for, as I said before, everybody under the same roof with Mr. Smith was, to a certain extent, affected with the same nervous gloom and apprehension.

===Chinese===
大约在这前后，我妻子做了一个梦，这梦搅扰她甚深，虽则她按照这类事情的寻常解梦之道，怎么也解释不清这梦所暗示的含义。梦中所见如下。

她梦见我们正忙忙碌碌地张罗着搬家的计划，我走进客厅——她正在里头收拾什么——神色相当激动地告诉她：接孩子们的车来了。她想，于是她便一手牵着小范妮、一手牵着那个男孩——也就是我们还一直唤他作"宝宝"的那个——走到门厅里去，只觉一阵说不出的阴郁、近乎恐怖的感觉，悄没声地爬上心头。她想，孩子们似乎也受了惊，快要哭出来了。

紧贴着大门、把光线都遮没了的地方，停着某种马车，她别的什么也瞧不见，只瞧见那车门大敞着，里头漆黑一片。她想，孩子们吓得直往后缩，她便好言好语地哄他们进去，说他们不过是"上新家去"。过了一会儿，小范妮便挨近了那马车；可就在这时，有人从背后飞快地赶上来，双手一举抱起了那个小男孩，恶狠狠地说："不成，宝宝先来"；便把他放进了车里。这个人正是我们的房客史密斯先生，一现便逝，转眼就不见了。我妻子即便在梦中，也动弹不得、出不了声；可当那孩子被举到车门口的时候，一个满脸美丽温柔与怜悯之色的男人，从车厢里探身出来，接过了那小小的孩童；那孩子向那陌生人伸出双臂，却回过头来，冲他母亲露出了一个古怪的微笑。

"他与我在一起，十分安稳；待你来时，我自把他交还给你。"

那人接孩子的工夫，一面望着她说了这几句话；话音刚落，车门便关上了，那关门的一声砰然，把我妻子从噩梦中惊醒了。

这个梦搅扰她甚深，甚至也叫我心头不快，挥之不去。然而我们彼此约定，对谁也不提这事，也不把我们对于那位生客的种种疑惧泄露出去。我们生怕孩子们也好、仆人们也好，染上我那可怜的小妻子——说句老实话，也染上了我自己几分——所已着上的那种恐惧。不过这一层小心，我想，其实大可不必，因为正如我方才所说，凡是与史密斯先生同住一个屋檐下的人，或多或少都沾上了同一种神经质的阴霾与忧惧。


===Original===
And now commences a melancholy chapter in my life. My poor little Fanny was attacked with a cough which soon grew very violent, and after a time degenerated into a sharp attack of inflammation. We were seriously alarmed for her life, and nothing that care and medicine could effect was spared to save it. Her mother was indefatigable, and scarcely left her night or day; and, indeed, for some time, we all but despaired of her recovery.

One night, when she was at the worst, her poor mother, who had sat for many a melancholy hour listening, by her bedside, to those plaintive incoherences of delirium and moanings of fever, which have harrowed so many a fond heart, gained gradually from her very despair the courage which she had so long wanted, and knelt down at the side of her sick darling’s bed to pray for her deliverance.

With clasped hands, in an agony of supplication, she prayed that God would, in his mercy, spare her little child﻿—that, justly as she herself deserved the sorest chastisement his hand could inflict, he would yet deal patiently and tenderly with her in this one thing. She poured out her sorrows before the mercy-seat﻿—she opened her heart, and declared her only hope to be in his pity; without which, she felt that her darling would only leave the bed where she was lying for her grave.

Exactly as she came to this part of her supplication, the child, who had grown, as it seemed, more and more restless, and moaned and muttered with increasing pain and irritation, on a sudden started upright in her bed, and, in a thrilling voice, cried﻿—

"No! no!﻿—the baby first."

The mysterious sentence which had secretly tormented her for so long, thus piercingly uttered by this delirious, and, perhaps, dying child, with what seemed a preternatural earnestness and strength, arrested her devotions, and froze her with a feeling akin to terror.

"Hush, hush, my darling!" said the poor mother, almost wildly, as she clasped the attenuated frame of the sick child in her arms; "hush, my darling; don’t cry out so loudly﻿—there﻿—there﻿—my own love."

The child did not appear to see or hear her, but sat up still with feverish cheeks, and bright unsteady eyes, while her dry lips were muttering inaudible words.

"Lie down, my sweet child﻿—lie down, for your own mother," she said; "if you tire yourself, you can’t grow well, and your poor mother will lose you."

At these words, the child suddenly cried out again, in precisely the same loud, strong voice﻿—"No! no! the baby first, the baby first"﻿—and immediately afterwards lay down, and fell, for the first time since her illness into a tranquil sleep.

My good little wife sat, crying bitterly by her bedside. The child was better﻿—*that* was, indeed, delightful. But then there was an omen in the words, thus echoed from her dream, which she dared not trust herself to interpret, and which yet had seized, with a grasp of iron, upon every fibre of her brain.

"Oh, Richard," she cried, as she threw her arms about my neck, "I am terrified at this horrible menace from the unseen world. Oh! poor, darling little baby, I shall lose you﻿—I am sure I shall lose you. Comfort me, darling, and say he is not to die."

And so I did; and tasked all my powers of argument and persuasion to convince her how unsubstantial was the ground of her anxiety. The little boy was perfectly well, and, even were he to die before his sister that event might not occur for seventy years to come. I could not, however, conceal from myself that there was something odd and unpleasant in the coincidence; and my poor wife had grown so nervous and excitable, that a much less ominous conjecture would have sufficed to alarm her.

===Chinese===
而今，我一生中一个悲惨的篇章开始了。我那可怜的小范妮染上了咳嗽，不久便咳得十分厉害，过了一些时日，又转成一场猛烈的热症。我们当真为她的性命忧心如焚，凡照料与医药所能尽力的，无不竭尽所能。她的母亲不知疲倦，几乎日夜不离她的床边；说实在的，有一阵子，我们几乎已绝望了，只当她是再也好不了了。

一天夜里，病情最险恶的时候，她那可怜的母亲，已在床边守了许多凄凉的时辰，听着那些曾搅碎过多少慈母心肠的呓语呻吟、高热中的胡言乱语——她从自己那份绝望之中，反倒渐渐生出了久违的勇气，跪倒在病中爱儿的床边，为她得救而祷告。

她十指紧扣，痛苦地哀求，求上帝开恩，饶她这孩子一命——虽说她自己罪有应得，配受他手中最严厉的责罚，可这一桩上，求他仍以忍耐和温柔待她。她在施恩座前倾吐苦情——敞开心扉，承认自己唯一的指望便是他的怜悯；若没有这怜悯，她便觉得，她的心肝宝贝唯有从所卧的病榻，被抬到坟墓里去。

恰恰在她祷告到这一节的时候，那孩子——本来似乎越来越烦躁，又因疼痛和焦灼而越发的呻吟嘟囔——忽然一下子从床上直挺挺坐了起来，用一种叫人胆战的声音喊道——

"不！不！——宝宝先来。"

这一句折磨了她许久的神秘之语，由这谵妄的、或许已命在垂危的孩子，以一种似乎是超乎自然的恳切与气力，如此尖锐地喊出来，一下子打断了她的祷告，把她冻在那里，心生一种近乎恐怖之感。

"嘘，嘘，我的心肝！"可怜的母亲几近癫狂地喊道，一把将病儿那瘦削的身子搂进怀里，"嘘，我的心肝；别这么大声喊——好啦——好啦——我的乖宝。"

那孩子像是既看不见她、也听不见她，却依旧坐着一动不动，两颊烧得通红，一双亮闪闪的眼睛骨碌碌地不稳，干裂的嘴唇嘟囔着听不真切的字眼。

"躺下，我的乖乖——为你亲娘躺下吧，"她说，"你若熬坏了自己，便好不了啦，你可怜的娘可就要失去你了。"

听了这话，那孩子忽然又叫了起来，用的还是方才那又响又亮的嗓音——"不！不！宝宝先来，宝宝先来"——说罢便躺下了，自打她生病以来头一遭，安安稳稳地睡着了。

我那贤良的小妻子坐在她床边，伤心地哭泣。孩子见好了——这确是叫人欢喜的。可那话里头，却藏着一桩从她梦中传来的征兆，这征兆她不敢自己去解，它却已像铁钳一般，攫住了她脑子里每一根神经。

"哦，理查德，"她搂住我的脖子哭喊道，"这一句来自幽冥世界的可怖的威吓，把我吓坏了。哦！可怜的、心爱的宝宝，我就要失去你了——我准知道我就要失去你了。安慰安慰我，心肝，你说他不会死的。"

我便如此安慰了她；我使出我全部辩才与劝解的功夫，要叫她相信她这份忧惧是何等无根无据。那小男孩好好的，一点毛病没有；退一步说，纵然他要比姐姐先死，那也可能是七十年以后的事。然而我也不能瞒着自己，这巧合里头确实有几分古怪、几分不妙；再说我的可怜的妻子已变得这般神经质、这般易受惊，便是远不如这般不祥的揣测，也足以叫她大惊失色了。


===Original===
Meanwhile, the unaccountable terror which our lodger’s presence inspired continued to increase. One of our maids gave us warning, solely from her dread of our queer inmate, and the strange accessories which haunted him. She said﻿—and this was corroborated by her fellow-servant﻿—that Mr. Smith seemed to have constantly a companion in his room; that although they never heard them speak, they continually and distinctly heard the tread of two persons walking up and down the room together, and described accurately the peculiar sound of a stick or crutch tapping upon the floor, which my own ears had heard. They also had seen the large, ill-conditioned cat I have mentioned, frequently steal in and out of the stranger’s room; and observed that when our little girl was in greatest danger, the hateful animal was constantly writhing, fawning, and crawling about the door of the sick room after nightfall. They were thoroughly persuaded that this ill-omened beast was the foul fiend himself, and I confess I could not﻿—sceptic as I was﻿—bring myself absolutely to the belief that he was nothing more than a "harmless, necessary cat." These and similar reports﻿—implicitly believed as they palpably were by those who made them﻿—were certainly little calculated to allay the perturbation and alarm with which our household was filled.

The evenings had by this time shortened very much, and darkness often overtook us before we sat down to our early tea. It happened just at this period of which I have been speaking, after my little girl had begun decidedly to mend, that I was sitting in our dining-parlour, with my little boy fast asleep upon my knees, and thinking of I know not what, my wife having gone upstairs, as usual, to sit in the room with little Fanny. As I thus sat in what was to me, in effect, total solitude, darkness unperceived stole on us.

On a sudden, as I sat, with my elbow leaning upon the table, and my other arm round the sleeping child, I felt, as I thought, a cold current of air faintly blowing upon my forehead. I raised my head, and saw, as nearly as I could calculate, at the far end of the table on which my arm rested, two large green eyes confronting me. I could see no more, but instantly concluded they were those of the abominable cat. Yielding to an impulse of horror and abhorrence, I caught a water-croft that was close to my hand, and threw it full at it with all my force. I must have missed my object, for the shining eyes continued fixed for a second, and then glided still nearer to me, and then a little nearer still. The noise of the glass smashed with so much force upon the table called in the servant, who happened to be passing. She had a candle in her hand, and, perhaps, the light alarmed the odious beast, for as she came in it was gone.

I had had an undefined idea that its approach was somehow connected with a designed injury of some sort to the sleeping child. I could not be mistaken as to the fact that I had plainly seen the two broad, glaring, green eyes. Where the cursed animal had gone I had not observed: it might, indeed, easily have run out at the door as the servant opened it, but neither of us had seen it do so; and we were every one of us in such a state of nervous excitement, that even this incident was something in the catalogue of our ambiguous experiences.

===Chinese===
与此同时，我们这位房客的存在所激起的那种说不清道不明的恐惧，仍在与日俱增。我家一个女仆辞了工，单只因为怕我们这位怪房客，又怕他身边那些阴魂不散的古怪伴当。她说——另一个仆人也替她作证——史密斯先生的房里，似乎总有一个同伴；虽说她们从未听见他们说话，却时时分明地听见两个人在屋里一同来回踱步的步履声，还能把一根手杖或拐杖笃笃叩击地板的那奇特声响形容得毫厘不爽——这声音我自己那双耳朵也曾听见过。她们还屡次瞧见我方才所说的那只又大又丑的猫，从那生客房里出出进进；更察觉到，每当我们的小女儿病势最凶险的时候，这只可憎的畜生入夜之后便总是在病室门口扭来扭去、献媚讨乖、爬来爬去。她们深信不疑，这只不祥的畜生便是那恶魔本人；我承认，纵然我是个怀疑派，也无法硬叫自己相信它不过是一只"无害而必不可少"的猫。这些以及诸如此类的传言——做这番话的人显然深信不疑——自然丝毫也不能平息我们全家上下的惶恐与惊惧。

其时白昼已大大缩短，天黑常常赶在我们坐下来喝早茶之前便已降临。就在我方才所说的这段日子里，我的小女儿已确凿无疑地开始好转了，有一回，我坐在饭厅里，膝上熟睡着我的小男孩，心里不知在想些什么——我妻子照旧上楼，到小范妮房里陪她去了。我如此枯坐着，四下里对我而言无异于彻底的孤寂，黑暗不知不觉便爬了上来。

冷不丁地，正当我坐着，一只胳膊肘撑在桌上，另一只胳膊搂着熟睡的孩子，我只觉额上似有一股冷气幽幽地拂过。我抬起头来，在我胳膊所撑的那张桌子的那一头，只见两只又大又绿的眼睛正对着我。我所能看见的，仅此而已，便立刻断定那是那只可憎的猫的眼睛。我一时又惧又憎，便抄起手边一只水杯，使尽全身力气，冲它砸了过去。我准是没砸中，因为那双亮闪闪的眼睛定了一秒钟，又朝我这边滑近了一些，再又滑近了一些。玻璃杯狠狠砸在桌上那砰然一声，把一个正好路过的仆人叫了进来。她手里端着一支蜡烛，许是那光亮惊着了这只可憎的畜生，她一进门，它便不见了。

我心里原有一种说不清的感觉，觉得它这逼近，多少与某种蓄意要加害那熟睡孩子的恶念有关。那两只又宽又亮、灼灼放光的绿眼睛，我是看得清清楚楚，断不会错的。那只该死的畜生跑到哪儿去了，我却没有留意：它或许当真是在仆人开门时溜了出去，但我们俩谁也没瞧见；况且我们这一家人，个个都处在一种神经质的亢奋之中，便连这一桩小事，也算得是我们那一笔暧昧不清的怪事里的一桩了。


===Original===
It was a great happiness to see our darling little Fanny every day mending, and now quite out of danger: this was cheering and delightful. It was also something to know that more than two months of our lodger’s term of occupation had already expired; and to realise, as we now could do, by anticipation, the unspeakable relief of his departure.

My wife strove hard to turn our dear child’s recovery to good account for me; but the impressions of fear soon depart, and those of religious gratitude must be preceded by religious faith. All as yet was but as seed strewn upon the rock.

Little Fanny, though recovering rapidly, was still very weak, and her mother usually passed a considerable part of every evening in her bedroom﻿—for the child was sometimes uneasy and restless at night. It happened at this period that, sitting as usual at Fanny’s bedside, she witnessed an occurrence which agitated her not a little.

The child had been, as it seems, growing sleepy, and was lying listlessly, with eyes half open, apparently taking no note of what was passing. Suddenly, however, with an expression of the wildest terror, she drew up her limbs, and cowered in the bed’s head, gazing at some object; which, judging from the motion of her eyes, must have been slowly advancing from the end of the room next the door.

The child made a low shuddering cry, as she grasped her mother’s hand, and, with features white and tense with terror, slowly following with her eyes the noiseless course of some unseen spectre, shrinking more and more fearfully backward every moment.

"What is it? Where? What is it that frightens you, my darling?" asked the poor mother, who, thrilled with horror, looked in vain for the apparition which seemed to have all but bereft the child of reason.

"Stay with me﻿—save me﻿—keep it away﻿—look, look at it﻿—making signs to me﻿—don’t let it hurt me﻿—it is angry﻿—Oh! mamma, save me, save me!"

The child said this, all the time clinging to her with both her hands, in an ecstasy of panic.

"There﻿—there, my darling," said my poor wife, "don’t be afraid; there’s nothing but me﻿—your own mamma﻿—and little baby in the room; nothing, my darling; nothing indeed."

"Mamma, mamma, don’t move; don’t go near him"; the child continued wildly. "It’s only his back now; don’t make him turn again; he’s untying his handkerchief. Oh! baby, baby; he’ll *kill* baby! and he’s lifting up those green things from his eyes; don’t you see him doing it? Mamma, mamma, why does he come here? Oh, mamma, poor baby﻿—poor little baby!"

===Chinese===
眼见我们心爱的小范妮一天好似一天，如今已全然脱离险境，真是一桩大喜事：这叫人又欣慰又欢喜。再说我们这位房客的租期，也已过了两个多月，这也是一桩可以宽心的事；如今我们已能预先体味到他离去时那种种说不出的轻松了。

我妻子竭力想借我们这孩子康复的时机，在我身上收点善果；然而惊惧的印象去得快，而宗教的感恩之情，又非得先有宗教的信心不可。这一切到如今，还不过是撒在磐石上的种子罢了。

小范妮虽一日日迅速康复，身子却还很弱，她母亲照例每晚要在她房里陪上好一阵——因为这孩子夜里有时睡不安稳。就在这段日子里，有一回，她又照旧坐在范妮床边，目睹了一桩事，叫她好不惊惶。

那孩子，看样子是渐渐犯困了，正没精打采地躺着，两眼半睁半闭，对眼前发生的事似乎全不留心。忽然间，她面上一副骇然欲绝的神情，把四肢蜷缩起来，缩到床头，死盯着一样东西；从她眼珠转动的方向看来，那东西准是从靠门的那一头，正慢慢地向她逼近。

那孩子发出一声低低的、打战的尖叫，紧紧抓住她母亲的手，一张小脸煞白、紧绷着，全是惊恐之色，两眼慢慢追随着某个看不见的鬼影那悄无声息的行踪，一刻比一刻更怕人地往后瑟缩。

"是什么？在哪儿？是什么吓着你了，我的心肝？"可怜的母亲问道，她自己也被恐惧攫住，徒然四下张望，想找那似乎已把孩子吓得几乎失了心窍的鬼影。

"陪着我——救救我——别让它过来——瞧，瞧它——它在冲我打手势——别让它伤害我——它在发怒——哦！妈妈，救我，救我！"

孩子说着这话，两只手死死地攀住她，已吓得魂不附体。

"好啦——好啦，我的心肝，"我那可怜的妻子说，"别怕；这儿除了我——你亲娘——和小宝宝，没别人；什么也没有，我的乖宝；当真什么也没有。"

"妈妈，妈妈，别动；别走近他"；孩子发狂似地接着说，"这会儿只瞧见他的背影；别叫他再转过身来；他在解他的围巾。哦！宝宝，宝宝；他会害死宝宝的！他正把眼睛上那两片绿玩意儿往上掀呢；你没瞧见他这么做吗？妈妈，妈妈，他上这儿来干什么？哦，妈妈，可怜的宝宝——可怜的小宝宝！"


===Original===
She was looking with a terrified gaze at the little boy’s bed, which lay directly opposite to her own, and in which he was sleeping calmly.

"Hush, hush, my darling child," said my wife, with difficulty restraining an hysterical burst of tears; "for God’s sake don’t speak so wildly, my own precious love﻿—there, there﻿—don’t be frightened﻿—there, darling, there."

"Oh! poor baby﻿—poor little darling baby," the child continued as before; "will no one save him﻿—tell that wicked man to go away﻿—oh﻿—there﻿—why, mamma﻿—don’t﻿—oh, sure you won’t let him﻿—don’t﻿—don’t﻿—he’ll take the child’s life﻿—will you let him lie down that way on the bed﻿—save poor little baby﻿—oh, baby, baby, waken﻿—his head is on your face."

As she said this she raised her voice to a cry of despairing terror which made the whole room ring again.

This cry, or rather yell, reached my ears as I sat reading in the parlour by myself, and fearing I knew not what, I rushed to the apartment; before I reached it, the sound had subsided into low but violent sobbing; and, just as I arrived at the threshold I heard, close at my feet, a fierce protracted growl, and something rubbing along the surbase. I was in the dark, but, with a feeling of mingled terror and fury, I stamped and struck at the abhorred brute with my feet, but in vain. The next moment I was in the room, and heard little Fanny, through her sobs, cry﻿—

"Oh, poor baby is killed﻿—that wicked man has killed him﻿—he uncovered his face, and put it on him, and lay upon the bed and killed poor baby. I knew he came to kill him. Ah, papa, papa, why did you not come up before he went?﻿—he is gone, he went away as soon as he killed our poor little darling baby."

===Chinese===
她正惊恐万状地盯着小男孩的床——那床正对着她的床，他正安安稳稳地睡在里头。

"嘘，嘘，我的心肝孩子，"我妻子强忍着一阵歇斯底里的眼泪，说道，"看在上帝份上，别这样胡言乱语，我的亲亲宝贝——好啦，好啦——别怕——好啦，乖宝，好啦。"

"哦！可怜的宝宝——可怜的小心肝宝宝，"孩子还像方才那样说下去，"就没有人救他吗——叫那坏人走开啊——哦——那儿——怎么，妈妈——别——哦，你总不至于由着他——别——别——他要取这孩子的命——你由着他那样伏在床上吗——救救可怜的小宝宝啊——哦，宝宝，宝宝，醒醒啊——他的脸正贴在你脸上呢。"

她说着这话，提高了嗓门，发出一声绝望的尖叫，震得满屋都是回响。

这一声叫喊，不如说是号叫，传到独自坐在起居室里读书的我的耳中，我一时也不知怕的是什么，拔腿便往那间屋子冲去；还没赶到，那声音已低落下去，化作一阵低低的、却又剧烈的抽泣；我刚到门口，便听得就在我脚边，一声凶狠而拖长的咆哮，还有什么东西蹭过踢脚线。我在黑暗里，只觉又惧又怒，一脚一脚地朝那可憎的畜生乱踩乱踢，却全不顶事。一转眼我便冲进了屋里，听见小范妮抽抽搭搭地哭喊——

"哦，可怜的宝宝被害死了——那个坏人把他害死了——他揭开自己脸上的遮盖，贴到他身上，伏在床上，把可怜的宝宝害死了。我就知道他是来害他的。啊，爸爸，爸爸，你为什么不在他走之前赶上来呢？——他走了，他一害死我们可怜的小心肝宝宝就走了。"


===Original===
I could not conceal my agitation, quite, and I said to my wife﻿—

"Has he, Smith, been here?"

"No."

"What is it, then?"

"The child has seen *some*one."

"Seen whom? Who? Who has been here?"

"I did not see it; but﻿—but I am sure the child saw﻿—that is, *thought* she saw *him*;﻿—the person you have named. Oh, God, in mercy deliver us! What shall I do﻿—what shall I do!"

Thus saying, the dear little woman burst into tears, and crying, as if her heart would break, sobbed out an entreaty that I would look at baby; adding, that she herself had not courage to see whether her darling was sleeping or dead.

"Dead!" I exclaimed. "Tut, tut, my darling; you must not give way to such morbid fancies﻿—he is very well, I see him breathing;" and so saying, I went over to the bed where our little boy was lying. He was slumbering; though it seemed to me very heavily, and his cheeks were flushed.

"Sleeping tranquilly, my darling﻿—tranquilly, and deeply; and with a warm colour in his cheeks," I said, rearranging the coverlet, and retiring to my wife, who sat almost breathless whilst I was looking at our little boy.

"Thank God﻿—thank God," she said quietly; and she wept again; and rising, came to his bedside.

"Yes, yes﻿—alive; thank God; but it seems to me he is breathing very short, and with difficulty, and he looks﻿—*does* he not look hot and feverish? Yes, he *is* very hot; feel his little hand﻿—feel his neck; merciful heaven! he is burning."

It was, indeed, very true, that his skin was unnaturally dry and hot; his little pulse, too, was going at a fearful rate.

"I do think," said I﻿—resolved to conceal the extent of my own apprehensions﻿—"I do think that he is just a *little* feverish; but he has often been much more so; and will, I dare say, in the morning, be perfectly well again. I dare say, but for little Fanny’s *dream*, we should not have observed it at all."

"Oh, my darling, my darling, my darling!" sobbed the poor little woman, leaning over the bed, with her hands locked together, and looking the very picture of despair. "Oh, my darling, what has happened to you? I put you into your bed, looking so well and beautiful, this evening, and here you are, stricken with sickness, my own little love. Oh, you will not﻿—you cannot, leave your poor mother!"

===Chinese===
我到底没能完全掩住自己的激动，便对妻子说——

"他，史密斯，来过吗？"

"没有。"

"那是怎么回事？"

"孩子看见了什么人。"

"看见了谁？谁？有谁来过？"

"我没有看见；可是——可是我敢肯定孩子看见了——或者说，自以为看见了——他；——就是你方才说到的那个人。哦，上帝啊，发发慈悲救救我们吧！我该怎么办——我该怎么办啊！"

说着，这亲爱的小妇人泪如雨下，哭得肝肠寸断，抽抽搭搭地求我去瞧瞧宝宝；又说，她自己已没有胆量去看她的宝贝到底是睡着，还是已经死了。

"死了！"我失声喊道，"呸，呸，心肝；你可不能由着自己往这些病态的胡思乱想上去——他好着呢，我瞧见他在出气呢"；说着，我便走到小男孩躺着的床边。他正在熟睡；不过在我看来，睡得极沉，两颊也红得厉害。

"睡得安安稳稳的，心肝——又稳又沉；腮帮子上还有红扑扑的颜色，"我说着，替他拢了拢被角，便退回到妻子身边——我查看小男孩的工夫，她坐在那里几乎气儿都不敢出。

"谢天谢地——谢天谢地，"她轻轻地说；又哭了起来；随即站起身，走到他床边。

"是啊，是啊——还活着；谢天谢地；可我瞧他喘气好像很短促、很费劲，他的脸色——他脸色是不是又热又像在发烧？是啊，他烫得很；摸摸他的小手——摸摸他的脖子；老天爷发慈悲啊！他烧得滚烫。"

一点不假，他的皮肤又干又热，热得不正常；他小小的脉搏也跳得飞快，叫人害怕。

"我瞧啊，"我说——我已横下心，要把自己忧虑的程度瞒下一大半——"我瞧他不过是有点儿烧罢了；从前他比这烧得厉害的时候多着呢；我敢说，到了明早，他便会全好了。我敢说，要不是小范妮那个梦，我们压根儿就不会发觉呢。"

"哦，我的心肝，我的心肝，我的心肝！"可怜的小妇人俯在床边抽泣着，两手紧紧扣在一起，那模样活脱是一幅绝望的写照，"哦，我的心肝，你出了什么事啦？今儿傍晚我把你放进被窝的时候，你还那么精神、那么好看，这会儿，你却叫病魔缠上了，我的小心肝。哦，你不会——你总不能，撇下你可怜的娘吧！"


===Original===
It was quite plain that she despaired of the child from the moment we had ascertained that it was unwell. As it happened, her presentiment was but too truly prophetic. The apothecary said the child’s ailment was "suppressed smallpox"; the physician pronounced it "typhus." The only certainty about it was the issue﻿—the child died.

To me few things appear so beautiful as a very young child in its shroud. The little innocent face looks so sublimely simple and confiding amongst the cold terrors of death﻿—crimeless, and fearless, that little mortal has passed alone under the shadow, and explored the mystery of dissolution. There is death in its sublimest and purest image﻿—no hatred, no hypocrisy, no suspicion, no care for the morrow ever darkened that little face; death has come lovingly upon it; there is nothing cruel, or harsh, in his victory. The yearnings of love, indeed, cannot be stifled; for the prattle, and smiles, and all the little world of thoughts that were so delightful, are gone forever. Awe, too, will overcast us in its presence﻿—for we are looking on death; but we do not fear for the little, lonely voyager﻿—for the child has gone, simple and trusting, into the presence of its all-wise Father; and of such, we know, is the kingdom of heaven.

And so we parted from poor little baby. I and his poor old nurse drove in a mourning carriage, in which lay the little coffin, early in the morning, to the churchyard of —﻿—﻿—. Sore, indeed, was my heart, as I followed that little coffin to the grave! Another burial had just concluded as we entered the churchyard, and the mourners stood in clusters round the grave, into which the sexton was now shovelling the mould.

As I stood, with head uncovered, listening to the sublime and touching service which our ritual prescribes, I found that a gentleman had drawn near also, and was standing at my elbow. I did not turn to look at him until the earth had closed over my darling boy; I then walked a little way apart, that I might be alone, and drying my eyes, sat down upon a tombstone, to let the confusion of my mind subside.

While I was thus lost in a sorrowful reverie, the gentleman who had stood near me at the grave was once more at my side. The face of the stranger, though I could not call it handsome, was very remarkable; its expression was the purest and noblest I could conceive, and it was made very beautiful by a look of such compassion as I never saw before.

"Why do you sorrow as one without hope?" he said, gently.

"I *have* no hope," I answered.

"Nay, I think you have," he answered again; "and I am sure you will soon have more. That little child for which you grieve, has escaped the dangers and miseries of life; its body has perished; but he will receive in the end the crown of life. God has given him an early victory."

I know not what it was in him that rebuked my sullen pride, and humbled and saddened me, as I listened to this man. He was dressed in deep mourning, and looked more serene, noble, and sweet than any I had ever seen. He was young, too, as I have said, and his voice very clear and harmonious. He talked to me for a long time, and I listened to him with involuntary reverence. At last, however, he left me, saying he had often seen me walking into town, about the same hour that he used to go that way, and that if he saw me again he would walk with me, and so we might reason of these things together.

It was late when I returned to my home, now a house of mourning.

===Chinese===
事情一查明孩子是病了，她便显然对这孩子绝望了。果不其然，她的预感应验得再真切不过。药剂师说孩子的病是"隐性天花"；医生则断为"斑疹伤寒"。唯一可以确定的是结局——孩子死了。

在我看来，世间少有比一个裹在尸衣里的幼童更美的事物了。在那死亡的种种冰冷可怖之间，那张无辜的小脸显得那样超凡地天真、那样毫无戒备——这个小小的生灵，无罪无惧，独自走过了那片阴影，探明了消亡之谜。这里呈现的是死亡最崇高、最纯净的形象——没有仇恨，没有虚伪，没有猜疑，没有对明天的忧虑，曾在这张小脸上投下过半点阴霾；死亡是满怀爱意地降临到他身上的；他的胜利里没有一丝残忍、一丝苛刻。爱的眷恋，自然是无法按捺的；因为那呀呀学语、那粲然一笑、那一整个可爱的小小思想世界，都已经一去不返了。在他面前，我们也会生出敬畏——因为我们看见的是死亡；然而我们并不为这个小小的、孤独的旅人担忧——因为这孩子已怀着纯真与信赖，走到他全知全能的天父面前去了；而这样的人，我们知道，正是天国的子民。

我们就这样与可怜的小宝宝诀别了。一大清早，我和他那可怜的老奶妈，坐着一辆送葬的马车，车里安放着那口小棺材，到了某某教堂的墓地。我跟着那口小棺材走向坟地，心里的痛，真是不堪言说！我们走进墓地时，另一场葬礼刚刚结束，送葬的人们三三两两聚在坟边，教堂司事正往坟里铲着泥土。

我摘了帽子站在坟边，听着我们仪式所规定的那崇高而感人的祷文，发觉有一位先生也凑了过来，正立在我肘边。我没有回头看他，直到泥土已把我心爱的孩子掩埋妥当；其后我走到一旁，想独自待一会儿，擦干了眼睛，在一块墓碑上坐下来，好叫心头的纷乱平复下去。

我正这样沉浸在忧伤的遐想里，方才在坟边立在我肘边的那位先生，又一次来到了我身旁。这陌生人的脸，虽说不上英俊，却极为不凡；那神情是我所能想象的最纯净、最高贵的，又因一种我从未见过的怜悯之色，显得十分美丽。

"你为何像一个没有指望的人那样悲伤呢？"他温和地说。

"我是没有指望。"我答道。

"不，我想你是有的，"他又答道，"而且我敢说，不久你便会有更多的指望。你为之哀伤的那个小小的孩子，已经逃脱了人生的种种危险与困苦；他的肉身是朽坏了；可他终必得着生命的冠冕。上帝早早地赐给了他一场胜利。"

我不知这人身上到底有什么，竟斥责了我阴沉的骄傲，叫我听着他的话，便觉谦卑而感伤。他一身重孝，神色比我生平所见任何人都更安详、高贵、可亲。他也如我所说，年纪轻轻，嗓音清朗和谐。他同我谈了好一阵子，我不由自主地怀着敬意听他讲。末了，他告辞去了，说他常瞧见我在大约他惯常走那条路进城的时候，步行进城；又说倘若再见着我，便要与我同行，如此咱们便可一同参详这些事。

我回到家中——如今这里已是一座服丧的宅子——已是暮色深沉的时分了。

## The Vision of Tom Chuff / 汤姆·查夫的异象

===Original===
At the edge of melancholy Catstean Moor, in the north of England, with half-a-dozen ancient poplar-trees with rugged and hoary stems around, one smashed across the middle by a flash of lightning thirty summers before, and all by their great height dwarfing the abode near which they stand, there squats a rude stone house, with a thick chimney, a kitchen and bedroom on the ground-floor, and a loft, accessible by a ladder, under the shingle roof, divided into two rooms.

Its owner was a man of ill repute. Tom Chuff was his name. A shock-headed, broad-shouldered, powerful man, though somewhat short, with lowering brows and a sullen eye. He was a poacher, and hardly made an ostensible pretence of earning his bread by any honest industry. He was a drunkard. He beat his wife, and led his children a life of terror and lamentation, when he was at home. It was a blessing to his frightened little family when he absented himself, as he sometimes did, for a week or more together.

===Chinese===
在英格兰北部那片阴郁的卡特斯坦荒原（Catstean Moor）边上，六棵古老的杨树参差矗立，树干粗砺斑白，其中一棵在三十年前的一个夏日被闪电拦腰劈断。这些树身形高大，反把旁边那座宅子衬得矮小局促。宅子是粗石砌成的，矮墩墩地蹲伏其间，有一根粗烟囱，楼下辟出一间厨房、一间卧房，木板瓦的屋顶下还有个阁楼，靠一架梯子上下，里头隔作两间。

这宅子的主人，是个声名狼藉的人物。汤姆·查夫（Tom Chuff）便是他的名字。此人一头乱发，膀阔腰圆，身板壮实，个子却不甚高，两道浓眉压得低低的，一双眼睛阴沉沉的。他是个偷猎客，至于靠什么正经营生糊口，连装装样子的功夫都省了。他又是个酒鬼。在家时，打老婆，叫一窝孩子终日活在惊恐哭号之中。他有时外出，一走就是个把星期不曾回家——每逢这种时候，他那受惊吓的小小一家子，竟如同蒙了天大的恩惠一般。

===Original===
On the night I speak of he knocked at the door with his cudgel at about eight o’clock. It was winter, and the night was very dark. Had the summons been that of a bogie from the moor, the inmates of this small house could hardly have heard it with greater terror.

His wife unbarred the door in fear and haste. Her hunchbacked sister stood by the hearth, staring toward the threshold. The children cowered behind.

Tom Chuff entered with his cudgel in his hand, without speaking, and threw himself into a chair opposite the fire. He had been away two or three days. He looked haggard, and his eyes were bloodshot. They knew he had been drinking.

Tom raked and knocked the peat fire with his stick, and thrust his feet close to it. He signed towards the little dresser, and nodded to his wife, and she knew he wanted a cup, which in silence she gave him. He pulled a bottle of gin from his coat-pocket, and nearly filling the teacup, drank off the dram at a few gulps.

===Chinese===
我要说的那一夜，约莫八点钟光景，他用棍子擂起门来。其时正值隆冬，夜色浓黑。便是有荒原上的妖怪来叩门，这小屋里的一家人听着，只怕也不至于比这更吓得魂飞魄散。

他妻子提心吊胆、手忙脚乱地抽开门闩。她那驼背的妹子立在炉边，直勾勾地望着门口。孩子们缩在后头。

汤姆·查夫手提棍子，一言不发地进了屋，一屁股坐进对着炉火的那张椅子里。他已出门两三日，一脸憔悴，两眼布满血丝。家里人都晓得，他这是又喝上了。

汤姆用棍子扒拉敲打那团泥炭火，把两只脚直凑到火跟前去。他朝那张小小的碗柜努了努嘴，又冲妻子点了点头，妻子便知他是要一只杯子，默不作声地递了过去。他从外衣口袋里掏出一瓶杜松子酒，斟了几乎满满一茶杯，几口便将那烈酒灌下肚去。

===Original===
He usually refreshed himself with two or three drams of this kind before beating the inmates of his house. His three little children, cowering in a corner, eyed him from under a table, as Jack did the ogre in the nursery tale. His wife, Nell, standing behind a chair, which she was ready to snatch up to meet the blow of the cudgel, which might be levelled at her at any moment, never took her eyes off him; and hunchbacked Mary showed the whites of a large pair of eyes, similarly employed, as she stood against the oaken press, her dark face hardly distinguishable in the distance from the brown panel behind it.

Tom Chuff was at his third dram, and had not yet spoken a word since his entrance, and the suspense was growing dreadful, when, on a sudden, he leaned back in his rude seat, the cudgel slipped from his hand, a change and a deathlike pallor came over his face.

===Chinese===
往常他总要先灌下两三杯这等烈酒，提一提精神，这才动手收拾屋里的人。他那三个稚小的孩儿瑟缩在角落里，从一张桌子底下偷偷拿眼瞅他，活像童话里的杰克盯着那吃人妖怪。他的妻子内尔（Nell）立在一张椅子后头，随时预备一把抄起椅子，去挡那不知何时便会劈头落下的棍子，一双眼睛一刻也不离他身上；驼背的玛丽（Mary）也一般无二，瞪着一双大眼睛，翻出大片眼白来——她倚着那只橡木橱柜立着，那张黧黑的脸隔得远了，几乎与身后褐色的柜板分辨不清。

汤姆·查夫正灌到第三杯，进门之后还不曾开过口，这难熬的悬疑越积越重——忽然之间，他往后一仰，靠在那张粗笨的椅背上，棍子从他手里滑脱，脸上泛起一层死人般的惨白。

===Original===
For a while they all stared on; such was their fear of him, they dared not speak or move, lest it should prove to have been but a doze, and Tom should wake up and proceed forthwith to gratify his temper and exercise his cudgel.

In a very little time, however, things began to look so odd, that they ventured, his wife and Mary, to exchange glances full of doubt and wonder. He hung so much over the side of the chair, that if it had not been one of cyclopean clumsiness and weight, he would have borne it to the floor. A leaden tint was darkening the pallor of his face. They were becoming alarmed, and finally braving everything his wife timidly said, “Tom!” and then more sharply repeated it, and finally cried the appellative loudly, and again and again, with the terrified accompaniment, “He’s dying﻿—he’s dying!” her voice rising to a scream, as she found that neither it nor her plucks and shakings of him by the shoulder had the slightest effect in recalling him from his torpor.

And now from sheer terror of a new kind the children added their shrilly piping to the talk and cries of their seniors; and if anything could have called Tom up from his lethargy, it might have been the piercing chorus that made the rude chamber of the poacher’s habitation ring again. But Tom continued unmoved, deaf, and stirless.

===Chinese===
一时间众人只呆呆望着；他们怕他怕到了这步田地，竟不敢出声，也不敢动弹，唯恐他不过是打了个盹儿，汤姆一旦醒转，便要立时发作脾气、操起棍子来逞威风。

然而不多几时，情形瞧着越发不对了，他妻子和玛丽壮着胆子交换了一个眼神，满腹狐疑与惊诧。他那身子大半截都歪出了椅子沿，若不是那张椅子笨重得如同独眼巨人之物，早叫他连人带椅栽到地上了。一层铅灰之色正渐渐盖住他脸上那片惨白。她们开始慌了，末了他妻子把心一横，怯怯地唤了一声："汤姆！"继而提高嗓门又唤了一遍，末了放大嗓子把这名儿喊了出来，一而再、再而三，伴着惊恐万状的叫嚷："他要死了——他要死了！"声音直拔到尖叫——她发觉，无论怎么叫喊，无论怎么揪他肩膀、摇晃他，都不能叫他那一阵阵木僵之中回过魂来。

这一来，孩子们也添上一股新冒出来的怕意，尖着嗓子叽叽喳喳地哭叫起来，与长辈们的言语哭喊搅作一团；若说还有什么能将汤姆从他那呆木之中唤醒，怕就是这一阵尖利嘹亮的齐声合唱，震得这偷猎客所居的粗陋屋子嗡嗡作响。然而汤姆依旧纹丝不动，充耳不闻，寂然如死。

===Original===
His wife sent Mary down to the village, hardly a quarter of a mile away, to implore of the doctor, for whose family she did duty as laundress, to come down and look at her husband, who seemed to be dying.

The doctor, who was a good-natured fellow, arrived. With his hat still on, he looked at Tom, examined him, and when he found that the emetic he had brought with him, on conjecture from Mary’s description, did not act, and that his lancet brought no blood, and that he felt a pulseless wrist, he shook his head, and inwardly thought:

“What the plague is the woman crying for? Could she have desired a greater blessing for her children and herself than the very thing that has happened?”

Tom, in fact, seemed quite gone. At his lips no breath was perceptible. The doctor could discover no pulse. His hands and feet were cold, and the chill was stealing up into his body.

===Chinese===
他妻子打发玛丽下村里去——村子就在不到四分之一英里开外——去求那位大夫。她原给大夫家做洗衣妇的，求他下来瞧瞧自家男人，他眼见是不中用了。

那大夫是个好性子的人，闻讯便到。他帽子也顾不得摘，看了看汤姆，诊视了一番，发觉自己凭玛丽的形容揣测着带来的一剂催吐药并不见效，柳叶刀刺下去也不见血，手腕上又摸不着脉，便摇了摇头，暗自思忖：

"这女人哭天抢地地嚎什么呢？眼下这桩事，对她自己、对她那窝孩子，岂不是天大的福气？她还能盼着比这更好的么？"

汤姆这副光景，确乎是已然断气了。唇边丝毫觉察不出气息。大夫寻不见脉。他手足冰凉，那股寒意正一寸寸往身上爬。

===Original===
The doctor, after a stay of twenty minutes, had buttoned up his greatcoat again and pulled down his hat, and told Mrs. Chuff that there was no use in his remaining any longer, when, all of a sudden, a little rill of blood began to trickle from the lancet-cut in Tom Chuffs temple.

“That’s very odd,” said the doctor. “Let us wait a little.”

I must describe now the sensations which Tom Chuff had experienced.

With his elbows on his knees, and his chin upon his hands, he was staring into the embers, with his gin beside him, when suddenly a swimming came in his head, he lost sight of the fire, and a sound like one stroke of a loud church bell smote his brain.

Then he heard a confused humming, and the leaden weight of his head held him backward as he sank in his chair, and consciousness quite forsook him.

===Chinese===
大夫逗留了二十分钟，重新把大衣扣子扣上，把帽子往下拉了拉，正告诉查夫太太说他再待下去也无济于事了——就在这时，忽然间，一丝细细的血流从汤姆·查夫太阳穴上那道柳叶刀的伤口里渗了出来。

"这可奇了，"大夫说，"咱们再等等看。"

这里我得把汤姆·查夫这一刻所经历的种种感受，一一叙述出来。

他两肘撑在膝上，下巴搁在手里，正盯着炉中余烬发愣，那瓶杜松子酒就搁在手边——忽然之间，他脑袋里一阵天旋地转，眼前的炉火模糊了，一声闷响，仿佛教堂里一口大钟重重敲了一下，直撞进他脑髓里去。

继而便听得一阵嗡嗡乱响，辨不清音，那颗脑袋沉甸甸如铅，将他往后坠去，整个人瘫进椅子里，知觉便全然弃他而去了。

===Original===
When he came to himself he felt chilled, and was leaning against a huge leafless tree. The night was moonless, and when he looked up he thought he had never seen stars so large and bright, or sky so black. The stars, too, seemed to blink down with longer intervals of darkness, and fiercer and more dazzling emergence, and something, he vaguely thought, of the character of silent menace and fury.

He had a confused recollection of having come there, or rather of having been carried along, as if on men’s shoulders, with a sort of rushing motion. But it was utterly indistinct; the imperfect recollection simply of a sensation. He had seen or heard nothing on his way.

He looked round. There was not a sign of a living creature near. And he began with a sense of awe to recognise the place.

===Chinese===
待他神志清醒过来，只觉周身发冷，正倚靠在一棵巨大的、叶落净尽的老树上。这夜没有月亮，他抬头一望，只觉得自己从未见过这般硕大明亮的星子，也未曾见过这般乌黑的天穹。那些星子眨眼之间，暗下去的工夫越来越长，再亮起来时却越发凶猛、越发炫目，隐约之间，他竟从中觉出一种沉默的威吓与狂怒之意。

他模模糊糊记得自己是到了此处的——更确切地说，是被人一路抬了来的，仿佛被扛在众人肩头，一阵风似的疾掠而至。然而这一切都浑浑噩噩，不过是某种感觉的一点残缺记忆罢了。一路上他什么也未曾看见，什么也未曾听见。

他四下里张望。近处不见一个活物的影踪。他怀着一种敬畏之心，开始认出了这地方。

===Original===
The tree against which he had been leaning was one of the noble old beeches that surround at irregular intervals the churchyard of Shackleton, which spreads its green and wavy lap on the edge of the Moor of Catstean, at the opposite side of which stands the rude cottage in which he had just lost consciousness. It was six miles or more across the moor to his habitation, and the black expanse lay before him, disappearing dismally in the darkness. So that, looking straight before him, sky and land blended together in an undistinguishable and awful blank.

There was a silence quite unnatural over the place. The distant murmur of the brook, which he knew so well, was dead; not a whisper in the leaves about him; the air, earth, everything about and above was indescribably still; and he experienced that quaking of the heart that seems to portend the approach of something awful. He would have set out upon his return across the moor, had he not an undefined presentiment that he was waylaid by something he dared not pass.

===Chinese===
他所倚靠的这棵树，乃是 Shackleton 教堂墓地（churchyard of Shackleton）四周疏疏落落长着的一株挺拔古老的山毛榉。这片墓地铺开它那绿意起伏的怀抱，倚着卡特斯坦荒原的边沿，而荒原的另一头，便是他方才失去知觉的那座粗陋小屋。穿过荒原回到他自己的住处，足有六英里开外，那片黑沉沉的旷野横亘在他眼前，凄然没入黑暗之中，望不见尽头。是以他若直瞪瞪望着前方，天与地便融作一片，分不出彼此，只剩一片可怖的虚无。
